en: First Chapter, First Section.
(In this section, there is an investigation of passages containing clear indicatory marks of Brahman.
Śaṅkara’s Commentary on the Brahma-sūtras.

I quickly take refuge in that Hari, whose form is infinite bliss, who holds Janaka’s daughter on his lap, and in whom even the brother of an enemy found the supreme state by seeking his compassionate protection— [he whom] Śrī Rāmānanda Yati has expounded in this *Bhāṣyaratnaprabhā* commentary. (1)

I bow to the auspicious Lord of Kāśī, who, together with Śrī Gaurī, grants all desires by his own lotus feet and bestows liberation; who is mature and destroys the forest of obstacles with the sword of his glorious, curved tusk; who is sinless and teaches that there is no bliss higher than the happiness of dispassion through his humble means of skins and begging bowls; and who is free from internal affliction. 2.
I worship that Goddess Vāṇī, who holds a lute in her hand and whose very body is the Vedas and Śāstras; by a mere fragment of whose grace even a mute becomes a scholar. 3.

I have found rest like a bee at the lotus-feet of the venerable Goddess of Speech, Śrī Govinda, whose face smiles with the light of supreme non-duality revealed by the words of the illustrious Gopāla—those who attained self-realization through the noble Śiva-Rāma, the worshipful lord of abundant food that delights the gods and abounds in the milk offered by Kāmākṣī. //4//

Having prostrated before the venerable Śaṅkara, the author of the Bhāṣya, and Vyāsa, who is Hari himself, the author of the Sūtras, I shall speak of that means which severs the bonds of the web of words for the satisfaction of the Parahaṃsas at the holy site of the Śrībhāṣya. (5)
For one whose mind has become weary from examining extensive texts, this commentary named *Bhāṣyaratnaprabhā* has been commenced for that purpose. (6)
"By attaining this glorious commentary on the Śārīraka, may my speech attain purity;
thus may my labor bear fruit, just as the water of a street becomes like the Ganges. (7)
This world is a magical illusion produced by ignorance;
I am that fearless Brahman, which is infinite bliss and true knowledge. //8//

The Section on the Desire to Know (Jijñāsādhikaraṇa). Sūtra 1: This is the first aphorism of the Vedānta-mīmāṃsā-śāstra, which is intended to be explained.
Now, therefore, the inquiry into Brahman.
In this context, the word "atha" (now) is understood in the sense of immediate succession, not in the sense of formal commencement,
because the inquiry into Brahman is not something that can be formally commenced.
Furthermore, because an auspicious word lacks syntactic connection with the meaning of the sentence,
it serves as an auspicious purpose only when employed for another primary purpose;
and because an expectation of what was previously mentioned is, in effect, not distinct from immediate succession (ānantarya).

And if it has the sense of "immediacy," then just as the inquiry into Dharma necessarily depends upon the prior study of the Veda, so too must that which the inquiry into Brahman necessarily depends upon be stated; however, the immediate succession to the study of one's own Vedic portion (*svādhyāya*) is common to both.
[Objection: But here there is a distinction for the sake of understanding ritual action (*karman*). [Reply: No.
Because the inquiry into Brahman (*brahmajijñāsā*) is possible even for one who has studied the Vedānta prior to the inquiry into Dharma (*dharmajijñāsā*);

and whereas there is a rule of immediate succession regarding the offerings of the heart and other organs because the sequence is intended to be significant, such a sequence is not intended to be significant here.
This is because there is no evidence for a relationship of subordinate and principal, or for a qualification based on a prior qualification;
furthermore, there is a difference between the inquiry into Dharma and the inquiry into Brahman regarding their respective fruits of inquiry.
Knowledge of Dharma has prosperity as its fruit, and that depends upon performance.

However, the knowledge of Brahman has as its fruit the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*) and does not depend on any other performance of action. Furthermore, the dharma that is to be investigated is something yet to be accomplished; it does not exist at the time of the knowledge itself, because it is dependent upon human activity.
But here, the Brahman that is to be investigated is an existing reality (*bhūta*); because it is eternal, it is not dependent upon human activity.
Furthermore, there is a difference in the operation of the injunction (*codanā*).
For the injunction that is the defining characteristic of Dharma informs a person only by enjoining him with respect to its own object.
But the injunction regarding Brahman merely brings about awakening in the person;
since awakening is produced by the injunction itself, the person is not enjoined to bring it about,
just as one is not enjoined to bring about the cognition of an object through the contact of the sense organ with that object.
Therefore, something must be stated that follows immediately before the inquiry into Brahman (*brahmajijñāsā*) is taught.
It is said: [it is] the discrimination between eternal and non-eternal entities, and detachment from the enjoyment of objects here and hereafter.
The perfection of the means such as tranquility and self-control, and the desire for liberation;
for when these exist, it is possible to desire to know and to know Brahman both before and after the inquiry into Dharma, but not otherwise.
Therefore, by the word *atha*, the immediate succession following the attainment of the aforementioned means is taught.
The word *ataḥ* has the sense of a reason (*hetu*).

For the Veda itself shows that rites such as the Agnihotra, which are means to the highest good, yield impermanent results: "Just as here the world acquired through action perishes, even so there the world acquired through merit perishes."
Thus it is stated in passages such as Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.1.6.
Likewise, it demonstrates that even through the knowledge of Brahman, there is a supreme human goal, as in Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.1: "The knower of Brahman attains the Supreme.
Therefore, immediately after the attainment of the aforementioned means, the inquiry into Brahman (brahmajijñāsā) must be undertaken.
The desire to know Brahman is *brahmajijñāsā*.
And Brahman has the definition that will be stated [in the next sūtra]: "That from which the origin, etc., of this [world proceed].
For this very reason, one should not suspect that the word "Brahman" has any other meaning, such as a genus (*jāti*) and so forth.

The genitive case in "brahmaṇaḥ" denotes the object (karma-ṣaṣṭhī) and not a residual relation (śeṣa), because the desire to know (jijñāsā) requires an object, and no other object of inquiry has been specified.

Now, one might object: even if the genitive of remainder (*śeṣa-ṣaṣṭhī*) is adopted, it does not contradict Brahman’s status as the object of the desire to know (*jijñāsā*), because a general relation necessarily resides in a specific relation.
Even so, for one who discards the direct objecthood of Brahman and instead postulates an indirect objecthood through the medium of a general relation, the effort would be in vain.

If it is argued that it is not useless because its purpose is to propose the investigation of everything based on Brahman, we say no; for when the primary subject is embraced, those things required by it are already implied by the sense.

For Brahman is primary because it is that which is most desired to be attained through knowledge. When that primary object of inquiry is embraced, those things without which Brahman cannot be inquired into are already implied by the sense; thus, they need not be stated as separate sūtras. Just as when it is said, "The king is going," the going of the king along with his retinue is thereby expressed, so it is here.
And because it is supported by scripture;
for there are scriptural passages such as, "From which indeed these beings are born" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 3.1).
"Desire to know that; that is Brahman"—thus [the scripture] shows directly that Brahman is the object of the desire to know.
And that [is consistent] with the Sūtra only if the genitive case is understood as denoting the object (*karma-ṣaṣṭhī*).
Therefore, in the expression "from Brahman," the genitive case is used in the sense of the object (*karmaṇi-ṣaṣṭhī*).
The desire to know is *jijñāsā*.
Knowledge culminating in comprehension is the object of the desire expressed by the desiderative suffix (*san*),
because desire has as its object the fruit of an action.
For Brahman is that which is intended to be understood by means of the instrument of knowledge (pramāṇa) that is cognition;
for the realization of Brahman is the human goal, because it eradicates the evils such as ignorance, which are the seeds of transmigratory existence without remainder.
Therefore, Brahman is to be sought after with the desire to know.
Furthermore, that Brahman must be either well-known or unknown.
If it is well-known, it need not be an object of inquiry;
if, on the other hand, it is unknown, it cannot possibly be an object of inquiry.
It is said: there indeed exists Brahman, whose nature is eternally pure, conscious, and free, omniscient, and endowed with all powers.
For when the word *brahman* is etymologically derived, meanings such as eternal purity and so forth are understood,
because they follow from the meaning of the verbal root *bṛh* ("to grow" or "to be great").
Furthermore, the existence of *brahman* is well-established because it is the Self of all.
For everyone indeed believes in the existence of a self;
no one thinks, "I am not.
If the establishment of the existence of a self did not occur, the whole world would perceive, "I am not."
And the Self is Brahman.
If, then, Brahman is already well-known in the world as being the Self, it follows once again that it is already known and thus not an object of inquiry. No;
for there are conflicting views regarding its specific nature.
Ordinary people and the Lokāyatikas maintain that the self is merely the body characterized by consciousness;
others hold that the senses themselves are conscious and constitute the self;
still others say it is the mind.
Some maintain that consciousness alone is momentary;
others hold that it is empty; and still others claim there exists a transmigrating agent distinct from the body and so forth.
Others say he is the enjoyer;
some say he is solely the enjoyer and not the agent;
and some maintain that there exists a Lord distinct from him, who is omniscient and the creator of all.
Others maintain that the self is the enjoyer;
thus, many are in disagreement, relying upon arguments and statements that appear to be either valid or fallacious.
In this regard, one who accepts anything without investigation may be thwarted from the supreme good and incur misfortune.

Therefore, under the guise of introducing the inquiry into Brahman (*brahmajijñāsā*), the investigation (*mīmāṃsā*) of the Vedānta texts—aided by reasoning that does not contradict them and having liberation as its purpose—is now commenced.

[Sūtra 1] [Note: An *adhikaraṇa* (topic) is to be understood as having five members: the subject matter (*viṣaya*), the doubt (*saṃdeha*), the connection (*saṃgati*), the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), and the established conclusion (*siddhānta*).
Thus, when there is effort arising from the desire to act produced by knowledge, dharma such as sacrifice and the like comes into being.]

Some maintain that because Brahman is free from all veils, it constitutes the very nature of the fruit; therefore, the fourth-case compound (caturthī-samāsa) should be accepted here as "for the sake of that" (*tadartha*), according to the rule beginning with *caturthī tadarthe*. Furthermore:
"Because he attains [everything], because he takes up [everything], because he eats the objects of the senses here, and because his existence is continuous, he is called the Self (*ātman*)."
An enumeration of those who hold erroneous views: the proponents of emptiness (*śūnyavāda*) among the Mādhyamikas; the proponents of momentary consciousness (*kṣaṇikajñānavāda*) among the Yogācāras;
and the proponents of external objects that are momentary and inferable from the forms of cognition (*jñānākārānumeyakṣaṇikabāhyārthavāda*) among the Sautrāntikas.
The doctrine of momentary external objects belongs to the Vaibhāṣikas; the doctrine of the body as the self belongs to the Cārvākas;
and the doctrine of the transformation of the body as something distinct from the body belongs to the Digambaras—such [positions] are to be inferred accordingly.

In this context, for one who has studied the Veda along with its auxiliary limbs by means of the injunction for compulsory study— "The Veda is to be studied"— there is found the injunction for hearing (śravaṇa), as in: "Seek to know that," "That is to be sought after, that is to be understood," and "Verily, the Self, my dear, is to be seen and heard."
The meaning of this is as follows: one who desires immortality must engage in the investigation of the non-dual Self by means of the Vedānta texts alone.

Thus, by virtue of this restrictive injunction (*niyamavidhi*) based on that desire, it follows as a matter of fact that the engagement with treatises concerning a separate Self is excluded, or else the predominance of Purāṇas and similar works for the followers of the Veda is set aside; such is the actual state of affairs.

In this regard, someone whose mind has become utterly pure through sacrifices and other rites performed either in this life or in another birth [might ask]: what is the subject matter of this method of hearing,
what is its fruit, and who is the qualified candidate?
One wonders what the connection [between the subject matter and the inquiry] is.

Perceiving that desire for knowledge, the venerable Bādarāyaṇa composed this aphorism— "Now, therefore, the inquiry into Brahman"— in order to determine, by means of logic, the fourfold set of preliminary requirements (anubandha-catuṣṭaya) that necessitate the commencement of the scripture consisting of oral study.
But surely, the collection of subsidiary matters can be known through the explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) situated in proximity to the injunctions;

for instance, by the scriptural text—"Just as here the world acquired through action perishes, even so there the world acquired through merit perishes"—which possesses the logical principle that "whatever is produced is impermanent," and [by the text] "The wise one is neither born nor dies," and "He who indeed... [and so forth].

From such scriptural passages as, "The Plenum (bhūman) is that which is immortal; other than this is afflicted," one obtains the discrimination that the Self, as the Plenum, is eternal, whereas that which is other than it is non-eternal and consists of the nature of ignorance.
The world consisting of crops and so forth, produced by the mind through actions such as agriculture, means the object of enjoyment.
*Vipaścit* is that whose nature is eternal knowledge.

"Having examined the worlds acquired through karma, a Brahmin should attain detachment, realizing that 'there is nothing uncreated [eternal] to be gained by what is created'; for it is only for the sake of the Self that everything becomes dear"— from such scriptural passages as these, detachment is obtained toward the non-Self alone, that is, toward the entire collection of objects consisting of the body, senses, and so forth, once they have been examined and determined to be impermanent.
The meaning is that liberation is not produced by performed action; thus, one should attain detachment from actions and their fruits.

From the Śruti text, "Having become calm, self-controlled, withdrawn, patient, concentrated, and possessing faith, one should see the Self in the very Self," the sixfold set beginning with tranquility (śama) is obtained.
"Having become concentrated" is the reading in the Kāṇva recension.
Cessation (*uparati*) is renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*).
Through the scriptural statement, "He does not return again," which declares the eternity of liberation—consisting of self-luminous bliss—the desire for liberation (*mumukṣā*) is obtained.
Thus, it can be understood that the qualified candidate (*adhikārī*) is one who possesses the specific qualifications such as discrimination (*viveka*) and the rest.

Just as in the injunction for the Rātri-sattra sacrifice—"those who perform these nights"—the statement "they attain firm standing" (pratiṣṭhanti) serves as an explanatory praise (arthavāda) for one desiring such firm standing, so it is here.

Likewise, in the case of the injunction "it should be heard" (śrotavyaḥ), the object of the suffix—the mandate (niyoga)—has as its content the investigation (vicāra), which is the meaning of the verbal root; and it can be understood that the Vedāntas are the object of that investigation, because the injunction to investigate ("it should be heard") is prescribed with reference to the vision of the non-dual Self, as in the statement "the Self is to be seen" (ātmā draṣṭavyaḥ).
For inquiry is not the direct cause of perception, because it is not a means of valid cognition; rather, it is so by virtue of being the object of a means of valid cognition.

And the Vedāntas alone are the authority regarding the non-dual Self, according to the Śruti: "That person who is known through the Upaniṣads," and "Those whose purpose is well-ascertained through the knowledge of the Vedāntas."
Furthermore, the subject matter of the Vedantas is the identity of the inner self and Brahman,
according to the scriptural texts: "That thou art" and "I am Brahman."

Thus, the fruit of the method of inquiry is liberation through the gateway of knowledge, according to such scriptural passages as, "The knower of the Self transcends sorrow," and "The knower of Brahman becomes Brahman itself."

Likewise, the relationship between the qualified person and the inquiry consists in the former's duty to perform it, while the relationship with the result consists in its being attained; thus, as appropriate, this is easily understood.
If it is argued that this sūtra is therefore redundant, we say no.

In the absence of sūtras providing the logical principles for determining the intended meaning (*tātparya*) of those scriptural passages concerning eligibility and so forth, one must investigate: is the qualified seeker (*adhikārī*) one endowed with the specific qualifications such as discrimination (*viveka*), or someone else; are the Vedāntas redundant in light of the *Pūrvatantra* (Mīmāṃsā), or do they convey a meaning not already established there;
and is Brahman non-different from the inner self (*pratyagātman*), or not?

Is liberation another world like heaven and so forth, or is it the very nature of the Self? This aphorism is necessary for the purpose of determining the qualified seeker and other factors, which are initially understood through scriptural statements, thereby removing such doubts.

This has been stated by the venerable Śrīcaraṇas, who are of the nature of Light: "Even though the qualified person (*adhikārī*) and other factors are established through scripture (*āgama*), this aphorism (*sūtra*) is for the purpose of determining them through reasoning (*nyāya*).

For those who hold that there is no injunction (*vidhi*) regarding hearing (*śravaṇa*), it would follow that the aphorism is useless, since there would be no need to determine the qualified person and so forth for a hearing that is not enjoined; but enough of this digression.

Thus, this Sūtra has a connection with the Śruti because it is raised for the sake of determining its own meaning by means of the Śruti passages concerning the qualification (*adhikārin*) and other factors required by the injunction to hear [this scripture];

it has a connection with the beginning of the Śāstra because it serves as an introduction (*upoddhāta*) by determining the preliminary conditions (*anubandha*) that are the cause for commencing the Śāstra;

and it has a connection with the Chapter on Concordance (*samanvayādhyāya*) because it declares the concordance (*samanvaya*) of the Śruti passages concerning the qualification and other factors with their own respective meanings.

The connection with the *pāda* is established by the statement of the concordance (*samanvaya*) of such scriptural passages as "All this has that as its self; that is the Truth; that is the Self; Thou art That," which contain clear indicatory marks (*liṅga*) of Brahman, such as being the Self of all.
Similarly, the connection with the *śruti* (scripture) exists because all the *sūtras* serve to determine the meaning of scripture.
Within each respective chapter (*adhyāya*) and *pāda*, the connection should be inferred based on the commonality of the subject matter (*prameya*).

The subject matter (*prameya*) of the entire treatise is Brahman; however, the subject matters of the chapters are respectively: the concordance (*samanvaya*), the absence of contradiction (*avirodha*), the means of realization (*sādhana*), and the fruit (*phala*). Among these, the subject matter of the first section (*pāda*) is the concordance of those scriptural passages (*śruti*) that contain clear indicatory marks (*liṅga*) of Brahman.
The distinction is that the second and third [sections] concern those passages where the indicative marks of Brahman are unclear,
while the fourth quarter concerns the coordination of words alone. Since this section is the very first, no prior connection with a preceding section is required.

Now, the formal inquiry (adhikaraṇa) is commenced: The subject matter (*viṣaya*) is the treatise of Vedānta-mīmāṃsā, which consists of the hearing (*śravaṇa*) enjoined by the injunction "it is to be heard. The doubt is whether this [treatise] should be commenced or not, based on the possibility or impossibility of its subject matter and its purpose.

In that regard, since there is a contradiction with perception—which grasps difference in the form "I am not Brahman"—and with inference, which has as its mark the possession of contradictory attributes such as agency and non-agency, the subject matter of the identity of Brahman and the Self is impossible.

The prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that the inquiry need not be undertaken because, for one bound by truth, the fruit consisting of liberation through knowledge is impossible. To this, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is: "Then, therefore, the desire to know Brahman" (*athāto brahmajijñāsā*).
Here, in order to accord with the injunction for hearing (*śravaṇa-vidhi*), the word "must be performed" (*kartavyā*) must be supplied.
And indeed, the Commentator [Śaṅkara] has supplied it, stating: "The desire to know Brahman must be performed."

In this context, since the knowledge and the desire denoted by the root and the suffix respectively cannot be construed as things to be performed (*kartavya*), the primary meaning (*prakṛti*)—knowledge as the result—is expressed through *ajahallakṣaṇā* (non-abandoning indication), while the suffix expresses the investigation (*vicāra*) to be accomplished by that desire through *jahallakṣaṇā* (abandoning indication).
Thus, the literal sense of the Sūtra is established as: "Investigation must be undertaken for the sake of the knowledge of Brahman."

In this context, since knowledge cannot be a fruit in its own right, its status as a fruit must be explained solely by its function of removing the misfortune consisting of the states of being a knower (*pramātṛ*), an agent (*kartṛ*), and an enjoyer (*bhoktṛ*). Since that misfortune cannot be removed by mere knowledge if it were real, it must be declared to be superimposed (*adhyasta*); thus, the superimposed nature of bondage is indicated by implication. And this [superimposition] is the cause for establishing that the scripture possesses both a subject matter (*viṣaya*) and a purpose (*prayojana*).
For thus it is that the treatise ought to be commenced, because it possesses a subject matter and a purpose, like the act of eating and so forth.
The treatise possesses a purpose,
because it is the cause of the knowledge that brings about the cessation of bondage, like such statements as "this is a rope."
Bondage is removable by knowledge because it is superimposed,
like a snake on a rope;
thus is the purpose established.

Thus, by aphoristically indicating as its fruit the cessation of the delusion of misfortune pertaining to the individual soul (*jīva*) through the knowledge of the Brahman that is one with this [Self], it also implies— by the force of the meaning— the identity of the *jīva* and Brahman as the subject matter (*viṣaya*),
because the cessation of delusion regarding one thing does not occur through the knowledge of something else.
[Therefore,] the *jīva* is non-different from Brahman.
Because it is the locus of superimposition (adhyāsa) which is to be removed by that knowledge;
for whatever is thus [characterized] is so [established],
just as the "this-portion" (idamaṃśa) is non-different from the mother-of-pearl— thus, superimposition is the cause for the establishment of the object.
Thus, because it possesses both a subject matter and a purpose, the treatise should be commenced.

Regarding this, the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa) holds that since bondage is real and is not removed by knowledge, liberation must be accomplished through other means; this is the result [of that view]. In the final conclusion (siddhānta), liberation arises from knowledge alone; such is the distinction.

Having thus kept all this in mind, the venerable author of the Commentary (Bhāṣyakāra), desiring to explain the Brahma-sūtras, first describes—by means of the two introductory commentaries (bhāṣya) concerning the presentation and resolution of the superimposition (adhyāsa), which serves as the cause for establishing that [the inquiry]—the fact that the subject matter and its purpose are implied by the very necessity of the scriptural meaning regarding the duty to investigate, as expressed in the sūtra: "Of the two objects of the notions of 'you' and 'I'... and so forth.
By this, the argument that the section on superimposition (*adhyāsa*) is not a commentary (*bhāṣya*) because it does not touch upon the literal meaning of the Sūtra is refuted,
since it does touch upon its implied meaning.
As for the claim that this commentary (*bhāṣya*) should not be explained because it lacks an auspicious invocation (*maṅgalācaraṇa*), that is not so;

for the purpose of composing the commentary ending with "all the more impossible is their mutual existence," there was a recollection of the reality (*tattva*)— the meaning of the inner self (*pratyagartha*) as a mass of consciousness (*vijñānaghana*) free from all afflictions—
and thus, being faultless, this commentary is indeed to be explained.

In the world, the error "this is silver" regarding a mother-of-pearl shell is observed to be produced by a latent impression (saṃskāra) generated by a prior valid cognition (*pramā*) that apprehended the identity between the substrate (*adhiṣṭhāna*) and the superimposed particular (*āropya-viśeṣa*), as in the case of real silver where one thinks "this is silver. Therefore, in this instance as well, regarding the superimposition of the non-self ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*) upon the Self, a prior valid cognition must be posited;
and that [prior cognition] requires an actual identity between the Self and the non-self.
For that is not the case; for indeed, the self and the non-self are devoid of identity,
because they are incapable of being one with each other.

Thinking that it is like darkness and light, he establishes the contradiction—which serves as the logical reason—through its actual nature, through cognition, and through conventional usage, by stating: "of the objects of the notions of *yuṣmad* and *asmat*.

Nor is there any issue, for by the rule "pratyayottarapadayośca," it is ordained that "when a suffix or a subsequent word follows, the substitutes *tvam* and *aham* take the place of the portions ending in *map* of *yuṣmad* and *asmad*."
It should not be argued that [the form] "tvanmat-pratyaya-gocayoḥ" would be appropriate, as in the expressions "your son" (*tvadīyaḥ putras*) and "my son" (*madīyaḥ putras*).
This is because the rule "tvamāvekavacane" (Pāṇini 7.2.97) governs the substitution of *tvam* and *aham* specifically within the domain of the singular number.

In the present case, however, there is no denotation of a single referent for *yuṣmad* and *asmad*; rather, the referents of *yuṣmad* are plural, and the consciousness that is the referent of *asmad* is also plural due to its limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*).
Now, this being the case, how is the analysis (*vigraha*) of this commentary to be understood?

Nor should it be said that the analysis is: "the cognition 'you' is the *yuṣmat-pratyaya*, and the cognition 'we' is the *asmat-pratyaya*; [it refers to] those two which are the objects of these cognitions."
If it is argued that even if the word is grammatically correct, it is semantically incorrect because the non-self—
such as the ego (ahaṃkāra)— cannot be the object of the cognition "you" (yūyam), we say no; for the word *gocara* refers to suitability (*yogyatā*).

The conscious self (cidātmā) is indeed the object of the notion "I" (asmat-pratyaya), because it is the recipient of the fruit consisting in the cessation of doubt and other such states induced by that notion; thus,
it is not entirely without an object.
And because of the statement in the Bhāṣya: "Because it is the object of our [our-pratyaya] cognition.

Although the ego (ahaṅkāra) and so forth are also fit for that [cognition], they are nevertheless described as being "fit for the *yuṣmat*-pratyaya" (the "you"-cognition) in order to establish their absolute difference from the conscious self (cidātman).
The venerable Āśramaśricaraṇas, however, state in their *Ṭīkāyojanā* as follows: "The conscious being denoted by the word *yuṣmad* is that which is to be addressed;
the conscious being qualified by the ego (*ahaṅkāra*) and so forth is denoted by the word *asmad*.
Thus, the rule regarding the substitution of *tvam* and so on applies only when *yuṣmad* and *asmad* are used in their primary sense (*svārtha*), not when they are used figuratively (*lākṣaṇika*)."

Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of contradicting the rule: "In place of *yuṣmad* and *asmad*, when standing in the sixth, fourth, or second case, [the substitutes] *vām* and *nau* [are optionally used].

Here, just as in the case of words that indicate [other things], even for those indicating pure consciousness (*cinmātra*) and pure insentience (*jaḍamātra*), the substitutes *tvam* and *aham* do not apply, because there is no difference in their being indicators.

If it were intended by this rule that the absence of the *tvam* substitute occurs only when those two [words] denote the actual word-forms themselves, then in this commentary (*bhāṣya*), the word *yuṣmat* would refer to the objective reality (*parāgartha*) capable of being the object of a cognition produced by the word *yuṣmad*.
By the word *asmad*, the inner self (*pratyagātman*)—which is capable of being the object of the cognition produced by the word *asmad*—is intended.
Thus, since the word itself is also understood as the delimiting factor of the indicated (*lakṣyatāvacchedaka*), it does not undergo the substitution of *tvam*.
Nor is it the case that only "extroversion" (*parāktva*) and "introversion" (*pratyaktva*) constitute the delimiting factors of the indicated.
It should not be said that [the cognition] does not apprehend the aspect of the word's fitness because of complexity;
for, in order to manifest the contradiction between the external object and the internal cognition, the contradictory fitness of the words must also be stated.

For this very reason, although one could have said "of these two, which are the objects of the notions of 'this' and 'I'," the word *idam* ("this") is used in the sense of "I" (the self) many times in both common usage and the Veda, as in "we are these," and "we are the Videhas."

Thinking that the word *yuṣmad* (you) does not contradict the word *asmat* (we), because one observes its usage in the expression "this is I," the word *yuṣmad* was employed; for when the word *idam* (this) is used, no contradiction [with *asmat*] is perceived.
By this [argument], since it denotes a conscious being, the word *asmat* ought to have been used first, according to the maxim: "That which is more venerable comes first."
The objection that the *ekaśeṣa* (retention of one) prescribed by the rule "tyadādīni sarvair nityam" might also apply here is refuted;

for, as in the rule "yuṣmadasmadoḥ," neither prior placement (*pūrvanipāta*) nor *ekaśeṣa* is applicable here, and furthermore, if *ekaśeṣa* were applied, the intended contradiction would not be manifested.

The elders, however, say: "The mention of *yuṣmad* at the beginning is intended to indicate the extraction of the pure element of consciousness (*ciddhātu*) from the non-self (*anātman*), which is the referent of *yuṣmad*, by means of the logic of superimposition and negation (*adhyāropa-apavāda*).
In that context, through the two words *yuṣmad* and *asmat*, the factual contradiction between the Self and the non-Self as the external and the internal is stated;
by the word *pratyaya*, the contradiction in terms of cognition is stated.
That which is cognized is the "cognition" (*pratyaya*), such as the ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*) and so forth; being non-self, it appears as an object of perception (*dṛśya*).
The self (*ātman*), however, because it is the very act of cognition (*pratīti*), is the "cognition" itself; it appears by virtue of its self-luminosity (*svaprakāśatā*).
By the term "object" (*gocara*), a contradiction has been stated from the perspective of conventional usage.

The threefold contradiction has been made clear: the referent of "you" (yuṣmad-artha), which is the object of such worldly usage as "I am the agent" by way of obscuring the inner self (pratyagātman); and the referent of "we" (asmad-artha), which is the object of such worldly usage as "I am Brahman" by way of the dissolution of the non-self (anātman).

The construction [of the sentence] is as follows: "yuṣmad" and "asmat" refer to the words for "you" and "I"; these two are both the cognitions (*pratyaya*) and the objects (*gocara*) of those cognitions, hence they are called "the objects of the cognitions of *yuṣmad* and *asmat*.

Since it has been established that the non-existence of one among these two—which possess threefold contradictory natures—is impossible, their absolute identity (*atyantābheda*) or essential oneness (*tādātmya*) is likewise untenable.
To the objection that even if identity is impossible, why could there not be a relation of identity (tādātmya) as in the case of "the white jar," he says: "of the object and the subject.
The meaning is that because consciousness and the insentient possess the nature of subject and object, they cannot have identity, just like a lamp and a jar.
"Thou" and "I" refer to the alien and the inward objects, respectively.
Alternatively, the analysis [of the compound] is: "those very [two] are the condition (*pratyaya*) and the object (*gocara*).

Here, by means of the two terms "condition" and "object," the fact of being consciousness (*cit*) and non-consciousness (*acit*) is stated as the reason for the inwardness (*pratyak*) and outwardness (*parāk*) of the Self and the non-Self respectively. Regarding that, he states the reason: "of the object and the subject.
Because the non-Self is that which is grasped (*grāhya*), it is non-conscious.
However, because the self (ātman) is the grasper, it must be said to possess consciousness (citva).

The meaning is that if it were non-conscious (acitva), its own grasping by itself would be impossible due to the contradiction of being both object and agent, which would result in its not being perceptible.
Alternatively, the relationship of cause and effect may be stated according to preference.

Now, one might object: since there is a contradiction between the self and the non-self—by virtue of being "inner" and "outer," "consciousness" and "unconsciousness," and "grasper" and "grasped"—and since, like darkness and light, their identity (aikya) or oneness-in-nature (tādātmya) is impossible, it follows that there can be no superimposition (adhyāsa) due to the absence of a means of valid cognition for such a relation; nevertheless, let there be a mutual superimposition of their respective attributes, such as consciousness and happiness on the one hand, and insentience and suffering on the other. To this, he says: "Of their attributes also... [taddharmāṇām api].

The properties (*dharma*) of those two—the self (*ātman*) and the non-self (*anātman*)—are "their properties" (*taddharma*). The meaning is that there is an impossibility of their mutual existence; that is, the existence or conjunction (*saṃsarga*) of those various properties in another substrate (*dharmyantara*) is untenable.
For indeed, there can be no exchange of properties without a conjunction of the two substrates.
In the case of a crystal, there is a connection with the quality of redness due to the proximity of a red object.

However, since the Self, whose nature is non-attachment, has no connection whatsoever with anything else, how could there be a connection with its qualities—which presupposes a prior connection with the substratum? With this intention, he said: "all the more so" (*sutarām*). Now, one might ask: even if there is no identity between the Self and the non-Self, nor a connection between their respective qualities, why should superimposition (*adhyāsa*) not still occur? To this, he says: "for this reason" (*ityataḥ*).

According to the manner stated above, because there is an absence of identity (*tādātmya*) and so forth, there is an absence of valid cognition (*pramā*) regarding that; therefore, since the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) produced by valid cognition—which is the cause of superimposition (*adhyāsa*)—is absent, the logical connection is: "it is proper that superimposition should be false" (*mithyā*).
For the word *mithyā* signifies both denial (*apahnava*) and the state of being indefinable (*anirvacanīyatā*).
And here, the purpose is denial.
Anticipating the objection, "Well then, where and whose superimposition is being denied?", he states—

beginning with the words "the object of the notion of 'I' (asmatpratyayagocara)"— that the superimposition of non-self and its attributes upon the Self, and of the Self and its attributes upon the non-self, is being refuted.
Thinking that even the intellect (*buddhi*) and other faculties possess the fitness for the notion "I am," he distinguishes the Self from them by describing it as "the subject" (*viṣayi*).
This means it is the witness (*sākṣin*) of the intellect and so forth. The reason for its being the witness is stated as "consisting of consciousness" (*cidātmaka*).
The meaning is: "in the aspect of consciousness (cid-aṃśa) which manifests as 'I'";
"of that which is the object of the notion of 'you' (yuṣmat-pratyaya-gocara)" means "that which is fit for the designation 'thou'."
This means "of this object" (idamartha).

Now, one might ask: how can the intellect and so forth, which appear as "I," have the status of being "this object"? To this he says: "of the object"—meaning, that which is manifested by the witness-consciousness (sākṣin).

The meaning is that, because the intellect (*buddhi*) and other internal organs possess the defining characteristic of being manifested by a witness (*sākṣibhāsyatva*), they do not appear as objects of the "this" (*idamartha*) category, unlike a pot or similar external objects. Alternatively, the previously stated nature of the Self— its primary inwardness (*pratyaktva*) as being the innermost of all, its self-evident character (*pratītatva*), and its being the object of the empirical usage "I am Brahman"— is unestablished, because it is perceived as "I."

Anticipating the objection that [the Self] is like the ego (ahaṅkāra), he says: "It is the object of the notion 'I'. The meaning is: it is that which is both the notion (*pratyaya*) of "us" (*asmad*) and the object (*gocara*).
The reason [for its being distinct from the ego] is either its being a manifestation made manifest by the function of "I" (*ahaṃ-vṛtti*), or its being the objective content of such a manifestation.

The meaning is that in the first example the reason (*hetu*) is unestablished (*asiddhi*), whereas in the second position that [reason] is unestablished; thus, it is logical that the primary nature of the self (*ātman*) consists in its being the subject (*pratyaktva*) and so forth.
Now, an objection: that the self is an object (*viṣayatva*) is itself unestablished.
Because it possesses the word "I experience," like the ego-sense (ahaṅkāra); to this he says: "as the object" (*viṣayiṇī*).
Whether being the denotable meaning (*vācyatva*) or the indicated meaning (*lakṣyatva*), this is the logical reason (*hetu*).
Not the first, because that [reason] is unestablished in that case;

not the last, because it is deficient in the example—this is the sense. One might object: even if there is a relationship of object and subject between the body and the ego-sense (ahaṅkāra) in the cognition "I know the body," there could still be an illusory identification (abhedādhyāsa) between the self and the ego-sense, just as there is the illusory identification of non-difference in the thought "I am a man. To this he says: "consisting of consciousness" (cidātmaka).

The sense is this: although there is superimposition (adhyāsa) because of the similarity between those two [the Self and the ego] due to their respective qualities of being non-material and limited, the non-material and limited ego and so forth are not superimposed upon the unlimited conscious Self.

Anticipating the objection that—since the ego is manifested as "I" and thus possesses inwardness (pratyaktva) like the Self, its inwardness is primary, and consequently the previously mentioned "outwardness" (parāktva) and other attributes cannot be established regarding it—the author says: "yuṣmad... (the word *yuṣmad*).
The state of being manifested by the activity of the "I" (ahaṃvṛtti) does not exist in the ego (ahaṅkāra), because of the contradiction between the status of agent and object;
nor does the state of being manifested by consciousness exist in the conscious self (cidātman). Thus, the reason [adduced] is unestablished (asiddhi).

Therefore, the sense is that although the intellect and so forth possess inwardness (pratyaktva) from the perspective of their appearance, their outwardness (parāktva) and other such qualities are indeed primary.

The analysis of the compound is as follows: it is that which is cognized (*prati-yata*) by you in relation to that [object], hence it is *pratyaya*; and it is the sphere of worldly transactions such as agency (*kartṛtva*) and so forth; [the genitive] "of that" (*tasya*) refers to this.
He states "of the poison" (*viṣasya*) for the purpose of showing that it is to be abandoned.
The root *piñ* means "to bind."
The meaning is that it is an "object" (*viṣaya*) because it binds or fetters (*visinoti*).
Let the superimposition of the non-self and its attributes upon the self be false;
why should the superimposition of the self and its attributes upon the non-self not also be so?
Anticipating the objection that [the self exists] because of such experiences as "I am vibrating" or "I am happy," he says: "by its opposite.
Therefore, the opposite of the non-self (anātman) is consciousness (caitanya), which is of a contrary nature.
The third case ending (*tṛtīyā*) is used here in the sense of "being thus" (*itthambhāve*).

It is logical that the superimposition (adhyāsa) of the conscious self, as the subject, and its attributes upon the object— the ego-sense and so forth— is false and non-existent, because the causal conditions for such a superimposition are absent. For in this case, there exists neither the latent impression (saṃskāra) deposited by prior valid cognition, nor similarity, nor ignorance.
Because in the Self, which is partless, devoid of qualities, and self-luminous, there is no possibility of ignorance consisting of similarity to qualities or parts.
If it is asked, "But how can the Bhāṣya statement 'of its attributes' be consistent with the self being devoid of qualities (nirguṇa)?", it is replied:
consciousness manifested through a modification of the intellect is *jñāna* (knowledge); that which is manifested as non-different from the object is *sphuraṇa* (manifestation).

Bliss (*ānanda*) is that which is manifested by a mental modification (*vṛtti*) produced by virtuous karma; thus, due to the distinction created by the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) of the modification, knowledge and the other attributes are designated as properties of the Self (*ātmadharma*).

As it is stated in the *Ṭīkā*: "Bliss, the experience of objects, and eternity—these are properties which, although non-different [from consciousness], appear as if distinct because of their nature as consciousness.
Therefore, in the view that the Self is the attributeless Brahman (*nirguṇabrahmātmatvamate*),...

Since the meaning of the cognition "I am doing" cannot be a superimposition (adhyāsa), it must be accepted that its validity and truthfulness are established, and that the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) in the expression "I am a man" is merely figurative (*gauṇa*).

Consequently, because bondage is real, its cessation—which is the intended fruit—cannot arise from knowledge; and because the identity between the bound individual soul (*jīva*) and Brahman is impossible, the subject matter (*viṣaya*) of the scripture is non-existent. Thus, the scripture should not be commenced.
This is the purport of the *pūrvapakṣa* (prima facie) commentary.
By the inclusion of the word "yukta" (proper), he indicates the weakness of the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*).
To explain: is the non-existence of superimposition (*adhyāsa*) due to its being improper, or due to its not appearing, or due to the absence of its cause?
Regarding the first [alternative], he says "even so" (*tathāpi*), meaning that this is accepted.
In accordance with this, the phrase "even though" (*yadyapi*) should be read at the beginning.
The intended meaning is that the impossibility of superimposition (*adhyāsa*) upon the Self—which is unattached and self-luminous—is itself an ornament (*alaṅkāra*).
He states that the second [alternative] is not the case with the words "this" (*ayam*).
The meaning is that the non-appearance of superimposition is unestablished, because of the direct experience of the ignorant person thinking, "I am the agent.
Nor should it be said that this perception is not a valid means of knowledge (*pramā*) regarding agency and so forth;
for [the scripture] is faultless due to its being of non-human origin (*apauruṣeya*).

Furthermore, because the sentence "That thou art" (tat tvam asi) has its purport determined by such marks as the introductory context (*upakrama*) and so forth, and because it imparts the realization of non-agency and Brahmanhood, one ascertains that [the prior perception] is an error.
Nor should it be argued that the knowledge arising from scripture (*āgama*) is sublated simply due to conflict with the more senior means of knowledge, namely direct perception (*pratyakṣa*);
for if that were so, it would lead to the absurd conclusion that the doctrine identifying the body with the self (*dehātmavāda*) is valid.

The notion "I am a human being" contradicts direct perception [of the Self], for through such scriptural texts as "Now, this [Self] is bodiless," it is established that the Self is distinct from the body.

Therefore, it must be accepted that the perception of grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya)—which is tainted by the suspicion of being an error—does not possess greater authority than scripture, just like the perception "this is silver.
Furthermore, does "seniority" mean occurring earlier in time, or being the basis upon which the knowledge of scripture depends?
The first [alternative] is not tenable,
because even a senior [cognition], such as the illusion of silver, is seen to be sublated by a subsequent cognition of mother-of-pearl.

Nor is the second, because when scriptural knowledge arises, it does so through the apprehension of the relationship [between word and meaning] via the usage of elders, which is rooted in perception and other means of knowledge.

Furthermore, although perception and other means of knowledge depend upon verbal testimony for their empirical validity (*vyāvahārika-prāmāṇya*), they do not depend upon its ultimate validity (*tāttvika-prāmāṇya*); and since it is impossible for scripture to sublate that aspect which is not required by them, [the objection fails]. As for the argument that—just as a momentary sacrifice becomes the cause of a fruit arising at a later time by the force of scriptural authority—it is possible for even reality to cease through knowledge by the force of the scriptural text, "Thus the knower is freed from name and form," and therefore the description of superimposition (*adhyāsa*) is unnecessary: [this is refuted as follows].
As for the claim that it is futile, that is not so;
for nowhere is anything seen to be real that is removable by mere knowledge, nor is the cessation of the real Self ever observed.
For if there were certainty regarding unfitness [to perform rituals], it would be impossible for the scriptural statement that "the real bond ceases through knowledge" to convey its meaning.
Nor should it be argued that there is no certainty of unfitness because we observe the destruction of even real sin through the sight of the Setu (the bridge),
since that [sin] is destroyed by knowledge only when that knowledge is dependent on faith, ritual observances, and so forth.
Furthermore, since the scripture stating "There is no other path" (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 3.8) indicates that bondage ceases through knowledge alone,
one must describe its status as a superimposition (adhyasta) in order to justify its being removable by the knowledge taught in the scriptures.
Moreover, what kind of reality could possibly belong to that which is removable by knowledge alone?
First of all, it is not the case that [the world] is not produced from ignorance (*ajñāna*),
because that would contradict the scriptural text, "But Māyā is Prakṛti," since Māyā and avidyā are one and the same.
Nor is it the case that [Brahman] is devoid of its own absence in its own substrate, because that would contradict scriptural negations such as, "It is neither gross" (*asthūlam*).
Nor is it the case that Brahman is incapable of sublation, for that would contradict scriptural statements regarding its cessation through knowledge.
If, on the other hand, you mean that it is free from sublation at the time of empirical transaction (*vyavahāra*), [then...]
In that case, it follows that truth is merely empirical, which means it is superimposed;
and this must indeed be described for the sake of knowing the compatibility (yogyatā) regarding the meaning of the Vedic scripture, just as the sacrificial act [is described] by way of the *apūrva*.

Nor is there any redundancy because that [superimposition] is described in the section concerning their difference (*tadanyatva*), since it is merely being recalled at the outset for the purpose of establishing the object and other factors that serve as the means for the commencement [of inquiry], which were already discussed therein; this is the general direction.
He shows superimposition (adhyāsa) in two ways with the words "worldly transaction" (lokavyavahāra).

"World" (loka) refers to the superimposition of objects, as one identifies [with them], thinking "I am a man"; the "transaction" (vyavahāra) regarding that object is the conceit (abhimāna), by which the superimposition of cognition (jñānādhyāsa) is shown.
He states the definition of the nature of the two-fold superimposition with the words beginning "in each other" and ending with "of the attributes and the substrata.
The substrata of the attributes such as insentience and consciousness are the ego (ahaṅkāra) and the Self (ātman).

Since these two are absolutely distinct, the construction is as follows: through the non-apprehension of their mutual difference, one superimposes upon each other the identity of the other and the attributes of the other in a reversed manner, and thus worldly transaction proceeds.

Therefore, the cognition "this is that" (*so 'yam*) is not a case of superimposition (*adhyāsa*), because even though a distinction is conceptually constructed between the referents "that" and "this" due to their difference in time, there is no absolute difference between them; this is why the word "absolute" (*atyanta*) was used.

Nor should it be argued that the phrase "and [its] attributes" (*dharmāṃśca*) is redundant, since the superimposition of attributes is established once the identity of the substratum (*dharmitādātmya*) has been superimposed.

This is for the purpose of making it known that, although the superimposition (*adhyāsa*) of the substratum (*dharmī*) upon the attributes of the senses such as blindness is not manifest, the superimposition "I am blind" is indeed manifest.

Now, one might raise the objection: "If the Self and the non-Self are mutually superimposed, would this not result in the doctrine of emptiness (*śūnyavāda*)? Anticipating this, he says: "having coupled the real and the unreal.

The "real" is consciousness, which is not this [body]; its superimposition upon the non-Self consists merely in its association (*saṃsarga*), not in the superimposition of its essential nature (*svarūpa*).

The meaning is that "unreality" has you as its object; because there is superimposition even upon its own nature, the coupling of those two is called superimposition (adhyāsa), and thus it is not a state of voidness (śūnyatā).

Surely, if the words *adhyāsa* (superimposition), *mithunīkaraṇa* (pairing), and *lokavyavahāra* (worldly transaction) have a single meaning, how can there be the use of the suffix *lyap*—which replaces the gerundive suffix *ktvā* to express priority of time—as in "having superimposed" (*adhyasya*) and "having paired" (*mithunīkṛtya*)?
[The answer is: because of the distinction between individual instances of superimposition.

In that regard, the use of *lyap* is intended to indicate that each preceding instance of superimposition serves as a cause for each succeeding instance of superimposition by way of its residual impression (*saṃskāra*), thereby establishing its priority in time.
He clarifies that very point with the word "intrinsic" (*naisargika*).
The meaning is that the stream of superimposition (*adhyāsa*) within the inner self (*pratyagātman*), by way of the relationship between cause and effect, is beginningless.
[Objection: But since a stream is not a real entity (*avastu*),...
If it is asked, "Since individual instances of superimposition (adhyāsa) have a beginning, how can they be beginningless?"— it is replied:

because it is accepted that the beginninglessness of effects consists in the non-occurrence of the beginningless time without at least one among the various instances delimited by the property of being a superimposition.
By this, the alternative that [the cognition arises] due to the absence of a cause is refuted,
because the word *naisargika* (innate) indicates that the impression (*saṃskāra*) is the instrumental cause (*nimitta*).
Nor should it be said that only an impression produced by a previous valid cognition (*pramā*) is the cause.
Because, for the sake of parsimony (*lāghava*), the impression (*saṃskāra*) produced by a prior experience is the cause;

therefore, it is established that there exists an impression produced by a prior superimposition (*adhyāsa*). He states the material cause (*upādāna*) of this superimposition: "having false cognition as its cause" (*mithyājñānanimitta*).
That which is both false (*mithyā*) and ignorance (*ajñāna*) is "false ignorance" (*mithyājñāna*). That whose cause is this [ignorance] is "caused by that" (*tannimitta*);
the meaning is that it has that as its material cause (*upādāna*).

Although ignorance is its material cause, because it veils the nature of the Self (*ātmatattva*) as it manifests, it is described as a "defect" (*doṣa*), serving as the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) for the Lord who is the agent of the superimposition of the ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra-adhyāsa*).
The term "cause" (*nimitta*) is used to indicate that [the Self] possesses causality by virtue of being transformed by causes such as mental impressions (*saṃskāra*), time, and karma; yet,
how can there be an attachment of ignorance (*avidyā*) to the Self, which is self-luminous and unattached, given the absence of the causal complex consisting of mental impressions and so forth?
The word "false" (mithyā) is used for the purpose of dispelling such a doubt. Just as darkness, though established by the experience of owls, cannot exist within the orb of the fierce sun,
so too the ignorance established by the experience "I am ignorant" is impossible to deny.
Because the imagined [object] does not touch its substrate,
and because knowledge of the eternal nature [of that substrate] is not contradictory [to it];
or else, the word "mithyā" (false) is used for the purpose of dispelling the doubt that ignorance is merely the absence of knowledge.
The definition of ignorance (*ajñāna*), expressed by the term "false knowledge" (*mithyājñāna*), is that it is directly removable by knowledge while being false.
For one who asserts that the prior absence of desire (*icchāprāgabhāva*) is directly removed by knowledge, the phrase "while being false" (*mithyātve sati*) is stated.
The word "directly" (*sākṣāt*) is used to exclude over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to bondage (*bandha*), which is removable by knowledge through the mediation of the removal of ignorance.
The definition is either "falsity while having beginningless material cause," where "falsity" is for the purpose of excluding Brahman,
and "beginningless" is for the purpose of excluding clay and the like.
The phrase "while being the material cause" is used for the purpose of refuting a relationship between ignorance (*avidyā*) and the Self (*ātman*).
Now, he seeks to strengthen the doctrine of superimposition (*adhyāsa*), stating: "I am this," "this is mine.
Among the superimpositions of internal effects, "I" is the first superimposition.
Nor should it be argued that this is not a false superimposition because the two parts—the locus (*adhiṣṭhāna*) and the object superimposed (*āropya*)—are not perceived;
for, just as in the expression "the iron burns," there is the perception of both the seeing subject and the seen object in the form "I perceive.
By the word "this" (*idam*), the aggregate that is the object of experience is denoted.

Here, by the expression "I am this," the superimposition of identity (*tādātmyādhyāsa*)—namely, "I am a human being"—is shown; by the expression "this is my body," the superimposition of association (*saṃsargādhyāsa*) is shown.

If it is objected: "But surely the very identity of the body and the self is their relation; so what is the difference between them?"—it is true that identity consists in mutual difference existing while there is oneness of existence (*sattaikya*).

In this context, the distinction is that "I am a human being" is the manifestation of the aspect of identity, while "this is mine" is the manifestation of the aspect of difference in the form of a relation. Thus, since the causal complex exists and experience exists, superimposition (adhyāsa) exists; therefore, because there is no contradiction regarding the identity of Brahman and the Self, the subject matter and the purpose exist, and the scripture should be commenced—such is the purport of the Siddhānta-bhāṣya. And so, having established the subject matter and the purpose as implied by the Sūtra, he asks for the definition in order to prove superimposition—which is the cause of those two—by means of its definition, possibility, and proof: "He says."
"What is the definition of superimposition (adhyāsa)?"—this is what the proponent (pūrvavādī) asks; that is the meaning.
The phrase "he says" (āha) is used to indicate that this treatise is a formal debate (vādakathā), since its primary purpose is the determination of truth. Thus, the words of another are cited.
The commentary beginning with "He said" and extending up to "How, moreover, in the inner self" is devoted to defining superimposition (*adhyāsa*).
From that point onward, it is devoted to establishing its possibility (*saṃbhāvanā*).
The section beginning with "This very [superimposition], called ignorance" and ending with "is evident to all the world" is devoted to providing proof (*pramāṇa*). Such is the division.
He states the definition: "It is said to be of the nature of memory.
The word "superimposition" (adhyāsa) is to be supplied from the context.
Here, the definition is simply "the appearance of one thing in another."

The remaining two words are for the purpose of establishing that [definition]. For instance: "that which is manifested" (*avabhāsa*) refers to an object such as silver; "an unsuitable locus" (*paratra*) refers to the substratum (*adhikaraṇa*) that is unfit for that [object].
The unsuitability of the locus consists in its being the absolute absence (*atyantābhāva*) of the superimposed thing, or its possessing that [absence].

And thus, the meaning is that superimposition (*adhyastatva*) consists in being manifested in that which is conjoined with itself under a single delimitation (*ekāvacchedena*), while simultaneously possessing its own absolute non-existence (*svātyantābhāva*).
This is a definition common to both beginningless and beginning superimpositions.
The phrase "under a single delimitation" is included to exclude over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to the case of conjunction (*saṃyoga*).

Regarding conjunction (*saṃyoga*), although it appears in the tree with which it is conjoined even while its own absolute absence (*svātyantābhāva*) exists there, there is no over-extension (*ativyāpti*) because the delimiters (*avacchedaka*) of the two absolute absences differ—namely, the root and the top [of the tree].

The term "conjoined with itself" (*svasaṃsṛjyamāna*) is included to exclude the over-extension that would apply to a jar, since a jar brought later may appear on a floor where it was previously absent;
by this term, it is stated that at the time of the absence of the counter-positive (*pratiyogin*), the conjunction of that counter-positive must exist, and thus there is no over-extension.

The phrase "existing in that which possesses its own absolute non-existence" (*svātyantābhāvavati*) is included to exclude over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to the smell manifested by the delimitation of [the earth] as such.
Since the absolute non-existence of silver exists at the time of its association with it, delimited by the "this-ness" (*idantva*) in mother-of-pearl, there is no lack of extension (*avyāpti*).
Now, an objection: this definition is impossible (*asaṃbhava*).
Because of the absence of the causal complex for silver in the mother-of-pearl shell, there is no real relation [between them].

Nor should it be argued that the term "superimposed" (adhyasta) refers merely to the appearance of a remembered, real silver elsewhere—in the mother-of-pearl—because that would entail the theory of misapprehension (anyathākhyāti). Therefore, he says: "having the form of memory" (smṛtirūpa).
That which is remembered is *smṛti*; real silver and the like are its objects. That which has a form similar to that [object] is *smṛtirūpa*.
The meaning is "resembling that which is being remembered.
By the mention of similarity, there is a distinction between the object being remembered and the superimposed object (*āropya*).

It is stated that there is no "apprehension of something as otherwise" (anyathākhyāti). He establishes this similarity [to his own view] with the words "previously seen," where "seen" means the act of seeing.
Because it appears through the medium of a mental impression (*saṃskāra*) as having been seen previously, it is called "the appearance of what was previously seen.

By this, it is stated that the similarity between the object being remembered and the object superimposed consists in their both being objects of a cognition produced by a mental impression; for both memory and superimposition are produced by a mental impression.

Nor should it be argued that because superimposition is produced by a mental impression (*saṃskāra*), it would follow that it is a memory; for we intend to include its being produced by the conjunction with a defect (*doṣasaṃprayoga*) as well, and thus it is not produced by mental impressions alone.
Here, the word "conjunction" (*saṃyoga*) refers to the cognition of the general nature of the substratum (*adhiṣṭhānasāmānyajñāna*).

Because there is no contact with the sense organs in the superimposition of the ego (ahaṅkāra-adhyāsa), it is established by the two terms "of the nature of memory" (smṛtirūpa) and "previously seen" (pūrvadṛṣṭa) that silver is produced in mother-of-pearl and the like through the power of defects (doṣa), contact (saṃprayoga), and latent impressions (saṃskāra); thus, the definition characterized by "appearing elsewhere" (paratrāvabhāsyatva) is justified.
Others, however, say that by those two terms, the definition of the superimposition of an effect (kāryādhyāsa) is stated as being produced by the triad of defects and so forth.

Others, however, maintain that "having the form of memory" means being similar to what is being remembered; and this similarity consists in being the object of a cognition not produced by a means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*), because both memory and superimposition are not produced by a *pramāṇa*. [The term "previously seen"] refers to the locus previously perceived or to something belonging to that same class.
Because there is an absence of having been previously perceived in a body with newly acquired silver, etc.,

they have stated that the definition of empirical superimposition (*prātītikādhyāsa*) consists in being of a nature similar to what was previously perceived, while being the object of a cognition not produced by a means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*).
By the two terms "in another" (*paratra*) and "appearance" (*avabhāsa*), the general definition of superimposition has indeed been explained.

In this regard, they say that the two words beginning with "pramāṇa" (valid means of knowledge) are included in order to exclude over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to the case of the Ganges and so forth when it is being remembered, as well as to a brand-new jar.
Therein, regarding the superimposition of an object (*arthādhyāsa*), the construction is: "that which resembles what is being remembered appears elsewhere due to a previous perception.

Regarding the superimposition of cognition (*jñānādhyāsa*), however, the sentence should be construed as: "that which resembles memory appears elsewhere due to a previous perception. This is the summary.

Now, one might object: "Since there are conflicting views among disputants regarding superimposition (*adhyāsa*), how can the definition stated above be established? Anticipating this doubt, [the author] considers that although there is dispute concerning the nature of the substrate (*adhiṣṭhāna*) and the object superimposed (*āropya*), the definition—"the appearance of one thing in another"—is a universally accepted tenet because it is established by both scriptural authority and reasoning that a false object appears upon a real substrate. Thinking thus, he states the views of those who maintain *anyathākhyāti* (misapprehension as otherwise) and *ātmakhyāti* (self-apprehension), beginning with the words "some [say] of that."

Some proponents of *anyathākhyāti* (misapprehension as otherwise) maintain that there is a superimposition (*adhyāsa*) of the attributes of another object—such as silver located in a different place—upon a substrate like mother-of-pearl, which actually possesses its own constituent attributes.

However, the proponents of *ātmakhyāti* (self-apprehension) maintain that there is a superimposition of the attribute of silver, which is of the nature of cognition, upon the external mother-of-pearl;
that is to say, they hold that internal silver appears as if it were external. This is the meaning.
He states the theory of non-apprehension (*akhyāti-vāda*) with the words "some" (*kecit*).

The meaning is that they say: when there is a non-apprehension of the difference between two objects or two cognitions whose superimposition upon one another is established in common worldly experience, there arises an error rooted in that [non-apprehension], namely the specific linguistic usage "this is silver."

The point is that even by them, a qualified error must be accepted because otherwise the specific conventional usage could not be accounted for; thus, there is an agreement regarding the appearance of one thing as another.
He states the view of the Śūnyavādins: "But others... and so forth.

The meaning is that they describe the "imagination of the contrary nature" of that very substrate, such as mother-of-pearl and the like; that is, the imagination of something absolutely non-existent, such as silver, which possesses a contrary—that is, opposed—nature.
Regarding these views, he states the agreement concerning the definition of "the appearance of one thing as another" (paratra parāvabhāsa) with the words: "But in every way... (sarvathāpi tu).

The meaning is that even though there is dispute regarding the specific mode [of error], such as whether it is *anyathākhyāti* (misapprehension of something else) and so forth, superimposition (*adhyāsa*) does not abandon its defining characteristic of being the appearance of one thing in another location.

The point is that since silver— which is directly perceived in the mother-of-pearl— cannot exist in another place or in the intellect, and since it cannot be non-existent because it is perceived, nor can it truly exist in the mother-of-pearl because it is sublated, its nature must be precisely falsity (*mithyātva*).
He says "And thus" (tathā ca) to show that there is no dependence on reasoning regarding the falsity of what is superimposed, because that is established by experience;
this experience occurs at a time subsequent to sublation, whereas [the superimposition] occurred prior to it.

Because it is impossible to have knowledge of the shell-nature [of the object], the word "mithyā" (false) expresses the falsity of the silver, which is established by the perception of its sublation (*bādhā*).

Having stated the illustration for the superimposition (*adhyāsa*) of the ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*) upon the attributeless Self, he states the illustration for the superimposition of the internal difference between Brahman and the individual soul (*jīva*), which is conditioned by adjuncts (*upādhi*) such as ignorance (*avidyā*), with the words "one" (*ekaḥ*).
The meaning is that, just as with the [appearance of] a second moon, a single object alone appears as twofold when pointed at by a finger.
The word "iti" (thus) serves to conclude the section on the definition [of superimposition].
Let it be granted that superimposition occurs in the case of mother-of-pearl and the like; however—
However, since [superimposition] is not possible in the case of the Self, he raises an objection with the words, "But how?

Where there is the status of being the substratum for immediate superimposition, there is invariably the state of being conjoined with the sense organs and the state of being an object; this pervasion (vyāpti) is observed in cases such as mother-of-pearl.
Intending to show that because the pervader is absent, the Self cannot be the substratum, he says, "In the case of the inner Self" (*pratyagātmani*).
The meaning is: how can there be a superimposition (*adhyāsa*) of objects such as the ego (*ahaṅkāra*) and their attributes upon the inwardly directed, full, and sense-unperceivable [Self]?
He states the aforementioned pervasion (*vyāpti*): "For everyone...
Here, "being situated in front" means being in contact with the senses.

[Objection: Might it not be the case that even for the Self, in order to serve as the locus [of superimposition], there must be objectivity and so forth? To this, he says: "yuṣmat... (the passage beginning with "you"). Following such scriptural texts as "The inner Self, which is unworthy of being the object of the notion 'this', is not grasped by the eye," you maintain that the Self is not an object.
The meaning is that if, out of greed for proximity, one were now to admit its objectivity, there would be a contradiction of both scripture and established doctrine.
He asserts the possibility of superimposition upon the Self with the words "it is said.
The pervading characteristic of superimposition is merely the appearance of both the substrate and the object of superimposition in a single cognition;
and that consists in being the locus of effects such as the cessation of doubt, which is occasioned by that appearance.

Thinking that this very objecthood (*viṣayatva*), as constituted by its non-difference from the manifestation (*bhāna*), is not a pervader due to its complexity (*gaurava*), he says: "Not, first of all... (*na tāvat*).
This self is not, by necessity, an object [of cognition].
He states the reason for this: "our" (asmad).
The meaning is that it appears there in the form of the "I"-notion (*aham-adhyāsa*), which is our cognition (*asmat-pratyaya*).

Alternatively, the meaning is this: that in which the conscious self (*cidātman*)—which is our own object—is perceived by way of being reflected is the "I-notion" (*asmad-pratyaya*), namely the *ahaṅkāra*, because it appears therein.

Nor should it be argued that there is a circularity—that appearance occurs when there is superimposition (*adhyāsa*), and superimposition occurs when there is appearance—because [the process] is beginningless (*anāditvāt*).
Because it is possible for that which appears as the self through prior practice to serve as the substratum for subsequent superimposition.
[Objection: "But how can the Self, which consists of the manifestation (*bhāna*) having the ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*) as its object—namely, the [notion] 'I am indeed'—be the knower?
For without being the object of that [manifestation], it would be impossible for it to be the recipient of its fruit. To this, he says: "And because of its immediacy" (*aparokṣatvācca*).
The word "and" (*ca*) is for the purpose of dispelling this doubt.
The meaning is "because of its self-luminosity.
He establishes its self-luminosity with the word "pratyak" (the inner self).
The meaning is that because the Self is well-known to everyone from children to scholars as being free from doubt and the like, it possesses self-luminosity.
Therefore, the intended meaning is that because the Self manifests through self-luminosity (*svaprakāśatva*), it is possible for it to be the substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*) of superimposition (*adhyāsa*).
Regarding the claim that being the substratum of immediate superimposition is pervaded by being an object of perception through sensory contact, he says: "And this [Self] is not...
He states the reason for this: "...even though it is not perceptible."
The meaning is: "even in that which is perceptible by the senses.
Ignorant people, lacking discrimination, superimpose upon the sky—which is like the surface of a sapphire bowl—the qualities of being dark or yellow as if it were directly perceived;
however, since the quality of being perceptible by the senses does not exist there, there is no pervasion (vyāpti) due to this deviation (vyabhicāra).
By this, the argument that superimposition (*adhyāsa*) is impossible between the self and the non-self due to a lack of similarity is refuted;
for superimposition is observed even in the absence of such similarity between the blue color and the sky.

According to our established doctrine (*siddhānta*), it should be understood that the sky is cognizable by the witness-consciousness (*sākṣin*) manifested through a visual modification (*vṛtti*) having the form of light.
He concludes the discussion on its plausibility with the word "evam" (thus).

Now, one might ask: why is superimposition (*adhyāsa*) described here when ignorance (*avidyā*), which was indicated in the Sūtra as that which is to be destroyed by the knowledge of Brahman, has been set aside? To this he says: "tametam" (this very [superimposition]).

The meaning is that they consider this superimposition—which has been introduced, resolved, and characterized by the aforementioned definition—to be ignorance itself, because it is the effect of ignorance.
He states that this [superimposition] is ignorance because it is to be removed by knowledge: "by its discrimination.
The meaning is that they say knowledge is that which removes superimposition, as it determines the true nature of the substrate through the negation of what is superimposed.
Nevertheless, setting aside causal ignorance (kāraṇāvidyā), why is effect-ignorance (kāryāvidyā) described? To this he says: "therein."
The meaning is that while that superimposition (adhyāsa) exists as consisting of ignorance (avidyā) according to the logic already stated.

The intention is that since the fundamental ignorance (mūlāvidyā) is not seen to be an evil (anartha) during deep sleep, its description here is intended to demonstrate that it becomes an evil through its manifested effects (kāryātmanā). The literal meaning [of the verse] is that the substratum (adhiṣṭhāna) is not tainted by the virtues or defects produced by what is superimposed upon it.
Having thus stated the definition and the possibility of superimposition (*adhyāsa*), he states the proof: "Taking this very [superimposition]...

The meaning is that, taking as its cause this aforementioned superimposition—which is established through the perception of the witness—threefold worldly activity proceeds: namely, that pertaining to ritual action (*karma-śāstra*), that pertaining to liberation (*mokṣa-śāstra*), and that which is worldly.
Among these, the ritual scriptures, such as the *Ṛgveda* and others, are devoted to injunctions and prohibitions.
The distinction is that the Vedānta texts, which constitute the scriptures on liberation, are solely intent upon the inner Brahman that is devoid of injunctions and prohibitions.
Thus, although superimposition is established by perception as the cause of worldly transaction, [the author] asks for further proof, saying: "But how?

The analysis of the compound *avidyāvadviṣayāṇi* is as follows: the self who possesses superimposition in the form "I am possessed of ignorance" is the knower (*pramātā*); those [scriptures] whose object and locus is such a [knower] are "those having the ignorant one as their object."
