Although it is evident that the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) have as their object one who possesses ignorance (*avidyāvat*), because the valid cognition—which serves as the cause for the linguistic usage of various objects of knowledge—resides in a knower (*pramātṛ*) whose nature is superimposition (*adhyāsa*), there remains the further inquiry: by what means of valid cognition is this status of having an ignorant person as the object established?
Alternatively, how can the means of valid cognition themselves have as their object one who is not a knower?
The objection is that [the cognition] would incur invalidity due to a defect in its basis (*āśrayadoṣa*).

In response to the inquiry regarding the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) therein, he states the presumption based on worldly practice (*vyavahārārthāpatti*) and the inference based on its mark (*talliṅgānumāna*) with the passage beginning "It is said" (*ucyate*) and ending with "therefore" (*tasmāt*).

The empirical usage having Devadatta as its agent is rooted in the superimposition of "I" and "mine" upon his body and so forth, because it follows the positive and negative concomitance with that [superimposition]; whatever is thus is so,
just as a pot is rooted in clay— such is the formal argument.
In this regard, he demonstrates the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) with the words "deha" (body).
It is observed that in the case of Devadatta, during deep sleep, when there is an absence of superimposition (*adhyāsa*), there is an absence of worldly activity (*vyavahāra*);
whereas in the waking and dreaming states, when there is superimposition, there is worldly activity. This positive concomitance (*anvaya*) is not explicitly stated because it is obvious.
The sense is that superimposition is established either by this mark (*liṅga*) as its cause, or else by the impossibility of accounting for the effect, which is worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*).

Now, one might object: "Let worldly transaction be established merely through the conceit of 'I' with respect to the body, which possesses the genus *manuṣyatva* (humanity) and so forth; what is the use of the conceit of 'mine' with respect to the senses and other organs? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "Not indeed" (*na hi*).
The word "senses" (*indriya*) is also indicative of the marks (*liṅga*) and so forth.
Because of the use of the word "etcetera" (*ādi*) in the phrase "perception and so forth" (*pratyakṣādi*), the meaning is as follows:

the conventional discourse (*vyavahāra*) prompted by perception, inferential marks (*liṅga*), and so on—taking the form of "I am the seer," "I am the inferrer," "I am the hearer," and so forth—is not possible without grasping the sense organs and other factors as objects of the notion of "mine" (*mamatā*).
Alternatively, the construction is: that conventional discourse which does not take those [factors] up as "mine" does not exist.
In the former case, since there is a single agent for the actions of non-appropriation and performing, the suffix *ktvā* is grammatically correct;
in the latter case, its correctness follows from the fact that non-appropriation and the act of usage have a single identical agent— this is the distinction.

The sense is that if there were no superimposition (adhyāsa) of "mine" with respect to the senses and so forth, then, like a blind person, there would be no such worldly functioning as being a "seer" and so on.
To the objection that since worldly functioning occurs through the superimposition of the senses alone, the superimposition of the body is redundant, he says: "And not...
The locus (adhiṣṭhāna) of the senses is their substratum (āśraya).

The meaning is "the body. Now, one might object: "Let it be that the body conjoined with the Self is their substratum; what is the use of superimposition (adhyāsa)? To this he replies: "And not by means of a non-superimposed state of being the Self. This means: that in which the state of being the Self—that is, identity with the Self (ātmatādātmya)—is not superimposed.

The meaning is that, according to the scriptural text "For [the Self] is unattached," the relationship between the body and the Self is purely superimposed (ādhyāsika), and not one such as conjunction (saṃyoga) or the like.
Now, one might object: let there be no superimposed relationship of the Self with the body and so forth either.

Because the status of being a knower (*pramātṛtva*) is established by its own inherent consciousness, and because there is no occurrence of the status of being a knower during deep sleep due to the cessation of the instruments (*karaṇa*), he says in response to that: "And not in this [state]...
For the status of being a knower consists in being the substratum of valid cognition (*pramā*).

If valid cognition (*pramā*) were merely eternal pure consciousness (*nityacinmātra*), then it would be impossible for it to have a substratum (*āśraya*), and the sense organs (*karaṇa*) would be rendered useless.
If, on the other hand, it were merely a mental modification (*vṛtti*), there would follow the undesirable consequence of the world being blind (*jagadāndhya*).
Because mental modification (*vṛtti*) is insentient, cognition (*bodha*) arising from that modification is the valid knowledge (*pramā*).

The point is that for the unattached Self (*ātman*), the state of being the substratum of that [cognition] is not possible without the superimposition (*adhyāsa*) of identity with the mind (*manas*), which possesses modifications.
The literal meaning is: "provided that there is no superimposition of the body and no superimposition of its attributes.
To one who might object, "In that case, let the self not be the knower," he replies: "And not..."

Therefore, he concludes the result of both inference and presumptive testimony (arthāpatti) by stating "tasmāt" (therefore): superimposition must be admitted for the sake of the empirical usage of the self as a knower and so forth.
The meaning is "because of the existence of means of valid cognition" (pramāṇa).
Alternatively, having resolved the question regarding the means of valid cognition, he dispels the objection by stating "tasmāt."

Since the superimposition (adhyāsa) of "I" resides within the knower (pramātṛ), it is not a defect; thus, the construction is that even the means of valid cognition (pramāṇas) have as their locus that which possesses ignorance (avidyā). A defect is said to be that which arises subsequently, once the knower already exists.
Just as a piece of glass or the like [is a defect],

ignorance (*avidyā*), however, is not a defect because it is internal to the cognizer; the point is that it is therefore not the case that perception and the other means of knowledge would thereby become invalid.

Now, as for the statement that worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*) is the effect of superimposition (*adhyāsa*) based on positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), that is incorrect because we observe worldly transactions even in the absence of superimposition among the learned; therefore, he says: "And with beasts, etc.
The word "and" (*ca*) is for the purpose of dispelling this doubt.
What constitutes "learnedness" (vidvattva): is it the direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*) that "I am Brahman," or is it the ratiocinative knowledge of the distinction between the Self and the non-Self?
In the first case, it will be stated in the *Samanvaya-sūtra* that worldly activity continues due to the persistence of sublated superimposition (*bādhitādhyāsānuvṛtti*).
In the second case, indirect knowledge (*parokṣajñāna*) cannot remove immediate error (*aparokṣabhramanivartaka*).

The meaning is that it is logical to say that empirical activity is the effect of superimposition (adhyāsa), because even for those possessed of discrimination, at the time of empirical activity, they are no different from animals and the like, being equal to them insofar as they possess superimposition.
Herein is the formal argument (prayoga): those possessed of discrimination possess superimposition, because they possess empirical activity, just like animals and the like.
Therein, explaining the summary statement, he clarifies the reason through an illustration with the words "Just as... (*yathā hi*).
The suitability or unsuitability of consciousness consists in its having as its object that which accomplishes what is desired or undesired;
he illustrates this very point with the word "Just as" (*yathā*).
This staff is a means for accomplishing what is undesirable to me,
because it is a staff,
like a staff previously experienced.
The meaning is that they act after inferring: "This grass is a means to achieve what is desired, like previously experienced grass.
Now, he states the presence of the reason in the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*) with the word "thus" (*evam*).
The logical connection is "even those whose minds are fully developed";
the meaning is "even those who possess discernment.
He states the conclusion with the words "therefore" (ataḥ).
"By the force of experience" is the meaning.
"Similar" means equal insofar as they are both effects of superimposition.

[Objection: "But it is not the case that animals and the like say, 'Our activity arises from superimposition,' nor is this [known] through the perception of others; therefore, the example is devoid of the probandum. [Reply: He says "And of animals, etc."—they possess only the knowledge of the self and the non-self, but not the discrimination between them.

Because there is no [explicit] instruction; therefore, the meaning is that their superimposition is established due to the existence of the causal complex (*sāmagrī*). He concludes with the words "tatsāmānya" (that generality).

The connection [of the sentence] is as follows: because its similarity to those [animals], such as goats and the like—namely, the state of being characterized by worldly transaction (vyavahāravattva)—is observed, it is determined that this worldly transaction is common even to the wise.
It was stated previously that this commonality of the transaction consists in its being an effect of superimposition (adhyāsa).
In that regard, he recalls the positive and negative concomitances (anvaya-vyatireka) mentioned there with the words "tatkā" (arising from that).

"Tatkāla" means that whose very time is the time of that superimposition (adhyāsa). Alternatively, it means that which possesses the positive concomitance (anvaya) and so forth already stated: namely, that when there is superimposition, there is worldly transaction (vyavahāra), and in its absence—as in deep sleep—there is its absence.

Therefore, it is faultless that even for those who possess discrimination, there exists the conceit of "I" and "mine" with respect to the body and so forth, due to this empirical sign. Now, one might object: "Even if worldly transactional activity is based on superimposition, ritual activities such as the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice are not produced by superimposition, because they are preceded by the knowledge of a self distinct from the body. Anticipating this doubt, the author accepts the reason [for their being based on superimposition] by stating: "But in the case of scriptural [activity]... (śāstrīye tu).

Then, raising the objection as to how the fact that Vedic ritual action is produced by superimposition (adhyāsa) can be established, [the author] asks: "Is it merely the cognition of the Self as distinct from the body that is required there, or is it the knowledge of the true nature of the Self?
To the first case, he says "Even so" (tathāpi), meaning that since such a cognition does not sublate superimposition, the establishment of [superimposition] is thereby proven.
He says that the second [alternative] is not [the case]: "not by Vedānta," etc.

The meaning is that for ritual action, what is required is the knowledge "I am a transmigrating being belonging to a particular caste, afflicted by hunger, thirst, and so forth"; it is not the knowledge of the true nature of the Self which is the opposite of that, because the latter is useless and would obstruct engagement in action.
He concludes that scriptural action is produced by superimposition with the words "prāk tu" (but previously).
He provides scripture as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for superimposition with the words "yathā hi" (for just as...).
The meaning is that just as perception, inference, and presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) are means of valid cognition regarding superimposition, so too is scripture.

The meaning is as follows: scriptural tradition (*āgama*)—expressed through such statements as "A Brāhmaṇa should sacrifice," "One should not beg after having bathed [for initiation]," "One should initiate a Brāhmaṇa at eight years of age," and "One whose hair is black should establish the sacred fires"—by referring to the qualified agent through words such as "Brāhmaṇa" and so forth, which denote pride in one's caste and the like, leads us to understand superimposition (*adhyāsa*). Thus, although superimposition is established by means of proof, since there arises the desire to know "of what is there a superimposition upon what?", he recalls the definition in order to illustrate it, saying: "Superimposition, indeed... and so on.
He provides an illustration with the words "tadyathā" (for example).
The meaning is that it is illustrated in such a way that its characteristic becomes clear.

One superimposes upon the self as qualified by the body—external objects such as sons and so forth, which are perceived as distinct from one's own body—their properties, such as totality and the like.
The meaning is that, due to the cognition of those attributes, one superimposes attributes similar to them upon oneself;

this should be understood because the superimposition of those attributes is impossible when there is direct perception of difference, and because the theory of "misapprehension" (anyathākhyāti) is not accepted.
He says "likewise" (tathā) to explain that one superimposes the attributes of the body, the senses, and the mind upon the Self characterized by [consciousness].

Since the body and so forth, which possess attributes such as thinness, are imagined as being identical with the Self, it should be understood that their attributes are directly superimposed upon the Self. He describes the superimposition of the attributes of the mind upon the Witness, whose nature is immediate and unknown, saying: "likewise, the internal organ... (tathāntaḥkaraṇa).
Having explained the superimposition of attributes (*dharmādhyāsa*), he states the superimposition of the substrate (*dharmyadhyāsa*) in the same manner with the word "thus" (*evam*).
It should be understood that, having superimposed the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) non-differently upon the Witness (*sākṣin*), one then superimposes its attributes, such as desire and the like.
The mental modifications (*manovṛttayaḥ*) are one's own movements.

It is "inner" (*pratyak*) because it moves toward (*añcati*), that is, manifests itself, as being of the nature of existence, consciousness, and bliss (*saccitsukhātmaka*), by way of its opposition (*prātilomyena*) to non-existence, insentience, suffering, and the ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*) and so forth.

Having thus illustrated the superimposition (*adhyāsa*) of the non-self and its attributes upon the Self, he now describes the superimposition of the Self as well upon the non-self through their mutual association, with the words "And that... (*tañca*).
In the superimposition of "I," the manifestation of the conscious self (cidātman) must be admitted;
otherwise, the world would fall into total blindness.
Furthermore, there is no manifestation of that which has not been superimposed.
Therefore, just as in the case of silver [superimposed] upon this [shell], the superimposition of association with the Self must be admitted for the Self;
and likewise by way of its reverse.
The "reverse" of that inert object of superimposition is its status as the substrate (adhiṣṭhānatva).
And consciousness exists as that very self—this is the meaning.
In that regard, the connection [of consciousness] with ignorance is by way of its pure self;
the distinction is that with the mind it is of that which is conditioned by ignorance, and with the body and so forth it is of that which is conditioned by the mind.

The sense is that, in this way, through the superimposition of the intellect and so forth upon the self, the self acquires agency and other such qualities; and through the superimposition of the self upon the intellect and so forth, the intellect and so forth acquire consciousness.
He concludes the described superimposition with the words "evamayam" (thus, this).

Because it consists of beginningless ignorance (*anādyavidyā*), the superimposition (*adhyāsa*) of effects is itself beginningless; from superimposition comes latent impression (*saṃskāra*), and from that, superimposition.
Thus, by way of this continuous flow, its naturalness (*naisargikatva*) is established.
In this manner, both the material cause (*upādāna*) and the efficient cause (*nimitta*) have been explained.
Because there is no destruction without knowledge, it is infinite.
As it is said in the Bhagavadgītā: "Neither its form is perceived here in such a way, nor its end, nor its beginning, nor its foundation.
Having stated the cause, he describes its essential nature with the word "mithyā" (unreal).

The meaning is as follows: "pratyaya" refers to that which is perceived through false illusion (*mithyāmāyā*), namely the manifold of effects (*kāryaprapañca*) and the cognition thereof; such is its essential nature.
He states its function with the words "kartṛtva" (agency) and so forth. He concludes the proof with the words "sarva" (all).

Intending that perception alone is the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) for apprehending the locus of superimposition (*adhyāsa*), while inference and other means serve only to establish its possibility, he concludes the discussion on perception.
Having thus described superimposition, he shows the subject matter (*viṣaya*) and the purpose (*prayojana*) accomplished by it with the words "of this" (*asya*).

Liberation (mokṣa) is the absolute destruction, along with its root, of superimposition (adhyāsa), which is the cause of misfortunes such as agency and so forth. To the question "By what means is this achieved?", he says: "By the Self" (ātman).
This means by the attainment—that is, the unobstructed acquisition through hearing (śravaṇa) and other means—of the direct realization (sākṣātkāra) of the identity of Brahman and the Self.
He states the cause for this knowledge (vidyā): "All" (sarva).
The meaning is that they are undertaken and studied;
for those who have investigated the Vedāntas, it is stated that the subject matter is the non-duality of Brahman and the Self,
and liberation is the fruit.

It should be understood that, by implication, those very same [topics] constitute the subject matter and the purpose of this treatise as well, which consists of an inquiry into that [Self]. Now, one might object: "Since meditations on the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) and so forth appear in the Vedāntas, how can it be said that their sole purpose is the unity of the Self? To this he says: "And just as... (*yathā ca*).
That which is the body (*śarīra*) itself is called *śārīraka*.
Because it is contemptible, the "Śārīraka" refers to the individual soul (jīva) dwelling therein; "Mīmāṃsā" is the inquiry into its being Brahman, and the meaning is "in that [work].

Since meditations (upāsanās) serve the purpose of attaining the knowledge of the oneness of the Self by means of one-pointedness of consciousness, it will be explained later that the primary purport (mahātātparya) of those passages as well lies in that oneness.

Thus, by means of the statement regarding superimposition (*adhyāsa*), it has been demonstrated that the scripture ought to be commenced, because there is no contradiction in the identity of Brahman and the Self, and because it possesses both a subject matter and a purpose.
Thus ends the first section.

The Vedāntas are the direct subject matter of this inquiry (vicāra); since there is doubt as to whether they have already been dealt with or not, [it is argued that] because the entire Veda is devoted to injunctions (vidhi),
and because injunction has already been investigated by the previous system (pūrvatantra) starting from the aphorism "Now, therefore, the desire to know Brahman" (athāto brahmajijñāsā).

The prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) being that since the Vedāntas have already had their meaning understood, there is no subject matter immediately preceding [this work] and thus no need for its commencement, the author says: "Regarding the Vedāntas.
This means that this is the first aphorism (*sūtra*) of the collection of aphorisms intended to be explained—a treatise consisting of a revered inquiry into the subject matter of the Vedāntas.
If the Veda were to have injunction (*vidhi*) alone as its meaning, then the omniscient Bādarāyaṇa would not have spoken of the "inquiry into Brahman" (*brahmajijñāsā*).
Because there is no means of valid cognition regarding Brahman [by other means],

the author of the Sūtras demonstrates by stating that Brahman is the object of inquiry (*jijñāsya*) that an investigation into the Vedānta— which has Brahman as its subject and which is not understood through any other system— must be commenced.
And the commentator explained this by the phrase "of that which he intends to explain" (*vyācikhyāsitasya*).
Thus ends the second section.

Having thus, by means of two sections, explained the two reasons—the possession of a subject matter and a purpose, as well as the fact that the subject has not been previously established—which constitute the implied meaning of the Sūtra regarding the necessity of investigating the Vedānta, [the author], beginning the word-by-word commentary, establishes the qualified candidate (adhikārin) by stating that the word *atha* signifies "immediacy," since doubt remains as to whether the scripture should begin depending on the existence or non-existence of such a candidate: "In this regard, the word *atha*... and so forth.
The meaning is "in the sūtra.

Since the word *atha* has many meanings— namely, "auspiciousness," "immediacy," "commencement," "question," and "entirety"— as expressed by the rule "the word *atha* [is used] in the senses of auspiciousness, immediacy, commencement, question, and entirety," in this context of "Now, the instruction on yoga" (*atha yogānuśāsanam*), [it signifies commencement].

One might ask: "Just as in the Sūtra the word *atha* signifies 'commencement'—as in 'the Yoga-śāstra is commenced'—why should it not be so here? To this he replies: "It does not have the sense of an introduction (*adhikāra*).
The underlying intention is this: does the term *jijñāsā* refer primarily to the desire for knowledge, or does it indicate the investigation (*vicāra*) itself?

Now, if the word "atha" (then/thereupon) has the sense of "commencement" in the first [interpretation], the meaning of the sūtra would be that "the desire for knowledge of Brahman is commenced"; but that is inconsistent, because such a desire is not something to be commenced.
For a desire is not undertaken at every section; rather, it is by means of that desire that the inquiry is undertaken.

Not the second [alternative], because it is impossible for [the word *atha*] to indicate "investigation" (*vicāra*) without supplying a word denoting an action to be performed (*kartavyapada*); and once such a word is supplied, since the commencement would be stated by that very word, the word *atha* would be redundant.

However, since it is more appropriate for the word *atha* to signify immediate succession (*ānantarya*) for the sake of establishing the eligibility [of the student], he now refutes the other possible meaning with the words "of the auspicious rite" (*maṅgalasya*).

The meaning is that the sentence-meaning is the necessity of undertaking the inquiry; for in that case, there is no syntactic connection (*anvaya*) of the auspicious rite as its agent or in any other capacity.
If it is objected that the author of the Sūtras has already indicated that an auspicious rite must be performed at the beginning of a treatise by using the word *atha*, [the reply is: True.
Its meaning is not auspiciousness; rather, its hearing and recitation perform the function of an auspicious rite.
However, its primary purpose is immediate succession; thus it says, "the meaning is immediate succession" (*arthānantara*).
Immediate succession is the other meaning.

Through hearing—that is, by the act of listening—the hearing of the syllable *oṃ* and the word *atha* yields the fruit of auspiciousness, just like the hearing of the sounds of conchs, lutes, and so forth.
As it is said: "In ancient times, these two—*oṃ* and the word *atha*—emerged from Brahman after piercing his throat; therefore, both of them are auspicious."
The meaning is that this is because of such a traditional teaching (*smaraṇa*).

Now, since the context is that "the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) is false," if it is thought that "the phenomenal world is real," then the word *atha* is observed to have the sense of introducing a subsequent topic that differs in meaning from the previously discussed subject.
To the question, "Why should it not be so here?", he says: "Because of the preceding" (*pūrva*).
This means "because of the result.

Since there is no specific subject matter (*arthaviśeṣa*) introduced prior to the inquiry into Brahman (*brahmajijñāsā*), for which the word *atha* could express its being something different from that [prior subject], [the word *atha* cannot be used in this sense].
The author of the Sūtras should not state that it is a different matter from anything whatsoever, because there would be no purpose [in doing so].

If it is argued that, by the force of expectation—since that which was previously introduced as the cause for the inquiry into the duty denoted by the word *jijñāsā* (the desire to know) expects it—one implies that prior cause and thereby asserts that it is a different matter; [we reply:]...

In that case, "being another thing" (*arthāntaratva*) is included within "immediacy" (*ānantarya*), because immediacy must necessarily be stated in order to understand the relationship between cause and effect.
For when it is said, "this is another thing," the fact of its being a cause is not understood;
however, when it is said, "this is immediate [to that]," the understanding of its being a cause certainly arises.

Nor should it be argued that there would be the undesirable consequence of the horse being perceived as the cause immediately prior to the cow in the case of "a horse and then a cow," because such immediate succession is not primary when there is a separation by either space or time.
Therefore, immediate succession is primary only between a causal complex (*sāmagrī*) and its result.

Because there is no intervention [between the two], once that [meaning] has been stated, it should not be called a different meaning (*arthāntaratva*), since it would be redundant and purposeless; this is the sense.

One should construe the commentary by supplying the thought: "Since the result, which is the inquiry, depends on the previously mentioned reason, that 'different meaning' which arises by force of that dependence is not a separate meaning of the word *atha*, because it is included within the category of 'immediacy' (*ānantarya*)."

Alternatively, the meaning is this: that "otherness of meaning" (*arthāntaratā*) which requires a preceding subject matter has as its result knowledge; since [the word *atha*] is not distinct from immediate succession (*ānantarya*) by way of that [resulting knowledge], and because that [otherness of meaning] is not included within the knowledge of it, it is not the meaning of the word *atha*. Now, raising the doubt: "Even if it has the sense of immediate succession, what is the limit (*avadhi*) of that succession? he says: "And when... (*sati ca*).
That which invariably precedes, occurs prior to, and is the uncommon cause—meaning the complete cause—is [the limit].
The meaning is that it must be stated that this very [study] is the limit (avadhi).

Now, one might object: "Let it be that, just as in the inquiry into Dharma, the study of the Veda is a sufficient cause (puṣkala-kāraṇa) for the inquiry into Brahman as well. To this he says: "svādhyāya" (one's own Vedic study).
The meaning is that while it is a common cause (sādhāraṇa-kāraṇa) in the inquiry into Brahman, it is not a sufficient cause.

[Objection: But surely, according to the principle of "separateness of conjunction" (*saṃyogapṛthaktva*), it will be stated in the *Sarvāpekṣā* section that by such scriptural texts as "by sacrifice, by charity," ritual acts such as sacrifice are enjoined for the sake of knowledge; and thus, the understanding [of those acts] through the *Pūrvatantra* (the Mīmāṃsā) is a sufficient cause [for knowledge]. Thus he raises this doubt with "But surely" (*nanu*). Here, in the inquiry into Brahman (*brahmajijñāsā*), there is a specific [requirement], namely the uncommon cause.

Regarding the Jaimini Sūtra, "But when one [action] serves both purposes, there is the distinctness of the conjunction" (*saṃyogapṛthaktvam*), its meaning is as follows: when a single action has both purposes—that is, a connection with multiple results—the "conjunction" (*saṃyoga*) refers to the sentence that makes known the connection to both; the "distinctness" (*pṛthaktvam*) of that [sentence] means its differentiation, and that is the reason [for the dual purpose].

Consequently, here too, although actions such as the *jyotiṣṭoma* have results such as heaven, they also serve the purpose of knowledge on account of scriptural statements such as "by sacrifice, by charity," and so forth.
He refutes this with the words "No," and so forth.

The intention is as follows: the thousandfold logic found in the previous systems (the Mīmāṃsā) is not a complete cause for the knowledge of Brahman or its inquiry, because that [logic] serves only as a means for determining Dharma.
Nor is there a definitive determination of karma,
because that [determination] serves as a cause for performance;
for there is no pervasion (vyāpti) between dharma and Brahman, as there is between smoke and fire.
By means of which, through the knowledge of Dharma, the knowledge of Brahman arises;

even though ritual actions are causes by way of discerning [the reality of] mother-of-pearl and so forth, nevertheless, they do not possess the status of being qualifications for the person entitled [to the inquiry].
Because those [actions] performed in other lifetimes are also causes for results even when they are unknown;
therefore, the qualification of the primary agent (adikāriviśeṣaṇa), when known, must be stated as the proximate limit (*ānantarya-avadhi*) that serves as the abundant cause for engagement.
Hence, these are the actions.

Since the comprehension of that [dharma] or the investigation into its means is not the limit [of inquiry], the desire to know Brahman (*brahmajijñāsā*) does not follow immediately after the desire to know dharma (*dharmajijñāsā*).

Now, one might object: even if there is no relationship of cause and effect between the desire to know dharma and the desire to know Brahman, the word "atha" (then) serves to indicate the sequence by way of stating immediate succession.

Anticipating the objection that the word *atha*—as in the scriptural passage, "First he cuts from the heart, then from the tongue, then from the chest"—is intended to indicate the sequence of the portions to be cut (*avadāna*), [the author] says: "Just as...

Just as the sequence (*krama*) consisting of the fixed order of succession among the portions to be cut is the meaning of the word *atha* because it is intended to be expressed there, so too here the sequence between the inquiry into Dharma (*dharmajijñāsā*) and the inquiry into Brahman (*brahmajijñāsā*) is not intended to be expressed;
for since they do not have a single agent, no sequence between them is required.
Therefore, the meaning is that the word *atha* does not signify sequence. Now, one might ask: why is there no single agent for those two? To this he says: "śeṣa" (subsidiary).
[This refers to] those things which are subsidiary to a single primary purpose.
As in the case of the *avadānas* and the *prayāja* offerings;
and as in the case of that which stands in the relation of subsidiary (*śeṣa*) and principal (*śeṣin*), such as the *prayāja* and the *darśa*.

And there is the case of that which has the status of being an entitlement for one already entitled, such as the *godohana* vessel prescribed for one desiring cattle by the rule "with the *godohana* for one desiring cattle," based upon the *praṇayana* of water which is an auxiliary (*aṅga*) of the *Darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices;

or, for example, the *Soma* sacrifice prescribed for the time subsequent to the *Darśapūrṇamāsa* by the rule "having sacrificed with the *Darśapūrṇamāsa*, one should sacrifice with *Soma*. In these cases, the *Soma* sacrifice has the status of being an entitlement for one already entitled to the *Darśa* and so forth, and they possess the quality of having a single agent (*ekakartṛkatva*).
[This] occurs;

and thus, because those [elements] grasped by a single injunction for performance can be executed simultaneously, an expectation for sequence arises, and sequence is understood through direct statement (*śruti*) and so forth.
However, there is no such authority—such as direct statement, indicative mark (*liṅga*), and so on—for the relationship of subordinate and principal between the two "desires to know" (*jijñāsā*).
Is it not so that the Śruti declares: "Having completed the student life, one should become a householder; having been a householder, one should become a forest-dweller, and then renounce"?

And: "Having studied the Vedas according to the rules, having procreated sons in accordance with dharma, and having offered sacrifices according to one's ability, one should direct the mind toward liberation."

It is not so, because the Smṛti text "one should renounce even from the stage of studentship" (*brahmacaryādeva pravrajet*) and "the one of purified soul attains liberation indeed in the first stage of life" (*āsādayati śuddhātmā mokṣaṃ vai prathamāśrame*) indicate that the qualification for [renunciation] is established by the Smṛti.

Thus, from the two scriptural passages (*śruti*) and traditional texts (*smṛti*) cited by you, it is understood that those two scriptural and traditional texts have as their subject matter the person whose mind is impure.
This is what is meant: if the mind has been purified by actions performed in previous births, then one should renounce even while still a student (*brahmacārin*) and desire to know Brahman;
but when it is known through passion that the mind is not yet pure, then one should become a householder.

If there is still impurity even there, one should become a forest-dweller; if there is still impurity even then, one should likewise wait for the [proper] time, thinking, "I shall renounce when purity is attained in the forest.
And thus says the Śruti: "On the very day one becomes dispassionate, on that very day one should renounce."
Therefore, the point is that there is no evidence whatsoever for these two [Mīmāṃsās] having the relationship of the subject matter and the qualified person (*adhikṛtādhikāra*).
Now, one might object: let it be that the two Mīmāṃsās do not stand in the relation of subordinate and principal (*śeṣa-śeṣitva*) nor in the relation of subject matter and qualified person;
nevertheless, since they both have the single fruit of liberation (*mokṣa*), they must certainly have a single agent (*ekakartṛkatva*).

For those who advocate for the combination [of means] say: "Liberation results from both knowledge and action. And because there is a single authorship, since the object to be investigated is one—the meaning of the Veda—so too it is with the six sacrifices, such as the Āgneya and others, which have a single fruit, namely heaven.

Having raised the objection that "since the twelve chapters have a single object of inquiry (*jijñāsya*), the sequence between them is intended, and therefore the word *atha* signifies sequence," he says:
"Because of the difference in results (*phala*) and the difference in the objects of inquiry. The ellipsis [to be supplied] is: "sequence is not intended.

This is because, for example, there is a difference in results—such as spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*), heaven, and long life—for the *saurya*, *āryamaṇa*, and *prājāpatya* sacrificial oblations (*caru*).

The sense is that, just as there is no requirement for a sequential order between the systems of medicine and erotics because their objects of inquiry differ, so too there is no requirement for a sequential order between the two Mīmāṃsās.
In this regard, he explains the difference in their results with the words "abhyudaya" (prosperity).

That which arises by being directed toward sense-objects is "abhyudaya"—that is, pleasure dependent on sense-objects such as heaven and the like; and the meaning is that this is the result of the [Pūrva] Mīmāṃsā, which has the knowledge of Dharma as its purpose.
He states that "that" [result]—not only is there a difference in the nature of the fruit, but also in its cause—by saying "tacceti.
He further states that the fruit of the inquiry (mīmāṃsā), which is the cause for the knowledge of Brahman, is contrary to that [other inquiry], by saying "niḥśreyaseti.
The meaning is: "niḥśreyasam" is the eternal, independent good; it is liberation (mokṣa), and that is the fruit.
And he says "nor" (na ca) to show that the knowledge of Brahman does not require any performance other than its own arising;
the sense is that there is no combination (samuccaya) because of the difference in their nature, cause, and fruit.
He explains the difference in the objects of inquiry with the words "and [it is] that which is to be brought into being" (bhavyaśca).
"One who comes into being" is *bhavya*;
the meaning is "that which is to be accomplished. He states the reason for its being that which is to be accomplished with the word "not."
In that case, [one might object that it] would be a mere nothingness;
to this he says "no," namely: "because of the dependence on human activity.
This means: because its cause is that whose essence is human effort (prayatna).

The meaning is that because [dharma] is to be accomplished through human effort (*kṛti-sādhyatvāt*), dharma does not exist at the time of the knowledge that generates that effort; it is not due to its being non-existent in an absolute sense (*tucchatvāt*).
He states the distinction of Brahman from dharma with the words "But here," which means "in the Uttara-mīmāṃsā."
That which has come into being is incurable.
The reason for this is "because it is eternal," meaning because it exists at all times.

Having stated the difference in essential nature between *dharma* and *brahman* by way of their being something to be accomplished (*sādhya*) and not something to be accomplished (*asādhya*), he states the difference also by way of the cause (*hetu*) with the word "not.
The meaning is that [Brahman] is not dependent on human action (*kṛti*) like *dharma*.
He also states the difference by way of the means of knowledge (*māna*) with the word "injunction" (*codanā*).
In this context, "codanā" refers to a statement that makes known what was previously unknown.
Its "activity" consists in its capacity to produce cognition; and because of its difference from that [other means of knowledge], there is a difference in the object of inquiry—this is the meaning.
He explains the summary statement with the words: "For that which... and so forth.

The definition of a means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) is as follows: a statement such as "One desiring heaven should sacrifice" (*svargakāmo yajeta*) informs a person only by impelling them toward their own object—namely, *dharma*, which consists of an efficient force (*bhāvanā*) having sacrifice and the like as its instrument and heaven and the like as its fruit, or toward the injunction (*niyoga) regarding the sacrifice and so forth which are the cause of that fruit, or toward the sacrifice and so forth which are the means to one's welfare.

On the other hand, [statements] such as "This Self is Brahman" (*ayam ātmā brahma*) inform only the meaning of "Thou" (*tvaṃ*), namely Brahman alone which is devoid of phenomenal expansion (*aprapañca*); they do not impel [one to action], because there is no [action-oriented] object [to be engaged in]. This is the meaning.
[Objection: But surely the object [of the Veda] is indeed comprehension; to this he replies: "not the person.
He states the reason why the person does not engage in comprehension through the injunction regarding Brahman in the preceding sentence: "of comprehension...
He provides an illustration for the point that a thing itself, as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), is not an instigator toward the knowledge produced by itself: "just as..."

Since understanding arises from the mere [hearing of] the statement, and since an injunction is inapplicable once [understanding] has arisen, there is no human activity directed toward the knowledge of the sentence-meaning.

And thus, since there is a difference between the objects of inquiry— dharma being the object of a means of knowledge that impels action, and Brahman being the object of a means of knowledge that is indifferent [to action]— the two differ.
The point is that the word *atha* does not serve the purpose of indicating a sequence for those two [Mīmāṃsās].

Thus, since no other meaning for the word *atha* is possible, and given that it expresses immediate succession (*ānantarya*), one must state the sufficient cause as its limit; with this in mind, he says "therefore" (*tasmāt*).
It is taught.
The word "sūtrakṛtā" (by the author of the Sūtras) is to be supplied as the remainder. To the question "What is that?", he says: "It is stated.
That the validity of discernment (*viveka*) and so forth is established by scripture has already been explained previously.

*Śama* is the cessation of the mind from worldly activities; *dama* is the cessation of the external organs; *uparati* is the renunciation of obligatory and other prescribed rites for the sake of knowledge;
and *titikṣā* is the endurance of the pairs of opposites, such as cold and heat.
The stabilization of the mind through the abandonment of sleep, laziness, and negligence is *samādhi*.
Faith is the state of being convinced of everything.
The attainment of these six factors constitutes the perfection of tranquility and the other qualities.
In this context, it should be understood that discrimination (*viveka*) and the other qualities serve as qualifications for the seeker (*adhikārin*) by virtue of being successive causes.

He states that these are the causes for the desire to know Brahman (*brahmajijñāsā*) through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) with the words "in those" (*teṣu*). Even for one who engages in the inquiry into Brahman out of mere curiosity, the knowledge of it does not arise until the attainment of the fruit; thus, the establishment of negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) is secured.
He concludes the explanation of the word *atha* with the words "Therefore" (*tasmāt*).
Now, it may be objected that the aforementioned discrimination (*viveka*) and other means are not possible,

because the fruit of action is eternal according to such scriptural passages as, "The merit of one who performs the Cāturmāsya sacrifices is indeed imperishable," and thus detachment (*vairāgya*) cannot be established from that [action].

The liberation of the individual soul (jīva) as having the nature of Brahman is untenable, because of their difference and because, like a clod of earth or similar objects, such liberation would not constitute the goal of human endeavor (puruṣārtha). Consequently, the desire for liberation (mumukṣā) would be impossible. To resolve this objection, the word "ataḥ" (therefore) is used; he explains that word as follows: "the word 'ataḥ'."

The word *atha* (then), signifying immediate succession, implies by its very meaning that the fourfold set beginning with discrimination (*viveka*) constitutes the cause for the desire to know Brahman (*brahmajijñāsā*). The word *ataḥ* (hence) is a restatement intended to refute any objection regarding this implied causality;
such is the meaning. He explains what was stated [by the word *atha*] with the words "because" (*yasmāt*).

The word "therefore" (tasmāt) is to be connected with what follows. The scriptural passage beginning with "Just as here... (*tadyatheha...*) is supported by the logical principles that "whatever is small is mortal" and "whatever is created is impermanent"; thus, it sublates the scriptural statement regarding the inexhaustibility of the fruits of action.

Therefore, the sense is that detachment (*vairāgya*) is attained through the discernment (*viveka*) of the impermanence of everything other than the Self, based on the scriptural text: "Other than this, everything is afflicted" (*ato 'nyadārtam*).
He fosters the desire for liberation with the word "tathā" (so).

The meaning is that just as the Veda demonstrates the impermanence of the fruits of ritual action, so too does it demonstrate the boundless, self-luminous bliss from which the wind of sorrow has been stilled, arising from the knowledge of Brahman.
The intention is that by the mention of superimposition (*adhyāsa*) upon [the self] as being a living being and so forth, the possibility of its being Brahman has indeed been stated.

Thus, since the qualified seeker who possesses the full set of causal conditions has been established by the words "atha" and "ataḥ," he says "tasmāt" (therefore) to indicate that the scripture should be commenced.

For the purpose of completing the sentence of the aphorism and for the purpose of connecting it with the supplied word "kartavyā" (to be performed), he shows the meaning of the individual components by stating his own preferred compound, while using the term "brahmajijñāsā" to indicate the inquiry (*vicāra*) through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*). [He begins: "Of Brahman..."
Thus [it is said].
Now, one might object: why could there not be a dative compound (caturthī-samāsa) such as *brahmaṇe jijñāsā*, just as in the case of *dharmāya jijñāsā*?
To this it is replied: for the primary meaning of the word *jijñāsā* is "desire" (*icchā*).
For that [action], the object (karman) as its primary factor is required first, and the result (phala) afterwards;
therefore, at the outset, a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*) is appropriate for the sake of understanding the object.
When the object has been stated, the result is stated by implication.
Because the fruit belongs to the object of desire itself;
just as when it is said "the desire for heaven," heaven acquires the status of being the fruit, so it is here.

For this very reason, in the case of "inquiry into dharma" (*dharmajijñāsā*) as well, a genitive compound is shown by taking "desire" (*icchā*) [as the final member], according to the rule: "for that is the desire to know it."

However, since investigation (*vicāra*)—which is characterized by deliberation—is of the nature of a mental affliction (*kleśa*), there is an initial desire for its fruit; thus, the fourth type of compound (*caturthī-samāsa*) was stated as "the desire to know for the sake of Dharma" (*dharmāya jijñāsā*).
Likewise, if the Commentator (*vṛttikāra*) had said "the desire to know Brahman" (*brahmaṇe jijñāsā*), let that be so, because Brahman is the fruit by virtue of being knowledge (*jñāna*).
Now, he states the meaning of the word *brahman*: "And Brahman... (*brahma ca*).

An objection is raised: "In Vedic texts such as, 'This [world] is Brahman and Kṣatra; Brahman comes forth; Brahman is the Self-existent (Svayambhū); Brahman is Prajāpati,' and in common usage as well, the word *brahman* is employed for the caste of Brāhmaṇas, for the individual soul (*jīva*), for the Veda, and for the lotus-seated deity (Brahmā). To this, he says: "For this very reason. The meaning is: precisely because [otherwise] there would arise the consequence of inconsistency with the sūtras that establish the definition of being the cause of the world.
He refutes the statement in another commentary that "the sixth case [is used] in the sense of the remainder (śeṣa)" by saying "of Brahman" (brahmaṇa iti).
The "remainder" refers to a general relation.
In the word *jijñāsā*, knowledge is the object (*karman*) of the desire expressed by the suffix *-san*.

Brahman is the object (*karman*) of that knowledge; for in that case, since an action accompanied by an object cannot be known without knowledge of the object, and because desire is produced by the knowledge of its object, the object itself—which is required first—is what must be expressed by the genitive case, not the "remainder" (*śeṣa*). This is the meaning.

[Objection: "But surely the means of knowledge (pramāṇa) and so forth are something else entirely; let them be the object of action (karman), while Brahman is connected as the primary beneficiary (śeṣin). To this he replies: "By [the phrase] 'another object of inquiry' (jijñāsyāntara).
The sense is that by abandoning the action mentioned in the scripture and postulating another that is not heard there, one follows the maxim: "Casting away the morsel of food, he licks his hand.
With a hidden intention, the objection is raised: "But surely... (nanu).

The meaning is that because of the rule "the genitive is used in the sense of the remainder" (*ṣaṣṭhī śeṣe*), although the genitive merely indicates a general relationship, it results in the status of being an object (*karman*) when there is a requirement for a specific relation due to the proximity of a transitive action.
As if not understanding this intention, he states the reply: "Even so... (*evam api*).

The meaning is that even though the status of being an object (*karmatva*) is directly evident through the rule "kartṛkarmaṇoḥ kṛti" (Pāṇini 2.3.65)— which prescribes such a status when there is a connection with a word ending in a *kṛt* suffix, as the word *jijñāsā* ends in the suffix *ākāra*— the proponent of the "remainder" (*śeṣavādī*) abandons that objecthood, which is required first, and instead postulates an indirect, non-verbal [objecthood].
The proponent of the "remainder" reveals his own intention by saying, "It is not useless."
By means of the residual genitive case, the desire to know (jijñāsā) related to Brahman is proposed.
In that context, the investigation of those things dependent upon Brahman—namely, its definition, means of knowledge, reasoning, knowledge, means of attainment, and results—is also proposed;
for even that desire to know is related to Brahman, since it exists for the purpose of knowing Brahman.

However, with the intention that the investigation would be established as having Brahman alone as its object if the genitive were taken in the sense of the *karman* (object), it is stated that the genitive is used in the sense of the *śeṣa* (remainder).
Therefore, my effort is not in vain;
the meaning is that it possesses as its purpose and fruit the promise of an investigation into Brahman and everything related to it.

The proponent of the established conclusion (siddhāntin) states that this fruit of your effort is not appropriate, because when the investigation of Brahman— the primary subject— is formally proposed by the Sūtra, the investigation of its auxiliary elements is already implied by that proposal. He explains the meaning summarized in the phrase "not [the investigation of] the Pradhāna," etc.,
by providing an illustration with the words beginning with "Brahman indeed," and so forth.

And because it conforms to the root scripture, "Desire to know that" (*tadvijijñāsasva*), he states that the genitive case is used in the sense of the object (*karmaṇi ṣaṣṭhī*)—namely, "and because of conformity with scripture" (*śrutyanugamācca*).
This means that one attains the fact that the scripture and the sūtra have the same meaning.
He explains the etymological meaning of the word *jijñāsā* as "to know" (*jñātum*).
Now, since desire is not observed toward an object that has not been cognized, it must be said that the knowledge of the object is the root of that desire.
But since the knowledge of Brahman is itself the fruit of the desire to know (jijñāsā), how can it be its root? Anticipating this objection, he says: "By cognition... (avagatyā).

The object of the desire to know (*jijñāsā*) and its fruit is that very knowledge consisting of an undivided direct realization (*akhaṇḍa-sākṣātkāra-vṛtti-jñāna*), which has as its ultimate limit consciousness manifested in the form of the cessation of veils (*āvaraṇa-nivṛtti-rūpa-ābhivyakti-mat-caitanya*).

However, it will be stated now that the "root" is initial, superficial knowledge (*āpātajñāna*); thus, because there is a distinction between the knowledge that is the fruit and the knowledge that is the root, the desire to know is not untenable—this is the meaning.

Now, one might object: "The village is the object (*karman*) of the act of going, and its attainment is the fruit (*phala*); since there is thus a distinction between them, how can it be said that the object itself is the fruit? To this, he says: "As for the fruit... The meaning is that although these two are distinct with respect to other actions, because desire has the fruit as its object, the object itself is the fruit.
Now, one might object that since knowledge (*jñāna*) and realization (*avagati*) are identical, the statement regarding their distinction is improper; to this, he says: "by knowledge" (*jñānena*).
The meaning is that there is a distinction in that knowledge is the mental modification (*vṛtti*), while realization is its fruit. [The word] "to realize" (*avagantum*) means to manifest.
He clarifies that realization is the fruit [of the inquiry] with the word "Brahman.
He states the reason expressed by the particle "hi" (for) with the words "niḥśeṣa... (without remainder).
The meaning is: because it destroys that misfortune which has ignorance as its seed and source.
Having explained the meaning of the individual words, he states the meaning of the sentence of the Sūtra with the words "Therefore" (*tasmāt*).
Here, he indicates by means of the suffix *tavya* that the suffix *san* (in *vicārayitavya*) characterizes the act of inquiry (*vicāra*).

Since the qualification of the seeker has been established by the two words "Now" (*atha*) and "Therefore" (*ataḥ*), the meaning is that inquiry must be undertaken for the sake of the knowledge of Brahman.
Thus ends the third section.

In the first exposition (*varṇaka*), having stated that bondage is superimposed (*adhyasta*), there arises a doubt regarding the commencement of the scripture (*śāstrārambha*) based on whether the subject matter (*viṣaya*) and other requirements are possible or impossible, depending on whether Brahman is already known or unknown—even though the subject matter and so forth are generally established. He states the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*): "But that [Brahman]...
The word "but" (*punaḥ*) is intended to indicate a different exposition.
If the knowledge of Brahman were already present prior to the inquiry into the Vedānta, then it would lack the status of being a subject matter characterized by being unknown (*ajñātatva*).
One should not consider that, due to the absence of ignorance, there is also no fruit consisting of its cessation;
for if it were unknown to anyone, then an inquiry could not be undertaken with that as its objective, since it is impossible to have an objective that is unknown.

And likewise, since it is impossible to establish [the truth] for one who has not ascended to the realization of the Buddha through a treatise consisting of inquiry and through the Vedāntas, there is no relationship in the form of being the subject matter of those [texts]; consequently, because knowledge does not arise, the fruit also does not exist, and thus the treatise is not to be commenced—this is the meaning.

He establishes the conclusion that [the inquiry] ought to be commenced because the object and other factors are obtained through common consensus (*āpātaprasiddhi*), by means of the passage beginning with "It is said" (*ucyate*).
The meaning is: "it is indeed well-known. This is because the word "exists" (*asti*) refers to common consensus, since existence itself is not the subject under discussion (*aprakṛta*).
Now, by what means of knowledge (*māna*) is Brahman established?

Nor should it be said that this is established by the Śruti text, "Brahman is Truth, Knowledge, Infinite," because the word "Brahman" lacks a grasped conventional relation (*saṃgati*) in common worldly usage, and thus a sentence containing it would be non-communicative. Anticipating this objection, he states that through the etymological derivation (*vyutpatti*) of the word "Brahman," there is first the establishment of both the attributeless (*nirguṇa*) and the qualified (*saguṇa*) Brahman. [He says: "Of the word *brahman*..."

The word "hi" (for/indeed) has this meaning: it is known that there must be some referent [for the term *brahman*], because its usage in the revealed scripture (*śruti*) and the aphorisms (*sūtra*) would otherwise be inexplicable;
for one never observes the use of meaningless words within authoritative statements (*pramāṇavākya*).
And that object is determined by etymology to have the nature of greatness, because of the traditional rule (smaraṇa) that "the root *bṛh* means 'to increase'.
Furthermore, since there is no limiting factor, that increase is unlimited greatness.
Furthermore, it is understood from its usage together with the word "infinite" (*ananta*) in the scriptures that [the greatness] is unlimited;
for such boundless greatness is impossible if one possesses defects such as finitude or is devoid of qualities such as omniscience,
since in the world it is well known that those who lack qualities and possess defects are small.
Therefore, from the etymological derivation as "that which expands" (*bṛṃhaṇāt*), eternity—characterized by the absence of limitation in terms of space, time, and substance—is understood.
Purity (*śuddhatva*) is the state of being devoid of defects such as ignorance (*avidyā*).
Enlightenment (*buddhatva*) is the absence of insentience (*jāḍya*).
Even at the time of bondage, its state of being bound by itself and its state of liberation are perceived;
thus, it is well known to be devoid of all defects and free from qualities (*nirguṇa*).
Likewise, that which is denoted by the term "That" (*tatpadavācya*) is well known to possess attributes such as omniscience.

Because if there were a remainder of either the object of knowledge (*jñeya*) or the task to be accomplished (*kārya*), it would follow that they are few in number; consequently, one would attain only partial omniscience and the capacity for only limited action.

Having thus stated that the inquiry (*jijñāsā*) is justified because the term *tat* (That) is well-known yet lacks authority as it stands—being merely superficial and not removing ignorance—he further states that the inquiry is likewise justified by the selfhood of the term *tvam* (Thou), saying "of all": the meaning is that Brahman is well-known through its non-difference from this very Self (*ātman*) which belongs to every person in the world.
Now, as to the question "What is the well-known nature of the Self?", he says: "For everyone...
It is not that one does not realize "I am"; rather, one certainly does realize it.
This very realization is the well-known nature of the Self as Being-Consciousness-Bliss (saccidānanda); this is the meaning.
Anticipating the objection that the self cannot exist because it is empty, he says "yadi hi" (for if...).
If the self were empty, people would perceive it as "I am not"; however, the world perceives "I am. Therefore, the meaning is that the existence of the self is established.
He states what follows from the well-known status of the Self with respect to Brahman: "And the Self...
The intention is that this is based on such scriptural passages as, "This Self is Brahman.
He recalls the defect stated regarding the position of [Brahman's] being well-known by means of the prima facie argument: "If..."

The meaning is that because there is an absence of non-cognition (*ajñātatva*), there is an absence of an object and so forth, which results in the conclusion that [Brahman] is not something to be investigated.

Just as in the case of "this is silver," where there is in reality the well-known presence of mother-of-pearl, so too in the case of "I am," there is in reality the well-known presence of Brahman by virtue of the commonality of its nature as existence and consciousness;

however, this [cognition] does not have as its object the specific quality of being the Brahman of perfect bliss, for if it did, it would follow that there would be no dispute among proponents [of different views].

For when there is the perception of the specific quality of being a mother-of-pearl shell (*śuktitva*), no conflicting doubt (*vipratipatti*) arises as to whether it is silver, vermilion, or something else.

Therefore, by the principle that a conflicting doubt cannot otherwise be accounted for (*anyathānupapatti*), the author establishes the conclusion with the words beginning "no" (*na*) and so forth, that even though the object is generally known, its specific nature remains unknown, and thus the existence of the subject (*viṣayin*) and other factors is established.

It should be understood that the relationship between the universal (*sāmānya*) and the particular (*viśeṣa*) is conceptually constructed (*kalpita*) based on the distinctions expressed by such terms as "Being" (*sat*), "Consciousness" (*cit*), and "Fullness" (*pūrṇa*) within the Self itself.
Therein, he sets forth the various misconceptions in a sequence from gross to subtle, beginning with "the body alone" and so forth.

Having stated the views of those outside the Veda who are devoid of knowledge of the scriptures— namely, the common folk— he now states the view of the logicians and others, beginning with "it exists."
He states the Sāṃkhya view with the words "the enjoyer" (*bhoktā*).

Regarding the point of dispute as to whether the self (*ātman*) is of the nature of the body and so forth, or distinct from them—he first sets forth the positions of the body, senses, mind, intellect, and the void;

then, regarding the point of dispute as to whether that which is distinct from these also possesses agency (*kartṛtva*) and so forth, or not—he presents the two views of the Logicians (*Tārkika*) and the Sāṃkhyas; and finally, [he shows that] even if it is a non-agent, it is distinct from God (*Īśvara*).
He states the position of the Yogins as one of the points of contention, asking "or not," namely: "There exists a Lord distinct from that [aggregate].
Having grasped the state of being unsurpassed, the Yogins declare that the Lord is endowed with omniscience and other such qualities.
Having stated the position of difference, he states the position of the established doctrine (siddhānta): "That is the Self of the enjoyer."

The meaning is that the Vedāntins declare that the Lord is the very nature of the self (ātman) of the enjoyer—the individual soul (jīva)—who is a non-agent and a witness. He concludes the conflicting views with the words, "Thus, many [are the opinions].

The detailed exposition and refutation of these conflicting views have been demonstrated through the presentation of the *Vivaraṇa* for the sake of easy understanding; therefore, we shall desist here.

In this regard, the proponent's position relies on both reasoning and scripture: the individual soul (*jīva*) is indeed Brahman because it possesses selfhood (*ātmatva*), just like Brahman; for such reasoning exists, and there is the presence of uncontradicted scriptural authority such as "That thou art" (*tat tvam asi*).
Others, however, [assert] through fallacious reasoning such as: "The body and so forth are the self, because they are the object of the notion of 'I',
unlike a jar and so forth," which is the opposite case.
"This very person consists of food" (in the dialogue of the senses); "the eye and the others said to speech"; "the mind said";
"this which consists of consciousness";
"in the beginning, this was indeed non-existent."
The distinction is that they have relied upon fallacious statements such as "the agent, the knower, the non-eater, the other" and "it rules from within the self.
[Furthermore,] the body and so forth are not the self.
By such logical arguments as "because it is composed of the elements" and "because it is visible," [it is established that] "the one consisting of bliss [is Brahman], because of the repetition."
The fallacious nature [of these views] will be stated in such sūtras as those beginning with "ityādi.

Now, one might object: "Let there be these conflicting opinions; nevertheless, since a person will achieve their own goal by relying on whichever doctrine they have faith in, what is the use of commencing an inquiry into Brahman? To this, he says: "In that regard, without having investigated...
The actual state of things is that liberation arises solely from the knowledge of the identity of Brahman and the Self.
By resorting to other doctrines, liberation cannot be achieved because of the absence of that [true knowledge].

Furthermore, by knowing the Self otherwise, one would fall into the dark well of saṃsāra through that sin, according to the Vedic scripture: "Into blinding darkness enter those people who are slayers of the Self."
"What sin has not been committed by that thief who robs himself, who represents himself as one thing when he is actually another?"
This is the meaning of the statement "iti vacanāt.

Therefore, he concludes the meaning of the sūtra—"tasmāt"—by stating that for the sake of the fruit of supreme beatitude (*niḥśreyasa*), inquiry into the Vedānta must be undertaken by all seekers of liberation (*mumukṣu*).
This is because, since bondage is superimposed (*adhyasta*), there exists a subject matter (*viṣaya*) and so forth, and thus the topic has not already been established.

The meaning is that this inquiry, which has the Vedānta as its subject matter, is undertaken for the sake of the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*), because it possesses an eligible candidate (*adhikārin*), because its subject matter and so forth are established from beginning to end, and because it has as its instruments those reasonings not in conflict with the Vedānta that reside in other systems (*tantrāntara*).
Now, one might object: since there is no word denoting "inquiry" (*vicāra*) in the Sūtra, how can its commencement be the meaning of the Sūtra? To this, he says: "Brahman... [and so on].
The intention is that, by means of the expression of the desire for the knowledge of Brahman, [the Sūtra] indicates "inquiry" and then declares its necessity.
Thus, four meanings of the first Sūtra have been shown through the fourfold exposition.
And it is an ornament for a Sūtra to possess multiple meanings.
Now, does this Sūtra initiate the treatise while standing outside of it, or by being included within it?
In the first case, it would be something to be rejected,
because it lacks connection with the treatise.
In the second case, its producer must be stated;
yet it cannot be its own producer, because that would entail the fallacy of self-dependence (ātmāśraya), wherein something arises from itself.
"And we do not perceive any other commencement [of this treatise].
It is said in reply: This treatise, having been commenced according to the rule of hearing (śravaṇa), establishes its own commencement as being internal to the treatise itself.
Just as the rule of study (adhyayana-vidhi), though internal to the Veda, impels one toward the study of the entire Veda, so it is here; thus there is no fault. //1//

Section on "Birth and so forth" (Janmādyadhikaraṇa). Sūtra 2.
It has been stated that Brahman is to be desired for inquiry.
But what is the characteristic of that Brahman? To this, the venerable author of the Sūtras says:
"From which [proceed] the birth and so forth of this [world]. (BS 1.1.2)
"Janmotpatti" (birth and origination) is its beginning; this is a *bahuvrīhi* compound where the qualities [of the members] are included in the meaning (*tadguṇasaṃvijñāna*).
"Birth, subsistence, and destruction" is the meaning of the compound.
Furthermore, the status of birth as the beginning is both in reference to the scriptural teaching and in reference to the actual nature of things.

First, as for the scriptural teaching: in the statement, "From which indeed these beings are born" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 3.1), there is an observation of the sequence of birth, subsistence, and dissolution;
and this is also the actual state of things.
Since the subsistence of a substratum (dharmin) that has acquired its existence through birth is possible,
the word "asya" (of this) is a designation by means of the pronoun *idam* for the substratum presented by perception and other means of knowledge.
The genitive case is intended to express the relationship between the substratum and its properties, such as birth and so forth.

The phrase "from which" (*yataḥ*) is an indication of the cause. The remainder of the sentence is: that from which—being omniscient and omnipotent—the origin, sustenance, and dissolution of this world occurs; a world that is differentiated by name and form, joined with many agents and enjoyers, which is the locus of actions and their fruits determined by specific places, times, and causes, and whose structure is inconceivable even by the mind—that is Brahman.
Since other modifications of existence (*bhāvavikāra*) are also included within these three, birth, subsistence, and destruction are what are grasped here.

However, if one were to take the [six] enumerated by Yāska—beginning with "is born," "exists," and so on—then because those occur during the period of the world's subsistence, the origin, subsistence, and destruction of the world from its primal cause would not be grasped.
To prevent such a doubt, it is held that the very birth which is Brahman is itself its subsistence and its dissolution; thus, those [three] alone are what are grasped.

It is not possible to conceive of the origin and so forth of the world— characterized as described above— from anything other than Īśvara, who is characterized as described above; nor from the Pradhāna, nor from insentient atoms, nor from non-existence, nor from a transmigrating soul (saṃsārin),
nor from inherent nature (svabhāva), because specific places, times, and causes are here accepted as the basis [for its production].
The proponents of God as the cause (Īśvarakāraṇins) consider this very inference to be the proof for the existence of a Lord distinct from transmigrating beings and so forth.
[Objection: But has not that same [inference] been presented here as well in the Sūtra on "Birth and so forth" (Janmādi-sūtra)? [Reply: No;
because the purpose of the Sūtras is to string together the flowers of the Vedānta passages.
For it is the Vedānta passages that are cited by the Sūtras and subjected to inquiry. This inquiry culminates in the ascertainment of the meaning of those passages.

However, since there exist Vedānta passages that declare the cause of the world's origin and so forth, inference—provided it does not contradict the Vedānta passages—is not precluded from being a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) for the purpose of strengthening the grasp of their meaning.
Furthermore, reasoning (*tarka*) is accepted as an auxiliary to scripture (*śruti*);

for instance, the scripture states, "It is to be heard and it is to be reflected upon" (*Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad* 2.4.5), and, "Just as a learned and intelligent man, having been taught the way, would reach Gandhāra itself, even so does a person who has a teacher know [the Self]" (*Chāndogya Upaniṣad* 6.14.2).
And thus, [the author] indicates that the inquiry into Brahman requires the assistance of human intelligence.

Unlike the inquiry into Dharma, where scripture (*śruti*) and so forth, as well as experience (*anubhava*) and so forth, serve as means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) according to their respective applicability, here they do not; for the knowledge of Brahman culminates in direct experience and has an already existent reality as its object. Indeed, regarding an object that is to be accomplished (*kartavya*), there is no dependence on direct experience, and thus scripture and the like alone would possess authority, since what is to be accomplished depends upon the person [for its realization].
Worldly and Vedic action can be performed, not performed, or performed otherwise,
just as one may travel by horse, on foot, or in some other way.
Or it does not go;
likewise, "One takes the *ṣoḍaśin* cup at the *atirātra*, one does not take the *ṣoḍaśin* cup at the *atirātra*."
Furthermore, injunctions and prohibitions such as "one offers after sunrise" and "one offers before sunrise," as well as options, general rules, and exceptions, would be meaningful in this context.
But the thing itself is not conceptualized as "it is thus," "it is not thus," or "it does not exist";
rather, conceptualizations depend upon human intellect.
Knowledge of the true nature of a thing does not depend upon human intellect.
Rather, that [cognition] depends solely on the actual state of things (vastutantra).
For regarding a single post, the cognition "it is a post" or "it is a man or something else" does not constitute knowledge of reality;
therein, "it is a man or something else" is false cognition.
The knowledge of reality is "this is indeed a post," because it is dependent upon the object itself.
Likewise, the validity of cognitions whose objects are real entities is dependent upon those entities.
This being so, even the knowledge of Brahman is dependent solely upon the reality itself, because its object is an existing entity (*bhūtavastu*).

[Objection: But if Brahman is an existing entity, it must necessarily be the object of other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*); thus, the investigation of the Vedānta texts would become useless. [Reply: No.
Because there is no apprehension of a connection due to [Brahman] not being an object of the senses;
by their very nature, the senses have [empirical] objects as their domain, not Brahman as their domain.
For if Brahman were indeed an object of the senses,
this effect would be perceived as being connected with Brahman;
however, when only the effect is perceived, it is impossible to determine whether it is connected with Brahman or connected with some other thing.
Therefore, the Sūtra beginning with "birth" (janmādi) is not intended to present an inference; rather, it is for the purpose of pointing out a Vedānta passage.
But what is that Vedānta passage which the Sūtra here intends to indicate?
"Bhṛgu, the son of Varuṇa, approached his father Varuṇa and said:
'Teach me, venerable sir, the Brahman.'"
Having begun thus: "That from which indeed these beings are born; by which, once born, they live; and into which they enter when they pass away."
"Seek to understand that;
that is Brahman. (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 3.1)
And its definitive statement is: "Verily, from bliss alone these beings are born; by bliss, once born, they live; into bliss they enter at their passing."

Other similar passages of this kind, which have as their subject matter the Cause whose nature is eternally pure, conscious, free, and omniscient, should also be cited. // 2 // Having established the commencement of the scripture by means of the first sūtra, the author, now beginning the scripture, recounts what has preceded in order to state the connection between the preceding and succeeding sections: "Brahman," etc. [The text continues: "It created all this, whatever exists here"—this is direct perception. [End of Note]
It has been stated that one who desires liberation must engage in the inquiry into the Vedānta for the sake of the knowledge of Brahman.

Although, by stating that Brahman is the object of inquiry, the inquiries into the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and so forth are implicitly promised, since these cannot be carried out without first knowing the means of valid cognition for Brahman, its definition (*lakṣaṇa*) must be stated at the outset in order to know its essential nature.
Having raised the objection that this is not possible, the author of the Sūtras honors the Sūtra itself by determining its definition—asking, "What is its characteristic?
The word "what" (*kim*) is used in the sense of an objection;
the meaning is that there is no characteristic at all.
Because it arises by way of an objection (*ākṣepa*), there is a connection by way of objection.

Since the Vedānta texts—which reveal the definition [of Brahman] and possess clear marks of Brahman—are stated to be in harmony (*samanvaya*) with respect to the defined object, Brahman, there is a connection with the Śruti, the Śāstra, the Book (*adhyāya*), and the Section (*pāda*).
To illustrate: the passage beginning with "From which indeed these beings are born" is the subject matter (*viṣaya*).
Thus, the doubt arises as to whether Brahman has a defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) or not.

In this regard, the distinction is that under the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), the non-attainment of liberation results from the failure to establish the true nature of Brahman, whereas under the final conclusion (*siddhānta*), its attainment results from its establishment.

Although, in the case of a contextual connection by way of objection (*ākṣepasaṃgati*), the result of the preceding section may be taken as the result here and need not be stated separately; [nevertheless, it is stated].

As it has been said: "In the case of an objection (*ākṣepa*), a refutation (*apavāda*), a primary meaning (*mukhya*), a secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*), an action (*karma*), and that which proceeds after having performed [something else]—the purpose (*prayojana*) need not be stated.
Nevertheless, it should be understood that it was stated for the sake of clarity.

Where the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*) is established by means of the principle of a settled conclusion from a previous section (*pūrvādhikaraṇasiddhānta*), there the connection is one of exception (*apavādikī*). The inquiry has that [exception] as its purpose.

In that regard, the prima facie view is that [the definition does not apply], because birth and so forth, being attributes of the world, are unfit to be the defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) of Brahman.
Nor should it be said that being both the material cause (*upādāna*) and the agent (*kartṛ*) of the world constitutes the defining characteristic [of Brahman];
for if the agent were also the material cause, inference could not function due to the absence of an illustrative example (*dṛṣṭānta*).
Nor should it be argued that since the scriptural Brahman has its defining characteristic established by scripture itself, what is the use of inference? [To this we reply:]...
