Since inference serves as a support for scripture, in its absence or in case of its contradiction, the meaning of scripture cannot be established.
Nor should it be argued that either being the agent of the world or being the material cause is individually the defining characteristic [of Brahman];
for a mere agent who is distinct from the material cause cannot be Brahman.

Since it follows [from your position] that [knowledge] arises from actual perception, and since inference— which consists merely of human conjecture— is unstable and lacks independence regarding supersensuous objects, it is possible to establish the dual causality taught in the faultless Śruti as being non-human (apauruṣeya) by means of the analogy of pleasure and so forth.
He establishes that very definition with the aphorism: "From which [proceeds] the birth, etc., of this [world].

Although here the definition is presented as the causality of the world's birth, maintenance, and dissolution, it will be explained later in the section beginning with "And the non-material cause" (*aprakṛtiśca*) that this causality is not merely that of an agent, but rather consists of both the nature of being an agent and the nature of being the material cause (*upādānatva*).
Since the definition is stated by taking the dual causality as an established fact, there is no tautology.

Now, it may be asked: how can the causality of the qualityless Brahman—which is the object of inquiry—be its definition? It is said in reply: just as silver is the definition of mother-of-pearl in the sense that "that which is silver is mother-of-pearl," so too is Brahman defined as "that which is the cause of the world" based on a conceptual construction (*kalpita*).
Thus, it is faultless that the nature of being the cause, existing as a peripheral characteristic (*taṭastha-lakṣaṇa*), is indeed the defining mark of Brahman.
He explains the Sūtra with the words beginning with "birth" (*janma*).
In a *bahuvrīhi* compound, all the word-meanings are qualifiers of the sentence-meaning, which is the meaning of the other member (*anyapadārtha*).

Just as in the case of Devadatta who has brindled cows (*citragu*), where the brindled cows are the qualifier, so too here, "birth" is the qualifier of the aggregate (*samāhāra*) indicated by the neuter singular [ending]—namely, the aggregate of birth, subsistence, and dissolution.

And thus, the meaning is that a *bahuvrīhi* compound in which the subordinate part of the summarized meaning (*samāsārthaikadeśa*)— in this case, "birth"— is understood as a qualifying attribute (*tadguṇasaṃvijñāna*) is called a *tadguṇasaṃvijñāna*.

In that context, it is improper to prescribe Brahman-hood for that which is the cause of birth, because Brahman-hood cannot be known if [the cause of birth] is perceived as distinct from the causes of maintenance and dissolution.

Therefore, it should be understood that the sūtra indicates a collective whole (samāhāra) because it considers the three causalities—defined by birth, subsistence, and dissolution—together as the defining characteristic (lakṣaṇa).
Now, one might ask: how is the primacy of birth to be known, given that saṃsāra is beginningless? To this, he says: "And of birth... [janmanaśca].

The meaning is that, having understood from the root scripture (*mūlaśruti*) and from the nature of things (*vastugati*) that [Brahman] is the beginning, the author of the Sūtras spoke of the "origin" (*janman*) in relation to that [beginning].
Anticipating the objection that the word *idam* (this) denotes only perceptible objects, he states that it refers to all effects that are present: "of this" (*asya*).
Since the world, beginning with ether (*viyat*), is eternal, there would be no connection with "origin" and so forth; to this he replies: "the genitive" (*ṣaṣṭhī*).
The intention is that the connection of the great elements, such as the objects of the senses, with birth and so forth will be explained.

Now, one might object that since the world’s birth and so forth lack a connection to Brahman, they cannot serve as its defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*). Anticipating this doubt, he states the meaning of the ablative case—“from which”—to show that being the cause of that [world] is indeed the defining characteristic.
By the word *yat* (which), the reality whose nature is bliss, infinite, and consisting of knowledge is denoted, because it has been determined [in scripture] by the words, “Verily, from bliss alone.”
And thus, it should be understood that the definition by intrinsic nature (*svarūpalakṣaṇa*) is established.

Having stated the meaning of the word (*padārtha*), he explains the meaning of the sentence of the Sūtra—by supplying the word "that" (*tat*) and by connecting it with the word "Brahman" from the preceding Sūtra—starting with the words "of this," etc.
The specific qualities of the world serve to establish the possibility of the Cause possessing attributes such as omniscience.

Just as a potter first conceives in his mind the form of a pot—its broad base, belly, and so on—as something undifferentiated from the word "pot," and then differentiates it by that very nature, manifesting it externally;
in the same way, it is inferred that the Supreme Cause also differentiates itself by means of its own intended name and form. Thinking this, he says: "by name and form" (*nāmarūpābhyām*).
Here, the instrumental case (*tṛtīyā*) is used in the sense of "being in such a manner."
The first effect is produced by a conscious agent, because it is an effect, like a jar; thus, Primordial Matter (pradhāna) and the Void (śūnya) are refuted.
He refutes the notion that [the world] is produced by individual souls (jīvas) such as Hiraṇyagarbha and others with the word "aneka" (many).

In rites such as the Śrāddha and the Vaiśvānareṣṭi, there is a separate mention because of the distinction between the agent and the enjoyer in the case of the father and son. Furthermore, according to the scriptural texts, "He who first creates Brahmā" and "All these emerge from the Self," individual souls—by way of the limiting adjuncts (upādhis) of the gross and subtle bodies—are effects; therefore, since they fall within the world itself, [the world cannot be produced by them].
It establishes the omniscience of the cause with the words "pratiniyata-":
the meaning is that it refers to the substratum of those actions and their fruits which have specific, fixed locations, times, and causes.
For instance, the summit of Mount Meru is the location for the fruit of action that is heaven.
After the fall of the body, the time [of death] is determined by such causes as dying during the northern solstice (*uttarāyaṇa*).
In this way, the specific locations such as villages and regions for the fruits of royal service are to be understood.
And just as the fruit of service is given by one who knows the [proper] regions and so forth, so too is the fruit of karma.
The sense is that the attainment of omniscience follows from [the fact that He] is the fruit [of meditation]. He establishes His omnipotence with the words "even by mind.

Now, one might object: since there are other modifications of being, such as growth and transformation, why are they not included under the phrase "birth and so forth"? To this he replies: "Of others... [and so on].
The meaning is that increase and transformation are included within birth, while decrease is included within destruction.
Now, it may be argued that the body is born,
exists, [and so forth].
It increases, it transforms, and it diminishes.
One might ask: "Could this statement of the sage Yāska, 'it perishes,' not be the source for this Sūtra? To this, he says: "Yāska...

It is said that the sage Yāska, while the great elements were in their state of persistence after having arisen, observed the sixfold process beginning with birth (*janma*) in material objects through direct perception and composed his *Nirukta* statement. If one were to take that as the basis and hold that the meaning of the Sūtra is the definition of Brahman as the cause of the sixfold process beginning with birth, then the author of the Sūtra [would have failed to provide] the definition of Brahman.

The meaning is this: lest there arise the suspicion that [the birth and so forth] are not included [in the Sūtra] but rather that the characteristics of the great elements (mahābhūtas) have been stated, [the author] intends to show that those very things—birth and so forth—which are mentioned in the Śruti are what are being taken up.

If even the etymological explanation (nirukta) has the Śruti as its source, and if the meaning of "birth and so forth" refers to the birth and so forth of the great elements, then let that very Śruti be the source for the Sūtra.
The sense is: "What is the use of this superfluous etymological explanation (*nirukta*)?
If there were a cause of the world other than Brahman, then the definition of Brahman would suffer from defects such as over-extension (*ativyāpti*);
therefore, in order to exclude that possibility, the Sūtra on the definition [states] that the origination and so forth of the world are not possible without Brahman.
The logical reason "because other causes are impossible" has been stated in brief;
it will be explained in detail in the Tarkapāda. Now, he demonstrates it concisely with the words beginning "not as stated," and so forth.

In the course of explaining the four qualifiers of the world—beginning with "determined by name and form" (*nāmarūpābhyāṃ vyākṛta*)—the refutation of Primordial Matter (*pradhāna*), the Void (*śūnya*), and the transmigrating soul (*saṃsārin*) was demonstrated.

This is because it is impossible for insentient atoms to act spontaneously; and because, since there is no proof of an omniscient Lord (*sarvajñeśvara*)—as there is no evidence for a creator other than the individual soul (*jīva*) due to the rule that everything else is devoid of knowledge—those [atoms] would lack a director.
The sense is that it is impossible for [Prakṛti] to be the originator of the world.
Regarding the Lokāyata view that the world is diverse by its very nature, he says "and not" (na ca);
the syntactical connection is that it is impossible to conceive of the origination and so forth of the world [from such a cause].
Does "being its own cause" mean that it is its own intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), or that it is independent of causes?
It cannot be the first, because that would entail the fallacy of self-dependence (*ātmāśraya*).
It cannot be the second; thus he says: "because of being qualified," and so forth.

The meaning is that specific and uncommon factors—namely place, time, and causal conditions—are employed by those seeking an effect; therefore, it is not logical for an effect to be independent of its causes.

The implication is that if there were such independence, those seeking grain would not engage in activity regarding specific plots of land, at times such as the rainy season, or with causal factors such as seeds.

The commentary states that the creation and so forth of the world are impossible apart from a Lord characterized by the previously mentioned attributes such as omniscience; thus, it expresses the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) that "there is no effect without a creator. By this, the universal pervasion (*vyāpti*)—that whatever is an effect has a creator—is known. The author introduces the misconception of the logicians (*tārkika*) who claim: "This very knowledge of pervasion, while establishing a creator within the subject (*pakṣa*) of the world, establishes an omniscient Lord; what need is there for scripture? This is expressed in the words: "etadeva... (this very [knowledge]).
The construction is as follows: they believe that this very [knowledge] is the means of proof (sādhana) through inference alone, and not through scripture (śruti).
Alternatively, the meaning is: they believe that this very knowledge of pervasion (vyāpti), being accepted by us merely as a reasoning that supports scripture, is an independent inference (anumāna).
The word "etc. (ādi) refers to omniscience (sarvajñatva) and so forth.
Alternatively, the meaning is that they consider this very definition, when conjoined with the cognition of pervasion (*vyāpti*), to be inference as an independent means of knowledge.
In that regard, the distinction is as follows: from the cognition of pervasion, the existence of a creator of the world is established;
subsequently, that creator—
He is omniscient because he is the cause of the world;
by contrast, like a potter and others— thus, the proof of his omniscience is established through his defining characteristic.
In this context, by the phrase "they think," the fallacious nature of the inference is indicated.

For instance, first of all, a living being (*jīva*) cannot be the agent of a sprout and so forth, because there is a certainty of negative concomitance (*vyatireka-niścaya*)—namely, that anything distinct from a living being is necessarily insentient like a jar, and thus no other agent exists;
consequently, the knowledge of the pervasion (*vyāpti*) that "whatever is an effect has an agent" is not established.
However, in the case of inference based on characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) and marks (*liṅga*), there is a sublation (*bādha*); for it is impossible for one who is bodiless to possess knowledge of birth.

Since the pervasion (*vyāpti*) that "whatever is knowledge is produced by the mind" contradicts this, eternal knowledge cannot be established; rather, there is a certainty of the absence of such knowledge.
Therefore, regarding supersensible objects (*atīndriyārtha*), scripture alone is the refuge.
The sense is that inference is merely a logical argument (yukti) intended to establish the possibility of the meaning of the scripture; it is not independent.

An opponent—the Vaiśeṣika—objects: "But this is incorrect," for, intending the inclusion of scripture within inference, your own author of the Sūtras should have presented only inference. Thus, the objection begins with "nanu.
The implication is that the statement regarding inference being a fallacy (in the phrase "ato manyante") is improper.

If the Vedas did not possess independent authority, then the author of the Sūtras would not have investigated their purport through such [sūtras] as "But that [Brahman is known] from the harmony [of the texts]" (1.1.4).

Therefore, since the subsequent sūtras are for the purpose of investigating the Vedas, it is established—even in the sūtra concerning "origination and so forth" (1.1.2)—that it is the Veda alone that is investigated independently, and not inference; thus he refutes [the objection] with "No. Furthermore, the comprehension of Brahman is desired by one seeking liberation, for the sake of which this treatise is commenced.
And that [knowledge] does not arise from inference,
because of the scriptural text, "But him, who is to be known through the Upaniṣads.
Therefore, he says "vākyārtha" (the meaning of the sentence) to indicate that inference is not to be investigated.

The meaning is that the realization of Brahman—which arises from the ascertainment [of truth] through the investigation of the sentence and its meaning, namely the determination of its purport (*tātparya*) and the ascertainment of the possibility of the object of knowledge (*prameya*)—leads to liberation.
"Possibility" (*saṃbhava*) means the absence of sublation (*bādhābhāva*).
Now, does he mean that inference is entirely disregarded? He says: "But when [the means of knowledge] exist... and so forth.

The subject of dispute has non-different material and instrumental causes, because it is an effect, like the threads and so forth produced by a spider; and the subject of dispute has a conscious nature as its material cause.
The meaning is that the inference— "because it is an effect, like pleasure and so forth"— is required for the firm establishment of the meaning of the scripture.
Firmness (*dārḍhya*) means the cessation of doubt and error.
The meaning of the scriptural statement "it is to be reflected upon" (mantavyaḥ) is that the meaning heard [from scripture] is to be rendered probable through reasoning.

For example, suppose a certain person from the Gandhāra region were abandoned by thieves in another forest with his eyes still bound; then, once released from those bonds, a wise man—capable of following the path described [to him], himself skilled in reasoning and endowed with intelligence—would reach his own country. In exactly the same way, here in this forest, one who has been led away from the bliss of his own true nature by ignorance, desire, and so forth, [reaches it through reflection].
"Though cast into saṃsāra by some teacher overcome with compassion, you are not a transmigrating being, but rather one whose true nature has been taught as 'That thou art.
If you yourself are skilled in reasoning, you would know your own nature; it cannot be otherwise.
Thus, the Śruti shows its dependence on reasoning that conforms to the human intellect, saying "the learned man."
The meaning is "because of the scripture concerning the Self.
Now, an objection is raised: it is not proper for Brahman to require reflection and so forth, because it is the subject matter of the Veda, just like Dharma.
But since it is the *śruti*, *liṅga*, *vākya*, and so forth that are required, he says "no.
It should be explained as: "just as in the case of *dharma* which is to be inquired into, so too in the case of *brahman* which is to be inquired into.
"Experience" (*anubhava*) refers to the experience of the wise, known as the direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*) of *brahman*.
By the word "etcetera" (ādipadāt), reflection (manana) and meditative absorption (nididhyāsana) are included.
He states the reason for this with the words "anubhava" and so forth:

because, for the sake of liberation, verbal knowledge of Brahman must culminate in direct realization (sākṣātkāra); and since [Brahman] is the established reality that is the inner self (pratyagbhūta), it is possible for such knowledge to have direct realization as its fruit.
Therefore, the requirement for reflection (*manana*) and so forth is logical [in the case of Brahman].

However, regarding *dharma*, which is by nature eternally beyond the senses and is to be established, direct perception is neither required nor possible; thus, for the sake of performance, only the determination [of its nature] through scripture (*śruti*) is required.

As for the indicative marks (*liṅga*) and other means of proof, they are included within scripture itself and are required as being useful for determination by way of scripture; reflection and the like are not required, because they are of no use. This is the meaning.
Direct assertion (*śruti*) is a word that is independent [of others].
Indicative power (*liṅga*) is a word’s capacity to manifest its meaning.
A sentence (*vākya*) is a word that requires another word capable [of syntactic connection].
*Prakaraṇa* (context) is the principal sentence that depends upon subsidiary sentences.
*Sthāna* (position) is the relationship between items recited in a sequence with those [items] recited in the same sequence, according to their order;

for example, ten sacrifices such as the *aindrāgna* are recited in sequence, and there are ten mantras beginning with "Indra and Agni, the luminaries in heaven," where the first mantra is applied to the first sacrifice.
Thus, and so forth, should be inferred. "Commonality of designation" (saṃjñāsāmya) means common appellation (samākhyā).
The distinction is that, for example, mantras designated as *ādhvaryava* are applied to a rite designated as *ādhvaryava*.
Thus, first of all, in the inference that "Brahman requires reflection and so forth because it is the subject matter of the Veda,
like Dharma," the property of Dharma is presented as the probandum (sādhya) and is therefore unfit for direct experience.

It has been stated that "not requiring experience" (*anapekṣitānubhavatva*) is the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*). Furthermore, it has been stated that due to the absence of this adjunct, Brahman does not require reflection (*manana*) and so forth.

In that case, if you were to assert that Brahman is identical to Dharma merely by virtue of being the subject matter of the Veda, then, like Dharma, Brahman would likewise be something to be accomplished through human effort (*kṛtisādhya*), and would be subject to injunctions (*vidhi*), prohibitions (*niṣedha*), alternatives (*vikalpa*), general rules (*utsarga*), and exceptions (*apavāda*).
"May they be so. He states the refutation regarding the counter-position (vipakṣa) with the words beginning "puruṣa" and so forth.

The grammatical connection (*anvaya*) is as follows: because the acquisition of its own nature—that is, its production—is dependent upon human activity, it is only the Vedas and other such sources that possess authority (*prāmāṇya*) regarding Dharma.
He clarifies that the Dharma is something to be accomplished by means of the example of worldly action with the words "to do";
the meaning is "just like in the world.
He clarifies the example with the word "as."
He states the illustrative example with the word "tathā" (likewise).
Having stated that it is possible to perform or not perform a *dharma* in that manner, he states that it is possible to perform it otherwise with the word "udita" (declared).
Having established that *dharma* is something to be accomplished (*sādhya*), he states its suitability for injunctions and so forth with the word "vidhi" (injunction).
The meaning is that those injunctions and prohibitions, as well as options and the like, which are purposeful and find scope when a dharma is to be established, would likewise apply to Brahman.
Examples of injunctions and prohibitions include "one should sacrifice" and "one should not drink liquor.
An example of a possible option is "one should sacrifice with rice or with barley," while the choice between taking up or not taking up [the soma] is a matter of personal preference.
Regarding the two options of offering the oblation after sunrise or before sunrise, there is a settled alternative.
"One shall not harm" is a general rule (utsarga), while "one should sacrifice an animal to Agni and Soma" is an exception (apavāda).
Likewise, the distinction is that "he offers in the Āhavanīya fire" is a general rule (utsarga), while "he offers at every step of the horse" is an exception (apavāda).
He refutes the objection that these [rules] might apply to Brahman by means of the words beginning with "no" (na).
Because its object is an existing reality;
up to this point [it has been explained that] "this thing is thus."
"It is not so":
this is a conceptualization regarding the mode [of being], such as "is it a jar or a cloth?
"It exists or it does not exist": this is a conceptualization regarding the essential nature of existence.

[Objection: But surely, even regarding real entities such as the self (*ātman*) and so forth, conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) such as "it exists" or "it does not exist" are observed among disputants. To this, he says: "But the conceptualizations... The literal meaning is as follows: the recollection of alternatives such as existence and non-existence is a human intellect; rooted in that, the conceptualizations consisting of doubt and error are mere fluctuations of the mind and do not possess the nature of valid cognition (*pramā*). The underlying point is this: since a phenomenon can be acted upon exactly as it is known, all conceptualizations based on human intellect in accordance with the scriptures are indeed of the nature of valid cognition.
"By parity with that [case], all conceptual constructions (vikalpa) regarding Brahman would also be real.
To the one who says "it is likewise even there," he replies: "No.

If the knowledge of an established entity were also produced in dependence upon human intellect, just like the knowledge of a thing to be accomplished, then conceptual constructions regarding the established would be real.
The cognition of an established object is not produced by a person; rather, it is produced by the object as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
And thus, because the object has a single nature, only one cognition is valid;
the meaning is that other conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) are simply non-conformable with reality (*ayathārtha*).
Regarding this, he states an illustration: "For it is not [the case] with respect to a post," and so forth.
The meaning is that once the restriction "it is indeed a post" is established, all alternative conceptualizations (*vikalpa*) are no longer in accordance with reality (*yathārtha*).
In that context, knowledge that is dependent upon the actual object is what is in accordance with reality.
He analyzes what is dependent on a person as being false with the word "therein" (*tatra*).
This means "in the case of a post" (*sthāṇau*). He extends the principle stated regarding the post to jars and other objects with the word "thus" (*evam*).
He states the subject at hand: "In that case, being so.

This means that since the validity of knowledge regarding an established object depends upon the thing itself, the knowledge of Brahman is likewise produced by the thing itself and is thus true; it is not dependent on the person [who knows], because its object is an existing reality, just like the cognition of a post.

Therefore, the meaning is that all conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) are independent in the case of an object to be established (*sādhya*), but not in the case of an already established object (*siddha*); thus, due to this distinction, there is no similarity of properties (*dharma-sāmya*) with a Brāhmaṇa, and it follows that the realization [of Brahman] depends upon reflection (*manana*) and so forth.
Now, one might object: "In that case, Brahman must be within the range of perception (*pratyakṣa*) and other means of knowledge, because it is distinct from *dharma*."
Like a jar and so forth;
and thus, in the *Janmādi-sūtra*, the inference regarding the cause of the world is to be investigated,
because it possesses authority with respect to an established fact (*siddhārtha*).

It is not the Śruti [that is the subject], because since it lacks authority regarding an already established fact (siddhārtha), an inquiry into it would be fruitless; thus he raises an objection with "na nv iti" (but surely not).
The implication is that, on the grounds that [the Śruti] is merely the object of other means of knowledge (pramāṇāntara), the inquiry should apply to those other means of knowledge themselves.
In this regard, the proponent of the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣin) should be questioned:
does the inference that "whatever is an effect is born from Brahman" establish Brahman, or is it that "whatever is an effect has a cause"?
It is not the first, because the universal concomitance (vyāpti) is unestablished; thus he says, "No."

The meaning is that because Brahman cannot be grasped by the senses, it is impossible to apprehend its pervasion (vyāpti) through perception; therefore, it is not an object of any other means of valid cognition (pramāṇa).
To the question "Why is it ungraspable by the senses?", he says: "By its very nature," based on the Vedic scripture: "The Self-existent pierced the openings [of the senses] outward."
The meaning is that this is because Brahman is devoid of form and other such qualities.

To the question, "Even if it is not perceivable by the senses, why could the apprehension of pervasion (vyāpti) not occur?", he says: "For when..."—the remainder of the sentence being "that [perception] does not exist."
The meaning is that a perceptual observation of the pervasion—that "this effect is born from Brahman"—is not possible because Brahman is beyond the senses.
Regarding the second [alternative], even if the cause is established, its identity as Brahman cannot be known without scripture; thus he says, "merely the effect.

Since no certainty can be attained that "Brahman is the cause of the world" without scripture once a relationship has been established, therefore, for the sake of attaining that certainty, scripture alone must be primarily investigated.

But inference, by means of generalities such as being the material cause (*upādānatva*)—just as in the case of clay and so forth—is to be considered as a subordinate factor (*guṇa*) for the purpose of establishing the possibility of the scriptural meaning that Brahman is identical with its own effects; thus he concludes with the words "Therefore" (*tasmāt*).
He asks what the scriptural passage (*viṣayavākya*) for this sūtra is with the words "What, then? (*kiṃ punar*);
the meaning is: what is the sentence intended to be examined here regarding Brahman for the purpose of providing its definition?
For here, having promised the inquiry into Brahman for a qualified seeker in the first aphorism, the definition of that which desires to know Brahman is stated in the second aphorism.

Likewise, in the Śruti as well, Brahman is made known to one who desires liberation and wishes to know Brahman by restating the defining characteristic of being the cause of the world; thus, in order to demonstrate that the aphorism follows the sequence of the scriptural meaning, he recites the passage beginning with "Bhṛgu" along with its introduction.
"Adhīhi" means "teach," that is, "cause [me] to remember.
Here, the singular number in "yena" is intended to be significant, because if there were plurality, it would be impossible to enjoin Brahman-hood.
The intermediate sentence is: "That which is the cause of the world is one.
The distinction between the great sentences (*mahāvākya*) is as follows: either "That which is the one cause is Brahman," or "That which is the cause is the one Brahman.

Anticipating the question, "What then is the definition of its essential nature (*svarūpa-lakṣaṇa*)?", he says, "And of that [it is said]..."—having determined the meaning of the word *yataḥ* from the remainder of the passage as being "Truth, Knowledge, and Bliss" (*satya-jñāna-ānanda*).

He states that even sentences from other recensions (śākhā), such as "He who is omniscient," "From Him this Brahman, name, form, and food are born," and "Brahman is consciousness and bliss," are also the subject matter [of the inquiry]. He says "others too" and explains their being of such a nature by the words "eternal," etc.
Thus, in all recensions, the statements defining the two characteristics are consistent with respect to Brahman, which is the object of the desire to know.
Thus, it is established that liberation results from that knowledge. //2//
END BsCom_1,1.2.2 START BsCom_1,1.3.3 3.
The Section on Scripture Being the Source [of Brahman] (Śāstrayonitvādhikaraṇa) / Sūtra 3.
Having introduced the idea that Brahman is omniscient by demonstrating its status as the cause of the world, [the author] confirms that very point, saying:
"Because it is the source of the scripture" (Brahma Sūtra 1.1.3).

Brahman is the source—that is, the cause—of the great scripture consisting of the Ṛgveda and the other Vedas, which is augmented by numerous branches of knowledge, which illuminates all objects like a lamp, and which is almost equivalent to omniscience itself.

The possibility of such a scripture— one that encompasses the Ṛgveda and other Vedas and is endowed with the qualities of omniscience— arising from anyone other than an omniscient being does not exist.
For whatever extensive scripture arises from a particular person,
as is the case with grammar and the like which concern even only a portion of what is to be known, it is well known in the world that he possesses knowledge far exceeding that [subject matter].

What more need be said? From that Great Being, who is the source and womb of all, there arose—without effort and as if in mere play, like a person's natural breath—the Veda known as the Ṛgveda and so forth; it is divided into numerous branches and recensions, serves as the cause for the classification of gods, animals, humans, castes, stages of life, and so on, and is a mine of all knowledge.
This is because of such scriptural passages as, "The Ṛgveda is the breath of this great Being" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.4.10).
Of that great Being, there is unsurpassed omniscience and omnipotence.

Alternatively, the scripture (*śāstra*) as previously described—the *Ṛgveda* and so forth—is the source, the cause, and the means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) for this Brahman in the attainment of its true nature.
The intended meaning is that Brahman, the cause of the origin and so forth of the world, is known solely through the authority of scripture.
The scripture was cited in the previous sūtra: "From which indeed these beings are born," and so on.
For what purpose, then, is this sūtra, since by citing such a treatise (śāstra) in the very first sūtra, the fact that Brahman has the treatise as its source was already demonstrated?

It is said in reply: Since it might be suspected that in that [first] case, because the treatise was not explicitly mentioned by the words of the sūtra, only inference based on "origination and so forth" was presented, this sūtra is intended to dispel that suspicion.
"It proceeded because it has the scriptures as its source" (Śāstrayonitvāt). [Note:

The four Vedas are to be supplemented; therein, the Purāṇas primarily supplement the passages teaching creation and so forth, as well as the explanatory narratives (*arthavāda*) consisting of accounts of the deeds of others and ancient legends, while incidentally supplementing the portion concerning non-duality and the portion concerning ritual action.]

The Nyāya-śāstra, however, supplements [the Veda] by discerning and making known the categories of existence through the definition of the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) and the objects of cognition (prameya).
The Pūrva- and Uttara-mīmāṃsās, for their part, are employed by way of determining the intended meaning (tātparya).
The Dharma-śāstra supplements the portion concerning injunctions (vidhi) found in either the Śruti or the Smṛti.

The *Śikṣā* reinforces the meaning of the injunction that "one's own recitation (*svādhyāya*) should be studied" by means of defining the places of articulation (*sthāna*), the effort (*karaṇa*), and so forth.
The *Kalpas*, however, are employed for the purpose of defining ritual applications (*prayoga*).
As for grammar (*vyākaraṇa*), it analyzes word-meanings (*padārtha*) in the sense of determining that "this word is correct (*sādhu*) in this particular meaning."

Nirukta demonstrates the etymological meaning within various words; Chandaḥśāstra elucidates the meters found in the Vedas, such as Gāyatrī and others, by means of their defining characteristics; and Jyotiṣa establishes the specific times prescribed [in the scriptures], such as "one should sacrifice with the Full Moon [offering] on the full moon day" and "one should sacrifice with the New Moon [offering] on the new moon day."
And thus, the greatness of that [work] is evident, since many great sages, the authors of treatises such as the Purāṇas, were engaged in providing explanations for its various regions.
The analysis of the compound is: "that whose subject matter (artha) is dharma in an extensive form";
the meaning is "extensive."
I worship Śrī Rāma, the knower of all, who is to be known through the Vedas, whose very breath is the Vedas—the powers of knowledge regarding all things. //1//
Stating the connection by way of restating the preceding topic, he introduces the subsequent sutra with the words "The world...":
By the statement that the conscious Brahman is the cause of the world, the author of the sutras has effectively asserted its omniscience,
because a creation by a conscious being must be preceded by knowledge.
And thus, Brahman is omniscient,
because it is the cause of all;
for whoever is the maker of something is the knower of that thing.
As it is established that [the Lord] is like a potter,

the meaning is that he speaks in order to strengthen that very omniscience— which is sought for the purpose of refuting [theories such as] *pradhāna*— by means of the reason of being the author of the Veda; for these two reasons establish a single objective.
The intermediate connection (*avāntara-saṃgati*) consists in having the same subject matter.

Alternatively, since the Veda is eternal, it might be objected that Brahman cannot be the cause of everything; thus, by way of this objection (*ākṣepa-saṃgati*), the fact that Brahman is the cause of the Veda is stated: "This Rigveda, Yajurveda, Sāmaveda, and Atharvāṅgirasa are the breath of this great Being."

Thus, the subject matter is this statement; the doubt is whether it establishes the omniscience of Brahman by virtue of being the cause of the Veda, or whether it does not establish it. In that regard, the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that it does not establish it, because if the Veda were of human origin—like grammar and other such sciences—it would result in a lack of authority due to its dependence on a foundational means of knowledge. In the final conclusion (*siddhānta*), the result is the establishment of the sentience of the cause of the universe. Thus, its establishment [is the goal].

Since this Vedāntic statement, which possesses clear marks of Brahman, is shown to be in harmony with the author of the Veda, there are consistencies with the Śruti, the Śāstra, the Book (Adhyāya), and the Section (Pāda).
In this manner, the consistencies with the Śruti and so forth are to be inferred up to the end of the Pāda.
For indeed, the capacity to illuminate all objects is perceived in the Veda.
That [power] is preceded by the power residing in Brahman, which is its material cause, or it resides in that [Brahman] itself;
for it is a power of manifestation,
or else it is a power residing in an effect.

Just as in the case of the power of a lamp, by virtue of being the material cause (*upādāna*) of the Veda, Brahman’s status as the witness of all (*sarvasākṣitva*)— in the form of the capacity to illuminate all objects connected to itself— is established. Alternatively, just as students compose the Veda after knowing its prior sequence, so too the Supreme Lord— who possesses the assistance of *māyā* with its manifold qualities and is unobscured, infinite pure consciousness alone— [produces the Veda] possessing a sequence similar to the sequence of the previous kalpa created by Himself.
Since he creates the collection of the Vedas and their meanings while knowing them simultaneously, the Veda is not of human origin (*pauruṣeya*).

For where the knowledge of a sentence is preceded by the knowledge of its meaning and serves as the cause for the creation of that sentence, there is human authorship; but here, because of the simultaneity, such authorship does not exist.

Therefore, he establishes the conclusion that the author of the Veda, like the Veda itself, necessarily knows its meaning as being connected to himself, and is thus omniscient— this is expressed by the word "śāstra.

Intending to apply the sūtra in accordance with these two connections— that Brahman is the cause of the scripture and that it is omniscient and the cause of all— he explains the words beginning with "mahataḥ" (of the great).
The qualifications of the Veda are for the sake of establishing its omniscience:
therein lies its greatness by virtue of its extent in terms of both text and meaning,
and its status as a *śāstra* because it teaches what is beneficial.
Considering that the word *śāstra* is intended to indicate sound (*śabda*) in general, he says "aneka" (many).

The ten branches of knowledge (*vidyāsthāna*)—namely, the Purāṇas, Nyāya, Mīmāṃsā, the Dharmaśāstras, and the six auxiliary sciences (*ṣaḍaṅga*: Śikṣā, Kalpa, Vyākaraṇa, Nirukta, Chandas, and Jyotiṣa)—are the means for knowing the meaning of the Veda.
The meaning is: "of one who is assisted by these."
By this, the authority of the Veda is indicated through its being accepted by Manu and others.
He states that its authority also follows from its lack of non-cognitiveness—saying "like a lamp.

Although it possesses the power to illuminate all objects, because it is insentient, it is "like the Omniscient One"; its "source" (yoni) refers to both the material cause (upādāna) and the agent (kartṛ).

[Objection: But surely, the quality of an omniscient being is the possession of the power to know all objects; even if the Veda possesses that [power], how can its source be omniscient? To this he says: "For not...
Since that power cannot exist in the effect without its presence in the material cause, the source of the Veda must be omniscient.
As for inference, it has already been shown previously.
Nor does it follow that [the Veda] is produced by ignorance;
the point is that even though it possesses power, it is insentient.
The Veda is produced by one who possesses knowledge of a subject matter exceeding its own scope, because it is a statement of valid authority (*pramāṇa*).
"Like grammar, the Rāmāyaṇa, and so forth"—this is another inference.
Regarding that, he states the pervasion (*vyāpti*) with the words "whatever...
*Vistara* means an abundance of words.
By stating [the author's] smallness in terms of meaning (*arthataḥ*), he indicates that the knowledge of the author regarding the subject matter (*artha*) is superior;

for an abundance of explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) is observed in the Veda. Here is the construction: whatever scripture originates from whichever authoritative person (*āpta*), that person possesses knowledge of a subject matter superior to that scripture.

Thus it is well known that even grammar and similar sciences— which have as their object only a portion of what is to be known, such as the correctness of words— arise from Pāṇini and others who know more than they teach. If even a science with a limited scope can arise from one who knows more, then [it follows] from the Vedic revelation beginning with "Of this Great One," that from the Great, Undivided, Real Source, the Veda— characterized by its many branches and so forth— arose without effort, like the breath of a person.
It goes without saying that his omniscience and possession of all powers are established.
In this context, in order to dispel the suspicion that the Veda is of human origin, he states the meaning of the word "breathing forth" (*niḥśvasita*) found in the scripture: "without effort.
This means without the exertion involved in knowing an object through other means of knowledge, according to the analogy of the blinking of an eye.

Here, by means of inference, for the sake of strengthening the omniscience declared in the scripture "He who is all-knowing," we establish merely the existence of knowledge of the primary meaning in the author of the Veda— just as in the case of Pāṇini and others— but not that such knowledge of the meaning is the cause of the Veda; for that would contradict the Śruti text regarding the "breath" (niḥśvasita),
and because the status of being the author of the Veda is possible through mere knowledge of the Veda, just as in the case of a student.

This is the distinction: the student is dependent on another, whereas the Lord, by his own memory, manifests at the beginning of the aeon the very same sequence of the Vedas he himself created to Brahmā and others; because his knowledge is unobstructed, he knows their meaning as something that cannot be avoided, and thus he is "omniscient"—this is beyond reproach.
Now, following the definition of Brahman, since there is a desire to know the means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*), he states another exposition with the words "ata eva" (for this very reason).
Since both the definition and the means of valid knowledge have the determination of Brahman as their purpose, they share a single result; this constitutes the connection (*saṅgati*).
Regarding the doubt as to whether or not the scriptural text, "But that person who is known through the Upanishads," declares that Brahman is to be known solely through the Vedas:

Since, by means of the effect as a logical mark (*kāryaliṅga*) alone, there is established through parsimony (*lāghava*) a single omniscient creator who is Brahman, [the opponent] concludes that [Brahman] is not [known] through [ordinary] speech. To this, the Siddhāntin replies: "Because [Brahman] has the scripture as its source" (*śāstrayonitvāt*).
He explains this with the words: "As it has been said."

In every case, the pair of arguments for the prima facie (pūrvapakṣa) and the final position (siddhānta) should be understood as the seeds of doubt. Here, the distinction is that the result of the prima facie view is the establishment of the necessity of investigating inference alone, whereas the result of the final position is the [investigation of] the Vedāntas.
The establishment of Brahman through inference and other means was incidentally refuted in the preceding Sūtra.

Furthermore, because the multiplicity of the world’s manifold elaborations (prapañca) contradicts its having a single creator—just as a palace and such do—the principle of parsimony (lāghava) does not apply here.

Nor is the possibility of a single creator established by his omniscience; for if one were to argue that omniscience is known from the knowledge of unity, and from that [omniscience] the [knowledge of unity follows], there would be a circular dependency (anyonyāśraya). Anticipating this objection, he says: "From scripture alone" (śāstrādeva).
"What is that treatise?"—to this he says: "The treatise.
He raises an objection regarding its separate composition: "For what purpose?"—the meaning is: "What is the purpose for which it has been shown? by whatever reason.

He states, "It is said," [in order to show] that this separate sūtra is intended to dispel the doubt that the inference characterized by "birth and so forth" (janmādi-liṅgaka) might be presented independently. //3//
END BsCom_1,1.3.3 START BsCom_1,1.4.4 4.
The Section on Concordance (Samanvayādhikaraṇa) / Sūtra 4.

But how, again, can it be said that Brahman has scripture as its means of valid cognition, given the [Mīmāṃsā] sūtra: "Since the Veda has action as its purpose, those parts which do not have that as their purpose are useless"?
Thus, it has been demonstrated that the scripture has action as its primary purpose;
consequently, the Vedāntas are purposeless, because they do not have action as their purpose.
Alternatively, they may serve as supplements to injunctions for ritual action by means of revealing the agent, the deity, and so forth,
or they may serve the purpose of enjoining other actions such as meditation;
for it is not possible to establish a fully accomplished, existing entity [through them].

Because an established entity is the object of perception and other means of knowledge, and because there is no human purpose in teaching such an entity when it is devoid of anything to be rejected or accepted;

for this very reason, so that passages such as "He wept" (so 'rodīt) do not become meaningless, it is said: "But because they form a single syntactical unit with an injunction, they exist for the purpose of praising that injunction."
Thus, by way of being commendatory (*stāvaka*), the purposefulness of [the explanatory passages] has been stated.
Furthermore, regarding mantras such as "For food, thee" (*iṣe tvā*) and others, their connection to ritual action (*karmasamavāyitva*) has been stated through their denoting the action and its means.
Nowhere is the purposefulness of Vedic sentences observed or established without contact with an injunction (*vidhi*).
Furthermore, an injunction is not possible with respect to the established nature of a thing,

because an injunction has action as its object. Therefore, the Upanishads (Vedāntas) are subordinate to injunctions regarding action by means of revealing the nature of the agent, the deity, and so forth, which are required for that action.

Now, even if this [position] is not accepted for fear of contradicting another context (*prakaraṇāntara*), nevertheless, because those [passages] are devoted to actions such as meditation mentioned within their own sentences, it follows that Brahman is not the source of the scripture (*śāstrayonitva*). To this, it is replied: [The objection of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is: "Of the Veda... [as stated in the sūtra]. *Note: The phrase "āmnāyasya" refers to the prima facie argument.*

The meaning of this is as follows: since the *āmnāya*, that is, the Veda, is intent upon the exposition of ritual action (*kriyā*), those passages which do not have that as their purpose—those which do not concern action, such as "He wept" (*sa arodīt*) and so forth—are purposeless.

Therefore, it is said that the authority of the Vedas is impermanent and non-universal. The established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that "the words already existing [in the Veda] are connected with the purpose of ritual action."

Therefore, among those Vedic statements, there is a syntactic connection (*anvaya*) between the sentences that establish established facts (*siddhārtha*) concerning beings and the sentences that enjoin action (*kriyārtha*), such as "One should not give silver on the sacrificial grass" (*barhiṣi rajataṃ na deyam*) or "One should sacrifice with an animal" (*paśunā yajeta*).

Thus, when the connection is made by supplementing the meaning through censure and so forth, their status as authoritative means of knowledge (*prāmāṇya*) is established by virtue of their being intent upon action (*kriyāparatva*).
The meaning is: "Because of the existence of the fruit [arising] from the knowledge of the perfected reality.
But that [existence] is due to "concordance" (*samanvaya*).
The word "but" (*tu*) is for the purpose of setting aside the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*).
That Brahman—the omniscient and omnipotent cause of the origin, sustenance, and dissolution of the universe—is understood solely from the Vedānta scriptures.
How so? Because of their harmony (*samanvaya*). For in all the Vedāntas, the statements are consistently harmonized with the intent of establishing this very meaning.
"In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.2.1); "One only, without a second"; "In the beginning, this was indeed the Self alone."
"This very Brahman is without prior, without posterior, without interior, and without exterior" (Aitareya Upaniṣad 2.1.1.1).
"This Self is Brahman, the perceiver of all" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.5.19).
"This immortal Brahman alone is before [us]" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.1.1).

(Muṇḍaka 2.2.11), and so forth. Furthermore, once the coherent connection (*samanvaya*) of the words contained therein regarding the nature of Brahman is ascertained, it is not logical to postulate another meaning, for that would entail the abandonment of what is heard in scripture (*śruti-hāni*) and the assumption of what is not heard (*aśruta-kalpanā*).

Nor is it understood that these [passages] are intent on establishing the nature of an agent, because of scriptural texts such as "Then by what and whom should one perceive? (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.4.13), which demonstrate the absence of action, factors of action, and results.
Furthermore, even though Brahman possesses the nature of an established reality, it is not an object of perception and the like;
for the identity of Brahman and the Self, expressed as "That thou art" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.8.7), cannot be understood without the scripture.
As for the objection that instruction would be purposeless because [Brahman] is devoid of anything to be rejected or accepted,
this is not a fault;

for the human goal is accomplished precisely through the realization of Brahman as the Self— which is empty of anything to be rejected or accepted— thereby resulting in the abandonment of all afflictions.
However, there is no contradiction whatsoever in the fact that the presentation of deities and so forth serves the purpose of meditation contained within its own sentence;

yet, in the same way, it is not possible for Brahman to be subordinate to an injunction for meditation, because in the case of oneness— being devoid of anything to be rejected or accepted— the sublation of the cognition of duality such as action and its factors necessarily follows.
For there is no possibility of the re-emergence of dualistic cognition once it has been eradicated by the cognition of oneness,
such that Brahman could be understood as being subordinate to injunctions for meditation (*upāsanā-vidhi*).
Even if elsewhere the validity of Vedic sentences is not seen to exist without contact with an injunction, [this does not apply here].
Nevertheless, because the knowledge of the Self culminates in its fruit, the authority of the scripture concerning that subject cannot be rejected.
Furthermore, the authority of the scripture is not something to be apprehended through inference, such that it would require an illustrative example observed elsewhere.
Therefore, it is established that Brahman has scripture as its means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

Here, others raise an objection: even if Brahman has scripture as its means of valid cognition, nevertheless, Brahman is presented by the scripture solely as the object of an injunction for realization (*pratipatti-vidhi*).
Just as sacrificial posts (*yūpa*), the *āhavanīya* fire, and so forth—though not known from ordinary experience—are presented by the scripture as subordinate elements of injunctions, so it is here.
Why is this so?
Because the purpose of a treatise (*śāstra*) consists in [prompting] engagement and cessation.
For those who know the intended meaning of a treatise have said: "Its visible purpose is indeed the comprehension of ritual action (*karman*)."
"An injunction (*codanā*) is a statement that prompts action.
"The knowledge of that [Dharma] is instruction (*upadeśa*). (Jaimini Sūtra 1.1.5).
"The collection of those [words] which have come into being [as parts of a sentence] is for the purpose of action. (Jaimini Sūtra 1.1.25).
And as it is said: "Since the Veda has action as its purpose, those parts which do not have that as their purpose are useless" (Jaimini Sūtra 1.2.1).
Therefore, the scripture is meaningful only insofar as it impels a person toward a specific object or restrains them from a specific object.
And other [passages] are employed as supplementary to that;
by analogy with this, the Vedāntas would likewise possess purposefulness in that same way.

Furthermore, if they are subordinate to injunctions, it is logical that just as the Agnihotra and other means are enjoined for one who desires heaven and so forth, so too the knowledge of Brahman is enjoined for one who desires immortality.

But has it not been stated here that there is a difference in the objects of inquiry (*jijñāsya*)? In the *karmakāṇḍa*, dharma—which is yet to be brought into being (*bhavya*)—is the object of inquiry; whereas here, Brahman—which is already existent (*bhūta*) and eternally accomplished—is the object of inquiry. Therefore, the fruit of the knowledge of Brahman ought to be distinct from the fruit of the knowledge of dharma, which depends upon ritual performance.
It cannot be so.
Because Brahman is presented as the object to be understood precisely for one who is impelled by the injunction regarding what is to be done,
as in: "The Self, indeed, my dear, is to be seen" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.4.5),
and "That Self which is free from evil— that is to be sought after, that is to be desired to be known" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.7.1).
"One should meditate upon it as the Self" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.4.7); "Meditate upon the Self alone as the world" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.4.15);
"He who knows Brahman becomes Brahman indeed" (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 3.2.9).

When such injunctions as these exist, there arises the inquiry: "Who is this Self? What is that Brahman? In response to this, all the Vedāntas are employed to impart its essential nature, beginning with such statements as: "Brahman is eternal, omniscient, omnipresent, eternally satisfied, and by nature eternally pure, conscious, and free;
Brahman is consciousness and bliss. Thus it is said.
And through the worship of that [Brahman], liberation— which is also seen as a fruit in the scriptures— will come to pass;
for when there is the mere statement of a thing without its entry into an injunction of action, the possibility of rejection or acquisition exists, as in the case of the statement,
"The earth consists of seven islands."
The Vedānta statements would likewise be as purposeless as sentences such as "the king is going. [Objection:
But even when stating a mere fact, usefulness is observed—as in "this is a rope, this is not a snake"—whereby the fear produced by delusion is removed;
similarly here too, by stating the reality of the Self which is not subject to transmigratory existence, the delusion of being a transmigrating being is removed, and thus there is usefulness.
This might be so,
provided that the delusion of transmigratory existence would cease through the mere hearing of the nature of Brahman, just as the delusion of a snake ceases upon hearing the true nature of the rope.
But it does not cease,
because even for one who has heard about Brahman, the worldly attributes such as pleasure and pain are observed just as before, according to the injunction:
"It is to be heard, it is to be reflected upon, it is to be meditated upon" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.4.5).

And because we observe that there is an injunction for reflection (*manana*) and meditative absorption (*nididhyāsana*) subsequent to hearing (*śravaṇa*), it follows that Brahman must be accepted as having the scripture (*śāstra*) as its sole means of valid cognition, precisely by virtue of being the object of an injunction for realization.
To this, it is replied: No.
Because of the difference between the fruits of ritual action (*karma*) and the knowledge of Brahman (*brahmavidyā*):
ritual action— whether physical, vocal, or mental— is that which is established by the *Śruti* and *Smṛti* and is designated as *dharma*,
the object of the inquiry expressed in "Now, therefore, the inquiry into *dharma*" (*athāto dharmajijñāsā*, Jaimini Sūtra 1.1.1).
Thus it has been stated;
for non-dharma, such as violence and the like, is also to be investigated for the sake of avoidance, since it is characterized by prohibitive injunctions.

Regarding these two—dharma and adharma, which are characterized by injunctions and result in benefit and harm—their fruits are pleasure and pain, which are directly perceived, experienced through the body, speech, and mind alone, produced by the contact of the senses with their objects, and [experienced] by beings from Brahmā downwards.
It is well known that among embodied beings,
from humans up to the level of Brahmā, there is a gradation of happiness.
From this, it is understood that there is a corresponding gradation in its cause, namely, dharma.
The gradation of qualification follows from the gradation of the nature of things (*dharmatā*).
Furthermore, the gradation of qualification established by factors such as desire (*arthitva*) and capability (*sāmarthya*) is well known.

And thus, it is only for those who perform sacrifices and other rites that there is travel by the northern path (*uttareṇa pathā*) due to the excellence of their knowledge (*vidyā*) and meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
By means of the practices of sacrifice (*iṣṭa*), public works (*pūrta*), and charity (*datta*) alone, there is travel by the southern path through the sequence of smoke and so forth;

even therein, both the gradation of pleasure and the gradation of its means are understood from the scripture, based on the passage: "having dwelt [there] as long as their works endure" (*Chāndogya Upaniṣad* 5.10.5).

Likewise, it is understood that among humans and other beings, down to those in hell and the stationary (sthāvara), even a minute fragment of pleasure is achievable only through dharma characterized by injunction; this is perceived as existing in varying degrees of intensity.

Similarly, because the gradations of suffering are observed among embodied beings in higher and lower realms, there is likewise perceived a corresponding gradation in its cause—adharma—as well as in the injunctions for its prohibition and in those who practice it. Thus, for those possessed of defects such as ignorance, the nature of saṃsāra—which is preceded by the assumption of a body and caused by the gradations of pleasure and pain resulting from the gradations of dharma and adharma—is well-established through Śruti, Smṛti, and reasoning.

And so the Smṛti says: "For one who is possessed of a body, there is indeed no removal of the pleasant and the unpleasant"—this reiterates the nature of transmigratory existence as it has been described. Furthermore, by the prohibition of contact with the pleasant and the unpleasant in the passage, "Verily, the pleasant and the unpleasant do not touch one who is bodiless" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.12.1), it is understood that the state of bodilessness known as liberation is denied to be an effect of dharma characterized by Vedic injunction.
For if it were the effect of dharma, the prohibition against contact with the pleasant and the unpleasant would not be tenable.
If it is argued that bodilessness itself is the effect of dharma, we say no,
because that is its very nature.
"Having realized the bodiless Self, which dwells within bodies that are unstable, the great and all-pervading Lord, the wise man does not grieve" (Kāṭhaka Upaniṣad 1.2.21);
"For it is without breath, without mind, and pure" (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 2.1.2).
This is because of such scriptural passages as, "For this person is unattached" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.3.15).
Therefore, it is established that bodilessness, known as liberation— which is distinct from the fruits of actions to be performed— is eternal.
Among these, some things are changing yet eternal (*pariṇāminitya*), such that even when they undergo transformation, the cognition "this is that very same thing" is not sublated;
for example, according to those who maintain the eternity of the world consisting of earth and so forth,
and likewise, according to the Sāṃkhyas, the *guṇas*.
But this [Self] is ultimate, immutably eternal,
and all-pervading like space.
Devoid of all modification,
eternally satisfied,
and without parts.
It is of the nature of self-luminosity,
wherein neither dharma nor adharma, along with their effects and the three periods of time, ever recur;
that state is bodilessness, known as liberation.
This is known from such scriptural passages as: "Other than dharma, other than adharma, other than this cause and effect, other than the past and the future" (Kaṭha Upaniṣad 2.14).
Therefore, if that Brahman for which this inquiry has been commenced were taught as something to be performed,
and if liberation were accepted as something to be accomplished by means of that performance, [then there would be a contradiction].
It would necessarily be impermanent.
This being the case, it would follow that liberation is merely some excellence among those aforementioned fruits of action—which are themselves impermanent and exist in varying degrees;
yet liberation is accepted by all proponents of liberation as being eternal.
Therefore, it is not logical that the instruction regarding Brahman should be subordinate to ritual action.
Furthermore: "He who knows Brahman becomes Brahman itself" (Muṇḍaka 3.2.9);
and "His actions perish when He, both the higher and the lower, is seen" (Muṇḍaka 2.2.8).
"Knowing Brahman as bliss, one fears nothing from anywhere" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.9);
"O Janaka, you have indeed attained fearlessness" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.2.4).

"Then he knew only himself: 'I am Brahman. Therefore, he became that All. (Vājasaneyibrāhmaṇopaniṣad 1.4.10) "In that state, what delusion, what sorrow can there be for one who perceives oneness? (Īśāvāsya Upaniṣad 7)
Thus, scriptural passages such as these, which show that liberation follows immediately after the knowledge of Brahman, preclude any other intervening activity.

Likewise, the passage, "Seeing this very [Self], the seer Vāmadeva realized: 'I was Manu and the Sun'" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.4.10), is to be cited in order to exclude any further duty between the vision of Brahman and the state of being the Self of all.
Just as in the expression "he sings while standing," it is understood that there is no other action performed by that agent between the acts of standing and singing; likewise:
"You indeed are our father, who carries us to the further shore beyond ignorance" (Praśna Upaniṣad 6.8);

and "I have indeed heard from those like your reverence that the knower of the Self overcomes sorrow; such am I, O venerable sir, I am in sorrow; may you, O venerable sir, carry me across to the further shore of sorrow" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 7.1.3).

And scriptural passages such as, "To him whose impurities have been washed away, the Blessed Sanatkumāra shows the further shore of darkness" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 7.26.2), demonstrate that the fruit of the knowledge of the Self is solely the cessation of the obstacles to liberation.

Likewise, there is the aphorism composed by the Teacher [Gautama], supported by reasoning: "Upon the successive removal of false knowledge, defects, activity, birth, and suffering, through the removal of each subsequent member, there is liberation" (Nyāya Sūtra 1.1.2).
Thus,
the removal of false knowledge arises from the realization of the identity of Brahman and the Self;
and this realization of the identity of Brahman and the Self is not of the nature of a meditative identification (*saṃpad*).
As it is said: "The mind is indeed infinite; the Viśvedevas are infinite; by that [meditation], he conquers an infinite world" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.1.9).
Nor is it of the nature of superimposition (*adhyāsa*), as in:
"One should meditate on the mind as Brahman" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 3.18.1).
Furthermore, in passages such as "The sun is Brahman" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 3.19.1), there is a superimposition of the vision of Brahman upon the mind, the sun, and so forth;
nor is it based on the connection with a specific ritual action, as in the cases of "Vāyu is indeed the absorber" and "Prāṇa is indeed the absorber" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 4.3.1).
It is not of the nature of a purificatory rite (*saṃskāra*) that is a subsidiary part of a ritual action, such as the act of looking at the clarified butter (*ājyāvekṣaṇa*).

For if the realization of the identity of Brahman and the Self were accepted as being of the nature of "attainment" (*saṃpad*) and so forth, [it would contradict] the scriptural texts such as "That thou art" (*Chāndogya Upaniṣad* 6.8.7) and "I am Brahman" (*Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad* 1.4.10).

The syntactical connection of words in such passages as "This Self is Brahman" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.5.19), which are intent upon establishing the reality of the oneness of Brahman and the Self, would be undermined [if the individual soul were not identical with Brahman]. Likewise: "The knot of the heart is rent asunder; all doubts are cut away" (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 2.2.8).
Furthermore, scriptural passages such as these, which declare that the fruit is the cessation of ignorance, would be contradicted; likewise,

statements regarding the attainment of that very state, such as "He who knows Brahman becomes Brahman itself" (Muṇḍaka 3.2.9), would not be consistently applicable under the view that [knowledge] is a mere mental identification (*saṃpad*).
Therefore, the realization of the identity of Brahman and the Self is not of the nature of a ritual accomplishment (*saṃpad*) or the like;
consequently, the knowledge of Brahman (*brahmavidyā*) is not dependent upon human effort.
Rather, it is dependent upon the thing itself, just like the knowledge of an object that falls within the scope of valid means of cognition such as direct perception.
For such a Brahman and its knowledge, it is impossible by any reasoning to conceive of an entry into the realm of effects (*kārya*).

Nor can Brahman enter into the realm of effects by being the object of the act of knowing, as stated in the *Kena Upaniṣad*: "It is indeed other than the known, and moreover, above the unknown. (KeU 1.3)
Thus, because the status of being the object of the act of knowing is denied—
as in, "By what should one know him by whom all this is known?

(Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.4.13)— and likewise, there is also a denial of its being the object of the act of meditative worship, after introducing the non-objectivity of Brahman with the words, "That which is not expressed by speech, but by which speech is expressed."
"Know that very Brahman, and not this which they worship here" (Kena Upaniṣad 1.4).
If it is argued that since Brahman is not an object [of cognition], its being the source of the scriptures is untenable, we say no;
for the scripture has as its purpose the cessation of the distinctions imagined through ignorance.

For this scripture does not intend to establish Brahman as an object characterized by "this-ness. Rather, by establishing it as the inner self (pratyagātman) beyond the range of objectification, it removes the distinctions of the known, the knower, and the act of knowing, which are imagined through ignorance. And so says the scripture: "He for whom it is not known—that one has known it."
"That whose thought he does not know; it is unknown to those who know, and known to those who do not know" (Kena Upaniṣad 2.3);
"You cannot see the seer of seeing."
And as it is said in such passages as, "You cannot know the knower of consciousness" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.4.2).

Therefore, because [the scriptures] establish the nature of the eternally liberated Self by removing the state of being a transmigrator imagined through ignorance, there is no defect of impermanence regarding liberation.
However, for one for whom liberation is something to be produced, it is logical that it must depend upon an action— whether mental, vocal, or physical.
Furthermore, if those two [the self and the world] were subject to modification, liberation would necessarily be impermanent;
for neither a modified product like curd nor a produced effect like a jar is eternal.

It is observed in the world that what is eternal does not require anything else to be attained; furthermore, there is no need for attainment even in the sense of reaching something, because when it is one's own essential nature, it cannot be attained.
Even though Brahman is distinct from its own nature [as an object], it is not something to be attained;
for, because it is omnipresent, Brahman's nature is eternally attained by everyone,
just as the case is with space.
Nor is liberation something to be refined, such that it would require an operation;
for what is called "refinement" must consist either in the imparting of qualities to that which is to be refined, or in the removal of its defects.
Liberation cannot be brought about by the addition of qualities, because the nature of Brahman, which constitutes liberation, is such that no excellence can be added to it;
nor can it be brought about by the removal of defects.

If it is argued that liberation is an inherent attribute of one's own self which, being already firmly established, becomes manifest when the self is refined by ritual action— just as the quality of brilliance is manifested in a mirror when it is refined by the act of polishing— it is not so. This is because liberation is the very nature of Brahman, which is eternally pure.
Because it is untenable for the self to be the locus of action:

that which serves as the locus of an action cannot even come into being unless it effects a modification in that [locus]. If the self were modified by action, the consequence would follow that the self is impermanent.
Furthermore, statements such as "this [Self] is said to be unchangeable" would be contradicted;
and that is undesirable.
Therefore, an action residing in its own substrate is not possible for the Self.
However, because an action that has another locus is not its object, the Self is not refined by it.
[Objection: But surely the embodied one is seen to be refined by actions such as bathing, sipping water, and wearing the sacred thread, which have the body as their locus. [Reply: No;
for it is only the Self as grasped by ignorance—that is, as identified with the aggregate of the body and so forth—which is being refined.
For it is directly perceived that bathing, sipping water, and so forth, are inherent to the body.
It is logical that by means of those [acts] which have the body as their locus, some entity—which is actually a composite of that [body] and is grasped as the Self through ignorance—is refined.

Just as the fruit of health results for one who identifies with the body through the equilibrium of the bodily constituents (*dhātu*) caused by medical treatment directed toward the body, [so too does purification result].
Wherever the cognition "I am healthy" arises,
and likewise wherever the cognition "I am pure and refined by means of bathing, sipping water, the sacred thread, and so forth" arises— that is what is being refined.
And that [refined entity] is indeed conjoined with the body.
For by that very agent— the cognizer who is the object of the notion of "I"— all actions are accomplished, and he alone enjoys their fruit,
as it is said: "Of these two, one eats the sweet pippala fruit, while the other looks on without eating" (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 3.1.1).
Thus it is from the wording of the mantra;
and also: "The wise say that the Self, when joined with the body, the senses, and the mind, is the enjoyer" (Kāṭhaka Upaniṣad 1.3.4).
And likewise: "The one God is hidden in all beings, all-pervading, the inner Self of all beings."
"He is the supervisor of karma, the abode of all beings, the witness, the conscious one, absolute and devoid of qualities" (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 6.11);
and "He has pervaded [all], being radiant, bodiless, unbreathing, without veins, pure, and untouched by evil" (Īśa Upaniṣad 8).
These two mantras demonstrate that Brahman is incapable of having any excellence added to it and is eternally pure;
and since liberation is the state of being Brahman,
liberation cannot be something to be refined by ritual action.
Therefore, no one can point out any other gateway for entering into action toward liberation.
Consequently, apart from knowledge alone, even the slightest trace of action has no place here.
[Objection: But is not what is called "knowledge" a mental action? [Reply: No.
Because of its distinct nature:
for that which is called "action" (kriyā) is indeed enjoined independently of the intrinsic nature of the object, and it is dependent upon the mental activity of the person.
As it is said in such passages as: "One should meditate mentally upon that deity for whom the oblation has been taken,
when about to utter the *vaṣaṭ* call," and "One should meditate upon the twilight mentally" (*AiB* 3.8.1).
Although meditation (dhyāna) is a mental reflection, it can nevertheless be performed, not performed, or performed otherwise by a person,
because it is dependent upon the person.
Knowledge (jñāna), however, is produced by the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa).
And since valid cognition has as its object a thing as it truly is, knowledge cannot be made, not made, or made otherwise; it depends solely on the thing itself,
not on scriptural injunction.
Nor is it dependent on the person;
therefore, even though cognition is mental, there is a great distinction [between it and perception].
And as it is said: "The person, O Gautama, is indeed the fire."
In the passage, "Woman indeed, O Gautama, is the fire" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 5.7.1), the mental conception of woman and man as fire occurs;
because it is produced solely by an injunction, that [conception] is indeed an action and dependent upon the person.

However, the cognition of fire with respect to a well-known fire is neither dependent on scriptural injunction (*codanā*) nor dependent on the person; rather, it is dependent solely on the perceptible object. Thus, this is indeed knowledge (*jñāna*), not an action (*kriyā*).
This should be understood to apply to all objects that are the domain of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
Such being the case, even the knowledge whose object is the *ātman* as Brahman, which exists exactly as it is (*yathābhūta*), is not dependent upon scriptural injunction (*codanā*).

Even when verbal suffixes such as the optative (*liṅ*) and so forth are heard in reference to that [Brahman-ātman], they become blunted because their object is one that cannot be enjoined, just like the sharpness of a razor applied to a stone.

Because its object is a reality that is neither to be abandoned nor to be acquired, what then is the purpose of those statements that have the appearance of injunctions, such as "The Self, indeed, is to be seen, to be heard," and so forth?
We reply: they are for the purpose of turning one away from the objects of natural worldly activity.
For a person who proceeds with an outward orientation, thinking "may what is desired be mine" and "may what is undesired not be mine," does not attain the ultimate human goal therein.

Therefore, for one who desires that ultimate human goal, [the scriptures] turn him away from the sphere of activity involving the natural aggregate of causes and effects and cause him to proceed as a stream directed toward the inner Self, [saying]: "The Self, indeed, my dear, is to be seen."
Such passages as these teach the true nature of the Self— which is neither to be abandoned nor to be acquired— to one who has set out in search of that Self:
"All this is what this Self is" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.4.6).

"Where, however, for him everything has become the Self alone—then by what and whom should one see? By what and whom should one know? O dear one, by what should one know the knower? (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.5.15);
and "This Self is Brahman" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.5.19), and so forth.
As for the claim that the knowledge of the Self, being primarily concerned with what is not to be done, serves neither for rejection nor for acquisition, we accept that very point as it stands.
For this is our ornament: that when the realization of Brahman as the Self occurs, all duties cease and one has accomplished all that was to be done.
And thus says the Śruti: "If a person should know the Self, thinking 'This exists,' desiring what, or for the sake of what desire, would he suffer along with the body?"
"Bhārata, having understood this, one becomes wise and has accomplished all that was to be done" (Bhagavad Gītā 15.20);
such is the Smṛti.
Therefore, Brahman is not presented as the object of an injunction for practice.
As for what some say— that "there is no portion of the Veda which speaks of a mere entity apart from injunctions for engagement or withdrawal and their subsidiaries"— that is not so,
because the person of the Upaniṣads is not subsidiary to anything else.

That person who is understood through the Upanishads alone— the non-transmigrating Brahman, distinct from the four kinds of substances such as produced things and so forth, situated within its own context, non-dual and without remainder—
it cannot be said that "he does not exist" or that "he is not apprehended," for it is said: "This Self is 'not this, not this'" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.9.26).
This follows from the word "it" (iti),
because the self cannot be denied, for whoever is the denier is himself that very self.
