[Objection: But surely it is untenable to say that the Self is known only from the Upaniṣads, since it is the object of the notion of "I. [Reply:
No, because it has been explained as being the witness of that [notion].

Indeed, apart from the agent who is the object of the notion of "I," no person—who is the witness of that [agent], residing in all beings, equal, one, immutably eternal, and stable—has ever been apprehended either in the section on ritual injunctions or in the systems of logic.
Therefore, it cannot be rejected by anyone, nor can it be reduced to a mere subordinate element of ritual injunction.
Precisely because it is the Self (*ātman*) of all, it is neither to be abandoned nor to be acquired.
For every collection of perishable modifications perishes only up to the limit of the Puruṣa.
The person (puruṣa) is indestructible because of the absence of a cause for destruction,
and because of the absence of a cause for modification, he is immutably eternal.
Therefore, its nature is eternally pure, awakened, and liberated.

Hence it is said: "There is nothing higher than the Puruṣa; that is the culmination, that is the supreme goal" (Kaṭha Upaniṣad 1.3.11), and "I ask you about that Puruṣa who is known through the Upaniṣads" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.9.26).
Thus, the qualification "belonging to the Upaniṣads" (aupaniṣada) is appropriate for the Person (puruṣa), as He is revealed as the primary subject matter within the Upaniṣads.
Therefore, the assertion that there is no portion of the Veda concerned with an existing reality (bhūtavastu) is mere temerity.
As for the enumeration by those who know the purport of the scriptures, such as: "For its purpose is seen to be the comprehension of ritual action," and so forth—
Since that [Brahman] is the object of the desire to know its nature (*dharmajijñāsā*), this must be understood as referring to the intention of the scriptures concerning injunctions and prohibitions.

Furthermore, for those who accept with absolute certainty the principle that "because the Veda has action as its purpose, those parts which do not have that [action] as their meaning are useless," there follows the undesirable consequence that teachings about existing entities (*bhūta*) would be useless.
For if the scripture teaches an existing entity apart from injunctions to engage or desist and their subsidiaries, it must do so for the sake of something yet to be accomplished (*bhavya*).
What is the reason for saying that [the scripture] does not teach an eternally immutable reality (*bhūta*)?
For a reality being taught does not become an action (*kriyā*).
If it is argued that even though a reality is non-action, the teaching of reality is solely for the sake of action because it serves as a means to accomplish action; [we reply:]...
This is not a fault;
for even though it has action as its purpose, the reality taught possesses the power to transcend action.
Its purpose, however, is simply to serve as a means for action.
And it is not the case that the reality has not been taught by this much alone. Even if it has indeed been taught, what would that avail you?
It is said in reply: the teaching of the reality of the self, which has not yet been understood, ought to be exactly like that.

By the realization of that [Brahman], the cessation of false knowledge—which is the cause of transmigratory existence—is effected as the purpose; thus, its purposefulness remains established through the instruction on entities that are the means for action.
Furthermore, cessation itself is taught in such injunctions as "A Brahmin must not be killed," and that [cessation] is not an action.
Nor is it a means for accomplishing an action.

If it were argued that the teaching of things that do not have action as their purpose is useless, then it would follow that teachings of abstention, such as "A Brahmin is not to be killed," would be purposeless;
and that is undesirable.

Nor can it be maintained that the negative particle (*nañ*)—through its association with the meaning of "killing" as established by its own nature—is capable of being construed as having the sense of a non-occurring action, apart from the state of indifference consisting in the cessation of the act of killing;
for this is the very nature of the negative particle: that it makes known the non-existence of that which is connected to itself.
And the cognition of non-existence is the cause of indifference;
that [cognition], like a fire whose fuel has been consumed, subsides of its own accord.

Therefore, we consider that in prohibitions such as "A Brāhmaṇa must not be killed," the meaning of the prohibition is simply indifference resulting from the cessation of the action that was previously engaged in.
This is the case except for those [passages] such as the *Prajāpati-trāta* and others.

Therefore, it should be understood that the statement regarding "uselessness" refers to those *arthavādas* which consist of mere descriptions of facts (*bhūtārtha*) that are not conducive to human goals (*puruṣārtha*).

As for what was also said—that a mere fact stated without entering into an injunction of what is to be done would be useless, like the statement "the earth consists of seven islands"—[that too is addressed].
That has already been refuted;
for even in the mere statement of a fact, such as "This is a rope, this is not a snake," a purpose is clearly observed.

Now, it was argued that since one who has heard of Brahman continues to be subject to transmigratory existence just as before, the teaching lacks purpose, just like the statement regarding the nature of the rope.

To this it is replied: It is not possible to show that one who has realized the identity of Brahman and the Self continues to be a transmigrating being as before, because that would contradict the realization of the identity of Brahman and the Self produced by the authority of the Veda.

For although it is observed that one who identifies with the body and so forth possesses suffering, fear, and the like, it cannot be imagined that the very same person, upon attaining the realization of the identity of Brahman and the Self through the authority of the Veda and thereby ceasing that identification, would still possess that same state of possessing suffering, fear, and the like caused by false knowledge.

For it is not observed that the suffering caused by the seizure of wealth belongs to a wealthy householder who possesses pride in his wealth, simply because that same suffering caused by the seizure of wealth occurs for that very person when he has become a renunciant and is devoid of pride in wealth. Nor is it observed that the pleasure caused by the pride of wearing earrings belongs to one who wears earrings, simply because that same pleasure caused by the pride of wearing earrings occurs for that very person when he is separated from the earrings.
This has been stated by the Śruti: "Indeed, while one is embodied, pleasure and pain do not touch him" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.12.1).
If it is argued that the state of being bodiless occurs only when the body has fallen away and not while one is living, we say no.
Because having a body is caused by false knowledge (*mithyājñāna*).

Indeed, apart from false knowledge characterized by the conceit of identifying the Self with the body, it is impossible to conceive of the Self's state of having a body as arising from any other cause.
We have already stated that its eternal bodilessness is due to the fact that it is not caused by karma.
If it is argued that embodiment is caused by dharma and adharma produced by that [self], we say no;
for the connection with a body is unestablished, and thus it remains unestablished that dharma and adharma are produced by the self.

Furthermore, there would be the fallacy of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśrayatva*) regarding the connection with a body, dharma and adharma, and their being produced by that [self]; therefore, this conception of beginninglessness is merely a succession of the blind.
Furthermore, because there is no inherence of action [in the self], agency is untenable for it.
If it is argued that agency is observed in kings and others by virtue of their mere proximity [to the action], we say no;
for in their case, agency is established through their connection with servants acquired by means of granting wealth and other such means.

However, it is not possible to conceive of any basis for the relationship between a body and its owner—such as the giving of wealth and so forth—that applies to the self, in the manner that it does to a person.
Rather, false identification (*mithyābhimāna*) is the perceptible cause of this relationship.
By this, the status of being a sacrificer (*yajamānatva*) of the self is also explained.

Regarding this, they say: "The conceit of 'mine' with respect to the body and so forth—which belong to the self that is distinct from the body and so forth—is figurative (gauṇa) and not false. If this is argued, we say no;
for the distinction between the figurative and the primary is well-established only for one who has a well-known difference between things.
For it is only in the case of one for whom the difference between entities is established...

Just as a specific form possessing a mane and so forth is established through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) as the primary referent of the word and cognition "lion," and another person, distinct from that, is established as being endowed with qualities such as cruelty and valor which are prevalent in a lion— therefore, for that person, the word and cognition "lion" are secondary (*gauṇa*), but not for one who does not recognize a distinction between established entities.
However, in that case, the word and the cognition regarding something else occur solely on account of error and are not figurative.
This is just as, in dim light, when the specific characteristics are not grasped, the word and the cognition "this is a post" have the post as their object;
or as, in the case of mother-of-pearl, there suddenly arise the certain word and cognition "this is silver."

In the same way, how can it be said that the word and the cognition "I" arising with respect to the aggregate of the body and so forth—without any figurative application (nirupacāra)—due to the non-discrimination between the Self and the non-Self, are secondary (gauṇa)?
Even for learned men who discriminate between the Self and the non-Self, the word and the cognition remain undiscriminated, just as they do for goat-herders.
Therefore, for those who maintain the existence of a Self distinct from the body and so forth, the notion of "I" with respect to the body and so forth is purely false (mithyā), not secondary.
Therefore, since embodiedness has false cognition as its cause, it is established that even for the wise person while living, there is bodilessness.
And thus there is a scriptural text concerning the knower of Brahman: "Just as the slough of a snake might lie dead and cast away upon an anthill, even so does this body lie."
"Then this bodiless, immortal life-breath is indeed Brahman, it is indeed radiance" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.7);

and also, "Having eyes, yet as if without eyes; having ears, yet as if without ears; having speech, yet as if without speech; having a mind, yet as if without a mind; having a life-breath, yet as if without a life-breath. And the Smṛti also says: "What is the description of one whose wisdom is steady? (Bhagavad Gītā 2.54).
Thus, by describing the characteristics of one whose wisdom is established (sthitaprajña), [the scripture] demonstrates that the knower has no connection with any worldly activity.
Therefore, for one who has realized the identity of Brahman and the Self, there is no state of transmigratory existence as before.
Conversely, he for whom there is transmigratory existence as before has not realized the identity of Brahman and the Self; thus, the position is faultless.

As for the further argument that because reflection (*manana*) and meditative concentration (*nididhyāsana*) are seen to follow hearing (*śravaṇa*), Brahman is subordinate to an injunction and does not culminate in its own nature—that is not so;
for reflection and meditative concentration have understanding (*avagati*) as their purpose.
For if Brahman, once understood, were employed elsewhere, then it would indeed be subordinate to an injunction.
But that is not the case, because reflection (*manana*) and meditative absorption (*nididhyāsana*), like hearing (*śravaṇa*), also have comprehension as their purpose.

Therefore, it is not possible for Brahman to be established by the authority of scripture as an object of an injunction for realization; hence, Brahman is an independent object of scriptural authority, based on the systematic coherence (*samanvaya*) of the Vedānta texts.

Success! This being the case, the commencement of a separate treatise with the words "Now, therefore, the desire to know Brahman" (athāto brahmajijñāsā) is justified as having that [Brahman] as its subject matter.

For if it were intended merely to enjoin a means of realization, a separate treatise would not be commenced, since [the inquiry into such means] has already been begun with the words "Now, therefore, the desire to know Dharma" (athāto dharmajijñāsā).

And if it were to be commenced in this manner, it would have begun thus: "Now, therefore, follows the inquiry into the remaining duties" (*atha ataḥ pariśiṣṭa-dharma-jijñāsā*), or "Now, therefore, follows the inquiry into that which serves the purpose of the sacrifice and that which serves the purpose of the person" (*atha ataḥ kratvartha-puruṣārthayoḥ jijñāsā*), as in [Jaimini Sūtra] 4.1.1.

However, since the realization of the identity of Brahman and the Self has not been previously promised, the commencement of the scripture for that purpose—namely, "Now, therefore, follows the inquiry into Brahman" (*atha ato brahma-jijñāsā*)—is appropriate.
Therefore, all other objects of knowledge and all other means of valid cognition culminate solely in the realization: "I am Brahman."

For when the non-dual Self—which is neither to be rejected nor to be accepted—is realized, the means of valid cognition (pramāṇas) can no longer exist, as they would then be devoid of objects and devoid of a cognizer (apramātṛkāṇi).

Moreover, they say: "When the secondary self and the false self cease to exist through the sublation of [identities with] the son, the body, and so forth, how could there be any duty (kārya) once there is the realization: 'I am the Being-Brahman-Self'?"
Prior to the realization of the Self that is to be sought, the self possesses the status of a knower;
once sought, it is the knower itself that becomes free from evil, defects, and the like.
"Just as the notion of the body being the self is conceived as a valid means of knowledge,
so too is this worldly means of knowledge valid until the certainty regarding the Self is attained.

Thus ends the group of four aphorisms. [Note: The intention is that the opponent has stated that Brahman is taught as being subsidiary to ritual action; this [section] is for the purpose of refuting that. Anticipating the objection that—just as the *juhū* ladle is subsidiary to the sacrifice by virtue of its completeness—the Self might also be subsidiary to ritual action by virtue of knowledge, and therefore the Vedāntas would be subsidiary to those injunctions, he says: "By what means? (tatkena).]
Subsequent ritual action (*pratipattikarma*) is a subsidiary member (*aṅga*) remaining from the primary ritual action (*pradhānakarma*).
It is, for example, like the offering to Sviṣṭakṛt, the presentation of oblations (*balidāna*), and so forth, performed with that same substance after the principal oblation (*caruhoma*);
or as in the *śrāddha* rite, the casting of the funeral cakes (*piṇḍa*) into the current of the Gaṅgā or another river after the offering of the cakes and worship.

Non-entry is non-connection. The injunction is the mandate for performance; the meaning is that it is the object [of the injunction] by way of delimiting the performance which constitutes its objective domain.
Sacrifice (*yāga*) is the offering of a substance such as a sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) with reference to a deity such as Agni.
It is bodiless and without a physical form; it is beyond the pleasant and unpleasant, pleasure and pain, and what is done and what is left undone.
From the effect that has been made and from the cause that has not been made—
he, Brahmā, knew it; he had understood it.

To him for whom the impurity of passion and the like— which colors the mind like bark-garments and the like— has been rubbed away, washed off, and destroyed by the alkaline water of the practice of knowledge and dispassion;
[to him] who possesses *adhyāsa*, which is the cognition of something as being that which it is not according to scripture,
and *ādeśa*, which is instruction.
At the time of dissolution, the wind envelops and withdraws fire and the other elements; thus it is called "the absorber" (*saṃvarga*).
During the state of sleep, the vital breath (*prāṇa*) withdraws speech and the other senses; thus, by virtue of its connection with the act of withdrawal, it is the "absorber.
That which is "other than" this means it is distinct from the object of knowledge.
Moreover, it is also other than that which is unknown— that is, other than the object of ignorance;
it is that Brahman by which speech is uttered,
or rather, by which speech is manifested and made known through sound.

Because it is the object of cessation (nivṛtti), [the word "dharma" is used]. Even though the Self does not serve as the substratum for its own attributes, the word "dharma" is employed with the intention that there will be an eternal attribute called liberation;
or else, it refers to the essential nature (svarūpa) itself.
The individual soul is one;
it is the fig, the fruit of karma;
it shines forth, that is, it manifests.
The "Supervisor of Karma" is the bestower of the fruits of action.
By the term "pure" (*śukram*), the absence of external impurity is expressed.

Although the denial of bodily defects is already established by the phrases "without wounds" (*avraṇam*) and "without veins" (*asnāviram*), their repeated denial is for the purpose of demonstrating that even the assumption of forms such as a boar through divine play (*līlā*) is not unreal.
And thus it is said: "O Nārada, this is indeed an illusion created by me that you see me as endowed with the qualities of all beings; you ought not to view me in this way.
The term "pure" (*śuddha*) refers to the absence of ignorance (*avidyā*), which is the material cause of the body.
The term "unstruck by evil" (*apāpaviddham*) is used for the sake of its being free from those causes [of sin].
Here, "entry" (*anupraveśa*) means a relationship;
for one becomes a person to be enjoined (*niyojya*) only when they possess the understanding, "This must be done by me."
Furthermore, that which is the object of an injunction (*vidhi*) is something to be accomplished through human effort (*kṛtisādhya*).
Since knowledge is not to be accomplished through effort, the self-knowledge (*ātmajñāna*) is neither of these two; this is the intended meaning.
Those [injunctions] having the "form of an injunction" (*vidhicchāyāni*) are similar to well-known injunctions such as those for sacrifice (*yāga*).
The "stream" (*srotas*) in the inner self (*pratyagātman*) is the flow of mental modifications (*cittavṛtti*).

One is satisfied [thinking], "What was to be done has been done; what was to be attained has been attained"—thus [one is content]. "One should not burn after" means one should not feel remorse as the body is being tormented.
The word "pratipatti" (realization) has as its object only the cognitions whose nature is either valid or invalid. As it is said:
"Because he attains [objects], because he takes [them up], because he eats the objects here, and because his state is continuous, he is therefore called the Ātman. (Ātmapurāṇa).
"The person taught in the Upaniṣads is the object of the notion of 'I';
[he is] distinct from that individual self (jīvātman) which is the agent and the object of the notion of 'I', being conditioned by the aggregate of the body and the senses"—
such are the words of the Bhāṣya.
The "vow of the student" (baṭorvrata), beginning with "One should not look at the rising sun," and so forth, refers to the Prajāpati-vrata.
"Inclusion in an injunction" (vidhyanupraveśa) means connection with an injunction.
The meaning is that because an immutable entity (kūṭastha) cannot be associated with action, it possesses no agency (kartṛtva).
The meaning is: "word" and "verbal cognition.
"Without figurative usage" means without the knowledge of [supreme] qualities;
that is to say, for those who are merely skilled in hearing and reflection—namely, for the learned whose direct realization has not yet arisen.

The sloughed-off skin of a snake (*ahinirlvayanī*)—cast away, deposited, and dead upon an anthill or similar place, abandoned by the snake and devoid of its sense of identity—remains just as it is; this and other such points are to be inferred. Since its purpose is the realization (*avagati*) of Brahman through direct intuition (*sākṣātkāra*), even the offering to Brahman is [included] as a subordinate element (*vidhiśeṣatva*) of that injunction.

Now, regarding the phrase "athātaḥ" (now, therefore): since the relationship between the subordinate (*śeṣa*) and the principal (*śeṣin*) has been established in the third [book] by means of direct scriptural statement (*śruti*) and other criteria, the inquiry—namely, "Who indeed is for the sake of the sacrifice, and who is for the sake of the person?"—proceeds at the beginning of the fourth [book], because it is only through the principal that the application of the subordinate is possible. Therefore, there is no sublation of the object of knowledge (*prameya*) or the knower (*pramātṛ*) by knowledge (*jñāna*).

"Gaumēti" [means]: the identification with the self (*ātma-abhimāna*) regarding one's sons, wife, and so forth, is secondary (*gauṇa*), because in those cases there is an experience of difference. However, regarding the body, senses, and so forth, it is not secondary because there is an experience of non-difference; rather, it is false (*mithyā*).

If both of these selves were non-existent— namely, if the secondary self (gauṇātman) were non-existent, there would be the sublation of son, wife, and so forth; and if the illusory self (mithyātman) were non-existent, there would be the sublation of the body, senses, and so forth—
then how could the maintenance of worldly affairs, the realization that "I am the existent Brahman," and the direct intuition of non-duality (advaita-sākṣātkāra) possibly occur?

From the knowledge of the Self that is to be sought— namely, "that Self which is free from evil" is what must be sought— it follows that prior to that realization, the self possesses the status of a knower (*mātṛ*) and there exists the distinction between the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), the object of knowledge (*prameya*), and the act of knowing (*pramā*). Therefore,
the meaning is that in the absence of those [distinctions], the effect [of realization] does not arise.

"From self-certainty" means up to the direct realization of the nature of Brahman. Regarding the doubt—whether the Vedāntas concern the already-established Brahman or concern an action to be performed—arising from the respective consequences of fruitlessness and dependence on other means, the author states the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) by way of an objection following the second interpretation in the previous sūtra, beginning with the words "But how... and so forth.

Because the concordance (*samanvaya*) of passages such as "Existence alone, my dear" (*sadeva somya*), which possess clear marks of Brahman such as being the Self of all, has been stated with respect to Brahman,
the connections (*saṃgati*) with the Śruti and so forth are established.
In the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), the engagement of those seeking liberation (*mumukṣu*) in the Vedāntas would not be established.
The distinction is that its establishment occurs in the final system (siddhānta). To the objection "How so? the reason is given by the phrase "as far as" (yāvatā).

Since the Jaimini-sūtra has shown that the scripture—the Veda—is intent upon action (kriyā), it follows [by implication] that because the Vedāntas do not have action as their purpose, they would be useless, meaning they are devoid of any fruitful meaning; such is the syntactical connection.

This is the meaning of the Sūtra: First, in the first Sūtra, it was stated that the Veda—being the object to be brought about (*bhāvya*) by the injunction (*vidhi*) whose instrument (*karaṇa*) is the act of study (*adhyayana*)—has as its purpose a meaningful result.

In the second Sūtra, "Dharma is a matter characterized by an injunction" (*codanā-lakṣaṇo ’rtho dharmaḥ*), it was determined that since an injunction is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) regarding Dharma as something to be accomplished (*kārya*), the Veda’s authority is pervaded by the fact that it has as its purpose what is to be done (*kārya-paratva*).
In this regard, there arises a doubt: do the explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) such as "Vāyu is indeed the swiftest" possess authority regarding Dharma, or not?

Since the authority of the Vedic tradition (*āmnāya*) is pervaded by its being for the sake of action (*kriyārthatva*), and since no dharma is perceived in the explanatory passages (*arthavādas*), those passages which do not aim at action are purposeless—

that is, they have fruitless meaning. Furthermore, it is not logical that those [passages] included under the injunction to study (*adhyayana-vidhi*) should possess authority regarding a fruitless, established matter.
Therefore, their authority is said to be non-eternal;
that is to say, due to the absence of the pervader (vyāpaka), the pervaded (vyāpya) authority simply does not exist.

Thus, even regarding the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*), he states the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) by means of the sūtra: "But because they form a single syntactical unit with an injunction, they [the mantras] serve the purpose of praising the injunctions"—namely, that they have action as their ultimate goal (*kriyāparatva*).
The meaning is that [the purpose of the explanatory passage] is shown when [the injunction] has been reached as "it is impermanent.
Wind is indeed the deity that moves most swiftly; therefore, a ritual action dedicated to that deity will bestow its fruit very quickly.

In this way, because they form a single syntactical unit with injunctive sentences such as "One should sacrifice a white animal to Vāyu," the explanatory passages (arthavādas) become fruitful by means of their function as praise for the objects to be enjoined.
Insofar as they are directed toward fruitful action by way of praise (*stuti*), explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) are authoritative; this is the meaning.
Now, one might object that it is not proper for the Vedāntas, which are included within the injunction to study the Veda, to be purposeless. To this he says: "The agent," etc.

We do not seek to prove the purposelessness of the Vedāntas; rather, [we argue that] in common worldly experience, there is no other means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) for what is already established, and because such a thing would be fruitless.

We maintain that if those [Vedic statements] were concerned solely with established Brahman, they would result in either dependence on other means of knowledge or fruitlessness, which would lead to their lack of authority; therefore, it must be said that they are concerned with the "task" (kārya) by way of revealing the agent, deity, and fruit that are subordinate to that task.
In that regard, however, sentences whose primary referent is an existing entity (siddha-padārtha) serve to praise the agent and the deity.
The sentences beginning with "the desire to know" (vividiṣā) serve as praises of the fruit [of action].

Now, one might object: since the Vedānta texts are studied in a different context without reference to any specific ritual action, how can they be subordinate to that [action]? For there is no evidence for this. Anticipating this dissatisfaction, the author states another position: "meditation" (upāsanā).

The meaning is that the injunction for meditation (upāsanā-vidhi) states: "One who desires liberation, having superposed non-difference between the unreal [individual self] and Brahman, should meditate [upon it], thinking 'I am Brahman'";
and by the word "etcetera" (ādi), hearing (śravaṇa) and so forth are included.
Alternatively, it must be stated that [the Upanishads] have as their purport that which is to be accomplished by that [meditation].

[Objection: But surely, having set aside the heard (śruta) Brahman, for what purpose should the unheard state of being intent on action (kāryaparatva) be stated? To this he says: "Not indeed" (na hi).
"Pariṣṭhitam" means standing firmly on all sides, determinedly, independent of any duty to be performed;
that is to say, it is established (siddha).

Its "establishment" (pratipādana) consists in making known through the Veda what was previously unknown; that is not possible, because when a sentence corresponds with an object that is capable of being known by other means of knowledge, it is merely repetitive (anuvādaka).

The meaning is that, like the sentence "Fire is the remedy for cold," [the Veda] possesses the quality of being informative; however, in the case of contradiction, it lacks this quality, like the sentence "The sacrificial post is the sun."

Having stated that the meaning of the Veda is not something already established because it is capable of being known through other means of knowledge— just like a jar— he says "likewise" (*tathā*) because it would also be fruitless.
The meaning is that since it does not concern what is to be avoided or pursued, there would be no result [in knowing it], and thus that [status of being already established] is impossible.
For the fruit is indeed the pervasion of happiness and the abandonment of suffering;
and that is to be accomplished through engagement and withdrawal.

These two, moreover, arise from the cognitions of that which is to be adopted—which is the effect of the effort of engagement—and that which is to be rejected—which is the effect of the effort of withdrawal.
The sense is that [the Veda] does not result from the knowledge of an accomplished being (*siddha*).

Then, anticipating the objection as to how the teachings of the Vedas—which convey the knowledge of accomplished beings—can have any efficacy, he explains the summary statement beginning with "of the tradition" (*āmnāyasya*) with the words "for this very reason" (*ata eva*).
The meaning is: precisely because there is no fruit resulting from the knowledge of an already-accomplished entity.

The meaning is that, just as the sentence "That fire, obstructed by the gods, wept" serves as a supplement to the prohibition of giving silver on the sacrificial grass (*barhis*)—by way of censuring silver through its being born of tears—the Vedāntas must likewise be stated to be supplements to injunctions and the like. Now, one might object: "Let them have independence like mantras; let them not be in syntactic unity with an injunction like an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*. Anticipating this doubt, he states that the example is unestablished: "And of the mantras... [and so forth].

In the first chapter, following the consideration of *arthavāda* within the definition of the means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa-lakṣaṇa*), the consideration of *mantra* was undertaken: since the action of cutting a branch is understood through the ellipsis (*adhyāhāra*) of "I cut" in the mantra "For food, thee" (*iṣe tvā*), and since deities and other means of action are understood in such [mantras] as "Agni is the head" (*agnirmūrdhā*), it follows that mantras are employed in the sacrifice by means of direct scriptural injunction (*śruti*) and so forth.
Do these mantras assist the sacrifice by producing an unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*) through mere recitation, or rather, by the visible means of reminding one of the ritual purpose?

When it is argued that mantras have an unseen purpose (*adṛṣṭārtha*) because—even through reflection and so forth during doubt—it is possible to remember the meaning of a mantra understood at the time of study, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is as follows: "But the meaning of the sentence is not different" (JS 1.2.40). Since there is no difference between worldly and Vedic sentences regarding their meaning, it is possible for mantra-sentences to assist the sacrifice through their visible function alone, namely, the manifestation of their own meaning.
Since it is improper to postulate an unseen factor when a seen one is possible,

the status of mantras as auxiliary elements of ritual action is established through the medium of the recollection of the action and its means, which is required for the performance that yields the fruit.
The restrictive rule (niyama) that "the object must be remembered by means of mantras alone" serves an unseen purpose.

Thus, the distinction is as follows: explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) form a syntactic unity with injunctions (*vidhi*) through the mediation of the meaning of the words used for praise, whereas mantras form a syntactic unity with them through the mediation of the knowledge of the sentence-meaning.
Now, let it be granted that sentences occurring within the context of ritual action (*karmaprakaraṇa*) form a syntactic unity with injunctions; however—
To the objection, "Why should the Vedāntas not possess validity regarding an established entity (siddha)? he replies: "Nowhere...
The Vedāntas are meaningful only as being in syntactic unity with injunctions (vidhi), because they do not convey an already established fact.
The meaning is: "like the case of mantras, arthavādas, and so forth.

To the objection that [the principle] might be postulated in the Vedāntas even though it is not seen elsewhere, he replies: "Or it is appropriate" (*upapannā vā*). The word "not" (*na*) is to be supplied [from the previous context].
The meaning is that it has already been stated that there is no purpose for an injunction regarding something already established.

[Objection: In that case, let an injunction be postulated with respect to Brahman itself as its own object; what is the use of making the Vedāntas subordinate to another injunction? To this, he says: "And not... [Objection: But surely an injunction is seen regarding an already established curd in the statement, "One offers with curd" (*dadhnā juhoti*). To this, he says: "Action... (*kriyā...*) [and so forth].

The meaning is that because curd, as a means for an action, is being employed, it is something to be accomplished (sādhya) and therefore subject to injunction; however, since Brahman, being devoid of action, cannot be accomplished by any means whatsoever, it is not subject to injunction. He concludes the Bhaṭṭa school's position with the words "Therefore" (tasmāt).
Expressing his own lack of approval, he states an alternative view with the word "atha.
He explains the aphorism of the established conclusion (siddhānta-sūtra) with the words "the word 'tu' [but].
He asks for the reason regarding the thesis that "that Brahman has the Vedānta as its means of valid cognition" with the word "how?"
He states the reason: "Because" (*samiti*).
Therefore, the reason is simply "because it is the object of the purport of the positive concomitance" (*anvayatātparyaviṣayatvam*).
The prefix *sam-* is included within the proposition itself to indicate that the correctness of the purport consists in its having an indivisible entity as its object (*akhaṇḍārthaviṣayakatvam*).
And thus, undivided Brahman is the object of the valid cognition arising from the recitation of the Vedāntas,
because it is the object of the purport of the Vedāntas;
for whatever is the object of the purport of a particular statement is the object of the valid knowledge produced by that statement.
For example, the formal argument is: "Dharma is that which is to be known through the sentence-meaning.
The indivisibility (*akhaṇḍatva*) of the sentence-meaning is its non-composite nature (*asaṃsṛṣṭatva*).

And the capacity of a sentence to have an indivisible meaning consists in its producing a valid cognition whose object is the relation among those word-meanings which are presented by their respective words.

Nor is this [point] unestablished; for in common worldly usage, definitional sentences such as "the moon is the most excellent light" function as causes for the valid cognition of the mere individual entity of the moon and so forth through indication (*lakṣaṇā*). Furthermore, the indication of all words is not contradictory, since it is accepted that a single eulogy is the object indicated by all the words of an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*).
Thus, since Brahman appears as an undivided whole through words such as "truth" (satya) and "knowledge" (jñāna), there is no lack of proof regarding the subject (*pakṣāsiddhi*).

Nor is there a lack of proof regarding the reason (*hetvasiddhi*), because the purport of the Vedāntas is determined to be the non-dual, undivided Brahman by means of indicators such as the introductory passages (*upakrama*) and so forth.
In the sixth chapter of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad, it shows the introduction: "Being alone," etc.
Uddālaka said to his son: "O Somya, O one of pleasing appearance, all this world..."
Before its origination, in the prior time, there was only Brahman, which is real and uncontradicted.
By the word "eva" (only), the separate existence of the world is negated.
The three words "eka," "eva," and "advitīyam" are intended to exclude respectively any distinction of the same kind, of a different kind, and internal difference.
Having thus introduced Brahman as non-dual, [the scripture] concludes with "All this has that as its self.
This uniformity between the introduction and the conclusion is an indicator of the intended meaning (*tātparya*),
just as in the case of "That thou art."
Thus there is a repetition nine times.

The "novelty" (apūrvatva) of the non-dual Brahman, which is devoid of form and so forth and is inaccessible to other means of knowledge, has been stated: "In this very place, my dear, you do not perceive that which truly exists.
The meaning is: "You do not know the innermost Brahman residing within the aggregate [of the body and organs]."
"For him there is delay only so long as he is not released; then he shall attain [Brahman]"—thus is the fruit for the knower stated through the knowledge of Brahman.
For him, the delay lasts only as long as his body is not released; that is, until the fall of the body.
Then, immediately after the fall of the body, the knower attains Brahman.
The meaning is that they experience disembodied liberation (*videhakaivalya*).
Passages such as "having entered by means of this living self" are explanatory statements (*arthavāda*) intended to convey the knowledge of non-duality.
Through analogies such as clay and so forth, the logical justification has been stated that there is no modification apart from the material cause (*prakṛti*).

Thus, these six kinds of indicators of purport (tātparya-liṅga) are seen, either individually or collectively, in each Vedānta text. He recites the opening statement of the Aitareya Upaniṣad: "The Self, verily... In the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad, the concluding statement of the Madhu-kāṇḍa speaks of the true Self as being devoid of distinctions: "That is this...
That Brahman appears in many forms through its powers of illusion (māyā).
This is immediate;
it is unprecedented, being devoid of a cause;
it is unsurpassed, being free from an effect.
"Anantara" means that there is no other state of birth for it;
the meaning is that it is of a single flavor (*ekarasa*). "Abāhya" means it is without a second.
He establishes its immediacy with the word "this" (ayam).
It is the "experiencer of all" (sarvānubhūḥ) because it experiences everything;
the meaning is that it is pure consciousness (cinmātra).
Having stated the sentences of the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma Vedas, he states the sentence of the Atharva Veda: "Brahman alone is this" (*brahmaivedam*).
The meaning is that whatever collection of objects in the eastern direction appeared previously as if it were non-Brahman to the ignorant, that very thing is the immortal Brahman, the sole reality.
By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), sentences such as "Truth, Knowledge" (*satyaṃ jñānam*) and so forth are included.
"Granted that Brahman is the object of the [Upanishads'] purport, why could the meaning of the Vedāntas not be simply *kārya* (something to be done)? To this he replies: "Not so.

The meaning is that when the purport of the Vedāntas is determined to be Brahman, it is not logical for their meaning to be *kārya*, according to the maxim: "That toward which a word is directed is the meaning of that word."
Regarding the claim that the Vedānta texts function as glorifications of the agent and so forth according to the principle of *arthavāda*, he says: "And not of those...

It does not appear that they serve as glorifications of what remains subordinate to ritual action; rather, through the means of knowledge (*jñāna*), they serve precisely to destroy that action along with its instruments.
The meaning is that this is based on the Śruti passage: "At that time of knowledge, who is the agent, by what instrument, and upon what object would one see?"

The point is that since explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) lack a fruit in their own literal sense, they possess the character of praise (*stuti*). Regarding the claim that Brahman—being an established entity—is cognizable by other means of knowledge and thus cannot be the subject matter of the Veda, he says: "Nor [is it known] by other...
This is to be connected with the phrase "without the scripture [saying] 'That thou art'."
Dharma is not the meaning of the Veda, because, like cooking, it is cognizable through other means of knowledge by virtue of being something to be accomplished (*sādhya*).
If it is argued that dharma is not cognizable through other means of knowledge because it cannot be determined without the Veda, then the same applies to Brahman as well.
Having restated the argument that Brahman is not the meaning of the Vedas because it is fruitless, he refutes it with the words beginning "But as for... and so forth.
[The reasons are] "because of being devoid" and "because of being distinct"; the word "of Brahman" is to be supplied as the remainder.

As for what was also stated—that "the Vedāntas have meditation as their primary purport"—in that regard, does this apply to sentences concerning the vital breath (prāṇa), the five fires (pañcāgni), and so forth, or to all of them? Regarding this, he accepts the first position with the words "deity and so forth.
The meaning of the word "and so forth" (ādi) includes qualities such as being the eldest (jyeṣṭhatva) and the resulting fruit.
Not the second [alternative],

because it is impossible to assume that statements such as "Truth, Knowledge" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.1), which are devoid of injunctions and are fruitful in their own sense, have meditation as their purport. Furthermore, regarding the Brahman that is their object, would its being subordinate to them occur prior to knowledge or subsequent to it?
Regarding the first [case], although that [Self] which possesses superimposed qualities may be subordinate to them, it is not so in the second case; thus he says, "but not in that way.
The meaning is: like the deities of the vital breaths (prāṇa) and so forth.
"I am Brahman."

He says "in oneness" (ekatve) to show that when oneness is known, since the Self as Brahman is devoid of anything to be abandoned or acquired, there is no fruit [to be attained]; and because the cause—the knowledge of duality between the object of meditation and the meditator—is destroyed, meditation cannot remain as a residual duty.

He says "not so" (na hi) to refute the claim that there might be an injunction for meditation even if the knowledge of duality were to arise again through the force of its latent impressions (saṃskāra).
The word "of the firm" is to be supplied as the remainder [of the sentence].
Firmness is the absence of certainty regarding its being an error;
however, that which arises from mental impressions (saṃskāra) is not a cause for an injunction when it is certain to be an error.
"By which" means by the existence of a cause for the act of worship.
He restates that being for the purpose of action is the pervader of the Veda's authority— beginning with "even though."
The meaning is that [this applies] to the explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) and so forth within the ritual section (*karmakāṇḍa*).

Thus, the intention is that since the pervader is absent, there is an inference of the absence of the pervaded in the Vedāntas. [Therefore,] the Vedāntas are not a means of valid cognition with respect to their own subject matter.

Regarding the inference that [the Vedas] lack injunctive purpose because they are like [passages such as] "He wept," he states "Nevertheless" (tathāpi) to show that "futility of purpose" is a limiting condition (upādhi).

The meaning is: even though the explanatory passages (arthavādas) do not have a fruitless meaning as their own object, [the same applies to] that which has them as its object—that is, the instrument [of knowledge] directed toward them.
The phrase "in its own meaning" has "Brahman, which is the Self," as its ellipsis.

The sense is that since the Vedāntas are established as authoritative with respect to their own meaning by virtue of being the instrument for knowledge that bears fruit, "having action as its purpose" cannot be their pervader (i.e., a necessary condition).
Now, it may be argued: let it be that having action as its purpose is not the pervader of Vedic authority; [but what then?]
"But the pervaded [object] will exist;
therefore, because of its non-existence, the meaning of the Vedāntas is difficult to know," [to this he says]:
"No," with the words "na ca" (and not).
The meaning is that there is no such instance elsewhere where the authority of the Veda is established through being cognizable by inference, which would require an observed example (*dṛṣṭānta*).
Because the Veda’s own authority is known intrinsically (*svataḥ*), like the eye and other senses, it does not depend upon a logical mark (*liṅga*) or the like characterized by pervasion (*vyāpti*).

However, in the case of doubt regarding its authority, certainty of authority arises from the fact that its purport concerns an uncontradicted object that is conducive to a result (*phalavat*), and not merely from its having action as its purpose.
The intention is that there is an inconsistency (vyabhicāra) in the statement "he might fall into a well.
He concludes the meaning of the syllables with the words "therefore" (tasmāt); the meaning is "because of the harmony" (samanvayāt).
It is established that even injunctive sentences possess authority because their meaning is unknown and they lead to a result; the same applies to the Vedāntas.

Thus, the view of those atheists who maintain that words have their linguistic competency regarding an already accomplished entity is [rejected], because Brahman is not accessible through other means of knowledge.

Furthermore, by stating that [Brahman] is cognizable solely through Vedanta because of its fruitfulness, [the objection] has been refuted. Now, another exposition of the Sutra is commenced in order to refute the view of the Vṛttikāras— who, desiring all words to have their power directed toward an object associated with an action (kāryānvita), maintain that the inner Brahman is taught by the Vedantas as a subordinate element of an injunction (vidhiśeṣatva) and not independently.

In this regard, there arises a doubt as to whether the Vedāntas teach Brahman as being subordinate to injunctions for meditation (*upāsanā-vidhi*), or rather independently; this doubt stems from the presence or absence of linguistic competency (*vyutpatti*) regarding an already established entity. The author states the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*): "Here others [say]... The meaning is that the Commentators (*vṛttikāra*) present the prima facie view when it is stated that Brahman is to be known through the Vedāntas.
In the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), liberation results from meditative worship (*upāsanā*);
in the established conclusion (*siddhānta*), it results solely from the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*). This is the fruit [of the discussion].
The injunction (*vidhi*) is the mandate (*niyoga*); its object is the practice of realization, namely, meditative worship.

In response to the inquiry, "What is the scope of this [injunction]?", he states that Brahman is presented by sentences such as "That thou art" precisely through their being intent upon injunction—meaning, by virtue of being the object of the comprehension that constitutes the scope of an injunction. He provides an illustration for how Brahman is obtained as a subordinate element of a sentence primarily intent upon injunction: "Just as... and so forth.

In the injunctions, "He binds the animal to the sacrificial post (yūpa)," "He offers in the Āhavanīya fire," and "One should sacrifice to Indra," when there arises the expectancy as to what the sacrificial post and so forth are, [the answer is]: the wood prepared by rites such as carving—expressed in "He carves the post; he makes it eight-cornered"—is the *yūpa*.
The fire prepared by the rite of installation (*ādhāna*), expressed in "One should install the fires," is the *Āhavanīya*.

The meaning is that just as [attributes] such as "Vajrahasta" (the wielder of the thunderbolt) and "Purandara" (the destroyer of cities) are presented by sentences primarily intended for injunctions, so too is Brahman.

The word "api" (also/even) is used to dispel the doubt that if a sentence primarily intended for an injunction were to convey another meaning as well, there would be a split in the sentence (*vākyabheda*). Since even those things not known through other means of knowledge are mentioned as subordinate elements (*śeṣa*) and not as the primary subject, there is no split in the sentence.
The sense is that it is precisely the difference in the primary meaning that constitutes a split in the sentence (*vākya-bheda*).

Now, one might object: "By means of the sixfold marks (*liṅga*) mentioned above, how can Brahman—the subject matter of the intended meaning—be a subordinate element (*śeṣa*) to an injunction? Thus he asks: "Why?
For the determination of the intended meaning of a scripture is indeed established through the linguistic usage of elders (*vṛddha-vyavahāra*).
Furthermore, in the linguistic usage of elders, the unprecedented application of words is observed with a view toward the listener’s engagement or withdrawal [from action].
Therefore, these two alone are the purposes of the treatise as well.
And since these two are produced by the knowledge of what is to be done (*kārya*), the treatise has "the state of being directed toward what is to be done" (*kāryaparatva*) as its primary aim.

Therefore, he states that Brahman is the "remainder of what is to be done" with the words "in activity," etc. He cites the consensus of the elders regarding the fact that the scripture has *niyoga* (the mandate) as its primary purport, beginning with the words "for it is not so," etc.
[The terms] *kriyā* (action), *kārya* (what is to be done),...
*Niyoga*, *vidhi*, *dharma*, and *apūrva* are synonymous.
When the question arises as to what the meaning of the Veda is, the author of the Śābara-bhāṣya stated: "For [it] is seen," and so forth.
Regarding that Veda, he cites the commentary from the *Codanā-sūtra* on the point that "the effect [of the Veda] is the meaning of the Veda": "An injunction (*codanā*)," etc.
The meaning is that an injunctive statement which impels one toward action through the mediation of knowledge is called an injunction.

Having stated the opinion of Śabarasvāmin, he states the opinion of Jaimini: "The knowledge of that. The meaning is that the instruction (*upadeśa*), which is the non-human (authorless) injunctive sentence, is the indicator (*jñāpaka*) of that dharma, because it is not distinct from dharma.

Regarding the view that words possess their power (*śakti*) with respect to meanings associated with an action (*kārya*), he cites the aphorism: "Of those [words] which have occurred therein... This means that in the Veda, there must be a recitation—that is, a simultaneous utterance—of words established as referring to accomplished entities (*siddhārtha*), together with a word expressing an action (*kriyārtha*), such as an optative suffix (*liṅ*) which denotes what is to be done (*kārya*). This is because the knowledge of the meaning of individual words is the cause for the cognition of the action that constitutes the sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha*).

The meaning is that words are capable of denoting objects associated with an action, and together with a word expressing an action, they bring about the understanding of the action itself as the sentence-meaning by means of the recollection of individual word-meanings. He states the conclusion: "Therefore," because the elders have spoken thus.
Therefore, only the sentences consisting of injunctions and prohibitions constitute the scripture (*śāstra*);
the explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) and so forth, however, are exhausted as being subordinate to them.
Thus, through that scripture of ritual action (*karma-śāstra*), it possesses the common characteristic of being a scripture.
Therefore, the meaning is that the Vedāntas must possess purposefulness solely by having an injunction as their purport.
Now, one might object: "Since neither a person to be enjoined (niyojya) nor a prescribed action (vidheya) is observed in the Vedāntas, how can there be a cognition of an action to be performed?
To this, he says: "And when [the Self] exists," and so forth.

But surely, by the authors of the sūtras for the inquiry into Dharma and the inquiry into Brahman, a difference in subject matter has been stated here in these two sections, since a division of the scripture would be untenable if they had a single purpose.
In that case, given the difference in the objects of inquiry in the two sections, a distinction in their respective fruits must be asserted.

And thus, knowledge is not something to be enjoined for the sake of the fruit of liberation; for if liberation were produced by an action subject to injunction, it would follow that it is no different from the fruit of ritual action (karman), and if there were no difference, the distinction between the objects of inquiry (jijñāsya) would be unestablished.

Therefore, since liberation is eternally established and distinct from the fruits of ritual action, the injunction of knowledge as its manifestor is improper—this is the objection raised in the words "But here... (nanviheti).
It cannot be argued that the distinction between liberation (*mukti*) and the fruit of ritual action (*karmaphala*) is unestablished, and therefore knowledge must be enjoined for that purpose;

nor can it be said that, in that case, only fruitful action would be the object of inquiry even among those who study the Vedas, resulting in the non-establishment of their difference, for this is actually desired.
Furthermore, there is no contradiction with the aphorism (*sūtra*) stating that Brahman is the object of inquiry.
He provides the rebuttal—“No”—on the grounds that the author of the Sūtras establishes Brahman as being subsidiary to the injunction for knowledge.
He clarifies that Brahman is not prompted by an injunction with the words, “The Self, verily...
It should be understood that in the passage “One who knows Brahman,” the injunction is transformed to mean: “One who desires the state of Brahman should perform the knowledge of Brahman.”
The world is of the nature of knowledge.
He shows the very meaning of the Vedāntas themselves by saying "eternal.
Now, one might ask: what is the fruit of the injunction? To that he says: "from the meditation upon That."

The meaning is that liberation, as taught in the scripture—“The knower of Brahman attains the Supreme”—is the fruit resulting from the meditation on the inner Brahman (*pratyagbrahman*), even though it is not as well-known in the world as heaven. He states the counter-argument against not accepting that Brahman is subordinate to an injunction regarding the meditation to be performed: "If [it were] not to be performed," etc. The meaning is that if there were a cognition of an already established entity unconnected to an injunction, there would be no result such as engagement in action, and thus the Vedāntas would be rendered futile.
The doubt expressed by "nanu" (surely) has a clear meaning.
He refutes it by pointing out the disparity between the example and the case at hand—using the word "syāt" (it might be).
The meaning is: "If it were so, then this [example] would indeed possess purpose."
Thus he states the meaning of the word "this" (yat):
furthermore, if liberation were to arise from knowledge alone, then there would be no injunction for reflection and so forth subsequent to the knowledge produced by hearing;
and since there is such an injunction, he states that liberation is to be accomplished through action: "It is to be heard."
Because words possess the capacity to denote things as connected to an action,
because only that which results in activity and so forth constitutes a treatise (śāstra), and because there is an absence of such a result in the case of an already established entity.
He concludes the prima facie view— that the Vedāntas are directed toward action because of injunctions such as "one should reflect" (manana)— with the words "Therefore" (tasmāt).

The Vedāntas do not have injunctions as their primary purpose, because, while possessing a fruit in their own literal sense, they lack a person to be enjoined (niyojya), just like the sentence "This is not a snake."

He establishes the final position— that two qualifications are attached to the reason in order to exclude the two statements, "He wept" and "One desiring heaven should sacrifice"— with the word "here.
He says "no" to the claim that knowledge is the enjoined duty for one who desires liberation as the person to be impelled (niyojya).
Liberation is not produced by ritual injunctions,
because it is distinct from the fruit of karma,
just like the Self; this is the meaning.

In order to explain the knowledge of the causes already mentioned, he elaborates upon karma and its fruit with the passage beginning "the bodily" and ending with "he reiterates the cycle of existence (saṃsāra) as described.
Now—"after the study of the Vedas";
"therefore"—because the Veda is intent upon a fruitful purpose.
The meaning of the aphorism is that an investigation of ritual injunctions (*karmavākya*) must be undertaken for the sake of determining what is Dharma.
He says, "and also Adharma," to show that it is not only the action called Dharma, but Adharma as well;
the meaning is that this is established by the authority of prohibitory statements (*niṣedhavākya*).
Having stated the action, he states the result with the words "of those two" (*tayoḥ*).

Liberation (*mokṣa*), however, is beyond the senses, free from sorrow, not an object of enjoyment for the body and so forth, not produced by sense-objects and so forth, and is not well-known even to non-self-knowers; thus, the qualifiers such as "perceptible" (*pratyakṣa*) and so on are used to indicate its distinction [from ordinary results].
Having stated the fruit of action in general, he elaborates separately upon the fruit of merit (*dharma*) with the words "humanity and so forth" (*manuṣyatvādi*).

"That is one human bliss, Ānanda; from that, the bliss of the Gandharvas and others is a hundredfold"—the meaning of the word "anu" (following) in this scriptural passage is that it conforms to experience.
And therefore, the meaning is: "due to the gradation of happiness."

Liberation, however, is unsurpassed, and its means—knowledge of reality—is of a single uniform nature; this constitutes the distinction. Furthermore, the qualified seeker of liberation with respect to ignorance is exclusively one who is endowed with the fourfold prerequisites.
He states the distinction by saying "in action, however, it is of various kinds," namely "dharma" and so forth;
the meaning is that it is not only understood [by inference], but is also well-known.
"Desire" (arthitva) means the longing for a result.

Worldly capacity consists of sons and so forth; by the word "and so forth," learning and being irreproachable according to the scriptures are also included. Furthermore, the fruit of action is that which is to be attained through the path.
He states the distinction that liberation is eternally attained by saying "likewise" (*tathā*).

The meaning is that through the excellence of mental steadiness in worship, one's journey to the world of Brahmā via the path of light (*arciḥ*) and so forth is heard of in the scripture beginning with "They [go] to the light" (*te 'rciṣam*). [Furthermore:
"The Agnihotra sacrifice, austerity, truth, and the preservation of the Vedas;..."
The rites of hospitality and the Vaiśvadeva sacrifice are designated as *iṣṭa*.
The construction of ponds, wells, tanks, and so forth, as well as temples for deities,
the gift of food, and groves— this is designated as *pūrta* (meritorious works).
Protecting those who have come for refuge, non-violence toward living beings,
and whatever gift is given outside the sacrificial altar— this is designated as "given" (datta).

"In that case as well" means even in the world of the moon (*candraloka*). "Saṃpāta" refers to action (*karman*), because by means of it one "falls together" (*saṃpatati*)— that is, goes— from this world to that world.
The meaning is that they remain there for as long as the karma to be experienced lasts, and then return again.
Having described the gradations of happiness among those who have gone upwards from the human state, he now speaks of those who have gone downwards—beginning with "In the same way.
Now, while stating the gradations of suffering, its causes, and those who practice them, he elaborates upon the fruit of unrighteousness (adharma)—beginning with "And likewise upwards."
He concludes the detailed exposition of the two kinds of karmic fruits, intended to make known their distinct characteristics from liberation, with the word "thus" (*evam*).
The meaning of the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) includes egoism (*asmitā*), desire, anger, and fear.
There is also the Smṛti passage beginning with: "Having abandoned him, they [attain] the vast world of heaven."
Since an increase in flame is observed to result from an increase in fuel-wood,
it is a logical principle (*nyāya*) that one may infer a gradation in the means (*sādhana*) based on a gradation in the results (*phala*).
He states the scriptural authority (*śruti*) with the words "And thus" (*tathā ca*).

Liberation is not the fruit of action, because it possesses attributes such as being contrary to the fruit of action, being beyond the senses, being free from sorrow, and being incapable of being experienced by the body and so forth; this is established by inference through the method of difference (*vyatireka*), like heaven and other such rewards. He cites the scripture supported by this reasoning: "The bodiless... and so on.
The word *vāva* is used for emphasis.
The meaning is that the Self, being in reality bodiless (*videha*), is not touched at all by the pleasure and pain associated with sense objects.
If liberation were the fruit of a dharma consisting of meditative worship (*upāsanā*), [then it would be subject to decay].
He states that "dharmakāryatve hi" (for if it were the effect of dharma) because it would be improper to negate that very thing which is dear [to us].
Now, one might object: what is called "the dear" is indeed sensual pleasure (*vaiṣayika-sukha*), and that is what is being negated;
however, liberation (*mokṣa*) is itself the fruit of dharma.
He raises an objection based on the capacity of actions to produce diverse results—namely, that there is indeed "bodilessness" (*aśarīratvam*).
Bodilessness is the soul's lack of attachment to a body;
since this is beginningless, it cannot be produced by action. To this he replies: "No."
It is bodiless, devoid of a gross body;
it is the one eternal reality abiding within many impermanent bodies;
it is great and all-pervading.
He precludes [the notion of] relative greatness by using the word "all-pervasive" (vibhu).

The meaning is that having known that Self, the wise person does not experience transmigratory existence, which is characterized by sorrow. He cites scripture regarding the absence of the subtle body: "without breath" (aprāṇa).
Because the powers of action and knowledge belonging to the vital breath (prāṇa) and the mind (manas) are negated,
and since the organs of action and knowledge are dependent upon them, they too are negated;
therefore, the meaning is that [the Self] is pure.
Regarding the absence of the two bodies, there is the scriptural text: "For [the Self] is unattached.
Since it has been established that liberation, which is the nature of the bodiless Self, is an eternal entity (anādibhāva), he states the conclusion: "Therefore, indeed.

Anticipating the objection that even if it is eternal, liberation might still be an effect of attributes (dharmakāryatva) due to its being subject to modification, he divides the eternal into two kinds: "Among these, some... and so forth.
The meaning is "in the midst of eternal entities.
That which is both subject to transformation (*pariṇāmin*) and eternal is called "transformative-eternal" (*pariṇāminitya*).
However, since the Self (*ātman*) is unchangingly eternal (*kūṭasthanitya*), it cannot be accomplished through action; thus he says: "But this," etc.
The permanence of that which undergoes transformation (*pariṇāmin*) is merely false, being constructed by recognition (*pratyabhijñā*).
However, for that which is immutable (*kūṭastha*), permanence is ultimate because of the absence of any cause for destruction.
To establish its immutability, he states its lack of motion with the words "like space" (*vyomavat*).
He states the absence of transformation by saying, "devoid of all modifications.
He states that there is no action even for the sake of a fruit because of the lack of expectation for a fruit by saying, "eternally satisfied.
Satisfaction is the state of being free from desire.
It is either sorrowless bliss;
because it is partless, there is no activity,
nor is there any activity even for the purpose of its manifestation.
Because it is self-luminous;
therefore, it has been stated that liberation is not achievable through action because of its immutability.
And because it is unattached to action and its effects, he says "where" to show that it is likewise so.
And he says "time" because it is not delimited by time; and the phrase "the three times do not apply" should be connected [to the subject] by way of logical fitness (*yogyatā*).
He states the proof for its not being delimited by dharma and so forth with the word "elsewhere."
The meaning is "other than": other than the effect that has been produced, and other than the cause that has not yet been produced.
The meaning is: "Tell me that which you perceive as other than the past (*bhūta*) and the future (*bhavya*)," the word "and" (*ca*) implying "and the present (*vartamāna*).
Now, one might object: let the cited scriptural passages indeed declare Brahman's immutability (*kūṭasthatva*) and non-attachment (*asaṅgitva*).
To the question, "Why should liberation not be the fruit of injunction? he says: "Therefore," etc.; that absolute liberation (kaivalya) is indeed Brahman itself.
The meaning is that [liberation] is distinct from the fruit of karma.
The intention is that because liberation is non-different from Brahman, it is immutable and unattached to dharma and so forth.
Alternatively, that which is to be inquired into is Brahman; therefore, the meaning is that because it is an object of inquiry distinct from that [karma], it is untouched by dharma and the like.
Therefore, even in the reading that includes the word "absence" (abhāva), this is the very same meaning:
if Brahman were touched by injunctions, there would be no distinctness of the scripture,
because it would fail to obtain an object that is different from what is to be accomplished (kārya) and not yet known.
The meaning is this: when the means of valid cognition for difference remains active, the identity of Brahman and the Self cannot be attained through a statement subordinate to an injunction;
nor is an injunction untenable without that [identity], since we observe injunctions for meditations on the identity of a woman and fire.
Alternatively, he states the established meaning of the Sūtra regarding the fact that liberation is not achievable through injunction (*niyoga*), beginning with "Therefore" (*ataḥ*).
The meaning is this: Brahman, which is the object of inquiry here, is taught by the Vedāntas as being entirely independent [of injunctions], because of the harmony (*samanvaya*) [of the texts].
He intends to impose a penalty, saying "if that were so" and "that being the case. The meaning is: if liberation were impermanent by virtue of being something to be accomplished (*sādhya*).

"From this" means: because liberation cannot be accomplished through an injunction (*niyoga*), there is no person to be enjoined (*niyojya*); that is to say, there is an absence of an injunction regarding something to be done.

Furthermore, he states that liberation—which consists in the cessation of ignorance through knowledge, like the removal of darkness by a lamp—does not have the nature of being an object to be accomplished by a ritual injunction (*niyoga*), because it is a visible result: "Moreover" (*api ca*).
He who knows "I am Brahman" becomes Brahman itself.

When that which is the cause (*para*) and the effect (*avara*)—in its true form and as their underlying substrate (*adhiṣṭhāna*)—is seen, the actions of this seer whose fruits have not yet begun (*anārabdhakalāni*) perish.
The knower of bliss, which is the true nature of Brahman, becomes fearless due to the absence of a second;
you have attained the fearless Brahman.
Through the destruction of ignorance, by means of the teacher’s instruction, that which is called the individual soul (jīva) realized itself as Brahman, thinking, "I am Brahman.
From that realization, that Brahman became full;
through the abandonment of the delusion of limitation, it attained oneness.
For one who has the realization "I am Brahman," at the time of that realization, neither delusion nor sorrow exists; this is the meaning of the Śrutis.
He states their purport: "Brahman.
This means: in the interval between knowledge and its fruit.
The point is that if liberation were the fruit of a ritual injunction, it would have to occur at a later time, just like heaven and so forth;
and in that case, there would be a contradiction with the Śruti. For this reason as well, he says "likewise" (tathā) to show that liberation is not the result of an injunction.
Perceiving that Brahman as "I am this inner self," from that knowledge the sage Vāmadeva, the lord of sages, indeed realized the pure Brahman;
remaining established in that knowledge, he saw the mantras concerning the Self which reveal his own nature as the universal Self—
the meaning is that he beheld such [mantras] as "I am Manu" and so forth.

Although there is a disparity in that "abiding" (*sthiti*) is the characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) of the act of singing, whereas the "vision of Brahman" (*brahmadarśana*) is the cause (*hetu*) of the act of realizing Brahman, nevertheless— by the rule *lakṣaṇahetvoḥ kriyāyāḥ*— the suffix *laṭ* [is applied] after a verbal root denoting either a characteristic or a cause with respect to an action.

Because the suffixes *śatṛ* and *śānac* are substitutes [for the present participle], by the force of the rule prescribing the *śatṛ* suffix, when it is said "he sings while standing," another action performed by that same agent does not intervene in the interim; it is on this basis that he provides the illustration for the phrase "perceiving" with the word "just as. Furthermore, the cessation of ignorance through knowledge is heard in scripture.
If knowledge were something to be performed (vidheya), it would be an object of action (karman), and thus its capacity to remove ignorance would be untenable;
therefore, he says "You indeed," etc., to show that the Vedāntas are merely enlighteners and not prescriptive injunctions.
The six sages, Bhāradvāja and the others, having prostrated at the feet of their teacher Pippalāda, said: "You are truly our father."
"You, who by means of the boat of knowledge (vidyā-plava) enable us to cross—that is, to reach—the further shore of the great ocean of ignorance, which is devoid of rebirth, namely Brahman;
that is to say, you destroy ignorance through knowledge.
Having thus stated the question, the Chāndogya text says: "It has been heard... (śrutam).
In this context, the distinction is that the portion ending with "may he deliver" (tārayatu) belongs to the introduction, while the remainder belongs to the conclusion.
For it has indeed been heard by me from those equal to the Blessed One that one who knows the Self crosses over sorrow, but it has not been seen [by me].
Therefore, O Blessed One, out of ignorance I grieve;
may the Blessed One alone, by means of the raft of knowledge, enable me— who am thus grieving— to reach the further shore of the ocean of sorrow.

The meaning is that Sanatkumāra, being addressed by Nārada, showed to him— the one whose impurities had been burnt away by penance— that "further shore" which is Brahman, consisting of the cessation of darkness (tamas), that is, ignorance, which is the root cause of sorrow, through the means of knowledge. The phrase "He who knows this— tears asunder the knot of ignorance" is the sense of the word "etcetera" (ādi).
Thus, it has been stated that valid knowledge of reality (*tatvapramā*) is the cause of liberation, and not ritual action (*karman*).
In this regard, he cites the consensus of the sage Akṣapāda Gautama, saying "And so it is":
upon the disappearance of the false cognition "I am fair-complexioned," there follows the destruction of defects such as attachment, aversion, and delusion.

The meaning is as follows: from the removal of defects (*doṣa*) comes the removal of the engagement in the nature of merit and demerit (*dharma-adharma*); from the removal of that engagement comes the removal of birth, which consists in the acquisition of a body; thus, according to the order of recitation, when each subsequent [cause] is destroyed through the destruction of its cause, then, due to the removal of birth—which is the immediate effect of its cause, namely engagement—there occurs *apavarga*, which is the destruction of suffering.

Now, since it was stated in the previous sūtra that "the attainment of the supreme good results from the knowledge of reality," a question arises as to how the knowledge of the true nature of the Self—which is distinct from other categories—accomplishes liberation. This sūtra is introduced to state that it does so by means of the cessation of false knowledge (*mithyājñāna*). Furthermore, one might object: "If a sūtra asserting that liberation comes from the knowledge of the Self as distinct [from others] were accepted, it would amount to an admission of the opponent's view. To this, he says: "It is false" (*mithyā*).

The point that liberation arises from the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*) has been stated as a matter of consensus. However, the notion that the cognition of duality (*bhedajñāna*) is the cause of liberation is not accepted; for, according to the scripture stating, "For where there is duality, as it were," such cognition is an illusion, and according to the scripture stating, "He goes from death to death who perceives here as if there were diversity," it is a cause of misfortune.
This is the intended meaning.

Now, one might object: "Is not even the knowledge of the identity of Brahman and the Self invalid, like the knowledge of difference, because it is an illusion consisting of meditative identification (*saṃpad*) and the like? To this, he says: "And this is not [so]," and so forth.
Meditative identification (*saṃpat*) is the contemplation of non-difference with a superior reality by setting aside a limited substratum.
Just as the mind is infinite because its own functions are infinite,

and since the Viśvedevas, who are superior to that [mind], are also infinite, there is the attainment of an infinite fruit through the identification (sampatti) of the Viśvedevas with the mind due to this similarity in infinitude; likewise, the non-difference of the individual soul (jīva) from Brahman is a "sampad" [identification] due to the similarity in sentience—
this is the meaning.
Meditation (*dhyāna*) is the worship of a symbol (*pratīkopāsti*), which is a superimposition (*adhyāsa*) primarily upon the object of focus;
for example, viewing the mind or the sun as Brahman.
Likewise, the knowledge "I am Brahman" would also be a superimposition—this he denies with the words "Not so."

"Ādeśa" means instruction. "Upadeśa" means a specific action; thus, it refers to that meditation for which yoga is the instrumental cause. It is like the wind at the time of dissolution, which is called "saṃvarga" because it encompasses and withdraws fire and the other elements.

In the *Chāndogya*, meditation is prescribed on the basis that the vital breath (*prāṇa*) is called "the absorber" (*saṃvarga*) because it performs the act of absorbing speech and the other senses during sleep;
likewise, one might think that the knowledge "the individual soul (*jīva*) is Brahman" is based on its connection with the act of growth. To this, he says "nor even," meaning:

just as the act of looking is prescribed as a purificatory rite (*saṃskāra*) for the clarified butter (*ājya*) used in the Upāṃśuyāja and other rites—according to the rule, "The clarified butter is to be looked upon by the wife"—so too [the notion of the soul being Brahman] would be for the purpose of purifying the self, which is an auxiliary factor in the performance of ritual action as its agent.
He says "no" to the claim that it is knowledge of Brahman, adding "nor [is it] the attainment of Ājya.
He states the reason for these four propositions as "because of [the nature of] identification (saṃpad) and so forth.

The established purport (*tātparya*)—which is the coherence (*samanvaya*) residing in the words of co-referential sentences and which serves as the cause for the valid cognition of the reality of the oneness of Brahman and the Self through indicators such as the opening statements (*upakrama*) and so forth—would be contradicted.
