Furthermore, through the knowledge of oneness, the knot of passion and so forth within the internal organ—the heart of the one who holds the view of agnosticism—or the knot of egoism consisting of identity with the intellect, perishes; thus, there is a contradiction of the scriptural statement regarding the fruit of the cessation of ignorance.
This is because knowledge such as that of "attainment" (*sampad*) is not authoritative and therefore does not remove ignorance.
Moreover, how could the state of being Brahman arise for the individual soul (*jīva*) through the mere attainment of its identity with Brahman?
Whether the prior form remains or has perished, it is impossible for one thing to possess the nature of another;

therefore, the meaning is that [the Self] does not consist of identification (*saṃpad*) and so forth. He states the conclusion resulting from the absence of such forms as identification with the words "Therefore" (*ataḥ*).
Because it is valid knowledge (*pramātva*), it is not to be accomplished by human effort (*kṛtisādhya*); rather, it is eternal.
The meaning is that it is not to be established by a means of knowledge (*pramāṇasādhya*).

He states, "of such a nature," because it is impossible to imagine that liberation—which is of the nature of the already-established Brahman—could be accomplished through action, nor that the knowledge of it could be the object of an injunction (*niyoga*), since it cannot be produced by effort.
If it is argued that Brahman is an auxiliary to the ritual action because it is an instrument of action, like the clarified butter (ājya) which is the object of the wife's inspection, we ask:
is Brahman the object of the action in the context of knowledge, or in the context of meditation?
He says "not now" (nādya), meaning "and not [otherwise]":
verbal knowledge is the meaning of the word "act of knowing" (vidikriyā); that which is known is the effect, and that which is unknown is the cause; therefore, the meaning is "other than that.
By what instrument could one know that Self by which this entire visible world is known?
Therefore, the meaning is that the Self is not an object [of cognition].
He states that it is not the second [alternative] with the word "tathā" (so).

By the scriptural text, "That which one does not think with the mind," the world declares that Brahman is not an object by stating that it is not known by the mind; he then says, "Know that very Brahman to be the unknowable."
The meaning is that people worship that [Brahman] as a deity and so forth, qualified by limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), and not as this Brahman itself.

One might raise the objection: "If Brahman is not an object of verbal cognition, there would be a loss of the initial proposition. To this, the reply is: although it is an object of the mental modification (*vṛtti*) produced by the Vedānta, it possesses the fruit of the cessation of ignorance brought about by that modification; thus, it is validated by the scripture. Even though it is an object of the modification, because Brahman—which is self-luminous—is not an object of the manifestation of consciousness (*sphuraṇa*) by that modification, it is not an object of knowledge (*aprameya*).
He sets it aside, saying "no.
This means because it is "other" (paratvāt) and because it is the "fruit" (phalatvāt);
or alternatively, it means because its purport is Brahman in the form of cessation (nivṛtti).
He explains what was stated with the words "nahi" (not indeed):
being an object of consciousness is "this-ness" (*idantva*);
being a non-object is "non-this-ness" (*anidantayā*).
Regarding its invisibility, he cites scripture with the words "And thus":
"He by whom Brahman is not thought [as an object] has understood it correctly;
but he who, being ignorant, thinks 'Brahman is an object of consciousness' does not know it."
He restates what has already been said for the sake of reinforcement: "It is unknown" (*avijñātam*).
The meaning is that for those who know Brahman through its state of being non-objective, the position is that Brahman is unknown and unseen;
whereas for the ignorant, the position is that Brahman is known and seen.

"Do not see the seer of seeing"—the witness of the visual and mental functions—"by means of this visible seeing"; likewise, do not objectify "the seer of cognition"—the witness of the determinative function of the intellect. Thus he says, "not. Now, one might object: even if the scripture possesses authority as the remover of ignorance and so forth, since that cessation is adventitious, liberation would be non-eternal. To this he says, "Therefore," [denying that objection].
The meaning is "from the knowledge of reality" (*tattvajñānāt*).

Since destruction (*dhvaṃsa*) is eternal and of the nature of the Self (*ātmarūpa*), there is no contingency of its being non-eternal; this is the sense. Furthermore, since the fruit of action is only fourfold—consisting of origination, modification, attainment, and purification—and liberation is distinct from these, it cannot be accomplished through ritual worship (*upāsanā*); thus he says, beginning with "But for one who... and concluding with "therefore, having set aside knowledge alone... (*tasmājjñānamekaṃ muktvā*).

By this much [of the argument], the connection is as follows: it is logical that [the object] requires [an agent] both in its capacity as something to be produced (*utpādyatva*) and in its capacity as something to be modified (*vikāryatva*). He refutes this with the words "of those two" (*tayor*).
Change is a different state of that which persists.
Now, one might argue: "To avoid [the charge of] impermanence, let it be that Brahman, while persisting through action, attains [the world] like a person reaching a village.
To this he says: "And not... (na ca).

Is Brahman non-different from the individual soul (jīva) or not? In either case, since it is already attained, there is no dependence on ritual action; this he states with the words beginning "svātma" (one's own self).
Just as rice grains require sprinkling because they are to be consecrated, liberation does not; this he states with the words beginning "nāpi" (nor even).
The imparting of qualities (*guṇādhāna*) occurs in rice through sprinkling and so forth; the removal of impurities from cloth and such occurs through washing and so forth.
He raises an objection: "It is a property of its own self" (*svātmadharma*).

Liberation is indeed the very nature of the Self as Brahman; though obscured by the impurity of beginningless ignorance (*anādyavidyā*), it becomes manifest when that impurity is destroyed through spiritual practice (*upāsanā*). Regarding this, there is the following illustration: "Just as... Here, *saṃskāra* refers to the destruction of impurity.
Furthermore, is this impurity in the Self real or imagined?
In the second case, its destruction occurs through knowledge alone, not through action.
Regarding the first case, one asks: is the action based on the self or based on something else?
It is not the first; thus he says: "No, [it is] action."
He clarifies the impossibility with the words "that which...
(yad iti). For an action (*kriyā*) is not produced unless it effects a modification, such as conjunction, in its own substratum;
and that [position] is contradicted by the statement.
He says "not the second" because it is "other," meaning that it is not its object; that is to say, because it does not possess conjunction with the substance that is the locus of the action.

The point is that a mirror, being composed of parts and being conjoined with substances such as powdered bricks which serve as the substratum for action, is indeed refined; thus, there is no deviation [from the rule] that one thing is not refined by the action of another. To this, an objection is raised regarding potential deviation: "But surely... [The response is: There is no deviation, because the Self—though actually reflected in primordial ignorance (mūlāvidyā) and grasped through the delusion "I am a person"—has attained identification with the body due to that error, and thus, through the delusion of being the substratum of action, it is erroneously thought to be the object of refinement.
Thus he says: "No.
"Someone" means one whose true nature as Brahman is not yet determined.

The logical connection (*anvaya*) is as follows: the fruit of health belongs only to that which is the aggregate of the body, in relation to which the notion of health arises within the self (*ātman*).

Now, one might object: "How can there be a refinement (*saṃskāra*) for that which is non-different from the body, since it is impossible for such a thing to be the enjoyer of fruits in the next world? To this, he says: "By that" (*tena*).

The meaning is that the fruit of action is experienced by the "experiencer"— that is, by the self which appears as the agent through its reflection in the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) when conjoined with the body, and which possesses cognitions such as desire due to its identity with the mind (manas). The sense is that it is logical for the latent impression (saṃskāra) to belong to this transmigratory experiencer who is qualified by the mind.
Regarding the point that the state of being an enjoyer belongs to the qualified [self] and not to the pure witness alone, he states the proof with the words "of those two.

Between the knower (*pramātṛ*) and the witness (*sākṣin*), the knower—who possesses imagined agency and so forth merely through contact with *sattva*—enjoys the "pippala," which is the fruit of karma;
that very same self, when purified, appears as something else, namely as the witness. This is the meaning.
"Self" (ātmā) means the body;
the meaning is the self as the cognizer endowed with the body and so forth.

Having thus stated that the conscious essence (ciddhātu), when possessed of limiting adjuncts (sopādhika), is subject to false conditioning, he states the proof for its unconditionability (asaṃskāryatva) when devoid of such adjuncts (nirupādhika) with the word "one" (eka).
The one God, who is non-dual among all beings, is self-luminous;
nevertheless, because he is veiled by *māyā*, he does not manifest—thus [the text] says "hidden" (*gūḍha*).

Now, an objection may be raised: the non-manifestation of the God is due to his lack of connection with the individual soul (*jīva*) or due to his being distinct from it, and not because of concealment by *māyā*.
"No," he says, "for it is all-pervading and the inner self of all beings.
The meaning is that due to the Lord's omnipresence and because He is the inner self of all living creatures, there is no manifestation [of Him] precisely because of the absence of any veil.
If it is argued that [if He were] the inner self, He would be an agent, [the answer is] no.
The term "supervisor of karma" means the witness of action.
If that is so, then since there is a witness, the consequence of duality follows.
It does not become a witness by becoming the substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*) of all beings;
rather, the meaning is that the status of being witnessed is superimposed upon the witness as its substratum.
He states the meaning of the word "witness" (*sākṣin*) as "the solitary cognizer" (*cetā kevalaḥ*).
It is well known in the world that one who is a knower is a non-agent and a witness.
The word "ca" (and) serves to include both faults and positive qualities together.
Because it is devoid of qualities and free from defects, there is no refinement consisting of either a quality or the destruction of a fault; such is the meaning.
Because it begins with the word "he" (saḥ), the words *śukra* and so forth must be expressed in the masculine gender.
He alone is the Self who has gone around and pervaded everything;
he is *śukra*, radiant.
It is bodiless and devoid of gender; it is without wounds and uninjured; it is without outflows and free from veins; or rather, it is imperishable.
By these two words, the emptiness of the gross body is expressed.
"Pure" means free from the impurities of passion and so forth; "unstruck by evil" means untouched by merit and demerit.

The word "ataḥ" means that there is no fifth fruit of action other than arising, attainment, modification, and refinement, which could serve as the gateway for liberation being achievable through action.
[Objection: But if liberation is unattainable, the commencement of the scripture is in vain. [Reply: No;
because its purpose is knowledge. Thus he says, "Therefore" (tasmāt), meaning:
because there is no other means.
He anticipates an objection with the word "nanu" (but surely).
The sense is that, in that case, it would be contradicted [by your own position] that there is no entry of action into liberation.
Even mental knowledge is not an action suitable for injunction.
He says "no" because [the Self] is not an object and because it cannot be accomplished by action;
he elaborates upon this distinction with the words "for action... and so forth.
The construction is as follows: "In whatever object that [activity] is enjoined independently of that [object], there indeed it is an action.
He provides an example for the point that an action is independent of the objective entity and is achievable through volitional effort (*kṛti*), beginning with the word "just as" (*yathā*).
The phrase "taken up by the Adhvaryu" is the ellipsis [to be supplied].
When the Hotṛ priest is about to utter the *vaṣaṭ* call,
and in such introductory formulas as "the twilight deity," whatever kind of meditative act (*dhyānakriyā*) occurs that is independent of an actual object— [...is what is meant here.]

The meaning is that such an action is enjoined by the *Purva Mīmāṃsā* Sūtras. To the objection that meditation (*dhyāna*) also is not an action because it is mental, like knowledge (*jñāna*), he says "meditation," etc.;
the ellipsis is "nevertheless, it is indeed an action."
The sense is that "being achievable through action" (*kṛtyasādhyatva*) is the limiting condition (*upādhi*).
Having described the activity of meditation, he clarifies the distinction of knowledge from it with the words "knowledge, however" (*jñānaṃ tu*).
Therefore, because it is a valid cognition (*pramātva*), it is not dependent on injunction (*codanātantra*) and is not the object of a ritual prescription (*vidhi*).

The meaning is that there is a great difference between meditation and knowledge because meditation depends on the person— meaning that which has the person as its cause by way of his effort— whereas knowledge does not deviate from the reality and is independent of the person.
He states this very distinction by means of another illustration with the words "and just as."
The meaning is that even though there is non-difference [between Brahman and the self], meditation can be performed according to scriptural injunction (*vidhi*), whereas knowledge cannot.

Now, one might object: "While perceptual knowledge (*pratyakṣajñāna*) is dependent on its object because it is produced by that object, verbal comprehension (*śābdabodha*) lacks such dependence; therefore, it is an action subject to injunction. To this he says: "In this way, all... and so forth. This is not so.
Knowledge regarding the objects of verbal testimony, inference, and so forth, must also be understood as being non-prescribable action;
the meaning is that even in those cases, since knowledge is attained through the means of valid cognition itself, there is no application of an injunction.
This being the case:
The meaning is: "given that knowledge is not something that can be enjoined in the world.
"Being as-it-is" (yathābhūtatva) means being uncontradicted.

Now, an objection is raised: in such [scriptural] statements as "one should see the Self," "know thou Brahman," and "the Self is to be seen," the optative (*liṅ*), imperative (*loṭ*), and gerundive (*tavya*) suffixes are heard, which enjoin cognition.
Therefore, since knowledge is not something to be enjoined, he says: "with respect to that object.
Regarding that object which is of the nature of knowledge, injunctions are incapable of impelling a person.

The meaning is that knowledge—being non-enjoinable (*aniyojya*), unachievable through action (*kṛtyāsādhya*), or devoid of an agent to be enjoined (*niyojyaśūnya*)—is such because it has that [knowledge] as its object.
The meaning is that there is no one to be enjoined nor any object of the injunction who would think, "This is my duty.
Well then, let Brahman, as the object of knowledge, be enjoined;
no, he says: "not [to be abandoned]," etc.
The meaning is that because the object is the very nature of reality (*vastusvarūpa*),
it is not something to be enjoined (*vidheya*) since Brahman is unsurpassed and is the inner self (*adhyātma*).
Furthermore, because its object is a neutral reality (*udāsīnavastu*), knowledge itself is not something to be enjoined.
The meaning is: "because there is an absence of results such as [worldly] activity and so forth.
He asks for the purpose of the injunctive passages: "For what purpose are they?
The meaning is: "They have the appearance of injunctions, being similar to well-known injunctions regarding sacrifices and the like."
The knowledge of the Self is praised as the means for attaining the supreme human goal by means of injunctive suffixes.

He states that the words of injunction have the result of removing that engagement with sense objects—which, through the delusion that such praise constitutes a cause for ultimate desire, acts as an obstacle to hearing about the Self and so forth—by saying "svābhāvika" (inherent), etc.
He explains this with the passage beginning "yo hi," and so on.
In that context, "in regard to objects" means the activity of the aggregate [of the senses] directed toward its domain, such as sound and so forth;
"stream" refers to the flow of mental fluctuations.
The ellipsis is "they cause [one] to engage" in such things as hearing the means for knowledge (*jñānasādhana*).
He states the nature of that hearing with the words "of that" (*tasya*);
"seeking" (*anveṣaṇa*) refers to knowledge (*jñāna*).
The meaning is this: since all this world is indeed the Self alone, the Self is realized through the realization of non-self.
Once there is the realization of the non-dual, invisible Self, where could the poor ritual injunction remain, which subsists upon the forest of duality?
He states the authoritative source for the absence of anything further to be done by the knower of the Self with the words "And so it is."

If some person were to know himself thus: "I am this very Supreme Bliss, the Supreme Self," then desiring what fruit, or for the sake of the pleasure of what enjoyer, would he suffer in sympathy with the body as it is being tormented? He would not suffer.
The intention is that the knower of the Self has accomplished all that was to be done because of the absence of duality between the enjoyer and the enjoyed.
Furthermore, the word "iti" is used to indicate the extreme difficulty of attaining such knowledge.
This is the most secret of truths.
He concludes the refutation of the commentator’s view with the words "Therefore" (*tasmāt*).
He introduces the position stated by the Prābhākara with the words "As for what some [say]" (*yad api kecit*). [The opponent argues:
"The agent is the self; because it is established in common worldly experience, it is not the subject matter of the Vedānta."
The meaning is that there is no other Brahman at all, because the Veda has as its purport only what is to be accomplished (kārya), and thus lacks any means of knowledge (māna) for such a thing.
To the objection that [Brahman] would be unestablished due to the absence of a means of knowledge, he says: "Not so."

Since the Self—whose nature is the fruit [of liberation], which is known solely through the Upaniṣads, and which leaves nothing further to be accomplished—is not subordinate to action, it is not established that the entire Veda is devoted to action. Nor should it be argued that, by means of the signs of engagement and withdrawal, the listener infers the speaker’s cognition of an action as the cause of those signs; and having ascertained the speaker’s sentence to be intent on action, one grasps the word-potency (*śakti*) of the words in the sentence as residing in that which is connected to an action; thus, an already established entity, being not itself a word-meaning (*apadārtha*), cannot constitute the sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha*). This is not tenable.

When a father hears the sentence "A son has been born to you," he infers the birth of the desired son through the sign of his joy; thus, he grasps the relationship (*saṃgati*) of words such as "son" with an already established entity (*siddha*).

Since it is more parsimonious (*lāghava*) to accept that the expressive power (*śakti*) of words resides in a meaning already connected [to others], rather than in an object connected only to a task to be accomplished (*kāryānvita*), an established entity can also constitute the meaning of a sentence—so much for this.

Furthermore, is it because Brahman does not exist that the entire Veda is devoted solely to action; or is it because Brahman does not appear in the Vedāntas; or else because [Brahman] is subordinate to action; or perhaps because [Brahman] is established by worldly experience; or finally, because of contradiction with other means of knowledge?
Therein, he refutes the first three positions with the words "He who...
The qualification "not subject to saṃsāra" and so forth is for the purpose of showing that [the Self] is not subsidiary to anything else.
Having stated that its existence is established by the mind of the Vedānta as the reason for its non-non-existence, he states another reason—its being the Self—with the words "That very one..."
The word *iti* is used in the sense of "this.
The meaning is that this very Self, which has been taught through the negation of all objects of perception by means of the formula "not this, not this," is this one.
He raises a doubt regarding the fourth [state]: "But surely the Self is 'I'?"

He says "no" because it is not established in common worldly experience, since the status of the Self as the object of the notion of "I"—by virtue of being the witness of the ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*) and so forth—has already been refuted.
He says "for not," meaning: what need is there to say that this [Self] is not known even by the founders of other philosophical schools (*tīrthakāra*), since it is devoid of all gradations?
In that [opponent's] view, the qualifiers indicate the non-apprehension of the self. He sets aside the fifth [alternative] with the word "ataḥ" (therefore).
The meaning is: by some proponent, either through a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) or through reasoning (*yukti*).
The sense is that because [the agent] is not an object of perception (*agamyatvāt*), there is no contradiction with other means of valid cognition (*mānāntara*).
Furthermore, the witness (*sākṣin*) is a subordinate factor of the action (*karmāṅga*) because it is manifested (*utpannatvāt*), just like the agent (*kartṛvat*).
Regarding this, he says: "vidhi... (Injunctions...).
The meaning is that the Witness is not a subordinate element of ritual action because an unknown Witness is useless, whereas a known Witness is contradictory [to the nature of action].

He further states that the Witness is not a subordinate element of action because, being the Self, it is the supreme remainder of all and is neither to be discarded nor acquired—this is expressed by the words "ātmatvāt" (because of being the Self).
Anticipating the objection that the self should be abandoned because it is impermanent, he says: "For everything...

He refutes the idea that it should be abandoned on account of its being subject to transformation by saying: "...it is sold... He refutes the idea that it should be accepted by saying: "...for this very reason..."
The meaning is "because of being changeless.
For the quality of being something to be attained (*upādeyatva*) belongs to the goal (*sādhya*), but not to the Self (*ātman*), because [the Self] is eternally established; this is the meaning.
Because the self must be abandoned for the sake of attaining the Supreme, he says: "Therefore, there is nothing higher than the Puruṣa. It is the *kāṣṭhā*, the ultimate limit of everything.
Thus, because the Self is not a subordinate remainder,
because it is non-sublatable,
and because it is unprecedented, [it is the primary object].
And because it is clearly manifest in the Vedāntas, its being knowable through the Vedāntas alone has been stated. Regarding that, he cites the scripture: "But him... (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 3.2.9).
The meaning is: "O Śākalya, I ask you about that Person, the full one, who is the substratum of the Sūtra together with its cause.
This is the sense of the word "ataḥ" (from this).

The meaning is that the Vedāntas are determined to have the reality of the Self as their sole purport by means of the aforementioned indicative marks and through direct scriptural statement (*śruti*).
He reiterates what was stated previously with the words "As for that which...
When the futility of the Veda is suspected, this subsequent commentary—"For it is seen..."—is intended to establish its meaningfulness.

In this context, although one should have said "the comprehension of a purposeful object" (*phalavadarthāvabodhanam*), the term "comprehension of ritual action" (*karmāvabodhanam*) was used because the discussion began with the investigation of *dharma*. This does not, however, exclude the fact that the Upanishads (*vedānta*) have Brahman as their ultimate purport. For this very reason, the author of the Sūtras [Jaimini] states, "Because it is not perceived [otherwise], it is the means of knowledge for that object" (*anupalabdher arthe tatpramāṇam*); by this, he shows that *dharma* is the meaning of the Veda precisely because it is an unknown entity possessing a fruit. Since Brahman remains as what is yet to be known, there is no contradiction with the statements of the elders; thus he says: "That *dharma*... and so forth.

The meaning is that even the scripture of prohibitions has as its purport the activity of cessation; thus, the collection of sentences from those sūtras and bhāṣyas intends to show that the ritual section (karmakāṇḍa) has as its purport an activity.
However, in reality, the purport of the ritual section lies in the sense of the optative suffix (liṅ).

And as for the meaning of the optative suffix (*liṅ*), it is simply the status of being a means to a desired end (*iṣṭasādhanatva*) residing in actions such as sacrifice— which is established in common worldly usage as the object of the motivating cognition—
and not some "task" (*kārya*) distinct from the action, because such a thing is as non-existent as a tortoise's hair; thus, even that [meaning] is distinct from the "task" postulated by the opponent.

It should be considered: once [the validity of the means of knowledge] is established, does it belong to the section concerning action (*karmakāṇḍa*) or to the section concerning knowledge (*jñānakāṇḍa*)?
Furthermore, the Vedāntas have as their ultimate purport an already established entity, because they consist of words denoting an existing reality that possesses a fruit.
He says "and also" (api ca), using the example of words such as "curd" (*dadhi*).
Is the meaninglessness of words that do not denote an action (*akriyārtha*) the absence of a denotable object (*abhidheyābhāva*), or is it the absence of a result (*phalābhāva*)?
The first [opponent] says: "Of the tradition" (*āmnāyasya*).

The meaning is that, according to the maxim [stated], for those who necessarily accept this lack of denotable content, words such as "curd" (*dadhi*) and "Soma" in sentences like "one should sacrifice with Soma" (*somena yajeta*) and "one offers with curd" (*dadhnā juhoti*) would be devoid of meaning.
Anticipating the objection, "But by whom was this lack of denotable content stated?", he says: "In the engagement... (*pravṛtti*).

If words such as "curd" (dadhi) denote an existing entity (*bhūta*) by virtue of being subordinate to an action (*kārya*), having a purpose to be accomplished (*bhavyārthatva*), and being a supplement to an action (*kāryaśeṣatva*), then what is the reason that words such as "Being" (*satya*) do not denote the immutable (*kūṭastha*)?
Is it because the immutable is devoid of activity (*akriyatva*), or because it is not a supplement to an action (*akriyāśeṣatva*)? This is the question.

Now, one might raise the objection: "Is it not the case that curds and the like are taught because they are effects (*kārya*) due to their connection with an action (*kāryānvayitva*), whereas the immutable [Self] is not taught because it is not an effect? Anticipating this, he refutes it with the words "Not so" (*na hi*).
If curds and the like were themselves effects, they would lose their status as being subordinate to an action (*kāryaśeṣatva*).
The point is that, therefore, the status of being the meaning of a word is obtained for things like curds (*dadhi*), which are real entities distinct from their effects.
He raises a second objection: "Even if it were not an action" (*akriyātve ’pi*).
The sense is that while [an entity] subordinate to an effect is subject to instruction, the immutable (*kūṭastha*) is not, because it is not subordinate to an effect.

Whether the status of being a remainder of an action (*kāryaśeṣatva*) for an existing entity (*bhūta*) is for the sake of the word's meaning or for the sake of the result, [the author] says "this is not a fault" to refute the first alternative:
even though curd and so forth are remainders of an action, only the thing-in-itself (*vastumātra*) is taught by the word; the word-meaning is not that which is connected to an action.
The meaning is that the potency of words lies solely in the connected sense (*anvitārtha*).
He accepts the second [position] with the words "But [the fact] that they have action as their purpose" (*kriyārthatvaṃ tu*).
The meaning is that the status of that particular existing entity, such as curd and so forth, as a subordinate element (*aṅga*) to an action is accepted with a view toward the result (*phala*).
The meaning of the word "but" (tu) is that [the world] does not [arise] from Brahman.
Now, one might object: if it is admitted that an existing entity is a subordinate part of an effect, how can it be the meaning of a word in its own right?
To this, he says: "And not... (na ca).

The meaning is that the status of being a word-meaning is not lost merely by accepting subsidiarity (*śeṣatva*) for the sake of a result, because subsidiarity does not enter into the definition of being a word-meaning.
He raises the objection regarding the position that "uselessness" means the absence of a result—namely, "If [it is argued]...

Even though curd and the like, though fruitless in themselves, are taught as being fruitful by way of an action, nevertheless, for one who maintains the doctrine of the immutable Brahman, there is an absence of any door to action; therefore, what result follows from that illustration?
The meaning is "it may be so.
There is no fixed rule that action alone is the means for the efficacy of what has come into being, because we observe efficacy through the mere knowledge of a rope; thus he says: "It is said."

"In the same way" means "just like curd and so forth. Although there is a distinction in that curd and the like achieve their fruitfulness through action (*kriyā*), whereas Brahman is fruitful by its very nature (*svataḥ*), it is nonetheless faultless to say that the Upanishads (Vedāntas) are similar to the instruction regarding curd and the like, simply by virtue of having as their content a reality that possesses fruitfulness.
Now, he states that the Vedāntas, like prohibitive sentences, have as their purport an already established fact (*siddhārtha*), beginning with the words "Moreover" (*api ca*).
Because the negative particle (*nañ*) is connected with the meaning of the verbal root, the meaning of the negative is the absence of killing;
the meaning of the suffix *tad* (the optative) is being a means to a desired end (*iṣṭasādhanatva*).
In this context, the desired [result] is the absence of the suffering of hell, and its protector is the absence of killing; such is the meaning of the prohibitive statement.

When it is stated that the absence of killing is the cause for the absence of suffering, the person desists from killing by implication, through the understanding that killing is a means to suffering.
There is no injunction here at all, because an injunction has as its object an action, the means for accomplishing that action, or substances such as curd and so forth;
nor is the cessation expressed by the negative particle (*nañ*), which consists in the absence of killing, an action.
Because it is non-existent,
it is also not the means for accomplishing an action;
the meaning is that since non-existence is not a cause for the purpose of an existent thing, and because the purpose of an existent thing is absent [in it].
Therefore, the sense is that the prohibitive scripture possesses authority regarding an established fact (*siddhārtha*).
He states the penalty for the contrary position: "non-action" (*akriyā*).

Now, it might be argued that by means of the connection with the negative particle (*nañ*), which is based on the attachment to the meaning of "killing" as naturally or through passion obtained, a volitional act opposed to killing is understood.

And that [non-killing], being of the nature of the meaning of the negative particle (*nañ*), is enjoined because it has not been previously established there, in the sense that "one should perform non-killing.
Anticipating the objection that this sentence would thus have a positive purpose (*kāryārthaka*), he refutes it with the words "and not" (*na ca*).

The essential nature (*svarūpa*) of the person (*puruṣa*) is indifference (*audāsīnya*), and that is characterized by the cessation of the act of killing; that is to say, it is an indifference consisting of cessation, which amounts to the non-existence of killing.
It is not possible to assume that the negative particle (*nañ*) has the function of denoting an action apart from that [non-existence].

This is because, when the primary meaning—non-existence—is possible as the referent of the negative particle, it is improper to resort to a figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of an action that contradicts it. Furthermore, if a prohibitive sentence were to have an action as its meaning, it would result in the collapse of the distinction between injunction (*vidhi*) and prohibition (*niṣedha*).

[Objection: But surely, why should the negative particle (*nañ*) not also have its denotative power (*śakti*) with respect to that which is other than the referent (*tadanya*) and that which is contradictory to it (*tadviruddha*), given that we observe such usage as *abrāhmaṇaḥ* ("non-Brahmin") and *adharmaḥ* ("unrighteousness")? [Response: No.
He states "and of the negative particle" because it is improper for a word to have multiple primary meanings.
However, words such as *go* (cow) possess multiple meanings only out of necessity (*agatyā*),
since [meanings like] heaven, directions, speech, and thunderbolt lack any possible connection with the primary meaning (the animal), and thus figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) cannot apply there.
However, it is logical that the two— namely, "other" and "contrary"— are the objects of definition, because of their possible relationship [with the term].
For instance, in the case of one who is other than a Brāhmaṇa, such as a Kṣatriya or the like...

Alternatively, because the negative particle (*nañ*) is capable of relating to the absence of Brahmins and so forth— which is sinful and contrary to the Dharma— it should be understood that, in the present context, due to its connection with the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*), the negative particle expresses only a simple negation (*prasajya-pratiṣedha*) and does not indicate an exclusion (*paryudāsa*). Or rather, there is no connection of the negative particle with the base word (*prakṛti*), because the meaning of the suffix takes precedence over the base word.

Furthermore, while subordinate elements are connected through their relation to the principal element, the negative particle (*nañ*) is connected with the meaning of the suffix as residing in the meaning of the base—that is, with "being a means to the desired" (*iṣṭasādhanatva*).

And that which is "desired" is precisely that which, in relation to oneself, is not followed by a more powerful undesired consequence; it is not merely momentary pleasure, for otherwise even the consumption of food mixed with poison would result in being considered "desired."
And thus, "one should not kill" means that killing is not a means of achieving a desired end when it is a means of achieving a powerful undesired end.

In this context, the phrase "one should kill" restates—on the basis of a misconception—the qualified status of killing as a means of achieving a desired end; then, by the communication of its negation through the word "not," the cognition arises that killing is a means of achieving a powerful undesired end.

This is because, while the property of being a means of achieving a temporary desired end (the qualificandum) exists in killing, the cognition of the absence of the qualified whole results in the understanding of the absence of the qualifier.

The qualification is "not being a means to a powerful undesirable [consequence]"; thus, its absence—namely, "being a means to a powerful undesirable [consequence]"—is established as the meaning of the negative particle (*nañ*). He states that the cognition of this [absence] maintains indifference with the words "In the case of non-existence...
The word *ca* has the sense of "also," indicating an alternative position.
The meaning is that just as there is a cognition of the absence of the object of the base (prakṛti), so too there is a cognition of the absence of the object of the suffix (pratyaya).
Since cognition is momentary, when that [cognition] is absent, one would fall from indifference and engage in actions such as killing;
to this, he says: "And that... [sā ca].

Just as fire is extinguished after burning its fuel, so too that cognition of the absence of the object denoted by the negative particle (*nañ*) is extinguished only after burning the fuel of passion—the root of which is the delusion that killing and such acts are means to a desired end; this is the literal meaning.
The sense is that when passion is destroyed, the [prohibition] ceases.
Alternatively, the meaning is that since that action was undertaken out of passion, it subsides of its own accord once passion has been destroyed.

In the opponent's view, however, even if it is stated that "an action contrary to killing must be performed," the fallacy [of the injunction] is unavoidable because the delusion that killing is a means to a desired end has not been dispelled.
Therefore, he concludes that the meaning of the negative particle (*nañ*) is simply the absence of that [action], stating: "Therefore" (*tasmāt*).

The meaning of the word "that" (*tat*) refers to the absence of the object to be accomplished (*kārya*), since there is no volitional effort (*kṛti*) directed toward an object when the meaning of the verbal root (*bhāvārtha*) is absent.

Alternatively, it should be explained that in the stated position, indifference (audāsīnya), which is characterized by cessation, is indeed dependent upon a qualified absence. It should be understood that the phrase "characterized by cessation" is intended to establish that this naturally established indifference is something to be accomplished through the meaning of the negative particle (nañ).

Regarding the Prajāpati-vrata, having introduced the task (kārya) with the word *vrata*—which denotes an action to be performed—as in "This is the vow of that boy," the Prajāpati-vow is then stated as "One should not look at the rising sun."

Therefore, by the force of the context (*upakrama*), the negative particle (*nañ*) in that instance is accepted as indicating an action consisting of a volition (*saṃkalpa*) that is opposed to seeing.

Likewise, in cases such as "non-cow" (*agauḥ*), "non-liquor" (*asurā*), and "unrighteousness" (*adharma*), since the negative particle joined with a noun or a verbal root cannot signify mere negation (*pratiṣedha*), it indicates something else or its opposite.
The meaning is that, apart from these instances such as the "vows of Prajāpati," we consider the meaning of the negative particle to be simply non-existence (*abhāva*).

The sense is that, just as the prohibitory scripture possesses authority once the meaning of the negative particle—which has the result of the absence of suffering—is established, so too do the Vedāntas possess authority regarding Brahman.
If it is asked, "In what domain then does the sūtra 'those [texts] not having action as their purpose are useless' apply? he says in response: "Therefore..."
The meaning is that because the Vedāntas possess fruitfulness regarding their own subject matter, they do not concern themselves with futile discourse.
The passage beginning with "As for what was said... has a clear meaning.

Although liberation does not occur merely through the knowledge gained from hearing [the scriptures] while one is still in saṃsāra, liberation even while living is undeniable when there is direct realization (sākṣātkāra); this he states with an illustration in the passage beginning with "To this it is replied... and so forth.
The meaning is that this contradicts the direct realization (sākṣātkāra) that "I am Brahman.
He states the scriptural authority for the liberation while living (jīvanmukti) of one who knows the Truth: "As it has been said by the Śruti.
He raises an objection, suggesting that being bodiless while living is a contradiction: "The body..."

Since the connection of the self with the body is caused by delusion, he states with the words beginning "no" that bodilessness—consisting in the destruction of that [connection]—is appropriate for the living person through the knowledge of reality.

He states with the word "eternal" that bodilessness, which is the nature of the unattached Self, is manifested in the living person through the knowledge of reality. He raises the objection that the connection between the body and the self is real with the words "caused by that."
The sense is that there is a requirement for an effect in order to bring about its destruction.

[The opponent objects: Once the self’s connection with a body has arisen, merit and demerit (dharma-adharma) are produced; and when those exist, the connection is born. Because of this mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*), since one is unestablished, the second would also be unestablished. He refutes this with the words beginning "No" (*na*).

But surely, if this dharma and adharma produced by this body were the cause of its connection with this very body, there would be the fallacy of mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*): the production of the connection with this body would depend on the karma of a previous body, and that previous body would depend on the karma performed by the body prior to that—like the seed and the sprout. Since this is beginningless (*anādi*), this fault does not apply; to this, he says: "Andha-... (blind...).
The meaning is that it lacks authoritative basis (*aprāmāṇikī*).

For the connection of the self with the body, produced by prior karma, is not perceived through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) in the same way that a sprout from a seed or another seed [from a sprout] is seen;
nor is there any scriptural tradition (*āgama*) [to that effect].
On the contrary, the intention is that such scriptural passages as "For [the Self] is unattached" preclude all agency.
He states the reasoning for this with the word "activity":
the meaning is that because an immutable (kūṭastha) entity is incapable of action, it cannot possess agency.
He dispels the doubt that even though [the Self] is inherently inactive, it may possess agency through proximity to causal factors, by means of a dissimilar example—saying "no.
The meaning is that while it is logical for kings and others to have agency through servants they have hired themselves, this is not the case for the Self.
He states "it is false" to show that the connection of the Self with the body and its actions—which revolve like seed and sprout on the ground of ignorance—is produced solely by delusion.

Now, it might be argued that because the injunction "one should sacrifice" (yajeta) would otherwise be untenable, the self's status as an agent must be accepted; to this, he replies with the words "by this" (etena).

The meaning is that the agency in performing sacrifices and so forth, resulting from the connection with the body and other such things produced by delusion, has been explained [as being non-real] up until the dawn of the knowledge of Brahman.
Regarding this, they say— the meaning is that the Prābhākaras hold that because there is no illusion, the connection with the body and so forth is real; such is their intention.
He says "no" because [the cognition] is not secondary due to the absence of knowledge of difference (*bhedajñānābhāvāt*).
The meaning is that for one by whom the difference between two things is well-known—that is, cognized—there is the established basis for the cognition of the secondary and the primary.
The syntactical connection (*anvaya*) is: "for whichever person those two are secondary according to you."
The meaning is that [the two] have as their objects qualities such as heroism.
"But of him" means:
of a person devoid of the cognition of difference.
"Word and cognition" means the word and the verbal comprehension. He provides an example for those two which have doubt as their root, beginning with "as when dull... and so forth.
When even those [metaphorical usages] rooted in doubt do not possess a secondary (gauṇa) status, then what need be said of those rooted in error? Thus he says: "Or as...
The word "akasmāt" means when there is the awakening of latent impressions (saṃskāra) by means of unexpected factors such as unseen merit (adṛṣṭa) and so forth.
The meaning is that [this occurs] without figurative usage and without knowledge of the qualities.

The phrase "of those who maintain a self distinct from the body and so forth" implies that for those who maintain the body as the self, there is merely the conceit of it being valid cognition (*pramā*).
He states the proof for liberation while living with the words "And so it is.
"There" means in that body of one liberated while living.
As in the illustration, the sloughed-off skin of a snake (*ahinirlvayanī*)—cast aside, deposited in an anthill or similar place, dead, and abandoned of its sense of identity by the serpent—remains.

In this very way, this body remains abandoned of self-identification by the wise man. Then, like a snake freed from its skin, he who dwells in the body is "bodiless"; because of the absence of self-identification in the body—just as there is none in the snake's slough—and because of being bodiless, he is immortal. Thus, though living, he is the *prāṇa* (the vital breath);
the meaning is that he is that Brahman, the light, the self-luminous bliss itself.
In reality, even though one lacks eyes, because the [notion of] eyes and so forth has been sublated yet not ceased, one is "as if possessing eyes," and so on; this should be applied accordingly.
Thus, it is faultless.
Since liberation is attained through the knowledge of Brahman as the Self, the authority of the Vedāntas is established.
The meaning is that its status as a *śāstra* (treatise) is established by its teaching what is beneficial and by its being free from defects.

With regard to the knowledge of Brahman, since both reflection (*manana*) and meditative absorption (*nididhyāsana*), like hearing (*śravaṇa*), are accepted as having their own distinct intermediate injunctions, Brahman does not become a subordinate element of an injunction; for it is primary because it is that which is to be attained through the knowledge aimed at [in the injunction]. Thus he says:
"No. Hearing is primary because it has as its object the Vedāntas, which are the instruments of knowledge.
Since reflection (*manana*) and meditative contemplation (*nididhyāsana*) have the object of knowledge as their domain, they must be understood as auxiliary to that [knowledge];

the utility of the unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*) resulting from the restrictive rule (*niyama*) lies in its contribution toward knowledge, according to the principle of "dependence on all" (*sarvāpekṣānyāya*).
If so, why was an injunction (*vidhi*) regarding knowledge abandoned?
To this he says: "If indeed" (*yadi hi*).

If, having accepted an injunction regarding knowledge, the Brahman known through the Vedas were employed as the object (*karman*) of the act of enjoined knowledge, then it would be subordinate to the injunction (*vidhiśeṣatva*). However, there is no such employment of that which has already been known.
The meaning is that when the fruit is obtained through the mere attainment of understanding, an injunction (vidhi) is inapplicable.
Therefore—because an injunction is impossible;
for this reason—because the status of being a subordinate element (śeṣatva) is impossible.

The meaning is: when the fruit, which consists in the cessation of ignorance, has been attained through knowledge acquired by means of the statements concerning truth and so forth. He applies the aphorism [saying], "independent," and "this being the case."
The word "ca" (and) is used for emphasis:

it is only because Brahman possesses independence in the manner described that the venerable Vyāsa’s composition of a separate treatise is justified, since he thereby attains a subject matter distinct from [the one treated in] the Dharmaśāstra.
The meaning is that [the inquiry] is not justified if the Vedāntas were intended to have action as their primary purport, because there would be no difference in the object of knowledge (*prameya*).
Anticipating the objection that a separate commencement is for the sake of investigating the dharma pertaining to the mind (*mānasa*), he says:
"And being commenced..."—that is, immediately after the investigation of dharma consisting of external means.

Therefore, since external dharma serves as a cause for mental worship through the gateway of purification, the remaining mental dharma is what ought to be investigated; thus, there should be a sūtra [to address this].
Regarding this, he provides an illustration with the word "atha" (now).

The meaning is that in the third chapter, after determining the relationship between the subordinate (*śeṣa*) and the principal (*śeṣin*) by means of scripture and other criteria, since the performance of the subordinate depends upon the principal, one will ascertain which is subordinate to the sacrifice (*kratu*) and which is subordinate to the person (*puruṣa*).

It would have to be commenced in this way; however, it has not been so commenced. Therefore, the sense is that it is incorrect to say that the commencement is for the sake of a subordinate property (*avāntaradharma*).
He states "brahma" to show that his own position is in accordance with the Sūtras;
the meaning is that since Jaimini did not investigate Brahman, it is appropriate for him [Bādarāyaṇa] to formulate the Sūtra concerning its desire to be known (*jijñāsya*).

Raising the objection, "If the subject matter of the Vedānta is non-duality (*advaita*), then what is the status of injunctions and the like, which depend upon duality? he replies with "Therefore," stating that their authority exists only prior to the arising of knowledge, and not afterwards.
The meaning is that knowledge sublates both the object of cognition and the cognizer.
Brahman is not a subordinate element of any effect;
rather, all worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*) occurs prior even to the awakening to That. In this regard, he cites a verse from the wise who know Brahman, beginning with "Moreover" (*api ca*).

When the realization arises—"I am the witness of all"—that Brahman, previously established as the Self, is eternally uncontradicted and that it is the Self which perceives objects, then, because the existence of son, body, and so forth is sublated and their nature as mere illusion is ascertained, there remains no basis for either the secondary identification with the Self (the notion "I" arising from association with the qualities of being the experiencer of one's own pleasure and pain through son, wife, etc.
or the false identification with the Self (the notion "I am a man, an agent, a fool"), which is the cause of all worldly transaction. In the absence of these, what [remains] to be done?
The meaning is: how could there be any worldly practice such as injunctions and prohibitions? It would not be possible in any way due to the absence of a cause.
Now, one might object: "The realization 'I am Brahman' is sublated, because the sense of 'I', which is the knower, cannot be Brahman.

Anticipating this doubt, he says, "It is to be sought," [meaning] there is no sublation, because the state of being a knower is produced by the identification with the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa), which is a manifestation of ignorance.

Based on the scriptural statement, "That Self which is free from evil, ageless, deathless, and sorrowless is to be sought," the meaning is that even before the realization of the Supreme Self—which is to be known—the conscious element (cid-dhātu), the Self, possesses the status of a knower; and it is precisely as a knower that, once known, it becomes the Supreme Self, devoid of evil, attachment, aversion, and death.

To the objection—"If the status of being a knower is merely imagined, how can the validity of the means of knowledge (pramāṇas) which depend upon it be maintained?"—the author replies with the words "deha" (the body).
The notion that the body is the self, though a constructed error, is accepted by the followers of the Vedas as valid because it serves as a factor in worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*).

Similarly, let ordinary perception and other means of knowledge be accepted as having empirical validity (*vyāvahārikaprāmāṇya*) during the time of transaction, since they remain uncontradicted until the realization of the Self.

However, the meaning of the word "but" (*tu*) is that the Vedāntas possess the validity of revealing ultimate reality (*tattvāvedakaprāmāṇya*), because they teach what is uncontradicted throughout the three periods of time.
"Until the ascertainment of the self. The prefix *ā* in "until the ascertainment of the self" (*ātmaniścayāt*) indicates a limit.
The sense is that even though the status of being a cognizer (*pramātṛtva*) is imagined, there is validity because the object is not sublated.

The harmony of all the Vedas with the supreme abode named Rāma has been established for the sake of pure understanding, by refuting the view that the purport of the scriptures lies in their injunctions regarding ritual action. //4//
Thus ends the Four Sūtras.

The Section on "Iksati" (Sūtras 5–11) The section concerning the word "Iksati" (he sees/contemplates). Sūtras 5 through 11.

Thus, it has been stated that the Vedānta passages— which have the realization of Brahman as the Self for their purpose and are coherent through their primary purport (tātparya) upon Brahman as the Self— reach their final conclusion in Brahman even without entering into the sphere of action (kārya).
And it has been stated that Brahman is omniscient, omnipotent, and the cause of the origin, subsistence, and dissolution of the world.

The Sāṃkhyas and others, however, considering that an established entity must necessarily be accessible through another means of valid cognition (pramāṇa), infer other causes such as Pradhāna and so forth; they then interpret the Vedānta passages solely with reference to those [causes].
Indeed, in all Vedānta passages concerning creation, they maintain that it is by means of inference alone—through the effect—that the cause is intended to be characterized.
The Sāṃkhyas hold that the conjunctions of Pradhāna and Puruṣa are eternally inferable.
The followers of Kaṇāda, however, infer from these very same passages that God is the efficient cause (*nimittakāraṇa*) and atoms are the material cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*).
Likewise, other logicians (*tārkika*), relying on fallacious statements and fallacious arguments, arise here as proponents of prima facie views (*pūrvapakṣavādin*).

In this regard, the Teacher—who is proficient in words, sentences, and the means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*)—sets forth those fallacious statements and fallacious arguments based on misconceptions as prima facie positions and refutes them, in order to demonstrate that the Vedānta passages have as their ultimate purpose the realization of Brahman.

In this regard, the Sāṃkhyas, who maintain that the Pradhāna— consisting of the three guṇas and being insentient— is the cause of the world, say: "Those Vedānta passages which you stated demonstrate that the omniscient and omnipotent Brahman is the cause of the world can also be applied to the position that the Pradhāna is the cause."
To begin with, the possession of all powers (sarvaśaktitva) is possible for even the Pradhāna with respect to its own transformations;
likewise, omniscience (sarvajñatva) is also possible.
How so?
As for that which you consider to be knowledge, it is a quality of *sattva*, according to the traditional teaching: "From *sattva* arises knowledge" (Gītā 14.17).
And by means of that knowledge, which is a quality of *sattva*, persons who possess cause and effect are well known as omniscient yogins.
For omniscience is established as occurring when *sattva* reaches its unsurpassed excellence.
It is not possible to conceive of omniscience—or even limited knowledge—belonging to the solitary *puruṣa*, who is neither an effect nor a cause and consists of mere consciousness.

However, because *pradhāna* is composed of the three *guṇas*, the *sattva* that serves as the cause of all knowledge exists within it even during the state of *pradhāna*; thus, omniscience is figuratively attributed to *pradhāna*, which is itself insentient.

Furthermore, even by you, who necessarily accept that Brahman is omniscient on the basis of the Vedānta texts, omniscience must be admitted as consisting precisely in the possession of the capacity for all knowledge; for Brahman does not exist as actually performing a cognition of every object. To explain: if cognition were eternal, Brahman’s independence with respect to the act of knowing would be lost.

Furthermore, if Brahman were to cease from the activity of knowing because it is impermanent, then omniscience would follow [only] by virtue of its possessing the capacity for all knowledge. Moreover, you maintain that prior to creation, Brahman is devoid of all causal instruments (kāraka).
Furthermore, the arising of knowledge in anyone is not possible in the absence of the body, the sense organs, and so forth, which are the instruments of knowledge.
Moreover, since transformation is impossible for the Pradhāna—which is composed of multiple constituents—it is logical that it can be a cause, just like clay and other such materials;
however, this is not the case for Brahman, which is uncomposite and of a single nature. This being the position reached, the following Sūtra is commenced:

Note: Even without a causal relation, [the objects] are inferable. The inference is as follows: that which is a reflection in the intellect is preceded by a corresponding original object (*bimba*), because it is a reflection, like the appearance of a face in a mirror.
Those who hold divergent views regarding grammar, Mīmāṃsā, and Nyāya— namely, the words, sentences, and means of valid cognition— as well as regarding fallacious sentences and fallacious arguments;
[this applies] with respect to the activity of knowing, that is, with respect to the meaning of the verbal root *jñā*.
Sovereignty is agency;
by the word "etcetera," the inclusion of the object of knowledge, the knower, and so forth is intended.
He refutes the causality of Pradhāna and other such principles through arguments in the Tarkapāda.

The causality of Brahman is established in the *Smṛti-pāda*: "On account of seeing [the Self], that which is not based on the Word [is not the cause]. (BS 1.1.5). The insentient *pradhāna* postulated by the Sāṃkhya cannot be accepted as the cause of the world in the Vedānta texts.
For that [cause] is indeed without sound.
How is it without sound?
Because of "seeing"—because the scripture declares that the cause possesses the quality of being a seer.
How so?

For it is heard thus: "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone, one only without a second" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.2.1), and having begun with that, [it continues]: "It thought: 'May I be many, may I procreate'; It emitted heat" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.2.3).

In this context, having determined that the world—which is denoted by the word "this" and differentiated by name and form—existed as the Self (ātman) prior to its origination, the text demonstrates that this very subject denoted by the word "Being" (sat), preceded by reflection, is the creator of fire and the other elements.
Likewise, elsewhere it is said: "In the beginning, indeed, this was the Self alone, one only."
"Nothing else whatsoever was moving.
He thought, 'Shall I now create the worlds?
He created these worlds. (Aitareya Upaniṣad 1.1.1)
Thus, [the scripture] declares that creation is preceded by deliberation (*īkṣā*). Furthermore, having introduced the Puruṣa consisting of sixteen parts, it says: "He reflected;
He created Prāṇa" (Praśna Upaniṣad 6.3).
And in the phrase "because of seeing" (īkṣateḥ), the intended meaning is the indication of the root's sense,
just as in the case of "because of sacrificing" (yajateḥ);
it is not an indication of the verbal root itself.

Therefore, passages such as, "He who is all-knowing and all-perceiving, whose austerity consists of knowledge— from Him is born this Brahman, name, form, and food" (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 1.1.9), which have the omniscient Lord as their cause, should also be cited.
As for what was said— that the Pradhāna will become omniscient through knowledge characterized by the quality of *sattva*— that is not tenable;
for in the state of Pradhāna, since the qualities (*guṇas*) are in equilibrium, knowledge as a property of *sattva* cannot exist.
Now, it was argued that [Prakṛti] will be omniscient by virtue of possessing the capacity for all knowledge;
that too is not tenable.

If, while the qualities are in equilibrium, Prakṛti is called omniscient by relying on the power of knowledge which rests upon *sattva*, then one might as well rely on the power that obstructs knowledge and rests upon *rajas* and *tamas*.
One might say that [the Self] knows only a little;
furthermore, the activity of a sentient being is not denoted by the verb "to know" (√jñā) unless it is witnessed by a witness,
and the non-conscious *pradhāna* lacks the status of being a witness.
Therefore, the omniscience of Pradhāna is untenable;
however, since yogins are sentient beings, their omniscience is tenable as being caused by the excellence of their sattva, and thus it does not serve as a valid example.
Furthermore, if it were further imagined that the state of being a seer is caused by a witness (sākṣin), [then...]
Just as a mass of iron and the like possesses the quality of being a burner by virtue of fire,
so too, it being thus, that very cause by which the Pradhāna possesses the quality of seeing is the omniscient, primary Brahman, and it is logical that He is the cause of the world.
As for what was further stated— that even for Brahman, primary omniscience is not tenable— [that is refuted].
"If [the Lord] possesses eternal knowledge and action, independence with respect to knowledge and action would be impossible.
To this it is replied: First, you must be asked this: how is it that the loss of omniscience follows from the possession of eternal knowledge and action?
For it is a contradiction to say that one who possesses eternal knowledge capable of illuminating all objects is not omniscient.
Indeed, if knowledge were non-eternal, one would know at some times and not know at others, and thus there would be a lack of omniscience.

This fault does not exist in the case of the eternity of knowledge. If it is argued that "if knowledge is eternal, the designation of independence regarding the object of knowledge is not tenable," we say no.
For even though the sun possesses pervasive heat and light, we observe the independent designation that "it burns" and "it illuminates.
Now, one might object: such a designation as "it burns" or "it illuminates" would indeed apply to the sun when there is contact with the object to be burned or illuminated;
however, since Brahman has no prior association with objects of knowledge or action before creation, the illustration is dissimilar. This is not so.

Since we observe the designation of agency in the statement "the sun shines," even though there is no action [inhering in it], so too, even in the absence of an object of knowledge, the designation of Brahman as agent in the passage "It thought" is appropriate; thus, there is no inconsistency. Furthermore, if an object were required, the scriptural texts concerning Brahman's status as a seer would be all the more justified.
What, then, is that karma which becomes the object of God’s knowledge prior to creation?
We reply: it is name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), which are undifferentiated (*avyākṛta*) yet intended to be differentiated; they are indefinable as being either identical with or different from [Brahman].
Since the experts in the Yoga-śāstra maintain that even for yogins there is direct perceptual knowledge regarding objects past and future by virtue of [the Lord's] grace,
what need is there to mention that the eternally established Lord possesses eternal knowledge regarding the creation, maintenance, and dissolution of the universe?
As for what was previously stated— that before creation, it is impossible for Brahman to be a perceiver without a connection to a body and so forth— [this is now addressed].
That objection does not apply;
for, just like the light of the sun, since Brahman is eternal in its very nature as knowledge, the requirement of means for the production of knowledge is untenable.

Furthermore, the arising of knowledge in a transmigrating being who possesses ignorance and the like may depend upon the body and other factors, but it cannot be so for the Lord, who is devoid of any causes that could obstruct His knowledge.

And these two mantras demonstrate that the Lord is independent of a body and the like, and that His knowledge is unobstructed: "For Him there exists neither effect nor instrument; neither one equal to Him nor superior to Him is seen.
His supreme power is heard to be indeed manifold, and His knowledge, strength, and action are innate" (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 6.8).
"Without hands or feet, He is swift and a grasper; He sees without eyes, and He hears without ears."
"He knows the knowable, yet there is no knower of him; him they call the foremost, the Great Person" (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 3.19).

Now, it might be argued that there is no transmigrating being other than the Lord who possesses causes obstructing knowledge, according to the Śruti: "There is no other seer, there is no other knower than He" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.7.23).
In this regard, why is it said that the arising of knowledge in a transmigrating being depends on a body and so forth, whereas for the Lord it does not?
To this it is replied: True;
there is no transmigrating being other than the Lord.

Nevertheless, the connection with the limiting adjuncts (upādhi) such as the aggregate of the body and so forth occurs precisely because of this; it is like the connection of space with limiting adjuncts such as a jar, a water-pot, or a mountain cave.

And the worldly usage of words and concepts based on that [connection] is observed, such as "the hole of a jar" or "the hole of a water-pot," even though there is no difference from space itself. Furthermore, the false notion of a distinction within space—such as "the space of a jar"—is seen to be produced by those [adjuncts].

Likewise, here too, there exists the false cognition of a distinction between the Lord and the transmigrating soul (saṃsārin), produced by the non-discrimination [of the Self] from its adjuncts (upādhi) such as the aggregate of the body and so forth.

And it is observed that even while the Self alone truly exists, there is an adherence to the notion of "Self" with respect to the non-Self—the aggregate of the body and so forth—by means of a prior false cognition consisting of mere imagination.
This being the case, the status of being a transmigrator is established, and for the transmigrator, the state of being a perceiver dependent upon the body and other factors is logically consistent.

As for what was also said—that because the *pradhāna* consists of multiple constituents, its status as a cause is possible like that of clay and so forth, whereas it is not possible for the uncomposite Brahman—that has already been refuted by the fact that the *pradhāna* is not based on scripture (*aśabda*).

Furthermore, he will elaborate later how, even by means of reasoning, the causality of Brahman alone can be established and not that of the *pradhāna* and other such principles: "Because this world is of a different nature" (Brahmasūtra 2.1.4).
By such [statements] as these. // 5 //
Having restated what has been established, he states the intermediate connection (*avāntara-saṅgati*) characterized by an objection (*ākṣepa*): "But the Sāṃkhyas and others [say]...

Let it be granted that the Vedāntas have a coherent unity (*samanvaya*) with respect to an established entity; nevertheless, because there can be no apprehension of the word's denotative power (*śakti-graha*) regarding Brahman—which is not accessible through other means of knowledge—and because, due to its immutability and changelessness, it cannot logically be a cause, there can be no such coherent unity.

However, the meaning is that they raise an objection [to the Sūtra] by asserting that there is a "concordance" (samanvaya) with the Pradhāna— which consists of the three guṇas and is knowable through inference— as follows: "The initial effect of creation is insentient in nature, because it is an effect, like a jar."
The insistence that what is established must be cognizable through another means of knowledge is for the sake of grasping the word’s expressive power (*śakti*).

For this very reason, it has been stated that since the grasping of expressive power is possible regarding the *pradhāna* presented by inference, one should interpret the scriptural passages as being directed toward that [inferred entity].
Furthermore, there are such scriptural texts as: "O dear one, seek the root of Being by means of the sprout of light."

Showing that the cause is sought by itself through its own "sprout" (effect) as its mark, [the author] states "In all... to indicate that they assert the cause of the world to be established by another means of knowledge.
Now, one might object: since Pradhāna and the like are beyond the senses, it is impossible to grasp their pervasion; how, then, can there be inference?
To this, he says: "Pradhāna..."

The meaning is that the conjunctions of *pradhāna* and *puruṣa* are to be understood through inference based on general observation (*sāmānyatodṛṣṭānumāna*): whatever is an effect is of an insentient nature, like a jar; and whatever is insentient is conjoined with a conscious being, like a chariot and so forth.
He states another opposing view regarding the causality of non-dual Brahman: "The followers of Kaṇāda, however...

The meaning is that from the very texts concerning creation—which take the form of inferences for the sake of others—they infer God as the agent, based on the principle that whatever is an effect has an intelligent creator; and they infer the atoms, based on the principle that whatever is a composite substance is produced by substances possessing a dimension smaller than its own.
Others, such as the Buddhists and so forth,
[cite] fallacious statements such as, "In the beginning, this was non-existent," and so on;
[they claim that] whatever is a real entity must end in emptiness.
"Just as [the example of] a lamp" refers to a fallacious argument (*yuktyābhāsa*).
Having thus stated the disagreements among disputants, he introduces the sequence of subsequent sūtras for the purpose of refuting them with the word "therein" (*tatra*).
The meaning is: "when there is a dispute among disputants."
Because he is a treasure-house of grammar, Mīmāṃsā, and Nyāya, he possesses knowledge of words, sentences, and the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

Regarding the doubt—arising from whether the "seeing" (*īkṣaṇa*) attributed to that which is the cause of the world is primary or secondary as to whether it is conscious or unconscious—the author states the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*): "In this regard, the Sāṃkhyas... and so forth.
The meaning of the word "api" (even/also) is the sense of the particle "ca" (and).

The connections with the Śruti and other sources are established by the statement that passages containing clear marks of Brahman, such as "Being only... (*sadeva*), are intended for Brahman, through the refutation of their being directed toward the Pradhāna.
In the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), there is the meditation on the identity of the individual soul (*jīva*) with the Pradhāna.
The distinction is that, according to our established doctrine (*siddhānta*), the knowledge of the oneness of Brahman [belongs to the conscious self];
whereas he states that omniscience belongs only to the insentient *sattva* and not to the conscious [self] by saying, "and by that quality of *sattva*."

"Not of the solitary [Self]" means that since the knowledge produced [by the intellect] is a property of *sattva*, and because eternal perception is not an effect, pure consciousness (*cinmātra*) does not possess the agency of being the knower of all things.

Now, one might ask: "In the state of equilibrium of the *guṇas*, since there is no predominance of *sattva*, how can there be omniscience? To this he says: "Because of the nature of the three *guṇas*."
The three *guṇas* alone constitute *pradhāna*; its state of equilibrium is called *pradhāna* because it is characterized by non-differentiation.
Even in that state of dissolution (*pralaya*), omniscience—in the form of possessing the capacity for all knowledge—remains intact; this is the meaning.
[Objection: Why should I accept a secondary (metaphorical) omniscience consisting merely in the possession of such capacity?
Regarding this, he says "no.

Since non-eternal knowledge perishes at the time of dissolution (pralaya), it must be said that [the self] possesses power; furthermore, because of the absence of causal factors, he says "moreover" (api ca).
Having stated the similarity between the two views, he states the distinction in his own view with "moreover" (api ca).
The causality of Brahman was established in the *Smṛti-pāda*;
the causality of the *pradhāna* and other principles was refuted by means of reasoning in the *Tarka-pāda*.
Now, however, it is refuted by means of scripture: "Because of [Brahman's] seeing, that which is not based on scripture [is not the cause]."

The construction of the sūtra is as follows: because of the mention of "seeing" (īkṣaṇa) and "hearing" (śravaṇa), the Pradhāna—which is not denotable by the Veda and is beyond the scope of words—is not the cause, since it is "without scriptural authority" (aśabda).
That cause, which is denoted by the word "Sat," saw [the world].
He describes that very act of seeing: "Much" (bahu).

For the purpose of existing in the form of manifold expansion, he says "I myself shall be born" by way of being the material cause, due to the non-difference between the cause and the effect; this is expressed by the word "progeny" (prajā).
Having thus looked upon that [reality] as "Being" (sat), and having created space and air, he says "That" (tat) regarding how he created fire.

"Moving with a glint"— that is to say, pervaded by living beings— that Supreme Self, who is non-different from the individual soul (*jīva*), created *aprāṇa* (the unbreathed), and from *prāṇa* (breath) he created faith,
space, air, light, water, earth, the senses, mind, food, and from food, vigor, austerity, sacred formulas, ritual acts, and the worlds within those worlds.

Thus the sixteen kalās have been described. Now, an objection may be raised: according to the traditional rule (smaraṇa) of Kātyāyana, "The suffixes *ik*, *śit*, and *tap* denote the verbal root," the word *īkṣateḥ* refers to the verbal root by means of the suffix *śtip*. Therefore, how can the meaning of the root (*dhātvartha*)—namely, "seeing" (*īkṣaṇa*)—be explained? Anticipating this doubt, he states "by means of *īkṣateḥ*" (*īkṣiteriti ceti*), indicating that it is done through metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*).

Regarding the Jaimini-sūtra, "The *yajati* [root] possesses the state of being preceded by the injunction of the procedure (*itikartavyatā*) as in the primary sacrifice," the meaning is that just as the root-meaning, namely the sacrifice (*yāga*), is expressed by the word *yajati* through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*), so it is here as well. Since the subsidiaries (*aṅga*) of modified sacrifices (*vikṛti-yāga*) such as the *saurya* are not explicitly enjoined, the meaning of the sūtra is that they possess the status of subsidiaries belonging to the archetypal sacrifices (*prakṛti*) such as the *darśa*, which precede them. He states the benefit resulting from the mention of the root-meaning with the words "by that" (*tena*).
The distinction is that he is "all-knowing" (sarvajña) in a general sense and "all-seeing" (sarvavit) in a specific sense.
Knowledge is indeed the very vision that constitutes austerity.
Regarding the fruit for the ascetic, he says: "Therefore," etc.
This effect called the Sūtra is Brahman.
Having accepted that knowledge consists of the activity of pure *sattva*, the omniscience of Pradhāna was refuted.

Now, however, the meaning of the word "knowledge" is not merely the activity of an insentient entity; rather, knowledge is either an activity qualified by the consciousness of the Witness (*sākṣin*), or it is the consciousness manifested through that activity.
And he says "moreover" (api ca) because that [witnessing] does not exist for the blind Pradhāna;
the ellipsis is: "there is witnesshood, by which it would possess the aforementioned quality of possessing knowledge."

Now, it might be argued that the omniscience of yogis has been stated to arise merely from the functioning of their *sattva*; to this, he says: "But for the yogis... He states the view of the Sāṃkhya with its Lord (*seśvara-sāṃkhya*) beginning with "Now" (*atha*).
Omniscience means the state of possessing knowledge whose range encompasses all objects.
Keeping in mind that there is no agency of knowing because knowledge cannot be produced by an action, he asks: "First of all, this...
