He raises the objection regarding the grammatical incorrectness of the expression "he knows everything" on the grounds that knowledge is eternal: "If knowledge is eternal..."

He states, with an illustration, that the designation of Brahman as the "agent" of knowledge is valid because, although knowledge is eternal, one may conceptually posit a distinction from the nature of Brahman by virtue of its being conditioned by various objects, and thus figuratively attribute to it the status of an effect: "Not [like] the continuous... (na pratateti). The meaning is "continuous" (saṃtata).
"Even though [the object] is not intended to be expressed"—that is, even though it is not meant to be spoken of.

Now, one might object: "Since the verb *prakāśati* (shines) is intransitive, the usage 'the sun shines' (*savitā prakāśate*) is appropriate; however, since the verb *jñā* (to know) is transitive, it requires an object, and thus the statement 'it saw' (*tadaikṣata*) would be incorrect in the absence of an object.
To this, he replies: "But when there is a requirement for an object..."

It was stated previously that there is no disparity [between the two cases], because even when the action of karma is not intended to be expressed, just as the sun— which is essentially light— is metaphorically designated as the "agent" (kartṛ) by virtue of being the substratum of the act of shining in some sense, so too the conscious self (cidātman) is metaphorically designated as the agent of the act of seeing (īkṣaṇa) by virtue of its conscious nature.

Now, however, [the point is made] that just as for a potter the act of seeing consists of a modification (vṛtti) of his own limiting adjunct, the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa), so too for the Lord (īśvara), it consists of a modification of his own limiting adjunct, ignorance (avidyā).

At the conclusion of the dissolution, a certain transformation directed toward creation occurs within Prakṛti, whose various creative impressions have been awakened; therefore, it indicates that there exists in her a vision regarding all effects latent in subtle form, and because that vision is an effect and involves the presence of action (*karman*), its agency is primary— this is emphasized by the word "sutarām" (all the more).
[Objection: But how can the Lord—who is pure consciousness as the prototype (bimba) conditioned by Māyā—be the primary agent with respect to seeing, given the absence of any action?

[Reply: This is not so, because agency belongs only to one who possesses knowledge conducive to the effect; and since the Lord also possesses eternal knowledge conducive to seeing, he is indeed the agent.
Nor should it be argued that since agency is established by eternal knowledge alone, what is the use of "seeing" (īkṣaṇa)?
For such an argument would lead to an over-extension (atiprasaṅga), whereby one might ask: "Since sound can exist in air and so forth, what is the need for space?

Therefore, because it is heard in scripture as the cause of air and the rest, just like space, this "seeing"—which is heard as adventitious—must be accepted as the cause of space and the other elements. This suffices.
The meaning is that when the unmanifest (avyākṛta) exists in a subtle state, it is desired to be "differentiated" (vyākartum), that is, to be made gross.

Having raised the objection that although the act of seeing in the form of consciousness colored by the effects of the unmanifest does not depend on an instrument, an instrument must still be stated for the seeing in the form of a mental modification (vṛtti), he says: "Moreover, [it belongs] to one who possesses ignorance and so forth.
The sense is that, because there is no rule that what is known by one must be known by another, even the Illusionist (māyin), though bodiless, can be the instrumental cause of produced seeing.

Anticipating the objection that there exists a pervasion (vyāpti) such that whatever knowledge is produced must be accomplished by means of a body, he states "And the two mantras," thereby refuting it with scripture.
"Effect" refers to the body;
"cause" refers to the sense organs.
The power (*śakti*) of this Lord is *māyā*; it is "supreme" (*parā*) in relation to its own effects, and it is twofold because it produces diverse effects.
He states that this [power] is established merely through tradition (*aitihya*) and not established by means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), saying: "It is heard."
The creative activity that occurs through the power of the nature of knowledge (*jñāna*) is inherent (*svābhāvikī*);
the meaning is that it arises from being of the nature of beginningless *māyā*.

Furthermore, the "power" of knowledge—that is, of consciousness—is its clarity as reflected in the modification of *māyā*; the "activity" of that [clarity] is the Brahman’s status as the progenitor by way of being the original image (*bimba*), and thus its status as the knower is also inherently inherent. This is another interpretation.
Though handless, he is a grasper;
though footless, he is swift.
The meaning is that the Lord has no dependence on worldly causes for his own activity.
The meaning is: the foremost, without beginning, the Person, infinite, great, and all-pervading.
He raises the objection of a departure from established tenets (*apasiddhānta*) with the words "Now, [it may be objected]...
The logical connection is as follows: since ignorance, attachment, and so forth—which are the obstructing causes regarding knowledge—are absent in the Lord, there is no one other than the Lord.

He replies, "To this it is said," because he has already stated that the distinction between the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Lord is merely adventitious (*aupādhika*). Thus, there is no departure from established tenets.
"Produced by that" means produced by the connection with limiting adjuncts (upādhi); it refers to worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*) consisting of words and the cognitions they generate.
The word "unconfused" (*asaṃkīrṇa*) is to be supplied as the remainder [of the sentence].
To the question, "How can there be non-confusion if there is no distinction [between the self and the adjuncts]?", he says: "And produced by that... and so forth.

The meaning is that [the self's limitation] is produced by its connection with limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*). "In that way" means that the cause of the connection with the body and so forth is non-discrimination (*aviveka*), which is beginningless ignorance (*anādyavidyā*); the meaning is that it is produced by that [ignorance].

For the distinction— that the individual soul (jīva) is the reflection in ignorance (avidyā) and the Lord (īśvara) is the original image-consciousness (bimba-caitanya)— has its existence dependent upon ignorance;
this is because an eternal distinction cannot be an effect.
The distinction between the knower and so forth, produced by the intellect and its functions, is itself merely an effect; this is the discernment.
Now, one might ask: how can there be non-discernment regarding the Self, which is partless and self-luminous?
To this, he says: "And it is seen."
In reality, the notion "I am a man" is difficult to deny because it is observed as an error regarding the Self, which is by nature distinct from the body and so forth and is self-luminous.
And the meaning of the word "ca" (and) is that this [notion] is imagined through mere false cognition—that is, through ignorance established by delusion, since it is measured by such false cognition.
Alternatively, he states the common worldly experience regarding the aforementioned false cognition: "And it is seen," etc.

The third case ending (*tṛtīyā*) is used here in the sense of "being in such a state. The meaning is that it is perceived as having the nature of an error; or alternatively, the meaning is that it is perceived solely through a succession of prior errors, and not as an object of cognition (*prameya*).
He states that even for the immutable (kūṭastha), an illusory causality is logical, beginning with "But as...
As for the objection that it is impossible to grasp the power of words regarding that which is not an object of knowledge, that is not so;

for words such as "Being" (satya) and others, whose powers are understood in common usage to refer to meanings such as "the uncontradicted," serve as indicators (lakṣaka) of the undivided Brahman presented as a portion of their own primary denotations (vācya). Thus it is established. //5//
Here it is said: That which was stated— that the non-conscious *pradhāna* is not the cause of the world because it possesses the quality of seeing (*īkṣitṛtva*)— is also explainable otherwise.
Because we observe metaphorical usage as if something were conscious even when it is unconscious—
for example, having observed that a riverbank is about to collapse, one says "the bank wishes to fall," and thus metaphorical usage as if conscious is seen even for an unconscious bank—
so too, although the *pradhāna* is unconscious, there will be metaphorical usage as if conscious when its manifestation is imminent, as in the statement, "It thought."

Just as in the world a certain conscious person, having bathed and eaten, looks toward the afternoon and thinks, "I shall go to the village by chariot," and subsequently proceeds accordingly with regularity,
so too does the Pradhāna proceed with regularity in the form of the Mahat and the other evolutes.
Therefore, it is figuratively described as if it were conscious.
For what reason, moreover, is the primary sense of "seeing" set aside and a figurative sense postulated, as in:
"That fire saw," and "Those waters saw" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.2.3, 4)?
Thus, since even water and fire— which are insentient— are seen to be treated as if they were sentient through metaphorical usage,
it is understood that the act of "seeing" (īkṣaṇa), though involving an agent, is merely figurative,
because the statement occurs in a context primarily consisting of metaphorical expressions.
This being the case, the following sūtra is commenced:
[The term] *sarvajña* (all-knowing) refers to one who knows everything in a general sense;
[the term] *sarvavit* (all-seer) refers to one who knows everything by taking up each specific property, such as a jar and so forth.
This "Brahman" being born is the effect known as Hiraṇyagarbha.
Having set forth the Sāṃkhya position as a defense of his own view, [the author] refutes it with the words "As for what was said.
The meaning of the word "that" (tat) is the lack of consciousness, that is, the state of not being a knower.
He states the Sāṃkhya doctrine that accepts a Lord (seśvara-sāṃkhya): "Now" (atha).
The meaning of "extended" (pratatā) is "continuous" (saṃtatā).
"Even though it is non-existent" (asaty api) means even when it is not intended to be expressed [as a primary object].
The word "sutarām" (even more so) is used because there is no sublation of the meaning of the suffix, just as there is none of the base.
"Kārya" means the body; "karaṇa" refers to the collection of sense organs.
"Insistence" refers to false pride.
[Objection: If it is argued that [the term "Self"] is used figuratively, [we reply] no, because of the word "Self.
As for what was stated—that the primary principle (pradhāna), which is insentient and denoted by the word "Sat," possesses the act of seeing (īkṣati) only in a figurative sense—[that is not so].
The claim that [the Self] is like fire and heat is incorrect.

Why? Because of the word "Self. Having begun with, "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.2.1), it continues, "It thought: 'Let me send forth these worlds,' and it sent forth fire" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.2.3).

Thus, having described the creation of fire, water, and food, [the text] refers back to that very same subject—the Existent as the Seer—and to those very elements of fire, water, and food by means of the word "deities," saying: "That deity thought: 'Come now, let me enter these three deities with this living self and differentiate name and form'" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.3.2).

In that context, if the Pradhāna were imagined to be the conscious observer through the function of the Guṇas, then it alone—being the subject under discussion—would be referred to by the phrase "this deity.
In that case, the deity would not denote the individual soul (jīvātman).
For the so-called jīva is indeed conscious, the presiding lord of the body, and the sustainer of the vital breaths.
Because of its well-known etymology,
how could that [Self] be the Self of the insentient *pradhāna*?
For "Self" (*ātman*) indeed means one's own essential nature (*svarūpa*).
The conscious individual soul (*jīva*) cannot be the essential nature of the unconscious *pradhāna*.
However, if the conscious Brahman is accepted as the primary subject of the act of seeing, then the application of the word "Self" (*ātman*) with reference to the individual soul becomes logical.
Thus it is said: "That which is this subtle essence—this whole world has that as its self; that is the Truth, that is the Self; That art thou, Śvetaketu" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.14.3).

In this passage, having taught the Self under discussion— the "Being" (sat) along with its subtle essence (aṇiman)— by means of the word "Self" in the phrase "That is the Self," [the text] teaches it as the Self of the conscious Śvetaketu in the words "That thou art, O Śvetaketu. However, water and fire are non-conscious because they are objects [of perception],
and because they are designated merely as things to be employed in the manifestation of names and forms and so forth.

And since there is no reason for it to be primary—as there is in the case of the word "Self"—it is proper to regard the power of seeing as being figurative, like [the word] "bank. Furthermore, even in those two cases, the power of seeing depends precisely upon being presided over by the Existent (Sat). However, it has already been stated that for the Existent, the power of seeing is not figurative on account of the word "Self. // 6 //
Now, he states the doubt to be refuted by the subsequent sūtra: "Regarding this, it is said.

[The phrase] "even otherwise" means even in the case of insentience (*acetanatva*). [Objection: But what similarity does the *pradhāna* have with a sentient being (*cetana*), such that its "seeing" (*īkṣaṇa*) could be considered figurative? To this, he says: "Just as... (*yathā*).
The meaning is that "similarity" refers to the performance of effects in a fixed sequence.
Regarding the phrase "because of the statement being mostly figurative," the meaning is because it is recited in a context abounding in secondary (gauṇa) meanings.
If it is argued that the term "seeing" (īkṣati) is used figuratively with respect to the insentient [ether], just as it is with water and fire, we say no.

He states the meaning of the Sūtra—"from the word *ātman* [there is] the determination of the existence [of the subject] as conscious"—with the words beginning "that which was said," and so forth. That aforementioned subject denoted by the word *sat*, this very deity who is the seer, being indirect (*parokṣa*), [says]: "Come now (*hanta*); immediately after the creation of the elements, these three created things in the form of fire, water, and food.
Because it is indirect, the word *devatāḥ* takes the accusative plural ending.

The syntactical connection (*anvaya*) is as follows: "Having entered into those [beings] by means of this living self (*jīva*), which is my own essential nature (*svarūpa*) experienced in previous kalpas, I shall make their names and forms gross so that they may become objects of enjoyment.

This is because it is well-known in common usage, and because the etymology of the verbal root *jīv*—from the sense of "sustaining life" (*prāṇadhāraṇe*)—is "that which lives (*jīvati*) sustains life (*prāṇān dhārayati*)."

"But here, however" means that in our own position (*svapakṣe*), since it is observed in the world that the distinction between the original image (*bimba*) and its reflection (*pratibimba*) is merely imagined, it is logical that the individual soul (*jīva*) is the Self (*ātman*) of Being (*sat*).

Having stated that the *pradhāna* is not the referent of the word "Being" because of the word "Self" (*ātman*) applied to the individual soul, he explains the reason in another way— that the *pradhāna* is not [the referent] with respect to the individual soul being within Being— by saying "so too."
That which is called "Being" (sat), this subtle essence within the minute, this entire world has that as its self;
that Being alone is the truth.
Because modification is false,
that existent reality is the Self of all. O Śvetaketu!
And you are not a transmigrating being; rather, the meaning of the Śruti is that you are that very Brahman, which is real, unsublated, and the Self of all—
thus it teaches here.
Therefore, because it is conscious by nature and because it exists, it is indeed conscious—this is the completion of the sentence.
Regarding the claim that the "seeing" of the existent [Being] is figurative, as in the case of water and fire, he says: "But in the case of water and fire..."
The differentiation of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) is creation;
the restriction [of beings] is from the word "water.

Since air and fire are objects of sight, are created, and are subject to restriction, they lack sentience; thus, there is an obstacle to the primary sense of "seeing" (*īkṣaṇa*), and no proof for it exists. For this reason, it is logical that the "seeing" is figurative.

The interpretation is as follows: the quality is the performance of an action characteristic of a conscious being; the meaning of "fire thought" (*teja aikṣata*) is the performance of an action characteristic of a conscious being.
Alternatively, by the word "fire," its substrate, *sat* (Being), is indicated.
And thus, he states that the act of seeing (īkṣaṇa) is primary with the words "of those two" (tayor iti).
This might be so if the seeing of the Existent (sat) were primary; but why is that? To this he replies: "But of the Existent... (satastu iti).

Since there can be no doubt between two things that are unequal—one being figurative and the other primary—the fact that the term "Self" (ātman) is used serves as a decisive factor; therefore, the meaning is that the seeing of the Existent is primary. //6//
Now,
it might be argued that the word "Self" (ātman) is applied even to the insentient *pradhāna*.
Because it accomplishes all the purposes of the Self (ātman),

just as the word "Self" is applied to a servant who performs all the king's tasks, as in the expression, "Bhadrasena is my self. For primordial matter (pradhāna), by effecting the experience and liberation of the person (puruṣa), acts as a benefactor to that Self.
It is like a servant attending to a king in matters such as peace and war;

or alternatively, the single word *ātman* may apply to both sentient and insentient objects, as seen in usages such as *bhūtātman* (the self of the elements) and *indriyātman* (the self of the senses).

Just as the single word *jyotis* (light) has both the sacrifice and the flame as its referents, how is it determined that the word *ātman* in this context refers to the Self in its primary sense rather than in a figurative one? To this, the author reads the following reply: "By means of this very Self—which was experienced during the previous creation and is the cause of the sustenance of the vital breaths—having entered those aforementioned deities after their manifestation, [the Lord] thought: 'I shall clearly and completely fashion name and form. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.3.2). By this, it is shown that the Self, whose nature is Being (*sat*), entered the deities after creation and intended to manifest names and forms. Thus, the word *ātman* here denotes the Supreme Self in its primary sense.
The meaning is that the supreme deity has looked upon [them].

By figurative application (*guṇavṛtti*), the capacity to see is attributed to water and fire, just as the desire to fall is attributed to the bank; this is the sense of their having "seen" in a secondary sense.
This is because liberation is taught for one who is established in That (the Supreme Self). (BBs 1.1.7)

The non-intelligent *pradhāna* cannot be the referent of the word "Self," because, having taken up the previously mentioned *sac-cit* (Being-Consciousness) as "That is the Self," the text teaches that it is the goal for the intelligent Śvetaketu, who is to be liberated, saying, "That thou art, O Śvetaketu"; and then continues, "The man who has a teacher knows; for him there is delay only so long as he is not released."
This is because of the instruction on liberation: "Then I shall attain [Brahman]" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.14.2).

For if the scripture were to teach a seeker of liberation—who is conscious—that the unconscious Pradhāna, denoted by the word *sat*, is what he is, saying "You are that," then it would be teaching something contrary to reality; as such, the scripture would lead to the person's detriment and would not be an authoritative means of knowledge.
It might be so;

however, it is not proper to consider a faultless scripture to be invalid. Furthermore, if a scripture that has attained the status of a valid means of knowledge were to teach an insentient non-self as the Self to one who is ignorant yet seeking liberation, that person—out of faith—would not abandon the view of that [insentient thing] as the Self, following the maxim of the blind man and the cow's tail.
And one would not realize the Self as distinct from that [body];
if that were the case, one would fail to achieve the goal of human existence and would encounter misfortune.

Therefore, just as it teaches the means such as the Agnihotra exactly as they are to one who desires heaven and the like, so too, for the seeker of liberation, it teaches the Self exactly as it is in the words, "That is the Self; That thou art, O Śvetaketu."
This is logical;
and this being so, the teaching of liberation for one whose intention is rooted in truth (*satyābhisandha*) becomes tenable through the analogy of grasping and releasing the heated axe.

Otherwise, if the instruction regarding the reality of the Self as Being were not primary, [the scripture] would have said: "One should know: 'I am the hymn' (*aham uktham asmi iti vidyāt*). (Ai. Ār. 2.1.2.6)
In that case, this [Self] would be merely a product of ignorance with impermanent results;
consequently, instruction regarding liberation would be untenable.
Therefore, the word "Self" cannot be used figuratively for the *aṇiman* (the minute atom).

In the case of a servant, however, because the distinction between master and servant is perceptible, the metaphorical use of the word "self" is appropriate, as in "Bhadrasena is my self. Furthermore, even if a word is seen to be used metaphorically in some instances, it is not on that basis alone—given that the word is a means of valid cognition—that it is logical to assume a metaphorical sense for the object; for otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of a lack of confidence in all cases.
As for the claim that the word *ātman* is common to both the conscious and the unconscious— just as the word *jyotis* (light) applies to both a sacrifice and a flame—
that is not so,
because it is improper for a single term to have multiple meanings.

Therefore, the word *ātman* primarily refers only to that which possesses consciousness; it is applied to the elements and so forth through a metaphorical attribution of consciousness, as in the expressions "the self of the elements" (*bhūtātman*) and "the self of the senses" (*indriyātman*).

Although the word *ātman* is common to both [the conscious and the unconscious], its application to one or the other cannot be determined without some determining factor, such as the context or a qualifying term.
And here, there is no reason whatsoever that determines the unconscious.

But the subject under discussion possesses a seer; and the sentient Śvetaketu is present nearby. For we have already stated that it is impossible for the sentient Śvetaketu to have a non-sentient self.
Therefore, it is certain that the word "self" (ātman) here refers to a sentient being.

Furthermore, the word *jyotis* (light) is conventionally established (*rūḍha*) in common usage to mean "flame" alone; its application to the ritual sacrifice is based merely on a similarity to flame as imagined through an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*). Therefore, this is not a valid parallel example.

Alternatively, having already explained the word *ātman* in the preceding sūtra itself by way of dispelling all doubts regarding its figurative or common usage, one should then explain the word *tanniṣṭhasya mokṣopadeśāt* ("because liberation is taught for one who is intent upon That") as an independent reason for refuting the Pradhāna as the cause.

Therefore, the non-conscious *pradhāna* cannot be that which is denoted by the word "Being" (*sat*). [Note: Here, the use of the first-person pronoun (*uttamapuruṣa*) in place of the third person is archaic, as in Vedic usage. The construction is as follows: if the scripture, by addressing the conscious seeker of liberation—who is already "Being"—with the words "You are non-conscious," were to speak erroneously and thus lead the person to misfortune, it would consequently fail to be an authoritative source of knowledge (*apramāṇa*).
In this context, "frustration" (vihati) means the absence of attaining liberation.
As it is said: "Just as one who is truthful does not burn when grasping a heated axe, but is released.
"Uktha" refers to the vital breath (prāṇa).
This knowledge arising from the Great Sayings (mahāvākya) is thus described.

With the words beginning with "Now" (atha), [the author] raises the objection that the word *ātman* is used in a secondary sense (*gauṇa*) for the Pradhāna because of its association with the quality of acting for the benefit of the Self.
He replies with "Or rather" (athavā) that the word *ātman* is primary even when applied to the Pradhāna, because it possesses multiple meanings.
The illustration for the state of having multiple meanings is given by "yathā" (just as).

The meaning is that just as the word *jyotis* is primary (*mukhya*) in the sense of the *Jyotiṣṭoma* sacrifice—characterized by a thousand-fold sacrificial fee—due to the scriptural statement "Now this is the *jyotis*," and also in the sense of fire due to common worldly usage, so it is here.

He states the meaning of the Sūtra—"Not so," etc.—by explaining that liberation is heard [to be attained] by one who is "established in *Sat*" (*sanniṣṭha*), meaning one whose realization of non-difference is fixed upon that reality which is *Sat*.
The *Śruti* has been explained under the *Samanvaya-sūtra*.
He elaborates on what was stated as "for the sake of harm" with the words, "And if [it were taught] to one who is ignorant," etc.
It is said that a certain wicked person spoke to a blind man who had fallen on the path through a great forest and was desiring to go to his own kinsmen's city.
"Why do you remain here suffering, O venerable one?
Hearing these pleasant words, the blind man, considering him a trusted friend, said:
"Oh, what good fortune is mine!"
When he said, "Sir, you speak thus to me, who am wretched and unable to reach my desired city," that man, wishing to deceive him, brought a rogue young bull and had him seize its blind tail;
and he instructed the blind man:
"This young bull will lead you to the city; do not abandon your tail.
Out of excessive faith, that blind man abandoned it, and failing to attain his desired goal, he fell into a succession of calamities.
The meaning is: "by that same principle.

"That being the case" means that in the absence of self-knowledge, one would be frustrated—that is, one would not attain liberation, but on the contrary, would encounter misfortune and cyclic existence (saṃsāra).
[Objection: "But surely this statement may be for the purpose of meditating on the identification of the individual soul (jīva) with Pradhāna.
To this, he replies: "And this being so," which means:
while the uncontradicted cognition of the Self exists.
It is observed that someone falsely accused of theft is released when he grasps a heated axe with truth;

by that example, liberation is taught for one who possesses the firm conviction "I am [Brahman]" regarding the Truth that is Brahman, as instructed in the Śruti: "He who is devoted to truth grasps the heated axe; he is not burned, and then he is released.
This teaching is not tenable under the view of *saṃpat* (symbolic identification), as the author states with the words "otherwise."
"Uktha" is the vital breath (prāṇa), because it causes the body to rise;

therefore, since the teaching of liberation is possible only in its primary sense, and because a secondary sense is improper when the primary sense is available, he says "api ca" (furthermore) to show that the word "Self" (ātman) is used in its primary sense.
[The word] "in some cases" refers to [the case of] a servant and so forth.

The meaning is that even in the case of "I am everywhere," the word *ātman* would not be used in its primary sense; rather, it is applied to the elements and so forth through a metaphorical attribution of consciousness (*caitanyatva*),
because of their identity with consciousness (*caitanyatādātmya*) in all cases.

It has been stated that the word "ātman" is unique to the conscious being alone. Or, even if it were common to non-pervasive entities, since there is no determining factor here in this Śruti passage to establish that it refers to the Pradhāna, it does not function with respect to the Pradhāna; thus he says: "Even though it is common. However, regarding its denotation of the conscious being, the context and the word "Śvetaketu" serve as determining factors; thus he says: "But the subject under discussion..."
He clarifies the determinative nature of the derivative term with the words "not indeed" (*na hi*).
To the question "What follows from that?", he replies with "Therefore" (*tasmāt*).
He refutes the example given—that the word *ātman* has multiple meanings like the word *jyotis*—with the words "light" (*jyotiḥ*).

How, then, is there the application [of the term] "jyotiṣṭoma" in the injunction "one should sacrifice with the jyotis"? To this he replies: "by means of an explanatory passage (arthavāda). Through the explanatory passage—"These indeed are those lights which are its stomas"—a similarity to a flame is figuratively established.

The *stomas*—namely the *trivṛt*, *pañcadaśa*, *saptadaśa*, and *ekaviṃśa*—are collections of verses denoted by the word "light" (*jyotis*) through the quality of manifesting their respective meanings. Thus, in the term *Jyotiṣṭoma*, meaning "that whose *stomas* are lights," the word "light" is used in a secondary (figurative) sense.

Now, one might object: it would have been more appropriate to dispel the doubt regarding the word "Self" (*ātman*) being common to both the primary and secondary senses in the preceding sūtra itself, rather than here.

Since a figurative sense or a multiplicity of meanings is a weaker objection when the primary meaning can be stated with brevity, there is no need for the effort of a separate sūtra to refute it. Thus, explaining the [following] sūtra as a response to such an objection does not appear particularly elegant; therefore, out of dissatisfaction, he says "Alternatively" (*athavā*).

The meaning is: that self-word (*ātma-śabda*) from which all suspicion of a figurative sense or a multiplicity of meanings has been removed—that is its "state of having those suspicions removed" (*tacchaṅkatā*), and by means of that.
Regarding the word "therefore":

since the term "Self" (ātman) refers to that which exists [the Brahman], and because [the individual soul] is non-different from it, the teaching on liberation—independently of the reason [concerning the soul's nature]—is itself the reason for refuting the Pradhāna as the cause; this is the meaning. //7//
Furthermore, for what reason is the Pradhāna not denoted by the word "Sat"?
"And because there is no mention of its being something to be discarded.

(Sūtra 1.1.8) If the non-self, namely *pradhāna*, which is denoted by the word "Being," were taught here as "That is the Self; thou art That," then [the teacher], desiring to point out the primary Self so that one would not—upon hearing that instruction—become fixed upon that [non-self] due to ignorance of the Self, would have stated that [the non-self] was to be discarded.

Just as one who wishes to show the star Arundhatī first causes [the pupil] to grasp a large, non-primary star situated near it, saying "This is Arundhatī," and having set that aside, subsequently causes him to grasp Arundhatī herself—
so too [the teacher] would say, "This is not the Self.
But he did not speak in this manner.
For it is observed that the conclusion of the sixth chapter indeed culminates in the realization of the Self as pure Being;
the word "and" [is used] because of the contradiction with the initial proposition.
This is for the purpose of demonstrating the contradiction with the thesis (*pratijñāvirodha*) and its further elaboration.
Even though there is the statement that [the world] is to be abandoned, a contradiction with the thesis would follow;
for it was previously asserted as a thesis that "by knowing the cause, everything is known."
"Furthermore, did you ask for that instruction by which the unheard becomes heard, the unthought becomes thought, and the unknown becomes known?

How, O Venerable One, does that instruction come about? "Just as, my dear, by means of a single clod of clay, all that is made of clay becomes known—the modification being a mere verbal handle, a name, while the reality is simply 'clay'—so it is."
For it is heard at the beginning of the passage: "Thus, my dear, is that instruction" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.1.1, 3).

Furthermore, when the Pradhāna—which is denoted by the word *sat* and is the cause of the category of objects of enjoyment—is known, whether as something to be abandoned or not to be abandoned, the category of enjoyers does not thereby become known.
Because the class of enjoyers is not a modification of the Pradhāna, therefore the Pradhāna is not what is denoted by the word "Being. // 8 //

One might object: "Is it not the case that, just as someone wishing to point out the star Arundhatī points to a nearby, large star and instructs it to be Arundhatī, so too is there an instruction that the Pradhāna itself—the entity denoted by the word 'Sat'—is the Self? This is the sense of the question "Why [not]? (kutaśca): why is it that the Pradhāna is not what is expressed by the word "Sat"?

The word "ca" (and) in the Sūtra has the sense of a collective inclusion of what has not been explicitly stated; thus he says, "the word 'ca'. He explains this with the words "even though," where the particle "api" indicates that [the object] does not exist at all.

When his son had returned after studying the Vedas, being conceited, the father said to him: "O son, you have even asked about the Self (Ātman)—that which is indicated [by the scriptures] and is obtainable solely through instruction—having questioned your teacher;
for by hearing, reflecting upon, and realizing that [Self], there arises the hearing and so forth of everything else. This is the grammatical connection.
The son raises an objection, wondering how one thing could be known through another that is itself unknown: "How? (verse 3).
The meaning is: "O Blessed One, how indeed can that [universe] come to be so?"
He states that there is no difference between the effect and its cause with the words "just as" (yathā).
"By the lump" (piṇḍena) means by its own form;
the word "by [it] being known" (vijñātena) is to be supplied as the remainder of the sentence.
Regarding this, he states the reasoning: "by speech" (*vācā*).
That which is commenced by speech—that is, by the organ of speech—is a modification, and thus it is called "a mere commencement by speech.
Now, one might object: is it not the case that by speech only the name (*nāman*) is commenced?
Anticipating the objection that [the world] is not merely a pot or the like, he states that modification is a mere name:
"This modification is a mere name; it is spoken of by speech alone.
In reality, it is not distinct from its cause; therefore, it is indeed false."
This is the intended meaning:
[one might argue that] if the modification (vikāra) is false, then its non-different cause must also be false; to this he says "clay" (mṛttikā).
The cause does not possess a separate existence from the effect, nor is the effect separate from the cause;

therefore, since there is no nature of the effect apart from the cause, the knowledge of that [cause] arises through the knowledge of the cause—this being established, he states the application of the example with the word "evam" (thus).
Just as clay, so too Brahman alone is real, while transformations such as space and the like are false; thus, when there is knowledge of Brahman, nothing remains to be known. This is the meaning.

Although knowledge of the modifications arises from the knowledge of the Pradhāna due to their identity with it, nevertheless, this does not apply to the Puruṣas, because they are not modifications of the Pradhāna; thus he says, "And not...
The sense is that for us, the individual souls (jīvas), since they are of the nature of Being (sadrūpa), there is knowledge [of all] through the knowledge of That. //8//
And for what further reason is the Pradhāna not denoted by the word "Sat"?
"O Śvetaketu, did you ever ask your teacher about that which is called *ādeśa*—that reality which is to be understood through the words of the scriptures and the teacher?

[He replied: 'The modification is merely a name arising from speech (*vācā-ārabhya*), being uttered; in reality, there is no modification over and above the clay, such as a jar or a bowl. In the ultimate sense, only the clay is real.'"
On account of merging into itself (svāpyaya).

With reference to that very cause denoted by the word "Being" (sat), the scripture declares: "When, my dear, a person is said to be 'sleeping,' then he has become united with Being; he has gone to his own (svam apītaḥ). Therefore they say of him 'he sleeps' (svapiti), for he has gone to his own."
"Then he becomes one with Being" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.8.1).
This scriptural passage explains the etymology of the name "he sleeps," which is well known in the world regarding the person.
Here, by the word *sva*, the Self (*ātman*) is meant.
He who has been introduced as that which is denoted by the word "Sat" (Being) becomes absorbed in it; the meaning is that he has gone into it.

It is well known that the root *i* preceded by the prefix *api* has the sense of absorption (*laya*), since we see its use for both origination and dissolution in such expressions as "origination and absorption" (*prabhavāpyayau*).

Through its connection with specific limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) consisting in the activities of the mind, the individual soul (*jīva*), perceiving the objects of the senses, becomes identified with those specific states and is said to be "awake.
Distinctly characterized by the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of those experiences, it becomes designated by the term "mind" while seeing dreams.

When both limiting adjuncts cease in the state of deep sleep (*suṣupti*), due to the absence of distinctions created by the adjuncts, it is as if dissolved into its own self; thus it is said, "For he has gone to his own (*svam hy apīto bhavati*)."

Just as the etymology of the word "hṛdaya" was shown after hearing it: "This very Self is in the heart; this is its etymological derivation: 'He is in the heart' (hṛdi ayam), therefore it is called 'hṛdaya'" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.3.3);

or just as the Śruti shows the root cause for the application of the words "aśanāyā" and "udanyā": "The waters indeed lead away that which has been eaten," and "The fire indeed leads away that which has been drunk" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.8.3, 5)—in the same way, [the text] shows through the etymology of the name "svapiti" (he sleeps) the meaning that he has gone (apīta) into his own Self, which is denoted by the word "Sat."
Furthermore, a conscious self could not realize the unconscious *pradhāna* as its own essential nature.
If, on the other hand, the *pradhāna* itself were denoted by the word "self" because it belongs to the self,
even so, the contradiction would arise that the conscious [self] attains the unconscious.

And another scriptural passage—“Embraced by the conscious Self (prājña-ātman), one knows nothing external, nor anything internal” (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.3.21)—shows this merging (apyaya) of consciousness during the state of deep sleep.
Therefore, that Consciousness in which all cognitions merge, which is denoted by the word ‘Sat’ (Being), is the cause of the world, and not the Pradhāna. // 9 //
FN: "Wherein, when a person is asleep, he receives the name 'he sleeps'—then the person has become united with Being (sat), having become one with it"—this is the construction.
"For what reason? means: for what further reason?

The application of the Sūtra is as follows: because it is heard in scripture that during deep sleep (suṣupti) the individual soul (jīva) merges into its own Self, which is Being (sat), it is indeed conscious Being.
Just as this sleeping occurs, so in that state of deep sleep where the name "he sleeps" (svapiti) applies, the person becomes united with Being; he attains oneness with Being.
But how can there be the application of a name even when there is oneness with Being?
Regarding this, he says "his own" (*svam*).
Therein, he states what is well-known in the world: "therefore" (*tasmāt*).
The meaning is: because he has gone into his own self (*sadātmānam*), therefore [he does not know].
He states the purport of the scripture with the words beginning "this" (*eṣa*).

To the question, "How does this much refute the Pradhāna? he replies, "by its own word. Having raised the objection—"Even though the root *i*, which has the sense of 'going,' is preceded by [the prefix *pra-*,] how can there be the dissolution (*laya*) of the eternal individual soul (*jīva*)?"—he states the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) for the waking and dreaming states in order to say that it is through the dissolution of the adjuncts. [The mind...]
Thus, the modifications of the senses and the mind are limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*).

Through them, because of the connection between the Self and specific gross objects such as jars, the Self— perceiving those sensory objects and having fallen into the delusion of identity with the gross body— becomes known as the "Universal" (*viśva*) and is awake.

When distinguished by the mind which is the substratum of waking impressions, that Self is designated as "taijasa" (the luminous); seeing in the dream state the transformations of māyā accompanied by diverse impressions, it becomes denoted by the word "manas" found in the Śruti passage, "O dear one, that is the mind. The meaning is that when both the gross and subtle adjuncts have ceased, that Self is metaphorically called "dissolved," because of the absence of specific egoistic conceits such as "I am a man" or "I am an agent."

Now, one might object that because the etymological derivation of the name "he sleeps" (svapiti) is merely an explanatory statement (arthavāda), it does not correspond to reality; to this, he says: "Just as...
This is the etymological explanation of that word *hṛdaya*.
Since they lead away the food eaten after having liquefied it and cause it to decay (*jarayanti*), water itself is the referent of the term *aśanāyā* (thirst).
Because it leads that water [drunk by the traveler] away and dries it up, it is *udanya*, which is indeed fire (*tejas*);
here the lengthening of the vowel is a Vedic archaism (*chāndasa*).
He states "thus" (*evam*) to show that this etymological derivation (*nirvacana*) is likewise consistent with the facts.
And he says "not so" because this is not tenable in the case of the Pradhāna theory.
Anticipating the objection that the word *sva* (self) possesses power to denote not only the self (*ātman*) but also what belongs to the self (*ātmanīya*), he says "if.

"Embracing by the Intelligent One" (*prājñena saṃpariṣvaṅgaḥ*) means non-difference through the absence of the delusion of difference, [the Intelligent One] being the Lord who is the reflected consciousness (*bimba-caitanya*). //9//
For what further reason is the Pradhāna not the cause of the world?
Because of the commonality of their destination.

(BBs 1.1.10) If, as in the systems of the logicians, there were a diversity of understandings regarding the cause even in the Vedāntas— such that in some places conscious Brahman is the cause of the world, while in others something else entirely were so— then, at times, one might have interpreted the scriptural passages concerning "seeing" and so forth in accordance with the doctrine that Pradhāna is the cause.
This is not so;
for in all the Vedāntas, there is indeed a uniform understanding of a conscious cause.

"Just as when a fire is blazing, sparks fly out in all directions, even so from this Self all the vital breaths (prāṇas) proceed each to its own abode, from the vital breaths the gods, and from the gods... [and so forth].
"The worlds" (Kauṣītaki Upaniṣad 3.3);
"From this very Self, indeed, space was produced" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.1);
"All this, verily, is from the Self alone" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 7.26.1).
Furthermore, all the Vedāntas demonstrate that the Self is the cause, as in the passage: "From the Self this vital breath is born" (Praśna Upaniṣad 3.3).
And we have already stated that the word "Self" (ātman) denotes a conscious being.

And this is a great ground for authority: that the Vedānta texts have a uniform purport regarding the fact that the cause of the world is a conscious being, just as the sense organs such as the eye have a uniform function regarding objects such as color-form.
Therefore, because of this uniformity of purport, Brahman, who is omniscient, is the cause of the world. 10.
FN: *Gati* means comprehension.
"They would stand opposed" means that all ten directions would be spread out as having diverse modes of movement.
Validity (*prāmāṇya*) consists in making known what was previously unknown.

Since the understandings produced by those various Vedānta texts are generally concerned with a conscious cause, the meaning of the Sūtra—that the non-conscious cannot be the cause of the world—is stated by way of a negative argument (*vyatireka*) in the passage beginning with "yadi tārkika... and continuing with "na tv etad," where "anything else" refers to atoms (*paramāṇu*) and so forth.
"But this is not [the case]" means that the world does not have such a cause.
The meaning is that there would be a discrepancy in their respective cognitions. "They would go forth in various directions" means they would proceed in many different ways;
that is, the vital breaths, such as sight and the others, would manifest according to their respective physical locations (the sense organs).
Immediately after the vital breaths (prāṇas) are the deities, such as the Sun and others, who are their sustainers;

immediately after those are the "worlds" (lokas), meaning the sense objects, so the sense is. Now, one might object: since the Vedāntas possess intrinsic authority (svataḥ-prāmāṇya), they are capable of determining their own respective meanings individually; what then is the use of a uniformity of purport (gati-sāmānya)? To this, he says: "And great... (mahacca).

Regarding the fact that the Vedāntas’ status as a means of valid knowledge consists in their being the cause for the cognition of a single [non-dual] reality, which serves to remove doubt, he provides an illustration: "The eye," etc.

Just as all eyes are the cause for the cognition of a single form, as hearing is the cause for the cognition of sound, and as the nose and other senses are the causes for the cognition of odor and so forth;
Thus, the meaning is that the uniformity of the purport of the Vedāntas with respect to Brahman is the reason for the firmness of their authority. //10//
And for what further reason is the omniscient Brahman the cause of the world?
And because it is so heard [in scripture].
By the very word itself, it is heard in the *Śvetāśvatara-mantra-upaniṣad* that the omniscient Lord is the cause of the world;
for, referring to the omniscient Lord, it says: "He is the cause, the lord of the lords of the organs, and there is neither his progenitor nor his lord" (Śve. 6.9).

Therefore, it is established that the omniscient Brahman is the cause of the world, and not the non-intelligent *pradhāna* or anything else. // 11 // [FN: The lords of causes are the individual souls (*jīvas*); their lord is [Brahman].]
The *vastutantra* (the system of reality) would be knowledge (*jñāna*), while the *karmatantra* (the system of ritual action) is worship (*upāsana*).
"More extensively" (*āvistarām*) means more preeminently manifest.

Thus, having refuted the coordination (*samanvaya*) of the Vedāntas with respect to the non-intelligent by means of such indicative marks as "seeing" (*īkṣati*) and so forth, he now refutes it even by means of words denoting a conscious being—with the words, "And because it is heard [in scripture]" (*śrutatvācca*).

He explains the Sūtra with the words "by its own term. The term "all-knowing" (sarvavit) denotes the conscious self. Since it is heard in scripture—referring to the Supreme Lord who is all-knowing—that "He is the knower, the time of time, the possessor of qualities, the all-knower," and that "He, the all-knowing, is the cause"—it follows that the cause is not insentient; such is the meaning of the Sūtra.
The individual souls (jīvas) are the lords of the instruments (the senses), and He is the lord of them.
He concludes the discussion on the subject of authority with the words "Therefore" (tasmāt).
Considering that [attributes] such as "seeing" and the word "Self" are also inappropriate for atoms and the like, he says "or something else" (anyat vā). //11//
END BsCom_1,1.5.11 START BsCom_1,1.6.12 6.
The Section Concerning the One Consisting of Bliss (Ānandamayādhikaraṇa) / Sūtras 12–19

Beginning with the sūtra "From which [proceeds] the birth, etc., of this" and ending with "And because it is so heard," the fact that the Vedānta passages cited by these sūtras establish the meaning— that the omniscient and omnipotent Lord is the cause of the origin, sustenance, and dissolution of the world—
has been demonstrated through reasoned argumentation.
And by the presentation of the commonality of their destination, it has been explained that all the Vedāntas maintain that the cause is conscious.
Therefore, one might ask: what is the purpose of the subsequent portion of the text?
It is said in reply: for Brahman is understood to be of two forms.
[The Self] is characterized by the limiting adjuncts of the distinctions and transformations of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), and [the Self] is its opposite, being devoid of all limiting adjuncts.

For it is said: "For where there is duality as it were, there one sees another; but where for him everything has become the Self alone, then by what and whom should he see? (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.5.15).

"Where one sees nothing else, hears nothing else, and understands nothing else—that is the Infinite (bhūman). But where one sees something else, hears something else, and understands something else—that is the finite (alpa). Verily, the Infinite is immortal, while that which is finite is mortal. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 7.24.1) "The Wise One, having fashioned all forms and created names, sits calling them forth. (Taittirīya Āraṇyaka 3.12.7)
"Partless, actionless, tranquil, irreproachable, and stainless;
the supreme bridge to immortality, like a fire whose fuel has been consumed" (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 6.19).
"Not this, not this" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.3.6).

Thus, thousands of scriptural passages— such as "neither coarse nor fine" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.8.8) and "one state is deficient, the other is complete"— demonstrate the twofold nature of Brahman according to the distinction between the spheres of knowledge and ignorance.
Among these, during the state of ignorance, all worldly transactions involving the object of worship, the worshipper, and so forth, pertain to Brahman.

Among those, some meditations on Brahman are for the sake of worldly prosperity, some are for the sake of gradual liberation, and some are for the sake of the successful accomplishment of ritual acts.
Their distinction arises from the difference in the limiting adjuncts (upādhi) consisting of specific qualities.

Although the one and only Supreme Self, the Lord, is to be meditated upon as qualified by various specific qualities, nevertheless, the fruits differ according to the meditation on those specific qualities, based on the Vedic scripture: "In whatever way one meditates upon Him, that very thing one becomes."
And as it is said in the *Chāndogya Upaniṣad* (3.14.1): "In whatever manner a person acts in this world, so does he become after departing from here.

And from the *Smṛti*: "Whatever state of being one remembers when leaving the body at the end, to that very state one goes, O son of Kuntī, having been constantly absorbed in that thought" (*Bhagavad Gītā* 8.6).

Although the one Self is hidden within all beings, both stationary and moving, nevertheless, due to the gradations of the specific limiting adjuncts of the mind (*cittopādhiviśeṣatāratamya*), a gradation is heard of even that Self—which is immutable, eternal, and uniform—as it becomes increasingly manifest through specific powers of sovereignty (*aiśvaryaśaktiviśeṣaiḥ*).
This is stated in the passage: "He who knows his Self as more fully manifested" (*tasya ya ātmānamāvistarāṃ veda*, AiĀ 2.3.2.1).

In the *Smṛti* as well, it is said: "Whatever exists that is possessed of majesty, splendor, or power, know each of those to be born from a mere fraction of my radiance" (*Gītā* 10.41). Wherever there is an excellence of majesty and so forth, that very thing is enjoined as the Lord to be meditated upon.
In the same way, here too, he will state that the golden person within the solar orb is indeed the Supreme Being, because of the mark of being free from all evil.
This is to be understood similarly in such passages as "The ether [is Brahman], because of its marks" (Brahma-sūtra 1.1.22).

Thus, even self-knowledge—which is the cause of immediate liberation—though taught by means of specific limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), must be determined through a careful consideration of the course of the statements [of scripture], as it may be doubted whether its subject matter is the higher or the lower [Brahman] because the specific connection with the adjuncts is not intended to be emphasized.
This is just as in this very [work], in the case of the sūtra: "The one consisting of bliss [is Brahman], on account of repetition" (*ānandamayo 'bhyāsāt*).

Thus, the subsequent portion of the text is commenced to demonstrate that even the one Brahman is taught in the Vedāntas both as the object of meditation (*upāsya*) and as the object of knowledge (*jñeya*), depending on whether it is connected with limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) or has its connection with limiting adjuncts removed. Furthermore, that refutation of a non-conscious cause which was stated under the sūtra "Because of the uniformity of the way of approach" (*gatisāmānyāt*) is now further elaborated by explaining other passages concerning Brahman through the negation of causes contrary to Brahman.
The one consisting of bliss [is Brahman] because of repetition;
in the Taittirīyaka, [there is mention of] the one consisting of food, the one consisting of vital breath, and so on.
Following the sequence of the mind-made (*manomaya*) and the consciousness-made (*vijñānamaya*), it is handed down in scripture: "From this very one, who consists of consciousness..."
"Another inner self consists of bliss" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.5).

Regarding this, there is a doubt: Is the term "consisting of bliss" (ānandamaya) used here to denote the Supreme Brahman itself, which was introduced as "Brahman is truth, knowledge, and infinite" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.1), or does it refer to something different from Brahman, such as those [sheaths] beginning with "consisting of food" (annamaya)?
What, then, is the prima facie conclusion? That the "consisting of bliss" (*ānandamaya*) is a secondary self (*amukhya ātmā*) that is something other than Brahman.
Why?
Because it falls within a series of secondary selves beginning with "consisting of food" (*annamaya*).
Now, it might be argued that because it is the innermost of all, the one consisting of bliss (*ānandamaya*) is indeed the primary Self.
This cannot be so, because of its connection with limbs such as "dearness" and because it is heard of as having a body.
If the one consisting of bliss were the primary Self, there would be no contact with dearness and the like.
But here, moreover, it is heard in scripture: "His very beloved is the head," and so forth;
and corporeality is also heard: "Of this [latter], this indeed is the embodied self (śārīra ātmā), which belongs to the former."
The meaning is that this very self consisting of bliss (*ānandamaya*) is the embodied self (*śārīra ātmā*) of the previously mentioned self consisting of consciousness (*vijñānamaya*).
And for one who possesses a body, contact with the pleasant and the unpleasant cannot be prevented.
Therefore, when it is thus argued that the self consisting of bliss is merely a transmigrating being (*saṃsārī*), this is stated: "The self consisting of bliss [is Brahman], because of repetition."
The Self consisting of bliss must indeed be the Supreme Self;
why?
Because of repetition.
For the word "bliss" (ānanda) is repeated many times with reference to the Supreme Self alone.

Having introduced the one consisting of bliss (ānandamaya), its nature as essence (rasa) is stated in the words, "He is indeed essence," and it is further declared: "For only by attaining this essence does one become blissful. [And: "Who indeed could inhale? Who could exhale?"
"If this bliss did not exist in space, this [Self] would not cause bliss;
for it is this very one that causes bliss" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.7). "This, then, is the inquiry into bliss."
"He attains this self consisting of bliss" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.8),
"Knowing the bliss of Brahman, he fears nothing from anywhere" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.9),
and "He understood that bliss is Brahman" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 3.6).
Moreover, in another scriptural passage, "Brahman is consciousness and bliss" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.9.28), the word "bliss" is seen applied to Brahman itself.
Thus, because the word "bliss" is repeatedly applied to Brahman, it is understood that the Self consisting of bliss is Brahman.
As for the argument that the "consisting of bliss" (ānandamaya) is also non-primary because it falls within a series of non-primary selves beginning with the "consisting of food" (annamaya),
that is not a valid objection;
for the one consisting of bliss is the innermost of all.

Indeed, the scripture, desiring to teach the primary Self alone, follows the common understanding of the world; having first referred to the food-made body— which is not the Self but is well-known as the Self among the utterly deluded— as being like a statue cast from molten copper poured into a mold,
it then proceeds to teach that each subsequent [layer] is the Self, while being similar to each preceding one, thereby leading one to grasp the Self through a succession of non-Selfs.
It is more appropriate [to hold] that the Self consisting of bliss (*ānandamaya*) was taught as the primary one because it is the innermost, considering the ease of practice.
Just as in the illustration of Arundhatī, when many stars that are not the actual Arundhatī have been shown, the one finally pointed out is indeed the primary Arundhatī;
so too here, because the one consisting of bliss is the innermost of all, it possesses the status of the primary Self.
As for what you say—

that the attribution of being the head and so forth to the primary Self (ātman) in relation to the beloved and others is untenable— the fault does not apply, because that [attribution] is produced by the immediately preceding limiting adjunct (upādhi) and is not inherent.

The fact that the one consisting of bliss (*ānandamaya*) possesses a body is also shown through the succession of bodies beginning with the one consisting of food (*annamaya*); however, it does not possess corporeality directly like a transmigrating being (*saṃsārin*). Therefore, the one consisting of bliss is indeed the supreme Self. // 12 //
FN: The meaning is that because of the scriptural statement of its partlessness (*niṣkalatva*), it is without parts (*niraṃśa*).
Who else could move, or who else could specifically breathe—that is, live?
"Causes bliss" means "causes one to experience bliss.
"Approaching" means "attaining"; the remainder of the sense is that it is the very nature of Brahman.
"Following the gross-grasping tendency of worldly intellect" is the meaning.
Even here, although [the topic] has fallen into a secondary stream,

[the author] introduces the composition of the subsequent sūtras by restating what has already occurred, beginning with the words "birth and so forth" (*janmādi*). It is said that [the discussion] begins from the sūtra on birth and so forth because the first sūtra serves as the introduction to the treatise (*śāstropodghāta*).

The purport is this: by refuting the interpretation that all Vedānta texts are concerned with the *pradhāna* and other non-conscious principles through their application (*samanvaya*) to the "task" (*kārya*), it has been explained that they have Brahman as their ultimate subject matter.
Therefore, since the meaning of the first chapter is thus completed, the question arises: what is the reason for commencing the subsequent portion of the work?
This is because, within the Vedāntas, a great many passages concerning both the qualified (*saguṇa*) and unqualified (*nirguṇa*) Brahman are observed.

In this regard, he states "it is said" because the very cause for the inquiry is the question: "Which statement has its reconciliation (*samanvaya*) with the attribute-less [Brahman] by means of an injunction for the meditation on the qualified [Brahman], and which has its reconciliation directly with Brahman itself without the intention to convey attributes?
He then states the meaning of the statements concerning the qualified and the attribute-less in brief: "For [Brahman] is of two forms."

The meaning of the sentence is that the entire world is a modification consisting of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), and its differentiation consists of specific attributes such as having a golden beard and so forth.
He cites the relevant passage beginning with "For where... (*yatra hi*).

Indeed, in that state of ignorance where duality is imagined as it were, one being "this" perceives "that," and thus the object appears as a thing qualified by its perceptible adjuncts (*dṛśyopādhika*).

But when, at the time of knowledge, the entire world has become nothing but the Self for the wise person, then—by the very implication of the question "who would see whom?"—the reality appears devoid of adjuncts (*nirupādhika*). That plenitude (*bhūman*) in which the wise person, being certain, knows no second thing whatsoever, is the non-dual plenitude, the Supreme Self, free from attributes (*nirguṇa*).
Now, immediately after the description of the attributeless (nirguṇa), the one with attributes (saguṇa) is described. That in which one abiding perceives a second is limited and finite;
but that which is the Plenum (bhūman) is immortal and eternal.
The word "atha" (now) is to be explained as before.

The Wise One is the Supreme Self alone; having fashioned all forms and created names, He enters into the intellect and other faculties, exists there under the designation of the "individual soul" (jīva), and engages in worldly activity. That [Self] which is thus endowed with qualities (saguṇa), he [the teacher] [describes] by way of its qualityless nature (nirguṇatvena).
Even the knower becomes immortal.
That from which parts (kalā) or portions have departed is "partless" (niṣkala).
Therefore, due to being partless, it is actionless (niṣkriya).
Therefore, it is peaceful and unchanging;
it is faultless, being devoid of defects such as passion and the like;
it is stainless (*nirañjana*), being free from "ointment" (*añjana*), which refers either to the connection with fundamental ignorance (*mūlatamas*) or to phenomena (*dharma*) and so forth.

Furthermore, it is the supreme, most excellent bridge (*setu*) for immortality—that is, liberation—because it stands upon the mental state (*vṛtti*) arising from its own words, just as a worldly bridge is a means of passage.
The meaning is that one should know the Self as tranquil and devoid of qualities (*nirguṇa*), having burnt away ignorance and its products, just as a fire whose fuel is consumed subsides;
thus [it is described] as "not this, not this" (*neti neti*).
This has been explained.
It is devoid of duality such as "gross" and so forth.
He cites the scripture regarding the two forms with the words, "deficient."

The meaning is that the state of duality is inferior, limited, of a qualified nature (saguṇa), and distinct from the unqualified (nirguṇa); likewise, the complete [state] is unqualified and distinct from the qualified.
To the objection that it is contradictory for a single entity to possess two forms, he says: "Knowledge" (vidyā).

The object of *vidyā* (knowledge) is that which is to be known (*jñeya*), namely the qualityless (*nirguṇa*) reality; the object of *avidyā* (ignorance) is that which is to be meditated upon (*upāsya*), namely the qualified (*saguṇa*) reality which is superimposed. Thus, there is no contradiction.
In this regard, he explains the object of *avidyā* with the word "therein" (*tatra*).

For the sake of attaining knowledge of the qualityless reality, various meditations for the sake of specific fruits are enjoined—by way of the analogy of the "sweetmeat on the tongue"—relying upon the superimposed phenomenal world prior to its sublation.

Since knowledge is the primary fruit for them by way of one-pointedness of mind (*cittaikāgrya*), it should be understood that the ultimate purport (*mahātātparya*) of those statements as well is Brahman.

For meditations such as "Name is Brahman," the fruit is prosperity consisting of the freedom to act according to one's desire; for meditations such as the "Small One" (*dahara*), the fruit is prosperity consisting of the freedom to act according to one's desire.

The distinction is that for meditations such as that on the "small one" (dahara), the fruit is gradual liberation, whereas for meditations such as the Udgītha, the fruit is the success of ritual action;
this is because these meditations are mental in nature.
And because it is internal to knowledge,
the intention is that its injunction belongs to the section on knowledge (jñānakāṇḍa).
Now, since the Brahman to be meditated upon is one, how can there be a distinction among the meditations?
Regarding this, he says: "of them" (teṣām).
The "specific qualities" (guṇaviśeṣāḥ) are such as having true desires and so forth;
the "limiting adjuncts" (upādhi) are the heart and so forth.
Here, having raised an objection himself, he provides the resolution: "One [is the same].

The sense is that although there is no difference in the essential nature (*svarūpa*) of the Supreme Self, when there is a distinction among meditations due to the distinction between the conditioned forms (*upahita*) resulting from different limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), there is a corresponding distinction in the fruits.

To whatever extent people meditate upon that Supreme Self as possessing specific qualities—just as they might meditate on a king—they obtain as their fruit the possession of those very same qualities.
*Kratu* means resolve (*saṃkalpa*) or meditation (*dhyāna*).
In this context, whatever kind of meditation one possesses, upon death one becomes that very form of the object of worship.
Regarding this very point, the Lord’s own statement is cited: "And from memory" (*smṛteśca*).

One might object: "Since the Self is one and without distinction among all beings, how can there be scriptural statements regarding the gradation between the object of worship and the worshipper? Anticipating this doubt, the author provides the following resolution: "Even though [the Self] is one. Due to the varying degrees of purity of the aforementioned limiting adjuncts (upādhis), there arise specific distinctions consisting of gradations in the powers (śaktis) whose nature is sovereignty, knowledge, and bliss.
Through these, a gradation of manifestation is heard of in the scriptures for the Self—which is uniform in essence—progressively from humans up to Hiraṇyagarbha.

The meaning is that he who knows—that is, meditates upon—the Self of that [Īśvara] as His own self, its very nature, more fully (*āvistarām*) or more manifestly (*prakaṭataram*), "attains that," according to the force of the suffix *-tarap*.

Thus, the intention is that there is no contradiction in this gradation based on limiting adjuncts (*aupādhika-tāratamya*): the Self with an inferior adjunct is the meditator, while the Lord with a superior adjunct is the object of meditation.
Regarding this point, he cites the Bhagavadgītā, saying "in the Smṛti.
Here it is stated that even the sun and other such entities are not to be meditated upon as the individual soul (jīva), but rather as the Lord (īśvara).
In that regard, he states the agreement of the author of the Sūtras, saying "thus."
Arising [of a new meaning] is [due to] a lack of connection.

Having stated that the composition of the subsequent sūtras begins in order to declare that a sentence in which an adjunct (upādhi) is intended to be expressed is devoted to meditation (upāsanā), he says "Thus, immediately" to state that the composition begins for the purpose of determining that a sentence in which [an adjunct] is not intended to be expressed is devoted to the Brahman as the object of knowledge (jñeya).
The sheaths beginning with the *annamaya* are specific limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*).
The "course of the sentence" refers to its intended purport (*tātparya*).
He concludes the justification for the undertaking [of the inquiry] with the words: "In this way, even though it is one..."
He states "And that which... because the subsequent section is commenced for the purpose of proving the general principle stated as if it were already established (*siddhavat*).

Here, "food" (*anna*) is well-known; "vital breath, mind, and intellect" (*prāṇamanobuddhi*) are of the nature of Hiraṇyagarbha; and "bliss" (*ānanda*) is the Lord (*Īśvara*), who is the consciousness of the archetype (*bimba-caitanya*).

The ultimate truth of those five modifications is that they are the internal [sheaths]—the body, vital breath, mind, intellect, and the individual soul—which are the five sheaths (*kośas*) beginning with the "consisting of food" (*annamaya*), according to the Śruti.

In the previous section, it was stated that because primary and secondary observation are not equal, there is no doubt [regarding the latter], and thus a reading in which secondary meanings predominate is not determinative; however, since the suffix *-maya* is primary in the sense of both "modification" and "abundance," when a doubt arises, the section on Bliss (*ānanda-adhikāra*) follows from the predominance of the sense of modification in the reading.

There is the conclusion that the *jīva* is "consisting of bliss" (*ānandamaya*). To introduce the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) by way of a counter-example, he asks "What then? following the inquiry.
He asks "Why? regarding the reason for taking the term *ānandamaya* in its non-primary sense.
He states the reason—namely, the context of a series of modifications—by saying "beginning with *annamaya*."

The connections with the Śruti and other sources are indeed clear. The distinction is that, according to the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa) held by the Vṛttikāra, the fruit is the attainment of "the dear" and so forth through the meditation on the individual soul (jīva), whereas in the final conclusion (siddhānta), it is the meditation on Brahman.
He raises an objection with "But even so," and he provides a rebuttal with "It would not be.
He explains what was summarized with the word "primary."
The meaning is "the Supreme Self. To the question, "Why should lordship not exist even if [the Self] is embodied? he says, "And not...
The meaning is that being a *jīva* (individual soul) would be unavoidable.

Now, having raised the objection as to how the one consisting of bliss (*ānandamaya*) can be Brahman even though the word "bliss" (*ānanda*) is merely repeated, [the author] says this, intending that—just as the word "light" (*jyotis*) in the context of the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice refers specifically to the Jyotiṣṭoma, so too the word "consisting of bliss" occurring within the section on the one consisting of bliss refers specifically to the one consisting of bliss; therefore, its repetition establishes that it is Brahman: ... [text continues] ...
Having introduced the one consisting of bliss (*ānandamaya*): "essence" (*rasa*) means the core; that is to say, bliss.
This is the world.
Even though this space is full of bliss, if it were not the witness and the impeller, then who else could move, or who could distinguish, breathe, or live?
Therefore, this very one causes bliss; the meaning is that he causes [others] to be blissful.

Beginning with the bliss of human youths—as will be described in the passage "He should be young, a virtuous youth," and so forth—this present investigation into the gradations of bliss proceeds from the bliss of human youths up to the bliss of Brahman.

The meaning for the proponents of the partial view (*ekadeśin*) is that the wise one "approaches" (*upasaṃkrāmati*) means he "attains. However, according to the primary established doctrine (*mukhya-siddhānta*), the "approaching" of the wise one should be understood as the dissolution of the sheaths (*kośa*) into the state of being merely the inner self (*pratyaṅ-mātratva*). The remainder has its meaning already explained.
He states "and in another Śruti" in order to show the uniformity of the understanding, meaning that the comprehension of Brahman from the word "Ānanda" is the same everywhere.
Thinking that there might be a sublation [of this] due to the proximity of the non-primary self based on an indicative mark (liṅga), he says "not that one.

Anticipating the objection that being the innermost of all is not heard [in the text], he explains "the primary one," showing that because nothing else is mentioned besides it, that very one is the innermost of all.
"Conforming to the world's understanding" means following its mode of grasping at gross objects.
Just as copper takes the form of a crucible, the vital breath (*prāṇa*) takes the form of the body; this is its similarity with the body.

Likewise, the mind has the form of the vital breath (prāṇa); therefore, he says "by the former" to show that it is equal to that. The two marks—the conceptualization of having parts produced by the immediately preceding limiting adjunct (upādhi) which is the sheath of consciousness (vijñānakośa), and "embodiment" (śārīratva) because of being knowable by the body—are weak.
Therefore, the sense is that there is a sublation of the proximity of the modification due to the absence of assistance and because of both practice and being internal. //12//
If it be argued that [the Self] is not [denoted by the word "Self"] because of words denoting modification, we say no, because of abundance. 1.1.13.
Here it is said: the Self consisting of bliss cannot be the supreme Self.
Why? Because of the word denoting a modification (*vikāra*).
It is understood that this other word, distinct from words denoting a material cause (*prakṛti*), is a word denoting a modification.
If it is argued that because the suffix *mayaṭ* has the sense of "modification," the term *ānandamaya*—
like the terms *annamaya* and so forth— must refer exclusively to a modification, we say no;
for the suffix *mayaṭ* is also recorded in the sense of "abundance."
For by the rule *tatprakṛtavacane mayaṭ* (Pāṇini 5.4.21), the suffix *mayaṭ* is prescribed even in the sense of abundance;
just as in the expression "the sacrifice consists of food" (*annamayo yajñaḥ*), that which abounds in food is meant.
Thus, that which abounds in bliss is said to consist of the bliss of Brahman (*brahmānandamaya*).

Furthermore, the abundance of bliss in Brahman is established by the determination of its unsurpassed nature, after it has been stated that starting from the human state, bliss increases hundredfold at each successive higher station; therefore, the suffix *mayaṭ* is used here in the sense of abundance (*prācurya*). 13.

Anticipating the objection that the suffix *mayaṭ* [in the word *annamaya*] must signify a modification (*vikāra*) because it is supported by scriptural authority, he replies with the words beginning "In a modification... (*vikāra...*) that this is not so, since *mayaṭ* is also prescribed in the sense of abundance (*prācurya*).
The meaning of the rule *tatprakṛtavacane mayaṭ* is as follows:

when there is a statement (*vacana*) regarding something under discussion (*prastuta*) that is characterized by abundance (*prācurya*), the suffix *mayaṭ* occurs after a word in the nominative case (*prathamāsamartha*) denoting that thing.

In this context, by the inclusion of the word "vacana" (statement), the predominance and distinction of the subject under discussion are established, because such usage of the suffix *mayaṭ* is attested in common parlance,
as in the expression "the sacrifice consists of food" (*annamayo yajñaḥ*).

For here, the word *anna* (food) signifies abundance, as it is used in the sense "abundant food exists in this"; thus, the suffix *mayaṭ* following it is seen to denote the abundance of the food that is the meaning of the base (*prakṛti*) of "sacrifice" (*yajña*), and not merely the base itself—this is how it should be understood. //13//
And because its cause is designated [as such]. (1.1.14)

Furthermore, the suffix *mayaṭ* here has the sense of abundance (*prācurya*), because the Śruti declares that Brahman is the cause of bliss: "For He alone causes bliss" (*eṣa hyevānandayāti*). The meaning is that He makes [beings] blissful.
For it is well known in the world that he who causes joy to others is recognized as one possessing abundant joy;
just as in common experience, he who brings about wealth for others is understood to be one of abundant wealth, so it is here.
Therefore, since the suffix *mayaṭ* can also signify abundance, the "consisting of bliss" (*ānandamaya*) is indeed the supreme Self. // 14 //
Considering that the word "ca" (and) in the Sūtra has the sense of including what has not been explicitly mentioned, he explains it with the words "itaśca" (for this reason also).
And that which was not mentioned—the ascertainment of the unsurpassed nature of the bliss of Brahman—has been stated previously. //14//
