And it is proclaimed as being based precisely on the wording of the mantras. (BS 1.1.15)
For this reason as well, the one consisting of bliss (*ānandamaya*) is the supreme Self alone;

because, having commenced with "The knower of Brahman attains the Supreme," the mantra "Brahman is truth, knowledge, and infinite" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.1) defines that very Brahman under discussion by means of the qualifiers "truth," "knowledge," and "infinite."
Because all beings, both stationary and moving, were born from space and the other elements in succession;
and because, having created those beings, it entered into them and abides in the secret cave of the heart,
being the innermost of all.

That Brahman which was introduced for the sake of being known in the mantra— "another inner Self, another inner Self"— is indeed that same Brahman described here in the Brāhmaṇa as "another inner Self, consisting of bliss" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.5).
And it is logical that the mantra and the Brāhmaṇa share a single meaning, as there is no contradiction between them.
For otherwise, there would be an abandonment of the subject at hand and the introduction of something irrelevant;
nor is any inner self mentioned as distinct from the one consisting of bliss, as was the case with those consisting of food and so forth.
And this very [teaching] is the "Bhārgavi Vāruṇī knowledge" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 3.6).
Therefore, the one consisting of bliss is indeed the supreme Self. [15] [Note:
The word "yasmāt" (because) is connected with the distant word "tasmāt" (therefore). The construction is:
that which was determined [in the preceding section] is precisely what is being sung here.
The meaning is: "because, while there is identity of referent, there exists the relationship of means and end.
Having stated the indicative mark (*liṅga*) for the blissful one (*ānandamaya*) being Brahman, he states the context (*prakaraṇa*): "māntra" and so forth.

The construction is as follows: since it is thus the subject under discussion, therefore that very Brahman described in the words of the mantra is sung of in the sentence "consisting of bliss" (*ānandamaya*).
Now, one might object: "Why this insistence that only what is stated in the mantra should be accepted here? To this he replies with the word "mantra":
because the Brāhmaṇa consists of explanations of the mantras, it serves as a means [to their understanding].
The mantra is the means for this;
thus it is said, "because there is no contradiction," which means because of the relationship between those two as the means (upāya) and the goal (upeya).
In that case, it might follow that those consisting of food (*annamaya*) and the others would also be Brahman based on the wording of the mantra; therefore, he says "And not...
Furthermore, the *Bhṛgu-vallī*, which was proclaimed to Bhṛgu and taught by Varuṇa, culminates in bliss (*ānanda*) in its fifth section.

In that regard, by the logic of the context, he states "this alone is its culmination" (etanniṣṭhaiva) to show that the Brahmavallī, which has that same single meaning, culminates in the Ānandamaya. //15//
It is not another, because that is untenable. (BS 1.1.16)
For this reason as well, the one consisting of bliss (ānandamaya) is the supreme Self alone, not the other;
"the other" means the transmigrating individual soul (jīva), which is distinct from the Lord.
The individual soul (jīva) is not denoted by the term "consisting of bliss" (ānandamaya).
Why?
Because it is logically untenable.
For, with reference to that which consists of bliss (*ānandamaya*), it is heard in scripture: "He desired: 'May I be many, may I procreate.
He performed austerity."
"Having performed austerity,
he created all this, whatever exists here" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.6).

In this regard, prior to the production of the body and so forth, the act of brooding (abhidhyāna), the non-difference of the creator from the modifications being created, and the creation of all modifications do not occur apart from the Supreme Self. 16.
That Lord performed austerity (*tapas*), which means he engaged in the contemplation of creation;
"meditation" (*abhidhyāna*) refers to desire.
"May I become many"—this is the non-differentiation [of the subject from the object]. //16//
And because there is a designation of difference. (BS 1.1.17)
For this reason as well, the one consisting of bliss is not a transmigrating being;
because, in the section concerning the one consisting of bliss, it is said: "He is indeed essence;
for only by obtaining essence does one become blissful" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.7).
Thus, he designates the individual soul (*jīva*) and the one consisting of bliss (*ānandamaya*) as distinct;
for that which has already been attained cannot itself be the object to be attained.
How then [is it said], "The Self is to be sought"?
The Śruti and Smṛti state, "There is nothing higher than the attainment of the Self," since it has been said that as long as [the Self] has not been attained, it remains something yet to be attained.
Certainly so.

Nevertheless, even while the Self remains unshaken from its own nature, a worldly perception is observed in which there is a determination of selfhood with respect to the body and other non-selves due to the non-comprehension of reality. Consequently, the designation of distinctions—such as "the Self, though already existing, must be sought; though not yet found, it is to be found; though unheard, it is to be heard; though unthought, it is to be thought; though unknown, it is to be known"—is logically justified.

However, from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), any seer or hearer other than the omniscient Supreme Lord is indeed denied by such passages as, "There is no other seer but He" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.7.23).
The Supreme Lord, however, is distinct from the body—which is constructed by ignorance and designated as the "knowing self" (*vijñānātman*) that acts and experiences.

This is just as a magician who, while holding a shield and sword and ascending into the sky by means of a rope, remains in reality a different person from that same magician when he is standing on the ground in his true form.
Or, for example, just as the unconditioned, unlimited space is distinct from the conditioned, limited space within a pot;

and it is with reference to such a distinction between the individual self (*vijñānātman*) and the supreme self (*paramātman*) that it has been stated: "Not the other, because of impossibility" and "And because of the designation of difference. (Sūtra 1.1.17)
FN: *Adhikāra* means the context.
That [context] is the essence consisting of the *ānandamaya* (the one filled with bliss), which is the undivided single flavor (*akhaṇḍaikarasa*).
"Laukika" means not departing from the world; it is non-authoritative. In the context of the section, that essence consists of bliss.

[Objection: "But even in the absence of the distinction between the attainer and the object attained, why should there not be non-difference? To this he says: "For it is not merely the attained [object]. [Objection:

"But if the distinction between the attainer and the object attained were necessary, there would be a contradiction with the Śruti and Smṛti. He raises this doubt with the word "How so? (katham). The syntactical connection is:
"Since you have stated 'by which' (yatastvayā), how then [can there be no contradiction] with the Śruti and Smṛti?"
He accepts the doubt raised by saying, "Certainly. Then,

suspecting that there would be a contradiction in the statement that the Self is obtained by the Self through the Self because of their non-difference, he says, "Even so," meaning that even though there is non-difference, there is no contradiction because of the imagined difference.
This is worldly delusion.

The meaning is that, due to the delusion born of one's own ignorance regarding the self as non-different from the body and so forth, there arises the erroneous notion of duality, leading to the assertion that the Supreme Self is an object of knowledge (*jñeya*).
It is "to be sought" (*anveṣṭavya*) in the sense of being known as distinct from the body and other such things.
It is to be attained through discriminative knowledge and realized directly;
for that purpose, it is to be heard.
Since "higher knowledge" (vijñāna) refers to profound reflection (nididhyāsana) or direct realization, there is no redundancy because this restates the meaning of another scriptural passage.
[Objection: "Let difference indeed be real. To this he replies: "is denied.

If it is argued that there is no individual soul (*jīva*) as a seer distinct from the Lord (*īśvara*), then by the very distinction of the individual soul, the Lord too would be false; therefore, he says: "the Supreme Lord" (*parameśvara*).
Because the Lord (Īśvara), who is pure consciousness (cinmātra), exists as distinct from the individual soul (jīva) which is imagined as a reflection of ignorance (avidyā), He is not unreal.

Regarding the fact that even though the imagined [reflection] is non-different from its substrate (adhiṣṭhāna), the substrate remains distinct from it, he provides an illustration with the word "yathā" (just as).
That which is mounted upon a thread is unreal even in itself.
Out of dissatisfaction with the [view that] "the soul does not exist," he states another illustration for the mere non-difference in the state of false belief (mithyātva), beginning with "or as if.
Now, one might object: "But surely, by the force of the Sūtra, difference is real"; to this he replies: "And such as this.
The meaning is that it is merely imagined (kalpita).
The intention is that in the Sūtra there is no mention of the word "difference" (bheda) as being real, and because the Sūtras beginning with "tadananyatvam" follow the Śruti. //17//
And because it is due to desire, there is no dependence upon inference. (BBs 1.1.18)

Furthermore, in the section concerning the one consisting of bliss (*ānandamaya*), because there is the designation of a desiring agent in the passage, "He desired: 'May I be many, may I procreate'" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.6), the insentient *pradhāna* postulated by the Sāṃkhyas—which is not based on direct scriptural testimony—should not be expected as the one consisting of bliss, nor as the cause.
This is according to the sūtra: "On account of [the Lord's] seeing, that which is not based on scripture [is not the cause]" (Brahma-sūtra 1.1.5).

Thus, although the Pradhāna has already been refuted, it is refuted once again here by way of a digression, relying on the scriptural passage concerning its being a "desirer" cited in the preceding sūtra, for the purpose of elaborating upon the uniformity of the goal (gatisāmānya). // 18 //
[Objection: Let it be that the *pradhāna*, which consists predominantly of *sattva* whose nature is bliss (*ānanda*), is "consisting of bliss" (*ānandamaya*).
To this, he says: "And because of desire" (*kāmācca*). That which is to be understood through inference is "inferential" (*ānumānika*).
Anticipating the objection of tautology, he says: "Because of seeing" (īkṣateḥ) //18//
And in this regard, it teaches his connection with that: BBs_1,1.19.
For this reason as well, the term "consisting of bliss" (ānandamaya) does not refer to either the Pradhāna or the individual soul (jīva):
because it teaches the union of this awakened jīva with that very Self which is the subject under discussion here as the "consisting of bliss.
"Union with that" (tadyoga) means union with that Self.
The attainment of that state is liberation; this is the meaning.
The scripture teaches union with that [state]: "For when he finds fearless support in that which is invisible, bodiless, indefinable, and without abode."
Then he becomes free from fear;
for when he perceives even a slight difference in this [Self], then fear comes upon him (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.7).
This is what is meant:
when one perceives even the slightest interval in this one consisting of bliss—an interval characterized by non-identity—then one does not turn back from the fear of saṃsāra;
but when one is established in this one consisting of bliss through uninterrupted identity, then one turns back from the fear of saṃsāra.
And that [characteristic] is consistent with the acceptance of the Supreme Self (paramātman), but not with the acceptance of the Pradhāna or the individual soul (jīva).
Therefore, it is established that the one consisting of bliss (ānandamaya) is the Supreme Self.

However, this must be stated here: "This very person consists of the essence of food (*annarasamaya*); different from this one consisting of the essence of food is the inner self consisting of breath (*prāṇamaya*); different from that is the inner self consisting of mind (*manomaya*); different from that is the inner self consisting of consciousness (*vijñānamaya*)" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.1, 2, 3, 4).

And since there is a continuous stream of the suffix *mayaṭ* used in the sense of a modification (*vikāra*), how can it be that, all of a sudden, by the logic of the "half-old woman" (*ardhajaratīya*), the suffix *mayaṭ* is taken to mean "abundance" (*prācurya*) and to have Brahman as its referent?
If you argue that this is because of the context of Brahman established by the words of the mantra (*māntravarṇika*), we say no;
for in that case, it would follow that even the "consisting of food" (*annamaya*) and the others are Brahman.

Here it is argued: It is appropriate that those consisting of food (*annamaya*) and the others are not Brahman, because a different, inner self is declared to follow each of them; however, no other inner self is declared after the one consisting of bliss (*ānandamaya*). Therefore, the one consisting of bliss is Brahman.
"Otherwise, there would be the consequence of abandoning the subject under discussion and introducing something irrelevant.

To this it is replied: Although it is not heard that there is another inner self within the one consisting of bliss (ānandamaya), as there is [another] within those consisting of food (annamaya) and so forth, nevertheless, the one consisting of bliss is not Brahman;
for, with reference to the one consisting of bliss, it is heard: "His joy alone is the head."
The right wing is joy;
the left wing is supreme joy;
the self is bliss.
"Brahman is the tail, the support" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.5). Therein,
that Brahman which was introduced in the wording of the mantra as "Brahman is truth, knowledge, and infinite," that very same one is here called "Brahman is the tail, the support."

It is precisely with the desire to make that [Brahman] known that these five sheaths (kośas), beginning with the one consisting of food (annamaya) and ending with the one consisting of bliss (ānandamaya), are postulated.
In that case, how can there be the consequence of abandoning the subject under discussion and introducing something not under discussion?
But is it not said that "Brahman is the tail, the support," [referring to Brahman] as a limb of the one consisting of bliss?
Just as in the case of the [self] consisting of food and the others, there are statements such as "this is the tail, the support.
In that regard, how can the primacy of Brahman be understood?
We reply: because it is the subject under discussion.

[Objection: "But surely, even if Brahman is understood as being a constituent part of the one consisting of bliss (*ānandamaya*), its status as the subject under discussion is not lost, because the one consisting of bliss is Brahman itself. [Reply:

To this it is said: If that were so, there would be an inconsistency, in that the very same Brahman would be the whole (*avayavin*) as the self consisting of bliss, and yet that same Brahman would also be the part (*avayava*) as the "tail," which is the support.

But since one must choose between the two, it is more reasonable to accept that the designation of Brahman occurs precisely in the phrase "Brahman is the tail, the support," because of the direct connection with the word "Brahman" there;
whereas in the passage concerning the "consisting of bliss" (ānandamaya), there is no such connection with the word "Brahman."
Furthermore, after it has been stated that "Brahman is the tail, the support," this is said: "Regarding this, there is also this verse:
'He becomes non-existent indeed, if he knows Brahman as non-existent.'"
And in this verse, "If one knows that 'Brahman exists,' then they know him as existing" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.6), the *ānandamaya* is not drawn back [as the subject].

From the statement of the merits and defects regarding the existence and non-existence of Brahman alone, it is understood that in the passage "Brahman is the tail, the support," Brahman itself is the primary subject. Furthermore,
it is not reasonable to suspect the existence or non-existence of the Self consisting of bliss (ānandamaya),
because the specific qualities of that ānandamaya— such as joy and delight— are well-known to all the world.
But how is it that Brahman, being the primary subject itself,
is designated as the "tail" of the one consisting of bliss in the statement, "Brahman is the tail, the support"?
This is not a fault.
By this, it is intended to be expressed that the tail is like a tail— that is, the support, the ultimate resort, and the single nest of all worldly joy is the bliss of Brahman;
not, however, that it is a physical limb.
This is because of another scriptural passage: "On a mere fraction of this very bliss do other beings live" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.3.32).
Furthermore, if the one consisting of bliss were Brahman, then Brahman would have to be admitted as possessing distinctions, since it would have "joy" and so forth as its constituent parts.
But Brahman is heard of as being without distinction in the remainder of the passage, because it is described as being beyond the range of speech and mind: "From whence words turn back,
together with the mind, not having attained it."
"One who knows the bliss of Brahman fears nothing from anywhere" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.9).

Furthermore, when it is said that [Brahman] "abounds in bliss," the existence of suffering is also implied, because in common worldly usage, abundance depends upon the relative scarcity of its opposite.

And that being the case, the scriptural statement regarding the Infinite Brahman— "Where one sees nothing else, hears nothing else, and understands nothing else, that is the Infinite" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 7.24.1)— would be contradicted, as it teaches the non-existence of anything distinct from it.
Furthermore, because there are distinctions such as "dear" and so forth for each individual body, the one consisting of bliss (*ānandamaya*) is also differentiated.
However, Brahman is not differentiated according to each body, as it is said: "Brahman is truth, knowledge, and infinite" (*Taittirīya Upaniṣad* 2.1).
This is because of the infinite scriptural testimony,
and also from another scripture: "The one God is hidden in all beings, all-pervading, the inner self of all beings" (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 6.11).
Nor is the repetition of the "consisting of bliss" (ānandamaya) heard;
for in every instance, it is only the meaning of the nominal stem itself that is repeated: "He is indeed bliss;
for having obtained bliss, this [person] becomes blissful."
"For who indeed could breathe, and who could live, if this bliss did not exist in the ether?
This is the inquiry into bliss."
"Knowing bliss as Brahman, one fears nothing from anywhere" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.7.8–9), and "He understood that bliss is Brahman" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 6.6).
And if it were certain that the term *ānandamaya* has Brahman as its referent, [then this would be established].
Consequently, even in the subsequent sections where there is the application of mere bliss (*ānanda-mātra*), one might assume the repetition of the "consisting of bliss" (*ānandamaya*);
however, we have already stated that the "consisting of bliss" is not Brahman, on account of reasons such as having joy as its head.
Therefore, since in another scriptural passage— "Brahman is consciousness and bliss" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.9.28)— the nominal stem *ānanda* is seen to be used for Brahman,

and since such usage regarding Brahman occurs in passages like "If this bliss did not exist in this space," it should be understood that this is a reference to Brahman and not a repetition (*abhyāsa*) of the term *ānandamaya*.

As for the repetition of the word "ānanda" itself ending in the suffix *-maya*— in the passage, "He reaches this self consisting of bliss" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.8)— that does not have Brahman as its object, because it is recited within a series of non-selfs such as those consisting of food (*annamaya*), which are modifications (*vikāra*) that are themselves to be transcended.

[Objection: But surely, if the one consisting of bliss (*ānandamaya*), which is to be reached, were Brahman—just like those beginning with the one consisting of food (*annamaya*)—then the fruit of the attainment of Brahman would not have been indicated for the knower.
[Reply: This is not a fault;
because by the very instruction regarding the reaching of the one consisting of bliss, the fruit, which is the attainment of Brahman that serves as the tail and support, has indeed been indicated.

Furthermore, this is because it is elaborated upon by the verse beginning with, "From which words turn back," and so forth. As for the scriptural passage cited in proximity to the one consisting of bliss (*ānandamaya*), namely, "He desired: May I be many, may I procreate"— [The answer is: It is not that. For that [passage] is intended to show that the Self is the cause of the world; it does not intend to teach that the Self consists of bliss. This is because the word *ānanda* (bliss) is used there in a figurative sense, as in the case of the word *anna* (food), and because it is mentioned merely as a subordinate element. Being connected with the Brahman that is in closer proximity by the phrase "Brahman is the tail, the support," this [passage] does not indicate that the one consisting of bliss (ānandamaya) is Brahman;

and because the subsequent portion of the text beginning with "He is indeed the essence" (raso vai saḥ) is dependent upon that [proximate Brahman], it does not have the one consisting of bliss as its subject matter.
[Objection: But surely the masculine designation in the phrase "He desired" (so 'kāmayata) is not appropriate for Brahman. [Reply:

This is not a fault, because in the passage "From that very Self, indeed, ether was produced" (tasmādvā etasmādātmana ākāśaḥ saṃbhūtaḥ), Brahman is the subject under discussion by means of the word "Self" (ātman), even though it is in the masculine gender.

However, as for the Vāruṇī knowledge of Bhārgava which states, "He understood that bliss is Brahman," since the suffix *mayaṭ* is not heard there, nor are the qualities such as having joy as its head mentioned, it is appropriate that bliss itself is Brahman. Therefore, without relying on even the slightest distinction, the attributes such as having joy as its head cannot be predicated of Brahman by its own nature alone.
And here, Brahman with attributes (saviśeṣa) is not intended to be taught,
because of the scriptural statement regarding its transcendence of the sphere of speech and mind.

Therefore, as in the case of "consisting of food" (annamaya) and the others, the suffix -maya in "consisting of bliss" (ānandamaya) should be understood in the sense of a modification (vikāra), not in the sense of abundance (prācurya).

The sūtras, however, are to be explained as follows: Regarding the passage "Brahman is the tail, the support," the question arises whether Brahman is intended here as a limb of the *ānandamaya* (the one consisting of bliss) or as the primary subject itself. Since the word "tail" (*puccha*) suggests it is a limb, the prima facie view is reached; in response, it is said: "The *ānandamaya* [is Brahman], because of repetition. In the statement "The self consists of bliss," Brahman is taught as the primary subject itself—namely, "Brahman is the tail, the support"—because of the repetition [of the term "Brahman"].
Because in this concluding verse, "He becomes as if present," Brahman alone is being repeatedly meditated upon.
If it is argued that [Brahman is not meant] because of the word denoting a modification, we say no, because of its abundance.
By the word "modification" (vikāra), the word "part" (avayava) is intended.
Regarding what was stated—that because "the tail" is a word denoting a subordinate part, Brahman cannot be the primary subject—its refutation must now be stated.
To this it is replied: this is not a fault.
Because the term for a part can also be justified on the basis of abundance; "abundance" means a preponderance,
so the meaning is that it is a statement regarding that which consists mostly of parts.

For, while in the case of those [sheaths] beginning with the "consisting of food" (annamaya), parts ending with the tail were mentioned in terms of limbs such as the head; in the case of the "consisting of bliss" (ānandamaya) as well, after mentioning other parts such as the head, the statement "Brahman is the tail, the support" was made by way of a figurative application of the pattern of parts, and not with the intention of denoting a literal limb.
For this reason, it has been established that Brahman is the primary subject on account of repetition (abhyāsa).
"And because it is designated as the cause of that":

Brahman is designated as the cause of the entire collection of modifications, including that which consists of bliss, in the passage: "It created all this, whatever there is" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.6).

Furthermore, it is not logically tenable that Brahman, as the cause, should be a constituent part (*avayava*) of its own modification, the one consisting of bliss (*ānandamaya*), in the primary sense of the term.
Other aphorisms (*sūtras*) as well should be understood as establishing that very Brahman which is designated in the passage concerning the "tail" (*puccha*), according to their respective contexts.

[Note: *Anātmye* means that which is devoid of identity with the "self" (*ātman*)—that is, the body—which is superimposed as having a relationship [to the self] and is the product of the elements transformed into the fivefold form by the collection of organs.]

The "defined" (*nirukta*) are those subtle elements (*bhūtasūkṣma*) which are spoken of by being extracted [from the unmanifest]; that which is devoid of non-difference from them is the "undefined" (*anirukta*).
The "abode" (*nilayana*) is Māyā, the locus of complete dissolution; it is "devoid of that" (*tacchūnya*).
"Udara" means *ut* (up) and *ara* (slight), referring to a slight interval or distinction (*antara*).
The meaning is that, compared to the "consisting of bliss" (ānandamaya), the state of being internal within Brahman is not heard [in the text], whereas the state of being a tail is indeed heard.
By "tail," mere support is meant;
by "foundation" (pratiṣṭhā), there is a single locus or substratum for the world together with its material cause.
For this reason— or rather, because words turn back without manifesting that [Brahman] through their power of denotation (*śakti-vṛtti*)—
its nature depends upon its opposite (*pratiyogin*), that is, its contradictory;
just as in the expression "a village consisting of Brahmins," there is the implication of the scarcity of Śūdras.

*Upakramaṇa* is the overcoming [of obstacles]. It refers to the discernment of those things that must be overcome and those that are to be abandoned. *Prāyāpatti* is the attainment within the intellect of the sequential order of the constituent parts.

The construction is as follows: since it teaches the union of the individual soul (*jīva*)—who possesses the awakening whose object is the one consisting of bliss (*ānandamaya*)—with that [bliss] by means of the locative case in the word "in this" (*asmin*), which denotes the object, it cannot be the primal matter (*pradhāna*).
To the objection that the individual soul also has a connection with the primal matter, he says: "as its self" (*tadātmanā*).
To the objection that the individual soul has identity with the individual soul, he says: "liberation" (*muktiḥ*).
In that which is invisible, devoid of the gross phenomenal world,

free from the subtle body (liṅgaśarīra)— which is the self's own nature consisting of the mere connection with the self— and distinct from that which is expressible by words; in that which is other than such [objects].

The meaning is as follows: when this wise person attains a firm, excellent state of mental steadiness (pratiṣṭhā) in Brahman—which is the void of that Māyā, the abode and the place of total dissolution—then at that very moment he attains the fearless Brahman.
Furthermore, the construction is: "Whenever this person perceives even the slightest interval (aram) or distinction (antaram), then at that time there is fear for him."
He refutes the opinion of the commentator (Vṛttikāra) with the words "But this... (*idaṃ tu*).

The syntactical connection (*anvaya*) is as follows: since the suffix *mayaṭ*—which signifies a modification (*vikāra*)—is present in the opponent's explanation, one must state how and by what analogy this "half-old-woman" (*ardhajaratīya*) logic can be accepted; namely, that within a single context, the same *mayaṭ* first has the sense of a modification and later has the sense of abundance (*prācurya*), all without any cause (*akasmāt*).
Having considered the question, it is suspected that "māntra" [is the answer]. The response is clear:
it is not heard [in the text] as "kimāntaraḥ."
Alternatively, having raised the doubt as to whether Brahman is not heard of even as something internal in reality, he accepts the first alternative, saying: "To this it is replied: although...

He states, "nevertheless," because of the scriptural mention of the suffix *-maya*, which is supported by its inclusion in a section primarily dealing with modifications (*vikāra*), and because of the indicative mark (*liṅga*) of having parts.
That which arises from the perception of a desired object is *priya* (pleasure).
Joy arises from mindfulness;
that [joy], when intensified through the absence of fear, is supreme joy (pramoda);
bliss (ānanda), however, is the cause.
The meaning of the Śruti is that the Self is the consciousness within the image (bimba-caitanya), which is the pure Brahman situated between the head and the tail;
he states the second [point] with the words "In that, that which... (tatra yad iti).
That Brahman which was the subject under discussion in the mantra as being hidden in the cave and situated within all, is recognized here in the sentence concerning the tail by the word "Brahman.
It is precisely for the purpose of making that [Brahman] known that the cave, in the form of the five sheaths, has been elaborated upon.
It was stated that they are postulated [as parts] because there is no intended meaning (tātparya) for them therein.

Thus, the meaning is that when the sentence concerning the tail is devoted to Brahman—which is the subject under discussion and the primary topic—there is no fault such as the abandonment of the subject matter (prakṛtahāni).
One raises an objection, saying "But surely," [arguing] that Brahman's status as the primary topic is contradicted by the scriptural mention of a "tail."
In this context, since the word "Brahman" brings about the recognition of the Brahman under discussion— which is the primary subject— there arises a conflict with the word "tail.
Considering that within a single sentence, between two words heard in first and last positions, the first is stronger as its meaning has not yet encountered contradiction,
he says "because it is the subject under discussion," intending that the status of being a subordinate quality (guṇatva) implied by the word "tail" is set aside.

He states the alternative possibility (*anyathāsiddhi*) of this [interpretation] with the words "Now, [it may be objected]... (*nanu*). He says, "To this it is replied" (*atrocyate*), because the status of being both a subordinate member (*aṅga*) and the primary object (*pradhāna*) for one and the same thing is contradictory.

Therein, in order to remove that contradiction, he says, "By one or the other," meaning that if Brahman is accepted in either one of the two sentences, then Brahman must be accepted in the sentence concerning the tail (*puccha*).

And he says "also" (api ca) because it is so from the remainder of the statement; the meaning is that there is even a verse regarding that Brahman. He asks for the explanation of the word "tail" (puccha): "But how? (kathaṃ punar iti).
Even for you, it is impossible to state the primary meaning of the word "tail," because Brahman lacks a tail consisting of bliss (*ānandamaya*).

Furthermore, if one resorts to the figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of a "tail" [in the sense of a support], it is more appropriate to understand it as the figurative indication of a substratum (*ādhāra-lakṣaṇā*).
Because it is joined with the word *pratiṣṭhā* (foundation) and because the word *brahman* attains its primary meaning,
and because in your own position the word *brahman* would also have to indicate a part [of a whole], he says: "This is not a fault."
By the word "puccha" (tail), mere substratum-ness is expressed. "Pratiṣṭhā" (foundation) means having a single nest;
the meaning is that there is one primary nest, that is, the foundational basis for the world together with its material cause.
Now, one might object: "The authors of the *Vṛtti* also accept that the Taittirīya passage is connected with Brahman;
why then do you cite it as an example of non-difference? Anticipating this doubt, he says, "Moreover" (*apica*).

Since there is a pervasion (*vyāpti*) such that wherever there is the state of having attributes (*saviśeṣatva*), there is the state of being within the range of speech and mind (*vāṅmanasagocaratva*), he says, "without attributes" (*nirviśeṣam*), meaning that here [Brahman] is described as being without attributes by stating the absence of the pervader (*vyāpakābhāva*).
The meaning is that they turn back because they are incapable;
furthermore, since that which possesses distinctions is false, fearlessness is untenable.
Therefore, the intention is that the sentence concerning the tail (*puccha*) alone is the illustrative example for the sake of attaining non-differentiated knowledge.
It was stated that when the suffix *mayaṭ* is used in the sense of abundance (*prācurya*), it contradicts the scriptural texts concerning the absence of distinctions (*nirviśeṣa-śruti*).
He states another defect with the words "Moreover" (*api ca*).
Since abundance, as the meaning of the suffix, is the primary element, the meaning of the base (*prakṛti*) serves as its qualifier.

That which is the counter-correlative (*pratiyogin*) of a distinction is its opposite; it requires [the presence of] a smallness [of that opposite], just as in the expression "a village consisting mostly of Brahmins," there is a smallness of Śūdras.
Let this be so—what is the fault?
To this he replies: "And thus...
This fault does not exist when the meaning of the base (prakṛti) is predominant, because in the expression "the sun is abundant light," even a slight darkness is not perceived.

However, one should consider that the term *ānandamaya* would entail the defect of having "abundant bliss" (*pracurānanda*) as its defining characteristic. Furthermore, because it is distinct [from Brahman], it cannot be Brahman—like a jar; thus he says, "in every body. Now, one might argue that since the word *ānanda* is repeated, it refers by implication (*lakṣaṇayā*) to *ānandamaya*, and thus the repetition is established; to this he replies, "And if... (yadi ca).

The sense is that there is a mutual dependence (*parasparāśraya*): once it is determined that the one consisting of bliss (*ānandamaya*) is Brahman, the repetition (*abhyāsa*) is established through the knowledge that the word "bliss" refers to that [Brahman]; and once that [repetition] is established, its determination [as Brahman] follows.
To show that this repetition pertains to the Brahman that is the tail, he says: "Therefore... (*tasmāt*).
"Approaching" (*upasaṃkramaṇa*) means "obstruction.

An objection is raised with the word "nanu": "Is it not the case that, having introduced the knower of Brahman with the words 'He who knows thus,' the fruit is indicated by the statement regarding approaching; therefore, if that [Self] were not Brahman, this would not be established?

Accepting that "approaching" means "attainment," he replies with "naiṣa doṣaḥ" (this is not so), stating that by the mention of the attainment of the qualified [entity], the fruit of attaining the qualifier is also stated.

In the established doctrine (*siddhānta*), it is stated that through knowledge there is the sublation (*bādha*) of the sheaths; thus, the attainment of the innermost bliss (*pratyagānanda*), which is the limit of that sublation, is implied. This is clarified by the subsequent verse, as the author says:
"That too... [and] "...because of its dependence on that.
The meaning is: because its object is the Brahman that is the tail of the desirer.

Regarding what was stated—that the Brahmavallī concludes at the section concerning the one consisting of bliss (ānandamaya) because it occupies the fifth position, as in the case of the Bhṛguvallī—the author says: "As for that... [yattviti].
The meaning is "but that which...
The intention is that the [notion of] location is sublated by the direct mention of the suffix *-maya* and by such indicative marks as having parts (*sāvayavatva*).
"Transcending the range" (*gocarātikrama*) means the absence of being within the range [of perception].

Regarding the conflict between the Veda and the Sūtras, he states "the Sūtras" [in the verse], meaning that the Sūtras must be interpreted otherwise according to the principle: "But when there is no quality [to be gained], the improper assumption [of a secondary sense] is not to be made.

Previously, it was argued by the reasoning that "because of the absence of doubt due to the act of seeing" (*īkṣateḥ*) that the context of the majority of readings (*prāyapāṭha*) is not determinative. Now, however, since the word "tail" (*puccha*) can equally denote either a support or a limb through figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*), there is indeed a doubt; thus, he presents the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*)—lacking the reasoning for the conclusion of the previous section—that the context of the majority of readings is determinative, on the grounds of the word "tail" (*pucchaśabdāt*).
And thus, there is a connection by way of a counter-example:
in the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa), the fruit is meditation on the qualified [Brahman], whereas in the final conclusion (siddhānta), it is the realization of the unqualified [Brahman].
The connections with the Śruti and other sources are indeed clear from the statement regarding the concordance (*samanvaya*) of the Vedānta texts.
By the term *ānandamaya* (consisting of bliss) in the Sūtra, the word *brahman* found in that passage is indicated.
That by which something is modified is a "modification" (*vikāra*), namely, a constituent part.
"Prāyāpatti" means the attainment of the sequence of parts within the intellect. For here,
the sheaths (kośas) are conceived as the limbs of a bird for the purpose of knowing Brahman, which is the subject under discussion.
There is no such intention here.

In that context, after the other limbs of the one consisting of bliss (ānandamaya) have been mentioned, something must be stated as its "tail" (puccha); it is the previously introduced Brahman that is expressed by the word "tail.
The meaning is that it must necessarily be stated as the substratum of the one consisting of bliss.
And because of the designation of that as its cause. //14//
Because that Brahman is designated as the cause of all effects;

and since the individual soul (jīva), consisting of bliss (ānandamaya), is an effect characterized by distinctions such as "dear" and so forth, it is not logical for Brahman to be subordinate to it—this is the meaning.
And it is proclaimed as being exactly what is described in the mantra-text. //15//

That Brahman, whose knowledge is said to bring liberation in the passage "The knower of Brahman attains the Supreme," and which is described in the mantra as "Truth, Knowledge," is celebrated right here in this sentence concerning the tail, because of its connection with the word "Brahman."
The meaning is that [the Self] consists of infinite bliss;
it cannot be either of the other two, because they are untenable. //16//
The other [interpretation], that the one consisting of bliss (*ānandamaya*) here is the individual soul (*jīva*), is not what is being propounded;
the meaning is that this is because [attributes] such as being the creator of all are untenable for it.
And because there is a designation of difference. (Sūtra 1.1.17)

The meaning is that because of the statement regarding difference—namely, "this one consisting of bliss (ānandamaya), having obtained the essence of Brahman (brahmarasa), becomes blissful"—it [the ānandamaya] is not what is being propounded [as Brahman].

Having raised the objection that "the ānandamaya is Brahman, because it is situated in the fifth stage [of the Taittirīyaka], just like the bliss mentioned in the Bhṛguvallī," he says: "And because of desire, there is no need for inference" (1.1.18).

The bliss of desire (*kāmananda*) is so called because it is desired; since that [bliss] is seen as Brahman in the fifth section of the *Bhṛguvallī*, there is no need for an inference that the "consisting of bliss" (*ānandamaya*) is also Brahman, because that would contradict the suffix *-maya* which signifies a modification (*vikāra*).

Having raised the objection that, due to the mention of difference, the Brahman with attributes (*saguṇa-brahman*) must be what is to be known here, he says: "And [the scripture] teaches its union with this [self] in this [state]. (1.1.19)

Since the *ānandamaya*— who possesses the realization "I myself am the supreme Brahman" regarding the Brahman described in the *puccha*-verse and summarized as "That is one"— is taught by the scripture beginning with "For when... (*yadā hi...*) to attain the state of Brahman through being hidden in the cave (the inner self),

[the author] says "others also" (sūtra 1.1.19) with the intention that the mention of the difference between the individual soul and Brahman is for the sake of knowing the identity with the attributeless Brahman.

Because there is instruction regarding His attributes within [the sun].

It is handed down in scripture: "Now, this golden person who is seen within the sun, with golden beard and golden hair, entirely golden down to his fingernails; his eyes are like a lotus blooming at dawn. "Of him, as a lotus is reddish-yellow... "From him rises the sun... and so forth.
"By that name he has risen above all evils; indeed, he who knows thus rises above all evils"—this is with reference to the deities (*adhidaivata*).
"Now with reference to the self (*adhyātma*): 'Now, this person who is seen within the eye'" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 1.7.1.5), and so forth.

In this regard, there is a doubt: Is it some transmigrating soul who has attained excellence through the power of the preeminence of knowledge and ritual action that is heard of as the object of meditation in the solar orb and in the eye, or is it the eternally established Supreme Lord? What, then, is the initial position? That it is a transmigrating soul.
Why? Because its possession of form is heard in scripture.
First, in the case of the person in the sun, form is illustrated by such passages as "golden-bearded" and so forth.
In the case of the person in the eye as well, that very same form is obtained through extension [of the description]: "The form of this one is the very same as the form of that one."

Furthermore, it is not logical for the Supreme Lord to possess form, because of the scriptural text: "Soundless, touchless, formless, undecaying" (Kāṭhaka Upaniṣad 1.3.15), and because of the mention of a support: "He who is within the sun."
"‘He who is here within the eye’—for no support would be taught for the Supreme Lord, who is all-pervading, established in His own majesty, and without a substratum.
[As it is said: ‘In what, O Venerable One, is He established? In His own majesty’ (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 7.24.1)."
And there are two scriptural passages: "He is omnipresent and eternal like space," and, from the scripture concerning the limits of his sovereignty:
"He rules over those worlds which are beyond that [sun] and over the desires of the gods" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 1.6.8).
Such is the limit of the power of the person in the sun;
"He rules over those worlds which are on this side of him, and over the desires of men," such is the case for the person in the eye.
And it is not fitting that the supreme Lord should possess a power limited by such boundaries.

"‘He is the Lord of all, He is the sovereign of beings, He is the protector of beings, He is the bridge, the supporter, so that these worlds may not be confounded’" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.22). Because of this scriptural statement which makes no distinction [between the two], the conclusion reached is that the Supreme Lord is not the one within the eye or the one within the sun. To this we reply: "The one within [is the Supreme Lord], because of the teaching of His attributes."
The person who is heard of in the scriptural passages, "He who is within the sun" and "He who is within the eye," is indeed the Supreme Lord, not a transmigrating soul.
Why? Because of the teaching of His attributes;
for the attributes of that Supreme Lord are taught here.

For example, having caused [the student] to hear that "His name is 'Ut' (uditi)," [the text] etymologically explains the name of this person in the sun by stating, "He has risen (udita) above all evils," thereby [showing it to be] free from all evil.
And that very name, once its etymology has been established, is extended to the person in the eye as well, [stating]: "Whatever is his name, that is his name.
Furthermore, freedom from all evil is heard in scripture as belonging to the Supreme Self alone, in such passages as, "The Self which is free from evil" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.7.1).

And likewise, in the passage concerning the person in the eye, [the text] determines that he consists of the Ṛg-veda, the Sāman, the Uktha, the Yajus, and the Brahman, stating: "He is the Ṛc, He is the Saman, He is the Uktha, He is the Yajus, He is the Brahman. And this is appropriate for the Supreme Lord, because, being the cause of all, it is logical that He is the self of all.

Having sequentially described the *Ṛk* and *Sāman* as consisting of earth, fire, and so forth with respect to the divine (*adhidaivata*), and as consisting of speech, breath, and so forth with respect to the self (*adhyātma*), [the text] says: "The *Ṛk* and the *Sāman* are its two joints" with respect to the divine; likewise with respect to the self: "Whatever are its two joints, those are the two joints."
And that [being praised] is possible only for the Self of all;

for the text, "Those who sing here on the lute, they sing of this [Self]; therefore they are winners of wealth" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 1.7.6), shows that even in worldly songs it is this very [Self] that is being sung about.
And that is consistent with the Supreme Lord’s appropriation [of all things], as it is said: "Whatever being is possessed of glory, or is majestic, or even powerful—
know each of those to have arisen from a fragment of my splendor."
(10.41) Thus, from the vision of the Bhagavadgītā,

even the lordship over the world and its desires, when heard as being absolute (*niraṅkuśa*), leads one to understand the Supreme Lord. As for what was said— that the hearing of a form characterized by golden beard and so forth is not possible in the case of the Supreme Lord— [that is not so].

To this we reply: It may well be that the Supreme Lord also possesses a form composed of *māyā* by virtue of His will, for the sake of favoring his practitioners; for it is recorded in the Smṛti: "O Nārada, this is indeed *māyā* created by me that you see me as endowed with the qualities of all beings; you ought not to know me in such a way."
Moreover, where the supreme Lord's form, in which all distinctions have been discarded, is taught, there the scripture says: "Soundless, touchless, formless, undecaying," and so forth.

However, because He is the cause of all, the Supreme Lord is also pointed out as an object of worship as qualified by certain attributes of transformation: "He who possesses all actions, all desires, all odors, and all tastes" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad).
By such passages as these,
the description of having golden hair and beard and so forth will also be accounted for.
As for the argument that [the Self] is not the Supreme Lord because an abode is heard mentioned, [that too is refuted].

To this it is replied: Even for that which is established in its own majesty, instruction regarding a specific substratum will serve the purpose of meditation (*upāsana*), since Brahman, like space, is all-pervading and thus its being within all things is logically established.

Furthermore, the scriptural mention of limitations on its sovereignty is likewise solely for the purpose of meditation, with reference to the distinction between the internal self (*adhyātma*) and the divine realm (*adhidaivata*).
Therefore, it is the Supreme Lord alone who is taught as being within the eye and within the sun.
[FN: "Within the sun" means within the solar orb;
"golden" means consisting of light.]
From the hairline extending to the tips of the nails,

his eyes possess a preeminent luster, like a lotus flower equal to the back (or tail) of a monkey— a *kapin*— which is exceedingly brilliant; just as that [lotus] is intensely radiant, so too are his two eyes supremely luminous.
Regarding the phrase "tasyoditi": *udita* means risen; the sense is that he is untouched by all evils along with their effects.
"He is this" is a statement concerning the person belonging to the divine realm (*adhidaivika*).
The meaning is that he is the lord of those worlds which are situated above this sun, as well as the lord of the desires and enjoyments of the gods.
Those two which consist of all the Ṛg and Sāman verses are the *geṣṇau*, that is, the feet and joints, of this chariot of the Sun;
for it is so stated in the context of the Nirvāhaṇīya hymns,
because their specific attributes are taught therein.
He cites the passage from the Chāndogya Upaniṣad: "Now, as for those who... The word "now" (atha) signifies the commencement of a meditation. "Golden" (hiraṇmaya) means a transformation of light.
The Person (Puruṣa), though all-pervading, is seen by the worshippers as possessing a form.
He describes that form with the words "golden" and so forth.
The term "praṇakha" refers to the tip of the nail; the prefix "ā" is used here in the sense of inclusion (abhividhi). He specifies the particularity of his eyes with the word "tasya" (of him).

The *āsa*—the tail-end—of a monkey is exceedingly brilliant; his two eyes are like a white lotus (*puṇḍarīka*) equal to that, meaning they are as radiant as a freshly blossomed red lotus. For the purpose of meditation, the solar orb is his location.
Having spoken of form, he designates "name" as "that which rises"; he etymologically explains that name: "he" (saḥ) means "risen" (uditaḥ), that is, "gone up" (udgataḥ).
The meaning is that he is untouched by all evil.
He states the result of knowing the Name with the words "He rises" and so forth.
After describing the meditation with reference to the sun, which is the abode of the deity, he says "Now" (atha) to state that same meditation with reference to the self, namely the body.

Just as in the previous [section], where the determination of the *nirguṇa* (devoid of attributes) was established by virtue of many proofs—namely the word "Brahman," the word "consisting of bliss" (*ānandamaya*), and the repetition of the word "bliss"—here, by virtue of many proofs such as the possession of form, the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is set forth for the purpose of providing an exception (*apavāda*) to the previously established general rule (*utsarga*) of the concordance with the *nirguṇa*, following the analogy of the previous example that "the golden one is the individual soul" (*jīva*). Thus, he states: "The transmigrating soul... In this context, the fruit of both the prima facie and the final positions is the meditation upon the individual soul (*jīva*) and Brahman respectively.
And because of the mention of the "eyes" as its locus, the connection is that it is a transmigrating being (*saṃsārī*).
He cites the scripture: "This very one...
[referring to] the person situated in the sun.
The meaning is that he is the lord of whatever worlds there may be above that sun, as well as of the enjoyments of the gods.

It is heard in scripture that this very person residing in the eye is the lord of those worlds which are below this eye, as well as of the enjoyments desired by humans; such is the boundary [of his domain].
Therefore, the meaning of the scripture is that [the Self] is the transmigrator;
the connection is with the scriptural statement "He is the Lord of all," which is without qualification.
Yama, the lord of beings, and Indra and others, the guardians of beings, are this very one.

Furthermore, just as a dam in the world is a restrainer for the non-intermingling of waters, so too is He alone the "dam" (setu) because He is the cause of the boundaries (maryādā) of these worlds, such as the castes (varṇa) and stages of life (āśrama).
Therefore, the meaning is that He is the Supreme Lord of all.
He explains the Sūtra with the words "ya eṣa" (this which...).
Although in a single sentence the latter part should be interpreted in accordance with what is heard first,
nevertheless, in this case, the quality of possessing form, being heard first, is fruitless.

Furthermore, while being free from all evil and being one with the Self of all can be attributed to the Lord for the sake of meditation, being free from all evil and being one with the Self of all is both fruitful and impossible to attribute to the individual soul (jīva); thus, it is more powerful [as an argument].

Nor should it be argued that, on the basis of the scriptural text, "Indeed, evil does not reach the gods," the individual soul (jīva) of the Sun-god is also untouched by evil; for the purport of that scripture is that the gods—who are currently ineligible for ritual action—are neither connected with the evil being committed nor touched by its fruit. Furthermore, since the statement, "When their merit is exhausted, they enter the world of mortals," would otherwise be inapplicable if those gods lacked accumulated sin, [the author] says with this intention: "And the departure from all evil belongs to the Supreme Self alone."
He states its universal nature with the word "tathā" (so).
Here, by the pronouns "tat," the person perceived through sight is denoted;
the change in gender is due to the reference to the *Ṛg* verses and so forth.
The *uktha* is a specific type of recitation (*śastra*); by association with that, the *sāman* is the hymn of praise (*stotra*),
and the *ṛc* is said to be the recitation other than the *uktha*.
The Yajurveda is the *yajuḥ*;
"Brahman" means the three Vedas.
It consists of the nature of the earth, fire, and so forth.

With respect to the deities (*ādhidaivata*), the *Ṛk* is said in the Śruti to be fivefold, consisting of the white light-forms residing in the earth, the intermediate space, the sky, the stars, and the sun; and the *Sāman* is likewise said to be fivefold, consisting of the exceedingly dark forms residing in fire, wind, the sun, the moon, and the sun.
With respect to the self (*adhyātma*), however, the *Ṛk*—

Speech, sight, hearing, and the eye—these four are said to have the form of white light; and the Sāman, consisting of breath, shadow, self, and mind, located in the eye, is said to have the form of deep blue. Having thus sequentially described the Ṛk and the Sāman, the Śruti says "of that" (tasya).

The two *geṣṇas* (feet) which consist of all the Ṛg-verses and Sāman-chants belonging to that [Self] residing in the sun—those very same two are the *geṣṇas* of the one residing in the eye; the meaning is that they are its "joints" (*parvaṇī*).
And that... [etc.]
The meaning is that it has the *ṛc*, *sāman*, and *geya* as its essence.
He states another indicative mark—that it is to be sung by all singers—with the words "Now, those... (*tadya iti*).
That is, in that world.

Those for whom there is the acquisition of wealth are "wealth-acquirers" (*dhanasanayaḥ*), meaning they possess prosperity. Now, one might object: "In the world, kings are praised, but not as the Lord (*īśvara*). To this he says: "Whatever... (*yadyat...*).
Prosperity consists of cattle, wealth, and so forth; splendor is radiance;
and vigor is strength.
The meaning is that the sattva, rajas, and so forth associated with that [body] are merely a portion of My own self; therefore, its singing belongs to the Lord alone.
"Unrestrained" means independent of anything else.
This form of diverse appearance is "māyā" because it is a transformation of māyā; the meaning is that it was created by Me as māyā.
Thus it has been said: "And moreover" (api ca), he states that the passage beginning with "without sound" (aśabda) is intended to refer to that which is to be known (jñeya).
To the question, "In that case, from where does its form [arise]?", he replies: "all" (sarva).

However, where it is stated that [the Lord] is to be meditated upon, one must supply the word "there" (tatra); the connection is that, because He is the cause of all, His possession of form—which might otherwise be inferred—is specified by such scriptural passages as "possessing all works" (*sarvakarmā*).
He refutes the claim that the Lord's sovereignty is limited by saying, "sovereignty...
The distinction between meditation on the internal self (*adhyātma*) and the divine (*adhidaivata*), as well as their separate application, is based precisely upon that [distinction].
The meaning is that it is for the purpose of defining the limits of sovereignty. //20//
And because there is a designation of difference, [the Self] is other [than the aggregate]. 1.1.21.
Furthermore, there exists a Lord who is the Inner Controller, distinct from the individual souls (jīvas) that identify with the bodies of the sun and so forth;

for another scriptural passage declares their distinction: "He who dwells in the sun, yet is within the sun, whom the sun does not know, whose body the sun is, who controls the sun from within—he is your Self, the Inner Controller, the Immortal" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.7.9).

For in that passage— "He who is within the sun, whom the sun does not know"— the inner ruler (antaryāmī) is clearly indicated as distinct from the knower, the sun, who is a conscious self (vijñānātman).
That very same being must also be the person within the sun here,
because of the identity of the scriptural statement.

Therefore, it is established that the Supreme Lord alone is taught here. Now, one might object: since this is an injunction for worship directed toward an object of worship, it must be stated that the object of the action to be performed (the karma) is established from another source, just as in the case of rice and other grains. Anticipating this doubt, he says "bhedā" (because of difference).

He states the meaning of the Sūtra—"He exists"—to show that because the difference between Āditya, the individual soul, and the Lord is declared in another Śruti, the Lord is established as being distinct from the individual soul.
In order to exclude the one who stands within the sun with its rays, he excludes the individual soul (jīva) by saying "whom.
To the question of how one who is bodiless can be a controller, he says "of whom."
He states the meaning of the term *antaryāmin* (the inner ruler) with the words "He who...";
he says "This is yours" (*eṣa te*) in order to refute the notion that it is not the Self;
the meaning is: "This is your own essential nature."
The meaning is that this is because the scriptural statement regarding [the Self] being within the sun is the same [in both cases].
Therefore, it is established that the Supreme Self alone is to be meditated upon as the Udgītha residing in the sun and other locations. //21//

Section on Ether (Ākāśādhikaraṇa) / Sūtra 22 8. [Topic]: Ether. Sūtra 22. "Ether is not produced. (Sūtra 22) The doubt arises as to whether ether is produced like earth and the other elements, or if it is unproduced. On this point, the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa) is that ether is produced, because it is mentioned in the same category as produced things; for instance, in the passage, "From that, indeed, was born ether" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.1), ether is mentioned alongside fire and the rest, which are known to be produced. To this, we reply: Ether is not produced. Why? Because it is eternal. How is its eternity known? From scripture. For scripture declares its eternity by stating that it exists even before the production of all other things, in such passages as, "In the beginning, my dear, this was indeed non-existent" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.2.1), and "That from which these beings are born" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 3.1). Furthermore, since ether is the substratum of sound, and sound is eternal, ether must also be eternal. Moreover, there is no scriptural statement regarding its origin comparable to those concerning earth and the others. Therefore, ether is unproduced. Alternatively, the word "ether" (ākāśa) may be understood here as referring to the Supreme Self, because of its characteristics. For the Supreme Self is described as having the characteristic of being the cause of all things, as in the passage, "From whom, verily, all these beings are born" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 3.1). And since the Supreme Self is established by scripture to be eternal, it follows that ether—meaning the Supreme Self—is not produced. Thus, the conclusion is reached. [End of Section 8] [Start of Section 9] Topic: Air (Vāyu-adhikaraṇa) / Sūtra 23. "Air [is not produced]. (Sūtra 23) The doubt arises as to whether air is produced or not. On this point, the prima facie view is that air is produced, because it is mentioned in the same category as produced things, as in the passage, "From that, indeed, was born air" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.1). To this, we reply: Air is not produced. Why? Because it is eternal. How is its eternity known? From scripture. For scripture declares its eternity by stating that it exists even before the production of all other things, in such passages as, "In the beginning, my dear, this was indeed non-existent," and "That from which these beings are born. Furthermore, since air is the substratum of touch, and touch is eternal, air must also be eternal. Moreover, there is no scriptural statement regarding its origin comparable to those concerning earth and the others. Therefore, air is unproduced. Alternatively, the word "air" (vāyu) may be understood here as referring to the Supreme Self, because of its characteristics. For the Supreme Self is described as having the characteristic of being the cause of all things, as in the passage, "From whom, verily, all these beings are born. And since the Supreme Self is established by scripture to be eternal, it follows that air—meaning the Supreme Self—is not produced. Thus, the conclusion is reached. [End of Section 9] [Start of Section 10] Topic: Non-existence (Abhāvādhikaraṇa) / Sūtra 24. "There is no non-existence. (Sūtra 24) The doubt arises as to whether non-existence (abhāva) is produced or not. On this point, the prima facie view is that non-existence is produced, because it is mentioned in the same category as produced things; for instance, in the passage, "From that, indeed, was born non-existence" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.7), non-existence is mentioned alongside ether and the rest, which are known to be produced. To this, we reply: There is no non-existence. Why? Because it is impossible. For non-existence is the mere absence of existence, and it is impossible for an absence to be produced. Furthermore, there is no scriptural statement regarding its origin. Therefore, non-existence is not produced. Alternatively, the word "non-existence" (abhāva) may be understood here as referring to the Supreme Self, because of its characteristics. For the Supreme Self is described as having the characteristic of being the cause of all things, as in the passage, "From whom, verily, all these beings are born. And since the Supreme Self is established by scripture to be eternal, it follows that non-existence—meaning the Supreme Self—is not produced. Thus, the conclusion is reached. [End of Section 10] [Start of Section 11] Topic: Water (Ap-adhikaraṇa) / Sūtra 25. "Water [is not produced]. (Sūtra 25) The doubt arises as to whether water is produced or not. On this point, the prima facie view is that water is produced, because it is mentioned in the same category as produced things, as in the passage, "From that, indeed, was born water" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.1). To this, we reply: Water is not produced. Why? Because it is eternal. How is its eternity known? From scripture. For scripture declares its eternity by stating that it exists even before the production of all other things, in such passages as, "In the beginning, my dear, this was indeed non-existent," and "That from which these beings are born. Furthermore, since water is the substratum of taste, and taste is eternal, water must also be eternal. Moreover, there is no scriptural statement regarding its origin comparable to those concerning earth and the others. Therefore, water is unproduced. Alternatively, the word "water" (ap) may be understood here as referring to the Supreme Self, because of its characteristics. For the Supreme Self is described as having the characteristic of being the cause of all things, as in the passage, "From whom, verily, all these beings are born. And since the Supreme Self is established by scripture to be eternal, it follows that water—meaning the Supreme Self—is not produced. Thus, the conclusion is reached.
