It is space, because of its characteristic marks.
Regarding this, they recite: "What is the goal of this world? "Space," he said. "For indeed, all these beings arise from space alone;
they dissolve back into space; for space is greater than these, space is the ultimate resort" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 1.9.1).
In this regard, there is a doubt: is the Supreme Brahman denoted by the word "ether" (ākāśa), or is it the elemental ether (bhūtākāśa)?
Why is there a doubt?
Because its usage is observed in both senses.
The word "ether" (ākāśa) is well-known in both common usage and the Veda as referring to a particular element.
It is also seen to be used occasionally for Brahman,
where Brahman is determined either by the force of the remainder of the passage or by the hearing of attributes unique to it.

As in such passages as: "If this bliss did not exist in the ether" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.7), and "The so-called ether is indeed the revealer of name and form; that which is within them is Brahman" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.14.1).
Hence there is a doubt: what, then, is appropriate here—
the elemental ether?
Why is this? Because that [meaning] enters the intellect quickly through its more well-known usage.
Furthermore, it is not possible to understand this word "ākāśa" as common to both [meanings], for that would entail the fallacy of having multiple meanings.
Therefore, the word "ether" (ākāśa) must be understood in a secondary sense with respect to Brahman;
for Brahman is similar to ether in many respects, such as omnipresence and so forth.
And when a primary meaning is possible, it is not appropriate to accept a secondary sense.
And here, the primary meaning of "ether" (ākāśa) itself can indeed be accepted.
But is it not the case that if the elemental ether (bhūtākāśa) were taken, the remainder of the passage—"All these beings, verily, arise from ether alone," and so forth—would be untenable?
This is not a fault.

For it is logically consistent that even elemental space (bhūtākāśa) can serve as a cause through the sequence of air and the other elements; indeed, it is known from scripture: "From this very Self, space was produced;
from space, air."
"From air, fire" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.1), and so forth.
Furthermore, both superiority and being the ultimate resort are possible for the elemental ether (*bhūtākāśa*) as well, in comparison with other elements.

Therefore, when the prima facie view is reached that the word "ether" refers to the elemental ether, we reply: "The ether [is Brahman], because of its characteristic marks. It is appropriate that the word "ether" refers to Brahman.
Why? Because of its characteristic mark (*liṅga*).
For this is a characteristic mark of the supreme Brahman: "All these beings indeed arise from space alone.
Indeed, it is the established rule in the Vedāntas that the origin of beings is from the supreme Brahman.
But has it not been shown that even the elemental ether (bhūtākāśa) possesses causality through the sequence beginning with air?
True, it has been shown;
nevertheless, because the primary cause, Brahman, was not accepted [therein], the restriction "from ether alone" (ākāśādeva) [is justified].
Furthermore, the qualification "all" would not be appropriate [if it referred to the elements].

Likewise, there is a characteristic mark of Brahman in the phrase "they merge into space," as well as in the attributes of being "greater" and "the ultimate resort" found in the passage: "For space is indeed greater than these; space is the ultimate resort.

For such non-relative greatness is taught in scripture only of the Supreme Self: "Greater than the earth, greater than the intermediate region, greater than the sky, greater than these worlds" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 3.14.3).
Likewise, the state of being the ultimate resort (*parāyaṇatva*) is also more appropriately applicable to the Supreme Self alone, because it is the supreme cause.
And there is a scriptural text: "Brahman is consciousness and bliss; it is the ultimate resort of the giver who bestows [wealth]" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.9.28).
Furthermore, having censured Śālāvatya’s position on account of the defect of its being finite, [the text continues:]

Jaivali, desiring to say something infinite, has selected space; and having identified that space with the Udgītha, he concludes: "This is that Udgītha which is higher than the high; this is that which is infinite" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 1.9.2).
And that infinity is a characteristic mark of Brahman.

As for what was further stated—that the elemental ether (*bhūtākāśa*) is understood first by the force of common usage—to this we reply: although it may be understood first, it is not accepted upon seeing the qualities of Brahman mentioned in the remainder of the passage.
Furthermore, the word "ether" (*ākāśa*) is shown to apply to Brahman as well in such passages as: "Ether, indeed, is the bringer-forth of name and form. etc.

Likewise, the use of words synonymous with "space" (*ākāśa*) is observed in reference to Brahman: "In the imperishable, supreme space (*vyoman*), all the gods have taken their seat" (*Ṛgveda Saṃhitā* 1.164.39);
"This very knowledge of Bhārgava and Vāruṇa is established in the supreme space" (*Taittirīya Upaniṣad* 3.6);
and "Om! Kaṃ is Brahman; Khaṃ is Brahman" (*Chāndogya Upaniṣad* 4.10.5).
And in passages such as "The ether is ancient" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 5.1),
even though the word "ether" occurs at the beginning of the sentence, it is proper to determine that its referent is Brahman on the basis of the remainder of the passage.
For even the word "fire" (agni), occurring at the beginning of the sentence "Agni studies the lesson," is seen to refer to the boy;
therefore, it is established that the word "ether" (ākāśa) refers to Brahman. // 22 // [FN:
Of the knower, the cognizer.]
"From the self consisting of consciousness," meaning from that which is conditioned by the internal organ;
"of this [world]," Śālāvatya, the Brāhmaṇa, asks Jaivali, the King;
"the sustainer" means the cause of its production and maintenance.

That which is between those two, from which they are distinct, or in the midst of which they exist—that is Brahman untouched by name-and-form; this is the meaning of the statement "the ether here is Brahman.
[The word] *rāti* refers to the giver of wealth, namely the sacrificer.
Its infinity in terms of space constitutes its transcendence (*paratva*).
Superiority by virtue of qualities (*guṇa*) is excellence (*varīyastva*);
infinity (*ānantya*) is the state of being unlimited in terms of time and substance;
or alternatively, "higher than the high" (*parovarīyastva*) refers to preeminence that surpasses others such as the *svara* and so forth.
In the sky within the sky, in the supreme, most excellent, unchanging, and immutable Brahman.
All the Vedas, including the Ṛgveda with its constituent Ṛks, serve as indicators [of Brahman].
Regarding that syllable upon which all the gods are seated— that is, established—
let there be a setting aside of weak indicative marks such as "possessing form" by means of the non-deviating indicative marks of Brahman, such as "untouched by evil."

But here, since the scriptural mention of the word "ether" (*ākāśa*) is stronger than the indicative mark (*liṅga*), [the author] provides a counter-example and replies: "The ether [is Brahman], because of its characteristic marks" (*ākāśas talliṅgāt*).
He cites the passage from the *Chāndogya*: "This... [etc.].
The Brāhmaṇa Śālāvatya asks King Jaivali:
"What is the support of this world of earth and of the other [worlds]?
The King replied, "It is space (ākāśa)," thus it is said.
Because of the hearing of bliss—which is the unique attribute of Brahman—in the passage, "This space," it was determined that space is Brahman.

In the passage "Ākāśa, indeed, by name," the division [of the meaning] is based on the supplementary statement (vākyaśeṣa), "That is Brahman. "Nirvahitā" means the cause of origination and maintenance.
Those two, name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*),
are so called because they are distinct from that which is within;
or rather, the meaning is that they exist in the middle as something imagined.

In the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), there is the meditation on the *udgītha* as the elemental ether (*bhūtākāśa*) and the Self (*ātman*); in the established conclusion (*siddhānta*), it is as Brahman and the Self—this is the result.

Since the reconciliation of the passage containing clear marks of Brahman regarding the object of meditation has been stated, the connections with the scriptures (*śruti*) and so forth extend throughout the chapter.
The commentary here is clear:

since air and the other elements are also causes of fire and the rest, there would be a contradiction with the scriptural mention of the word "only" (eva), and the universal scriptural statement would have to be restricted to refer to something other than space; thus [the author] says: "It is true that this has been shown."
The sense is that because Brahman is the self of all, the scriptural statement "from that alone everything [arises]" is logical;
likewise, it possesses the state of being the substratum of the dissolution of all things and unsurpassed greatness.
He states that even in the context of "abiding," there is the quality of being the supreme substratum, and thus these are clear marks (*liṅga*) of Brahman, by saying "Likewise, space... and so forth.
[The word] *rāti* means a giver of wealth;
if the reading is *rāti*, it means a kinsman.
He states another indicative mark with the words "Moreover" (*api ca*).
Three individuals—the two Brahmins Dālbhya and Śālāvatya and the King—skilled in the knowledge of the Udgītha, deliberated: "What is the ultimate resort of the Udgītha?"

In this regard, Śālāvatya, having criticized the position of Dālbhya— who held that because the *udgītha* is performed with water brought from heaven and by means of life-breath, heaven itself is its ultimate resort (*parāyaṇa*)— on the grounds of the defect of being "without foundation," stated that even for heaven, this world is the foundation (*pratiṣṭhā*), being the cause through the medium of ritual action (*karman*).

Having censured that position of Śālāvatya with the words, "Indeed, your *sāman*, O Śālāvatya, has an end," the King speaks of space (*ākāśa*) as being infinite; the meaning is that if the elemental space were intended, the defect of having an end would remain as it was.
Anticipating the objection that it is not heard in scripture that space is infinite, he says: "And that... and so forth.
The point is that because the *udgītha* is identified with space (*ākāśa*), its infinity and other qualities do not belong to it inherently.
That *oṃkāra*, which is a part of the *udgītha*,
has space as its essence.
"Supreme" means pre-eminent by virtue of qualities such as being the most flavorful;
therefore, it is "varīyān," meaning more excellent than other syllables.
The sense is that it is the best.
The word *paraḥ* is either an indeclinable ending in *s*,
as seen in the usage *paraḥ kṛtsnam*;
or it refers to one who is supreme (*paraḥ*) and superior (*varaḥ*) beyond all others.
The meaning is "far superior.

He recalls what was stated—that the word "ether" (ākāśa) is stronger because of its preeminence and because it is explicitly mentioned in the scripture—with the words "As for that which... and so forth.

In order to support the numerous marks such as "endlessness" (ānantya) which are favored by both the word *eva* and the word *sarva*, he says, "To this we reply," [implying] that the sublation of a single scriptural passage is appropriate according to the maxim, "One should sacrifice an individual for the sake of the family.
By the word *api*, it is indicated that there is no rule that the element [ākāśa] must be understood first from the word *ākāśa*.
He states the reasoning for this: "And it has been shown."
The point is that even Brahman, as a secondary (gauṇa) meaning of the word "ākāśa," is perceived first,
because of the frequent usage of that term and its synonyms for Brahman.
In the imperishable, immutable, and all-pervading space (vyoman), the Ṛg-verses— that is, the Vedas— exist.

The meaning is that in which syllable all the gods are established as the means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*). One should meditate upon the syllable *oṃ* as "Ka," which is bliss (*sukha*), and "Kha," which is the pervasive Brahman.
He cites the usage from another Śruti: "the ancient Kha."
The meaning is that Brahman is all-pervading and without beginning.
The distinction is that the *Chāndogya* states, "Ka is Brahman, Kha is Brahman," while the *Bṛhadāraṇyaka* states, "Oṃ, Kha is Brahman, Kha is the ancient."
Furthermore, in that very context, the subsequent [statement] should be interpreted in accordance with the preceding one, provided it can be so interpreted; however,
where it cannot be so interpreted, the preceding one must be interpreted in accordance with the subsequent one— this is what he states by the words "vākya" (sentence).
Therefore, he concludes that the scriptural passage is consistent with Brahman as the object of meditation, stating: "Therefore... (sūtra 22).

The Section Concerning Prāṇa / Sūtra 23.

For this very reason, the vital breath (prāṇa) [is the deity]. In the Udgītha section, beginning with "O Prastotṛ, that deity which is dependent upon the Prastāva," it is heard: "Which is that deity? "The vital breath," he said; "for indeed, all these beings enter into the vital breath alone and emerge from the vital breath."
"This very deity is connected with the Prastāva" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 1.11.4, 5).
In this regard, the doubt and its resolution are to be understood as before.
"For the mind, my dear, is fastened to breath" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.8.2).
Furthermore, in passages such as "the breath of breath" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.18), the word *prāṇa* is seen to refer to Brahman;
yet, in both common worldly usage and the Veda, it is more widely established as denoting a modification of air.
Therefore, a doubt arises here as to which [meaning] of the word "prāṇa" is appropriate to be taken up. What, then, is appropriate here?
It is appropriate to take up the prāṇa that is a modification of air (vāyu) and possesses five functions.
For we have already stated that the word "prāṇa" is more commonly established in that sense there.

But is it not the case that, as before, here too it is proper to understand Brahman alone because of its characteristic marks? For even here, in the remainder of the passage, the entering into and emerging of beings is perceived as the work of the Supreme Lord. No.
Even though the chief vital breath (*prāṇa*) is the primary subject, it is observed that the entry and emergence of the elements occur within it;

for thus it is recorded in scripture: "When a person sleeps, then speech merges into the vital breath, the eye into the vital breath, and the mind into the vital breath. When he awakens, they are born again from the vital breath alone" (Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa 10.3.3.6).

This is directly perceived: at the time of sleep, while the function of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) remains unimpaired, the functions of the sense organs (*indriya*) cease, and at the time of waking, they reappear.

Furthermore, since living beings consist essentially of the sense organs, the subsequent scriptural passage—which speaks of the dissolution and emergence of beings into the primary vital breath—is not contradictory.
Moreover, the Sun and Food are designated as the deities of the *udgītha* and *pratihāra*, and are thus mentioned as being distinct from the vital breath, which is the deity of the *prastāva*.
Furthermore, those two do not possess the nature of Brahman;

and because of that similarity, the vital breath (prāṇa) also does not have the nature of Brahman—this being the position reached, the author of the Sūtras says: "For this very reason, the vital breath [is Brahman].
This refers back to what was indicated in the previous Sūtra by the phrase "on account of its characteristic mark" (talliṅgāt).
For this very reason, on account of those marks, the word *prāṇa* must also refer to the Supreme Brahman.
For the connection of *prāṇa* with the marks of Brahman is also heard in scripture: "All these beings indeed enter into *prāṇa* alone, and from *prāṇa* they emerge" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 1.11.5).
The origin and dissolution of all beings, which are stated to be caused by *prāṇa*, lead one to understand that *prāṇa* is Brahman.

But was it not said that even if the principal vital breath (mukhyaprāṇa) is accepted as the subject, the observation of entering into and emerging from [the body] is not contradictory, because this is seen during sleep and waking?
To this it is replied: in the cases of sleep and waking, what is observed is the entering into and emerging from the support of the vital breath belonging to the sense organs alone.
It does not refer to all elements (bhūta) whatsoever;

rather, here it refers to those elements that possess sense organs, possess bodies, and are inhabited by living beings (jīva), according to the Vedic revelation: "Verily, all these elements [are pervaded by the Self]."

Even when the scriptural mention of "beings" (*bhūta*) is understood as referring to the gross elements (*mahābhūta*), even then it is not contradictory that this constitutes a characteristic mark of Brahman.
But surely we hear of the dissolution of the sense organs, together with their objects, into the vital breath (*prāṇa*) during sleep and waking, and of their emergence from the vital breath:
"When one is asleep and sees no dream whatsoever, then he becomes one with this very vital breath; then [they lead him]..."
"Speech merges together with all names" (Kauṣītaki Upaniṣad 3.3).
Even there, because of that indicative mark, the word "prāṇa" refers to Brahman alone.
As for the argument that prāṇa is not Brahman due to its proximity to food and the sun—
That is incorrect;
for when it is understood through the force of the supplementary statement (*vākyaśeṣa*) that the word "prāṇa" has Brahman as its referent, proximity (*saṃnidhāna*) is of no consequence.
As for the further point that the word "prāṇa" is more commonly established in the sense of the fivefold vital functions (*pañcavṛtti*), [that is irrelevant].
In that case, it must be answered just as in the instance of the word "space" (*ākāśa*).
Therefore, it is established that the vital breath (*prāṇa*), who is the deity of the *prastāva*, is Brahman.
On this point, some cite the passage: "The breath of the breath."
And as for the statement, "For the mind, my dear, is bound by the vital breath" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.8.2), that is incorrect;
because of the difference in terminology and the context, the doubt [regarding the identity of the two] is untenable.

Just as in the expression "the father of the father," it is understood that one father is indicated by the genitive case and another is indicated by the nominative case— as in "the father of the father"—
so too, because of the difference in words in the phrase "the breath of breath," it is determined that the "breath of breath" is distinct from the well-known breath;
for the same thing cannot appropriately be designated with a distinction such as "of that."
Furthermore, when someone is mentioned within a particular context, even by another name, it is understood that this very person is the subject referred to in that context.
For example, in the section concerning the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, the word "jyotis" (light) in the passage, "One should sacrifice with the Jyotis every spring," refers to the Jyotiṣṭoma itself;

likewise, how could the word "prāṇa" heard in the passage, "For the mind, my dear, is fastened to prāṇa," while occurring in the context of the Supreme Brahman, be understood as referring merely to a modification of air?
Therefore, because it is an object of doubt, this is not a suitable example.
However, regarding the deity of the *prastāva*, the doubt, the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*), and the final conclusion (*nirṇaya*) have already been established.
[Note: The sage Cākrāyaṇa, seeking wealth, went to a king's sacrifice and said: "O Prastotṛ!"]
The deity who is inherent in and follows the *prastāva* division of the *sāman*,
as well as its dissolution and emergence— that is, its disappearance and appearance—
then, in that state:
Speech is indicative of the remaining organs of action;
sight and hearing are indicative of the corresponding organs of perception; and the intellect, too, is indicated by the mind.

The sense organs are the "essence" among the elements because of their subtlety and their proximity to the enjoyer; therefore, by the statement regarding their dissolution and emergence, the same is established for the others as well—this is the meaning of the phrase "the completion of the remainder.
The meaning is that proximity [of the subject] to the sentence is difficult to obtain.
The analysis of the compound is: *prāṇa* (the Supreme Self) is the *bandhana* (bond), that is, the support or essential nature (*svarūpa*), of which [it is said].
He extends the logic stated in the passage concerning space to the subsequent passage: "For this very reason, [the word] 'prāṇa'.
The term "udgītha" in the commentary is intended to indicate that this occurs within the context of the Udgītha; the grammatical connection is that it is heard in the section on the Udgītha.
A certain seer named Cākrāyaṇa said to the Prastotṛ priest: "O Prastotṛ, which deity is followed by the Prastāva— the division of the Sāman— for the purpose of meditation?"
"If you recite it before me, who am learned, without knowing its meaning, your head shall fall off.
Terrified by this, he asked, "Which deity is that?"
The answer is: "In the vital breath (prāṇa).
This means that they enter and dissolve completely with reference to the vital breath; having that as their point of reference, they emerge—that is, they are born.
He explains what was stated—that because this is an extended application (*atideśa*), the doubt and so forth are to be understood as being the same as before—by saying "prāṇa" and so on.

The individual soul (*jīva*), which has the mind (*manas*) as its limiting adjunct (*upādhi*), is bound by the vital breath (*prāṇa*), which is Brahman; during deep sleep (*suṣupti*), it becomes one with it.
The meaning is that those who know the Self—which impels the vital breath, the wind, and which bestows existence and manifestation upon it—are the knowers of Brahman (*brahmavid*).
He raises the objection that since the meaning has already been established by the preceding [sūtra], this separate sūtra is redundant: "But [it is] as before.
Considering that this sūtra of extended application (atideśa-sūtra) is intended to dispel a further doubt, he states the objection: "No;
even in the case of the primary [meaning]."
In that case, the connection is to be understood everywhere in this manner: "the eye also goes there," and so forth.

Now, one might ask: "Since the dissolution and emergence of the sense organs into the vital breath (prāṇa) are heard of here, how is the consistency of the subsequent portion of the text—which teaches the dissolution of the great elements and so on—established? To this, he says: "Because [the elements] have the sense organs as their essence."
For this is the essence of that, according to the Śruti.

The meaning is that since the sense organs—which consist of the subtle body (liṅga-ātman) and are the essences of the unevolved elements (apañcīkṛta-bhūtas)—are stated to dissolve [into the prāṇa], it is established by that logic that the dissolution of the elements also occurs in the prāṇa; thus, the consistency of the remainder of the passage is maintained.
Furthermore, he states "also" because the prāṇa is not Brahman, as it is mentioned alongside non-Brahman entities.
When Cākrāyaṇa was asked by the Udgātṛ and Pratihartṛ priests, "What is the deity in the Udgītha and what is the deity in the Pratihāra?", he pointed to the sun and food respectively;
the meaning is that the Śruti states, "He said, 'The sun,'" and "He said, 'Food. This constitutes a general proximity.

The result of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that, since the primary vital breath (*mukhya-prāṇa*) is determined by the force of the first-mentioned *prāṇa*—which is supported by its proximity—the meditation on the *prastāva* is performed through the perspective of that [primary breath]. In the final conclusion (*siddhānta*), however, the meditation takes the form of viewing it as Brahman.
The distinction is that this section is an extension (*atideśa*) of the previous one, and thus its connection with the preceding is precisely that of an extension.

Having stated that, according to the etymology "they have become" (*bhūtāni*), it is not logical for the dissolution and emergence of any mere effect characterized by the property of becoming to occur within *prāṇa*, which is a modification of air, [the author] says "even when... (*yadāpi*) to show that even if the word *bhūta* is taken in its conventional sense, the dissolution and so forth still lead to the determination of Brahman; the meaning is that the elemental *prāṇa* cannot be the source of the elements (*bhūtayoni*).
The text raises a doubt regarding its being the source [of speech] by means of the word "nanu" (but surely).

The meaning is: when the individual soul (*jīva*) is in deep sleep and becomes one with the vital breath (*prāṇa*), which is Brahman, then speech and the other senses, along with their objects, merge into that vital breath.

To this, he replies, "In that case also," stating that because there is the indicative mark (*liṅga*) of being the substratum for the dissolution of all things—which is not distinct from the living soul—the vital breath is not the primary [Brahman].
He says, "That is incorrect," because an indicative mark (*liṅga*) contained within its own sentence is stronger than the proximity of another sentence.
The meaning is: "sentence-remainder" (*vākyaśeṣa*) refers to syntactic unity (*ekavākyatva*); "by that" means by the indicative mark contained therein.

He states that by the restrictive particle "only" (*eva*) in the phrase "prāṇam eva," and by the indicative mark of being the source of all beings, the word *prāṇa* indicates (*lakṣya*) Brahman as its cause—just as is the case with the word "ether" (*ākāśa*).
He states that the examples provided by the authors of the commentaries (*vṛttikṛt*) are untenable due to the absence of doubt, beginning with the words "In this case" (*atra*).
Having stated the difference in terminology, he elaborates on the context with the words "And for whom" (*yasya ca*). //23//

**The Section Concerning Light as the Foot (Jyotiścaraṇādhikaraṇam)** Sūtras 24–27 **Sūtra 24:** "On account of the word 'light' (jyotis) [the Brahman is meant], because it is seen [in the context]. **Sūtra 25:** "And on account of the mention of the feet. **Sūtra 26:** "And on account of the subsequent statement. **Sūtra 27:** "And on account of the Smṛti. **Commentary:** In the Vājasaneyaka, the following passage is found: "That which is the person consisting of light (jyotiṣmat), whose form is luminous, who is beyond darkness—he indeed is that, this is the immortal, this is Brahman, this is all" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.16). Regarding this, a doubt arises as to whether the "person consisting of light" is the individual soul (jīva) or the Supreme Self (paramātman). The opponent maintains that it is the individual soul, because the qualities of being "consisting of light" and "luminous" are more appropriate to the individual soul, who is associated with the subtle body (liṅgaśarīra), than to the Supreme Self. Furthermore, the term "immortal" is used in contrast to the preceding "mortal," which suggests a relative distinction rather than the absolute nature of Brahman. To this, the Sūtrakāra replies: It is the Supreme Self, because the word "light" (jyotis) is used here. In the context of the preceding section, the Supreme Self is described as having four quarters (pāda): "This is the four-quartered Brahman: Speech is one quarter, breath is one quarter, the eye is one quarter, the ear is one quarter" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 3.18.2). Since the word "light" is synonymous with the "eye"—as in the common expression "the sun is the light of the eyes"—it refers back to that same Supreme Self. Moreover, the mention of "feet" (caraṇa) in the phrase "He has four feet" (catuṣpāt) confirms this, as it refers to the previously mentioned quarters. The subsequent statement, "He is all this" (sa eṣa sarvam idam), further establishes that the subject is the all-pervading Supreme Self. Finally, the Smṛti texts also declare that the Supreme Lord is the light of all lights: "The light beyond darkness, the radiant, the supreme" (Gītā 13.17). Therefore, the "person consisting of light" is the Supreme Self.
Because of the mention of "light" as its feet.

They recite this: "Now, that light which shines beyond this, on the backs of all, on the backs of everything, in the worlds that are unsurpassed and supreme—this indeed is that light which is within this person" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 3.13.7).

In this regard, there arises a doubt: does the word "light" (jyotis) here denote the sun and other such physical lights, or does it denote the Supreme Self? Although it was previously stated that even a word whose primary referent is something else may have Brahman as its object on account of its characteristic marks (liṅga), here it is investigated whether those characteristic marks are indeed present or not.
What, then, is the prima facie position?
That the word "light" (jyotis) refers only to the sun and so forth.
Why? Because of its well-known usage.
For these two words, "darkness" (tamas) and "light" (jyotis), are well known as designating mutually opposed objects.
Darkness is said to be that which obstructs the functioning of the eye, such as the gloom of night;
light is that which assists that very same function, such as the sun.
Likewise, this scriptural passage "it shines" is well known to refer to the sun and other luminous bodies;
for it is not possible that the primary sense of the word "shines" applies to Brahman, which is devoid of form and other such qualities.
Furthermore, this is supported by the scriptural mention of its having heaven as its boundary.
For it is not fitting that the sky should be the boundary of Brahman, who is the seed of all things moving and non-moving and the Self of all;
however, the sky could be the boundary of light as an effect, which is limited.
Moreover, there is a Brāhmaṇa text stating, "The light beyond the sky."
But surely, since even the light that is an effect is perceived everywhere, it is inconsistent for it to have heaven as its boundary.
Let it then be the unevolved (atrivṛtkṛta) light produced first. No; because there is no purpose for unevolved light.

If it is argued that this very fact [of being a means] constitutes the purpose for being an object of meditation (*upāsya*), we say no; for we observe that even the sun and other such objects are taken as objects of meditation precisely because they are prompted by some other purpose.
As it is said: "Of these, I shall make each one threefold" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.3.3).
And because of this scriptural statement without qualification;
moreover, it is not well-known that even non-tripartite fire has heaven as its boundary.
Let it be, then, that only tripartite fire is denoted by the word "light."
But has it not been stated that light such as fire and so forth is perceived even below the sky?
This is not a fault;
for although light is perceived everywhere, its restriction to a specific location "beyond the sky" is not contradictory, as it is intended for the purpose of meditation.
However, the assumption of specific spatial divisions for Brahman, which is itself without parts, is untenable;

furthermore, the scriptural mention of a multiplicity of supports in the passage, "In worlds that are on all sides, beyond, unsurpassed, and supreme" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 3.13.7), is much more appropriate if the light is an effect. This is confirmed by the text: "This indeed is that light which is within a person here" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 3.13.7).
And thus, the light within the belly is seen as being superimposed upon the supreme light;
for superimpositions occur on the basis of similarity, as in the passage: "Of that [syllable Om], *bhūḥ* is the head—this is its single syllable" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 5.5.3).
However, it is well known that the light within the stomach is not Brahman,
because of the scriptural statements, "This is its sight" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 3.13.7) and "This is its hearing," which describe it as being characterized by heat and sound.
Furthermore, because of the Vedic text, "One should meditate upon this as both seen and heard," and because of the mention of a minor fruit in the passage,
"He who knows this becomes beautiful to look at and famous" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 3.13.8),
it is not Brahman.
For the meditation on Brahman is intended for a great fruit;
moreover, there is no other mark of Brahman in its own sentence than that of light, as in the cases of the vital breath (prāṇa) and space (ākāśa).
Nor is Brahman indicated even in the preceding sentence.
Because of the mention of a meter in the passage, "The Gāyatrī indeed is all this that has come to be"; furthermore,
even if Brahman were somehow indicated in the preceding sentence, there is nevertheless no recognition of it here, for in that context it says,
"Three quarters of Him are the immortal in heaven" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 3.12.1, 6).
Thus, the sky is heard of as the locus [of the light].
But here, in the phrase "the light beyond the sky," the sky is mentioned as a boundary.
Therefore, when it is argued that the natural (elemental) light should be understood here, we reply: the light here must be understood as Brahman.
Why? Because of the mention of "feet" (caraṇa); that is to say, because of the mention of "quarters" (pāda).
For in the preceding passage, Brahman was indicated as having four quarters: "Such is His greatness; yet the Puruṣa is greater than that."
By means of this mantra, "One foot of his is all beings; his three-footed immortal self is in heaven" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 3.12.6),

that very same form of Brahman which was previously indicated as having four feet— of which the three-footed immortal portion is connected with heaven— is here recognized as being indicated again by virtue of its connection with heaven.
If one were to abandon that [Brahman] and imagine an ordinary light, there would result the fallacy of discarding what is under discussion and introducing what is not.
Not only does the continuity of Brahman follow from the preceding sentence into the passage concerning the light,
but Brahman will also continue in the subsequent Śāṇḍilya-vidyā.
Therefore, in this context, Brahman is to be understood as "light.
As for what was said— that the two words "light" (*jyotis*) and "shines forth" (*ādīpyate*) are well-known to refer to the effected light—
this is not a fault.
Because, given the context of the realization of Brahman, there is no distinction between these two words;
for it is possible to employ them even with respect to Brahman as characterized by the luminous effect [of light], as in:
"By that splendor kindled, the sun shines" (Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa 3.12.9.7).
And this is because of the wording of the mantra.
Alternatively, this word "light" (jyotis) does not refer exclusively to the luminous energy that assists the function of the eye,
since its usage is observed elsewhere as well.
"By speech alone as his light he sits" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.3.5),
and "May the mind, as light, enjoy [the oblation]" (Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa 1.6.3.3).
Therefore, whatever illuminates anything is designated by the word "light."
This being so, the term "light" (*jyotis*) is appropriately applied even to Brahman, who is of the nature of consciousness and is the cause of the manifestation of the entire universe.
As it is said: "Everything shines after Him as He shines; by His light all this is illumined" (Kauṣītaki Upaniṣad 2.5.15);
and, "The gods worship Him as the life and the immortal light of lights" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.16).
This is also established by such scriptural passages as these.

As for what was said—that the limitation by heaven is not possible for the all-pervading Brahman—it is replied: even though Brahman is all-pervading, its appropriation of a specific location for the purpose of meditation is not contradictory.
But was it not said that for Brahman, which is without parts, the postulation of specific parts is untenable?
This is not a fault;
for even though Brahman is without parts, the postulation of specific parts is tenable due to its connection with specific limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*).
For instance: the sun is in the eye and in the heart.
Thus, meditations on Brahman connected with specific locations are heard in scripture.
By this, the multiplicity of substrates in the phrase "on all sides behind" has been established. Furthermore, as for that which was said:
[The opponent argues: "Since the light within the belly—inferred from heat and sound—is superimposed [upon the sun], the light beyond the sky must also be an effect [of Brahman].
This too is incorrect;
for even the Supreme Brahman can appropriately serve as a symbol (pratīka) for the light within the belly, just as it serves as a symbol for names and so forth.
As for the statement, "One should meditate [on it] as seen and heard," the status of being "seen" and "heard" will occur by way of the *pratīka* (symbolic representation).
Furthermore, the argument that it is not Brahman because of the mention of small fruits is also untenable.
There is no restrictive reason why Brahman must be resorted to for some results and not for others;
for where the Supreme Brahman, from which all connections with particular attributes have been eliminated, is taught as one's own Self, [there is no such distinction].
In that case, liberation is understood as the fruit that is of a single nature.

However, where Brahman is taught in connection with specific qualities or specific meditative forms (*pratīka*), there fruits belonging to the sphere of transmigratory existence—both high and low—are observed, such as: "He who knows this becomes an eater of food, a giver of wealth, and finds wealth" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.24).

In such scriptural passages as these, although there is no mark (liṅga) of Brahman pertaining to the "light" within its own sentence, nevertheless, that which is seen in the preceding sentence must be accepted.

This was stated by the author of the Sūtras: "The light [is Brahman], because of the mention of the feet. But how can the mention of the word "light" be diverted from its own subject matter by the proximity of Brahman found in another sentence?

This is not a fault; for when the pronoun *yat* (which), being read earlier in the phrase "that which is the light beyond this," refers by its own inherent power to the Brahman previously specified in the preceding sentence— being recognized as such through its connection with the celestial realm (*dyu*)— it follows that the word *jyotis* (light) must also have Brahman as its object.

Therefore, in this context, "light" (jyotis) is to be understood as Brahman. [FN: The word "atha" serves to introduce another form of meditation following the meditation on Brahman through the limiting adjunct of the Gāyatrī.
Thus, that light which shines beyond and further than the heavenly world is superimposed upon the gastric light, with the thought, "This is that."]
The meaning is "above" (pṛṣṭheṣu), that is, above all classes of living beings and all worlds beginning with the earth.
The phrase "for there is none" means that only that which possesses form and parts can be associated with radiance.
That which is not mixed with fire, water, and food is here called "made by Atri."
The other purpose is the destruction of darkness and so forth.

Having divided each of those—tejas, water, and food—into two parts, and having further divided each of those parts into two, and having deposited [each half] into the other parts, the process of tripartition (*trivṛtkaraṇa*) is accomplished. It is logical that they are the possessors of these portions.

Just as the visualization of Prajāpati’s head was taught in the syllable *bhūḥ* on account of their identity in being "one," so too must a similarity be stated here; otherwise, superimposition (*adhyāsa*) would not be established.
This is the "sight" when one perceives this heat by touch;
this is the "hearing" when, having closed one's ears, one hears as it were a roar—this is the remainder of the sense.
Pleasant to the eye and beautiful to behold;
renowned and famous;
ordinary, born of nature.
This means "that which is to be accomplished.
The state of being a differentiator is the quality of imparting fire (*tejas*) by distinguishing it from Brahman; the absence of that is non-differentiation.
The meaning is: because of non-differentiation, that is, because of not excluding [the object] from Brahman.
Its limitation is due to its being for the purpose of cognition or for the purpose of meditation;
the grammatical connection is "even beyond the sky.

For the light within the body (*kaukṣeyaka-jyotis*) is a modification of the Supreme Self who has entered into the state of the individual soul (*jīva*); it arises because the body becomes flaccid in the absence of the soul, and because there is heat in one who is living.
Therefore, meditation on the symbol is justified.
He is "the eater of food" (annāda) because he eats food in the form of the individual soul (jīva),
or because he is the giver of food everywhere.
"Vasudāna" (the giver of wealth) is a connection with a specific quality, based on the fact that he gives "vasu," which is gold, the fruit of ritual action.

The construction is as follows: by the inherent power of the pronoun (*sarvanāman*), there is the inherent capacity of that pronoun to denote what is proximate; when [the object] is referred to by the force of that [capacity], it is so joined.
[This is established] because light is mentioned as having feet.
He cites the Chāndogya Upaniṣad itself with the words "this" (*idam*).

The word "now" (*atha*) is for the purpose of indicating the sequence following the meditation on Brahman through the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) of Gāyatrī. That light which shines beyond, that is, above the sky (*divaḥ*), the heavenly world—that very light is superimposed (*adhyasyate*) upon this [light], namely, the digestive fire within the stomach (*jāṭharāgni*).
Where does it shine?

To this he says: "viśvataḥ" (from all sides). Above the entire class of living beings, and above all the worlds beginning with Bhūr, in those highest worlds—those than which there are no higher (anuttameṣu)—it shines as the Supreme, transcending the entire sphere of saṃsāra.
The meaning is "that which resides in the body.
Stating that this does not have a meaning already conveyed by the preceding [sūtra], he provides a counter-example, saying "in another sense" (*arthāntare*).

Here, although there is an absence of clear marks of Brahman (*brahmaliṅga*) in its own sentence, there is the mark of being a "foot of beings" (*bhūtapādatva*) in the preceding sentence, "A foot of him," and thus there is a connection with the section on "feet" (*pāda*).

The distinction is that the fruit [of practice] consists in the worship of either the insentient Brahman-light or the sentient light, depending on the prima facie (pūrvapakṣa) or the final (uttarapakṣa) position.
Now, one might object: since it is opposed to the darkness of ignorance, Brahman is also well-known as being denotable by the word "light" (jyotis); to this he replies, "the eye," etc. (cakṣur iti).
That which exists in the night (*śarvarī*) is "nocturnal" (*śārvaram*);
that is to say, blue.
By this, it is implied by the sense that darkness is a positive entity (*bhāvarūpa*), because, like a wall, it possesses the quality of obscuring and the quality of having color (*rūpavat*).
He states the supporting indicative marks (liṅgas) for the scriptural mention of "light" with the words beginning "tathā" (so).
He says "na hi" (for not), explaining that radiance consisting of a luminous form is indeed an indicative mark of fire alone.
Anticipating the objection that there may be no such boundary, he says "paro divaḥ" (beyond the heaven), asserting that it cannot be so because it is explicitly stated in scripture.
The ellipsis is "state the boundary" (*maryādām brūta*).
Someone objects that the Brāhmaṇa is useless because, like Brahman, even the effect possesses a boundary (*maryādā*); this objection begins with "nanu.
The proponent of a partial view (*ekadeśin*) replies: "Let it be so" (*astu*).
The meaning is that there exists some supersensuous light born in heaven and so forth beyond the sky, on account of the authority of the Śruti.
Having raised the objection that a fruitless thing cannot be the subject matter of the Śruti which is acquired through the injunction to study, he says: "No."

Anticipating the objection that meditation might be the fruit [of knowledge], he states "this very [is the fruit]" and so forth, asserting that there is no meditation whatsoever for that which is fruitless.
"Another purpose" refers to the destruction of darkness and the like.
Having stated the lack of fruit by accepting the existence of non-tripartite light (*tejas*), he says "of those" and so forth, asserting that such light itself does not exist.

The meaning is that there is nothing that has not been made tripartite (trivṛtkṛta), because it is stated without qualification: "Having divided each of the deities—fire, water, and food—into two parts, and having again divided each of those portions into two, and having placed [each part] into the other portions, I shall make them threefold, like a cord of triple-strands.
Furthermore, in this context, the phrase "that which is beyond this" uses the word "yat" to refer back to the well-known limit of heaven for the purpose of meditation.
And since that [light] which has not been made tripartite is not established anywhere as such, he says: "And not...
Having refuted the view of the partial school (ekadeśimatam), the proponent of the prima facie position (pūrvapakṣī) speaks directly: "Let it be so, then...
A particular region is a specific portion of the light of the sun and other luminaries, shining intensely beyond the sky.
The syntactical connection is that its acceptance for the purpose of worship is not contradictory; the intention is that this very [fire] is worshipped as the light within the belly,
because it too is of the nature of fire (*tejas*).
One might suppose that even for Brahman, there is a localized position for the sake of meditation;
to this he says "not so" (*na tu*).

The construction is as follows: it is not proper to imagine a portion of Brahman—which is without location (*niṣpradeśa*) and without parts (*niravayava*)—shining brilliantly beyond the sky, even though such a distinction [of meditation] exists.
The meaning is that it would result in the fallacy of attributing weight to what lacks authoritative basis.
To the question "What follows from this?", he says: "By similarity" (*sārūpya*).

Just as in the case of the utterance "Bhūḥ," the perception of Prajāpati’s head is heard due to the similarity of oneness, so too, non-Brahmanhood is well-established in the digestive fire (*jāṭharāgni*) by the scriptural mention of sound and other qualities; thus, there is a similarity in its being an insentient light (*jaḍajyotiṣṭva*).
The meaning is that it must be stated:

that well-known cognition of heat through the touch of the body is the perception of this internal digestive fire (jāṭharāgni), and that hearing a sound by closing the ears is likewise its perception.
The meaning is that this very [passage] is his scriptural authority (*śruti*).
He states another indicative mark (*liṅga*) for the insentience (*jaḍatva*) of light: "This, indeed, is..."—the meaning is "light."
He is pleasing to the eye, beneficial to the eyes, and beautiful;
he is renowned and famous;
nor is there anything else [to be desired].
The syntactical connection (*anvaya*) is that there is no other mark of Brahman (*brahmaliṅga*) whatsoever.

Now, one might object: "Let the Brahman mentioned in the preceding sentence—'Three quarters of Him are the immortal in heaven'—be understood here by the word 'light' (*jyotis*. Anticipating this doubt, he says: "And not so" (*na ca*). Furthermore, one might argue: "Brahman has been indicated by the two attributes of being the self of all and immortality. To this, he says: "Even so" (*athāpi*).
The meaning is "in some way through the door of the *śabda*.
The meaning is that there is no recognition [of identity] because of the difference in case endings in the forms *divi* and *divaḥ*.
That which is born from *prakṛti* is *prākṛta*.
The meaning is "it must be done. He rejects [the idea of] mere conduct with the words "by the feet," etc.:
"Gāyatrī indeed is all this that has come to be," "Speech indeed is Gāyatrī," "That which is this earth," and "That which is this body."

"In this person, there is the heart," "these vital breaths"—thus, consisting of the elements, speech, earth, body, heart, and vital breaths, the *gāyatrī* is sixfold and has four feet with six syllables.

As it has been said: "All this manifold universe (*prapañca*) is of that same measure; it is the majesty (*mahiman*), the manifestation (*vibhūti*), of this Brahman which is conjoined with the *gāyatrī*."
The Puruṣa, however, is of the nature of the full Brahman;
therefore, he is greater than and superior to the phenomenal world (prapañca).
He states this very superiority with the word "pāda" (foot/quarter).
The entire world is one foot, or part, [of Him], according to the Smṛti: "Pervading all this, I stand with one part, supporting the world.
Of this Puruṣa, there exists an immortal form consisting of three parts in the "Heaven"—that is, in His own self-luminous nature.
Or, it exists in the solar orb in heaven for the purpose of meditation;
the meaning is that there is an infinite Brahman-nature beyond the conceptualized world.
Just as in the world three quarters are greater than one quarter, so too this [Brahman] is greater; it is called "the immortal three-quarters" for the sake of making this understood.
It should not be thought that the state of having three feet is what is intended to be expressed.

Since the word "yat" (which) in the phrase "yad ataḥ paraḥ" (that which is beyond this) denotes a well-known entity, it refers to Brahman as established in the preceding passage; thus he says, "therein.

An objection is raised: "In the case of 'yad āgneyo 'ṣṭākapālaḥ' (that which belongs to Agni is on eight potsherds), the word 'yat' is seen to have a meaning not connected to the subject under discussion"; to this he replies, "abandoning that [objection]."

In that case, because the sacrifice was not established by any other means and was thus unprecedented (*apūrva*), there was no alternative but to resort to the fact that the word *yat* has an unknown referent.

Here, however, since Brahman—already established in the preceding passage—is recognized through its connection with the "heavenly world" (*dyu*), it is determined that *yat* refers to that very same entity; therefore, the word *jyotis*, which shares the same referent as *yat*, must have that same meaning as well.
He states "not only... to show that this is so even by the logic of the "pinch" (*saṃdaṃśanyāya*).
The meaning is that because Brahman is carried forward from the subsequent passage, "All this, indeed, is Brahman," the intermediate statement concerning light refers to Brahman.
This is established by the context (*prakaraṇāt*),
which means by the word "that" (*yat*) which refers back to the subject at hand, and by the indicative marks (*liṅga*) such as its connection with heaven and its being the foot of the earth.

Therefore, the objection that it is not proper to set aside the scriptural mention of "light" on account of the context has been refuted by the statement "because it is non-discriminatory"; the meaning is that it lacks the capacity to exclude Brahman.

The meaning is that one who does not know the Veda does not perceive that Great One by which mind—that is, by which consciousness—the sun is kindled and illumined, such that it shines and illuminates.

Having accepted that the word *jyotis* (light) has its primary denotation (*śakti*) only in the effect-light [the sun] and has stated that it indicates the causal Brahman, he now declares that it also has a direct denotation in Brahman itself: "Or else...
The meaning is that in deep darkness, people perform activities such as sitting and so forth by means of the light of speech alone.
"May the clarified butter (ājya) enjoy and drink [it]; the mind becomes the illuminating light"—this is the praise of the clarified butter.
Just as one who follows another who is walking also possesses movement, so too might there be a manifestation residing in everything; therefore, he says, "By its light.
The meaning is that the gods worship that Brahman—which is not limited by time—as the witness of the lights such as the sun, and as life and immortality.

He states with the words "To this it is replied," etc., that it is appropriate for Brahman to have qualities such as being bounded by heaven and so forth, imagined for the purpose of meditation, just as the quality of being fire is attributed to a woman.
The syntactical connection is "even beyond heaven.
He says "even of another" to show that there is no rule requiring similarity between the superimposed object (the meditative focus) and the substratum (the actual object of meditation).
The remainder [of the sentence] is "it will become the light of Brahman.
He says "it does not diminish" because of the Vedic scripture: "In whatever manner one meditates upon it, such is the fruit that accrues.
One might ask: why should the fruit of meditation not be uniform, like the fruit of knowledge? To this he replies: "For where... [and so forth].
The meaning is that the object of knowledge (*jñeya*) is one; however, he states that the object of meditation (*dhyeya*) is manifold with the words "But where...

The Lord is the "eater of food" (*annāda*) because he eats food in the form of individual souls (*jīva*), or he is the "giver of food" (*annada*) because he bestows it all around; or he is the "giver of wealth" (*vasudāna*) because he gives wealth (*vasu*) and gold. He who knows this connection with these specific qualities finds wealth.
And he becomes one whose digestive fire is kindled.

The first phrase is intended to include the scriptural injunctions regarding meditation on specific symbols (*pratīka*), such as "Speech is the highest [symbol] of Name" or "Mind is greater than Speech."
He raises an objection, thinking that direct scriptural statement (*śruti*) is stronger than proximity (*saṃnidhi*), by asking: "But how [is this so]?
Then he says: "This is not so," meaning that the subsequent scriptural statement is governed according to the first scriptural statement.

The construction is as follows: when [the pronoun] refers [to something] by the power of its own capacity—namely, the pronoun's capacity to denote what is proximate (*saṃnihita-vācitva*)—then [the subsequent statement is governed].
The meaning is: because of the grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya) with that word [denoting] the object and so forth. //24//

If it be argued that [the passage] does not refer to Brahman because it mentions a meter, we say no; for there is an injunction to fix the mind in that way, and there is a scriptural indication to that effect. (BS 1.1.25)

Now, as for what was said previously— that Brahman was not denoted even in that preceding passage because the meter named Gāyatrī was denoted in the statement, "The Gāyatrī indeed is all this being, whatever exists here" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 3.12.1)— that [argument is refuted].
That must be refuted.
But how can it be said that Brahman is not denoted because of the mention of the *chandas* (metres),
when in this very Ṛgvedic verse, "Such is its greatness," Brahman is shown to have four quarters?
This is not so;

for, having introduced the Gāyatrī with the words "The Gāyatrī indeed is all this," and having explained that very Gāyatrī through the distinctions of the elements, the earth, the body, the heart, speech, and the means of knowledge, [the text] concludes regarding that same [Gāyatrī]:
"This is that four-footed, sixfold Gāyatrī; this has been declared by a Ṛg-verse: 'Such is its greatness... (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 3.12.1). Thus, it refers to that very [Gāyatrī].

How could the mantra cited in the Gāyatrī, whose nature has already been explained, suddenly denote Brahman as having four feet? Even the word "Brahman" found there in the passage, "That which is indeed that Brahman" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 3.12.5, 6), refers exclusively to the meter because the meter is the subject under discussion, as seen in the statement, "He who knows this secret doctrine (upaniṣad) of Brahman thus" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 3.11.3).
If it is argued that because they explain the phrase "the Veda and the Upanishad" here as referring to the meters, Brahman is not the subject under discussion due to the mention of the meters—
this is not a valid objection.

"Likewise, because of the restriction of the application of the mind": likewise, by means of the meter named Gāyatrī, the application of the mind—that is, the concentration of the thought—upon the Brahman that follows it is declared by this Vedic statement:
"The Gāyatrī, indeed, is all this.
For it is not possible for the mere arrangement of syllables that constitutes the Gāyatrī to possess the nature of being the Self of all.
Therefore, that Brahman which is the cause of the world and is inherent in the modification called Gāyatrī is here referred to as "all.

This is just as in the passage, "All this, indeed, is Brahman" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 3.14.1). Furthermore, we shall explain in the section beginning with "The non-difference from That [is established] on account of such words as 'originating' etc. (Brahma Sūtra 2.1.14) that the effect is not distinct from its cause.

Likewise, elsewhere too, the meditation upon Brahman through its modifications is observed: "For it is this very [Brahman] that the Bahvṛcas investigate in the Great Hymn (mahad-uktha), the Adhvaryus in the fire, and the Chandogas in the Mahāvrata" (Ai.
Therefore, even though the meters are mentioned, Brahman with four feet is indeed indicated in the preceding passage.
That very same [Brahman] is referred to in the Jyotis passage as well, for the purpose of enjoining another form of meditation.
Another teacher says: Brahman is directly denoted by the word "Gāyatrī" itself, on account of the commonality of number.
Just as the *gāyatrī* has four feet consisting of six syllables each, so too Brahman is four-footed.
Furthermore, elsewhere we see words denoting a meter being applied to a different object due to a commonality of number;
for example, beginning with "These five and those other five, being ten, constitute the *kṛta*," the text says, "This is that *virāj*, the eater of food" (*Chāndogya Upaniṣad* 4.3.8).
In this view, since it is Brahman itself that has been denoted, there is no mention of the *chandas* (Vedic meters).
In any case, Brahman remains the subject under discussion in the preceding passage. [FN:
The meaning is that for one who knows this present "Brahmopaniṣad"—the secret of the Veda consisting of the Madhu-vidyā—there occurs the attainment of Brahman, which is free from rising and setting.]
The followers of the Ṛgveda worship him during the recitation of the Great Hymn (mahad-uktha);
the Adhvaryus, followers of the Yajurveda, during the sacrifice; and the Chandogas, followers of the Sāmaveda, during the Mahāvrata sacrifice.
In the Saṃvarga-vidyā, with respect to the divine realm, fire, sun, moon, and water are absorbed into air.
Internally, speech, sight, hearing, mind, and breath merge into one another.
These five others are related to the divine (ādhidevika), and the other five are related to the self (ādhyātmika); these ten, when combined, are called "the completed" (kṛta).
The game of dice has been played.
An adherent of a particular school (ekadeśin) refutes the doubt that Brahman is not the subject under discussion because it was designated by the term "metre" (chandas), asking: "How so?
He establishes this doubt with the words beginning "Not this," and so forth.
The fact that it consists of four quarters and so forth has already been explained.

As for the phrase "whoever [knows] this thus": the meaning is that whoever knows this Madhu-vidyā—which is the secret essence of the Vedas—in the manner just described, attains Brahman, which is devoid of rising and setting.
Thus, the sense is that the word "Brahman" is appropriate for the Gāyatrī because it is Vedic.

Regarding the objection that there is no basis for using the word "Gāyatrī" to indirectly indicate (lakṣaṇā) Brahman—which is the common substrate by virtue of being its material cause—he states: "For not in the syllables... [and so on].
Furthermore, how can even Brahman possess the nature of being the self of all?
Regarding this, he says: "And [it would be] an effect.

The sense is that one should not say that the attribution of being the self of all is for the purpose of meditation on the Gāyatrī; for since it is possible to meditate on the self of all as such by its very nature, the attribution of what is unreal is untenable.
He explains the remainder of the sūtra, "for thus is the observation," with the words "so elsewhere.
"Observation" (darśana) means that which is seen; the meaning is "that which has been perceived."
The Bahvṛcas, the followers of the Ṛgveda, meditate upon this very Supreme Self in the Great Hymn (mahaduktha) during the recitation of the Śastra;
likewise, according to the scriptural text, "The Adhvaryus, the followers of the Yajurveda, meditate upon Him as Agni" in the Agnirahasya, they meditate upon Him in the sacrificial fire;
and it is observed in the Aitareyaka that the Chanters, the followers of the Sāmaveda, meditate upon this very same One in the Mahāvrata sacrifice. This is the meaning.

Having explained that the word *gāyatrī* is indicative (*lakṣaka*) of Brahman, he says "the other" (*aparaḥ*) to indicate that it is figurative (*gauṇa*). "Directly" (*sākṣād eva*) means without even grasping the literal meaning (*vācyārtha*).
Previously, however, both Gāyatrī and Brahman were indicated by the word "Gāyatrī" through a non-exclusive indication (*ajahallakṣaṇā*) because it was to be meditated upon;

nor is there any impossibility of the syntactical connection "Gāyatrī is all," just as in the case of the connection of color with an individual, which is a part of the referent of the word "the pot is colored."

The sense is that, since the connection with "being the self of all" is possible when Brahman—which is the primary referent and is followed by the Gāyatrī—is taken as a part of the meaning of the word "Gāyatrī.

Thus, the meaning of the portion of the Sūtra representing the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) is as follows: "In the same way, because of the commonality of the quality of having four feet (*catuṣpāttva*), just like the Gāyatrī;

[the term] 'bestowal of the mind' (*cetorpaṇa*) refers to that word 'Gāyatrī' by which the mind is directed toward Brahman. Therefore, because it is declared [in scripture] as denoting Brahman itself, the claim that it denotes a meter (*chandas*) is unestablished."
Now he explains the remainder of the passage, "For thus is the vision," with the word "tathā" (thus):

In the Saṃvarga-vidyā, it has been stated that, on the cosmic level (*ādhidaiva*), fire, sun, moon, and water merge into air; and on the personal level (*adhyātma*), speech, sight, hearing, mind, and breath pass away into the vital breath (*prāṇa*).
These five others pertain to the divine (ādhidaivika), and the other five pertain to the self (ādhyātmika); when combined, being ten in number, they are called "Kṛta.
For there are four dice known by the names Kṛta, Tretā, Dvāpara, and Kali, which respectively have four, three, two, and one dot.
In that regard, the *kṛta* [yuga] consists of ten [units],
because three are included within four, two within three, and one within two; thus,
by virtue of this factor of ten, wind and the other elements are designated by the term *kṛta*.
Having introduced the state of being created (*kṛtatva*) regarding air and the other elements, he says: "This very [one]... The feminine gender is used in reference to the object to be enjoined.
The term *virāṭpada* denotes a meter (*chandas*).
According to the Vedic scripture, "The Virāj consists of ten syllables," the wind and the other elements are called Virāj by virtue of their commonality with the number ten.
Thus, through the medium of the number ten, one should meditate upon the state of being composed of the *kṛta* [syllable] and the state of being Virāj within the wind and the other elements.
In that regard, by meditating on [the Self as] Virāj, everything becomes his food, according to the Vedic scripture: "Virāj is food.
By meditating on [the Self as] Kṛta, he becomes an eater of food.

Because the *kṛta* [die] consumes the others by incorporating their values, such as three, within itself; for when it incorporates the values of its own four sides, it is observed as if it were eating the food [of the others].
For this very reason, the victory over the other dice following the victory of the *kṛta* is stated in the Śruti: "When the *kṛta* has been won, the lower ones gather around it."
"Ayo" refers to gambling; "kṛtāya" means one who has won by the throw known as *kṛta*. For such a person, the lower throws—the three-pointers (*tryaṅka*) and so forth—converge and submit to him;
the meaning is that they become defeated by him.

And thus, this Virāj, consisting of the tenfold elements such as air and so forth, is called "Kṛta"; the meaning is that she is the food (anna) because she is the "Kṛta," and she is the eater of food.
"In every way" means: [as follows].
The meaning is that even when the word "Gāyatrī" functions as an indicator (lakṣaka) or is used in a secondary sense (gauṇa).
Here, by the phrase "another says," the author indicates through the word "another" that this [interpretation] is not his own view regarding the secondary sense.

For, according to the theory of non-abandoning indication (ajahallakṣaṇā), it is more appropriate for Gāyatrī to be meditated upon as having speech as its essence—as in "Speech indeed is Gāyatrī"—and to possess the etymological name derived from the fact that she "sings" (gāyati) and "protects" (trāyate), since these qualities serve as her limiting adjuncts (upādhi) in meditation.

In the secondary sense, because the term "Gāyatrī" would have to be abandoned, both [the qualities of being four-footed and having six syllables] would have to be established merely by virtue of [Brahman's] being the Self of all;

thus, there is much that is inconsistent: the abandonment of the primary meaning of the word "Gāyatrī," and a remote indication (lakṣaṇā) based on the quality of having four feet, which is not well-known. //25//
And because the designation of the quarters beginning with "Being" (bhūta) is thus appropriate. 1.1.26.
For this reason as well, it must be accepted that Brahman is the subject under discussion in the preceding sentence;
for [the text] designates the elements and so forth as its feet.
For, having pointed out the elements, the earth, the body, and the heart, [the text] says: "This is that Gāyatrī, four-footed and sixfold.
Indeed, if Brahman were not the basis, it would not be logical for the elements and so forth to be the feet of mere meter (chandas).
Moreover, if Brahman were not the basis, this verse—"Such is its extent"—would not be understood as a reference to Brahman.

For by this verse, Brahman alone is denoted by its own inherent power, because its status as the self of all is established by the statement: "All beings are one quarter of Him; His three quarters are the immortal in heaven" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 3.12.6).
In the Puruṣasūkta as well, this verse is recited precisely with reference to Brahman.
And Smṛti also shows that Brahman has such a nature: "Pervading all this, I stand with a single portion, supporting the world" (Bhagavad Gītā 10.42).
Also: "That which is indeed Brahman" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 3.12.7).
And when it is explained in this way, the primary meaning becomes appropriate;

for the scriptural mention of "five persons of Brahman" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 3.13.6) in reference to the apertures of the heart is possible only if the intention is to express their connection with Brahman.
Therefore, it is established that Brahman is the subject under discussion in the preceding passage;
that very same Brahman is referred to in the *jyotis* (light) passage as being recognized through its connection with the celestial realm (*dyu*). [Note:
Six aspects of Brahman, known as Gāyatrī, are heard in scripture: the elements, the earth, the body, the heart, speech, and the vital breath.]

The term *suṣayaḥ* means "holes. Now, one might object: since the word "Gāyatrī" is heard first in the statement, "The Gāyatrī indeed is all this," how can there be a figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*)? Anticipating this doubt, he says "bhūtādipāda" (having the elements, etc., as its feet), explaining that because the intended meaning (*tātparya*) is understood to be Brahman through corroboration by numerous powerful means of knowledge—such as its being the Self of all found in the remainder of the passage—there is indeed figurative indication.
Thus he states the meaning of the word "also" (*itaśca*).
He shows the meaning of the word "etc. (*ādi*) found in the Sūtra with the words "the elements, earth, etc. (*bhūtapṛthivīti*).
In this regard, it is the consensus of both the author of the Sūtra and the author of the Bhāṣya that the Gāyatrī consists of four feet by means of the elements and so forth.
The fact that it consists of four quarters by means of six syllables, as stated by the author of the *Vṛtti*, is not well-known and is indicated by the word "ca" (and).

He states another reason with the words "api ca" (furthermore): because it is produced from a hymn (*sūkta*) dedicated to Brahman, it has that [Brahman] as its ultimate referent; this he expresses with the words "puruṣa" (Purusha).
He refutes the claim that the word *brahman* denotes a meter by stating, "That which is indeed Brahman.
This means that in the preceding verse, Brahman was spoken of.
There are five apertures in the heart: four in the four directions and one above.

Regarding those [five], for the purpose of meditation, the Śruti has conceived that the five—prāṇa, vyāna, apāna, samāna, and udāna—are the gatekeepers of the city of the heart, which is the abode of Brahman, stationed respectively at the eastern and other gates.

In this context, the scriptural statement regarding these vital breaths (prāṇas) located in the cavities of the heart as being "the persons of Brahman" (brahmapuruṣa) is possible because, in connection with the meditation on the Brāhmaṇa known as Gāyatrī within the heart, they serve as the gatekeepers of Brahman;
thus he says: "The five are Brahman... (26).
If it be argued that [the doctrine of Brahman] is not so because of the differences in instruction, we say no; for there is no contradiction in either case. (BS 1.1.27)
Furthermore, as for what was stated previously— that in the passage "Three quarters of it are the immortal in heaven," the sky is taught as a locus by means of the locative case (*saptamī*),
whereas in the subsequent passage "Now, that which is beyond the sky," it is taught as a limit by means of the ablative case (*pañcamī*)—
therefore, due to this difference in instruction, there is no recognition of that [same entity] here.
That must be refuted.
To this it is said: this is not a fault, because there is no contradiction in either case.
In either case—whether the instruction is given with a locative ending or an ablative ending—there is no contradiction with recognition.
Just as in common worldly usage, a hawk, though actually connected to the top of a tree, is seen to be described in both ways:
"the hawk is on the treetop" and "the hawk is beyond the treetop."
Thus, the eternal Brahman, though actually in heaven itself, is taught as being "beyond heaven.

Another says: Just as in the world, even though a hawk is not actually connected to the top of a tree, it is seen to be described in two ways—as "the hawk on the treetop" and "the hawk ahead of the treetop."
And thus, although Brahman, which exists beyond heaven, is taught as being "in heaven," there is therefore a recognition here of the Brahman previously specified.
Consequently, it is established that the Supreme Brahman alone is denoted by the word "light. // 27 //

It was stated that because of the difference in case endings in the phrase "divi divaḥ," there is no recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) of the subject under discussion; [the author] says that this should not be overlooked, stating, "that must be refuted. He anticipates the refutation with the word "here" (*atra*), and states the refutation while explaining the meaning of the negative particle (*nañ*) in the Sūtra: "this is not [the case]."
This explanation applies everywhere.

Since the recognition [of the object] occurs through its connection with the primary meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*), namely *dyu* (heaven), the difference in the case-meanings (*vibhaktyartha*) does not constitute an obstacle,
because it is possible for the locus (*ādhāra*) itself to function as a limit (*maryādā*) in some sense.

Just as the top of a tree, while being the support for a hawk perched upon its own part, serves as the boundary for that very same hawk relative to the part not touching it; so too, having conceived the heaven (div) in the sun or in the primary space within the heart as the support, and having conceived Brahman—delimited by the space not touching that heaven—as the limit, it is said to be "beyond the heaven. This is the meaning. However, if one takes Brahman as undelimited by space, then the status of being a limit for the heaven expressed by the ablative case is primary, and the status of being a support expressed by the locative case is figurative, characterized by proximity, as in the expression "the crocodile in the Ganges."
He says "the other" [to indicate] that this must be explained:
the primary sense of being a substratum (*pratyādhāratva*) with respect to what is connected was previously stated as "it exists only in heaven";
now, the primary sense of being a boundary (*maryādātva*) with respect to what is unconnected is stated as "even beyond heaven"—this is the distinction.
Therefore, it is established that the passage concerning light is consistent with Brahman as the object of meditation. //27//

Section on Pratardana (Pratardanādhikaraṇam) / Sūtras 28–31 START BsCom_1,1.11.28 END BsCom_1,1.10.27 The section concerning Pratardana begins with sūtra 28 and concludes with sūtra 31. This section examines whether the Self described to Pratardana as the one to be meditated upon is the individual soul (*jīva*) or the Supreme Self (*paramātman*). The discussion hinges on the interpretation of the passage in the *Kauṣītaki Upaniṣad* where Indra instructs Pratardana on the nature of the Self that is to be realized. The sūtras establish that the Self in question is indeed the Supreme Self, based on the characteristics mentioned therein, such as being the giver of life and the lord of all. Thus, the conclusion is that the object of meditation taught to Pratardana is the Highest Self.
