"Likewise, the vital breath [is Brahman] because of following after [the attributes of Brahman]. (BBs 1.1.28) In the Kauṣītaki Brāhmaṇa Upaniṣad, there is the narrative of Indra and Pratardana: "Pratardana, the son of Divodāsa, indeed approached the beloved abode of Indra through battle and manliness. In that [narrative], it is heard: "He said: 'I am the vital breath, the conscious self; meditate upon me as life and immortality.'"
Likewise, later on as well: "Now, indeed, it is *prāṇa* alone, the conscious self (*prajñātman*), which, having taken hold of this body, causes it to rise" (Kauṣītaki Upaniṣad 1.1, 2, 3).
Similarly: "One should not seek to know speech; one should know the speaker," and so forth.
And at the end: "This very *prāṇa* is the conscious self, blissful, undecaying, and immortal" (Kauṣītaki Upaniṣad 3.8), and so forth.
In this regard, there arises a doubt: what is denoted here by the word "prāṇa"—is it mere air, or the self of a deity, or the individual soul (jīva), or else the supreme Brahman?
But was it not already explained in the passage "Therefore, prāṇa" that the word "prāṇa" has Brahman as its ultimate referent?
Moreover, there is a mark of Brahman here as well, namely, "blissful, undecaying, immortal," and so forth.
How, then, can a doubt arise here?
We reply: because multiple marks are observed.
In this passage, not only the characteristic marks of Brahman are perceived; for there are indeed other marks as well, such as:
"Know me alone" (Kauṣītaki Upaniṣad 3.1).
Thus, "the word of Indra" is a characteristic mark of the deity;
"having taken hold of this body, he causes it to rise" is a characteristic mark of the vital breath (prāṇa);
and "one should not seek to know speech, but should know the speaker," and so forth, is a characteristic mark of the individual soul (jīva).

Therefore, a doubt arises. Since it is well known in common usage that "the breath is air" (*vāyu*), the prima facie view is established; however, it is stated [in response] that the term "breath" (*prāṇa*) should be understood as Brahman.
Why? Because it is so followed through the context.
For instance, when the sentence is examined from beginning to end, the coherence of its constituent word-meanings is found to be directed toward the exposition of Brahman.

To begin with, at the outset, Pratardana—having been told by Indra, "Choose a boon"—proposed the supreme human goal as his boon, saying: "You yourself choose for me that which you consider most beneficial for a human being."
How could the *prāṇa*, which is taught as the most beneficial for that [seeker], not be the Supreme Self?
For there is no attainment of the most beneficial state other than through the knowledge of the Supreme Self; as it is said:
"Only by knowing Him does one pass beyond death; there is no other path for the journey" (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 3.8).
This is because of such scriptural passages as these;

likewise, [the statement] "He who knows me— by no deed whatsoever is his world diminished, neither by theft nor by the killing of an embryo" (Kauṣītaki Upaniṣad 3.1), and so forth, is consistent only with the acceptance of Brahman.

For the destruction of all karma through the knowledge of Brahman is well-established in such scriptural passages as, "And his karmas are exhausted when He, the higher and the lower, is seen" (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 2.2.8).
Furthermore, the state of being the Self of intelligence is logically possible only in the case of Brahman.

For it is not possible for the insentient wind to possess the nature of the conscious Self (prajñātmatva). Likewise, in the concluding summary as well, qualities such as bliss—expressed in the words "blissful, undecaying, immortal"—cannot properly belong to anything other than Brahman. Furthermore: "He does not become greater by good action, nor indeed smaller by evil action; for he alone causes him to perform good action whom he wishes to lead up from these worlds."
"This one, moreover, causes him to perform evil deeds whom he wishes to lead downward from these worlds," and "This is the lord of the world, this is the ruler of the world" (Kauṣītaki Upaniṣad 3.8).
All of this can be consistently understood if the Supreme Brahman is relied upon as the referent, but not if the primary vital breath (prāṇa) is meant.
Therefore, *prāṇa* is Brahman. (28) [Note: This means that the sequence of words is seen to be connected solely for the purpose of establishing Brahman.
By the passage beginning with "He is not... (*sa na*), everything has been stated: his being untouched by merit (*dharma*) and so forth, his being the cause of all action, and his lordship over all.
"Prāṇa [is Brahman] because it is followed [by all things].
Divodāsa’s descendant was a king named Pratardana, the son of Divodāsa; by means of battle and personal prowess, he became Indra's beloved guest in his home.
To him, Indra said:
"I shall grant you a boon," [the Lord said].
Pratardana replied,
"Grant me that very boon which you consider most beneficial for a mortal, after you have reflected upon it yourself."
Then Indra said this: "I am Prāṇa," and so forth.
The statement that he is the "Self of Intelligence" (prajñātman) was made in order to exclude the primary vital breath (mukhya prāṇa).
He excludes the mere consciousness devoid of attributes (nirviśeṣacinmātra) by saying, "That Me."
This is the indicative mark (*liṅga*) for [the fact that] the vital breath (*prāṇa*) has the sense-faculties as its presiding deities.
He states the indicative mark for [its being] the principal vital breath (*mukhyaprāṇa*) with the word "Now" (*atha*).
The meaning is: immediately after the determination that speech and the other [faculties] lack the power to sustain the body.
The word "khalu" (indeed) is used to state that it is well known that the vital breath (*prāṇa*) sustains the body and causes it to rise.
He states that the capacity for speech is a mark (*liṅga*) of the vital breath's being the individual soul (*jīva*) with the words "not speech.
He states that qualities such as infinity are marks of Brahman with the words "and at the end."

Since many indicative marks (liṅgas) are seen here, he says "anekaliṅga" to state that this is the section for determining their relative strength (balābala), so as to clarify the meaning not already understood.
In the previous [section], it was stated that the scriptural mention of "light" (jyotiḥ-śruti) refers to Brahman due to the force of the word "yat" which denotes the previously mentioned Brahman;
however, there is no such force here to override the scriptural mention of "prāṇa."
He presents the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) through the connection of a counter-example (*pratyudāharaṇa*), stating: "Because multiple mutually contradictory marks (*liṅga*) are non-conclusive.

Alternatively, let there be a connection by way of an analogy: just as previously the meaning of the case-ending (*vibhaktyartha*) was set aside due to the force of the primary nominal stem (*pradhānaprātipadikārtha*), so too here, the unity of the sentence (*ekavākyatā*) is broken due to the force of multiple primary word-meanings.
Thus, according to the prima facie view, there is meditation on multiple [entities] such as the vital breath (*prāṇa*) and others.
In the final conclusion (*siddhānta*), the distinction is that there is knowledge of Brahman as the inner self (*pratyagbrahmadhī*).
He states the meaning of the reason—"for thus"—because the connection of the words is understood to have Brahman as their ultimate purport.

He explains what was stated—that the relationship between the meanings of the words "the most beneficial" (*hitatamatva*), "the destruction of karma" (*karmakṣaya*), and so forth, is perceived as the determiner of the purport regarding Brahman—by means of the passage beginning with "in the introduction" (*upakrama*).
The meaning is: "Grant that very boon which you deem fit.

He who knows me in the form of Brahman—that is, whoever directly experiences me—his world, his liberation, is not destroyed even by a great sin; it is not harmed, nor is it obstructed, because the heap of cotton that is karma has been burnt away by the fire of knowledge. Thus he says: "He who..."
Good and evil refer to merit and demerit;
[the state of being] untouched by them,
and the state of causing them to be performed.
And the meaning is that all this constitutes unbridled sovereignty. //28//

If it be argued that [the Self taught here] is not the Supreme Self because the speaker teaches himself, we say no; for in this [text], there is an abundance of references to the inner self (adhyātma).
That which was stated— that "breath is Brahman"— is now challenged:
the Supreme Brahman is not denoted by the word "breath."
Why? Because the speaker teaches his own self.

For the speaker, a certain specific embodied deity named Indra, taught his own self to Pratardana, beginning with "Know me alone," and continuing with the expression of ego—"I am Prāṇa, the conscious self.
How could this Prāṇa, being taught as the very self of the speaker, be Brahman?

For the status of being a speaker is not possible for Brahman, according to such scriptural passages as, "He is without speech, without breath" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.8.8). Likewise, [the author] praised himself by means of attributes connected with a physical body which are impossible in Brahman: "I slew the three-headed son of Tvaṣṭṛ; I delivered the Arunmukhas and the Atis to the jackals."
By such statements as these,
Indra's status as the vital breath (*prāṇa*) is established on account of his possessing strength;
for it is known from scripture that "the vital breath is indeed strength."
Furthermore, Indra is well known as the deity of strength;
for they say, "Whatever is an act of strength is indeed the work of Indra.
Moreover, the state of being the self of wisdom is possible for the divine self because its knowledge is unimpeded.
For they say that the deities possess unimpeded knowledge.
And since the instruction regarding the self of the deity is thus certain, statements concerning its being "most beneficial" and so forth must be applied to that very subject as far as possible.

Therefore, having raised the objection that Prāṇa is not Brahman because Indra is instructed as the self, it is answered: "Because there is an abundance of references to the inner self in this [section]."
In this chapter, an internal connection—that is, an abundance or preponderance of connection with the inner self—is perceived.

By the statement, "As long as the vital breath (prāṇa) dwells in this body, so long is there life," it shows that the inner self, which is the conscious principle (prajñātman), possesses independence regarding the commencement and withdrawal of life; it does not show such independence for any particular external deity.
Thus, by stating that "the highest good [depends] on the existence of the vital breaths," he shows that the vital breath (*prāṇa*) is indeed the internal support of the senses.
Likewise, [it is said]: "The vital breath alone, being the self of wisdom (*prajñātman*), having grasped this body, causes it to rise" (Kauṣītaki Upaniṣad 3.3);
and having begun with, "One should not seek to know speech, but should know the speaker," [it continues]: "Just as the spokes are fixed in the hub of a chariot... (ibid.).

"Just as the rim is fixed on the hub and the spokes are fixed on the hub, even so these elements (bhūtamātrāḥ) are fixed on the elements of consciousness (prajñāmātrāḥ), and the elements of consciousness are fixed on the vital breath (prāṇa).

This very vital breath is the conscious self (prajñātman), blissful, undecaying, and immortal"— thus [the text] concludes by referring to the innermost self (pratyagātman) alone, which is not overcome by the activities of the objects and the senses.
And the concluding statement, "One should know that as my Self," is appropriate for the acceptance of the inner self (pratyagātman), not for the acceptance of something external.
Furthermore, there is another scriptural passage: "This Self is Brahman; it has become all" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.5.19).
Therefore, because of the abundance of internal connections, this is indeed an instruction concerning Brahman, not an instruction concerning the self of a deity. // 29 //

How, then, is there a teaching regarding the Self by the speaker? [The answer is: Having slain the Brahmin Viśvarūpa, the son of Tvaṣṭṛ, he gave those who were not *runmukhas*—those other ascetics who were turned away from the Vedāntas, as opposed to those whose mouths (*mukha*) contain the Vedāntic words (*ruta*, meaning that which sounds according to reality)—to the *sālāvṛkas*, the wild dogs of the forest. (Note: *Tvaṣṭṛputraṃ viśvarūpaṃ brāhmaṇam ahanan*; *arunmukhān*: they are called *runmukhas* because they utter (*ru*) the Vedāntic statements; those other than them are *arunmukhas*, i.e., those whose faces are turned away from the Vedāntas.)
I have granted [this].

Just as in a wheel, where the rim is fixed upon the spokes and the hub, and the spokes are fixed upon the nave—the central block of the wheel—so too are the five elements, beginning with earth, measured out; thus, the five objects of experience, sound and so forth, are the "measures" (*mātrā*). These ten are the "elements and measures" (*bhūtamātrā*).
By means of the doctrine of the ego (ahaṅkāra), he spoke—that is, he said—using words denoting his own self.
He states another indicative mark (*liṅga*) showing that the sentence has as its purport the meditation upon Indra as having a body: "Likewise, [the mention of] a body," etc.

"Triśīrṣā" refers to the son of Tvaṣṭṛ named Viśvarūpa, a Brahmin who possessed three heads; him I have slain. "Rut" means that which sounds according to its true meaning, namely the words of the Vedānta; those whose mouths are such [words] are "runmukha. The meaning is that I have given other ascetics (yatīs) who are turned away from the Vedānta to the wild dogs of the forest.
He states the justification for applying the word "prāṇa" to Indra with the words "And [the quality of] being prāṇa...
The meaning is that even common people say this.
The intention is that by the word *prāṇa*, which denotes strength, the deity of strength (*baladevatā*) is indicated through secondary signification (*lakṣaṇā*).
He says "And when [the meaning] is determined" to explain that Indra is the most eminent because he is a bestower of benefit, and is sinless because he lacks eligibility for ritual action.
Does the word "Indra" denote pure consciousness (cinmātra) as indicated by the physical form (vigraha), or does it denote the physical form itself?
The first [alternative] establishes that the sentence has Brahman as its purport;
the second does not, as he says: "Regarding *adhyātma*.
That which is understood in the self—that is, in the body—is *adhyātma*, namely the inner self (*pratyagātman*).

The meaning is that those attributes, such as being situated within the body and so forth—which are impossible in the case of Indra’s body—that connect [the self] are the "ground" (bhūmi) for their internal connection (*adhyātma-sambandha*).
Here, "life-force" (*āyus*) refers to the circulation of the vital breath (*prāṇavāyu*) in this body.
Regarding "existence" (*astitva*), which means the persistence of the vital breaths, there is the persistence of the senses (*indriya*); thus, he cites the Śruti by the words "in existence."
The scripture beginning with "Now, therefore, the attainment of the highest good" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 7.1.3) is cited.
The phrase "in the same way" (tathā) indicates that [the Self] causes the body to arise, just as it establishes the senses.
Having stated its nature as a speaker, he says "and thus, by the opening statement," showing that it is the substrate of all.

In that regard, concerning the conceptualization of various manifold phenomena within the Self, there is an illustration: in the world, it is well known that the rim (*nemi*), which constitutes the circumference of the wheel, is fixed upon the spokes (*ara*)— the rods situated between the felly and the hub—
and the spokes are fixed upon the hub (*nābhi*), which is the central mass of the wheel.
Thus, the five elements beginning with earth are "measured" (mīyante), and thus they are the "measures" (mātrāḥ);
the five objects of experience, sound and so forth, are likewise measures. These ten elemental measures are deposited within the ten cognitive measures.

The five cognitive faculties of the senses, which consist of the cognitions of objects such as sound, are called "measures" because by means of them [the elements] are measured; these are the five organs of perception.

Having stated that [the spokes] are imagined upon the grasping subjects as if on the rim of a wheel, he says, "resting in the vital breath" (prāṇe 'rpitāḥ), meaning that everything is imagined upon the vital breath which stands in the place of the hub.
He says, "That is me" (sa ma), meaning that this vital breath is my own essential nature.
If so, there is a coordination (samanvaya) with the inner self (pratyagātman), but not with Brahman.
Regarding this, he says: "This... //29//
But the instruction is based on the vision gained through the scriptures, as in the case of Vāmadeva. (BS 1.1.30)

Indra, perceiving his own self—the divine essence—as the Supreme Self through the vision of a seer (*ārṣa-darśana*), according to the scriptures, taught: "Know me alone. This is just as the seer Vāmadeva, seeing this very reality, realized: "I was Manu and I was the Sun. It is exactly like that.
This is because of the Vedic scripture: "Whosoever among the gods awakened to this, he alone became that" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.4.10).
As for what was further stated—that after saying "Know me alone," Indra praised himself by means of his corporeal attributes such as the slaying of Tvaṣṭṛ's son—that must be refuted.

To this it is replied: The mention of the slaying of Tvaṣṭṛ and so forth is not for the purpose of praising Indra as an object of knowledge—on the grounds that "since I am one who has performed such deeds, therefore know me"—but rather for the purpose of praising knowledge itself.
How so?
For the sake of praising knowledge.
For, having introduced such acts of violence as the slaying of Tvaṣṭṛ's son, the text subsequently connects this with a praise of knowledge through the passage beginning:
"In that regard, my merit is not diminished; he who knows me, his world is indeed not diminished by any action whatsoever."
This is what is meant:
since not even a single hair of mine, who have become Brahman, is harmed despite having performed such cruel deeds,
so also for anyone else who knows me, no world whatsoever can be harmed by any action.
But that which is to be known is Brahman itself, as will be stated in the passage, "I am the breath, the conscious self.
Therefore, this is a statement concerning Brahman.
He asks about the course of the doctrine of egoism (ahaṅkāravāda) with the word "how" (katham). The Sūtra provides the answer.
He explains that [answer] with the word "Indra."
The vision of the seers (*ārṣa-darśana*) is self-evident in this life due to hearing [the scriptures] and other means performed in previous births.
If it is argued that the mention [of Indra] is not for the purpose of praising the object of knowledge, then how is it so? He asks, "How?
He replies, "By the word 'vijñāna' (knowledge)," stating that its purpose is to praise the knowledge of Brahman.
He states the regulator with the word "yat" (which); the syntactical connection is that it is by the subsequent sentence beginning with "tasya me" (of that mine), and so forth.
He states the praise with the words "this has been said.
The ellipsis is to be supplied as "therefore, knowledge is supreme.
Since Indra is the object of the praised knowledge, he says: "But that which is to be known... (30).

If it be argued that [the Self spoken of here] is not the Supreme Self because of the indicative marks of the individual soul (jīva) and the chief vital breath (mukhyaprāṇa), we say no; for there is a threefoldness of meditation, and because [these two] are resorted to [as subordinate], they are connected with it in this context. (BS 1.1.31)
Even if this is not an instruction concerning the supreme divine Self because of the observation of an abundance of internal connections, nevertheless, it cannot be a statement about Brahman.
Why? Because of the marks of the individual soul (jīva) and the marks of the principal vital breath (mukhya-prāṇa).
First, a clear mark of the individual soul is found in this passage: "One should not seek to know speech; one should know the speaker," and so forth.

For here, the state of being the object of knowledge is predicated of the individual soul (jīva), who is the supervisor of the body and the organs and is active through the instruments such as speech.

Likewise, there is also a characteristic mark of the chief vital breath (mukhyaprāṇa): "Now, indeed, it is the vital breath alone, the conscious self (prajñātman), which, having taken hold of this body, causes it to rise.
And the sustaining of the body is the specific function of the chief vital breath.

In the dialogue concerning the vital breaths (*prāṇasaṃvāda*), after introducing the vital breaths beginning with speech, it is heard [in the *Praśna Upaniṣad* 2.3]: "The most excellent among them, the vital breath (*prāṇa*), said: 'Do not fall into delusion; I alone, having divided myself fivefold and having firmly supported this body, sustain it.'"
However, for those who read "having taken hold of this body," it should be explained that [the Self] raises up the body by taking hold of this living soul (*jīva*) or the aggregate of the senses.
Furthermore, the state of being the self of wisdom (*prajñātmatva*) is appropriate for the *jīva* because of its nature as consciousness;
it is also entirely appropriate for the primary vital breath (*prāṇa*), since it is the substratum of the other vital breaths which are the means of wisdom.

Furthermore, if the individual soul and the chief vital breath (prāṇa) are accepted [as the subject], then both modes of description are justified: the description of non-difference through their co-existence, and the description of difference through their distinct natures—as in: "That which is prāṇa is indeed prajñā; that which is prajñā is indeed prāṇa. For these two dwell together in this body and depart together."
But if [the passage] refers to Brahman, how and why would there be a distinction?
Therefore, if it is argued that here both the individual soul (*jīva*) and the chief vital breath (*mukhya-prāṇa*) are to be understood as distinct from each other, and not Brahman,
this is not so.

[The opponent argues: "From the mention of the *upāsā* (meditations) and the *traividyā* (the three Vedas), it follows that there must be a threefold meditation—namely, meditation on the individual self (*jīva*), meditation on the chief vital breath (*mukhyaprāṇa*), and meditation on Brahman. And it is not proper to accept this within a single sentence."
Indeed, the unity of the passage is understood through its opening and conclusion.

Having begun with "Know me alone," and having stated, "I am Prāṇa, the conscious Self; meditate upon me as life and immortality," the text concludes, "This very Prāṇa is the conscious Self, blissful, undecaying, and immortal.
Thus, the opening and the conclusion are seen to be of a single form.
In this case, it is proper to accept a single meaning;
nor can the characteristic marks of Brahman be interpreted as referring to something else,
because it is impossible for the ten elements (bhūtamātrās) and the ten elements of cognition (prajñāmātrās) to be assigned to anything other than Brahman.
Furthermore, because the word "prāṇa" occurs elsewhere in the sense of Brahman due to the presence of Brahman's characteristic marks (liṅga),
and because here too it is joined with Brahman's characteristic marks such as the presentation of the "most beneficial," it is understood that this is indeed an instruction regarding Brahman.
As for the characteristic mark of the primary vital breath (mukhyaprāṇa) that was shown— namely, "having taken hold of this body, it makes it rise"— that is incorrect.
Since even the activity of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) is dependent upon the Supreme Self (*paramātman*), it can be figuratively attributed to the Supreme Self;
for the Śruti declares: "No mortal lives by means of *prāṇa* or *apāna*; rather, they live by something else, upon which these two depend" (Kāṭhaka Upaniṣad 2.5.5).
As for the indication of the individual soul (*jīva*) shown in such passages as, "One should not seek to know speech, but should know the speaker," that too does not preclude the position of Brahman;
for the individual soul is not absolutely different from Brahman,
as expressed in "That thou art" (*tattvam asi*).
This is established by such scriptural passages as "I am Brahman.
However, by relying on the distinctions created by limiting adjuncts (upādhi) such as the intellect (buddhi), Brahman itself is called the living being (jīva), the agent, and the enjoyer.

To show its true nature as Brahman by abandoning those distinctions created by the adjuncts, the teaching beginning with "One should not seek to know speech, but should know the speaker" is intended to direct one's attention toward the inner Self (pratyagātman).
It is not contradicted:
"That which is not expressed by speech, that by which speech is expressed—
know that alone to be Brahman, and not this which people worship here."

Furthermore, another scriptural passage such as *Kevala Upaniṣad* 1.4, "He who speaks, he who hears," shows that the very Self, while engaged in activities such as speaking and hearing, is Brahman. As for the objection raised— that the perception of a distinction between the vital breath (*prāṇa*) and the conscious self (*prajñātman*), expressed in the statement, "For these two dwell together in this body and depart together from it," is not tenable within the doctrine of Brahman—
that is no fault.

Since it is logical to designate as non-different the intellect (*buddhi*) and the vital breath (*prāṇa*), which are the two substrates of the powers of knowledge and action and serve as the limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) of the inner self (*pratyagātman*), there is no contradiction in identifying them as "the vital breath itself is the conscious self" (*prāṇa eva prajñātmā*), because the inner self, though conditioned by these two adjuncts, is non-different from them in its essential nature. Alternatively, the meaning of the sūtra *na vā upāsātraividhyād āśritatvād iha tadyogāt* is this: even in a passage concerning Brahman, the presence of characteristics belonging to the individual soul (*jīva*) and the chief vital breath (*mukhya-prāṇa*) is not contradictory.
How so? Because of the threefold nature of meditation (*upāsā*).

Here, in this meditation on Brahman, a threefold aspect is intended: by means of the attributes of the vital breath (*prāṇa*), by means of the attributes of wisdom (*prajñā*), and by means of its own inherent attributes.
Among these, [it is said]: "Meditate on life as the immortal; life is the vital breath."
"This body, having grasped it, causes it to rise," and "Therefore, one should venerate this very thing as the Uktha"— these are attributes of the vital breath (prāṇa).
Having begun with, "Now we shall explain how all beings become one in this consciousness (prajñā)," [the text continues].
"Speech alone was one limb that she milked out of this [body]; beyond that, the constituent of being (bhūtamātrā) is fashioned as its name.

Having mounted speech by means of discernment (prajñā), one attains all names through speech. Such is the attribute of discernment. Indeed, these ten constituents of being are based on discernment, and the ten constituents of discernment are based on being.
For if there were only the elements and not the factors of consciousness, they would not be factors of consciousness;
and if there were only the factors of consciousness and not the elements, they would not be elements.
Indeed, no form whatsoever could be established from within.

"This is not a plurality. Just as the rim of a chariot wheel is fixed to the spokes and the spokes are fixed to the hub, even so these elements (bhūtamātrāḥ) are fixed to the elements of consciousness (prajñāmātrāḥ), and the elements of consciousness are fixed to the vital breath (prāṇa). This very vital breath is the self consisting of consciousness"—such are the attributes of Brahman.
Therefore, this single meditation upon Brahman itself is intended to be threefold, by means of the attributes of the two limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) and its own inherent attribute.

Elsewhere as well— in passages such as "consisting of mind, having breath for its body" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 3.14.2)— meditation on Brahman through the attributes of the limiting adjuncts is resorted to.
Here too, this is appropriate, because the unity of meaning of the passage is understood from its opening and conclusion, and because the characteristics of Prāṇa, Prajñā, and Brahman are perceived.
Therefore, it is established that this is a statement concerning Brahman. // 31 //

Thus ends the first quarter of the first chapter in the *Śrīmacchārīrakamīmāṃsābhāṣya* composed by the venerable Śrī Śaṅkarabhagavatpāda. [Note: The meaning is that, as appropriate, some passages here concern the individual soul (*jīva*), some concern the principal vital breath (*mukhyaprāṇa*), and some concern Brahman. Regarding the dialogue of the vital breaths: speech and all the other organs, each considering itself to be superior, approached Prajāpati with the desire to determine which among them was truly preeminent.
He said to them: "That one among you by whose departure the body becomes most wretched is the best.
Then, as each of them—beginning with speech—departed in turn, the body remained healthy.
But when the principal vital breath (mukhyaprāṇa) was about to depart, there was a state of agitation among them all.

The preeminent Prāṇa said: "I alone, having divided myself fivefold into the forms of prāṇa, apāna, and so forth, support—that is, take recourse in—the *bāṇa*, which is the unstable body (etymologically, that which shines or moves is *vāna*; that itself is *bāṇa*). [These consist of] the ten *bhūtamātrās*: the five objects such as sound and the five elements such as earth;
and the ten *prajñāmātrās*: the five sense organs and the five perceptions."
This is the case elsewhere, such as in the passage beginning with "Therefore, [it is] Prāṇa.
That very consciousness by which speech is raised up—impelled and endowed with the capacity for speaking—is Brahman itself, which is inaccessible to speech and the other senses.
Regarding the word "one should meditate," there would be a syntactical split (vākya-bheda) if one were to meditate on the three [entities] independently.
The meaning is not that [the name applies] to the single Brahman by virtue of its own inherent quality;
rather, it is because life depends upon it that it possesses the nature of "life-span" (*āyus*).
Furthermore, the quality of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) is expressed by the term *utthāpayati* ("it causes to rise"), from which it is called *uktha*.
The word "atha" (now/then) refers to the property of being alive. One might ask: why could the raising of the body not be a sign of life? To this, he says: "and the maintenance of the body."

All the vital breaths (prāṇas), beginning with speech, came to Prajāpati while disputing among themselves, each claiming, "I am the best. He said to them, "He among you who, upon departing, causes this body to fall into the most wretched state—he is the best among you. Accordingly, as speech and the others departed one after another, the body remained healthy despite becoming mute and so forth.
But when the chief vital breath (*mukhyaprāṇa*) was about to depart and all [the senses] fell into agitation, the preeminent Prāṇa said to those [senses], beginning with Speech:
"Do not fall into delusion, for I alone do this.

What is that? Having divided myself fivefold into the forms of Prāṇa, Apāna, and so forth, I support—meaning I sustain—this unstable body, which is called *bāṇa* because it moves (*vāti*) or goes; that is the meaning.

He states that Brahman is not to be understood [as the subject] on account of the scriptural mentions of dual number, cohabitation, and departure—namely, "the individual soul and the chief [vital breath]" (jīvamukhya);
he states the designation of non-difference with "or whoever" (yo vā);
and he states the distinction with "together" (saha).

If the individual soul (*jīva*) and the chief vital breath (*mukhya-prāṇa*) are objects of meditation because of their indicative marks (*liṅga*), then Brahman would also have to be an object of meditation since its indicative marks have likewise been stated. Nor can this be accepted as a desirable consequence, for it would entail the disruption of the single unified meaning determined by the introductory context (*upakrama*) and other criteria. Thus he says, "This is not so," and so forth.
Nor should it be argued that there is a split in the sentence (*vākya-bheda*) merely because of the difference between independent word-meanings.

Since the characteristics mentioned in relation to the individual soul (jīva) and the chief vital breath (mukhya-prāṇa) cannot be established as independent because they can be interpreted as referring to Brahman, and since a word-meaning that lacks a fruit must be subordinate to the sentence-meaning that possesses a fruit— making it appropriate to interpret those characteristics in accordance with the primary sentence-meaning—
it is not possible to interpret the characteristic of Brahman found in the primary sentence-meaning otherwise.
Nor is that appropriate, as he says: "And it is not a mark of Brahman.
He explains the remainder of the Sūtra with the words: "And because of being dependent" (āśritatvāt).

Since [the word *prāṇa*] is used in other contexts—such as in the passage beginning "Therefore, *prāṇa*"—in the sense of being dependent on something else, here too, because of the connection of that mark of Brahman, the meaning is that the word *prāṇa* refers exclusively to Brahman.
He states, beginning with "But that which... [and so forth], that the marks such as the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) can be effortlessly led into Brahman, which is the self of all.

The meaning is that by means of that other [entity], namely Brahman, in whom these two abide as objects to be impelled, all [the organs] perform their functions such as the vital breaths. "Distinction" (*viśeṣa*) means the conceit of limitation.

In the statement "one should know the syllable 'vat'," it is not the speaker's status as an object of knowledge that is being expressed, since that is already established in the world; rather, his identity as Brahman is what is being made known.

Regarding the statement that "the marks (liṅga) and so forth are for the sake of being oriented toward the realization of That," he cites another scriptural passage: "That by which speech is impelled" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.4).
The meaning is that Brahman, which is inaccessible to speech and the other senses, is that very consciousness by which speech is impelled—that is, urged toward its own function.

He states, "This is not a fault," because while there is a difference between the referents of the terms *tat* and *tvam* in terms of their specific forms (*svarūpa*), their identity is indicated through the non-difference of the Self as characterized by them.
Having explained the Sūtra according to his own view, the author explains it according to the view of the Vṛttikāra, beginning with "Or rather" (athavā).
It was previously stated that this is because of the contingency of there being three types of meditation;
here, the meaning is that what is intended is a single meditation characterized by three modes directed toward one specific Brahman.

Therefore, the sense is that there is no syntactical split (vākyabheda). The nature of the vital breath (prāṇa) as the cause of life—consisting of bodily movement—is its "longevity" (āyuṣṭva); its "immortality" (amṛtatva) is due to its remaining for as long as the body exists until liberation; and its "being the Uktha" (ukthatva) is because it causes one to rise up; such are the attributes of the vital breath.
He states the attributes of the living self (*jīva*) with the word "Now" (*atha*).
This means immediately after the statement regarding the coexistence and departure of the intellect (*buddhi*) and the vital breath (*prāṇa*).
Here, by the term "wisdom" (*prajñā*), the intellect known as the living self, together with its luminous aspect (*sābhāsā*), is denoted.
Having begun by stating, "We shall explain how all visible beings related to her become one through the conscious Self (cidātman) which is their substrate," it was said: "Speech alone," and so forth.
The summarized meaning of the successive sections beginning with "The eye alone milked out for her one limb" is stated [as follows]:

For the intellect (buddhi), accompanied by its appearance (sābhāsa), which has arisen from the false imagination of the unreal, the objective world of names and forms (nāmaprapañca) constitutes one half of its body.

The state of having as its object the manifold of forms consisting of both the objective (artha) and the subjective (ātman) constitutes one half of the body; thus, taken together, the full body known as "objectivity" is accomplished by the sense organs.
Among these, speech alone among the organs of action (karmendriya) produced—that is, completed—one limb of this Intellect (prajñā), namely one half of its body.
The meaning is that through the door of the organ of speech, the intellect acquires the state of having the manifold of names (nāma-prapañca) as its object.
The fourth [case-ending] has the sense of the sixth.

Furthermore, it is said that its name—being established and made known through the eyes and so forth—is the cause for another [cognition] in the subsequent half [of the process], having the nature of objects such as form which consist of mere untruth.
The meaning is that cognition (buddhi) attains the state of having the manifoldness of objects as its domain by means of the cause of knowledge.

Having thus established that the intellect (buddhi) is the seer of all objects, he explains the superimposition of the status of being a seer upon the Witness (sākṣin) by means of the reflection of consciousness (cit-pratibimba) resting therein, with the words "by means of intelligence" (prajñayā).

The meaning is as follows: through the medium of the intellect, the conscious Self (cid-ātman), having mounted speech—the sense organ—and becoming its impeller, attains all names as things to be spoken by means of speech as an instrument; likewise, by means of the eye, it sees all forms and thus becomes a seer.

And thus, it is stated that omniscience resides in the conscious self (cidātman), while the status of being the cause for the superimposition of the capacity to see belongs to the intellect (buddhi). Furthermore, he states that attributes such as being the support of all and being the giver [of all] are the qualities of Brahman, by saying "tā vā" and so forth.
The state of being ten has already been explained.
With reference to the elements as the objects of perception, the sense-faculties exist as the instruments born from wisdom;

with reference to the collection of elements as the object to be perceived, the sense-faculties exist as mere wisdom. Thus, he establishes the mutual dependence of the perceived and the perceiver by means of the words "that which" (yad).
He clarifies this very point with the words "for not" (na hi).
The nature of the apprehended object is not established by the apprehended object itself, but rather by the apprehending subject;
likewise, the apprehending subject is not established independently of the apprehended object.
Therefore, because they are mutually dependent, this pair—the apprehended and the apprehender—is not distinct in reality, but is superimposed upon the conscious self (cidātman). Thus he says:
"No.
The passage beginning with "tadyathā" has already been explained.
He concludes the meaning of the Sūtra with the words "therefore" (tasmāt).
Anticipating the objection as to how there can be meditation on one thing by means of the attributes of another, he says, "Even elsewhere," because [the attributes] are based [upon it].
The limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) is the individual soul (*jīva*).
Thus, there is meditation by means of the attributes of another.
This is an inconsistent interpretation;

for, firstly, an injunction regarding Brahman as qualified by the three meditations is not possible— just as there is no injunction for the purchase [of Soma] already obtained as qualified by various qualities such as ruddiness— because that which is already established is unfit for an injunction.
Nor is there an injunction for three meditations by way of restating Brahman, because that would result in a split of the sentence (*vākyabheda*).
Nor should it be said that a single meditation qualified by multiple attributes is being enjoined.
Because no such injunctive statement is heard here;
nor [is it the case that] in the passage "Meditate on me as life and immortality," the word "me" refers to the individual soul (jīva) and "life" refers to the vital breath (prāṇa).

It must be stated that "immortality" refers to a specific rule for meditation by one who possesses his own particular duties (*svadharma*), because no duties are heard of in this context and because Brahman is not mentioned.

Because of the scriptural declaration that "breath indeed is immortality" (*prāṇo vā amṛtam*), which attributes immortality specifically to breath, one who is greedy for injunctions regarding meditation must abandon the unity of the passage by accepting that the injunctions— "one should know the speaker," "one should meditate on this very *uktha*," and "one should know 'that is my Self'"— are injunctions for the meditation on the individual self (*jīva*), breath, and Brahman respectively, while the others are injunctions regarding qualities.
And that is incorrect, because the unity of the passage is determined by its introductory context and other factors.
Therefore, he concludes that this sentence has as its ultimate meaning Brahman, the inner self which is the object of knowledge: "Therefore... (31).

Thus ends the first quarter of the first chapter in the *Bhāṣyaratnaprabhā*, a commentary on the *Śrīmacchārīrakamīmāṃsābhāṣya* composed by the venerable Paramahaṃsa Parivrājaka Ācārya Śrī Govindānanda Bhagavatpāda. //1//
Thus ends the first quarter (pāda) of the first chapter, titled "The Harmonization of Scriptural Passages Containing Clear Indications of Brahman.
The Second Quarter of the First Chapter.
[In this section, there is an investigation of those scriptural passages containing non-clear indications of Brahman which have as their subject matter Brahman as the object of meditation.]
1. The Section on Being Established Everywhere (Sarvatra-prasiddhy-adhikaraṇa). Sūtra 1.8.

In the first quarter (pāda), it was stated [in Sūtra 1.1.2] that "Brahman is the cause of the origin and so forth of this [world]," meaning that Brahman is the cause of the origin, etc., of the entire world, including ether and the rest.
Of that Brahman, who is the cause of the entire world, there is pervasiveness (vyāpitva).
eternal nature, omniscience, and omnipotence.
Attributes of this kind, such as "being the self of all," have indeed already been mentioned.

Furthermore, by demonstrating the reasons why certain words— well-known in other senses— have Brahman as their object, several passages containing clear marks of Brahman that were previously ambiguous have been determined to refer to Brahman.
Furthermore, other passages containing indistinct marks of Brahman are subject to doubt: do they establish the supreme Brahman, or do they have some other meaning?
To resolve this, the second and third quarters (pādas) are commenced.
This is the second quarter of the first chapter.
I worship Śrī Rāma, the perfected one who intoxicates the mind, who reclines within the cave of the heart, the inner witness, the unknowable, the Vaiśvānara fire. //1//

Because of the teaching of what is well-known everywhere. BBs_1,2.1:
This is recorded in scripture: "All this, indeed, is Brahman, as it originates from, dissolves into, and breathes within That; therefore, one should meditate with a tranquil mind."
Now, indeed, a person consists of volition (*kratu*); as is his volition in this world, so does he become after departing from here.
"He should form a volition: 'Consisting of mind, having the vital breath for its body, and having light for its form'" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 3.14.1, 2), and so forth.
In this regard, a doubt arises: is the embodied self (*śārīra ātman*) taught here as the object of meditation by means of these attributes such as "consisting of mind," or is it the supreme Brahman?
What, then, is the prima facie view?
That it is the embodied self.
Why? Because a connection with the mind and so forth is well known for that [self], which presides over the body and the organs, but not for the supreme Brahman.
This is known from such scriptural passages as, "For he is without breath, without mind, pure" (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 2.1.2).
[Objection: But surely Brahman has already been grasped by its own name in the passage, "All this, indeed, is Brahman."
How can it be suspected here that the embodied self (śārīra ātman) is to be meditated upon?
This is not a fault;
for this passage is not intended as an injunction for the meditation on Brahman, but rather as an injunction for tranquility (śama).

For this reason, [the scripture] says: "All this, indeed, is Brahman; as that from which it is born, that in which it dissolves, and that into which it enters, one should worship it with a tranquil mind.
What is meant by this is: because all this collection of modifications is Brahman alone, since it is born from that, dissolved into that, and enters into that.
Furthermore, if everything were of one single Self, passion and the like would not be possible;
therefore, [the text says], "one should meditate with tranquility.
Moreover, if the sentence is intent upon enjoining tranquility, it is not possible for this same sentence to enjoin meditation on Brahman.
However, worship (*upāsana*) is enjoined by the passage, "He should form a resolve" (*sa kratuṃ kurvīta*). "Resolve" (*kratu*) means intention or meditation (*dhyāna*).
And its object is heard in the text, "Consisting of mind, having breath for a body" (*manomayaḥ prāṇaśarīraḥ*), which is a characteristic mark of the individual soul (*jīva*).
Therefore, we say that this meditation has the individual soul (jīva) as its object.
Furthermore, even such scriptural descriptions as "possessing all works, possessing all desires," when heard, are appropriately applicable to the individual soul in a figurative sense.

Moreover, the qualities of having the heart as its abode and being "smaller than a grain of rice or a grain of barley"—as in the passage, "This is my Self within the heart, smaller than a grain of rice or a grain of barley"—are possible only for the individual soul, which is the size of the tip of an awl, and not for the unlimited Brahman.
But surely, even such statements as "greater than the earth" and so forth would not be possible if [the Self] were limited.

To this we reply: first of all, both minuteness and greatness cannot be attributed to one and the same thing because of their mutual contradiction. And if one must be accepted, then, because it is mentioned first, it is proper to accept minuteness.
However, its "superiority" will be in relation to the state of Brahman.

And since it has been determined that the subject matter concerns the individual soul (jīva), the mention of Brahman at the end— namely, "This is Brahman" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 3.14.4)— is also concerned with the individual soul alone, as it serves to refer back to the subject under discussion.
Therefore, [the Self] is to be meditated upon through attributes such as being "consisting of mind" (manomaya) and so forth.
Why? Because of the teaching that is well-established everywhere.
That which is established in all the Vedāntas as the referent of the word "Brahman"—namely, the cause of the world—is heard here at the beginning of the passage, "All this, indeed, is Brahman."
Therefore, it is logical that it is precisely that [Brahman] which is taught as qualified by attributes such as "consisting of mind" (*manomaya*).
In this way, there will be neither the abandonment of the subject under discussion (*prakṛtahāna*) nor the introduction of something not under discussion (*aprakṛtaprakriyā*).

But was it not stated that, at the beginning of the passage, Brahman was mentioned with the intention of prescribing tranquility (*śama*), and not with the intention of referring to It in its own right?

To this it is replied: although Brahman was indicated with the intention of enjoining tranquility (*śama*), nevertheless, when qualities such as "consisting of mind" (*manomaya*) are being taught, that very same Brahman remains proximate.
The individual soul (*jīva*), however, is neither proximate nor is it denoted by its own specific term; thus there is a distinction.
[Note: *tajja* means "born in that," i.e., produced therein.]

"In that" (*tasmin*) means "in that which is *tat*"; "it breathes and moves in that" means "it moves in that" (*tadana*); and "born from that" means "born from that" (*tajja*). Thus, it is "that-which-is-born-and-moves-in-that" (*tajjalān*). According to the rule of *śākapārthiva* (king of vegetables) compounds, the middle word "that" (*tat*) is elided.
Although it should have been stated as "taj-jalānam," there is an elision of a member [of the compound] according to Vedic usage (*chāndasa*).

By means of a transposition of case endings, the meaning is that one should meditate upon that which consists of mind (*manomaya*), has vital breath for its body (*prāṇaśarīra*), and has light for its form (*bhārūpa*).
Since it speaks thus, the meaning is that this passage is primarily intended to enjoin tranquility (*śama*).
The meaning is "of the size of an iron needle-point fixed on a spindle.

For one who, by means of the pronoun situated in the compound *prāṇaḥ śarīram asya* ("whose body is breath"), abandons the relevant Brahman and instead desires the irrelevant individual soul (*jīva*), the meaning is that there is both an abandonment of the subject under discussion and the introduction of what was not the subject; the ellipsis to be supplied is "there is a disparity between the individual soul and Brahman."
In order to state the connection between the first quarter and the subsequent two quarters, he restates what has preceded with the words "In the first [quarter].
By the statement that Brahman is the cause of the world, its all-pervasiveness and other attributes are established by implication.
Since the subsequent two quarters proceed depending upon that, the connection consists in the relationship of cause and effect.

Anticipating the question, "How is there a division of the quarters? he states the difference in the objects of knowledge (*prameya*) for each quarter with the words "in another sense" (*arthāntara*).
It has been shown that words such as "ether" (*ākāśa*) are harmonized with Brahman through clear marks of Brahman (*brahmaliṅga*);
the harmonization of sentences containing indistinct marks of Brahman will be explained in the [remaining] two quarters.
The sense is that there is a distinction between the two quarters due primarily to the difference between Brahman as the object of worship (upāsya) and Brahman as the object of knowledge (jñeya).
He cites the passage from the Chāndogya Upaniṣad: "This [world]," etc.;
"born from that" means *tajjam* (that-born).
It dissolves into that, therefore it is *tat-la*; it breathes and moves within that, therefore it is *tad-ana*;
and because it is both born from that (*taj-ja*) and that which dissolves (*tal-la*) and that which breathes (*tad-ana*), it is *tajjalān*.

In this *karmadhāraya* compound, by the maxim of "vegetable-king" (*śākapārthiva*), there is the elision of the middle member, the word *tat*. While one might have expected the form *tajjalānam*, the elision of a constituent part is a Vedic archaism (*chāndasa*).
The word *iti* is used in the sense of a reason (*hetau*).
The meaning is that this entire world is Brahman alone, because it is an illusory manifestation (*vivarta*) of it.

And that [context] is established otherwise for the purpose of enjoining the quality of tranquility.

The logical connection (*anvaya*) is that because it speaks in this way, it is therefore "devoted to the method of tranquility" (*śamavidhiparam*).

peace" (*śama*).

And because the intended qualities are established. (BBs 1.2.2)
"Intended to be spoken" (*vivakṣita*) means those things desired to be expressed.
Although in the case of the Veda—which is not of human origin—there is no speaker and thus no literal intention, it is nevertheless figuratively designated by its result, namely adoption (*upādāna*).
For in common worldly usage, that which is expressed by words and is to be adopted is said to be "intended."
Whatever is not to be accepted is what is not intended to be expressed;
therefore, even in the case of the non-Veda, that which is stated as being worthy of acceptance is what is intended to be expressed, while the other is not intended to be expressed.
However, what is to be accepted and what is not to be accepted is understood from the intended purport (*tātparya*) of the Vedic statements.

Thus, in this context, those qualities intended for meditation—which are taught as attributes to be adopted, such as "having true resolve" (*satyasaṃkalpa*) and so forth—are appropriate in the case of the Supreme Brahman.
