"Possessing ears everywhere" means one whose auditory organs (śrotra) extend in all directions, toward all things.
The statement that he is the self of all is because hands and other limbs are well-known to belong to all living beings. //2//
But because it is not possible [for the individual soul], it is not the embodied one. (BS 1.2.3)
By the preceding sūtra, the possibility of those qualities intended [to belong] to Brahman was stated;
by this [sūtra], however, their impossibility in the embodied soul (śārīra) is stated.
The word "tu" (however) serves the purpose of restriction.
By the reasoning already stated, it is Brahman alone that possesses the qualities of consisting of mind and so forth, and not the embodied individual soul (jīva),
because [Brahman is described as] "one whose resolve is true."
His self is space;
he is without speech and without regard.
Furthermore, qualities of this kind, such as "greater than the earth," do not apply directly to the embodied soul (*śārīra*).
The term *śārīra* means "that which exists in the body.
But surely the Lord (*īśvara*) also exists in the body?
True;
it exists in the body, but it does not exist in the body alone,
for it is "greater than the earth, greater than the intermediate space."
And because its all-pervasiveness is heard in the text, "It is omnipresent and eternal like space";
whereas the individual soul (jīva) exists only within the body, since it has no activity outside the body, which is the locus of its experience. // 3 //

FN: "Vākī" means one who possesses speech (*vāk*); "avākī" means one who does not possess speech, being devoid of all senses such as speech and the rest. Because his desires are fulfilled, he has no concern for anything; thus, he is "anādaraḥ" (without regard).
Now, if the attributes of the individual soul (*jīva*) are applied to Brahman, why are the attributes of Brahman not likewise applied to the individual soul?
Regarding this, he says: "Because it is untenable.
He explains the Sūtra with the words: "By the former," referring to the previously stated reasoning concerning [the impossibility of] being the self of all and so forth.
The meaning is that the properties of the imagined (kalpita) are connected to the substratum (adhiṣṭhāna), but the properties of the substratum are not imagined;
for at the time of the knowledge of the substratum, the properties of the imagined do not exist.
Or rather, that which possesses speech (*vāk*) is "the speaker" (*vākī*); one who does not possess speech is "non-speaker" (*avākī*).
The meaning is: one who lacks the sense-faculties (*anindriya*).
"Indifference" (anādara) means that he has no desire for respect toward anything;
the meaning is that he is eternally satisfied.
Since [the status of] being "superior" and so forth is untenable, the limitation expressed as "the embodied one" (śārīra) is the reason stated in the Sūtra.
But he says that this belongs to the individual soul (jīva) alone and not to the Lord (īśvara), starting with the words "It is true," and so forth. //3//
And because of the designation of the action and the agent. BBs 1.2.4.

For this reason as well, the embodied soul is not the possessor of qualities such as being "consisting of mind" (*manomaya*), because there occurs a designation of object and agent: "Having departed from here, I shall attain him" (*Chāndogya Upaniṣad* 3.14.4).
By the word "him" (*etam*), the text designates the Self under discussion—the one possessing qualities such as being "consisting of mind"—as the object, that is, as the goal to be attained.
"I shall fully awaken"— thus [he speaks] regarding the lay follower Śarīra as the agent and the one who attains; "I shall fully awaken" means "I shall attain."
Furthermore, when a distinction exists, it is not logical to designate one and the same entity as both the object of an action and its agent.
Likewise, the relationship between the object of meditation and the meditator is based solely upon difference.
Therefore, for this reason as well, the embodied self (śārīra) is not the one characterized by being "consisting of mind" (manomaya) and so forth. // 4 //

The connection is that [the text] designates "this" as the means of attainment (*prāpaka*). Regarding the phrase "designation of object and agent," he states another meaning: "thus, by means of meditation" (*tathopāsya*). //4//
Because of the distinction in sound. (BBs 1.2.5)

For this reason as well, the one characterized by qualities such as consisting of mind is other than the embodied soul, because there is a specific scriptural statement in another text within the same context: "Just as rice, or barley, or śyāmāka grain, or the kernel of a śyāmāka grain, so is this golden person within the self" (Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa 10.6.3.2).

The word "śārīra" (the embodied one) is a denotative term ending in the locative case, namely "antar-ātman" (within the self). Distinct from that is another word, "puruṣa," ending in the nominative case, which denotes the Self characterized by qualities such as being composed of mind (*manomaya*).
Therefore, a difference between the two is understood. [Note:
"Belonging to the same context" means having the same subject matter of knowledge.]
In the word *antarātmann*, there is an elision of the case ending according to Vedic usage (*chāndasa*);
the meaning is *antarātmani*.
"Having a single purpose" means having a common subject matter within the context.
In the word *antarātmann*, the elision of the case-ending (*vibhaktilopa*) is a Vedic archaism (*chāndasa*).
The distinction between the two words lies in their different case-endings;
therefore, there is a difference between their respective meanings—this is the meaning of the Sūtra. //5//
And the Smṛti demonstrates the distinction between the embodied self and the Supreme Self, as in: "The Lord dwells in the heart-region of all beings, O Arjuna,
causing all beings to revolve by His power of illusion, as if they were mounted on a machine" (Gītā 18.61), and so forth.

Here [the opponent] asks: Who, moreover, is this so-called embodied self (*śārīra*) distinct from the supreme self (*paramātman*), who is negated by such statements as "But because of impossibility, not the embodied self" (*Anu. 1.2.6*)?
For scripture states: "There is no other seer than He, no other hearer" (*Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad* 3.7.23).
Thus, passages of this kind preclude the idea of a self other than the Supreme Self.
Likewise, the Smṛti also says: "And know Me also as the Knower of the Field in all fields, O Bhārata" (Gītā 13.2), and so forth.
To this it is replied: This is true.
The Supreme Self alone, when delimited by the limiting adjuncts (upādhi) of the body, senses, mind, and intellect, is figuratively designated as the "embodied" (śārīra) by the ignorant.
Just as the ether, though unlimited, appears to be limited due to the influence of limiting adjuncts such as jars or water-pots, so it is in this case.
And with reference to that [distinction], the conventional usage of distinctions such as "object" and "agent" is not contradicted prior to the instruction of the oneness of the Self, "That thou art.
But once the oneness of the Self is grasped, there would indeed be a complete cessation of all conventional usages, such as bondage and liberation. (6) [Note:
"With reference to that" means with reference to the distinction based on limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*).]

Because the *Smṛti* speaks of a distinction between the one residing in the heart and the individual soul (*jīva*), he states here as well that the one consisting of mind (*manomaya*) residing in the heart is the Lord— namely, "and because of the Smṛti. Here, "beings" refers to the individual souls (*jīvān*),
and "machine" refers to the body.

Here, in order to dispel the misconception that a distinction between truths has been stated by the author of the Sūtras, he raises and refutes an objection—though one already refuted in the *Īkṣaty-adhikaraṇa*—with the words beginning "Here [someone] says" (*atrāha*).
He states, "True," [meaning]: according to the method you have described, there is indeed only oneness in reality, while the distinction is merely imagined and is merely restated in the Sūtras. //6//

If it be argued that [the Self] is not [the subject of the comparison] because of its smallness and because of that designation, we say no; for it is to be perceived as such, and it is also like space. 1.2.7.

The term "arbhaka" means small or limited; for its abode is circumscribed by the statement, "This is my Self within the heart," and because it is designated as minute by the word itself in the passage, "It is smaller than a grain of rice or a grain of barley."
It must be addressed that which was stated: that it is the embodied soul (*jīva*) alone, the size of a thumb-tip, who is taught here, and not the Supreme Self (*paramātman*) residing in the agent.
To this, it is replied: this is not a fault.
To begin with, it is in no way possible to designate that which occupies a limited space as being all-pervading.
However, for that which is all-pervading, because it exists in all places, the designation of occupying a limited space is also possible through some particular perspective.

For example, although one is the sovereign of the entire earth, one may nevertheless be designated as the "Lord of Ayodhyā. But by what perspective is the Lord, who is all-pervading, designated as having a body the size of a thumb and as being minute?
Thus we say: "Because he is to be perceived in this way.
In this manner, the Lord, endowed with a multitude of qualities such as subtlety and so forth, is taught there in the lotus of the heart as one who is to be perceived—that is, to be seen.

Just as Hari resides in the Śālagrāma stone, so too is his cognition and consciousness the means of apprehension therein; for although the Lord is omnipresent, he becomes gracious when worshipped in that specific place.
And this should be viewed as being like space:
just as space, although all-pervading, is designated as "smaller than the eye of a needle" and so forth in relation to such things,
so too is Brahman.
Thus, since it depends on being perceived in that way, the fact that Brahman has the heart as its abode and is minute in size is not ultimate;

for in this regard, it might be suspected that because Brahman has the heart as its abode, and because the hearts as abodes are different in every body, and because defects such as multiplicity, having parts, and non-eternality are observed in the case of Śuka and others who have different abodes, [these attributes would apply to] Brahman.
The objection that this [consequence] would also apply to that case is likewise refuted. (7) [Note:
The term "small" (*alpa*) is stated as a synonym for the word "child" (*arbhaka*) in order to negate its restriction to the sense of an infant.]
In some way, even with respect to the state of Brahman,

because it is to be perceived and to be seen, it has a small abode; that which has such an abode is "arbhakaukāḥ," and its state or essence is "arbhakaukatva"— from that [comes] the implied smallness.
He states that [the Self] is heard even by a word expressing minuteness, such as "smaller," using the phrase "by its own word.
He explains that this is not a fault with the words "not, first of all," etc.,
meaning "in no way whatsoever."
The meaning is "even with respect to the state of Brahman.

The intention is that since the nature of Brahman is impossible without the abandonment of limitation, and when that limitation is abandoned, it follows that Brahman itself becomes the object of worship.
He provides an illustration for the statement regarding the limitation of the omnipresent one: "just as in the case of an equal," and so forth.

The meaning is that this statement regarding limitation is made because [the Lord] is to be meditated upon in such a way within the small heart, just as one might speak of the location of the All-Pervasive Lord (Sarveśvara) in Ayodhyā.
Now, why is it generally said to be in the heart specifically?
To that, he says: "Therein... (tatra).
In the heart, the modification of the intellect (*buddhi-vṛtti*) becomes the grasper of the Supreme Self.
Therefore, the meaning is that it is so called because it is the locus for the manifestation of the Lord (*īśvara*).
He states, beginning with "In that regard, when it is suspected," etc., that even some creeper of doubt has been cut down by the sword of the analogy of space.
The meaning is that even though space consists of distinct locations (*āyatana*), there is an absence of any real distinction [between them] and so forth. //7//
If it is argued that there is attainment of enjoyment [in the intermediate state], we say no, because of the difference in nature.
Since Brahman is all-pervading and thus connected to the hearts of all living beings,
and since it is not distinct from the embodied soul by virtue of its nature as consciousness (cidrūpa),
the consequence would follow that the experience of pleasure, pain, and so forth would also be non-distinct [for Brahman].
And because of oneness:
for there exists no transmigrating self other than the supreme Self,
as it is said, "There is no knower other than this" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.7.23).
Because of such scriptural passages as these,
if it be argued that, therefore, the experience of transmigratory existence is attained by the Supreme Being itself,
we say: no, because of the difference in nature (vaiśeṣya).

First of all, it does not follow that Brahman experiences enjoyment in the same way as the body simply because it is connected to the hearts of all living beings, for there is a distinction (*vaiśeṣya*).
Indeed, there is a difference between the embodied soul (*śārīra*) and the Supreme Lord (*parameśvara*):
the one is the agent, the enjoyer, the means of merit and demerit, and possesses pleasure, pain, and so forth; [the other is not].
The other is the opposite, possessing qualities such as being free from evil.
Due to this distinction between these two, one experiences [the results of actions] and not the other.
Furthermore, if the connection with an effect were admitted to occur by mere proximity, without relying on the inherent capacity of the object, [there would be no distinction].
It would follow that even space and the like would be subject to burning and so forth.
These same objections and refutations apply equally to those who maintain that the self is omnipresent and manifold.
As for the argument that because Brahman is one and there is no other self, it follows that Brahman must experience the experiences of the body—[this is likewise untenable].
To this we reply: First, this "Beloved of the Gods" must be questioned:
How have you determined that this self is non-existent?
If you say, "From such scriptural passages as 'That thou art,' 'I am Brahman,' and 'There is no other knower than this,'" [we respond:]...
Therefore, the scriptural meaning must be understood in accordance with the scriptures; one cannot adopt a "half-old-woman" approach (applying it selectively) in this matter.

Furthermore, the scripture—in the passage "That thou art"—teaches that Brahman, characterized by freedom from sin and other such attributes, is the Self of the embodied soul. This very teaching precludes the status of being an experiencer for the embodied soul itself.
How, then, could there be the consequence of Brahman experiencing through the experience of that [soul]?
Now, if the oneness of the embodied self with Brahman is not grasped, then the experience of the embodied self is caused by false knowledge;
it does not, however, affect Brahman in its ultimate reality.
For when the sky is conceptualized by the ignorant as having a floor or being soiled and the like, the sky does not, in ultimate reality, become characterized by a floor, dirt, or the like.
To this he says: "Not so, because of the difference" (*na vaiśeṣyāt*).
Even if there is oneness, it does not follow that Brahman undergoes experience through the experience of the embodied soul, because of their difference.
For there is indeed a distinction between false knowledge and right knowledge.
Experience is constructed by false knowledge,
whereas unity is seen through right knowledge;
and the reality perceived through right knowledge is not touched by experience constructed by false knowledge.
Therefore, not even a trace of enjoyment can be attributed to the Lord. [Note:
The meaning is that the nature of merit and demerit (*dharmādharmatva*) is the limiting condition (*upādhi*).
This very distinction is what constitutes "particularity" (*vaiśeṣya*).]

The suffix *ṣyañ* is used in the sense of the base itself (*svārthe*), or it signifies the excellence of a particular quality (*viśeṣa*). The meaning of the sūtra is that "excellence" (*atiśaya*) consists in the fact that dharma and so forth serve as causes for their own substratum's fruit; [the suffix is applied] because of that.
For those who maintain that there are many selves, [it is said]:
"half.
This refers to the "maxim of the half-old woman" (*ardhajaratīnyāya*): one desires only the half—the face—of an old woman, but not her limbs.

The meaning is that even though the Lord, characterized by qualities such as being "consisting of mind" (*manomaya*), is designated as being within the heart (*hārda*) for the purpose of meditation, the statement "in that very [place] all this is contained," etc., is consistent with Him alone because He is free from defects.

To address the doubt that if Brahman were within the heart, there would be the contingency of experiencing undesirable things, and therefore the individual soul (*jīva*) alone must be the object of worship within the heart, he explains [the answer] with the words "like space" (*vyomavat*).
[He argues that] Brahman would not be a subject of experience (*bhoktṛ*).

He refutes the argument that "because it possesses sentience while being the heart, and because it is non-different from the individual soul (jīva), it is like the individual soul," by stating: "No, because of the difference in nature (vaiśeṣya)."
The meaning is that "possessing dharma and adharma" is the limiting adjunct (upādhi).
This very distinction is "vaiśeṣya";
the suffix *ṣyañ* is used here in its own sense (*svārthe*).
Alternatively, "viśeṣa" means excellence (*atiśaya*).
Excellence is the quality of being a cause for a fruit within its own substratum, such as merit (*dharma*) and so forth;
the meaning of the sūtra is "because of that."

Furthermore, for those who maintain that there are many selves (*ātman*) due to the diversity of bodies, there arises the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that all selves would be enjoyers within a single body.

As for the rebuttal that experience occurs only in the body acquired through one's own karma, we reply that this is an equal [problem] for both sides; thus, we are not to be questioned. He says "all-pervading" (*sarvagata*). In reality, however, it will be explained later that for them alone there is a confusion of experiences (*bhogasāṃkarya*).

Having ascertained through scripture that Brahman is non-different from the individual soul (jīva), [the author] states that the inference of its being an enjoyer is sublated by the scripture upon which it depends, with the words "according to the teaching" (*yathāśāstram*).
To desire only the face of an old woman and not her limbs is the "half-old-woman maxim" (*ardhajaratīyanyāya*);
and that is not appropriate here.

For it is not proper to accept non-difference and yet abandon the state of being a non-enjoyer, since the scripture itself precludes the state of being an enjoyer for the sake of establishing non-difference; thus he says, "And the scripture...
Now, one might object: "I have not grasped oneness through the scripture."
[Otherwise] there would be an injury to that which is the source of subsistence.

However, suspecting that [the opponent might argue] it is apprehended according to your own statement, [the author] says "Now, if it were not apprehended," etc., because the distinction between being an enjoyer and a non-enjoyer is established through the imagined difference between the original object (bimba) and its reflection (pratibimba); thus, the reason [adduced by the opponent] is irrelevant.
Furthermore, he cites the Sūtra—"That he says"—to establish this point: that the substrate (adhiṣṭhāna) possesses the specific quality of being untouched by what is imagined.
Since there is no sublation to Brahmā being the object within the heart, it is established that the Śāṇḍilya-vidyā passage is connected with Brahman as the object of meditation. //8//
END BsCom_1,2.1.8 START BsCom_1,2.2.9-10 2.
The Section on the Internal Organ (Antaradhikaraṇa) 9–10.
The Self [is the cause] because of the inclusion of both the moving and the non-moving.
In the Kaṭhavallī it is recited: "He for whom both Brahminhood and Kṣatriyahood are food, and for whom death is the sauce—who knows where He is? (1.2.24).
In this context, a consumer is understood, indicated by the mention of boiled rice and its condiment;
therein, could fire be the consumer, or rather the individual soul (jīva)?
Alternatively, there is the doubt as to whether it is the Supreme Self (paramātman),
because no specific distinction has been determined,
and because all three— the fire, the individual soul (jīva), and the Supreme Self— are found to be introduced as subjects of inquiry in this treatise.
What, then, is the prima facie position? That fire is the eater. Why? Because of the scriptural statement: "Fire is the eater of food" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.4.6).
This is because of both scriptural authority and common renown;
for the individual soul (jīva) might be the eater, as seen in the passage: "One of them eats the sweet pippala fruit."
It is not the Supreme Self, because of the scriptural vision: "The other, not eating, looks on" (Muṇḍaka 3.1.1).
This being the position reached, we reply: the Eater here must be the Supreme Self.
Why? Because of the mention of "the moving and the unmoving" (carācara).
For here, the moving and the unmoving—that is, the stationary and the animate—is understood as food with death as its condiment;
and for such food, no eater other than the Supreme Self is possible in its entirety.
But it is logical that the Supreme Self, withdrawing the entire collection of modifications, devours them all.

Now, one might object: "In this context, the mention of 'the moving and the unmoving' is not actually found; how then can the mention of the moving and the unmoving be taken as an established fact and employed as a reason?"
This is not a fault;
for it is understood that death is the condiment for the entire multitude of living beings,
and since Brahmins and Kṣatriyas are the most prominent, it is appropriate for them to be mentioned as representative examples.
As for the claim that even the Supreme Self cannot be an enjoyer, because of the scriptural observation, "The other looks on, not eating," it is said in reply:
this observation is a prohibition against the enjoyment of the fruits of karma.
Because that [destruction] is present;
it is not a negation of the withdrawal of transformations, for Brahman is well-known in all the Vedāntas as the cause of creation, maintenance, and dissolution.
Therefore, the Supreme Self alone must be the "Eater" (attā) here.

[For] that Supreme Self for whom both the Brahmin and the Kṣatriya castes are like two well-known dishes of boiled rice, and for whom Death—being the destroyer of all—stands as the condiment like clarified butter mixed with the rice; [that Self is the Eater].

Wherein that Eater, the causal Self (kāraṇātman), resides—that undifferentiated Self—one who possesses the means mentioned in the mantra, "Not one who has not desisted from evil conduct," knows it as it is; whereas another, devoid of that [means], does not know it in this way. This is the meaning. The mention [of this specific case] is illustrative.
Nor are only the Brahmins and Kshatriyas intended here, because by means of "death as the sprinkling," all living beings are brought to mind;
and it is appropriate to mention the Brahmin and the Kshatriya among living beings because of their preeminence.
And on account of the context. For this reason as well, the Supreme Self alone must be the "Eater" here, because this context pertains to the Supreme Self.
The reference to the subject under discussion in passages such as "The wise one is neither born nor dies" (Kaṭha 1.2.18) is logical;
furthermore, the fact that [the Self] is difficult to know, as expressed in "Who indeed knows where he is? (Kaṭha 1.2.6), is a characteristic mark of the Supreme Self. // 10 //
Because it includes both the moving and the non-moving as its own self:
"He for whom the world, consisting of Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, and so forth, is the rice,
and for whom even Death— the slayer of all living beings— is the condiment, serving much like clarified butter that seasons the rice."

That Self, which exists within the pure consciousness-only (cinmātra) through the conceptualization of non-difference—that pure Brahman, who is likewise the substratum (adhiṣṭhāna) of even the Lord—whom does he know?
The meaning is that no one knows it without means such as the purification of the mind.
He states the seed of doubt: "viśeṣa... (through specific [distinctions]).
The question regarding Agni is "Tell me about that Fire"; the question regarding the individual soul (jīva) is "This doubt which arises when one has died";
and the question regarding Brahman is "Other than dharma [and adharma]."

The meaning is that a reply is found for Agni in the words, "He spoke to him about that fire which is the beginning of the worlds," and for the other two [Vāyu and Āditya] in the words, "Come, I shall declare this to you.
It was stated previously that Brahman does not possess the status of an enjoyer.
Relying on that, he sets forth the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa) with the words "What, then, is it?
Due to dissatisfaction with the idea that the context concerns the fire-altar (agni), he says "or the individual soul (jīva).
In the prima facie view, there is meditation upon the individual soul.
In the final conclusion (*siddhānta*), the difference in result is that it is the knowledge of the undifferentiated Brahman (*nirviśeṣabrahmajñāna*).
The prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that the word "rice" (*odana*) denotes that which is to be enjoyed.
However, the final conclusion is that the word "rice" is used figuratively (*gauṇa*) for the entire range of effects (*kāryamātra*) indicated by the words "Brahmins" and "Kṣatriyas."

And here, the quality (guṇa) is understood as the perishability inherent in ordinary rice, which is brought to mind by the phrase "moistened with death" (*mṛtyūpasecana*), because a word used in a figurative sense (*gauṇa-śabda*) grasps a quality that is proximate.
Thus, since everything appears as something perishable, the Lord is said to be the "eater" by virtue of this indicative mark (*liṅga*); therefore, [the author] says, "this is not a fault."
"Because of its proximity"—the meaning is that enjoyment has been previously mentioned in the statement, "He eats the sweet fruit. // 9 // // 10 //
END BsCom_1,2.2.9-10 START BsCom_1,2.3.11 3.
The Section Concerning Those Entered into the Cave (guhāpraviṣṭādhikaraṇam) / Sūtras 11–12.
For it is because of the perception of that [Self] that the two selves are said to have entered the cave;

indeed, it is recited in the Kaṭha Upaniṣad: "Drinking the Truth, having entered the cave in the highest supreme realm, those who know Brahman call them shadow and light, as do those who maintain the five fires and the triple Nāciketa sacrifice" (Kaṭha 1.3.1).
In this regard, there is a doubt:
are the intellect (buddhi) and the individual soul (jīva) indicated here, or are the individual soul and the supreme self (paramātman)? If they are the intellect and the individual soul, [then...]
Thus, the individual soul (jīva) is shown to be distinct from the aggregate of the body and the instruments of action, which are dominated by the intellect (buddhi).
That too must be established here [in this context]:
"Regarding this doubt concerning a man who has died—some say 'he exists,' and others say 'he does not exist.'"
Because it was asked, "Instructed by you in this knowledge, this is the third of the boons" (Kaṭha Up. 1.1.20),
it follows that the individual soul and the supreme Self are [distinguished], and thus the supreme Self, which is distinct from the individual soul, is established.
That too must be established here:
"Other than dharma and other than adharma, other than what is done and what is not done, other than what has been and what is to be— tell me that which you see" (Katha Upaniṣad 1.2.14).
Since it was asked thus, the objector says here: "Neither of these two positions is possible. Why? Because the drinking of *ṛta* is the enjoyment of the fruits of karma."
Furthermore, by using the dual number in the phrase "in the world of good deeds," the Śruti demonstrates that both [of them] drink;
therefore, the position that they are the intellect (buddhi) and the knower of the field (kṣetrajña) is not possible.
For this very reason, the position that [the two] are the individual soul (kṣetrajña) and the Supreme Self (paramātman) is also not possible,
because even in the case of the conscious Supreme Self, the drinking of the *ṛta* is impossible,
as stated in the mantra-text: "The other, not eating, looks on."

To this it is replied: this is not a fault. For we observe the metaphorical designation of "those with umbrellas" (*chatriṇaḥ*) for many people even when only one among them possesses an umbrella; likewise, even when only one is drinking, two are said to be "drinking."
Alternatively, the individual soul (jīva) drinks,
while the Lord (īśvara) causes it to drink; yet, even while causing it to drink, He is said to drink Himself.
Since the status of being an agent is also observed in one who causes cooking,
it is possible to understand the term as referring to the intellect (*buddhi*) and the knower of the field (*kṣetrajña*), by metaphorically attributing agency to the instrument.
Because we observe such usage as "the fuel is cooking," and because within the context of the internal self (adhyātma), no other two who drink the covered [fluid] are possible,
it must therefore be the intellect (buddhi) and the individual soul (jīva).

The doubt arises whether these two are the individual soul (jīva) and the supreme self (paramātman). What, then, is the initial position? That they are the intellect (buddhi) and the knower of the field (kṣetrajña).
Why? Because of the qualification "having entered the cave."
Whether the body is the cave or the heart,
in either case it is logical that the intellect and the knower of the field have entered the cave.
Furthermore, when it is possible [to interpret it otherwise], it is not reasonable to assume that the omnipresent Brahman has a specific location;
moreover, the phrase "in the world of good deeds" shows that it does not transcend the sphere of karma.
But the Supreme Self does not abide within the sphere of either good or evil deeds.

This is because of the Vedic scripture: "He increases not by action, nor does he become less. Furthermore, the designation of these two as "shadow and light" is appropriate, for they are mutually distinct from one another, just like shadow and light.

Therefore, when it is argued that the intellect (*buddhi*) and the knower of the field (*kṣetrajña*) are what are being spoken of here, we reply: it is the individual self (*vijñānātman*) and the supreme self (*paramātman*) that are being spoken of here.
Why? Because both of them are conscious and possess a common nature.
Furthermore, in common worldly usage, when a number is heard, the understanding is seen to apply only to things that share a common nature.
When it is said, "A second for this cow must be sought," only a second cow is sought,

not a horse or a human being. Likewise, here, since the individual self (vijñānātman) has been determined by the indicative mark of drinking the *ṛta*, when a second is sought, only the Supreme Self (paramātman)— which is conscious and of a similar nature— is understood.
But was it not said that the Supreme Self is not to be understood because of the observation of its being hidden in the cave?
We reply that it is precisely because of the observation of its being hidden in the cave that the Supreme Self is to be understood.

For the state of being hidden in the cave is seen repeatedly in the Śruti and Smṛti as belonging to the Supreme Self alone: "Hidden in the cave, dwelling in the deep, the Ancient" (Kaṭha Upaniṣad 1.2.12).

In such passages as "He who knows [it] hidden in the secret cave, in the highest heaven" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.1) and "Seek the Self that has entered the cave," it has already been stated that even for Brahman, which is omnipresent, instruction regarding a specific location is not contradictory, as it serves the purpose of its perception.

However, the state of abiding in the world of well-performed deeds, like that of possessing an umbrella, is not contradictory even when residing in a single entity for both [the individual soul and the Supreme Self].
Nor is it contradictory to speak of "shadow and sunlight," because being in saṃsāra and being beyond saṃsāra are mutually distinct, just like shadow and sunlight.
Because the state of being a transmigrating being (saṃsāritva) is produced by ignorance, whereas the state of being non-transmigrating (asaṃsāritva) is ultimate reality;
therefore, it is understood that both the individual self (vijñānātman) and the supreme self (paramātman) have entered the cave. // 11 //
And for what reason are the individual self (*vijñānātman*) and the supreme self (*paramātman*) understood here?

[Because they are described as] "drinking" (*pibantau*)—that is, experiencing—the *ṛta*, which is the fruit of action (*karmaphala*), in this world of well-performed deeds; that is, abiding in the body, which is the effect of the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*) resulting from right exertion, they are the two who occupy the half of the Supreme Brahman.
That which is worthy of being the place is the "other shore" (parārdha), the heart; having entered that cave within the supreme and most excellent [space],
they abide there— like shadow and sunlight, which are mutually opposed— and of these two, the knowers of Brahman and the performers of ritual action speak.
Those who have built the threefold Nāciketa fire-altar also say this:
regarding a human being who has passed away and died, there is this doubt or uncertainty—
some say that there is an enjoyer in the next world, while others say there is not.
The meaning is: "Instructed by you, I desire to know this reality.
"Elsewhere than dharma and adharma" means other than these; "other than what has been done and not done" means untouched by dharma and adharma.
That which is distinct from cause and effect, whether produced or unproduced, is Brahman.
Or alternatively: agency is characterized by sovereignty, and since that [sovereignty] exists for the one who causes another to drink just as it does for the one who drinks, he too is an agent.
Therefore they say: "He who causes another to act is also a doer.
[The Lord] is hidden in the cave, situated in the intellect; He dwells in the cavern of the body, which is crowded with manifold misfortunes; He is the Ancient One, the Primordial Person.
"In the highest heaven"—in the most excellent space of the heart; "there, in the cave," that is, in the intellect (*buddhi*). "Seek"—that is, investigate.
With the words "the cave" (*guhām*), he states the concordance (*samanvaya*) of the subsequent sentence as well with the Knowable Self, following immediately after the sentence concerning the Eater.

Drinking—that is, enjoying—the *ṛta*, the inevitably occurring fruit of their actions, in the world of well-performed deeds, namely in the body which is the effect; having entered that cave situated within the "supreme half" (*parārdha*)—the heart, so called because it is worthy of being the supreme abode of the other [i.e., the individual soul], the most excellent [part]—they abide there. This cave is either of the nature of space or of the nature of consciousness.
Those who know Brahman and those who perform ritual acts say that these two are mutually opposed like shade and sunlight;
"those by whom the three-fold Nāciketa fire has been built" (triṇāciketa)— meaning they too say this—
the sense being that they have studied the Nāciketa passages.
The triad consisting of the knowledge of that meaning and the performance of that [knowledge] is to be understood.

Since both the individual soul (jīva) as limited by intellect and the Supreme Self (paramātman) have been introduced as the subjects under discussion, he states the doubt with the word "tatra" (in that regard).
He himself states the result of the prima facie (pūrvapakṣa) and the established (siddhānta) positions with the words beginning "yadi" and so forth.
The meaning is that even that [result] pertains to the difference between the individual soul (jīva) and the intellect (buddhi).
When a human being has departed—that is, when he is dead—there arises this doubt or uncertainty: some say there is an enjoyer in the next world; others say there is not.
Others say it does not exist;
therefore, the meaning is that you have instructed me so that I might know this reality of the Self (ātmatattva).
The meaning of "that too" is that it is also the essential nature of the Supreme Self (paramātmasvarūpa).

He raises a doubt regarding the impossibility of both being enjoyers, saying: "To this, he says. He states: "To this, it is replied," meaning that just as the word "umbrella-bearer" refers to those who are traveling, the word "drinking" refers by means of *ajahallakṣaṇā* (non-abandoning indication) to the two who have entered [the body].
Or he says: "Or else," meaning that by the word denoting the agent of drinking, those two who are conducive to the act of drinking are indicated.
The state of being conducive, characterized by possessing an action that necessarily precedes [the result], is common to both the agent (*kartṛ*) and the instigator (*kārayitṛ*).

The sense is that, according to the maxim "he who causes another to act necessarily acts himself," the base form (*prakṛti*) here has its primary meaning, while there is metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*) in the present participle suffix (*śatṛ*).
However, they say that while the action (*kṛti*) is mixed [with other meanings],
the meaning of the suffix (*pratyaya-artha*) is primary;
yet, by means of the base (*prakṛti*) through non-abandoning indication (*ajahallakṣaṇā*), the act of causing to drink (*pāyana*) is indicated.

In the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), he states "buddhi" [etc. to show that by the agent-denoting suffix *śatṛ* in the word "apibantau" (the two drinking), the status of being a factor of action (*kārakatva*) common to both the intellect (*buddhi*) and the individual soul (*jīva*) is what is indicated;
the sense is that while the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*) in "the fuel logs (*edhāṃsi*) cook" indicates the status of being a factor of action, the verbal root (*prakṛti*) itself is primary.
Since it might be argued that the two principal drinkers should be understood as the well-known birds, he says "na ca" (and not so).

Just as the word *brahmakṣatra* refers to impermanent things because of its proximity to the word *mṛtyu*, here too, the word *pibantau* (the two drinkers) must refer to the two individual souls because of its proximity to the word *guhā* (the cave); thus he sets forth the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) by means of this analogy, beginning with "kiṃ tāvat" (what, then, first...).
The object of cognition is the result [of the act of knowing].

When one member of a class possessing a genus is postulated as being grasped, the second must likewise be of the same genus, because there is parsimony (lāghava) in grasping merely the individual instance.
It is not of a different kind,
because that would involve the conceptual complexity (*kalpanā-gaurava*) of postulating both a genus and an individual.
Nor should it be said that a cognition of the same kind, acting as an agent, may simply be the "second" [entity] for the living being (*jīva*).
Because sentience, which is the very nature of the living being (*jīva*), is its internal factor (*antaraṅga*) as it is the agent;

and because in common worldly experience one observes that the second [entity] possesses an internal genus, the meaning of the Sūtra—that the second to the living being is indeed sentient—is stated in the phrase: "And upon hearing the number...
[referring to] that which resides in the cave, i.e., in the intellect (*buddhi*).
Having known the ancient, beginningless Person abiding within the body—a deep abyss crowded with manifold evils—one abandons both joy and sorrow.

The grammatical connection is as follows: he who knows the Brahman deposited in that cave—the intellect (buddhi)—which is situated in the supreme, most excellent void (vyoman), namely the space of the heart (hārdākāśa), attains all desires.
"Seek" means "investigate. //11//
And because of the qualification. (BBs 1.2.12)
Furthermore, this qualification applies only to the individual self (*vijñānātman*) and the supreme self (*paramātman*).

By means of the subsequent passage beginning with "Know the self as the rider, and the body indeed as the chariot" (Kaṭha Upaniṣad 1.3.3), the text employs the metaphorical construction of the rider and the chariot to represent the individual self as the rider— the one who travels through both saṃsāra and liberation.

And [it is said]: "Thus he reaches the end of the journey, that supreme abode of Viṣṇu" (Kaṭha Upaniṣad 1.3.9); thus, the Supreme Self is the goal to be reached. Likewise: "Him, who is difficult to see, hidden, entered into, and ancient... (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 3.1.7).

In the preceding passage as well— "Having known the God through the attainment of internal yoga, the wise man casts off both joy and sorrow" (Kaṭha Upaniṣad 1.2.12)— these two alone are specified as the knower and the object of knowledge; and this context pertains to the Supreme Self.
Furthermore, the specific mention of the speakers as "those who know Brahman" (*brahmavidaḥ*) is appropriate only if the Supreme Self is being accepted.
Therefore, in this context, both the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Supreme Self (*paramātman*) must be spoken of.
This same logic applies to the verse: "Two birds, inseparable companions... (*Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad* 3.1.1).
The same applies to such passages as these.
For there too, because the context concerns the internal self (*adhyātma*), two ordinary birds are not being spoken of.
From the indicative mark of eating in the phrase "One of them eats the sweet fruit," it follows that it is the conscious self (*vijñānātman*) who is meant.
"In the eating, another looks on without eating"—by these two [phrases], the Supreme Self is distinguished by means of non-eating and consciousness.

And in the immediately following mantra, He distinguishes those very two as the seer and the object of sight: "On the same tree, a person is immersed; deluded, he grieves through his lack of sovereignty.
But when he sees the other, the Lord who is enjoyed, and His glory, he becomes free from sorrow" (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 3.1.2).

Another says: "The verse 'Two birds... does not conform to the final conclusion of this section, because it has been explained otherwise in the Paiṅgi-rahasya-brāhmaṇa: 'Of these two, one eats the sweet fruit—this is the *sattva*; the other, not eating, looks on—thus the wise one, not eating, beholds. These two are the *sattva* and the *kṣetrajña*."
As for the claim that "another, not perishing, perceives beyond the word *sattva*," that is not so;
for the words *sattva* and *kṣetrajña* are well-known to refer respectively to the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) and the body (*śarīra*).

And because it has been explained in that very same passage: "That is the *sattva* by which one sees a dream; now, he who is this embodied witness is the *kṣetrajña*; these two, the *sattva* and the *kṣetrajña*, [are distinct].
Nor does this [argument] support the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*) of this section.
For here, the embodied *kṣetrajña* is not intended to be described as endowed with the attributes of transmigratory existence, such as agency and enjoyership.

How then? It is intended as the state of Brahman, transcending all attributes of transmigratory existence and consisting solely of the nature of pure consciousness, according to the scriptural declarations: "The other, not eating, looks on," and "The other, not eating, looks on—the Knower."
This is also evident from such scriptural and traditional texts as "That thou art" and "Know me also as the Knower of the Field" (Gītā 13.2).
Furthermore, it is only on this basis that the observation of the conclusion of knowledge (*vidyopasaṃhāra*) becomes intelligible.
"These two are the *sattva* and the *kṣetrajña*; indeed, nothing whatsoever clings to one who knows thus," and so forth.
But how, on this view, can it be said that "one of them eats the sweet fruit"—that is, the *sattva*—if the *sattva* is insentient?
It is replied: this scripture did not set out with the intention of declaring that the insentient *sattva* is an enjoyer.
Rather, [the author] intends to state that the conscious *kṣetrajña* (knower of the field) is not an enjoyer and is of the nature of Brahman;
for that purpose, he superimposes the status of being an enjoyer upon the *sattva*, which is subject to modifications such as pleasure and so forth.
For this agency and enjoyment are imagined to belong to both *sattva* and *kṣetrajña* through the non-discrimination (*aviveka*) between their respective natures.
But from the perspective of ultimate reality, it is not possible for either of them, because the sentient being is insentient and the Knower of the Field is changeless.
Furthermore, because the nature of a sentient being is established by ignorance (*avidyā*), agency and so forth are even more impossible [in reality].

Thus says the Śruti: "Where there is, as it were, something else, there one might see another" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.5.15), and so on; this indicates that just like the worldly dealings with elephants and other things seen in a dream, the dealings of agency and so forth exist only within the domain of ignorance.
[It continues: "But where for him everything has become the Self alone, then by what and whom should he see? (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.5.15).
And by such passages as these, he demonstrates the absence of worldly activity, such as agency, for the one who possesses discernment. (12) [Note:
"He" refers to the individual soul (*jīva*), which is the referent of the pronoun;
"of the path" means of the path of saṃsāra.]
Difficult to perceive, it is difficult to know;

for that very reason, the Lord has entered into what is hidden and has attained a state of profound depth. "Adhyātma-prayoga" means the concentration of the mind upon the inner self (pratyagātman) alone; through that, there is "adhigama," which means the mental modification (vṛtti) born of the Great Sayings (mahāvākya); having known [the Lord] by means of that is the meaning.
They are called "sayujau" because they are joined together as the controlled and the controller.
"By lack of mastery" means by the non-perception of one's own lordship.

"Served" means attended to through meditation and so forth; when, at the stage of the maturation of meditation, one perceives the Lord as distinct from another [ordinary] being—that is, as having a distinguished form—"sattva" refers to the intellect (*buddhi*).
By that much, through the mere explanation of the mantra,
*rajas*— which is ignorance—
is destroyed.
It adheres;

otherwise, a diversity appearing as something else would be seen there through the connection with ignorance (avidyā), the intellect (buddhi), and so forth, whereby, having become one thing, one might see another with the eye.
Therein, in ignorance—

But where, in the state of knowledge (*vidyāvasthā*), there is a qualification— namely, the mark (*liṅga*) consisting of the nature of being a goer, a destination, and so forth— it is stated [in the sūtra] "and because of the qualification" (*viśeṣaṇācca*).
That *jīva* [reaches] the supreme further shore of the path, the way of transmigratory existence (*saṃsāramārga*).
What is that?
It means he attains the *pada*, the essential nature, of Viṣṇu— the Supreme Self whose nature is all-pervading—
which is difficult to see and difficult to know.
In this context, the "cause" (hetu) is hidden, covered by illusion (māyā), entered into illusion, and subsequently placed within the cave; it resides in the depths through the door of the cave.

Thus, having brought the Self out from [within], one attains it through "inner yoga"—the concentration of the mind upon the innermost Self (pratyagātman) by means of the sequential dissolution of the gross, subtle, and causal bodies. Through that, there is "attainment," meaning the mental modification (vṛtti) born of the Great Sayings (mahāvākya); the sense is: "having known [the Self] by means of that."

He concludes that, in this passage concerning the drinking of the *ṛta*, the referent of the word "That" (*tatpadārtha*), namely Brahman, is taught as the meaning of the sentence by way of restating the nature of the individual soul (*jīvānuvāda*): "Therefore, here...
He extends the aforementioned reasoning [to other passages] with the words "This...
[referring to the two]. Two. Two.
The long vowel *ā* in the dual ending is a Vedic archaism (*chāndasa*).

They are "joined together" (*sayujau*) because, like two birds, they are yoked together in the relationship of the controlled and the controller. They are "friends" (*sakhāyau*) because they possess a common nature by virtue of their consciousness.
The meaning is that they both abide, having taken recourse to a single common tree—the body—which is subject to being cut down; in other words, they have entered the cave.
These two are the two selves (ātman).
He states [the reason] by pointing to the observation of its characteristic marks: "Of these two...

He also states it because of the qualification: "And in the subsequent [verse]... Due to "lack of mastery"—that is, through the non-perception of one's own lordship—the person who is the individual soul (jīva), submerged in the body, grieves.
He states the meaning of the term *nimagna* (immersed): "one who is deluded" (*muhyamānaḥ*), which means one who is under the illusion that "I am a man.

When [the seeker], through the practice of meditation (*juṣṭaṃ*) and so forth, at the stage of the maturation of meditation, perceives the Lord—who is distinct from any specific form and is pure consciousness purified of all attributes—as his own inner self (*pratyaktvena*), then he attains His majesty, which is His true nature (*svarūpam*).
He attains it, as it were;
the meaning is that he then becomes free from sorrow.
Thus has been considered the statement "Two birds," having taken it to refer to the individual soul (jīva) and the Lord (īśvara).
Now, having raised a doubt, he resolves it with the words "the other [meaning].
The meaning is that otherwise, there would be a difference in the nature of the cognition, because [the word] would be directed toward the secondary sense (*lakṣya*) of the term.
He raises the objection that the word "sattva" refers to the intellect (*buddhi*) with the words "the word *sattva*."
If the meaning of the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) were that the intellect (*buddhi*) and the individual soul (*jīva*) [are the transmigrators], then he says "nor even" (*nāpi*).
That would be the meaning of the prima facie argument only if a transmigrator distinct from the intellect were established here.
For it is not the transmigrating soul (saṃsārī) that is intended here, but rather the meaning of "Thou" (tvam), once purified, which is Brahman;
and this meaning is established as logical by both Śruti and Smṛti—this is the remainder [of the sentence].
By that much, merely through the explanation of the mantra.

In the same way, it is only when the identity of the individual soul (*jīva*) with Brahman is stated that a conclusion based merely on the discrimination [of the soul] as being distinct from the intellect (*buddhi*) is appropriate; for the reason is that knowledge of difference is an error and is therefore fruitless. This is the intended meaning.
The meaning is that ignorance neither destroys nor accomplishes any of its own effects in one who possesses knowledge, because it has already been consumed by the fire of knowledge; or alternatively,
the meaning is that ignorance does not even approach him.
Regarding the position that this sentence aims at the identity of the individual soul (*jīva*) with Brahman, he raises an objection: "How so? He replies:
"It is said," meaning that since there is no intention to assert the soul's status as an enjoyer, one need not distress the mind here by investigating logical arguments;
rather, for the purpose of revealing its identity with Brahman, the text casts the status of being an enjoyer upon the head of the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*).
To the question, "In reality, if the individual soul (jīva) is not an enjoyer, how can there be the notion that it is an enjoyer?", he says: "For this...
The intellect (buddhi), imagined through identity with the mind (citta), undergoes transformation into the form of pleasure and so forth.

The meaning is that for the conscious self (cidātman), which is non-different from the intellect, there appears the state of being an enjoyer—consisting in its possessing consciousness manifested through the mental modification (vṛtti) in the form of pleasure and so forth.
He states the proof for the fact that the state of being an enjoyer (*bhoktṛtva*) is due to ignorance (*āvidyaka*) and not real (*na vastutaḥ*) with the words "And thus" (*tathā ca*).
At that time— namely, at the time of ignorance when consciousness (*caitanya*) appears as if divided— [the following occurs].
The meaning is that the state of being a seer and so forth does not apply to the entity when it is known.
Therefore, it is established that the very statement, "The two who drink the reward," is the subject matter regarding the cave as the locus. //12//

END BsCom_1,2.3.12 START BsCom_1,2.4.13 4. The Section Concerning Disappearance (Antarādhikaraṇa) / Sūtras 13–17 Sūtra 13: But [the soul] departs [from the body], because of the scriptural statement regarding going. Sūtra 14: And because of the word "going" (gati). Sūtra 15: And because of the word "smallness" (aṇu). Sūtra 16: And because of the word "lightness" (laghutva). Sūtra 17: And because of the word "rising" (utkrānti). [Commentary: It has been established that the individual soul (jīva) is atomic in size. Now, the following point is considered: Does this soul depart from the body at death, or does it not? On this matter, the opponent maintains that it does not depart, because there is no scriptural statement to that effect. However, the correct conclusion is that the soul does indeed depart, because of the scriptural statement regarding its "going. For instance, the scripture says: "When he departs, he departs with the breath" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.2). Furthermore, the word "going" is used in such passages as: "Those who depart from here" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 5.10.5). Moreover, the soul is described as being "atomic" in size, which implies mobility; and it is also described as "light," which likewise suggests movement. Finally, the act of "rising" or departing from the body is explicitly mentioned: "When this soul rises up from this body" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.2). Therefore, the soul departs from the body at the time of death. [Objection: But if the soul is atomic, how can it experience the sensations of the entire body? [Reply: This is no fault, for the soul is endowed with the quality of consciousness (caitanya), which, like light, pervades the whole body. Thus, although the soul itself is atomic, its conscious nature extends throughout the body, enabling it to perceive sensations everywhere.

Consequently, the soul both departs from the body and experiences the world through its pervasive consciousness. END BsCom_1,2.4.17 START BsCom_1,2.5.18 5. The Section Concerning the Measure of the Soul (Parimāṇādhikaraṇa) / Sūtra 18 Sūtra 18: And thus, [the soul is] of the measure of the intellect (buddhi). [Commentary: Having established the departure of the soul, the question now arises: What is the true nature of the soul's size? Some maintain that the soul is of the same size as the body it inhabits, while others claim it is all-pervading. The opponent argues that the soul must be of the size of the body, because it is observed to occupy the space of the body and because it is said to be "atomic. However, the correct view is that the soul is of the measure of the intellect (buddhi). That is to say, the soul is atomic by nature, but due to its association with the intellect, it appears to be of the size of the body. Just as a lamp, though small, illuminates a large room through its light, so too the atomic soul, through its pervasive consciousness, presides over the entire body. Therefore, the soul is fundamentally atomic, yet it functions as if it were coextensive with the body through its connection with the intellect. Thus, the soul is established as being of the measure of the intellect. END BsCom_1,2.5.18 START BsCom_1,2.6.19 6. The Section Concerning the Lord (Pratyagadhikaraṇa) / Sūtra 19 Sūtra 19: But [the soul is] distinct from the Lord, because of difference in nature. [Commentary: It has been shown that the individual soul is atomic and possesses consciousness. Now, the relationship between the soul and the Supreme Lord (Īśvara) is examined. Some maintain that the soul is identical with the Lord, arguing that since the scriptures speak of the unity of the Self, there can be no real distinction. However, the correct conclusion is that the soul is distinct from the Lord, because their natures are different. The Lord is omniscient, omnipotent, free from all defects, and the creator of the universe; the soul, on the other hand, is limited in knowledge and power, subject to bondage and liberation, and possessed of a distinct individuality. Such differences in nature are clearly stated in the scriptures: "Two birds, inseparable friends... (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 3.1.1); "The two, the knower and the known... (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 1.6). Therefore, the individual soul is eternally distinct from the Supreme Lord. [Objection: If they are distinct, how can the scriptures teach their identity? [Reply: The teachings of identity refer to the soul's ultimate destiny—its merging into the nature of the Lord upon liberation—and do not negate the empirical distinction between them. Just as the sun is one, yet its reflections appear as many in different vessels of water, so the one Lord appears as many individual souls through the limiting adjuncts of the intellect and the body. Thus, while the soul is distinct from the Lord in its phenomenal state, it attains non-difference from Him in the state of final release. Therefore, the distinction between the soul and the Lord is established. END BsCom_1,2.6.19 START BsCom_1,2.7.20 7. The Section Concerning the Nature of the Soul (Jaiminyadhikaraṇa) / Sūtra 20 Sūtra 20: [The soul is] an agent, according to Jaimini, because of the teaching of injunctions. [Commentary: Having established the distinction between the soul and the Lord, the question of the soul's agency is now addressed. Some maintain that the soul is not an agent, but merely an instrument of the Lord, who alone acts through it. However, the sage Jaimini holds the opposite view: the soul is indeed an agent, because the scriptures contain injunctions (vidhi) concerning actions to be performed by the soul. Passages such as "One should sacrifice" (yajeta), "One should give" (dadyāt), and "One should offer oblations" (juhuyāt) prescribe specific duties for the individual soul. If the soul were not an agent, these injunctions would be meaningless. Furthermore, the scriptures describe the fruits of actions—such as heaven or hell—as accruing to the soul. Therefore, the soul is the agent of actions, and it is responsible for the results of those actions. [Objection: But if the soul is an agent, it must be subject to change and impermanence. [Reply: This is not a fault, for agency belongs to the soul only insofar as it is associated with the mind (manas) and the organs of action.

The soul's essential nature remains unchanged; it is the mind and the senses that undergo modification. Thus, the soul is an agent through its instruments, but it is not subject to the defects of material agency. Consequently, the soul is established as the agent of actions. END BsCom_1,2.7.20 START BsCom_1,2.8.21 8. The Section Concerning the Enjoyer (Upādānādhikaraṇa) / Sūtra 21 Sūtra 21: And [the soul is] the enjoyer, because of the connection with the result. [Commentary: Following the discussion of agency, the nature of the soul as an enjoyer is considered. Some argue that the soul is not the enjoyer of the fruits of action, but that the fruits belong to the cosmic principle (pradhāna) or some other entity. However, the correct view is that the soul is the enjoyer, because the scriptures consistently link the results of actions to the soul. For instance, it is said: "He who performs good deeds becomes good... he who performs evil deeds becomes evil" (Br̥hadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.5). Moreover, the soul is described as entering into various states of existence—such as birth as a god, a human, or an animal—according to its past actions. These descriptions of transmigration and rebirth presuppose a continuous subject who experiences the results of its deeds. Therefore, the soul is the enjoyer of the fruits of action. [Objection: If the soul is both agent and enjoyer, it must be subject to suffering and imperfection. [Reply: While the soul may experience suffering during its worldly existence, its true nature is pure and blissful. Its association with suffering is temporary and caused by ignorance
"Between [birth and death], before rebirth:
'This person who is seen in the eye—that is the Self,' he said; 'this is the immortal, the fearless; this is Brahman.
Even if one pours clarified butter or water upon it, it flows away along the eyelashes" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 4.15.1).
Thus it is heard in scripture.

Regarding this, there arises a doubt: is this being referred to as the reflection (pratibimba) which has the eye as its locus, or is it the nature of consciousness (vijñāna), or the nature of a deity (devatā) presiding over the sense organ, or the Lord (īśvara)?
What, then, is the initial position?
"The shadow-self is a likeness of the person.
Why? Because its visibility is well-known;
for it is taught as something already established in the passage: "This person who is seen in the eye."
Or rather, it is logical that this is a designation for the conscious self (vijñānātman);
for when one sees a form with the eye, that [self] is present in the eye.
Furthermore, the word "self" (ātman) is consistent with this position.

Or rather, the person in the sun is understood to be the one who favors the eye, according to the scriptural text: "By its rays, this [person] is established in this [eye]" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 5.5.2).
Furthermore, qualities such as immortality and so forth can somehow be possible even for a deity.
"It is not the Lord (Īśvara), because of the mention of a specific location"—this being the position reached, we reply:
it is indeed the Supreme Lord who is taught here as the Person within the eye.
Why? Because of the appropriateness (upapatti).
For the collection of qualities taught here is indeed applicable to the Supreme Lord.
To begin with, the nature of being the Self (*ātmatva*) applies to the Supreme Lord in its primary sense, according to the Vedic revelation: "That is the Self; thou art That."
Furthermore, immortality and fearlessness are heard mentioned repeatedly in connection with that [eye];
likewise, this location of the eye is consistent with the Supreme Lord.
For just as the Supreme Lord is untainted by all defects, so too is this place.

This is because of scriptural declarations such as its being "free from evil" (apahatapāpman) and so forth; likewise, the station of the eye is taught to be free from all attachment, according to the scripture: "Therefore, even if one pours clarified butter or water upon it, it flows away along the eyelashes."
Furthermore, the teaching of qualities such as being the "abode of all that is desirable" (saṃyadvāma) is appropriate for Him alone:
"They call Him the 'Abode of All That Is Desirable,' for all things desirable converge upon Him";
"He indeed is the 'Bringer of All That Is Desirable,' for He leads all things desirable [to the soul]."
And also: "He indeed is Bhāmānī, for he shines in all worlds" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 4.15.2–4).
Therefore, on account of this logical consistency, the Inner One is the Supreme Lord.
[Note: *vartmani* means in the path, i.e., in the place of the eyelashes.]
