and "the abode of union."
Depending upon this Person in the eye as their cause, desirable fruits of action come together—that is, they arise.
She is "Vāmanī" because she leads to desirable things; she is "Śobhanī" because she leads to beautiful things;
she is "Bhāmanī" because she leads to all splendors and lights everywhere.
"Because of the intermediate birth.
He cites the passage concerning the Upakośala-knowledge as "He who...

The meaning is that this location in the eye is suitable for Brahman because of its non-attachment; for when [something] is cast into it, it goes between the two paths, namely, the eyelashes themselves.
He states a doubt regarding "vision" (darśana) based on its being either worldly or scriptural, using the word "therein" (tatra).
Previously, in accordance with the sentience heard first in the phrase "the two drinking," the later-mentioned features such as entering the cave were interpreted accordingly;

similarly here, in accordance with the fact that it is "seen"—that is, its visibility—the immortality and other attributes should be interpreted as being imagined for the purpose of meditation. Thus, he presents the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa) by means of the analogy: "the shadow-self" (chāyātma).
The result is that in the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa) there is meditation on the reflection, whereas in the final conclusion (siddhānta) there is meditation on Brahman;
this is indicated by the phrase "as if well-known."
The meaning is "by way of being visible.
He states another alternative by means of mere possibility with the words "of the nature of consciousness," and so forth,
just as in the case of [the statement] "Mind is Brahman."

The prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that because the sentence "This is Brahman" (*etad brahma iti*) is headed by the particle *iti*, it does not have its own literal meaning as its primary purport.

The final conclusion (*siddhānta*), however, establishes that it refers to the Supreme Lord alone; for while in the passage "One should meditate on the mind as Brahman" (*mano brahmety upāsīta*) the particle *iti* refers to the mental cognition (*pratyaya*), here—in the construction "He said, 'Brahman'" (*brahmety uvāca*)—the particle *iti* relates to the speech itself and thus has the literal meaning as its purport, making the two cases dissimilar.

According to the principle that "corroboration by multiple authorities supports the intended meaning," he states—beginning with the words "saṃyadvāma"—that the visible mark is sublated by the scriptural passages concerning the Self and Brahman, which are supported by this logic.
"Saṃyadvāma" means that desirable things—the fruits of actions—converge toward, or arise from, this Person in the eye;
the sense is that He is the cause for the emergence of all fruits.
He says that this very [Brahman] is also the bestower of fruits upon the worlds— “vāmanīḥ” means it leads forth the fruits, that is, it causes the worlds to attain them;
it says “bhāmanīḥ” because it leads forth the lights (bhāma).
The meaning is that it illuminates all objects. //13//
And because of the designation of place and so forth. (BS 1.2.14)
But how, it may be asked, is it possible for Brahman, which is all-pervading like space, to have its location in the eye?
To this it is replied: this objection would indeed be valid if this were the only location specified for it.
For other locations for this [Brahman], such as the earth and so forth, have indeed been specified by the passage beginning, "He who dwells in the earth" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.7.3).
For in those [passages], the eye is also specified: "He who dwells in the eye.

By the inclusion of the word "and so forth" in the sūtra phrase "Because of the mention of location and so forth," he shows that it is not only an unsuitable location that is seen being mentioned for Brahman.

What then? Even such things as "name-and-form" (nāmarūpa), though inappropriate for Brahman which is itself devoid of name and form, are seen being designated [of it], as in: "His name is 'Ut' (he rises)" and "He has golden beard" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 1.6.7, 6).

It has already been stated that although Brahman is indeed without qualities (nirguṇa), it is taught in various places as possessing qualities (saguṇa) by means of the qualities belonging to name and form, for the purpose of meditation (upāsana).

It has already been stated that even for Brahman, who is omnipresent, a specific location is not contradictory for the purpose of its perception, just as in the case of Viṣṇu at Śālagrāma; this has indeed been explained. (14) [Note:

Regarding the phrase "sthānādanyādayaḥ," those which have their origin in place and so forth are the "place-originated" varieties of name and form; because of the designation of these, a restriction to a single location for that which is omnipresent is not tenable.]

The construction of the sūtra is as follows: there is no fault in the statement here that the eye is the location [of the person within the sun], because the location, name, and form are taught for the purpose of meditation even in another Vedic text (śrutyantara).
"Impossibility" (anavakḷpti) means the assumption of what is not established; the syntactical connection is: "that would be so if it were specified in this very context."
Anticipating the objection that "the statement of an abundance of inappropriate [qualities] is a lack of resolution," he states the reasoning: "Even though it is devoid of qualities... (14).
And because it designates [the Self] as distinguished by happiness. 1.2.15.
Moreover, there should be no dispute here as to whether Brahman is denoted by this sentence or not;
for it is established that the very designation of that which is distinguished by bliss constitutes Brahman-hood.

For it is Brahman, distinguished by bliss, which was introduced at the beginning of the passage as "Prāṇa is Brahman, Ka is Brahman, Kha is Brahman," that is indeed what is referred to here; for it is logical to maintain the subject matter under discussion.
[As stated: "But the teacher will tell you the way" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 4.14.1).
And because there is a promise to explain only the path [to Brahman], how then is Brahman qualified by bliss understood at the beginning of the discourse? It is said:
Having heard these words of the fires—"Prāṇa is Brahman, Ka is Brahman, Kha is Brahman"—Upakosala said: "I understand that prāṇa is Brahman, but what is Ka and what is Kha?"
"I do not perceive.
To this, the reply is: "That which is indeed *kaṃ* is the same as *kha*; that which is *kha* is the same as *kaṃ*" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 4.10.5).
In this context, the word *kha* is established in common usage as referring to elemental space (*bhūtākāśa*).
If the word *ka*, denoting happiness, were not employed as its qualifier,
it would follow that the word *brahman* is applied to mere elemental space with the intention of treating it as a mere symbol (*pratīka*), just as it is applied to names and so forth.
Likewise, since the word *ka* is well-known to denote the conventional pleasure produced by the contact of the sense organs with their objects,
if the word *kha* were not employed as its qualifier,
there would arise the misconception that worldly pleasure is Brahman.
However, when "kaṃ" and "khaṃ" are mutually qualified, they lead one to understand Brahman as consisting of bliss.

In that regard, if the second word "brahman" were not employed and it were merely said, "kaṃ khaṃ brahma," then because the word "kaṃ" would be used solely as a qualifier, the quality of bliss (sukha) would become something to be meditated upon rather than the object of meditation itself.
To prevent this, both words "kaṃ" and "khaṃ" have the word "brahman" as their head, resulting in the expression: "kaṃ brahma, khaṃ brahma."
For it is indeed desirable that even the quality of bliss should be meditated upon as possessing qualities.
Thus, at the beginning of the passage, Brahman is taught as qualified by bliss.

Furthermore, each of the fires—the Gārhapatya and the others—having taught its own respective majesty, conclude by saying, "This, my dear, is your knowledge of us, and the knowledge of the Self. This indicates that Brahman was pointed out previously.
They make it known;
and the promise to declare the goal alone in the words, "But the Teacher will tell you the way" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.14.2), excludes the intention to speak of any other matter.
As it is said: "Just as water does not cling to a lotus leaf, even so evil action does not cling to one who knows this" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 4.14.3).
Thus, by declaring that one who knows the Person residing in the eye is not afflicted by evil, the text demonstrates that the Person residing in the eye is Brahman.

Therefore, having stated that the very Brahman under discussion resides in the eye and possesses qualities such as being the "conductor of blessings" (*saṃyadvāma*), the text begins with the intention: "I shall describe the path consisting of light and so forth for the knower of That": "That person who is seen in the eye, this is the Self," he said.
A *pratīka* is the transfer of a cognition from one substratum to another substratum.
"Accompanied by *āmaya*" means accompanied by that which is subject to decay, dependence, and so forth.
Because their referents are specified, the two words are also said to be specified.

By virtue of being qualifiers (*viśeṣaṇatvena*), they serve to exclude [the possibility] of its being a past entity (*bhūtatva*). That which has "Brahman" as its head is *brahmaśiras*; the state of being such is *brahmaśirastva*.
He states that Brahman must also be understood from the context by saying, "qualified by bliss.

The meaning of the Sūtra is this: since Brahman, which is the subject under discussion and qualified by the attribute of bliss, is designated by the pronoun "this" (*ya eṣa*) through a conceptual differentiation for the purpose of meditation, the Inner One must be the Supreme Self (*paramātman*).

An objection is raised: "But surely the reflected self (*chāyātman*), brought forward by the mark of being visible (*dṛśyatva*), which is more powerful than the context, is the referent of the pronoun"; to this he replies, "The Teacher, however... (*ācāryastu*).
A certain student named Upakośala served the teacher Jābāla as a *brahmacārin* for twelve years.

When Jābāla had gone abroad and failed to instruct him, [Upakośala’s father] out of compassion taught him the knowledge of the Self (*ātmavidyā*) through the fires of the *gārhapatya* and others, saying, "Brahman is the breath" (*aprāṇo brahma*). Then it was said: "The teacher, however...
The meaning is that he will tell you the path consisting of light (*arcis*) and so forth, for the sake of attaining the fruit of the knowledge of the Self.
Subsequently, the Teacher having arrived, said, "This which is in the eye," and thus described the path beginning with light (arcir-ādi).
In this way, the syntactic unity (*ekavākyatā*) of the passage concerning the knowledge of the Self (*ātmavidyā*) spoken by the fires must be asserted with the passage concerning the path;

and that unity is established when the pronoun (*sarvanāman*) refers back to the Self under discussion. Therefore, the sense is that the context (*prakaraṇa*), which effects such syntactic unity, is stronger than the indicative mark (*liṅga*) which would otherwise cause a split in the sentence (*vākyabheda*).
The scripture explains this: "It is said.

The meaning is: "I know that the vital breath (prāṇa), which is the thread-self (sūtrātman), is Brahman because of its vastness; however, I am unable to know 'ka'—the pleasure of sense objects—and 'kha'—the elemental ether—as Brahman."
Of what nature is space (*kha*)?
That which is bliss (*ka*) is itself space; thus, by qualifying space with bliss, its status as a mere element is excluded. Likewise, of what nature is bliss (*ka*)?

"That which is space (kha) is indeed bliss (ka)"—this excludes the possibility that space, as qualified by its omnipresence (vibhutva), could be something produced. He expresses this through the method of negative concomitance (vyatireka) with the words "therein, space," etc.
The sense is that meditative worship of a symbol (pratīkadhyāna) is not intended here, because it would contradict the Vedic revelation stating "the knowledge of the Self" (ātmavidyā).
[The term] "sāmaya" means...
"Affliction" (*āmaya*) refers to defects such as dependence on means of accomplishment, impermanence, and so forth; the meaning is "accompanied by that.
Having stated the fault in grasping [the two] individually, he states the result of grasping them together in the words "mutually... (*itaretara*).
The meaning is that [the two words] have distinct referents.
Now, one might ask: "If Brahman alone is to be meditated upon here, what is the purpose of the other word 'Brahman'? To this he says: "Therein" (*tatra*).
The meaning is that it serves as a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*), specifically by excluding [the possibility of] the ether being an element (*bhūta*).
The analysis of the compound is: "that whose head is the word *brahman* is the reality (*tattva*).
To the question, "What fault is there in its being an object of study? he replies: "For it is desired... and so forth.
The sense is that by the mention of the "path," it is understood that [the subject] is a knowledge possessing excellent qualities (*suguṇavidyā*).
Furthermore, he states that the subject under discussion is Brahman because of the concluding summary using the term "knowledge of the Self" (*ātmavidyā*): "And each...
The Gārhapatya fire taught: "Earth, fire, food, and the sun—these are my four bodies, my manifestation (*vibhūti*)."
"The waters, the quarters, the stars, and the moon"—thus spoke the Anvāhāryapacana fire.
"The vital breath, space, the sky, and lightning"—thus the Āhavanīya fire proclaimed its own majesty. This is the knowledge of our fires, stated individually for each.

The meaning is that the knowledge of the Self (*ātmavidyā*), however, was previously stated by us collectively as "Breath is Brahman. To the objection that Brahman might be spoken of by the fires [of the body] and the shadow-self (*chāyātman*) by the teacher—due to the difference in speakers—the author replies: "But the Teacher... [and so forth].
The meaning is that because there is certainty regarding the unity of the statement, there is no difference in meaning even when there is a difference among the speakers. //15//
And because there is a description of the path for one who has heard the Upaniṣads. (BS 1.2.16)
Furthermore, the person residing in the eye is the Supreme Lord,

because the scripture declares that for the knower of Brahman— who has heard the Upaniṣads and realized the secret knowledge— the well-known path called Devayāna is his destination: "Then, having sought the Self through austerity, celibacy, faith, and knowledge, they conquer the sun by the northern route."
"This indeed is the abode of the vital breaths, this is the immortal, the fearless; this is the supreme goal, from which they do not return" (Praśna Upaniṣad 1.10).
Also in the Smṛti: "Fire, light, day, the bright fortnight, the six months of the northern solstice—departing there, people who know Brahman go to Brahman" (Bhagavad Gītā 8.24).
That very [path] is seen being described for those who know the Person within the eye, beginning with:
"Now, whether they perform funeral rites for him here or not, they pass into the light (arcis)"; and continuing:
"From the sun to the moon, from the moon to the lightning; there a person who is not human leads them to Brahman."
"The path of the gods, the path of Brahman; those proceeding by this do not return to this human whirlpool" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 4.15.5).
Thus, here, by means of the well-known destination pertaining to the knower of Brahman, it is determined that the one situated in the eye is Brahman. [Note:
The meaning of the word "atha" (then) is the immediate succession following the fall of the body.]
This is the station of Hiraṇyagarbha, consisting of both the individual and the collective cause.
When a practitioner of this meditation dies, his sons and others perform the funeral rites and other ceremonies pertaining to the corpse (*śavya*). This occurs within the creation of Manu (*mānava*).
"In the whirlpool" (āvarte) means that which is joined with the cycle of birth, death, and so forth.

"Whose secret doctrine" (upaniṣad)—meaning the meditation on the qualified Brahman—has been heard and practiced; the destination (gati) of such a person, well-known from both Śruti and Smṛti, is mentioned here. He states the meaning of the Sūtra—"for this reason also"—as follows:
the syntactical connection is "because it is seen [in scripture], therefore it is so here."
He cites the scriptural authority with the words "atha" (now).
The meaning is: immediately after the fall of the body.

Having meditated upon the Self through one's own duty—namely, austerity consisting of penance, celibacy, faith, and knowledge—one attains the northern path of the gods (*devayāna*) by means of that knowledge of meditation; it is not [attained] by the northern path [in the ordinary sense].
By way of the sun, they go to the abode of the qualified Brahman;
this indeed is the abode of the vital breaths, both in their individual and collective forms—the subtle body (liṅga-ātman) in the form of Hiraṇyagarbha.
In reality, however, this is the attributeless foundation of all, consisting of immortality and so forth.

Therefore, the meaning is that having attained the Brahman that is the effect and having known its nature to be devoid of qualities (nirguṇa), they are liberated. Fire itself is the deity of light; in this manner, the deities of the day and so forth are mentioned in the Smṛti. When this practitioner has died, whether his sons and others perform the funeral rites (*śavya*) such as the consecration of the corpse or do not perform them—in either case, by the power of their meditation, [they proceed] successively through the deities beginning with the Rays of Light (*arcis*).
They go to the fire with its flames,
and from there to day.
From the day to the bright fortnight,
from there to the northern solstice, and from that to the year.
From there to the world of the gods, from there to the wind,
and from the wind to the sun.

From there, having gone from the moon to lightning, a non-human person (amānavaḥ puruṣaḥ) comes from the world of Brahmā and leads the worshippers stationed in that world of lightning to the world of Brahmā, which is their destination.

This is the "Path of the Gods" (devapatha), distinguished by the deities beginning with Light, and it is also called the "Path of Brahmā" (brahmapatha) because of its connection with the Brahmā who is to be reached.
Those worshippers who attain this Brahman as their goal do not return—that is, they do not come back—to this human creation of Manu, which is characterized by the cycle of birth and death. //16//
Because of non-abiding and because of impossibility, it is not the other.
Furthermore, as for what was said— that the one situated in the eye might be the self consisting of shadow, the self consisting of consciousness, or the self consisting of divinity— this is not so.
To this it is replied: Here, the reflection-self (chāyātman) and others are not fit to be grasped as the "other" [the Self].
Why? Because of instability. For it is not possible for the reflection-self to have a permanent abiding in the eye.
For whenever a certain person approaches the eye, the reflection of that person is seen in the eye,
and when he has departed, it is no longer seen.
Furthermore, the scriptural text, "This person who is in the eye," by virtue of proximity, teaches that the person being seen in one's own eye is to be meditated upon.
Nor is it reasonable to assume that one performs meditation by placing some person who serves as a shadow near the eyes;
for the scripture, stating "He perishes following the destruction of this very body" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.9.1), shows that even the shadow-self is unstable.
Furthermore, because of the impossibility [of those qualities] in it, there can be no perception of qualities such as immortality in the reflected self (chāyātman).
Likewise, since the individual conscious self (vijñānātman) is connected to the entire body and its sense organs in common, it cannot be said that it resides only in the eye.
However, although Brahman is all-pervading, its connection with specific locations such as the heart is observed for the purpose of apprehension.
And likewise, even in the case of the individual self (*vijñānātman*), there is no connection with attributes such as immortality;

for although the individual self is indeed non-different from the supreme self (*paramātman*), nevertheless, mortality and fear— which are produced by ignorance, desire, and action— are superimposed upon it, and thus immortality and fearlessness are not possible [for it].
Furthermore, qualities such as being the "conductor of blessings" (*saṃyadvāma*) are entirely untenable in this [individual soul] because it lacks sovereignty.

As for the self of the deity, although its abiding in the eye might exist— according to the scriptural text, "By means of rays, he is established in this"— nevertheless, its being the Self (*ātmatva*) is not possible,
because it is of an outward-turned nature (*parāgrūpatvāt*).
Even immortality and other such qualities are not possible,
because their birth and dissolution are heard of in scripture;
even the immortality of the gods is relative to their remaining for a long period of time.
Even sovereignty is dependent upon the Supreme Lord and is not inherent; for it is said: "From fear of Him the wind blows, from fear the sun rises;
from fear of Him Agni and Indra, and Death as the fifth, run forth" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.8).

Thus, from the wording of the mantra, it must be understood that this one residing in the eye is indeed the Supreme Lord. And in this view, the expression "is seen" is to be explained as a reference to what is well-known, depending upon the scriptures and so forth, and intended for the sake of inspiring the wise. // 17 //

The Section on the Inner Ruler (Antaryāmy-adhikaraṇa) / Sūtras 18–20 Sūtra 18: "The inner ruler who dwells within the earth, yet is other than the earth, whom the earth does not know, whose body the earth is, and who rules the earth from within—He is Your Self, the inner ruler, the immortal.

Sūtra 19: "The inner ruler who dwells within the water, yet is other than the water... Sūtra 20: "The inner ruler who dwells within the fire, yet is other than the fire... [The sūtras continue in this manner for all elements and beings, up to: Sūtra 20: "The inner ruler who dwells within the self, yet is other than the self, whom the self does not know, whose body the self is, and who rules the self from within—He is Your Self, the inner ruler, the immortal. Regarding this, a doubt arises: Is the inner ruler mentioned here the individual soul (jīva), or is it the Supreme Lord? The opponent maintains: It must be the individual soul, because the attributes of being "other than" and "not known by" the respective entities (earth, etc. are appropriate for a conscious being distinct from them. Furthermore, the term "Self" (ātman) is commonly used for the individual soul. Therefore, the inner ruler is the individual soul. To this, we reply: The inner ruler is the Supreme Lord alone. Why? Because of the characteristics of ruling and so forth. The scripture describes Him as one who "rules the earth from within," and so on. Such sovereign power over all things is possible only for the Supreme Lord. Moreover, the attributes of being "other than" and "not known by" the earth and the rest indicate that He is distinct from all created beings. The term "Self" is used here in its primary sense to denote the Supreme Self, just as in the passage, "This is your Self, which is within all" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.4.1). Furthermore, the mention of immortality confirms that the Supreme Lord is intended. Therefore, the inner ruler is the Supreme Lord. Thus ends the section on the Inner Ruler. Sūtras 18–20. END BsCom_1,2.5.18 START BsCom_1,2.6.19 6. The Section on the Breath (Prāṇa-adhikaraṇa) / Sūtras 19–32. [Note: The provided text fragment ends at the conclusion of the Antaryāmi section.]
The Inner Ruler (Antaryāmin) [is Brahman], because his attributes are designated in relation to the deities, the worlds, and so forth.
Beginning with the passage, "He who rules from within this world and the other world, and all beings," the scripture continues:
"He who dwells in the earth, yet is within the earth, whom the earth does not know, whose body the earth is... [and so on].
"He who, dwelling within the body, controls the earth—He is your Self, the Inner Controller, the Immortal" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.7.1, 2), and so forth.

Here, it is heard that there is a certain Inner Controller (*antaryāmin*) who, dwelling within, acts as a ruler with respect to the deities (*adhidaivata*), the worlds (*adhiloka*), the Vedas (*adhiveda*), the sacrifice (*adhiyajña*), the elements (*adhibhūta*), and the self (*adhyātma*).

Regarding this, a doubt arises because an unfamiliar designation is seen: Is He some deity-soul presiding over the deities and so forth? Or is He some yogi who has attained powers such as *aṇimā*? Or is He the Supreme Self (*paramātman*)? Or is He something else entirely?
What first occurs to us is this: since the designation (*saṃjñā*) is not established, the designated object (*saṃjñin*) must also be some other entity that is itself unestablished.
Alternatively, it is impossible to accept the existence of another entity whose form has not been determined.
Furthermore, the word *antaryāmin* (the inner controller) is not entirely unfamiliar, as it is applied in the sense of "one who controls from within.
Therefore, some deity presiding over the earth and other elements might be the *antaryāmin*.
And so it is heard in scripture: "He whose abode is the earth, whose world is fire, whose light is the mind," and so forth (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.9.10).
And since that [Self] possesses the nature of cause and effect, it is logical that the deity-self, abiding within the earth and other elements, controls them;
or else, some perfected yogin might possess controlling power by entering into all things.
However, the Supreme Self would not be so understood.

Since it might be argued that [the inner ruler] is not the Supreme Self because he performs actions, the following is stated: That which is heard of as the inner ruler (antaryāmin) with respect to the divine and other spheres must be the Supreme Self alone and nothing else.
Why? Because of the designation of His attributes;
for the attributes of that Supreme Self are indeed seen being pointed out here.

The attribute of being the controller is appropriate for the Supreme Self, as it presides within and governs the entire aggregate of modifications—beginning with earth and so forth—which is divided according to the distinctions of deities and other categories;
for since it is the cause of all modifications, the possession of all powers is logically established.
Furthermore, the attributes of being the Self and being immortal are primarily applicable to the Supreme Self in the statement, "This is your Self, the inner controller, the immortal."

Furthermore, by stating "whom the earth does not know," the text shows that the inner controller (antaryāmin) is distinct from the self of the deity, as it speaks of an inner controller who is unknowable even to the deity of the earth;
for the deity of the earth would indeed know itself as "I am the earth.
Likewise, designations such as "unseen" and "unheard" are appropriate for the Supreme Self because it is devoid of form and other such qualities.
As for the objection that the status of being a controller is not possible for the Supreme Self, which is devoid of organs of action—
this is not a fault;
for He controls by means of those very organs of action [belonging to those He governs].
Because its status as both cause and instrument is logically established;
furthermore, the fault of infinite regress— whereby one would have to postulate another controller for it— does not arise,
owing to the absence of any distinction [between them].
For if there were a distinction [between them], the fault of infinite regress would result.
Therefore, the Inner Controller (antaryāmī) is indeed the Supreme Self alone. (18) [Note:
"Āyatana" means the body.]
The "eye of the world" (lokya-cakṣus) is that by which the world is perceived; it is the light-mind (jyotiḥ-manas).
This is because its attributes are designated in relation to the inner ruler (antaryāmin) with respect to the divine realm and so forth.
He cites a passage from the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad with the words "yaḥ" (he who).
He states the meaning as it appears in the context of the Antaryāmin-Brahman with the word "atra" (here):
by the passage beginning with "yaḥ pṛthivyām" (he who [is] in the earth), a controller is heard of in reference to the deities such as the Earth and others.
Likewise: "He who [dwells] in all worlds" refers to the locus of the worlds (adhiloka); "He who [dwells] in all Vedas" refers to the locus of the Vedas (adhiveda);
"He who [dwells] in all sacrifices" refers to the locus of sacrifice (adhiyajña).

The division is as follows: "He who [dwells] in all beings" refers to the objective realm (adhibhūta); and from "He who dwells in the vital breath" up to "He who dwells in the self" refers to the subjective realm (adhyātma).
Doubt arises from the question of whether or not it is possible for that which is bodiless to be a controller.

In the preceding section, the mention of abodes such as the earth was stated as an illustration (*dṛṣṭānta*) for the purpose of establishing that the Lord has the eye as His locus; here, the claim that this illustrative statement refers to the Lord is challenged and then resolved—this constitutes the "contextual connection by way of an objection" (*ākṣepasaṃgati*).
Therefore, this section possesses the character of a "sub-branch" (*phala*) in relation to the result of the preceding one.

However, it should be understood that the intermediate result in the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is the meditation on [Brahman] as non-lordly (*anīśvara*), whereas in the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) it is the knowledge of Brahman as the inner self (*pratyagbrahma*).
Stating his own lack of satisfaction, he proposes an alternative position, beginning with "Or rather" (*athavā*).
The meaning is that since there is an absence of fruit when the object is uncertain, it is impossible for that which lacks fruit to be the meaning of the Veda.
Thus it is heard in the Veda:
"The earth is the abode, the body, of that deity..."
"World" (*loka*) means that by which one sees, namely the eye;
"light" (*jyotis*) means the mind, which illuminates all objects.

Because the identity of the inner ruler (*antaryāmin*) is determined through the introductory context and other means, the position of multiple deities is not tenable; expressing dissatisfaction with this, he says, "or of the yogin."

Since it would involve the conceptual complexity of postulating an unestablished means for something that is established as adventitious, he establishes the final position—that the Inner Controller (antaryāmin) is indeed eternally established—by stating, "This being the case...
He states another reason for rejecting [the idea that] a deity [is the controller] with the words, "Whom the earth...
[He concludes that] the Lord (Īśvara) is not the controller.
He refutes the argument "because of being bodiless, like a jar" by stating, "this is not a fault.
Alternatively, the reason may be "the absence of a body distinct from that which is to be controlled."
Or [the definition may be] "not being connected with a body.
In the first case, there is a deviation (vyabhicāra) in the case of the individual soul (jīva), which is the controller of its own body.
The second [definition], however, is unestablished (asiddha).
He says, "those whom He controls," because the Lord possesses all connections acquired through His own ignorance (*avidyā*).

This statement—that He is the controller while possessing a body—is made in accordance with worldly perception. In reality, however, the activity of the insentient (*jaḍa*) due to proximity to the conscious principle is "control" (*niyamana*); the state of possessing that power is "controllership" (*niyantṛtva*).

And that [agency] is possible for the conscious self (cidātman) through its inconceivable power of illusion (māyā-śakti), even without a body. Now, one might object: "If there is a controller other than the individual soul (jīva) who controls the body, then there must be yet another controller for him, leading to an infinite regress. To this, he says: "Of him also... The Lord's (Īśvara’s) unrestricted sovereignty as the controller of all is established by scripture.
The meaning is that there is no infinite regress (anavasthā) because the inference of another controller for him is sublated by scripture (śrutibādha).

Alternatively, since the statement that the individual soul (jīva) is the controller is made based on a conceptual distinction from God (īśvara), and not because of an actual difference, there is no infinite regress. //18//
And it is not based on Smṛti, because there is no mention of its specific characteristics. 1.2.19.
It might be argued as follows:
properties such as being unperceived and so forth are also applicable to the *pradhāna* (primordial matter) postulated in the Sāṃkhya tradition,
because they accept that it is devoid of form and other such qualities.
For they record in their tradition: "It is beyond reasoning, unknowable, as if entirely asleep" (Manu Smṛti 1.5);
and its status as the controller is established because it is the cause of all modifications.
Therefore, the term *antaryāmin* (the inner controller) should refer to the Pradhāna.

Although the Pradhāna was already refuted in the sūtra "Because of seeing [it], it is not that which is not based on scripture" (Brahma-sūtra 1.1.5), it is raised here again by way of a doubt, since designations such as "not being seen" and so forth could possibly apply to it.
To this, the following is said: Furthermore, the Pradhāna, which is known through Smṛti, cannot be the referent of the word "Antaryāmin.
Why? Because of the description of qualities that do not belong to it.
Even though the designation of being unseen and so forth is possible for the Pradhāna, nevertheless, the designation of being a seer and so forth is not possible.
For they admit that the *pradhāna* is insentient;
indeed, the supplementary passage here is: "The unseen seer, the unheard hearer, the unthought thinker, the unknown knower" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.7.23).
Furthermore, the nature of a self is not tenable for the Pradhāna. 19.
If the Pradhāna is not accepted as the Inner Controller because qualities such as selfhood and being a seer are impossible for it, then let the embodied soul (śārīra) be the Inner Controller;
for the embodied soul, being conscious, is indeed a seer, a hearer, a thinker, and a knower.
And the self is [the agent] because of its inwardness;
it is also immortal, because the experience of the fruits of merit and demerit is logically possible.

Furthermore, attributes such as invisibility and so forth belong to the embodied self according to the opponent’s own tenets, since there is a contradiction in the activity of actions such as seeing being directed toward the agent itself.
And from such scriptural passages as, "One should not see the seer of seeing" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.4.2),
it follows that its nature is to inwardly govern the aggregate of the body and the organs.
Because [the embodied soul] is an enjoyer;
therefore, the embodied soul is the Inner Controller (antaryāmī). To this, he recites the following answer:
"And because it is immortal"—meaning that for one who is perishable, the enjoyment of experiences in another body would be impossible.
Regarding the term "agent" (*kartṛ*): in an action, the agent is subordinate (*guṇa*) while the object (*karman*) is primary (*pradhāna*).
Since it is contradictory for a single entity to possess both subordination and primacy within a single action, the meaning is that the agent cannot simultaneously function as the object.
He states that "it is beyond reasoning" (apratarkya) because it is not an object of logical inquiry as to how the Pradhāna proceeds through the sequence beginning with Mahat.
Because it is devoid of form and other such qualities, it is unknowable;
the meaning is that, due to its insentience, it remains as if asleep in all directions.
That which is non-principal is insentient;
the meaning of the reason is that it is because [the Sūtra] designates its properties (dharmas). //19//
For both [schools] also study this as distinct from the body. (BBs 1.2.20)
The word "not" (na) is carried over from the preceding sūtra.
Furthermore, the embodied self (śārīra) is not intended to be the inner ruler (antaryāmī).
Why?

Although attributes such as being a seer are possible for it, nevertheless, because it is delimited by limiting adjuncts (upādhi) like the space within a jar, it is not able to abide within or to rule over the earth and other elements in their entirety. Furthermore, both branches of the Veda—the Kāṇvas and the Mādhyandinas—teach this embodied self as distinct from the Inner Ruler (antaryāmin), as its locus and as that which is to be ruled, just like the earth and so forth: "He who [dwells] in consciousness..."
The Kāṇvas read: "He who dwells" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.7.22);
the Mādhyandinas read: "He who dwells in the self.
In this reading, "He who dwells in the self," the word *ātman* denotes the embodied soul (*śārīra*).
Even in this reading, "He who dwells in consciousness," the word "consciousness" (vijñāna) refers to the embodied self (śārīra),
for the embodied self consists of consciousness.
Therefore, it is established that the Inner Controller (antaryāmī) is the Lord, distinct from the embodied self.
But how, again, can two seers be possible within a single body—
one who is this Lord, the inner controller (antaryāmī), and the other who is this embodied soul (śārīra)? What, then, is the impossibility here?
Otherwise, scriptural statements such as "There is no other seer than this" would be contradicted;
for in this context, [the scripture denies] any seer or hearer other than the Antaryāmin under discussion.
It negates the self as a thinker and a cognizer.
If it is argued that this statement is for the purpose of negating another controller, we say no.
Because it would otherwise follow that there must be another controller, and because no distinction [between them] is heard in scripture.
To this it is replied:

This designation of a difference between the embodied self (śārīra) and the inner ruler (antaryāmin) is caused by the limiting adjuncts (upādhi) consisting of the body and organs presented by ignorance (avidyā); it is not ultimate (pāramārthika).
For the inner self is indeed one; two inner selves cannot possibly exist.
However, the conventional usage of distinction regarding that which is one alone is caused by limiting adjuncts (upādhi), just as [one speaks of] the space within a jar and the great space.

Consequently, all of this becomes intelligible: the scriptural texts concerning the distinction between the knower and the known, the means of valid cognition such as perception, the experience of transmigratory existence, and the scripture of injunctions and prohibitions.
Thus, the Śruti says, "For where there is duality, as it were, there one sees another," showing that all worldly activity pertains to the sphere of ignorance (*avidyā*);
and, "But where for him everything has become the Self alone, then by what and whom should he see?"—this prohibits all worldly activity in the sphere of knowledge (*vidyā*). (20)
He states the doubt to be refuted by the *Attara-sūtra* with the words "If [it were] the Pradhāna," and so forth.
Regarding the phrase "and being immortal":
the meaning is that for one who perishes, the experience of another body would be impossible.

Just as in the act of going performed by Devadatta, the village is the object (*karman*) and not Devadatta himself, so too in the acts of seeing and so forth performed by the self (*ātman*), the non-self (*anātman*) is the objective domain (*viṣaya*) and not the self, because it is impossible for an action to have its own agent as its object; thus he says: "In the agent... (*kartari*).
In an action, the agent is subordinate (guṇa) and the object is primary (pradhāna);
since it is contradictory for one and the same entity to possess both subordination and primacy within a single action, the meaning is that the agent cannot simultaneously be the object.

"One should not make the Self, the seer of seeing, an object of that very seeing which is itself seen," according to such scriptural passages; therefore, he says "no" because attributes such as being unseen belong to the embodied self (śārīra).
Having stated the reason implied by the word "also" (api), he states the reason explicitly expressed: "Moreover, both [the Sāṃkhya and the Vaiśeṣika]...
He raises an objection—asking "How so?"—in order to dispel the delusion of real difference arising from the word "difference" (bheda) in the Sūtra.

Now, one might raise the objection that there is no contradiction here, since the individual soul (*jīva*) is the enjoyer while the Lord (*īśvara*) is not the enjoyer; this is expressed by the question "But what [is the difference]?
The opponent replies, "None other," asserting that the distinction between the two is contradicted by scripture.
He states the meaning of the scripture itself with the words "herein.
Having raised a doubt regarding another possible meaning of the scripture, he refutes it with the words beginning "by another controller," and so forth.
It is not merely a negation of what is not even suspected.

However, since the scriptural statement prohibiting other seers is made without qualification, there would be a contradiction if it were intended to prohibit an inner seer within [the Self]; thus he says, "aviśeṣa" (without qualification).
Therefore, the mention of a difference between seers in the Sūtra and in the scriptural passage, "He who dwells in the Self," is untenable.

When it is argued that difference is refuted by the supplementary statement "not another" (*nānyaḥ*), [the author] provides the resolution: "To this it is said," [meaning] that difference is merely constructed through limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) and is restated [by scripture] in both the Śruti and the Sūtra.
To the question, "Why might difference not be real? he says: "For [Brahman] is one."
Because it is impossible for both [the self and the pot] to be objects of the cognition "I" out of respect [for the Vedic authority], only one can be that object.
Since that which is its object is non-self, like a pot, there is no real plurality of selves; this is the meaning.
And therefore... [tataśca].
The meaning is that because the acceptance of imagined difference (kalpitabheda) is admitted, everything that depends on difference is logically consistent.
Therefore, it is established that the Antaryāmi Brāhmaṇa is consistently integrated with Brahman as the object of knowledge. //20//

Section on "Invisibility," etc. (adṛśyatvādhikaraṇam) / Sūtras 21–23. START BsCom_1,2.6.21 END BsCom_1,2.5.20 The section concerning the one who is invisible, etc., begins here. It addresses the inquiry as to whether the subject described by such attributes as invisibility and so forth is the Pradhāna (the primordial material cause) or the Supreme Lord. Sūtra 21: *Adṛśyatvādiguṇako dharmokteḥ* // "The one whose qualities are invisibility and so forth [is the Supreme Lord], because of the mention of His specific attributes. Sūtra 22: *Rūpopanyāsāc ca* // "And because of the presentation of His form. Sūtra 23: *Vaiśeṣyāt tu tadvādastadvādaḥ* // "But on account of the distinction, there is the mention of that; there is the mention of that. [The commentary explains: The scripture speaks of a being characterized by invisibility, ungraspability, and other such qualities. Some maintain that this refers to the Pradhāna, which is the cause of the world. However, it is not so; the one possessing these qualities is the Supreme Lord. Why? Because of the mention of His specific attributes—such as being the creator of all, the ruler of all, and the source of all—which are impossible for the Pradhāna. Furthermore, the subsequent passage describes His form, stating, "He who is without parts, without activity, tranquil, irreproachable, stainless, with true wishes, whose wishes are fulfilled," and so on. Moreover, the term "that" (*tat*) used in the text refers to the Supreme Brahman, as established by the context of the preceding passages. Therefore, the one described by invisibility and other qualities is indeed the Supreme Lord. The repetition of "the mention of that" emphasizes the conclusion. Thus ends the section on invisibility.
