That which possesses the qualities of invisibility and so forth [is Brahman], because of the statement of its attributes:
"Now, the higher [knowledge] by which that Imperishable is apprehended;

that which is invisible, ungraspable, without lineage, without color, without eyes or ears, without hands or feet, eternal, all-pervading, omnipresent, exceedingly subtle, and imperishable—that which is the source of beings, which they behold. (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 1.1.5–6)
It is heard in scripture: "The wise... (Muṇḍaka 1.1.5, 6).

Regarding this, there is a doubt: Is this source of beings, characterized by qualities such as invisibility and so forth, the Pradhāna, or is it the embodied soul (śārīra), or rather the Supreme Lord?
In that context, it is logical that the *pradhāna*— which is insentient— is the source of beings (*bhūtayoni*),
because only insentient things are presented as its analogies:
"As a spider emits and reabsorbs [its thread], as herbs arise from the earth," and so forth.
"Just as the hair of the head and body arises from an existing person, so does this universe arise here from the Imperishable" (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 1.1.7).
Now, one might object that the spider and the person cited here as examples are both conscious beings.
We reply: No.
For consciousness alone does not possess the status of being the source of the thread or the source of hair and body-hair; rather,
it is well known that the insentient body of the spider, presided over by consciousness, is the source of the thread,
and the human body is the source of hair and body-hair.

Furthermore, although the desire for being seen and so forth might have been possible in the previous [sūtras], the Pradhāna was not accepted because the desire for being the seer and so forth was impossible there.
In this case, however, attributes such as invisibility and the rest are possible in the Pradhāna,
and no attribute that is contradictory is mentioned here.
But surely, this supplementary statement, "He who is all-knowing, all-perceiving" (Muṇḍaka 1.1.9), is not possible in the case of the insentient pradhāna;
how then can the pradhāna be asserted as the source of beings?

To this it is replied: Having taught that the source of beings (*bhūtayoni*) as possessing qualities such as invisibility by means of the word "syllable" (*akṣara*) in the passages, "by which that imperishable is attained" and "that which is invisible," the text will later teach again at the end, "higher than the high Imperishable" (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 2.1.2).
Therein, he who is heard as being higher than the Imperishable will be the omniscient and all-knowing one.
Pradhāna alone, designated by the word "akṣara," is the source of beings; however, when the word "yoni" denotes a cause, then the embodied self (śārīra) could also be the source of beings,
because the multitude of beings is produced through merit and demerit.
This being the case, it is replied: that source of beings characterized by qualities such as invisibility must be the Supreme Lord alone and none other.
How is this understood?
From the declaration of His attributes.
For it is seen that the attributes of the Supreme Lord (parameśvara) are being described here: "He who is all-knowing, all-perceiving.

Indeed, neither the insentient primordial matter (pradhāna) nor the embodied soul (śārīra), whose vision is limited by its adjuncts (upādhi), can possibly possess omniscience or all-perceiving nature.

But was it not already stated that this omniscience belongs only to that which is higher than the source of beings (bhūtayoni) indicated by the word "Imperishable" (akṣara), and does not pertain to the source of beings itself?
To this it is replied: this is not possible.

For the reason that, having first pointed out the source of beings under discussion in the phrase "from the Imperishable everything here arises" as the material cause of what is being born, the text immediately thereafter also points out the Omniscient One as the material cause of what is being born: "He who is all-knowing, all-perceiving, whose austerity consists of knowledge."

"Therefore, from this Brahman, name, form, and food are born. Since the subject is recognized as being the very same through this identical description, it is understood that omniscience and all-knowingness are predicated as attributes of the very same Akṣara, the source of beings (bhūtayoni), which was under discussion. Furthermore, in the passage "higher than the high Imperishable," no one other than the Akṣara—the source of beings under discussion—is denoted as being higher.

How is this understood? Because, having introduced the subject with the words, "He who knows that true Person, the Imperishable— for him he [the teacher] truly proclaimed that knowledge of Brahman" (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 1.2.13), it is promised that it is precisely that Imperishable, the source of beings, characterized by qualities such as invisibility, that is to be explained.
How then is it designated as "higher than the high Imperishable" (akṣarāt parataḥ paraḥ)? We shall explain that in the subsequent sūtra.
Furthermore, two kinds of knowledge are stated here as being to be known: "the higher and the lower" (parā caivāparā ca).

In that context, after describing the lower knowledge characterized by the Ṛgveda and so forth, the text says: "Now, the higher [knowledge], by which that Imperishable (akṣara) is attained," and so on. Therein, the Imperishable is heard of as the object of the higher knowledge.
If, however, an Imperishable possessing qualities such as invisibility were postulated as something other than the Supreme Lord, this would not be the higher knowledge.

For this distinction between higher and lower is conceived on the basis of the two types of knowledge having, respectively, worldly prosperity (*abhyudaya*) and the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*) as their fruits;
yet, no one accepts that the primary knowledge has the supreme good as its fruit. Furthermore, [if your view were correct,] three distinct knowledges would have to be postulated.
In your view, this is because the Supreme Self, who is higher than the Imperishable—the source of beings—is being propounded.
Furthermore, only two kinds of knowledge are specified here as objects to be known:
"O Venerable One, when what is known does all this become known? (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 1.1.3).
And thus, this reference to the knowledge of all through the knowledge of one is only possible when Brahman, whose nature is everything, is intended to be expressed;
it is not possible in the case of *pradhāna*, which is merely insentient and the sole substratum, nor in the case of the enjoyer who is distinct from the objects of enjoyment.

Furthermore, having introduced the knowledge of Brahman as the primary subject in the passage, "He taught that knowledge of Brahman, the foundation of all knowledge, to Atharvan, his eldest son" (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 1.1.1), [the text] shows the higher knowledge— which leads to the realization of the Imperishable— by means of the division into higher and lower, thereby demonstrating its status as the knowledge of Brahman. Moreover, that designation as the "knowledge of Brahman" would be contradicted if the Imperishable to be realized through it were not Brahman.

The knowledge of ritual action, characterized by the Ṛgveda and other Vedas, is introduced at the beginning of the inquiry into the knowledge of Brahman for the purpose of praising that knowledge of Brahman:
"For these are rafts, unstable, having the form of sacrifice; eighteenfold is said to be the inferior karma among them.
Those fools who rejoice in this [karma] enter again and again into old age and death" (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 1.2.7).

Because of such censuring statements as these, and having censured the other knowledge, the text shows that for one who has become dispassionate, there is the qualification for the higher knowledge: "Having examined the worlds acquired through karma, let a Brāhmaṇa attain detachment; there is nothing uncreated [eternal] to be gained by what is created.
For the sake of realizing That, he should approach a Guru alone, with fuel in hand—a learned man firmly established in Brahman" (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 1.2.12).

As for the argument that because non-conscious entities such as earth and so forth are employed as examples, the source of beings (*bhūtayoni*) which serves as the exemplified (*dārṣṭāntika*) must also be non-conscious—
that is incorrect. For there is no rule that the example and the exemplified must possess absolute similarity.

Furthermore, since gross entities such as earth and the rest are presented as the illustrative examples (dṛṣṭānta), it cannot be accepted that the source of beings (bhūtayoni) as the subject of the illustration (dārṣṭāntika) is itself gross.
Therefore, the source of beings, characterized by qualities such as invisibility and so forth, is none other than the Supreme Lord. (Note:
"Invisible" [adreśyam] means not visible to the organs of knowledge.)
Ungraspable by the organs of action;
*ūrṇanābhi* is a spider;
"in the former" means in each preceding section.
"No," [it is replied].

Just as in the case of "He places the moistened pebbles," where the determination is made from the supplementary statement "Ghee is indeed brilliance," here too, the determination is made from the supplementary statements such as "the invisible" and so forth.
By that knowledge, one knows the Imperishable, the source of beings, the Puruṣa, who is the Truth, which is the subject under discussion.
It is that in which all sciences find their foundation and completion.
"Floaters" (*plavāḥ*) refers to those who drift or move about, being unstable.
"Eighteen" refers to the sixteen officiating priests (*ṛtvij*), together with the patron (*yajamāna*) and his wife, making eighteen.
It has been said by Yājñavalkya that ritual action (*karma*) and sacrifice (*yajña*) are inferior and impermanent.
Having understood through perception and other means that the worlds attainable through action are impermanent, one should reach *nirveda*— that is, detachment (*vairāgya*).
Why? Because liberation, being uncreated, cannot be produced by performed action.
This is because of the scriptural teaching that [the Self] possesses qualities such as invisibility.
He cites the statement from the *Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad* with the words "Now," etc.

Immediately after the description of action, the lower knowledge (*aparavidyā*) consisting of ritual acts, that by which the attributeless [Brahman] is known is called the higher knowledge (*parā vidyā*).
He points to that very [knowledge] by describing its object: "That which...
It is "unseen" (*adreśyam*), meaning it cannot be perceived by the organs of perception (*jñānendriyas*).
It is ungraspable by the organs of action;
"lineage" (gotra) refers to the family line,
and "caste" (varṇa) refers to the birth-class such as Brahminhood and so forth.

The meaning is that it is empty of eyes and ears, yet not devoid of eyes and ears; it is empty of hands and feet, yet not devoid of hands and feet; that is to say, it is deficient in the organs of cognition and action.
He is all-pervading and sovereign;
He is extremely subtle because He is difficult to know.
By the two terms "eternal" and "imperishable," destruction and decay are excluded.

The connection [of the words] is as follows: that which the wise and learned perceive as the source and the primal nature (*prakṛti*) of all beings—that is the Imperishable (*akṣara*); they know it as the "Beyond" (*para*).
Since the qualities such as "unseeability" (*adreśyatva*) and so forth are common to both Brahman and the Primal Matter (*pradhāna*), there is a doubt.

By way of a counter-example—since qualities belonging to a conscious being, such as "being a seer" (*draṣṭṛtva*) and others, are not mentioned here as in the previous case—it is argued that the Primal Matter must be intended; thus he presents the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) with the word "therein" (*tatra*).
In the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa), the fruit is the meditation on Pradhāna and so forth; in the final conclusion (siddhānta), it is the realization of the attributeless (nirguṇa) reality.
A spider (ūrṇanābhi), that is, a silkworm, emits threads from its own body.
The meaning is that he brings it about;
[this refers to] one who exists, i.e., one who is living.
[Objection: But how can the *pradhāna*, which was previously refuted, be raised again?
Regarding this, he says "Moreover" (*api ca*).
Here, he raises an objection, fearing that a supplementary statement (*vākyaśeṣa*) contradictory to the primary subject is heard as being impossible: "But [the word] *yaḥ*...

He replies, "To this it is said," explaining that because of the hearing of the word *akṣara* in the ablative case, there is a recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*) of the primordial material cause (*bhūtaprakṛti*), whereas the omniscience and other attributes belong to the Lord (*īśvara*), the efficient cause of the universe, who is denoted by the word *para* in the nominative case.

He establishes the final conclusion by means of the maxim, "But when there is doubt, [it is determined] from the remainder of the sentence" (*saṃdigdhe tu vākyaśeṣāt*), stating, "This being the case" (*evaṃ prāpte*).

An objection is raised: "But surely" (*nanu*)—it is improper to determine that the source of beings (*bhūtayoni*) is the Lord (*īśvara*) on the basis of the remainder of the sentence, "He who is all-knowing," because there is no identifying mark for the source of beings in that remainder of the sentence where doubt exists as to whether it is sentient or insentient.

He provides the following resolution: "To this it is replied," on the grounds that by the rule *janikartuḥ prakṛtiḥ*, the material cause (*prakṛti*) receives the technical designation of the ablative (*apādāna*), and thus the use of the fifth case (ablative) is prescribed; therefore, there is recognition of the syllable (*akṣara*) mentioned as the material cause in the phrase "it originates from the syllable" as being the source of beings (*bhūtayoni*) in the subsequent sentence, due to the indicative mark (*liṅga*) of its being the material cause expressed by the word "from that" (*tasmāt*).
This effect is Brahman in its subtle form, namely name and form;
from that comes the gross "food," meaning rice and other such things.

As for the claim that the source of beings (bhūtayoni) is insentient because of the recognition [of it] through the scriptural mention of the fivefold suffix *-ant* (in *akṣaram*), [that is refuted as follows].
Regarding this, he says: "Beyond the Imperishable" (*akṣarāt parataḥ*).

This word "Imperishable" (*akṣara*) does not refer to the source of beings (*bhūtayoni*), because the source of beings—the Imperishable which was previously described as being attainable through higher knowledge—has already been identified as Brahman by the scriptural mention of "the Imperishable" (*akṣara*) in the passage "He knows the Imperishable Person," which possesses the indicative mark of being an object of knowledge. Thus he says: "by whom... (*yena*).

The meaning is that, having begun with the statement, "One should proclaim that knowledge of Brahman by which one knows the imperishable source of beings, the omniscient Person," it is understood that the supreme source of beings is the one being described as "breathless, mindless, and pure" and "higher than the high beyond the Imperishable."

Then, raising the objection as to what the meaning of the word "syllable" (akṣara) ending in the fifth case is, he says "How so? intending to state that it is "ignorance. Furthermore, he says "Moreover" (api ca), indicating that by the designation "higher knowledge" (paravidyā), its object is Brahman.
Now, one might argue that even the knowledge of the Pradhāna is "higher" because its object is the cause; to this he replies: "The distinction between higher and lower..."

The meaning is that, having censured the lower knowledge (*aparavidyā*) because its fruit is impermanent, [the scripture] declared the higher knowledge (*brahmavidyā*) for the sake of one seeking liberation; this is what is stated in the remainder of the passage.
Let it be granted that even the knowledge of *pradhāna* is "higher" insofar as it has liberation as its fruit; to this he says: "And not... [He objects:
But surely, in the subsequent passage, "He who is all-knowing," the subject of the higher knowledge is stated?
However, since the primary knowledge (pradhānavidyā) is expressed by the statement "indescribable" (adreśya), he says, "And three.
Furthermore, he states, "In what? to show that Brahman is the source of the elements (bhūtayoni).
A single abode and material cause for all that is insentient alone does not lead to the knowledge of the Selfs—which are not its effects—even when there is knowledge of those effects.
The meaning is that when the individual soul (*jīva*) is thus known, there can be no knowledge of that which is not its effect—that is, the object of experience (*bhogya*).
Furthermore, by the term "knowledge of Brahman" (*brahmavidyā*), he states that the source of beings (*bhūtayoni*) is Brahman; for this reason he says, "Moreover" (*api ca*):
"He [the Creator] spoke the knowledge of Brahman—the foundation and the culminating ground of all knowledge."
Since all branches of knowledge (*vidyā*) and the fruits of those knowledges are included within the knowledge of Brahman (*brahmavidyā*), the knowledge of Brahman is the foundation of all knowledge.
Now, one might ask: for what purpose is "lower knowledge" (*aparavidyā*) mentioned in the context of the "higher" (*para*)? To this he says: "The lower...
[The word] *plava* means that which floats or moves; thus, they are perishable.
Incapable of producing results that are unstable and impermanent, they consist of eighteen members: the sixteen officiating priests (ṛtvij), the wife, and the sacrificer (yajamāna).
They are called "forms of sacrifice" (yajñarūpa) because they are defined by the name "sacrifice."
For instance, they are called *ṛtvij* because they solicit during the seasons (*ṛtu*) and cause the sacrifice (*yajña*) to be performed;
one is a *yajamāna* because he sacrifices (*yajate*);

and according to the rule "the word *pati* takes the substitute *na* when connected with a sacrifice," the final letter of the word *pati* is prescribed as *na* in connection with a sacrifice, thus forming *patnī*.

Thus, since the basis for the application of names such as "sacrificial priest" (ṛtvij) and so forth is the sacrifice, they are "of the form of sacrifice. The meaning is that those fools who— regarding the inferior action with transient results prescribed in the Śruti— delight in the thought, "This very action is the highest good, not the knowledge of the Self," undergo birth and death again and again.
The rule is that one must indeed approach a teacher for the sake of knowing That—that is, for the sake of knowing Brahman.
By the term "learned in the Vedas" (*śrotriya*), the text excludes from the status of a teacher one who, though established in Brahman, has not studied the Vedas.
The example provided concerns the point that the effect is non-different from its material cause.
Even if there were equality in all respects, an undesirable consequence would still follow; thus he says: "Moreover, [if they were] gross... (21).
And because of the distinction and the designation of difference, the other two [the individual soul and the pradhāna] are not [the cause]. (BS 1.2.22)
For this reason as well, the Supreme Lord alone is the source of beings, and not either the embodied soul or the primal matter (pradhāna).
Why?
Because of the mention of specific attributes and because of the designation of difference.
For the text distinguishes the source of beings under discussion from the embodied soul by its dissimilarity: "For the divine, formless Person is both within and without, unborn;

for he is without breath, without mind, pure" (Muṇḍaka 2.1.2). Indeed, these attributes such as being "divine" and so forth are not possible for the embodied soul, who—due to the conceit of limitation by name and form presented by ignorance—superimposes those qualities upon itself.

Therefore, the person belonging to the Upaniṣads is directly spoken of here. Likewise, it designates the source of beings under discussion as distinct even from the Pradhāna, stating: "Higher than the high Imperishable" (akṣara).

The Imperishable is the unmanifested (avyākṛta), which consists of the causal power of the seeds of name and form; it is the subtle state of the elements, resting upon the Lord, and serving as His limiting adjunct (upādhi).
The designation "higher than the highest" by way of distinction— referring to that which is changeless and beyond all modification— shows that the Supreme Self (paramātman) is intended here;
it does not mean that some independent principle called "Pradhāna" is accepted as existing, and the designation of difference is made in relation to that.

What then? If even the Pradhāna, when postulated, could be conceived as the subtle elements (bhūtasūkṣma) denoted by terms such as "the Undeveloped" (avyākṛta) in a manner that does not contradict scripture, then let it be so postulated.
Therefore, it is established here that the Supreme Lord is the source of beings (bhūtayoni), on account of the designation of difference. // 22 //
And for what further reason is the Supreme Lord the source of beings?
[The term] *akṣara* (the Imperishable) is so called because it pervades (*aśnoti*) its own collection of transformations;
it is the unevolved (*avyākṛta*), the unmanifest (*avyakta*).
The Lord is the seed of name-and-form; His nature is that of power (*śakti*).
He explains the two reasons—namely, "because of the qualification" and "because of the statement of difference"—by distinguishing them through the passage beginning with "He qualifies," and so forth.
"Divine" means having the nature of luminosity, being self-luminous (*svayañjyotis*).
Formless and full,
the Person (puruṣa) who dwells within the city (puriśaya) is the inner self (pratyagātman);
because he exists as the substratum together with both the external gross [body] and the internal subtle causal [body], he is "with the external and the internal" (sabāhyābhyantara).
The meaning is that this is indeed well-known in the Śrutis.
"Limitation" refers to smallness caused by the body, which consists of name and form and is produced by ignorance (avidyā).
The meaning is that from the properties of that body—such as insentience and corporeality [the Self appears limited].
But would not the claim that the Pradhāna is "without sound" (aśabda) be contradicted if the word "syllable" (akṣara) were used to denote the Pradhāna?
To this he replies: "The syllable is the unmanifested (avyākṛta).
It is called the "syllable" (akṣara) because it pervades (aśnoti) its own collection of transformations.
It is indeterminate and unmanifest;
that is to say, it is beginningless. God (Īśvara) is the seed of name and form, existing as his very power (śakti).
Because it is dependent, the material cause (*upādāna*) is also called "power" (*śakti*).

That which possesses the subtle impressions (*saṃskāra*) of the elements is the "subtle element" (*bhūtasūkṣma*); that which has the Lord (*īśvara*), who is pure consciousness (*cinmātra*), as its substratum is likewise [described].
It is this very pure consciousness that serves as the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) for the distinction between the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Lord (*īśvara*).

As for the interpretation of those who maintain the doctrine of manifold individual souls (*nānājīvavādins*)—that [the term "Brahman"] has God as its locus and object—that falls outside the scope of the Commentary (*Bhāṣya*).

This is because the Śruti, in the passage, "In this very Imperishable, O Gārgī, the ether is woven like warp and woof," teaches that the unevolved (*avyākṛta*) has consciousness as its locus through the relationship of being woven; thus, there is no basis for resorting to a figurative meaning (*lakṣaṇā*) for the word "locus.
Furthermore, there is no evidence whatsoever for a difference between [the Brahman of the Upanishads] and the Root-Nature (*mūlaprakṛti*).

Nor is the scriptural text "Indra by means of māyās" an authoritative proof [for the plurality of māyā], because—by the force of numerous other scriptures such as "the one unborn"—and aided by the reasoning of parsimony (lāghava), that scripture merely restates a plurality of māyās corresponding to the diversity of individual intellects.
As it was said by Sureśvarācārya: "But in reality, not even the slightest difference of avidyā exists here."
The teachers of Sāṃkhya and Yoga, as well as the authors of the Purāṇas and Itihāsas, assert the identity of the primordial nature (mūlaprakṛti).
Now, if there is indeed an identity of ignorance (avidyā), how can the distinction between bondage and liberation be maintained?
Nor should it be said that such a distinction does not exist.
If it is argued that this leads to the contradiction of precluding the engagement in hearing [the scriptures] and so forth, it is replied:
Even by those who maintain the manifoldness of ignorance (*avidyā*), the fact that ignorance possesses parts must be admitted because it is subject to transformation (*pariṇāmin*).

Thus, the systematic order [of experience] is established through the distinction between individual souls (*jīva*) as conditioned by those parts of ignorance that have transformed into the nature of one's own aggregate consisting of what is essentially harmful.
For one in whose internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) knowledge arises, liberation occurs through the destruction of portions of ignorance that transform the internal organ;
and thus, for the listener, there is the attainment of the bliss of one's own true nature (svarūpānanda) and engagement in hearing [the teachings] and so forth.
Thus, both the experience of the wise and the scripture on liberation while living (jīvanmukti-śāstra) remain entirely uncontradicted.
Nor does this result in no distinction from the position that there are many individual souls (nānājīva-pakṣa).
There is no plurality in the primal nature (*mūlaprakṛti*); enough said. As for the reason for its being "other," it is stated to be "unchanging" (*avikāra*).

Now, one might object: since the author of the Sūtras has stated in the Śruti that there is a designation of difference from the Pradhāna, how can the statement of difference from ignorance (*ajñāna*) be explained in that context?
To this he replies: "Not here. That which is deposited (*pradhīyate*) in the form of an effect is *pradhāna*, which is simply ignorance (*ajñāna*);
the meaning is that anything other than that lacks any basis in valid cognition (*apramāṇika*).
Therefore, having established the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) that here it is ignorance alone which is the source of beings (*bhūtayoni*), this is refuted.
It should be understood that by the refutation of that [ignorance], the *pradhāna* postulated by the Sāṃkhyas is effectively refuted as well. //22//
And because of the presentation of form. (BBs 1.2.23)

Moreover, immediately after the passage "Higher than the Imperishable is the High," we observe that following the description of the creation of the principles beginning with Prāṇa and ending with Earth, the form of that very source of beings (*bhūtayoni*) as consisting of all modifications is presented:
"Fire is its head, the sun and moon its eyes, the quarters its ears, and the Vedas its opened mouth."
"Vāyu is his breath, the universe is his heart; from his feet the earth arose—for he is the inner self of all beings" (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 2.1.4).
And this [description] is appropriate for the Supreme Lord alone, because he is the cause of all transformations.
This presentation of form is not possible for the embodied soul, which possesses limited greatness, nor is it possible for the Pradhāna,
because [the Pradhāna] cannot be the inner self of all beings.
Therefore, it is understood that the Supreme Lord alone is the source of beings, and not the other two.
But how is it understood that this presentation of forms refers to the source of beings?
From the context.
And because of the reference back to the subject at hand by the word "this" (eṣaḥ);

for, having introduced the source of beings (bhūtayoni) with the statements, "From this the vital breath (prāṇa) is born," and "This is the inner self of all beings," the subsequent declaration must indeed refer to that very source of beings.
Just as the statement, "Study from this teacher, for he has mastered the Vedas and the Vedāṅgas," refers specifically to the teacher, so it is here.
But how can the source of beings, which possesses qualities such as invisibility, have a corporeal form?
This is stated with the intention of expressing its nature as the Self of all, and not with the intention of asserting that it possesses a physical body; thus there is no fault.
This is like [the passage] beginning with "I am food, I am the eater of food" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 3.10.6).
Others, however, hold the view that this is not a presentation of the form of the source of beings, because it is presented as being born.
"For from this [Brahman] is born the vital breath (prāṇa), the mind, and all the sense organs;

[as well as] space, air, light, water, and the earth which supports the universe"—thus, in the preceding passage, the collection of principles beginning with the vital breath and ending with the earth was indicated as being born.
And in the subsequent passage as well, it says, "From that [arose] fire, its fuel, and the sun," and so forth.
Furthermore, up to the passage "and from him all herbs and juices," he will describe [the source] solely as that which is being born.
Why, then, would he introduce the form of the source of beings here in the middle quite unexpectedly?
Moreover, its nature as the Self of all will be taught after the completion of the creation, starting with "The Person alone is this whole world, action... (Muṇḍaka 2.1.10).

Furthermore, we observe that the birth and other states of Prajāpati, whose body is the three worlds, are pointed out in both Śruti and Smṛti: "Hiraṇyagarbha arose in the beginning; once born, he was the sole lord of all that exists.
He supported this earth and yonder heaven. To which god shall we offer our oblation? (Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 10.121.1).
The phrase "samavartata" means "was born."
Likewise, [it is said]: "He indeed is called Puruṣa;
he is the first creator of beings, and Brahmā appeared at the beginning.
Furthermore, it is possible for even the *vikāra-puruṣa* (the person as a modification) to be the inner self of all beings.

Because [the Self] exists within all beings as their vital breath (*prāṇātman*), in this view the presentation of all forms in passages such as "The Person alone is all this, action... should be explained as the means for realizing the Supreme Lord.
[Note: *Agni* is the heavenly world; *vivṛtā* is the speech of the Vedas.]
With his two feet, [he placed] his two feet; he whose majesty is subtle and whose power is slight; and who is the illuminator, like fuel for the fire of the celestial world, namely the sun.
"In the beginning, Hiraṇyagarbha came into being;
having been born, he became the sole lord of the multitude of beings"—this is the sense.
For what? For Prajāpati.
"Let us worship," that is, let us serve.
According to the opinion of the author of the *Vṛtti*, he first explains the Sūtra with the words "Moreover" (*api ca*), etc.
The Śruti states: "Prāṇa, mind, and all the senses; ether, air, light, water, and earth."
Fire is the world of smoke, according to the Vedic scripture: "That world, O Gautama, is indeed fire.
The connection is that the Vedas, when manifested, are speech.
"By the feet" means "the two feet.
The meaning is that he whose form is this is the inner self (antarātman) of all living beings. Regarding the phrase "of the small magnitude": [it refers to the subtle body].
The meaning is "due to limited power.

For example, a certain knower of Brahman sings the Sāman chant "I am food" for the purpose of manifesting his identity with the Self of all, yet he does not intend to assert that his own nature is actually food and so forth, because such a result would be unattainable.
He says "so it is here too" with the words "I am food.
He refutes the commentary of the Vṛttikāra with the words "others,

however," meaning that since this Inner Self of all beings, the Sūtrātman, is presented here as being born from this source of beings (*bhūtayoni*) in accordance with the sequence of the Śruti text, it refers to Hiraṇyagarbha.
"Niradikṣat" means "he spoke. "Agni whose world is heaven"—that is, he whose form as fuel is the sun—was born from that fire which has heaven as its world; such is the meaning.
This is because of another scriptural passage stating, "Therefore, the sun itself is the fuel.
Thus, the intention is that even in the middle [of the text], only the process of creation is to be described, not a specific form.
As for what was said—that in the verse "Agni is the head," the intention is to express that the source of beings (bhūtayoni) is the Self of all—[that too is addressed here].
Regarding this, he says: "even the state of being the self of all.
Now, one might object: since the birth of Hiraṇyagarbha has not been mentioned elsewhere, how can it be stated here?
To that, he replies: "by scripture" (śruti).
Having come into being, he alone existed at the beginning as the sole Lord of the multitude of beings by the grace of the Supreme Lord.
That *sūtrātmā* (the thread-self) supported this heaven and this earth—indeed, everything gross.

Since the word *ka* is a name for Prajāpati, it lacks the status of a pronoun (*sarvanāman*), and thus the form *smā* would be inappropriate; therefore, it should be explained as *ekāya* (with the elision of the vowel *e*), meaning "to the one God, the self of Prāṇa, let us worship with oblation" or "let us serve."
According to the Vedic scripture, "Which is the one god? Breath.
Alternatively, it means "to that one god from whom this [universe] was born," based on another scriptural passage: "The one god is hidden in all beings."
Now, one might ask: how can that [Self] be the inner self of the elements? To this, he says: "By modification," etc.

Due to the performance of the combination of excellent meditation and ritual action in a previous kalpa, in this kalpa, [it becomes the inner self] of all the individual subtle bodies (liṅga) of living beings.

The meaning is that the pervasive collective subtle body (*samaṣṭi-liṅga-śarīra*), which consists of the organs of knowledge and action, the vital breaths (*prāṇa*), and the self (*ātman*), and which resides within all living beings, is produced; thus, it is logical that the *sūtrātman*, whose nature is that [subtle body], is the inner self (*antarātman*) of all beings.
Regarding his own position, he states the meaning of the *sūtra*: "In this view," and so forth.

The meaning is that all action—whether Vedic (śrauta) or traditional (smārta)—as well as austerity, is fruitful only when directed toward the Person alone; and because the text presents Him as being within all, the statement is consistently applicable to the Source of Beings who is to be known. //23//

END BsCom_1,2.6.23 START BsCom_1,2.7.24 Section on Vaiśvānara (Sūtras 24–32) The term *vaiśvānara* refers to the gastric fire (*jāṭharāgni*), because it is taught as such in the context of eating food. Furthermore, the characteristics of the gastric fire are observed here: the mention of the head, etc., is figurative, just as the head and other limbs are attributed to the sacrificial fire in the passage, "The fire is indeed the head of the sacrifice" (*Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa* 10.6.1.11). Moreover, the connection with the act of eating food is appropriate for the gastric fire, as seen in the passage, "He who eats food becomes one with this [fire]" (*Chāndogya Upaniṣad* 5.19.2). Also, the statement, "Whoever worships him as the measure of a span does not become small" (*Chāndogya Upaniṣad* 5.18.1), is consistent with the gastric fire, since it is measured by the span of the hands. Therefore, the *vaiśvānara* mentioned here is the gastric fire. To this, we reply: The *vaiśvānara* mentioned here is the Supreme Self, because the qualities of the Supreme Self are taught. For the qualities of the Supreme Self—such as being the support of heaven, earth, and so forth—are taught in the passage, "He in whom heaven, earth, and the sky are woven" (*Chāndogya Upaniṣad* 5.18.2). Furthermore, the statement, "Whoever worships him as the measure of a span does not become small; he becomes great" (*Chāndogya Upaniṣad* 5.18.1), is appropriate only for the Supreme Self. Moreover, the teaching that the whole world is contained within Him—as in, "In Him are all beings, and He is all beings" (*Chāndogya Upaniṣad* 5.18.1)—is possible only if He is the Supreme Self. Therefore, the *vaiśvānara* is the Supreme Self. If it be argued that the Supreme Self cannot be the object of worship because He is formless, we say no; for the Supreme Self can be worshipped through His attributes, just as the ether is worshipped as the "Fullness" (*Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad* 2.5.19). Furthermore, the Supreme Self is described as having a form consisting of the cosmic body, as in, "His head is the good, His eye is the sun, His breath is the air, His trunk is the space, His bladder is the water, His feet are the earth" (*Chāndogya Upaniṣad* 5.18.2). Thus, the Supreme Self is the *vaiśvānara*. Nor is there any contradiction in attributing the head and other limbs to the Supreme Self, for such figurative descriptions are common in the Vedas, as in the case of the sacrificial fire. Moreover, the connection with eating food is not a reason for limiting the term to the gastric fire, for the Supreme Self is the ultimate cause of all actions, including eating. The reference to the span of the hands is also not contradictory, as it serves to indicate the Supreme Self through a familiar medium. Therefore, the *vaiśvānara* is the Supreme Self. Furthermore, the word *vaiśvānara* is etymologically derived from *viśva* (all) and *nara* (beings), meaning "the Self of all beings," which is a designation belonging to the Supreme Self alone. Hence, the *vaiśvānara* is the Supreme Self. Also, the mention of the heart as the abode—as in, "He who knows this as the heart of the fire" (*Chāndogya Upaniṣad* 5.18.2)—is consistent with the Supreme Self, who is the inner controller of all. Therefore, the *vaiśvānara* is the Supreme Self. And finally, the teaching that the whole universe is contained within Him—as in, "In Him are all beings, and He is all beings"—is possible only if He is the Supreme Self. Thus, the *vaiśvānara* is the Supreme Self. Therefore, the *vaiśvānara* is the Supreme Self. [End of Section] END BsCom_1,2.7.24 START BsCom_1,2.8.25 Section on Akṣara (Sūtras 33–36) The term *akṣara* (the Imperishable) refers to Brahman, because of its association with the qualities of Brahman. In the passage, "O Gārgī, that Brahmin who departs from this world without knowing this Imperishable... he is like one who performs sacrifices for the sake of a thief" (*Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad* 3.8.10), the word *akṣara* denotes Brahman, because it is associated with the qualities of Brahman, such as being the support of all things. Furthermore, the description of the Imperishable as the support of heaven, earth, and everything else is appropriate only for Brahman. Also, the passage, "That which is above heaven, that which is below the earth, that which is between these two, heaven and earth, and that which is in the past, present, and future—all this is supported by the Imperishable" (*Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad* 3.8.4), shows that the Imperishable is the support of all. This is a characteristic of Brahman alone. Therefore, the *akṣara* is Brahman. If it be argued that the *akṣara* is the syllable *om*, because the word *akṣara* is commonly used for a syllable, we say no; for the context here is not about phonetics, but rather about the knowledge of the Supreme Reality. Moreover, the passage, "By what is the Imperishable supported? By the Imperishable which is the Immutable" (*Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad* 3.8.11), indicates that the *akṣara* is itself supported by something else, which is impossible for a mere syllable. Therefore, the *akṣara* is Brahman. Also, the passage, "That which is above heaven... all this is supported by the Imperishable" (*Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad* 3.8.4), shows that the *akṣara* is the support of all, which is a characteristic of Brahman. Therefore, the *akṣara* is Brahman. Furthermore, the passage, "The seers see it, the wise know it, and the meditators meditate upon it" (*Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad* 3.8.11), indicates that the *akṣara* is the object of meditation and knowledge, which is appropriate for Brahman. Therefore, the *akṣara* is Brahman. Thus, the *akṣara* is Brahman. [End of Section] END BsCom_1,2.8.25 START BsCom_1,2.9.26 Section on Antaryāmin (Sūtras 37–41) The term *antaryāmin* (the Inner Controller) refers to Brahman, because of the characteristics of Brahman. In the passage, "He who dwells in the earth, yet is within the earth, whom the earth does not know, whose body the earth is, and who controls the earth from within—he is your Self, the Inner Controller, the Immortal" (*Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad* 3.7.3), the *antaryāmin* is Brahman, because the characteristics of Brahman are taught. For the quality of being the inner controller of all elements, while remaining distinct from them, is a characteristic of Brahman alone. Furthermore, the passage, "He who dwells in all beings... he is your Self, the Inner Controller, the Immortal" (*Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad* 3.7.15), shows that the *antaryāmin* is the Self of all beings. This is possible only for Brahman. Therefore, the *antaryāmin* is Brahman. If it be argued that the *antaryāmin* is the individual soul (*jīva*), because the soul is the controller of the body, we say
Vaiśvānara [is the Self] because of the specific qualification of a common term:
"What is our Self? What is Brahman? and "You are now studying this very Vaiśvānara Self; tell us about that. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 5.11.1, 6)

Having thus begun, and having taught that heaven, the sun, air, ether, water, and earth possess the qualities of "excellent luster" and so forth by associating them with Vaiśvānara as his head and other limbs—while simultaneously censuring the worship of each one individually—the scripture declares: "But he who worships this Vaiśvānara Self, which is of the measure of a span and all-pervading, eats food in all worlds, in all beings, and in all Selves. Of this very Vaiśvānara Self, the head indeed is *sutejas* (of excellent luster), and the eye is *viśvarūpa* (multiform)."

"The breath is the separate-pathed self; the trunk is the fuel; the bladder is wealth; the feet are the earth; the chest is the altar; the body hair is the sacrificial grass; the heart is the Gārhapatya fire; the mind is the Anvāhāryapacana fire; the mouth is the Āhavanīya fire" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 5.18.2), and so forth.
In this regard, a doubt arises: is the gastric fire taught by the word "Vaiśvānara," or the elemental fire, or the deity presiding over that [fire], or the embodied soul, or the Supreme Lord?
What, then, is the cause for doubt here?

It is because the term "Vaiśvānara" is used as a common designation for the digestive fire, the elemental fire, and the deity; and the term "Self" (ātman) is used for both the embodied self and the Supreme Lord.
Thus, a doubt arises as to which [meaning] it is proper to adopt and which is to be rejected.
What, then, is the initial position?
That it is the digestive fire.
Why?

For in that context, the use of the qualification is seen in certain instances, such as: "This is Agni Vaiśvānara, who is within the person, by whom this food is cooked, which is eaten" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 5.9).
Or it may refer to fire in general, since usage is also seen in a general sense, such as: "The gods made Agni Vaiśvānara the banner for the entire world" (Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 10.88.12).
Or the deity might be one whose body is fire;

for that too, we observe its application in such scriptural passages as "May we be in the good favor of Vaiśvānara; for he is the king, the glory of all beings" (Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 1.18.1), since [the term] is possible when applied to a deity endowed with sovereignty and other such attributes.

Now, if it is argued that because of the grammatical coreferentiality with the word "Self" (ātman), and because the word "Self" alone is used at the beginning in the passage "What is our Self? What is Brahman?", the word "Vaiśvānara" must be interpreted in accordance with the word "Self"— even so, it would refer to the embodied self (śārīra ātmā),
since that [self] is the enjoyer and is thus closely connected to Vaiśvānara.
Furthermore, the qualification "measuring a span" is possible only in that [Self] which is delimited by limiting adjuncts (upādhi).
Therefore, when it has been argued that Vaiśvānara cannot be the Lord (Īśvara), this is said in reply: Vaiśvānara must be the Supreme Self (paramātman).
Why? Because of a specific common term.
The distinction between two common terms is "the distinction of common terms.
Although both these terms, *ātman* and *vaiśvānara*, are common terms,
the term *vaiśvānara* is common to three [meanings].
Furthermore, although the word "Self" (ātman) applies to both, a distinction is nevertheless observed by which their reference to the Supreme Lord is accepted, as in:
"Of this very Vaiśvānara-Self, the head indeed is Sutejas," and so forth.

For here it is understood that the Supreme Lord alone— characterized by having heaven as his head and so forth, and having entered into another state— is presented as the inner self (pratyagātman) for the purpose of meditation,
because he is the cause.
For since the cause possesses all the states belonging to its effects, it is logical that he has the heavenly world and other elements as his limbs.

Furthermore, the fruit described as being based on all worlds, all beings, and all selves—expressed in the passage, "He eats food in all worlds, in all beings, and in all selves"—is possible only if the Supreme Cause is accepted.
Likewise, there is the scriptural statement regarding the knower of That: "Thus, indeed, all his evils are burned away" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 5.24.3).

Furthermore, the opening statement, "What is the Self? What is Brahman? introduces the subject through the words "Self" (ātman) and "Brahman. Thus, these indicative marks lead to the understanding that the Supreme Lord alone is Vaiśvānara.
