Therefore, he says, "Or rather... (athavā).
The meaning is that this is the instruction regarding [the deity] whose head is the sun and so forth.

The meaning is that one should meditate upon that elemental fire which, in the form of light, has stretched across and pervaded this earth and even the sky—those two, heaven and earth, known as *rodasī*—as well as the intermediate space between them.
Since that which is merely insentient is not an object of meditation, he says "or rather" (*athavā*).
He establishes his conclusion: "Not so, because of the teaching of the vision [of the Supreme], etc.

Having stated that the Lord, characterized by having heaven as His head and so forth, is indicated (lakṣya) by the two words *agni* and *vaiśvānara*—which denote the gastric fire as a symbol (*pratīka*) to be meditated upon through the vision of the Supreme Lord—he states another alternative: "Or rather, [it refers to] the gastric [fire].
In this view, the distinction is that the Lord is the primary object of meditation here, whereas in the previous case He was secondary.
The meaning is that the object to be indicated (*lakṣya*) is "conditioned" (*upahita*) by the two words expressing the limiting conditions (*upādhi*).
He explains the impossibility (*asaṃbhava*), which is the seed of the metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*), with the words "If, moreover... (*yadi ca...*).
He explains the remainder of the sūtra, beginning with "And if [it were] the person alone" (*yadi ca kevalaḥ...*), with the words "And if... (*yadi ca...*).
The intended meaning is that [the Self] is devoid of being a symbol or an adjunct of Īśvara; "tadā" (then/at that time) is the ellipsis to be supplied.
"Yat" means "yaḥ" (who); the meaning of the Śruti is that this very person is the one characterized by the adjunct of the digestive fire (jāṭhara-agni) designated as Vaiśvānara.
The meaning is that he who knows [this] enjoys everything.

Having stated that the state of being a *puruṣa*—that is, fullness (*pūrṇatva*)—does not belong to the insentient digestive fire (*jāṭhara*), [the author] says in another reading, "But those who... to declare that its having the form of a person (*puruṣavidhatva*), i.e., the shape of a body, does not belong to it.

Now, one might object: since the digestive fire also pervades the body, it should possess that same form; to this he replies: "And the state of having the form of a person [is denied] because of the context."

The "person-like form" (puruṣavidhatva) does not mean pervading the body, but rather having the shape of the Virāj-body; the meaning is that the Lord's person-like form consists in His possessing the same proportions as the limbs of the meditator—from the head down to the chin—with respect to the divine sphere (adhidaiva) and the internal sphere (adhyātma). //26//
For this very reason, it is neither a deity nor an element. (BS 1.2.27)

Furthermore, as for what was stated— that because the elemental fire is also seen in the Vedic mantras to have a connection with the heavenly world and so forth, the attribution of limbs such as "the head itself is the brilliant" must belong to that very [elemental fire]—
and that this is due to the possession of sovereignty by the deity who has a body, that must be refuted.
To this it is replied: For these very reasons already stated, Vaiśvānara is not the deity;
likewise, even the elemental fire is not Vaiśvānara.
For it is not possible to conceive of the elemental fire—which consists merely of heat and light—as having the sky for its head and so forth.
Because it is impossible for one modification to have another modification as its essence;
likewise, even though a deity possesses lordly power (*aiśvarya*), the conceptualization of having heaven as its head and so forth is not possible,
because [the deity] is not the ultimate cause and because its lordly power is dependent upon the Supreme Lord.
Furthermore, the impossibility of the term "self" [applying] to any of these positions remains established. // 27 //
The perfection [of the qualities] in the limbs of the Lord will be stated later.
Having thus refuted the two positions regarding the digestive fire (*jāṭhara*), he refutes them by means of the phrase "for this very reason.
He explains the Sūtra with the words beginning "yat punar" (as for that which...).
Having the sky as its head and so forth,
the partaking of the fruits of all worlds,
and the complete burning away of all evils.

The reasons stated at the beginning regarding the terms *ātman* and *brahman* are recalled by the passage starting with "for [the fire] of the elements" (*na hi bhūtāgneḥ*), and so forth. The intention is that in the mantra "He who [shines] with light" (*yo bhānunā*), the greatness is described from the perspective of the Lord (*īśvara*). //27//
Jaimini [maintains] that there is no contradiction even with direct [perception]. (BS 1.2.28)

It was previously stated that the Supreme Lord is to be meditated upon either as having the gastric fire as His representative form (*pratīka*) or as having the gastric fire as His limiting adjunct (*upādhi*), in accordance with [the scriptural mention of] being "established within" and so forth.

Now, however, the teacher Jaimini considers that there is no contradiction whatsoever in accepting the meditation on the Supreme Lord directly, even without the postulation of a representative form or a limiting adjunct. [Objection:
But surely, if the gastric fire is not accepted, the statement regarding being "established within," as well as the reasons such as the word [of scripture], would be contradicted?

To this it is replied: First of all, the statement regarding being "established within" is not contradicted. For here, the phrase "he knows him who is man-like and established within man" is not spoken with reference to the digestive fire (jāṭharāgni), because that is neither the subject under discussion nor has it been mentioned.

How then is it that this is said—namely, "One knows [the Self] as man-shaped, established within the person"—with reference to that which was previously introduced: the attribution of the form of a person to the limbs of the person from the crown of the head down to the chin?
It is just as when one says, "He sees a branch established upon a tree."

Alternatively, with reference to that very Supreme Self which was introduced as the basis for the anthropomorphic forms in the adhyātma and adhidaivata aspects, it is said— intending its aspect as the pure witness— that "one knows [Him] established within the person. And since the Supreme Self has been determined through the consideration of the preceding and following context, the word *vaiśvānara* will apply to that very subject by means of some etymological derivation (*yoga*).
He is called Viśvānara because he is the "all-man" (viśvaś cāyam naraś ca), or because he is the "man of all" (viśveṣām vā ayam naraḥ), or because "all men" (viśve vā narāḥ) belong to him.
The Supreme Self,
because it is the self of all;
Viśvānara himself is indeed Vaiśvānara.
The secondary derivative (taddhita) suffix has no other meaning [than that of the base],
as in the case of words such as *rākṣasa* and *vāyasa*.
Furthermore, the word *agni* will also refer exclusively to the Supreme Self by resorting to its connection with qualities such as being the foremost (*agraṇī*).

The conceptualization of [the fires] such as the *gārhapatya* and their status as the locus for the oblation of breath (*prāṇāhuti*) are also possible for the Supreme Self, because it is the Self of all. // 28 //
But how, then, is the scriptural mention of being "the size of a span" (*prādeśamātra*) compatible with the Supreme Lord being the subject? He begins to explain that:
[The meaning is: "Being established within" (*antaḥpratiṣṭhitatva*) means being situated in the middle, that is, being a witness (*sākṣitva*).
Here, the lengthening of the vowel in the first member of the compound [in *prādeśamātra*] occurs according to the rule *nare saṃjñāyām*.
"Having no other referent" means being devoid of any meaning beyond the primary sense of the word.
Previously, it was stated that the words "Agni" and "Vaiśvānara" are indicative (lakṣaka) of the Lord;

now, by setting aside the [notions of] symbols and limiting adjuncts, [the text speaks of] the Blessed One Vaiśvānara, who has the form of the Virāṭ-puruṣa, with respect to the internal self (adhyātma).

Even if one accepts that [the Self] is to be meditated upon as being realized from the crown of the head down to the chin, there is no contradiction with the words [of scripture], because the two terms [“I” and “this”] have their primary meaning in the Lord through figurative application (yogavṛtti), and because qualities such as being "situated within" are possible in Him; thus he says: "Even directly... (sākṣād api).
He states the meaning of the word "directly" (*sākṣāt*) with the words "even without":

the sense is that Jaimini considers there to be no contradiction regarding sound and so forth, even though the Lord is the object of meditation, provided there is no connection with the digestive fire (*jāṭharāgni*).

This state of being "within" (*antasthatva*) is not said to mean residing in the belly; rather, within the body of a person—which consists of a collection of parts from the nails to the crest—the limbs from the head to the chin are established like branches upon a tree.
He who is perfected in those [elements] is said to be Vaiśvānara, established within the person.

Therefore, just as a bird situated on a branch is said to be "within the tree," so too is Vaiśvānara "within the person"—this is what the text expresses with the words beginning, "For here [it is] not like the person," and so forth.
Since words such as "fire" (agni) and others denote the Lord (Īśvara), the gastric fire is not what is being designated here.
The meaning is that the Lord possesses the form of a person (*puruṣavidhatva*) and is situated within because He is superimposed upon the limbs of the Person.
He states another alternative with the words "Or rather" (*athavā*);
the possession of the form of a person is as explained previously.
"Being situated within" (*antaḥsthatva*) means being neutral (*mādhyasthya*) or being a witness (*sākṣitva*).
Having thus explained "being situated within" in relation to the Lord (*īśvara*), he explains the words beginning with "sound" (*śabda*) and so forth: "And when [the mind] is determined," etc.
This person is the "Universal" (*viśva*) and the "Individual" (*nara*) or "living being" (*jīva*), because he is the self of all.

Alternatively, he is the "Viśvānara" because he is the maker (*kartā*) of all transformations (*vikāra*). Or, he is Viśvānara because all (*viśve*) beings (*narāḥ*), that is, all living creatures (*jīva*), exist within him either as his self (*ātmatvena*) or as those to be governed by him (*niyamyatvena*).
The secondary suffix (*taddhitapratyaya*) is used here in its own sense (*svārthe*), just as in the case of *rakṣas* becoming *rākṣasa*.
In the word "nare," there is lengthening of the first member according to the rule "nare saṃjñāyām.
The form "agni" is derived from the root *ag*, meaning "to go," with the suffix *ni*.
Because it leads (*aṅgayati*)—that is, causes one to reach—the goal, which is the fruit of action, Agni is called the "leader" (*agraṇī*).
Or, Agni is so called because he goes around (abhito 'gati).
For one who worships Vaiśvānara, the Prāṇāgnihotra is prescribed as an ancillary to knowledge prior to the feeding of guests;

for that purpose, the conceptualization of the three fires and so forth must be interpreted in a way that does not contradict the primary subject, as stated in the commentary beginning with "the Gārhapatya fire. //28//
"It is because of manifestation," says Āśmarathya. (BS 1.2.29)
Even for the Supreme Lord, who is beyond all measure, there may be a state of being "measured by a span" (prādeśamātra) for the purpose of manifestation.
It is said that the Supreme Lord manifests Himself as having the dimension of a span for the sake of His worshippers;
or rather, He is manifested through specific attributes in various locations, such as the heart and other sites of perception.

Therefore, the teacher Āśmarathya maintains that even in the case of the Supreme Lord, the scriptural mention of being "the size of a span" (*prādeśamātra*) is appropriate on account of His manifestation. [Note: This means either "that whose measure (*mātrā*) has transcended [ordinary limits]" or "that which is measured (*mīyate*) in specific locations (*pradeśeṣu*)."]

"Exceeding measure" (*atimātra*) means having transcended all dimensions; the meaning is "of that All-pervading One" (*vibhoḥ*). For the sake of favoring the lay devotees (*upāsaka*), He manifests as being "the size of a span" (*prādeśamātra*);
or, He is measured and manifested within specific locations (*pradeśeṣu*), thus He is called "the size of a span. //29//
Bādari [holds that the soul's departure occurs] because of remembrance. (BBs 1.2.30)
Or rather, because he is remembered by the mind as being established within the heart, which is the size of a span (*prādeśamātra*), he is called "span-sized.

It is just as barley grains measured by a *prastha* are called "a *prastha* [of grain]. And although the measurement inherent in the barley grains themselves is merely manifested through its connection with the *prastha*, [the same logic applies here].
In this case, there is no dimension pertaining to the Supreme Lord that could be manifested through its connection with the heart;
nevertheless, it is said that some form of recollection may serve as a support for the scriptural mention of "the size of a span" (*prādeśamātra*), however that may be.

Or rather, even though he is not of the size of a span, he is to be recollected as being of the size of a span, so that the meaning of the scriptural statement regarding his being "of the size of a span" may remain purposeful.
Thus, the teacher Bādari maintains that the scriptural mention of the Supreme Lord as being "measured by a span" (prādeśamātra) is based on the sign of remembrance (anusmṛti)— that is,
it refers to Him who is measured by the mind (prādeśena manasā mīyate), or it occurs because [the word] is employed in that sense.
He states another opinion with the words "anusmṛteḥ" (from remembrance).
"Measured by a span" means measured by a mind [the size of] a span; the sense is that it is merely a span in size.
"In some way or other" [means as follows].

The meaning is that the state of being the size of a span (prādeśamātratva), which resides in the mind and is imagined within the object being remembered by means of recollection, serves as the basis for the Śruti.
He states another interpretation of the Sūtra: "prādeśa... (Sūtra 1.3.24).
"Because of the attainment [of Brahman]," says Jaimini; for the scripture shows it thus. (BS 1.2.31)
Or rather, the scriptural mention of the measure of a span (*prādeśamātra*) may be intended as a sign of attainment.
Why?
Because the Vājasaneyi Brāhmaṇa, in the same context, [describes] the three worlds consisting of heaven and so forth down to the earth.

By correlating the limbs of Vaiśvānara with the parts of the body beginning from the head down to the chin, the text demonstrates that the Supreme Lord is to be realized as being "measured by a span" (*prādeśamātra*): "The gods, indeed, having well understood him, attained [him] as one measured by a span. Therefore, I shall explain these to you in such a way that I shall cause you to attain him as one measured by a span."
He said, pointing to the head: "This indeed is Vaiśvānara as the Summit.
Pointing to the eyes, he said: "This indeed is Vaiśvānara of Excellent Splendor.
Pointing to the nostrils, he said: "This indeed is Vaiśvānara whose Path is Diverse."
Pointing to the principal ether, he said: "This indeed is Vaiśvānara the Abundant.
Pointing to the principal waters, he said: "This indeed is Vaiśvānara the Wealth. Pointing to the chin, he said: "This indeed is the Foundation."
The term *cubuka* refers to the lower part of the face, the chin.
Although in the Vājasaneyaka the sky is recorded as having the quality of being "standing above" (*atiṣṭhātva*) and the sun as having the quality of "good brilliance" (*sutejastva*),
in the Chāndogya, however, the sky is recorded as having the quality of "good brilliance" and the sun as having the quality of "multiformity" (*viśvarūpatva*).
Nevertheless, nothing is lost by this distinction,
because the scriptural mention of being "the size of a span" is without distinction [in all cases],
and because [the teachings] are to be understood as corroborated by all the Vedic branches (śākhās).
The teacher Jaimini considers the scriptural statement regarding the span of a thumb's breadth to be more appropriate as a sign of prosperity. // 31 //
Now, he states the interpretation of the scriptural passage concerning the "span-long" (prādeśamātra) measurement: "On account of [the Lord's] attaining [that state]" (saṃpatteḥ).
He cites the Brāhmaṇa text: "As if span-long.

Although the Lord is unlimited, the gods—who had correctly understood Him as being conceived as span-long through His attaining that state—attained and reached that very Lord as their own inner Self (pratyak).
Indeed, in former times,
I shall then describe to you those parts beginning with heaven, in such a way that they do not exceed the measure of a span (*prādeśa*).

Having made a promise to Prācīnaśāla and the others—thinking, "I shall identify Vaiśvānara with the internal limbs beginning with the head"—the King, pointing to his own head and showing it with his hand, said: "This indeed is my head; that which stands above, transcending the worlds beginning with Bhūḥ, is the world of heaven (dyuloka), which is Vaiśvānara."
"His head" means up to that point;
the meaning is that by identifying the internal head with the divine head, one should meditate upon it.
In this same manner, it should be inferred for the eyes and so forth.
Showing his own eyes, he said, "This indeed is the well-luminous sun; it is the eye of Vaiśvānara.

By the word "nose," that which resides therein—namely, the vital breath (prāṇa)—is indicated. Regarding that internal vital breath, he prescribes the vision of the cosmic vital breath, Vāyu, saying, "the nose.
In all these instances, the word "Vaiśvānara" refers to its respective limbs.

The primary [element] is located in the mouth; regarding that, one should perceive the vast space as the presiding deity (adhidaiva). In the water in the form of saliva within the mouth, one should perceive the water located in his bladder, which is denoted by the word "rai. At the chin, the "foundation" (pratiṣṭhā) is to be seen as the earth in the form of the feet. Now, raising the objection: "Since there is a difference between the two meditations due to the inequality of their qualities, how can the mention of the 'span-long' (prādeśamātra) in the Chāndogya be explained in accordance with the Śruti in the Agnirahasya?"—anticipating this, he says: "Even though," and so forth.
By this much slight discrepancy, the identity of the knowledge (vidyaikya), established by a greater number of recognitions (pratyabhijñā), is not lost;

for it will be stated later that even when there is a difference of recensional branches (śākhābheda), the meditation on Vaiśvānara and others perceived in all the branches is one and the same, according to the established principle.
Furthermore, the quality of being "the foundation" (atiṣṭhātva) found in the Chāndogya must be integrated [into the Bṛhadāraṇyaka].
And the quality of having a universal form (viśvarūpatva) is to be accepted by the Vājin [Chāndogya] school.

Thus, while the possession of intense splendor is common to both the heaven and the sun, there is a distinction between the two regarding their being the "support" (atiṣṭhātva) and their being the "universal form" (viśvarūpatva).

Alternatively, the intention is that the distinction in qualities may exist according to the difference in Vedic branches (śākhā), but this does not imply a difference in the knowledge (vidyā) itself. //31//
And they record him in this [context]. (BBs 1.2.32)
Moreover, the Jābālas enjoin that this Supreme Lord is located within this space between the crown of the head and the chin: "That which is this unmanifest Self within, it is established in Avimukta.
"In what is that Avimukta established? "It is established between the Varaṇā and the Nāsī."

"What indeed is Varaṇā and what is Nāsī?"—having explained that it is this very nose which is called Varaṇā and Nāsī, [it is said]: "Because it wards off (*vārayati*) all evils committed by the senses, it is Varaṇā;
because it destroys (*nāśayati*) all evils committed by the senses, it is Nāsī."
Furthermore, they declare: "What is its location?
That which is the junction of the eyebrows is indeed the junction of the heavenly world and the world beyond" (Jābāla Upaniṣad 1).
Therefore, the scriptural mention of the Supreme Lord as being "measured by a span" is appropriate.
The term "abhivimāna" intends the sense of being the inner self (*pratyagātman*).
It is called "abhivimāna" because it is measured out (*vimīyate*) by all living beings as their own inner self;
or alternatively, it is "abhivimāna" because it has reached (*abhigata*) the state of being the inner self and is devoid of measurement (*māna-viyoga*).
Or, it is called "Abhivimāna" because it measures itself across (abhivimīyate) all things due to being the cause of the entire world;
therefore, it is established that the Supreme Lord is indeed Vaiśvānara. // 32 //
Thus ends the second quarter of the first chapter in the Śārīrakamīmāṃsābhāṣya composed by the venerable Śrī Śaṅkara Bhagavatpāda. [Note:

In Avimukta—meaning that which is established within the limited sphere imagined through the adjunct of ignorance—the Lord is to be meditated upon by means of the conceptualization of the distinction between the individual self (jīvātman) [and the Supreme Self].
Varaṇā is the eyebrow.
It is measured (*vimīyate*) means it is known;
*abhivimīmīte* means he fashions it.
Regarding the fact that the state of being a span (*prādeśatva*) is connected with the attainment [of perfection], he cites another scriptural passage in agreement: "He says, 'Oṃ! etc.

Regarding Atri’s question, "How may I know that which is infinite, undivided, and therefore unmanifest and difficult to discern? Yājñavalkya’s answer is that the Lord is to be worshipped as established within the *jīva*—the individual soul bound by desire and other afflictions—through the conceptualization of difference. Then follows Atri’s further question: "That [Lord]..."
"Beyond Varaṇā"—
in this way, the question and answer are to be understood in what follows as well.
And in that regard, the application of the commentary [to the Śruti] is that it explains this very nose together with the eyebrows.

The *varaṇā* is the eyebrow because it wards off all defects produced by the senses; the *nāsī* is the nose, for the etymological derivation (*nirvacana*) heard in the Śruti is that it destroys all defects.
It should be understood that the power to ward off evil arises from meditating upon the eyebrows and the nose as the abodes of the Lord of the Gate of Life.
Between those two as well, he asks specifically for the location of the individual soul (jīva), "Which one? The answer is: "Between the eyebrows.
Even if the reading is "of the breath" (prāṇasya), the meaning is "of the nose" (ghrāṇasya).

"This very one" is said to be meditated upon as the junction (*saṃdhi*) between the heavenly world, the celestial realm, and the supreme world of Brahman. Regarding this, he says "this very one": the inner self (*pratyagātman*) is called "all-pervading" (*abhivimāna*) because it is measured, known, or realized as "I am Brahman" in its direct presence; it is both "attained" (*abhigata*) and "all-pervading" (*vimāna*).
Because, while possessing the nature of all things, it is infinite;
here "māna" means measure.
It measures itself forth; it creates itself.
Therefore, it is established that the Vaiśvānara passage is consistent with Brahman as the object of meditation. //32//

Thus ends the second quarter of the first chapter in the *Bhāṣyaratnaprabhā*, a commentary on the *Śrīmacchārīrakamīmāṃsā* composed by the venerable Paramahaṃsa Parivrājaka Ācārya Śrī Govindānanda Bhagavatpāda. //2//
Thus ends the second quarter (pāda) of the first chapter, titled "The Concordance of Non-Evident Śruti Passages Denoting Brahman as the Object of Meditation.
Now begins the third quarter of the first chapter.
[In this section, there is an investigation primarily concerning those passages where the marks of Brahman are non-evident, but which relate to Brahman as the object of knowledge.]
Thus, the investigation of the sentence is also [concluded] by three quarters [of the chapter]. 1. The Section on Heaven, Earth, and so forth (Dyubhvādyadhikaraṇa). Sūtra 1–7.
First Chapter, Third Quarter.
The abode of heaven, earth, and so forth [is Brahman], because of its own word. //1//
I worship Śrī Rāma—the imperishable state beyond heaven, earth, and the intermediate space, worthy of contemplation, shining within the small heart as the supreme ruler;
known by Indra and others, the governor of all, the light that is the state of the sky, sleepless, unborn, and eternal. //1//
START BsCom_1,3.1.1:
That which is the abode of heaven, earth, and so forth [is Brahman], because of its own word.
BBs_1,3.1: This is heard in scripture: "In whom heaven, earth, and the intermediate space are woven, as well as the mind together with all the vital breaths."
"Know that alone as the one Self; abandon other words; this is the bridge to immortality" (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 2.2.5).

Here, since something is understood to be the "abode" because it is stated to be that which pervades heaven and so forth, a doubt arises as to whether that is the Supreme Brahman or some other entity.
In that case, it follows that there must be some other entity as a locus.
Why? Because of the scriptural statement, "This is the bridge to immortality.
For in the world, a bridge is well known to have a further shore.
Furthermore, it is impossible to admit that the supreme Brahman has a limit, because of the scriptural declaration: "It is infinite and without end" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.4.12).

And if another entity were to be accepted as the sense-base (*āyatana*), then that which is well-known in the Smṛti, namely *pradhāna*, should be accepted, because it is logical for it to be an āyatana due to its being the cause;
or else, it might be the wind (*vāyu*) well-known in the Śruti.
"O Gautama, the wind indeed is that thread; by the wind, O Gautama, as by a thread, this world and all beings are held together" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.7.2).
Since the wind is also heard to possess the quality of supporting, it might be the embodied self (śārīra).

Since that [Self] too, being an enjoyer, can logically be the substratum (*āyatana*) for the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) which is the object of enjoyment, this being the position reached, the Sūtra says: "The abode of heaven, earth, and so forth" (*dyubhvādyāyatana*).
Heaven (*dyu*) and earth (*bhū*) are "heaven-and-earth" (*dyubhuvau*); that of which these are the beginning is "heaven, earth, and so forth" (*dyubhvādi*).
That which is indicated in this passage as the support of our entire world—namely, heaven, earth, the intermediate space, the mind, and the vital breaths—that must be the Supreme Brahman, the abode.
Why? Because of its own word; that is to say, because of the word "Self" (ātman).
For the word "Self" occurs here in the passage: "Know Him alone as the one Self."
Furthermore, the word "Self" (ātman) is properly applicable when understood as the Supreme Self (paramātman), and not when understood in any other sense.

In some places, Brahman is heard of as the abode by its own very name: "All these creatures, my dear, have Being (sat) as their root, Being as their abode, and Being as their support" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.8.4).

And here too, Brahman is celebrated by its own name both before and after this passage: "The Person alone is all this—the work, austerity, Brahman, and the supreme Immortal" (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 2.1.10).
And also: "Brahman alone is this immortal one in front; Brahman behind, Brahman to the south and to the north" (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 2.2.11).
For in that passage, there is the hearing of the relationship between the abode and that which abides, and there is the grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya) expressed as "all is Brahman."

Just as a tree consists of multiple components—branches, trunk, and roots—an apprehension may arise that the Self is likewise manifold and variegated in its nature; to dispel this, the text states with emphasis: "Know Him alone as the one Self.
What is meant by this is that the Self to be known is not a variegated entity characterized by the diversity of the phenomenal world of effects.

Rather, it means that by means of knowledge (*vidyā*), one should dissolve the manifold of effects produced by ignorance (*avidyā*) and know that very Self (*ātman*)—which is the single substratum—as being of one essence (*ekarasa*).

Just as when someone says, "Devadatta is not here; bring him," the person brings only the seat and not Devadatta, in the same way, it is taught that the object of knowledge is precisely the Self, which is the single substratum of one essence.
Furthermore, a censure is heard regarding one who is intent upon the unreality of modifications: "He goes from death to death who perceives here as if there were diversity" (Kaṭha Upaniṣad 2.4.11).

However, the grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya) expressed as "All is Brahman" is for the purpose of dissolving the phenomenal world (prapañca), not for the purpose of establishing a plurality of essences.

As it is said: "Just as a mass of salt has no interior and no exterior, but is entirely a mass of flavor, even so, my dear, this Self has no interior and no exterior, but is entirely a mass of consciousness" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.5.13).
Because of the hearing of its being of one single flavor;
therefore, the abode of heaven, earth, and so forth is the supreme Brahman.

As for what was said—that because of the scriptural mention of a "bridge" (setu), and because a bridge necessarily has a further shore, the abode of heaven, earth, and so forth must be something other than Brahman—[that is not so].
To this it is replied: here, by the scriptural mention of a "bridge" (setu), only the quality of supporting or holding up is intended, not qualities such as having two banks.
For it is not the case that because a bridge made of clay or wood is seen in the world, a bridge made of clay or wood must necessarily be accepted here as well.

Furthermore, the meaning of the word "setu" is merely the act of supporting; it does not consist in having two banks and so forth, since the word "setu" is etymologically derived from the root *ṣiñ*, which means "to bind."

Another says: "That which has been proclaimed here as the knowledge of the Self— namely, 'Know that one alone as the Self'— and that which is the relinquishing of speech— namely, 'Relinquish other words'—
these two constitute the means to immortality."
By the scriptural mention of a "bridge" in the passage, "This is the bridge to immortality," it is the [Self] that is celebrated, and not the abode of heaven, earth, and so forth.
Therefore, what was stated—that because of the mention of a "bridge," the abode of heaven, earth, and so forth must be something other than Brahman—is incorrect. (Note:
The construction is "because of the hearing of the word 'immortality'" and "because of the hearing of the word 'bridge'".)
He explains [the phrase] "because it is heard as a bridge" with the words "for it has two shores.
"Woven together" means interlaced.
Due to grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya), the connection is that the Self is manifold.
One who possesses *abhisandhi*— that is, conceit (*abhimāna*)— regarding a modification that is unreal and imagined; [the word] *setu* means "that which binds" (*sinoti badhnāti*),
signifying a partial aspect of an object that acts as a support.
Thus, in the second quarter (pāda), the reconciliation of passages consisting mostly of conventional terms (*rūḍhi-pada*) and generally containing qualifying attributes (*saviśeṣa*) has been shown.
Now, the third quarter begins to explain the reconciliation of passages consisting mostly of etymological terms (*yaugika-pada*) and primarily concerned with the attributeless (*nirviśeṣa*).
Therefore, the connections of the topical sections (*adhikaraṇa*) here are with the scripture (*śruti*), the chapter (*adhyāya*), and the quarter (*pāda*).

In that case, just as it was previously stated that the common term situated in the opening [of the text] refers to Brahman by virtue of the supplementary passage’s mention of "having heaven as its head" and so forth, so too here, the common attribute of being a "dwelling place" situated in the opening must, by the scriptural mention of a "bridge" in the supplementary passage, be restricted to the *pradhāna* and other such entities which are in fact limited. This constitutes the connection with the previous section (the *lakṣaṇādhikaraṇa*) by way of illustration;
according to the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), there would be meditation upon the *pradhāna* and so forth.

In the final conclusion, the fruit is the knowledge of Brahman devoid of distinctions. He cites the statement from the Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad with the words "this," [referring to] that in which the Virāṭ, consisting of the three worlds, [is contained].

Together with all the vital breaths (*prāṇa*), know through hearing and other means that the mind—which is of the nature of the *sūtrātman*—as well as, by the force of the word "and," the unmanifest cause (*avyākṛta*) which is woven [as the substrate] and imagined; know that very Self, the substratum, as non-different from the innermost self (*pratyagātman*).
Abandon all other words concerning the non-self, casting them off completely and without remainder.

This realization of the Self, preceded by the liberation of speech, is like a bridge (*setu*)—a means of reaching the further shore of the immortal (*amṛta*), that is, of liberation (*mokṣa*), which is the opposite shore of the insubstantial, boundless, and irresistible ocean of saṃsāra. Thus the Śruti instructs those seeking liberation as if it were a mother.
Regarding this, a doubt is raised because of the observation of the common attribute of being a "resort" (*āyatana*): "What then?

Since the genitive case in the phrase "the bridge of the immortal" (*amṛtasya setuḥ*) indicates that the bridge is distinct from Brahman, [the opponent] says that the resort of heaven, earth, and so forth—which is referred to by the word "this" (*eṣa*)—is not Brahman at all, but is merely "like a bridge" (*setur iva setuḥ*). This is stated in the words: "of the immortal."
The meaning is: because of the hearing of difference and because of the hearing of it being a "bridge" (setu).
Among these, the hearing of difference has been explained.
He himself elucidates the hearing of it being a bridge by saying, "it has a further shore" (pāravān).
It is infinite in terms of time and shoreless in terms of space.

Since it is impossible to grasp the primary bridge— which holds back the waters— when one must resort to grasping a secondary bridge, one must select something that possesses the quality of having a further shore, which is invariably concomitant with the primary bridge.
The sense is that the Lord is not merely one who possesses the quality of holding [the world] in an indefinite manner.

Just as in the world gems are strung together by a thread, so too, O Gautama, all gross things are bound and strung together by the wind which constitutes the collective subtle body (liṅga); such is the meaning of the Śruti.
Since it might be argued that both positions have already been stated by the word "Self" (ātman), he says: "or the embodied one" (śārīro vā).
The meaning is that the term "bridge" (setu) is appropriate because [the Self] is accompanied by a second.
Now, if it is objected that the word "Self" can apply to the individual soul (jīva), he says: "And the word 'Self'... [and so forth].
The meaning is that for the individual soul (jīva), which is delimited by limiting adjuncts (upādhi), there is no primary existence with respect to every single object.

The intention is that the determination of Brahman occurs through the term "Self" (ātman) heard first, because the common locus established at the beginning possesses the indicative mark (liṅga) of being figuratively a "bridge.
He states another meaning of the phrase "from its own word" (svaśabdāt): "In some places... and so forth.
In the origination of beings, Being alone is the root; in their maintenance, it is the abode; and in their dissolution, it is the foundation.

This is because, according to the Chāndogya Upaniṣad, Brahman is heard to be the "abode" (āyatana) by means of the word "Being" (sat); thus, the meaning here is that it is likewise so in this context as well.
He states another point: "by the word itself.

The meaning is that since Brahman is proclaimed by words such as "Puruṣa" and "Brahman" in the sentences preceding and following the sentence "In whom heaven... (yasmin dyauḥ), Brahman must also be understood in the middle [of this passage].
The preceding sentence is "Puruṣa... (puruṣa iti).
"Brahman alone" is the subsequent statement;
the meaning is that everything situated in all directions is indeed Brahman.
"By the north" means in the northern direction.
Having raised the objection that the cited passage refers to Brahman with attributes (*saviśeṣa*), he explains the sentence starting with "In that regard" (*tatra*).
The connection is that "the Self is manifold" due to grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*).

Having stated that the object of knowledge is without attributes by means of the words "that alone" (*tam eva ekam*)—whereby everything is woven—together with the particle "alone" (*eva*) and the word "one" (*eka*), he states another reason: "because of the unreality of modifications" (*vikārānṛta*).

The meaning is that because one who has an intention toward or an identification with a modification—which is unreal and imagined—partakes in misfortune, and because of scriptural censure [of such a person], the immutable reality (kūṭastha-satya) is what must be known.
If so, how then is there grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya)?
To this he says: "All is Brahman."

The meaning is that, just as in the statement "that which is a thief is a post," the injunction that "whatever is all that is Brahman" is for the purpose of sublation by enjoining Brahmanhood with respect to everything;
it is not for the purpose of establishing a manifold nature in the sense that "whatever is Brahman is all. He states the restrictive rule regarding this: "As he... (sa yathā).
Just as a lump of salt is devoid of any other taste within or without and is entirely of the single taste of salt,
even so, O Maitreyī,
the Self has the single taste of consciousness; this is the meaning.

Although having a far shore, possessing parts, and so forth are invariably concomitant with the primary sense of a "bridge," nevertheless, that which constitutes the bridge—namely, the supporting or holding together of water and the like—is to be accepted as a secondary quality (guṇa) because it is a constituent part of the referent of the word "bridge," even though it is variable;
however, properties such as having a far shore, which fall outside the scope of the referent itself, are not to be so accepted. Thus he says: "To this it is replied."
He states that there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) if it were grasped merely because it is seen [in usage], saying "nahi" (not so).
Here, the word "by another" (*pareṇa*) is to be supplied as the remainder of the Vedic passage. He clarifies that "holding back" (*vidhāraṇa*) is the meaning of the word by saying "ṣiñ.
The meaning is that "holding back" is a part of the referent of the word *setu*, since the root *ṣiñ* means "to bind" or "to fasten" (*sinoti badhnāti*).
And likewise, since the term *amṛtapada* emphasizes the state (*bhāva*), Brahman is the bridge—the supporter—of immortality;
the meaning is that immortality belongs to this [Brahman] alone and not to anything else.
Alternatively, he says "the other" (*apara*) to show that Brahman, the support of heaven, earth, and so forth, is not the literal meaning of the word "bridge," but rather immediate knowledge.
He states the conclusion: "In that regard, what was said" means when the bridge of knowledge has been grasped. //1//
For this reason as well, Brahman alone, which is beyond this world, is the abode of heaven, earth, and so forth;
because its state of being approached by the liberated is seen to be designated. "Muktopasṛpyam" means that which is to be approached by those who are liberated.
Ignorance (*avidyā*) is the notion of "I" and "mine" with respect to the body and other non-self objects;

from that arises attachment to their worship and so forth, aversion toward their humiliation and so forth, and fear and delusion upon seeing their destruction. Thus, this mass of evils with infinite subdivisions is constantly manifest to all of us.

In contrast to that, there is the designation concerning the abode of heaven, earth, and so forth, stating that it is to be approached and reached by those who are free from the defects of ignorance, attachment, aversion, and the like.
Having stated, "The knot of the heart is severed, all doubts are cut asunder, and his karmas are exhausted when He, who is both high and low, is seen" (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 2.2.8),
[the text] further says: "Thus the knower, liberated from name and form, attains the divine Person who is higher than the high" (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 3.2.7).

Moreover, the fact that Brahman is to be approached by the liberated is well-established in the scripture, as in such passages as: "When all desires that dwell in his heart are cast away, then the mortal becomes immortal; here he attains Brahman" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.7).
However, it is nowhere well-known that the Pradhāna and other such principles are "to be approached by the liberated.

Furthermore, here, the status of being the object to be known—preceded by the relinquishing of speech—is attributed to the abode of heaven, earth, and so forth, in the passage: "Know Him alone as the one Self; abandon other words; He is indeed the bridge to immortality.
And this [quality] is seen in another Śruti with respect to Brahman: "The wise Brāhmaṇa, having known Him alone, practices wisdom."
"One should not meditate on many words, for that is a weariness of speech" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.21).
For this reason as well, the abode of heaven, earth, and so forth is the Supreme Brahman.
[Note: *Prajñā* refers to the cognition of the meaning of the sentence.]
The term "brāhmaṇa" (Brahmin) is an indicator for all twice-born castes (*dvija*) not explicitly mentioned.
The meaning of the Sūtra is that it speaks here of that Brahman which is to be approached by the liberated as their inner self (*pratyak*), and which is to be attained.
It shows bondage, which is the opposite of liberation, with the words: "in the body and so forth."
"By the reversal of that" means it exists as the cessation of the bondage consisting of the five aforementioned afflictions (*kleśa*).
Just as rivers such as the Gaṅgā, having abandoned name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), abide in the nature of the ocean, so too does the knower of the Self of Brahman.

Having abandoned *saṃsāra*, he remains having attained—as the inner self (*pratyaktvena*)—the state that is beyond the supreme cause, the unmanifest (*avyakta*), which is supreme, full, self-luminous, and blissful; thus it says, "so the knower.
One might ask: why could this not be [the attainment] of *pradhāna* and so forth? To this, it says: "and of Brahman."
For this seeker of liberation,
by the word "in the heart" (*hṛdi*), the fact that desires are attributes of the Self is refuted.
When there is the cessation of desire, then one becomes immortal.
Because there is no cause for death;
the meaning is that not only is there the cessation of misfortune, but while remaining in this very body, one enjoys the bliss of Brahman.
He states another indicative mark with the words "Moreover" (apica).
The wise and discerning person, having realized that very Self and having known the pure object of perception, should cultivate the knowledge of the meaning of the Great Sayings (*mahāvākya*).
To express the turning away from the ritual section (*karmakāṇḍa*) and other means which obstruct the knowledge sought by one desiring wisdom, he says "not" (*na*).
By the use of the word "many," he indicates that he does not accept a few words from the Vedānta.
"There are eight places for the articulation of sounds: the chest, the throat, the head, the root of the tongue, the teeth, the nose, the lips, and the palate."
"These [organs] are called by the word 'speech' because they are the locations of the organ of speech.
Their mere exhaustion is the result of uttering the word 'not-self'; the meaning is that it is merely a weariness of the mind resulting from that exertion. //2//
Inference is not [the means of knowledge], because the word for it does not apply to that [object]. (BBs 1.3.3)
He says that while a specific reason (*vaiśeṣika-hetu*) has been stated to establish Brahman, there is no such specific reason to establish any other entity.
That which is inferred—the *pradhāna* imagined in the Sāṃkhya tradition—is not to be understood here as the abode of heaven, earth, and so forth.
Why? Because it lacks the word for that (*atacchabdāt*).
The word "that" (*tat*) is a term that denotes that insentient *pradhāna*; "not that" (*atad*) is a term that does not denote it.
For there is no word here whatsoever that denotes an insentient *pradhāna*.

There exists here a word that establishes a conscious being (*cetana*) which is the opposite of that [insentient *pradhāna*]—such as "He who is all-knowing, all-perceiving" (Muṇḍaka 1.1.9)—by which the insentient *pradhāna* might be understood either as the cause or as the abode.
For this very reason, even the wind (*vāyu*) is not accepted here as the abode of heaven, earth, and so forth. // 3 //

"Vaiśeṣika" means that which is unique, such as the word "self" (ātman) and so forth. He states another meaning for the phrase "from a word not denoting that" (*atacchabdāt*): "of that which is the opposite of that."
For this very reason, that is, precisely because of the word "atacchabda" (not that word). //3//
And [the word] *prāṇabhṛt* [is also used]. BBs 1.3.4.

Although it is possible for the individual living being (*prāṇabhṛt*), who is the self of consciousness, to possess selfhood and sentience, nevertheless, since omniscience and other such qualities are impossible for one whose knowledge is limited by adjuncts (*upādhi*), even the living being must not be accepted as the substratum of that which is denoted by the word "That" (the Supreme Self).
Furthermore, it is not at all possible for the limited and non-omnipresent living being, constrained by adjuncts, to be the substratum of heaven, earth, and so forth.
The formulation of a separate rule is for the sake of what follows.
Regarding the phrase "and [it is] a living being" (*prāṇābhṛcca*):
in the sūtra, the word *ca* (and) serves to carry over (*anuṣaṅga*) the negative particle (*nañ*) from the preceding sūtra.
Since the word "self" (*ātman*), when used in grammatical apposition with the term "omniscient," does not denote a living soul (*jīva*), the word "therefore" (*ataḥ*) means "for that reason."

[Objection: Why was the single sūtra "Not [the self] is the vital breath, because of the word 'that'" not composed as one? [Response: Because the reason for refuting both is one and the same. To this he says: "Separately. "Yoga" means the sūtra.

The meaning is that although the reasons found in the subsequent sūtras are connected with the refutation of the vital breath alone, the sūtra was made separate by adding "and the vital breath" (prāṇabhṛcca) for the sake of easy understanding. //4//

And for what further reason should the individual living being (prāṇabhṛt) not be accepted as the abode of heaven, earth, and so forth?— START BsCom_1,3.1.5-6 END The individual soul cannot be regarded as the abode of heaven, earth, and so forth, for the following reason as well:— START BsCom_1,3.1.7 END

Because of the designation of difference (bhedavyapadeśāt). And here there is a designation of difference in the passage, "Know that one alone as the Self," by way of the relationship between the object of knowledge and the knower.
In that context, the individual soul (*prāṇabhṛt*) is the knower because it desires liberation.
By process of elimination, it is understood that Brahman, which is denoted by the word "Self," is the abode of heaven, earth, and so forth,
and not the individual living being.
Furthermore, for what reason should the living being (prāṇabhṛt) not be accepted as the abode of heaven, earth, and so forth?
Because of the context (prakaraṇa). And this context pertains to the Supreme Self (paramātman).
"O Venerable One, when what is known does all this become known? (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 1.1.3).

Because of this expectation of knowing everything through the knowledge of one thing, it must be the Supreme Self—which is the self of all—that, when known, makes all this known, and not merely the individual living being. // 6 //
He explains those very reasons by way of inquiry with the words "From what [reason]? and so forth.

Although it is the pure inner self (*pratyagātman*) alone that is to be known here, nevertheless, because the knower—in its form as a living being (*jīvatva*)—is distinct from the object of knowledge, it does not possess the nature of the object of knowledge; this is the meaning.

And thus, it should be understood that the status of the living being (*jīva*) as the subject matter of the passage concerning heaven, earth, and so forth (*dyubhvādivākya*) is refuted by virtue of its being qualified by the characteristic of being a living being, and not in its pure form. // 5 // // 6 //
And on account of abiding and eating:
with reference to the abode of heaven, earth, and so forth, in the passage "Two birds, inseparable companions and friends" (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 3.1.1),
abiding and eating are indicated.
"One of them eats the sweet fruit"—this refers to the consumption of the fruits of action; "the other looks on without eating"—this refers to abiding in indifference.
And by these two states of abiding and eating, the Lord (Īśvara) and the Knower of the Field (Kṣetrajña) are understood therein.
If the Lord is intended here as the abode of heaven, earth, and so forth, then the separate mention of that very Lord under discussion from the individual soul (kṣetrajña) is appropriate;
otherwise, the mention of something not under discussion would be accidental and disconnected.
[Objection: But for you as well, the separate mention of the individual soul from the Lord would result in being equally accidental. [Reply: No.
Because that [the individual soul] is not intended to be expressed.

For it is well known in the world that the two field-knower (kṣetrajña) are connected to adjuncts such as the intellect (buddhi) in each body by virtue of being the agent and the enjoyer; thus, they are not what the scripture intends to express with its primary purport.

However, since the Lord (Īśvara) is not established through worldly knowledge, He is what the scripture intends to express with its primary purport; therefore, it is not reasonable for His statement to be considered accidental.
In the passage, "The two selves have entered the cave," this is also shown: that in the verse "Two birds... (Ṛg Veda 1.164.20), the Lord (Īśvara) and the individual soul (kṣetrajña) are spoken of.

Even when, according to the interpretation provided by the Paiṅgi Upaniṣad, the qualities (sattva) and the individual soul (kṣetrajña) are said to be spoken of in this verse, there is still no contradiction whatsoever.
How so?

For here, the individual soul (*prāṇabhṛt*), which is perceived in every body through its identification with limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) such as the quality of sentience (*sattva*)—just like the space within a jar or other vessels—is denied [to be] the abode of heaven, earth, and so forth.
However, that which is characterized as being free from all limiting adjuncts in all bodies is not denied [to be the abode];
rather, that which is thus characterized in all bodies is the Supreme Self (*paramātman*) itself.

Just as the apertures of jars and the like, when no longer characterized by limiting adjuncts such as the jars themselves, become nothing other than the great space (mahākāśa), so too, since it is impossible for living beings to be anything other than the Supreme, the denial [of their being that] is not tenable. Therefore, the denial of being the abode of heaven, earth, and so forth applies only to those who identify with the limiting adjuncts of the individual soul (sattva) and the rest.
Therefore, the Supreme Brahman alone is the abode of heaven, earth, and so forth.
This very point is established by the sūtra itself, "That which has the qualities of invisibility and so on, because of the mention of its attributes.
For this passage, "In whom heaven, earth, and the intermediate space [are woven]," is recited in the midst of that very section concerning the Source of Beings (bhūtayoni).
However, it is presented again for the sake of further elaboration. // 7 //

Now, one might object: even though the Lord and the individual soul are mentioned in the verse "Two birds... (*dvā suparṇā*) with respect to their abiding together, for what purpose is the Lord to be understood here through the statement regarding the "abode" (*āyatana*)? To this, he says: "And if the Lord...
Here, the Lord to be understood is pure consciousness alone (*śuddhacinmātra*), not one qualified by omniscience and other such attributes.
Because that [objection] is not what is intended to be established here;

and since it is impossible for something that is not the subject of the discourse to be mentioned abruptly in the middle, the intention is that it must be grasped by the initial statement. Not understanding this, he raises an objection: "But even for you... and so forth.

He provides the rebuttal with "No," [meaning] that for the purpose of establishing the nature of Brahman, it is possible to refer (anuvāda) to the individual soul (jīva), even though it is not the subject at hand and is introduced abruptly, because it is well-known in the world.
Now, one might ask: since the two birds were mentioned in the verse "Two birds" (*dvā suparṇā*), how can this Sūtra apply here? To this he says: "The cave" (*guhām*).
The meaning is that by means of their abiding and eating, the identity of the Lord (Īśvara) and the Knower of the Field (Kṣetrajña) is shown through a reference to them.

Now, one might object that here the individual soul (jīva) and the Lord (īśa) are not the subjects of the restatement (anuvādya), because this would contradict the commentary of Paiṅgi; therefore, there is a lack of consistency with the Sūtra. To this, he says: "yadāpi" (even when...). The meaning is that even then, there is no inconsistency with the Sūtra.

Having referred to the intellect (*buddhi*) by means of the sentence concerning "eating" (*adana*), and having stated in the sentence concerning "abiding" (*sthiti*) that the object of knowledge is the pure inner Self (*pratyagātman*), which is Brahman and distinct from the intellect and other faculties, [the author] explains the connection with the Sūtra—stating that in the *dyubhvādi* passage it is precisely that [Brahman] which is to be understood, and not the individual soul (*jīva*) conditioned by the intellect—by saying "How? and so forth.
Now, one might object: "But here it is the unconditioned individual soul that is spoken of, not the Supreme Brahman"; to this he replies: "He who... (*yas tu*).
He raises the objection of redundancy with the words "This very [point]" (tadetad).
The meaning is that the passage concerning heaven, earth, and so forth has Brahman as its purport.
He provides the resolution with the words "For the sake of elaboration" (prapañcārtham).
The meaning is that, by means of the explanation of the word "bridge" (setu), the purpose is to clarify that the source of beings is the inner self (pratyagātman).
Therefore, it is established that the Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad is consistently integrated with Brahman. //7//
Section on the Abundance (bhūmādhikaraṇa), Sūtras 8–9. 2. The section concerning the Abundance. Sūtras 8–9.
"The Infinite [is Brahman] because of its being taught as superior to the serene faith.

This they recite: "The Infinite indeed is what one should desire to understand; 'Venerable Sir, I desire to understand the Infinite. Where one sees nothing else, hears nothing else, understands nothing else—that is the Infinite. But where one sees something else, hears something else, understands something else—that is the finite," and so forth (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 7.23.24).
In this regard, there is a doubt:
first of all, the term *bhūman* denotes plurality, according to the rule "there is elision of the suffix *bahu*, and *bhū* replaces *bahu*" (Pāṇini 6.4.158).
Thus, because it is recalled that the word *bhūman* ends in an abstract suffix (*bhāvapratyaya*),

when there arises a specific desire to know what the nature of that "muchness" (*bahutva*) is, it appears from the proximity [of the text] that "Breath (*prāṇa*) is indeed more than hope" (*Chāndogya Upaniṣad* 7.15.1) that Breath is *bhūman*.

Likewise, from the introduction of the context—“For I have heard from those like your venerable self that the knower of the Self crosses over sorrow; I, O venerable sir, am in sorrow; may your venerable self carry me across to the further shore of sorrow” (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 7.1.3)—it also appears that the Supreme Self is the ‘Bhūman.
In this regard, a doubt arises as to which [interpretation] should be accepted as correct and which should be rejected.
What, then, is the initial position?
That the vital breath (prāṇa) is the plenitude (bhūman).
Why?
This is because a succession of questions and answers is observed, as for instance: "Is there, O Venerable One, anything greater than name? and "Speech, indeed, is greater than name."

Likewise, there is a continuous stream of questions and answers regarding what is greater than name and so forth, up to the vital breath (*prāṇa*), beginning with "Is there, O Venerable One, anything greater than name? and "Mind, indeed, is greater than speech.

However, no such question or answer regarding something greater than the vital breath is seen, such as "Is there, O Venerable One, anything greater than the vital breath? or "This, indeed, is greater than the vital breath."

Having explained in detail, through such passages as "Prāṇa indeed is greater than name and all that precedes it up to hope" and "Prāṇa is indeed greater than hope," that one who perceives Prāṇa is an "exceeding speaker" (ativādin)—and having authorized this by saying, "If one says, 'Are you an exceeding speaker? he should say, 'I am an exceeding speaker,' and not deny it"—the text then draws back upon this state of being an exceeding speaker, which is the vow of Prāṇa, without abandoning it, stating: "But he indeed is an exceeding speaker who exceeds by means of Truth."
By introducing the "plurality" (bhūman) through the succession beginning with truth and ending with vital breath (prāṇa), it is understood that they consider vital breath itself to be the plurality.
But how, when the plurality is explained as being vital breath, can the statement "where one sees nothing else," which is intended as the definition of the plurality, be explained?

It is said in reply: because in the state of deep sleep, when the organs have been swallowed by vital breath, the cessation of activities such as seeing is observed, this definition—"where one sees nothing else"—is possible for vital breath as well.

And so the Śruti, after describing the state of deep sleep as the cessation of the activity of all the organs with the words "He does not hear, he does not see," and so forth, declares in that very same state the waking of the fivefold vital breath (prāṇa) with the words, "The fires of the vital breaths alone remain awake in this city" (Praśna Upaniṣad 4.2.3), thereby showing that the state of deep sleep has the vital breath as its primary constituent.
Furthermore, that which is heard in scripture regarding the blissfulness of the Infinite—namely, "That which is the Infinite is bliss" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 7.23)—is also not contradictory;
for it is said: "In this state, this deity does not see dreams, and then there is the bliss that exists in this body" (Praśna Upaniṣad 4.6).
Thus, because bliss is heard of specifically in the state of deep sleep;
and as for the statement, "That which is the Plenum (bhūman), that is the Immortal" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 7.24.1), that too is not inconsistent with the vital breath (prāṇa).
This is because of the scriptural text: "Breath indeed is the immortal" (Kauṣītaki Upaniṣad 3.2).

But how is it appropriate for this section to arise from a desire to know the Self—given the statement, "He who knows the Self overcomes sorrow"—if one considers the breath to be the "plurality" (bhūman)?
We reply that it is the breath itself which is intended here as the Self.

For instance, [the text] makes Prāṇa itself the self of all: "Prāṇa is indeed the father, Prāṇa is the mother, Prāṇa is the brother, Prāṇa is the sister, Prāṇa is the teacher, Prāṇa is the Brāhmaṇa" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 7.15.1).

And through the two illustrations of being the self of all and of the spokes and the nave—namely, "Just as the spokes are fixed in the nave, so everything is fixed in this Prāṇa"—there arises the nature of plenitude (bhūma), which consists in vastness.
[Objection: Because [the word *bhūman*] occurs in connection with *prāṇa*, it follows that *prāṇa* is *bhūman*.
To this, the following is said: Here, the Supreme Self alone must be *bhūman*, not *prāṇa*.
Why?
Because it is taught as being superior to the state of serene confidence (*saṃprasāda*). The term "serene confidence" refers to the state of deep sleep.
Because it is etymologically defined as that "in which one becomes perfectly serene" (*samyak prasīdati*),

and because it is mentioned alongside the states of dreaming and waking in the *Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad*, where it is stated that "the vital breath (*prāṇa*) remains awake in that state of perfect serenity," it is the vital breath (*prāṇa*) that is intended here by the term "perfect serenity.
The meaning is that the "Abundance" (*bhūman*) is taught as being superior to the vital breath.
If the *bhūman* were indeed the vital breath (*prāṇa*), then that very breath would have been taught after [the teaching on] it; however, this would be inconsistent.
For it was not the case that after "name" (*nāman*), "name" itself was taught as being greater than name.
Rather, something else distinct from name, namely speech (*vāk*), was taught: "Speech, verily, is greater than name."
Likewise, in each instance, that which is taught as superior to speech and the other organs is indeed something distinct from them;
similarly, the "Fullness" (bhūman) taught as superior to the vital breath (prāṇa) must be something distinct from the vital breath.
But is it not the case that here there is no question such as, "Venerable Sir, is there anything greater than the vital breath?"?
Nor is there any reply stating that "there is indeed something greater than breath"; how then could Bhūman be taught as being superior to breath?

Furthermore, we observe that the status of being an "ativādin" (one who speaks beyond) concerning breath alone is carried forward in the subsequent passage: "But he indeed is an ativādin who speaks beyond by means of Truth."
Therefore, it is not the case that there is no instruction regarding the attainment [of the Self].

To this, it is replied: First of all, it cannot be said that this is merely a reference back to the status of being "one who speaks beyond" (ativādin) with respect to the vital breath (prāṇa) alone, because of the specific statement: "He who speaks beyond by means of Truth."
But surely this statement of distinction must also concern the vital breath alone.
How so?
Just as when it is said, "He is an Agnihotrin who speaks the truth," one does not become an Agnihotrin merely by speaking the truth; [so too here].
By what means, then? By the Agnihotra itself;
however, speaking the truth is stated as a specific qualification for the performer of the Agnihotra.

Likewise, when it is said, "But he indeed speaks transcendentally who speaks transcendentally by means of truth," transcendental speech does not consist in the mere speaking of truth; rather, it consists precisely in the knowledge of Prāṇa under discussion.
"But it is intended that speaking the truth is a specific quality of those who know the vital breath.
We say: no, because that would entail the abandonment of the meaning of the scripture.

For here, by the direct statement (*śruti*), it is understood that "speaking beyond" (*ativāditva*) consists in speaking the truth—as in: "He who speaks beyond by means of truth, he truly speaks beyond.
There is no mention here of the knowledge of the vital breath (*prāṇa*);
however, the knowledge of the vital breath might be connected [to this passage] by virtue of the context (*prakaraṇa*).
In that case, the direct Vedic statement (*śruti*) would have to be set aside in deference to the context;

furthermore, the word "but" (*tu*) in the phrase "But he indeed speaks more than this" (*eṣa tu vā ativadati*) would not be appropriate for the purpose of excluding what has been previously discussed. [This is also seen in:
"Truth, however, must indeed be sought to be known" (*satyaṃ tveva vijijñāsitavyam*, Chāndogya Upaniṣad 7.16).
And thus, the employment of a further effort indicates the intention to express a different meaning.

Therefore, this should be viewed as being similar to how, when the praise of a single Veda is the subject at hand, one praises a person who has studied four Vedas—saying, "But he is a great Brāhmaṇa who has studied the four Vedas"—wherein the one who knows four Vedas is praised as being something distinct from those who know one Veda;
nor is there a rule that the intention to express a different meaning must necessarily take the form of a question and its answer.

Because the intention to convey another meaning arises from the impossibility of [the previous teaching] being connected to the subject at hand, Sanatkumāra himself instructs Nārada—who has become silent after hearing the instruction ending with the vital breath (prāṇa)—as follows:

"That which constitutes being an 'exceeding speaker' (ativādin) by means of the knowledge of the vital breath, which concerns what is unreal and a mere modification, is in fact not being an exceeding speaker at all; rather, 'he indeed is an exceeding speaker who exceeds as the Truth (satya)'."
In this context, "Truth" refers to the Supreme Brahman, because it is of the nature of the ultimate reality; as it is said:
"Brahman is Truth, Knowledge, and Infinite" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.1).
And this is so because of another scriptural passage (*śrutyantara*).

To Nārada, who had been thus instructed and who approached with the words, "O Venerable Sir, may I speak beyond the truth," [the Teacher] taught the *bhūman* (the Infinite) through a succession of means such as knowledge and the like.
It is understood that what was promised there as the "truth" (*satya*) to be spoken of as superior to the vital breath (*prāṇa*) is precisely what is here called the *bhūman*.
Therefore, since there is an instruction regarding the "Full" (bhūman) which is superior to the vital breath (prāṇa), the "Full" must be the Supreme Self, distinct from the vital breath.
In this way, the commencement of this section with the desire to know the Self will be logically justified.
Furthermore, the claim that the vital breath alone is intended here as the Self is also untenable.
For the vital breath does not possess the nature of the Self by its primary function;
nor is there any cessation of sorrow other than through the knowledge of the Supreme Self, as it is said: "There is no other path for going" (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 3.8).
This is because of another scriptural passage;

furthermore, having begun with "May the Blessed One carry me across to the further shore of grief" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 7.1.3), it concludes: "To him whose impurities had been wiped away, the Blessed Sanatkumāra showed the further shore of darkness" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 7.26.2).
"Darkness" refers to ignorance, which is the cause of sorrow and other afflictions.
Furthermore, in the instruction ending with the vital breath (*prāṇa*), it would not be stated that the vital breath is dependent on anything else, as in:
"From the Self comes the vital breath" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 7.26.2).
And such is the Brāhmaṇa.
If it be argued that at the end of the section there will be an intention to speak of the Supreme Self, [and that] "the Bhūman is indeed Prāṇa," we say: no.
"O Venerable One, on what is that established? "On its own greatness" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 7.24.1).
Because of this and other passages, the Bhūman alone is carried forward until the conclusion of the section.
Furthermore, the nature of being *bhūman*—which consists of vastness—is all the more appropriate for the Supreme Self, as it is the cause of all things. // 8 //
FN: The *bhūman* is the full reality that transcends empirical discourse (*vyavahāra*). "To those like you who possess the vision of the Blessed One" means to those such as yourself.
"The deity" refers to the individual soul (*jīva*) conditioned by the limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) of the intellect and so forth.
However, by virtue of the context, it should be connected as the reason for being "one who speaks beyond"; this is the remainder [of the sense].

The Existent (*bhūman*).
