When Sanatkumāra had thus stated to Nārada that "one who seeks unsurpassed happiness must investigate the Infinite (bhūman) alone," Nārada says: "The Infinite.
He states the definition of the Infinite as being non-dual with the words: "Wherein...
He clarifies the definition of the Infinite by stating the definition of the finite with the words: "But where..."
Regarding this, he states the seed of doubt by way of a question, beginning with "Why? (*kutaḥ*).

In the analysis of the compound *bahoḥ bhāvaḥ* ("the state of being much"), when the suffix *iman* is applied according to the rule *apṛthvādibhya imanij vā*, the rule *bahoḥ lopo bhū ca bahoḥ* dictates that there should be an elision of the initial vowel *i* of the suffix *iman* following the word *bahu*.

Since it has been stated that "in place of *bahu*, the substitute *bhūḥ* should occur," the word *bhūman* is formed. Because it ends with the suffix *iman* which denotes the sense of "being" (*bhāva*), its expressed meaning is "muchness" (*bahutva*).
When there arises the expectancy as to what possesses this quality (*dharmi*), the vital breath (*prāṇa*) situated in the immediate context appears as the substrate of that quality.

The meaning is that the Self, situated at the beginning of the sentence, also appears as the subject (*dharmin*) in need of its own definition; thus, a doubt arises from both the proximate and remote contexts.
Previously, it was stated that because of the word "Self," the abode of heaven, earth, and so forth is Brahman;
however, that is incorrect.

The proponent of the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣin) objects on the grounds that the term "Self" (ātman) is used even for what is not Brahman—as in the statement, "He who knows the Self overcomes grief"—and thus argues that "the vital breath (prāṇa) is the Infinite (bhūman).
One should understand the grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya) here as arising from the non-difference between the attribute and the substratum.
Furthermore, it should be understood that the fruits of the prima facie and final views are, respectively, the meditation upon the vital breath and the knowledge of Brahman.
In this chapter, a difference in meaning is observed through the distinction between questions and answers.

However, the "More" (bhūman), which is superior to the vital breath (prāṇa), is declared to be non-different from the vital breath by means of the previously mentioned indicative mark, even without a further question regarding what is more than that—this he states with the words beginning "Why? (kasmāt).
The connection with the preceding section is that [the state] "more than the vital breath" is not seen [as a separate entity].

Now, one might object: "Since the word 'but' (tu) in the passage 'But he indeed speaks surpassingly' marks a break in the context concerning the vital breath (prāṇa), the 'Abundant One' (bhūman) cannot be the vital breath. To this, the author replies: "The vital breath alone," and so forth. Having transcended the objects of meditation beginning with Name and ending with the Breath—which is the most excellent—one is called an "ativādī" (one who speaks surpassingly), meaning a knower of the Breath. It has been stated that when someone asks such an ativādī, "Are you an ativādī?", he should say, "I am," and should not make a denial by saying, "I am not an ativādī."

Having identified this [Self] as "the knower of the vital breath" (*prāṇavit*), and having established a succession of qualities such as truthfulness, meditation, reflection, and faith, there is no break in the context because of the instruction on the "Full" (*bhūman*).
The word "but" (*tu*) is for the purpose of refuting the status of being an "exceeding speaker" (*ativāditva*) for one who meditates on names and so forth; this is the meaning.

He connects the description of the characteristics of the Full—namely its nature as bliss and immortality—with the vital breath by means of the question beginning with "How, then? (*kathaṃ punar...*).

When the vital breaths (prāṇas) are swallowed up—that is, when they have dissolved—the person in deep sleep does not hear; this is the implied sense. According to the Vedic scripture, "The Gārhapatya fire is indeed this apāna, the Vyāna is the Anvāhāryapacana, and the Prāṇa is the Āhavanīya," the vital breaths are the fires that remain awake—meaning they stay fully active—within this city, which is the body.
The "deity" is the individual soul (jīva).

Now, the logical connection (*anvaya*) is that at the time when one does not see dreams, the fact that the vital breath (*prāṇa*) is blissful is not contradictory, because it is heard [in scripture] as such.
He removes the contradiction with the opening statement regarding the term "Self" by saying, "the vital breath itself.
Having raised the doubt as to how the vital breath can be the Self, he says, "for thus it is," because it is so stated in scripture.

The syntactical connection (*anvaya*) is that the Śruti accepts *prāṇa* as the substrate of all by stating, "everything has been surrendered. Therefore, it shows that being the Self (*ātmatva*) is its primary meaning, using the term "the state of serene clarity" (*saṃprasāda*).
This is also because of the usage: "Having remained in this state of serene clarity, he returns again.
He states that the word *tat* denotes deep sleep (*suṣupti*), citing the *Bṛhadāraṇyaka*.
He states that the vital breath (prāṇa) is the indicated meaning (lakṣya) because of its connection with the literal meaning (vācyārtha), saying "And in that" (tasyāṃ ca).
The meaning here is "in this Sūtra.
In this chapter, the Expanse (bhūman) is distinct from the vital breath.
The meaning is: "because it is taught after that," just as speech and the other [organs] are taught after name and the rest.
He states the subverting argument (bādhaka) which eliminates the reason in the counter-example: "If it were the vital breath alone... and so forth.
The meaning is that it is illogical for something to be taught by itself from itself, and this is not observed in the case of names and so forth.
He raises a doubt regarding the unestablished nature of the reason: "But here... and so on.

This word "this" (eṣa) is not a referent for the subject matter at hand— the knower of the vital breath— because, being dependent on the relative pronoun "that" (yat), it denotes one who speaks the truth.
Therefore, he says, "To this it is replied," establishing the reason that the context of the vital breath has been interrupted.
The meaning is that "speaking the truth" (*satyavāditva*) is the specific distinction; because the text says "he who possesses that [truth]," there is no reference back to what preceded.

One might object by way of an analogy: "But surely," [the opponent argues], "since the text restates, 'He who knows the vital breath (*prāṇa*) speaks beyond [others],' and then enjoins, 'he should speak the truth,' there is no break in the context of the vital breath. This is the objection raised with the example.

For the word *satya* (truth) is conventionally established as denoting that which is uncontradicted (*abādhita*), and thus it is a direct designation (*vācaka*) for Brahman, since everything other than that is false (*mithyā*).

However, when used in the sense of "speaking the truth," it is figurative (*lākṣaṇika*) due to its connection with the act of speaking an uncontradicted object; therefore, there is no injunction here regarding the expression of the thing to be indicated. Thus he says: "We say, 'No'."

Furthermore, by the use of the instrumental case in the scriptural text, "He speaks surpassingly by means of the Truth-Brahman" (*satyena brahmaṇātivadati*), it is heard that the state of speaking surpassingly has Brahman as its instrument;
therefore, it is not proper to sublate this through the context (*prakaraṇa*). Thus he says, beginning with "For by the scripture...
and so forth. Regarding the word "here":
The meaning is "one whose speech is truth.

Having stated that the context (*prakaraṇa*) is set aside by the scriptural statement (*śruti*) "by truth," he says with the word "but" (*tu*) that it is also set aside [by the force of the words themselves]: "the subject under discussion" (*prakṛta*).
And because of the indicative mark (*liṅga*) of being something to be known, he says "but truth indeed" (*satyaṃ tveva*) to show that it is different from what was previously mentioned.
He provides an illustration for the interruption of the context with the words "Therefore" (*tasmāt*).

The meaning is that, by the force of direct scriptural statement (*śruti*) and indicative mark (*liṅga*), this [Self] must be seen as truly distinct from the Prāṇa under discussion in its primary sense.
Thus, by stating the connection of being an "exceeding speaker" (*ativāditva*) with Brahman, its status as a characteristic mark (*liṅga*) of Prāṇa is refuted.
As for the claim that the "plurality" (bhūman) refers to the vital breath (prāṇa) because it is stated without a prior question,
that is not so;
he says "and not," meaning that such a reason is not decisive.
The meaning is that there is no fixed rule that a difference in questions necessitates a difference in subject matter,

because Maitreyī asked about the single Self many times; furthermore, even without a formal question, it is observed that what is stated regarding mastery of the four Vedas is distinct from the single Veda under discussion.

In this regard, just as there is a difference in meaning because the state of being "versed in the four Vedas" (*caturvedatva*) has no connection with the subject at hand, so it is here as well; he clarifies this with the words beginning with "therein" (*tatra*).
Since the word "truth" (*satya*) refers to the vital breath (*prāṇa*), he says: "Therein, truth... (*tatra satyam iti*).
Vijñāna is profound contemplation (*nididhyāsana*).
From the first word, reflection (*manana*), faith (*śraddhā*), hearing (*śravaṇa*), purity of mind (*manaḥ-śuddhi*), steadfastness (*niṣṭhā*), and the actions that cause it are included.
These, beginning with hearing, are the marks (*liṅga*) indicating that the object of knowledge, which is truth, is Brahman.

Thus, having set aside the intermediate context of the vital breath (prāṇa) by means of direct scriptural statements (śruti) and indicatory marks (liṅga), he says "tatra yat" to show that the subject under discussion is the True Brahman, which possesses the attribute of manifoldness expressed by the word "bhūman. Furthermore,

according to the maxim that "that which is remote but has a syntactic expectancy (sākāṅkṣa) is stronger than even that which is proximate," he says "evaṃ ca" to show that, having seen the proximate and self-sufficient vital breath, the "Self" mentioned at the beginning of the passage must be understood here as the "bhūman," since it requires the "bhūman" section for its own full elucidation.

Furthermore, since the passage begins with "the further shore of sorrow" (*śokasya pāram*) and concludes with "the further shore of darkness" (*tamasaḥ pāram*), and because it is impossible to cross over sorrow without uprooting its very foundation, the word "sorrow" (*śoka*) here refers to the fundamental ignorance (*mūlatamaḥ*).
He states that the Self is Brahman on the basis of the inferential mark (*liṅga*) of being cognizable by the knowledge that brings about its cessation—expressed as "nor elsewhere.

The connection is that the Brāhmaṇa declares the dependence of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) upon the Self. Now, one might object: let this final Brāhmaṇa be intended to have Brahman as its primary subject.

Then, one might raise the doubt that the "plurality" (bhūman) previously mentioned is the vital breath (prāṇa), based on the phrase "at the end of the section. He says "No," meaning it is not so, because the word "that" (tat) draws back the reference to the plurality. //8//
And because of the attainment of dharma. BBs_1,3.9 / END BsCom_1,3.2.8 START BsCom_1,3.2.9
Furthermore, those attributes that are heard in relation to the *bhūman* are applicable to the Supreme Self.

For the text, "Where one sees nothing else, hears nothing else, and understands nothing else—that is the *bhūman*," makes known the absence of activities such as seeing within the *bhūman*. And this absence of activities such as seeing is understood to belong to the Supreme Self.
This is because of other scriptural passages such as, "But when for him everything has become the Self alone, then by what and whom should he see? (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.5.15).

Furthermore, that absence of activities such as seeing which was mentioned regarding the state of deep sleep is stated with the intention of expressing the non-attachment (*asaṅgatva*) of the Self itself, not with the intention of expressing the nature of the vital breath (*prāṇa*).
Because this occurs within the context of the Supreme Self (paramātman);
furthermore, even that bliss which was mentioned regarding that state was spoken with the intention of expressing that the Self itself is of the nature of bliss.
For it has been said: "This is his supreme bliss; other beings live on only a fraction of this very bliss" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.3.32).

Here too, by the statement, "That which is the Plenum (bhūman) is bliss; there is no bliss in the small; the Plenum alone is bliss," [the text] shows that Brahman alone is bliss by refuting conventional happiness. Furthermore, the immortality heard here in the phrase, "That which is the Plenum is immortal," leads one to understand the Supreme Cause.
Because the immortality of modifications is merely relative, and because of another scriptural passage stating, "Therefore, everything else is perishable" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.4.2).

And thus, these attributes—truthfulness, being established in one's own glory, omnipresence, and being the self of all—which are heard [in the scripture], are applicable only to the Supreme Self and not to anything else.
Therefore, it is established that "Bhūman" refers to the Supreme Self.
(9) [Note: This was stated previously by the passage beginning with "he does not hear," etc.]

That which is accompanied by illness and suffering is *sāmaya*; it is afflicted and perishable. Regarding the state of Brahman as the Abundant (*bhūman*), he states another indicative mark: "Dharma," etc.
The Sūtra:

Having restated what was said regarding the characteristics of the *bhūman*—namely, that its nature as bliss and immortality is to be applied to the vital breaths (*prāṇa*)—it refutes that [view] with the words "And he who... and so forth.
For the self's status as a seer and so on exists only when there are limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) such as the intellect (*buddhi*).

In the absence of that [dreaming], there is the absence of that [seeing and hearing] during deep sleep; this was stated in the *Praśnopaniṣad* with reference to the Supreme Self—"he does not hear, he does not see"—for the purpose of knowing its state of non-attachment (*asaṅgatva*).
Likewise, in that very same text, the nature of bliss is attributed to the Self and not to the vital breath (*prāṇa*).
The meaning is: because another scriptural passage declares that bliss belongs to the Self alone, therefore [the Self is the enjoyer].
*Āmaya* is a defect such as destruction; that which is accompanied by this is *sāmaya*.
*Ārta* means perishable.
"He is below, He is above"—this refers to His omnipresence.
Furthermore, its being the Self of all is heard in the scripture: "That very one is all this.
Therefore, it is established that the section concerning the Bhūman is in harmony with the attributeless (nirguṇa) Brahman. //9//

Section on the Three Syllables (Akṣarādhikaraṇa) / Sūtras 10–12.
"The Imperishable [is Brahman], because it supports everything up to the ether.
"In what, then, is the ether woven, warp and woof? He said, "Gārgī, the Brāhmaṇas call this that Imperishable; it is neither coarse nor fine" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.8.7–8).
Thus it is heard in such passages.
Regarding this, there arises a doubt: does the word *akṣara* denote a phoneme (*varṇa*), or does it denote the Supreme Lord?

In this regard, since the word *akṣara* is well-known in such expressions as "the traditional collection of phonemes" (*akṣarasamāmnāya*) to mean a phoneme, and because it is improper to override its conventional meaning, [one might think] that "Oṃ is indeed all this" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 2.23.3).

And because in other scriptural passages such as these, even a phoneme (varṇa) is determined to be the self of all by virtue of being an object of meditation, it follows that the word "akṣara" refers to a phoneme;
this being the position reached, it is replied: the Supreme Self alone is denoted by the word "akṣara."
Why?
Because of the support of all things up to the end of space—that is, because it supports the entire collection of modifications from earth up to space.
For in that regard, it is said: "In space alone is all this collection of modifications, divided by the three periods of time, woven."

Having stated that [the ether] is woven across and through [Brahman] with the words "and woven across," and having introduced this Imperishable (akṣara) by means of the question, "In what, indeed, is the ether woven across and through?",
it is likewise concluded: "In this very Imperishable, O Gārgī, the ether is woven across and through."
This support of the ends of space is not possible for anything other than Brahman.
As for the statement, "The syllable Om is indeed all this," that too should be understood as being for the purpose of praise, because it serves as a means for the realization of Brahman.
Therefore, because it neither perishes (akṣarati) nor moves (aśnute), the Imperishable (Akṣara) is the supreme Brahman alone, by virtue of its eternity and omnipresence. 10.
FN: According to the maxim "conventional usage supersedes etymological derivation," he says: "by common renown. [The Sūtra states:
"The Imperishable [is Brahman], because it supports everything up to the ether.
He recites the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad: "In what, then..."

When Gārgī asked Yājñavalkya, "In what are all things—those that have been, those that are, and those that will be—woven? the sage replied that the unmanifested ether (*avyākṛtākāśa*) is the support for everything that has come into being.

To her second question, "In what is that ether woven?", the sage said that the substratum of that unmanifested is this Imperishable (*akṣara*), whose nature is defined by such qualities as not being gross and so forth. This is the meaning.
Because the word *akṣara* is used in both instances, a doubt arises.

Just as the word *satya* is conventionally established (*rūḍha*) in the sense of Brahman, and thus it was stated that "Brahman is the Bhūman," so too the word *akṣara* is conventionally established in the sense of a phoneme (*varṇa*); this is the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) based on that analogy.
In that case, the fruit would be the meditation (*upāsti*) upon the syllable *oṃ*.
The distinction is that, according to the established conclusion (siddhānta), the cognition of Brahman is devoid of attributes (nirguṇa).

Now, one might object: since the word *akṣara* (the Imperishable) is applied to Brahman in its primary sense due to its connection with immobility and indestructibility—as in "it does not perish" (*na kṣarati*)—the author says: "because of the transgression of common usage.
The meaning is that this follows the maxim: "Conventional meaning (rūḍhi) sets aside etymological derivation (yoga)."

Having raised the doubt as to how the syllable *oṃ* can be the support of all, [the author] states "The syllable *oṃ*" (*oṃkāra*) and so forth, saying that this is for the purpose of meditation, just as its being the self of all is stated in another Śruti.
Since the intention is determined to be that it is the substratum of the entire world up to the ether through the question and answer, the purpose is not merely meditation;

therefore, by the force of those indicative marks (*liṅga*), one should accept the etymological function (*yogavṛtti*) while setting aside the conventional meaning (*rūḍhi*). He establishes this conclusion with the words beginning with "Thus" (*evam*). //10//
It might be argued: if the dependence of an effect upon its cause is accepted, then the support of everything up to the ether is admitted.

This [objection] is applicable even to the proponents of primordial matter (pradhāna) as the cause. How can Brahman-hood be established on the grounds of "the support of the ends of space" (ambarāntadhṛti)? To this, he recites the following reply:
And that [support] is due to his command.
(BBs 1.3.11) And that support of the ends of space is the work of the Supreme Lord alone.
Why?
Because of the command.
For a command is heard here in such passages as: "By the command of this Imperishable, O Gārgī, the sun and the moon stand held apart" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.8.9).
And commanding is the activity of the Supreme Lord.
There can be no governance of the insentient *pradhāna*;
for there is no governance regarding jars and the like on the part of clay and other insentient causes of jars and such things. // 11 //
Having treated space as an element, he raises an objection with the words "this might be so.
He says "and that" to show that it is not so, because the scripture heard here concerns instruction regarding a conscious agent.
He explains the Sūtra with the words "and that."
The word "ca" (and) is for the purpose of excluding [the element] space from being a primary element (*bhūta*).

Since elemental space, as a product, cannot logically be the substratum of all products mentioned in scripture, it follows that "space" here refers only to the unmanifested ignorance (*avyākṛtājñāna*) designated by the term *pradhāna*. Therefore, because the Imperishable (*akṣara*) is its substratum, the Imperishable is not the *pradhāna*; this is the meaning.
[The phrase] "in the support" (*vidhṛtau*) means in the state of being supported as an object. //11//
And because of the exclusion of other states. (BBs 1.3.12)
Furthermore, because of the exclusion of any other state of being, Brahman alone is denoted by the word "akṣara" (the Imperishable).
Its specific function is the upholding of everything up to the ether, and this belongs to no one else.
What is meant by this "exclusion of any other state of being"?
The existence of another is "other-existence" (*anyabhāva*); the exclusion of that is "exclusion of other-existence" (*anyabhāvavyāvṛtti*).
What is meant by this is as follows:

that which is suspected here to be something other than Brahman denoted by the word "Imperishable" (*akṣara*)—the exclusion of the existence of that [other] constitutes this Imperishable which supports all things up to the ether.
The Śruti refutes this: "Now, that very Imperishable, O Gārgī, is unseen but seeing, unheard but hearing, unthought but thinking, unknown but knowing" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.8.11).
In this regard, the designation of being "unseen" and so forth is possible even for the Pradhāna.
Furthermore, designations such as "the seer" and so forth are not possible for the embodied soul because it is insentient.

Likewise, because of the negation of any difference in selfhood in the passage, "There is no other seer than this; there is no other hearer than this; there is no other thinker than this; there is no other knower than this," even the embodied soul, when characterized by limiting adjuncts (upādhi), cannot be denoted by the term "the Imperishable" (akṣara).
And because the possession of limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) is denied in the passage, "It is without eyes, without ears, without speech, without mind" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upani�sad 3.8.8);
for there can be no such thing as a "bodily self" (*śārīra*) that is devoid of limiting adjuncts.
Therefore, it is certain that the supreme Brahman alone is the Imperishable (akṣara). // 12 //
He explains the Sūtra by means of a question: "What is this?
He dispels the misconception that there is an exclusion based on the nature of a jar with the word "this.
The meaning is that the Śruti excludes the Imperishable as the support of everything up to the ether because it is insentient.
He also applies the Sūtra with the intent of refuting the existence of the individual soul (jīva), using the word "tathā" (likewise).
The meaning of the Sūtra is that "anyabhāva" means difference, and [the soul is not the Imperishable] because that difference is negated.
To the objection that, in that case, the purified individual soul itself would be the Imperishable and not the Supreme, he says: "na hi" (it is not so).
The meaning is that once [the self] has been purified, there is no state of being a living soul (jīvatva).
Therefore, it is established that the Gārgī-brāhmaṇa is consistent with the attributeless Imperishable (akṣara). //12//

Section on the Designation of the Object of Vision (Īkṣatikarmavyapadeśādhikaraṇa) / Sūtra 13. 4. [The Brahman is the object of the act of seeing,] because of the designation of the object of vision. (Sūtra 13)

"He is that [Brahman], because of the designation of Him as the object of the act of seeing. (Brahma Sūtra 1.3.13) Having introduced the subject with the words, "O Satyakāma, this *oṃkāra* is indeed both the higher and the lower Brahman; therefore, the knower, by means of this very support, attains one or the other," the scripture further declares: "But he who meditates upon the highest Puruṣa by means of this very syllable *oṃ*, consisting of three measures" (Praśna Upaniṣad 5.2, 5).
In this sentence, is it the Supreme Brahman that is indicated as the object of meditation, or rather the non-Supreme?
A doubt arises because of the context: "By this very abode, one attains either the Supreme or the non-Supreme.
On this point, the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa) is that this Brahman is the non-Supreme.
Why?

Because it is stated that for one who knows that [Self], there is a fruit delimited by a specific location, as in the passages: "He becomes united with the heat in the sun" and "He is led up to the world of Brahman by the Sāmans.
For it is not logical that one who knows the supreme Brahman should obtain a fruit delimited by a specific location.
Because the supreme Brahman is all-pervading.
[Objection: But if the lower Brahman is accepted, then the qualification "the Supreme Person" would not be appropriate.
[Response: This is not a fault.
Because the superiority of the vital breath (prāṇa) is established in relation to the body;
such being the position reached, it is replied: it is the Supreme Brahman alone that is taught here as the object of meditation.
Why?
Because of the designation of the object of the act of seeing.
"Seeing" (īkṣati) means perceiving;
that which is pervaded by the act of perceiving is the "object of the act of seeing."

In the supplementary portion of the passage, there is a designation of this Person who is to be meditated upon as the object of the act of seeing: "He sees the Person dwelling in the city, who is higher than the highest, beyond this mass of living beings.

In that context, even a thing that does not exist in reality can be the object of the verb *abhidhyai* (to meditate upon), because even that which is imagined by the mind can be the object of meditation.

However, since in the world it is observed that the object of the act of seeing (*īkṣati*) is a real entity, it is understood that this very Supreme Self, which is the object of perfect vision, is designated here as the object of the act of seeing. And it is He alone who is recognized here through the two terms "the other" (*para*) and "Person" (*puruṣa*) as the one to be meditated upon.
But was it not the "other Person" (*paraḥ puruṣaḥ*) who was mentioned in the context of meditation (*abhidhyāna*)?
But regarding the act of seeing, [the opponent asks]: "How can the other be recognized as the other?
To this it is replied: First of all, the words *para-puruṣa* (the Supreme Person) are common to both [contexts].
And here, the supreme Person under discussion who is to be meditated upon is not referred to by the term "mass of living beings" (jīvanaghana),
such that this Person to be seen would be something other than that supreme one.
What, then, is the "mass of living beings"?
It is said: "Ghana" means a solid mass or form. A "jīva-ghana" is a solid mass characterized as a living being.

Just like a lump of salt, that state of being a fragmentary portion (*khilya*) of the Supreme Self in the form of the individual soul (*jīva*), which is produced by limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) and is distinct from the objects and the senses—that is what is meant here by "jīva-ghana."

Another says: "That Brahmaloka which was indicated in the immediately preceding sentence, 'He is led by the Sāman chants to the Brahmaloka,' and which is superior to the other worlds, is here called the *jīvaghana* (the mass of individual souls).

For, since all individual souls (*jīvas*) accompanied by their instruments [of perception] are gathered together within Hiraṇyagarbha—who dwells in the Brahmaloka and is the self of all instruments—that Brahmaloka is termed the *jīvaghana*.

Therefore, that which is beyond it—the Supreme Self, who is the object of the act of seeing—is understood to be the very same one who is the object of the act of meditative reflection (*abhidhyāna*)."
Furthermore, the qualification "the Supreme Person" (paraṃ puruṣam) is appropriate only if the Supreme Self (paramātman) is understood;

for the Supreme Person is indeed the Supreme Self, since there is nothing else whatsoever beyond Him, as another scriptural passage states: "There is nothing higher than the Person; that is the culmination, that is the supreme goal."

Furthermore, by analyzing the statement, "The syllable *oṃ* is both the higher and the lower Brahman," and subsequently declaring that the higher Person is to be meditated upon by means of the *oṃ*, the text leads one to understand that the higher Person is indeed the supreme Brahman.

Moreover, the mention of the fruit consisting in liberation from evil—expressed in the words, "Just as a snake is freed from its skin, even so is he freed from evil"—indicates that the Supreme Self is the object of meditation here.
As for what was said—that for one meditating on the Supreme Self, a fruit limited by space is not appropriate—[that objection is thus answered].

To this it is replied: for one who meditates upon the Supreme Self by means of the three-measured *oṃkāra* as a support, the fruit is the attainment of the world of Brahman (*brahmaloka*), and through that, the gradual arising of perfect knowledge; thus, this will have the intention of "gradual liberation" (*kramamukti*), and so there is no fault.
(FN: The "higher" is the undifferentiated [Brahman]; the "lower" is the effected [Brahman].)
By means of the "abode" (āyatana), which is the instrument for attainment,
he follows after— that is, he reaches—
the other Brahman, Hiraṇyagarbha.
The meaning of the *samādhi* is that the gross aggregate (*piṇḍa*) is the Virāj; in relation to that, the Sūtra is "higher" (*para*).
The object of pervasion is the domain.
A "lump of rock-salt" (*saindhavākhilya*) is a mass of salt.
The state of being a remnant is smallness.
"Pādodara" means a snake.
It is [the Self] because of the designation of the act of seeing.
He cites the *Praśnopaniṣad*: "This," etc.
The teacher Pippalāda, being questioned by Satyakāma, says:
"O Satyakāma!"
This very syllable *oṃ* is Brahman—both the supreme, attributeless (*nirguṇa*) and the non-supreme, qualified (*saguṇa*).
For it is its symbol (*pratīka*), just as an image is of Viṣṇu.
Therefore, the knower who perceives the *praṇava* as the Self of Brahman, by means of this meditation on the *oṃkāra* as a locus and a means of attainment, [reaches that goal].

Having introduced the subject by stating that one "follows" or "attains" either the higher or lower meditation according to one's practice (*yathādhyānam*), [the text] speaks in the middle after describing the meditation on the *oṃ* syllable consisting of one and two measures (*mātrā*), saying: "But he who...
Here, the instrumental case (*tṛtīyā*) is used in the sense of "being in such a state" (*itthaṃbhāve*).
This is because the non-difference between Brahman and the *oṃkāra* is established from the outset.

For he who knows the seer (*ṛṣi*) and so forth, as well as the manifestation (*vibhūti*) of waking and the other states, for each of the three morae (*mātrā*) beginning with 'A'—specifically the single mora 'A'—by him that one mora of the *oṃkāra* is correctly known; thus it is "one-mora" (*ekamātra*).
Likewise, when there is correct knowledge of the manifestations of two morae, it is "two-mora" (*dvimātra*), and similarly "three-mora" (*trimātra*).

The meaning is that he who meditates upon the Puruṣa as the syllable *oṃ* goes to the world of Brahman through the door of the sun by means of the Sāman chants meditated upon as the manifestations of the syllable *oṃ*, and beholds the Supreme Self, the Puruṣa.
He states the doubt and its seed with the words beginning "What... and so forth;
the meaning is: in this statement regarding the three measures (*trimātra*).

In the preceding [section], it was determined that the object to be meditated upon—which had been presented as the prima facie view regarding the syllable *oṃ*—is that which resides in the intellect; thus, there is a contextual connection (*prasaṅga-saṃgati*).

Alternatively, just as in the previous case the word *akṣara*, though conventionally established in the sense of a "syllable," was shown by a mark (*liṅga*) to refer to Brahman, so too here he establishes the prima facie view by means of an analogy: that the word *para*, because of the mark of attaining the world of Brahman, refers to Hiraṇyagarbha. This is expressed in the words: "In that regard, the other... (*tatrāparam*).

The fruit in both cases is the meditation on the form of the Karya-Brahman (the effected Brahman). He is the worshiper; having become one with and entered into the sun, [one might object]: "Since it is heard that even for a worshiper of Brahman there is a small fruit—namely, that 'by meditating on the Lord as the giver of wealth, he obtains wealth'—" to this he says: "Not so."

Even if it were otherwise elsewhere, here— given that the opening statement is "the knower of the Supreme reaches the Unexcelled Beyond"— it is illogical for the knower of the Supreme to attain the non-Supreme, as this would contradict the initial premise.
Nor should it be argued that the attainment of the Supreme alone is what is being described here.
Since the Supreme [Self] is all-pervading, it would already be reached right here; thus, proceeding by way of the sun would be purposeless.

Therefore, the meaning is that the scriptural word "the Supreme" (*para*) must be set aside by the inferential mark (*liṅga*)—which consists in reaching something other [than the Supreme] and is supported by the opening statement. He asks about the interpretation of the word "Supreme": "But surely... (*nanu*).
The meaning of the resolution is that the *piṇḍa* (the gross body) is the *virāj*, and in relation to that, the *sūtra* is "higher" (*para*).
Since it has been asserted that the word "he" (*sa*) in the *sūtra* refers to the Lord (*īśvara*), he explains it as "the Supreme" (*parameva*).
The meaning is that this practitioner perceives the Person who is higher than this Hiraṇyagarbha as "I am Brahman."
"But let there be another [Self] who is the object of seeing";
to this he replies: "In that case, because of the verb *abhidhyai*.
Now, since seeing is a valid means of knowledge (*pramā*), it requires a real object; therefore, let the Supreme be the real object of seeing.
To the objection that there might be another [entity] different from the Supreme which could be meditated upon, he says: "That very one" (*sa eva*).

Because of the recognition through the two scriptural passages, the word *sa* (that) in the Sūtra is explained as "this very one. Here, the construction of the Sūtra is as follows: that which is to be meditated upon in the syllable *Oṃ* is indeed the Supreme Self, because the state of being worthy of contemplation (*īkṣaṇīyatva*) is mentioned in the remainder of the passage.
And here, because of the recognition [of the same] through scripture, it is said: "This is that very one.
Now, one might object: "But surely there is no recognition because of the difference in words," and thus the author introduces the objection with "nanu" (but surely).

Having admitted the difference in words such as "parātpara" (higher than the high), he states that there is no contradiction with the recognition expressed by the two scriptural passages, saying: "atra" (here).

[Objection: Is it not the case that, because of the reference to the object of meditation introduced by the phrase "from this supreme mass of living beings" (*etasmājjīvadhanātparāt*), the one to be seen must be the Supreme Self, which is different from the object of meditation? [Reply: To this, he says, "And not here.
Since in the world, meditation and the perception of its fruit have the same object, that which is to be meditated upon is indeed what is to be seen.
The intention is that in this way, there is a single coherent statement between the introduction and the conclusion.

He explains, starting with "Who then... and so forth, by means of a question, how the Lord of the Brahmaloka—who is most proximately referred to by the phrase "he [is led] from this mass of living beings"—is intended;
the sense is that this follows from the Sūtra: "A solid mass in the form of a body."
A "saindhavakhilya" is a lump of salt.
One whose state or portion is small, like a fragment, is "khilyabhāva.
By this term, he says that the world of Brahmā (brahmaloka) is referred to; thus he says, "the other."

He shows that the term *jīvaghana* (the mass of living beings) is used figuratively (*lakṣaṇā*) with respect to the world of Brahman by saying, "For of the living beings... The meaning is as follows: the "mass" (*ghana*) is the aggregate of those individual living beings who identify with the subtle instruments (*vyaṣṭi-karaṇa*); that [aggregate] which identifies with all instruments is the *jīvaghana*. Because he is their master, the world is indicated (*lakṣya*) through an indirect connection (*paraṃparā-sambandha*). Therefore, "beyond that" means transcending all worlds; the meaning is that he is pure (*śuddha*).
Furthermore, because the word *parapuruṣa* (the Supreme Person) has its primary meaning in the Paramātman, He alone is the object of meditation; thus he says, "The Supreme" (*param*).
Since there is nothing else higher than Him, He alone is the primary "Supreme," and not the Sūtrātman who is "higher than the body"—this is the meaning.

Moreover, since the Supreme Brahman was determined by the word "Supreme" at the beginning, it is that very same Supreme Brahman which must be meditated upon here in the remainder of the passage; thus he says, "The Supreme and the Lower" (*paraṃ cāparam ca*).
He says "as follows" (yathā) to indicate that this is also because of the sign of the cessation of evil.
"Pādodara" means a snake.

By meditating upon the Supreme Brahman through the syllable Om (oṃkāra), one goes to the world of Brahman by way of the sun, beholds the Supreme Brahman, and attains that very same state which is peaceful, fearless, and supreme; thus he states there is no contradiction, saying "to this it is replied."

Thus, it is established that by means of the two scriptural passages concerning the Supreme Person—supported by the section on establishing syntactical unity—the recognition of the Supreme Brahman sublates the indicative mark (liṅga) of reaching the world of Brahmā; consequently, the sentence is harmonized with Brahman as the object of meditation upon the syllable Om. //13//

The Section Concerning the Small [Space] (Daharādhikaraṇa) / Sūtras 14–21
The small [self] is [the Brahman] because of subsequent passages.

For the following statement is recorded in the tradition: "Now, in this city of Brahman, there is a small lotus-palace; within it is a small space (ākāśa). That which is inside that [space] is what one must seek, what one must desire to understand" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.1.1). And so forth.

In this regard, a doubt arises as to whether this "small space" (dahara ākāśa) heard of within the small lotus of the heart is the elemental ether (bhūtākāśa), or the individual self consisting of consciousness (vijñānātman), or the supreme self (paramātman).
Why does this doubt arise?
Because of the two terms "ether" (ākāśa) and "city of Brahman" (brahmapura).
For this word "ether" (ākāśa) is seen to be used both for the elemental ether and for the Supreme [Brahman].
In this regard, there arises a doubt: is the "small" (dahara) one the elemental ether itself, or is it the Supreme?

Likewise, regarding the term "city of Brahman" (brahmapura): does "Brahman" here refer to the individual soul (jīva), so that its city—the body—is the "city of Brahman," or is the "city of Brahman" the city of the Supreme Brahman itself?
In this regard, a doubt arises as to whether the "small ether" (daharākāśa) is the individual soul (jīva), the Supreme Self (para), or one of the two—the lord of the city (purasvāmin).
Since the word "ether" (ākāśa) is conventionally established in the sense of the elemental ether (bhūtākāśa), it follows that the "small" (dahara) refers to the elemental ether itself;
and its smallness is relative to its being the abode of that which is even smaller.

Furthermore, the relationship of comparison between the external space and "this space within the heart" expressed in the passage, "As large as this external space is, so large is this space within the heart," presupposes a distinction based on their external and internal states; moreover, the heaven, earth, and so forth are contained within that [space], because space is one in its nature as the principle of vacuity (*avakāśa*).
Alternatively, it might follow that the individual soul (*jīva*) is the "small" [space].
From the term "city of Brahman":
for this city of the individual soul (jīva), namely the body, is called the "city of Brahman" because it has been acquired through its own karma.
And it is by virtue of devotion (*bhakti*) that he is designated by the term "Brahman.
For the Supreme Brahman has no relationship with the body in the form of a master-and-possessor relation (*svasvāmibhāva*).
In that regard, it is observed that the master of a city resides in a single part of that city, just as a king [resides within his capital].
Furthermore, the individual soul (jīva) has the mind as its limiting adjunct,

and since the mind is generally established in the heart, this abiding within the heart must belong to the soul alone. Its smallness (daharatva) also becomes intelligible for that very soul, because it is compared to the point of an awl.

Furthermore, the comparison with space and so forth will be intended to express non-difference from Brahman. Moreover, it is not the small space that is heard of here as being the object to be sought after or desired to be known;
for, in the phrase "that which is within it," it is mentioned as a qualification of the Supreme (Brahman).
To this we reply: here the Supreme Lord alone must be the "small ether" (daharākāśa), and not the elemental ether or the individual soul (jīva).
Why?
Because of the reasons found in the subsequent portion of the text.

For instance, regarding the small ether (*dahara-ākāśa*) which is enjoined as that which is to be sought after, there occurs a statement of resolution preceded by an objection, beginning with "If they should say to him": "What is there in it that is to be sought after, what is there to be understood by inquiry? [The answer follows:
"He should say: 'As large as this external ether is, so large is this ether within the heart; both heaven and earth are contained within it,'" and so forth (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.1.3).

In this context, by negating the smallness of the ether—which had attained smallness through its comparison with the small lotus—by means of a comparison with the well-known [outer] ether, it is understood that the status of the small ether as the elemental ether is being negated.

Although the word "ether" (ākāśa) is conventionally established in the sense of the elemental ether, nevertheless, a comparison of that very thing with itself is not tenable; thus, the suspicion that it refers to the elemental ether is set aside.
But has it not been stated that the relationship of analogy between the two is possible through an imagined distinction of "outer" and "inner" even within a single space?
This is not at all possible;
for this is indeed a resort of last resort.
This involves resorting to a conceptual distinction.

Furthermore, even if one were to describe the relationship of comparison (*upamānopameyabhāva*) by assuming such a distinction, it would not be logical for the internal space to possess the same magnitude as external space, because the internal space is limited.
[Objection: But is it not said that even the Supreme Lord is "greater than space" (*jyāyān ākāśāt*)? (Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa 10.6.6.2)
Thus, on account of another scriptural passage, it is not tenable that [the space within the heart] has the same dimension as the physical ether.
This is not a fault;
for this statement aims at removing the smallness [previously] attributed to it by its enclosure within the lotus, and does not aim at establishing that it is merely of that size.
For if both were taught [simultaneously], the sentence would be split.
Furthermore, even if a distinction is imagined, it is not possible for heaven, earth, and so forth to be contained within a single part of space that is enclosed by a white lotus.

Moreover, qualities such as being the Self, freedom from evil, freedom from old age, freedom from death, freedom from sorrow, freedom from hunger, freedom from thirst, having true desires, and having true resolves—as stated in the passage, "This is the Self, free from evil, ageless, deathless, sorrowless, without hunger or thirst, whose desires are true and whose resolves are true"—do not belong to the elemental ether (bhūtākāśa).
They are possible.
Even though the word "self" (ātman) can apply to the individual soul (jīva), nevertheless, by other reasons, even the suspicion that it refers to the soul is removed.

For it is not possible to remove the smallness of the individual soul—which is limited by its adjuncts (upādhi) and compared to the point of an awl—merely because of its being enclosed within the lotus.
If it is argued that the omnipresence and other attributes of the individual soul (*jīva*) are intended to be expressed by way of its non-difference from Brahman,

then it is more logical to intend to express the omnipresence and other attributes directly of that very Brahman, whose nature the soul possesses. The meaning is this: immediately after becoming dispassionate toward the fruits of karma, those who— having understood through the instruction of a teacher and experienced through meditation the Self as subtle (dahara) in this state of life, along with the qualities such as "true desires" (satyakāma) residing therein— depart for the next world, for them there arises infinite sovereignty over all worlds, including the power to move about at will and so forth.
