This is just as the sentence "he sleeps with his mouth open" is explained as "having slept, he opens his mouth."
He refutes the notion that light is the Self with the words "This [is the Self].
Another scriptural passage states: "Having rejoiced and moved about in the state of deep sleep (saṃprasāda)...
He further states that rising from that state is also an indicative mark (liṅga) of the individual soul (jīva), saying: "In the same way..."
The illustration for the emergence of that which is dependent on Him from Him is given with the word "as.

Now, one might object: "The word 'ether' (ākāśa) is never seen applied to the individual soul (jīva). Anticipating this, he says "and as" to show that it must be inferred by the force of the evidence regarding the emergence from the state previously described. When it is argued that the individual soul might be the small [ether] due to a lack of a restrictive rule, he states the restrictive rule with the words "not this," and so forth.
The meaning is that the individual soul (jīva) is not the "small one" (dahara), because the hearing of the Dharma is impossible for one who is small.
If it is then asked why this is a redundant statement, he replies: "Because of the excess," and so forth.
The meaning is that this is for the purpose of dispelling further doubts regarding what follows.
What, then, is the interpretation of the reference to the individual soul (*jīva*)?
To that he says: "He will state [later]."
It will be stated that this reference has the purpose of making known the Brahman which is the soul's state of deep sleep. //18//
If it is argued that [the soul is different] because of the subsequent [scriptural statement], then [we reply]: "But [it is not so], for its true nature has become manifest. (BS 1.3.19)
The suspicion regarding the individual soul (*jīva*) that arose from the previous consideration of other [interpretations] has been refuted on the grounds of impossibility.
Now, however, a renewed suspicion regarding the *jīva* is raised—like the rising again of one who was dead through the sprinkling of nectar—from the subsequent statement of Prajāpati.

For there, having first promised that the Self characterized by qualities such as being "free from evil" (*apahatapāpman*) is to be sought and desired to be known, he says: "This person who is seen in the eye, this..."
By saying this (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.7.4), he points out the individual soul (jīva) as the seer residing in the eye.

And by repeatedly referring back to that very same one with the words, "I shall explain this very thing to you further" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.9.3), [the text continues]: "He who moves about in sleep, being honored—this is the Self" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.10.1).

Thus, by the passage, "Now, when one is thus asleep, composed, serene, and does not perceive any dream—this is the Self," [the text] explains that it is indeed the individual soul (*jīva*) that has entered into another state.
And it shows that this very [soul] possesses qualities such as being free from evil: "This is the immortal, the fearless; this is Brahman" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.7.3).
Furthermore, [it says]: "Indeed, at this time he does not know himself as 'I am this,' nor does he know these beings" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.11.1, 2).

Having thus perceived the defect in the state of deep sleep, and having begun with the words, "I shall explain this very same [Self] further to you, and not anything other than this," [the text] describes the individual soul (jīva) itself, preceded by a censure of its connection with the body: "This serene being (saṃprasāda), arising from this body and reaching the highest light, manifests in its own true form; he is the supreme Person."
It shows the Supreme Person (uttama-puruṣa) as having arisen from the body.
Therefore, there is the possibility that the attributes of the Supreme Lord exist in the individual soul (jīva).
Consequently, if someone were to say that the phrase "the small ether within this" refers to the individual soul alone, [we reply:]...
One should reply to that [objection]: "But [the Self] has its true nature manifested" (*āvirbhūtasvarūpas tu*).
The word "but" (*tu*) serves to set aside the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*).
The meaning is that even from the subsequent statement, no suspicion regarding the individual soul (*jīva*) can arise here.
Why?
Because even there, the individual soul (jīva) is intended to be understood as one whose true nature has become manifest. One whose true nature has become manifest is "āvirbhūtasvarūpaḥ."
The term "living being" (jīva) is used here by way of conventional usage.

This is what is meant: having first pointed out the seer characterized by the eye with the words "This one who is in the eye," and having then raised him above the notion of the body as the self through the Udaśarāva Brāhmaṇa, [the text] draws him back as the subject of exposition by repeatedly explaining that very same person with the words "But this one indeed to you."
By means of the sequence of presenting the states of dream and deep sleep, the text— stating that "having reached the highest light, he manifests in his own true form"—
explains this individual soul (jīva) as having the nature of that which is its ultimate reality, namely the Supreme Brahman, and not in its individual (jaiva) form.
That which is heard in scripture as the "highest light" to be attained is the Supreme Brahman.
And that [Self] possesses attributes such as being free from evil;
furthermore, according to scriptural texts such as "That thou art," this alone is the ultimate essential nature of the individual soul (jīva),
and not the other [nature] which is imagined through limiting adjuncts (upādhi).

For as long as one does not realize "I am Brahman"— the Self whose nature is immutable, eternal consciousness— by dispelling the ignorance characterized by duality, which is like the notion of a person in a pillar, so long does the state of being a *jīva* persist for the living soul.
But when, having been awakened from the aggregate of body, senses, mind, and intellect, one is enlightened by the Śruti:
You are not the aggregate of body, senses, mind, and intellect; you are not a transmigrating being.
What then? That which is the Truth is the Self, whose nature is pure consciousness—“That thou art.”

Then, awakening to the Self whose nature is the immutable, eternal Consciousness, and rising above this identification with the body and so forth, that very Self becomes the immutable, eternal Consciousness by nature;
for this is established by such scriptural passages as, "He who knows that supreme Brahman becomes Brahman itself" (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 3.2.9).

And that very [nature] is its ultimate essential form (*pāramārthika-svarūpa*), by which it, having risen out of the body, manifests in its own true nature. But how is it possible for something that is immutable and eternal to "manifest in its own nature by itself"? [This is not so in the case of things like gold], for in the case of gold and the like, whose true nature is obscured by contact with other substances and whose unique characteristics are unmanifest, [the manifestation occurs] through the application of alkaline salts and so forth.
For things that are being purified, there would be a manifestation in their own essential form;
likewise, for stars and the like, whose light is suppressed during the day, there would be a manifestation in their own essential form at night when they are free from the suppressor.
But such suppression of the eternally existing light of the self's consciousness by anything is not possible, because it is non-contacting, like space.
And because it contradicts what is observed:
for sight, hearing, thought, and cognition constitute the very nature of the individual soul (*jīva*);
and that [nature] is seen to be eternally perfected even for the soul that has not yet emerged from the body.
For every living being engages in worldly activity by seeing, hearing, thinking, and knowing; otherwise, such activity would be impossible.
If that [activity] were to occur only after one has risen from the body, then the observed activity prior to that rising would be contradicted.
Therefore, of what nature is this "rising from the body"?
Or, what is the nature of its manifestation as its own essential form?

To this it is replied: prior to the arising of discriminative knowledge, the nature of the individual soul (*jīva*), which is the light of vision and so forth, appears as if non-discriminated from the limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) of the body, senses, mind, intellect, objects, and sensations.
Just as the natural transparency and whiteness of a pure crystal appear as if non-discriminated from limiting adjuncts such as red or blue before their distinction is perceived.

However, due to the apprehension of discrimination produced by the means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*), the crystal—which was already existing in that very same way even previously—is said to "emerge" with its own nature of transparency and whiteness subsequent to that [contact].

Likewise, for the individual soul (*jīva*) which exists as non-discriminated from limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) such as the body, the "rising up from the body" is the discriminative knowledge brought about by scripture; the "emergence in its own nature" is the result of that discriminative knowledge, namely the realization of the nature of the absolute Self (*ātman*).
Thus, the bodilessness and the embodiedness of the Self consist merely in discrimination and non-discrimination.

This is because of the wording of the mantra, "The bodiless among bodies" (Kauṣītaki Upaniṣad 1.2.22), and because of the traditional teaching that there is no distinction between being embodied and being bodiless, as stated in, "Though dwelling in the body, O son of Kuntī, he neither acts nor is tainted" (Bhagavad Gītā 13.31).

Therefore, due to the absence of discriminative knowledge, one whose true nature is unmanifest is said to have a manifest true nature upon the attainment of discriminative knowledge. However, no other kind of manifestation or non-manifestation of the true nature is possible, precisely because it is the very essence of that nature.
Thus, the distinction between the individual soul (jīva) and the Supreme Lord (parameśvara) is created solely by false knowledge (mithyājñāna), not by the reality of things.
Because there is no difference in its being unattached, like space;
this must be understood from the following: having taught, "This person who is seen in the eye," he then teaches, "This is the immortal, the fearless; this is Brahman."

If the seer who is well-known in the eye and is perceived as the seer were different from Brahman, which is characterized by immortality and fearlessness, then there could be no grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with Brahman, who is immortal and fearless; nor is this person indicated as the reflection-self (*praticchāyātmā*) marked in the eye,
because that would entail the consequence of Prajāpati being a speaker of falsehood.

Likewise, in the second passage as well, this one who "moves about being honored in a dream" is not indicated as anyone other than the seer, the person in the eye, who was designated in the first passage;
for it begins with, "I shall explain this very same one to you further. Moreover, upon waking, one rejects what was seen by saying, "Today in a dream I saw an elephant; I do not see it now."
However, one recognizes that very same seer, thinking: "I who saw the dream, I am the very same person who now see the waking state.

Likewise, in the third instance as well—"For indeed, in this state [of deep sleep], he does not know himself thus: 'This is I,' nor does he know these beings"—this merely shows the absence of specific cognition during the state of deep sleep; it does not negate the knower.
As for the statement there, "He has gone to utter annihilation," that too intends only the destruction of specific cognitions, not the destruction of the cognizer;
for another Śruti text declares: "For there is no loss of the knower's knowledge, because of its indestructibility" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.3.30).

Likewise, in the fourth section as well, beginning with "I shall explain this very same thing to you further, and nothing other than this," and proceeding with the detailed exposition starting from "O Maghavan, this body is indeed mortal," [the text] shows the individual soul— denoted by the term *saṃprasāda*— as having attained the nature of Brahman, according to the statement "he manifests in his own true form," by means of the rejection of the connection with limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) in relation to the body.
[The text] shows the individual soul (jīva) to be distinct from the Supreme Brahman, whose nature is immortal and fearless.

However, some—considering it improper to refer back to the individual soul with the words "But him alone to you" if the intention is to speak of the Supreme Self—interpret it thus: "I shall explain further to you that very Self, characterized by qualities such as freedom from sin, which was indicated at the beginning of this section."
For them, the use of the pronoun "this" (etad), which refers to what is proximate, would be displaced; furthermore, the repetition of the word (bhūyaḥ-śruti) would be contradicted,
because that which was expressed in one formulation is not expressed in another formulation.
Moreover, having made the promise, "This very one [I shall explain] to you," Prajāpati would be guilty of deception if he were to explain something other than that before the fourth section;

therefore, by means of knowledge (vidyā), the supreme nature of the Lord— which is the opposite of that, characterized by qualities such as being free from sin— is established through the dissolution of that individual (jaiva) form which is presented by ignorance (avidyā), which is real only in that limited sense, and which is defiled by the defects of agency, enjoyership, passion, hatred, and so forth, and joined with manifold evils.
Just as [one perceives] ropes and the like through the dissolution of [the appearance of] snakes and so forth,
other disputants— and even some among our own [followers]— believe that the individual form of the self (*jaiva-rūpa*) is indeed ultimately real.
This *Śārīraka* [Brahmasūtra] has been commenced for the purpose of awakening all those who stand in opposition to the correct vision (*samyag-darśana*) of the oneness of the Self (*ātma-ekatva*).

The Supreme Lord alone—the eternally unchanging substratum of consciousness—is manifested in manifold ways through ignorance (*avidyā*) and *māyā*, like a magician; there is no other substratum of consciousness.

As for the fact that the author of the Sūtras, suspecting the individual soul (*jīva*) in the passages concerning the Supreme Lord, refutes it with the words "Not so, because of impossibility" (Brahma-sūtra 1.3.18) and so forth, the intention therein is this: in the one, non-attached Supreme Self—which is by nature eternally pure, conscious, and free, and is eternally unchanging—the individual form of the soul, which is the opposite of that [nature], is superimposed just as dust, stains, and the like are imagined in the sky.

He confirms the distinctness of the supreme self from the individual soul (jīva) with the thought: "I shall remove [the notion of duality] by means of sentences intended to establish the oneness of the Self, supported by logic, and by refutations of dualistic doctrines.

However, he does not intend to establish that the individual soul is distinct from the supreme; rather, he merely restates the distinction between souls as it is well-known in the world and imagined through ignorance (avidyā).
He considers that in this way, the injunctions for ritual action (karma-vidhi), which proceed by restating the inherent status of being an agent and an enjoyer, will not be contradicted.

However, [the author] demonstrates that the very unity of the Self is the meaning of the scripture to be established, by means of such passages as "But the instruction is according to the vision of the scripture, like that of Vāmadeva" (Brahmasūtra 1.1.30). Furthermore, we have already explained the removal of the contradiction with the injunctions for ritual action by means of the distinction between the knower and the agent. // 19 // [Note:
"Being honored" means being worshipped by objects consisting of latent impressions; this occurs in the context of the dream state.]
The syntactical connection (*anvaya*) is as follows: in that section concerning deep sleep (*suṣupti*), Prajāpati explains the *jīva* itself.
The particle *aha* expresses dejection. "Other than this" means other than this self under discussion; "another" means something different.
"Udaśarāva" means in a water-filled bowl; the meaning of the Śruti is that one's own body, which is the reflected self and unknown to oneself, is what must be told to me.
"Having risen up" (vyutthāpya) means having investigated.
The connection is that this is what is expressed by the phrase "he emerges" (abhiniṣpadyate).
The sun’s light is the overcomer when separated from it;
feelings are joy, sorrow, and so forth;
and discriminative knowledge is the purification of the meaning of the "thou" (tvaṃpadārtha).
The two truths are of different natures;
being devoid of parts and so forth is non-attachment.
This is deep sleep.
Now, regarding deep sleep,
[the text says] "he does not know himself"— that is, he does not know the self which is the locus of the ego-sense.
The meaning is that it is not so, because there is no alteration of the consciousness that constitutes the very nature of the self, owing to its inherent capacity.
By means of dissolution and purification,

and by means of knowledge— that is, the Great Sayings (*mahāvākya*) such as "That thou art" (*tat tvam asi*)— the logical principle is that because there is no distinction between the consciousness of the individual soul (*jīva*) and Brahman, no difference can exist between them, whether in their own form or in any other form.
Statements such as "Not this, not this" (neha nānā) and so forth are negations of dualistic doctrine.
Anticipating the objection that the reason "because of impossibility" (asaṃbhavāt) is unestablished, the author refutes it with the words "If [it is argued] from the subsequent [text]" (uttarāccet).
The doubt regarding the individual soul (jīva), which had been set aside by the Sūtra, is raised once again on the strength of the passage concerning Prajāpati.
The meaning is that, in that context, the impossibility [of the attributes] is not established because the qualities such as "freedom from sin" are attributed to the individual soul (jīva) itself.
To the question, "How is it stated there that this refers to the individual soul?", he replies with the words beginning with "tatra."

Although the word "jīva" does not appear at the beginning [of the passage], nevertheless, since the Self characterized by qualities such as being free from sin (*apahatapāpmatva*) is introduced at the outset, and because the three states of waking and so forth are subsequently presented for that Self, the jīva is determined by the mark of these states; thus, it is the conclusion that those very qualities belong to that [jīva]. This is the overall sense of the passage. Prajāpati says to Indra: "This one who... and so on.

The mention of the "eye" is used because of its predominance; he says "the seer" (*draṣṭāram*) to indicate that one has reached the waking state, which consists in the perception of objects through all the sense organs. In the section on dreaming, "being honored" (*mahīyamānaḥ*) means being worshipped by objects consisting of latent impressions (*vāsanā*). And in the section on deep sleep, [the text] says "whatever [he sees there]. The syntactical connection is that Prajāpati explains the individual soul (*jīva*) alone in each of these stages.
At that time, he has slept in such a way as to be in this state of sleep;
he is "samasta," meaning one whose collection of organs (karaṇagrāma) has been completely set aside or withdrawn;
and for that very reason, because his organs have been withdrawn, he is free from the turbidity produced by them and is thus "saṃprasanna" (serenely tranquil).

He dissolves the dream-state and the phenomenal world into mere ignorance; therefore, because of the existence of ignorance, this *prājña* (the state of deep sleep) is distinct from the liberated one. This *prājña*, as the witness of the causal body by means of his own consciousness, possesses qualities such as being "free from sin" (*apahatapāpmatva*), since these are attributed to him as *brahman* in the fourth section [of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad]. Anticipating this objection—that these qualities belong to that very [state]—he states that even this section refers to the individual soul (*jīva*) with the words "No, indeed" (*nāha*). The particle *aha* is used here in the sense of expressing weariness or emphasis.
Feeling distressed, Indra said:
"Indeed, this person while asleep—in the state of deep sleep—does not know himself as 'I am Devadatta' and so forth;
nor does he know these beings at all, but rather he has reached utter destruction."
Having perceived the defect, thinking "I see no object of enjoyment here," he approached Prajāpati once more.
Having heard of that defect, Prajāpati said, "This [one]" (etam).

The meaning is that, having begun with the words "other than this Self under discussion, I shall not explain another," he demonstrates the individual soul (jīva) itself by means of a censure, starting with, "Maghavan, this body is indeed mortal."
Therefore, from that statement of Prajāpati;
since, for this reason, the possibility [of the opponent's position] is not established, he states the final conclusion: "With reference to that."

The meaning is that "purified" refers to the manifestation [of the Self] through the purification of the three states, or that the object has been manifested by the mental modification (vṛtti) arising from the sentence.

If so, how can the individual soul (jīva) be referred to in the masculine gender in the Sūtra, since its status as a living being has ceased through knowledge? To this he says: "as having previously existed" (bhūtapūrva).

The meaning is this: since prior to knowledge there existed the state of being a *jīva*—characterized by being reflected in ignorance (*avidyā*) and its effects—it follows that even after knowledge, although one is of the nature of Brahman, one is still designated by the name "jīva.

He states the purport of Prajāpati’s discourse, which consists of the four stages of Viśva, Taijasa, Prājña, and Turīya, with the words "etad" (this), because [the *jīva*] possesses birth and destruction.

In order to demonstrate that the body, which is like a reflection, is not the Self, Prajāpati spoke to Indra and Virocana, saying: "Look at yourselves in a water-filled bowl; whatever form of the Self you do not discern, tell me that," and so forth. Thus he says, "In a water-filled bowl" (*udaśarāve*). The meaning of the cited scripture is: having seen the body as the reflected self in a bowl filled with water, that which is unknown to oneself must be told to me.
The connection is as follows: "having emerged and reflected, he accomplishes"—this is what is meant here.
To the question "What is meant? he says: "That which belongs to him... and so forth.

He does not define the *jīva* by its nature as a living being, because that is already established in common worldly experience; rather, having referred to it (*anūdya*), he distinguishes it from its mutually exclusive states and thereby makes known the true nature of Brahman.

Therefore, what is meant is this: that which is Brahman is precisely that which possesses attributes such as freedom from sin (*apahatapāpmatva*) and so forth, and not the *jīva*; for the meaning is that once [the self] has been purified, its attributes are stated in distinction from those of Brahman.
It should be understood that because this presentation of states is intended for the purpose of discernment (*viveka*), it does not constitute a characteristic mark of the individual soul (*jīva*);
for it would contradict the scriptural statement endowed with such marks: "This is the immortal, the fearless; this is Brahman.
Now, one might object: how can there be non-difference between two things possessing the contradictory attributes of being the individual soul and being Brahman?
Regarding this, he says: "That very [state]" (*tadeva*).

Considering that the state of being a living soul (*jīvatva*) is imagined through ignorance (*avidyā*) by means of positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), there is no contradiction; thus, he states the positive concomitance (*anvaya*) by way of an illustration with the words "as long as" (*yāvat*).
He states the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) with the words "when" (*yadā*).

The meaning is that as long as ignorance exists, there is the state of being a living soul (jīvatva), and through the dawn of knowledge arising from the [great] sentence, upon its cessation, that [state] ceases; thus, it is of the nature of ignorance (āvidyaka).
He concludes the established point regarding the imagined nature of transmigratory existence (saṃsāritva) with the words: "And that very [state] belongs to him."
He raises an objection in order to explain the scriptural text, "Having arisen, he manifests in his own form," beginning with the words "But how?
The grammatical connection is: "the nature of that which is immutable and eternal.

He says "as in the case of gold" to show that manifestation occurs through the destruction of impurity by action for that which is associated with the mind, but not for the immutable one, which is unassociated.
The impurity is a distinct substance consisting of earth.
The term "overpowered" is explained as "unmanifested.
Its specific quality is luminosity and so forth.
The sunlight is the overpowering factor. Regarding the sublation of the nature of the individual soul (jīva), he states the refutation: "It is seen," etc.
According to the scripture, "He is indeed a mass of consciousness," the Self is, at least, pure consciousness (cinmātra).

That consciousness, manifested by the modifications (vṛtti) produced by the eyes and other senses, becomes the very nature of the individual soul (jīva), denoted by terms such as "seeing" and so forth, and serves as the basis for empirical transaction. Therefore, if that [consciousness] were suppressed, observed empirical transactions would be contradicted;
the meaning is that in the absence of the cause, no empirical transaction could occur.
Furthermore, it must be admitted that even for the ignorant person, their true nature is manifested within the modifications.
He says "that" (tat ca) because [it occurs] from the observation of worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*).
He clarifies what was stated as "otherwise" (*anyathā*) with "if that" (*tac cet*):
the meaning is that if the true nature (*svarūpa*) were manifested only for one who possesses knowledge, then worldly transaction would be cut off prior to that knowledge.

Therefore, the meaning is: "because its own nature is always manifest. Since the Self—which is in reality unattached—is always manifest during its various states (vṛtti), yet appears to be associated with impurity in the form of non-discrimination from the body and so forth produced by nescience (avidyā), the scriptural texts concerning its "arising" and so forth are intended with reference to that [apparent] discrimination. To this he gives the answer: "In this context, 'sensation' (vedanā) refers to joy, grief, and the like."
The phrase "as if not distinct" expresses that the identity and the attachment are imagined (*kalpita*).
Regarding that imagined attachment, the example is given with the word "just as.
The term "produced by the Veda" refers to [the knowledge] derived from scripture.

The meaning is that this is established by the hearing of the referent of the term *tvam* (the "thou"), such as in the passage beginning, "He who consists of cognition among the vital breaths" (*yo 'yaṃ vijñānamayaḥ prāṇeṣu*).

He states with the word "purely" (*kevala*) that the fruit of the knowledge of the referent of the term *tvam*—which is pure and distinct from the vital breaths and so forth—is the direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*) of the meaning of the sentence.

Anticipating the objection that since embodiedness is real, "rising up" (*samutthānam*) must be explained as "departure" (*utkrānti*) rather than "discrimination" (*viveka*), he says: "In the same way, through discrimination... (*tathā vivekena*).
The meaning is "in accordance with the stated scripture.
According to the scripture, "The bodiless abides within bodies," embodiedness is merely imagined through a lack of discrimination (*aviveka*).
Therefore, the meaning is that discrimination (*viveka*) itself is the "emergence" (*samutthāna*).

Now, one might object: "Since enjoyment is unavoidable in a body acquired through one's own karma, how can there be the manifestation of one's true nature while still living? To this, he says: "Even while staying in the body.

The meaning is that liberation while living is logical, because there are traditional teachings (smṛti) stating that even for one staying in the body, there is an absence of bondage, just as there is for one who is bodiless.
He says "Therefore" to show that the remainder of the Sūtra is appropriate once the meaning of the Śruti has been established without contradiction.
The meaning is that the two truths are of different natures.

Since manifestation and concealment are established as being caused by knowledge and ignorance respectively, the distinction based on the relation of part and whole is also refuted; thus he says, "In this way.
Being devoid of parts and so forth is non-attachment (*asaṅgatva*).

The meaning is that because the self (ātman) is devoid of any genus (jāti) pervaded by substantiality (dravyatva), owing to its all-pervasiveness (vibhutva)—just like space—the oneness of the self is established, and thus difference is false. Furthermore, he states "from what [source]? and so forth, preceded by an inquiry, to show that difference is false based on the words of Prajāpati.

The logical connection is: "How can it be that this difference has no reality at all? [To the objection that] this statement is intended to enjoin the perception of Brahman in the reflection (chāyā) and is not intended to establish non-difference, he says: "Nor... The meaning is: if Prajāpati were to point out the non-self, namely the reflection, to Indra and Virocana—who had set out with the thought, "We shall seek that Self by the knowledge of which one has accomplished all that is to be done and attained all desires"—then he would be a speaker of falsehood.

He says "likewise" (*tathā*) to state that, as in the first instance, in the second and subsequent stages, the self that persists through the various changing states is described as Brahman. He provides the reasoning for its persistence despite the difference in states with "moreover" (*kiñca*). Anticipating the objection that the knower might cease to exist in deep sleep (*suṣupti*), he says "likewise in the third" (*tathā tṛtīye*).
Regarding the point that the Self exists in the form of non-conceptual knowledge during deep sleep, he cites the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Śruti with the words "nahi" (not so).
The meaning is that there is no destruction of the witness of the intellect, because there is no cause for such destruction.
He states "likewise" (tathā) to show that the very Self, which was described as being unattached through these [three] states, is also described as Brahman in the fourth state (turīya).

He refutes the interpretation of certain partial authorities (ekadeśin) with the words "but some," the sense being that there is a distinction between the individual soul (jīva) and the Supreme (para).
He says "not so" because it would contradict the Vedic revelation;
the meaning is that the word "all" refers precisely to the individual soul (jīva) which is present [in the context].
Furthermore, the use of the word "again" (*bhūyaḥ*) is appropriate when there is a repetition of what has already been stated.
But for you, who have begun with the Supreme Self, since [the text] speaks of the fourth [state], that would be a contradiction; thus he says, "Furthermore" (bhūyaḥ).
He concludes his own view—that Brahmanhood is taught by restating the individual soul as established in common worldly experience—with the words, "Therefore" (tasmāt);
the meaning is that other interpretations are possible.
"Dissolution" (*vilayana*) means purification;
that is to say, by means of knowledge, namely the Great Sayings (*mahāvākya*).
To those, however, who maintain that *saṃsāra* is real, he states that this very [treatise on] the embodied self (*śārīraka*) is the answer, beginning with the words "But others," and so forth.
He teaches the meaning of the Śārīraka in brief: "He is indeed one.

The grammatical coordination (sāmānādhikaraṇya) is used to refute the distinction between ignorance (avidyā) and illusion (māyā); their simultaneous employment is due to the difference in the grounds for the application of the respective terms, namely, the powers of concealment (āvaraṇa) and projection (vikṣepa).
The meaning is that the purport of the *Śārīraka* (Brahma-sūtras) is that Brahman alone transmigrates through ignorance, and there is no individual soul (*jīva*) other than that;
[if this is so], why then does the author of the Sūtras speak of a distinction?
To this he replies: "But as for that which... and so forth.

He establishes the difference [of the Supreme Self] from the individual soul (jīva) in order to prove that the Supreme Self is not subject to transmigratory existence (asaṃsāritva). The meaning is that as long as there is no certainty regarding its being free from transmigratory existence, then even if non-difference from it is stated, the transmigratory nature of the jīva cannot be removed. He says, "But of the jīva," [implying] that although the substrate (adhiṣṭhāna) is distinct from the imagined [superimposition], the imagined has no existence apart from the substrate.
He states the purpose of restating the imagined difference with the words "For thus...
He dispels the misconception that non-difference is not taught in the Sūtras by stating "is what is to be established.
The phrase "the Self, indeed, they approach," etc., constitutes the meaning of the word "etcetera" (ādi).

"Surely, if non-duality (advaita) is the meaning of the scripture, there would be a contradiction with injunctions (vidhi) that depend upon duality; to this he replies: 'And it has been described'. The meaning is that all is consistent, because injunctions based on imagined duality apply to one who does not know non-duality, but not to the knower. //19//
And the reference has another purpose. (BS 1.3.20)

Now, as for the reference to the individual soul (*jīva*) shown in the supplementary passage of the "small" (*dahara*) section—beginning with "Now, this serene one" (*atha ya eṣa saṃprasādaḥ*, Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.3.4)—if that were explained as referring to the Supreme Lord within the small space, it would follow that the passage has the sense of neither being an instruction on the meditation upon the individual soul nor an instruction on the specific subject under discussion.
Therefore, he says: "This reference to the individual soul has another purpose; it does not terminate in the nature of the individual soul, but rather terminates in the nature of the Supreme Lord."

How so? The individual soul (jīva), denoted by the word *saṃprasāda*, having become the presiding overseer of the cage of the body and senses during the activities of the waking state, and having experienced dreams constructed from the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of those [activities] while moving through the channels (*nāḍī*), becomes weary and, desiring a refuge, rises up from the identification with the body in both its forms [the gross and the subtle].

In the state of deep sleep, having attained the supreme light designated by the word "ether"— the supreme Brahman— and having abandoned the possession of specific cognitions, one emerges in one's own true nature. That supreme light which is to be attained, and that own nature in which this person emerges, is this Self characterized by qualities such as freedom from sin.
This reference to the individual soul (jīva) as being "to be worshipped" is also consistent for one who maintains that the Supreme Lord is the subject.

Thus, since Prajāpati’s statement—by way of restating the individual soul (jīva)—teaches that qualities such as freedom from sin belong to Brahman alone, and because those qualities are impossible in the individual soul, it was stated that the individual soul is not the "small one" (dahara). To the question, "In that case, what is the purpose of the reference to the individual soul? he says: "And for another purpose.
He explains the Sūtra with the words beginning with "Now" (atha).
The meaning is that there is no specific quality nor even any instruction regarding such a quality in the case of the small [space] under discussion (*dahara*).

Therein, he explains the passage concerning "perfect serenity" (*saṃprasāda*), which forms a supplementary portion of the discourse on the small [space], as being intended for Brahman, by means of the words beginning with "How? and so forth, after first raising an objection. //20//
If it be argued that [the word "small"] refers to limited hearing, that has already been answered. (BBs 1.3.21)
Furthermore, as for what was said—

that the smallness of the ether heard in the passage, "In this, within, is a small ether," is not possible in the case of the Supreme Lord, whereas the smallness of the individual soul (jīva), which is comparable to the point of an awl, is plausible— an answer to that must be stated.

For the resolution of this [objection] has already been stated in the passage: "If it be said that [the Lord is not the cause] because of his having a small abode and because of the designation of him as such, we say no, because he is to be perceived in this way, and because [the case] is like that of space" (Brahmasūtra 1.2.7).
This indicates that that very same resolution is to be applied here as well.

This smallness has already been refuted by the scripture itself, which compares it with the well-known space: "As large as this external space is, so large is this space within the heart. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.1.3) // 21 //

Having explained that its smallness was mentioned because it is to be meditated upon, he states another point—that this has been refuted by scripture itself—with the words, "And this [smallness] by scripture itself.

Thus, it is established that both the passage concerning the "small" (dahara) and the passage concerning Prajāpati are consistently applicable to both the qualified (saguṇa) and the unqualified (nirguṇa) Brahman. //21//
END BsCom_1,3.5.21 START BsCom_1,3.6.22 6. The Section on Imitation (Anukṛtyadhikaraṇa). Sūtras 22–23.
And because of the imitation of that [Brahman]:

"The sun does not shine there, nor the moon and the stars; these lightnings do not shine, much less this earthly fire. Everything shines only after Him who shines; by His light all this is illumined" (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 2.2.10).
Thus they recite:

"In whom all that shines shines along, and by whose light all this is illumined—what is he? Is he some element of light, or is he the wise Self? When such a doubt arises, the initial position is that it must be an element of light;
why? Because it is precisely elements of light, such as the sun and so forth, that are here denied the power of shining.
For it is well known that the moon, the stars, and so forth, which are of the nature of light, do not shine during the day when the sun—which is likewise of the nature of light—is shining.
Similarly, it is understood that that in which all this—the moon, the stars, and so forth—along with the sun, does not shine must itself be something of the nature of light.
Furthermore, non-shining is logically possible only for that which is of the nature of light.

Because imitation is observed among things of a similar nature—just as in the expression "he follows one who is walking"—it follows that the fire element must be some [independent] entity. To this we reply: it must be the intelligent Self alone.
Why?
Because of imitation.
Imitation is "anukṛti."
This "shining after" expressed in the passage, "Everything shines only after Him who shines," is possible only if [the Self] is understood as the Prājña (the Supreme Self).
[As stated in Chāndogya Upaniṣad 3.14.2: "He is of the nature of light, whose resolve is true."
For thus they declare the Self to be wise;
however, it is not well known that the sun and other luminaries shine after some other element of light.
Moreover, because the elements of light such as the sun and others are equal, there is no need for them to depend upon another element of light which they might shine after.
For a lamp does not illuminate another lamp.
As for what was said— that imitation is observed among things of a similar nature—
that is not an absolute rule.
For even among things that possess distinct natures, imitation is observed;
just as a red-hot iron ball, which imitates fire, burns after the burning fire, or as earthly dust, carried by the wind, is carried along after the blowing wind.

By the word "anukṛteḥ" (from imitation), the commentary has indicated the mention [of the sun's light]; and by the words "tasya ca" (and of that), it points to the fourth quarter of this verse: "By its light all this shines. This manifestation of the sun and other luminaries, which is stated to be caused by that [Self], leads one to understand the Self as the Prājña (the Conscious One).
For the scriptures declare the conscious Self to be "the light of lights, which the gods meditate upon as life and immortality" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.16).
Furthermore, it is both unestablished and contradictory to claim that the light of the sun and other luminaries shines by means of another light.
Because one light is obstructed by another light;
or rather, it is not only of the sun and so forth mentioned in the verse that this manifestation caused by them is spoken of.

What then? Because of the hearing of the term "all this" without qualification, the manifestation of this entire collection of names, forms, actions, agents, and fruits is caused by the existence of the Brahman-light.
Just as the manifestation of all forms of matter is caused by the existence of light such as the sun, so it is here;
and by employing the word "there" in the phrase "the sun does not shine there," [the text] shows that the subject under discussion is being referred to.
And the subject under discussion is Brahman, as established by the passage beginning, "In whom the heaven, the earth, and the intermediate space are woven" (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 2.2.5).
And immediately following that [it says]: "In the supreme golden sheath is the stainless Brahman, devoid of fruit;
it is the pure light of lights, which those who know the Self know.
To the question, "How is it the light of lights?", this [verse] arises: "The sun does not shine there... and so forth.

As for what was also said— that the negation of the manifestation of the luminaries such as the sun is possible only in another element of light, just as [the sun's light is eclipsed] by other [luminaries]—
it has already been established that no other such element of light exists there.
Furthermore, the negation of their manifestation is also possible in the case of Brahman.
For whatever they perceive, all that is perceived by the light of Brahman alone;
but Brahman is not perceived by any other light, because it is itself of the nature of light, such that the sun and other luminaries shine within it.
For Brahman manifests another, but Brahman is not manifested by anything else; "By its own light this one sits" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.3.6),
and "It is ungraspable, for it is not grasped" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.2.4).
From such scriptural passages as these [it is known]. (22) @---------------------- FN: In that state, other stars, the moon, and so forth do not shine; that is to say, they do not illuminate it.
Its "state of being the knower" (*prājñatva*) means its self-luminosity, which is stated for the purpose of explaining its capacity to illuminate.
Anukāra means resonance.
Viraja means empty of adventitious impurities. Śubhra means empty of innate impurities.
"And because of its imitation.
He cites the statement from the *Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad*: "Not there," meaning it does not shine within that subject, Brahman.
"It does not illuminate that" means up to this point.
When even the moon, the sun, and so forth do not illuminate it, then what can be said of fire, which possesses little light? To this he says: "From where?
Furthermore, since everything such as the sun is itself illuminated by it, it does not possess the quality of being an illuminator; to this he says: "That very [light]."
He dispels the doubt that inference is merely internal (subjective) like following after [a cow] by saying "of that" (*tasya*).
Regarding the word "there" (*tatra*), since the locative case is common to both the sense of "in the presence of" and "in the object," he expresses a doubt with "there.

In the previous instance, because of the force of the mention of the Self (*ātman*) and so forth, the conventional meaning of the word "ether" (*ākāśa*) was set aside, and its application to the Lord was accepted.

Likewise here as well, by the force of the locative absolute (*satisaptamī*), one must abandon the sense of the present tense and resort to a future meaning: "That particular light in the presence of which the sun and others do not shine is the object of meditation. This is because there is a contradiction in saying "it does not shine" while the sun and others are currently shining; thus he presents the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) with the example: "It is a material element of light (*tejodhātu*).
That is, a mass of light.
The fruit in both cases is the knowledge of the Self as devoid of qualities and self-luminous.
He states the inferential mark for its being the element of light with the words "of the elements of light.
He states the pervasion—that whatever overcomes light is itself light—with the words "having the nature of light."
"It is contradictory to say that when something exists, another does not shine, yet subsequently that other shines"; therefore, he says "anubhānam" (shining after).
The sense is that what is intended here is a shining that is inferior to the former.

Since an intended meaning is untenable when the primary sense is possible, he states the established conclusion—that the Supreme Self, who is the illuminator of all and self-luminous, is to be understood here—by means of the indicative mark of "primary shining," saying "prājña" (the wise one).
The state of being wise (*prājñatva*) is described as self-luminosity for the purpose of [establishing] its illuminating nature.
Regarding this, he cites scripture: "He whose form is light" (*bhārūpa*).
Furthermore, he states "but not... because the constituent element of fire (*tejodhātu*) cannot be accepted due to a lack of evidence.

Furthermore, he says "and because of equality" to show that the sun and other luminaries do not shine independently of the manifestation of another light, because they possess the nature of light, like a lamp.
He states that there is no rule that "whatever imitates something must belong to the same genus" by saying, "this is not an absolute certainty.
Anticipating the objection of tautology, he explains the alternative reason stated in the Sūtra—following the restatement of what was already said—with the words "because of imitation" (*anukṛteḥ*).

By the word "only" (*eva*) in the phrase "that very [Self] shining," the absence of any separate shining of everything else apart from its shining—which constitutes "subsequent shining"—is expressed by the term "because of imitation"; this is indicated by the words "and of that" (*tasya ca*).
The meaning is that there is no tautology, because it has been stated that [the Self] is the illuminator of all.
He says, "The gods... (tad devāḥ), to show that the Self's status as the illuminator of the sun and so forth is well-known from other Vedic texts (*śruti*) and is not contradictory.
The word "all" (*sarva*) has been explained here as referring to the sun and the others under discussion.
Now, considering that its scope is unrestricted, he states another point with the words "Or rather" (*athavā*).
He explains that by the use of the pronoun "therein" (*tatra*), the Brahman under discussion is to be understood, saying "There the sun does not [shine]" (*na tatra sūryaḥ*).

Furthermore, he states that this mantra refers to Brahman because it fulfills the expectancy of the preceding mantra, which clearly has Brahman as its subject, saying "And immediately after" (*anantaram ca*).

In the golden, luminous, and supreme sheath known as the *ānandamaya*, which transcends the sheaths beginning with the *annamaya*, resides Brahman—designated by the word "tail"—which is stainless (*viraja*), meaning free from adventitious impurities; partless (*niṣkala*), meaning devoid of components;
and radiant (*śubhra*), meaning free from innate impurities.
The meaning is that it is well-known among those who know Brahman as being witnessed by the sun and other luminaries.
He restates the position involving the locative absolute (*satisaptamī*) with the words "yadapi" (even though).
There might be a suspicion of its inclusion here [in the list] if there were an authoritative basis for a luminous element capable of overpowering the sun and so forth.
He says "there" (*tatra*) because there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) regarding that [non-appearance].
Having raised the doubt as to how the meaning of the sentence is established in the Siddhānta, he says "even in Brahman" (*brahmaṇyapi*).

Under the view that the locative case is used in the sense of "when existing" (*satisaptamī*), one must abandon the present tense heard in the scripture—that "it does not appear"—and instead assume the future tense not heard in the text, namely "they will not appear when that exists," in order to avoid contradiction with direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).

In the case where the locative case denotes the object (*viṣaya-saptamī*), however, one need only assume the addition of the unspoken suffix *ṇic* (in the sense of "it does not cause to shine"), and there is no abandonment of what is actually heard; thus, there is parsimony (*lāghava*).
Therefore, the meaning is that by negating the capacity of the sun and other luminaries to illuminate with respect to Brahman as their object, it is stated that Brahman is itself the illuminator.

The construction is as follows: for that reason—namely, because they are illuminated by something else—the sun and others might be illuminators with respect to that Brahman as their object; however, Brahman is not perceived by anything else, because it is self-luminous (*svaprakāśatvāt*).
He confirms what has already been stated by means of another scriptural passage with the word "Brahman.
There are two scriptural texts regarding its self-luminosity and its not being illumined by anything else.
The meaning is that it is "ungraspable" (agrāhya) because it is incapable of being grasped [by the senses]. //22//
Moreover, it is also recorded in the Smṛti: BBs_1,3.23.
Moreover, such a nature is recorded in the *Bhagavadgītā* as belonging specifically to the wise Self: "Neither the sun, nor the moon, nor fire illumines that;
having gone to which they do not return, that is My supreme abode" (15.6); and "The splendor residing in the sun which illumines the entire world... (15.12).
And also: "Know that light which is in the moon and that which is in the fire to be Mine" (15.12). // 23 //
He states that there is also the power of memory in the case of supplying an ellipsis with the words "Moreover" (apica).
He explains the Sūtra with the words "Moreover" (apica).
Two verses are to be understood regarding its being non-luminous and its being the illuminator of all.
Therefore, it is established that the *anubhāna-mantra* is fully integrated within Brahman. //23//
END BsCom_1,3.6.23 START BsCom_1,3.7.24 7. Section on the Measured (Pramitādhikaraṇa) / Sūtras 24–25. The section concerning the measured [extent]. Sūtras 24–25.
He is known through scripture alone.
It is heard in the Śruti: "The person the size of a thumb dwells in the middle of the self.
Likewise: "The person the size of a thumb is like a flame without smoke."
And [it says]: "The Lord of what has been and what is to be; He alone is today, He is tomorrow—this indeed is that" (Kauṣītaki Upaniṣad 2.4.13).

Regarding this, a doubt arises as to whether this person who is heard of as being the size of a thumb is the individual self (*vijñānātman*) or the supreme self (*paramātman*). On this point, it is initially concluded that it must be the individual self because of the teaching concerning its limited dimension.
For the measure of a thumb is not possible for the Supreme Self, which is infinite in length and breadth;
however, because the conscious self possesses limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), its being the size of a thumb is possible through a certain figurative conception.
And from Smṛti: "Then, from the body of Satyavat, [the soul] bound by a noose and fallen under control..."
Yama forcibly dragged out the person the size of a thumb.
(Mahābhārata 3.297.17). For the Supreme Lord cannot be extracted by force; therefore, it is determined that in that context, the transmigrating soul (*saṃsārī*) is the one the size of a thumb.
This being the case, we reply: this person measured by the size of a thumb must be the Supreme Self alone. Why? Because of the scriptural word:
"the Lord of what has been and what is to be."
For there is no other besides the Supreme Lord who possesses unimpeded sovereignty over the past and the future;
and the phrase "This indeed is that" connects here what was previously introduced and asked about.
The meaning is: "This indeed is that which was asked about as Brahman."

The meaning is that Brahman is asked here in the passage, "Tell me that which you see as other than dharma and other than adharma, other than this cause and effect, and other than the past and the future" (Kaṭha Upaniṣad 1.2.14);
and because of the scriptural statement of the name itself, namely "the Ruler" (īśāna), it is understood that this is the Supreme Lord.
But how can there be a teaching regarding the size of the omnipresent Supreme Self? To this we reply:
[The phrase] "in the self" means in the middle of the body, specifically the heart.
The mention of "the past and the future" is for the purpose of illustration; the meaning is that He is the controller of the three periods of time.
"By some [means]" means by the thumb-sized dimension of the sheath of the heart-lotus, which is the locus where the individual soul (jīva) is perceived.
He is measured by the word itself.
He recites the Kāṭhaka passage: "The thumb-sized... and so forth.
Although the Puruṣa is all-pervading, he is said to be "thumb-sized" because he abides within the self, in the middle of the body, in the heart which is the size of a thumb.
To state another scriptural passage asserting that he alone is the Supreme Self, the text says "likewise" (tathā).
It should be read as "adhūmakam" (without smoke).

Having clarified the point that the individual soul (*jīva*), which is the size of a thumb, is in reality of the nature of pure light like smokeless fire, he declares its identity with Brahman by saying "the Lord" (*īśāna*). He declares its non-duality by saying "that alone" (*sa eva*);
it exists as that alone throughout the three periods of time, and nothing else whatsoever exists.
The meaning is that this very thing is the Brahman which was questioned by Naciketas.
Regarding the doubt [arising] from the two words "measure" (*parimāṇa*) and "ruler" (*īśāna*), he says: "In that case...

Just as it was stated that Brahman—which is not within the range of the sun and other luminaries—is [the subject] because of the indicative mark (*liṅga*) of its light and so forth, by supplying the causal suffix *ṇic*, so too, upon the perception of the individual soul (*jīva*) due to the indicative mark of "measure" heard first, [there arises the doubt: "Is it the ruler? (*īśānaḥ*)...

He presents the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) that the sentence is primarily concerned with meditation by supplying the injunction "one should meditate" [with the words] "'I am'— " in the phrase "tatra parimāṇa-.
It should be understood that according to the prima facie view, there is the worship of the individual soul (*jīva*) through the vision of Brahman,
whereas according to the established conclusion (*siddhānta*), the fruit is the knowledge of the identity of the inner self and Brahman.
Length is longitudinal extension, while breadth is width; this is the distinction.
"By some" [is said].
The meaning is that [the soul] is the size of a thumb through the conceptual superimposition (adhyāsa) of a distinction within the intellect (buddhi), which is designated as consciousness (vijñāna).
He states "and from Smṛti" because the soul is thumb-sized according to the agreement with the Smṛti texts.
Furthermore, "after death" means having been bound by the nooses of Yama and having come under the power of karma.
To the objection, "Why could he not be Īśvara even there?", he says: "No.
The sense is that this is because of the traditional teaching (smaraṇa) that Yama himself is subject to the control of Īśvara, as in the statement: "Viṣṇu has power even over my restraint.

Furthermore, because there is no subverting factor due to the presence of the qualifying term "of the past and the future" (bhūtabhavyasya), and because the word "Īśāna" (the Ruler) conveys an unrestrained lordship, he establishes the final conclusion—that it is the Supreme Self alone—by showing that the indicative mark (liṅga) must be set aside by the Śruti.
And because of the context, he says "this" (etad) to show that this sentence has Brahman as its supreme referent.
Anticipating the objection that a word (śabda)—that is, syntactical connection—is weaker than an indicative mark (liṅga), he says "from the word" (śabdāt). //24//
But with regard to the heart, [the meditation] is for humans, because the qualification belongs to humans. (BS 1.3.25)
Although the Supreme Self is omnipresent, this state of being the size of a thumb is stated with reference to its abiding within the heart;
it is like the space [within] being the size of a cubit in relation to the joint of a bamboo.
For it is not possible for the Supreme Self, which is beyond all measure, to be literally the size of a thumb.
And it has already been stated that nothing other than the Supreme Self can be understood here, on account of terms such as "Lord" (īśāna) and so forth.

Now, an objection is raised: since the hearts of individual living beings are not fixed in size, even the requirement of being "the measure of a thumb" is untenable; to this, the following answer is given: "Because the scripture concerns human beings.
For although the scripture applies without distinction, it actually confers authority only upon human beings.

This has been explained in the section on qualification (*adhikāra-lakṣaṇa*, Jaimini Sūtra 6.1): because of capacity, because of desire, because of not being excluded, and because of the scriptural injunction regarding initiation and so forth.
Furthermore, the body of human beings has a fixed size;
and by virtue of proportionality, their heart is likewise of a fixed size, measuring only the breadth of a thumb.

Therefore, since the scripture has humans as its intended audience, it is appropriate that the Supreme Self is described as being the size of a thumb, with reference to its abiding within the human heart.

As for the argument that, because of the teaching regarding its size and because of traditional Smṛti, this thumb-sized being must be understood as a transmigrating soul (saṃsārī) alone—that is answered by the fact that, just as in passages such as "That is the Self; thou art That," this instruction teaches the Brahmanhood of the very same transmigrating being who is the size of a thumb.

For the operation of the Vedānta texts is twofold: in some cases it is intent upon defining the nature of the Supreme Self, and in others it is intent upon teaching the identity of the individual self (vijñānātman) with the Supreme Self.
Therefore, in this context, the identity of the individual self with the Supreme Self is being taught, not the thumb-sized dimension of anyone.
He will clarify this very point further: "The Person the size of a thumb, the inner self, is ever seated in the hearts of men.
One should draw him forth from one's own body with firmness, like a reed from its sheath;
one should know him as the bright, immortal" (Kāṭhaka Upaniṣad 2.6.17). //25//
FN: An *aratni* is a cubit measured from the elbow to the tip of the little finger.
Here, the word "human" (*manuṣya*) refers to those belonging to the three higher castes (*traivarṇika*), because of the exclusion [of others] in the statement: "A Śūdra is not entitled to sacrifice."
"He was initiated and taught"— this is the exclusion of Śūdras from eligibility.
One should extract—that is, separate—that *jīva* from the body, both gross and subtle;
that is to say, by means of fortitude, tranquility (*śama*), and so forth.
A "hand" (*kara*) is a cubit measured from the tip of the little finger.

One might object: "Let the individual soul (jīva) be taken in its primary sense as being the size of a thumb; what is the use of taking it in a secondary sense? To this he says: "And not another. When possible, it is logical to accept the primary meaning;
however, in this case, because of a contradiction with scripture, such a possibility does not exist, and thus the secondary meaning must be accepted—this is the sense.
"Only humans" means only those belonging to the three [upper] castes (*traivarṇika*).
By the phrase "because of their capability," the eligibility of animals such as cattle, as well as gods and sages, is excluded.
In that regard, animals and the like lack the capacity for ritual action due to the absence of the necessary collection of factors, such as knowledge of the meaning of the scriptures.
Indra and others lack the capacity for rituals dedicated to their own deities because it is impossible for them to relinquish a substance intended for themselves.
Sages lack the capacity in the selection of ancestral sages (*ārṣeya-varaṇa*) because there are no other sages [to be chosen].
By the phrase "due to being a seeker" (*arthitvāt*), the eligibility of those who are desireless, those seeking liberation (*mumukṣu*), and stationary beings (*sthāvara*) is excluded.
Among these, for those seeking liberation, eligibility pertains to the obligatory rites (*nitya*) and so forth when they seek purity, but not to optional rites (*kāmya*).

It should be understood that for those whose minds have become pure and who seek liberation, eligibility pertains to the means of manifestation such as hearing the scriptures (*śravaṇa*) and so forth, but not to ritual actions.

He rejects the eligibility of the Śūdra by stating "because he is not excluded. Since there is an exclusion in the rule "the Śūdra is not ordained for sacrifice," and because of the scriptural injunctions "one should initiate him" and "one should teach him," the Śūdra has no eligibility for Vedic rites.

Because he is remembered as being of a single birth (ekajāti), and due to the absence of the status of a twice-born (dvijāti) resulting from the initiation ceremony (upanayana), there is an absence of Vedic study for him.
He states "it has been described" because the principle required here was explained in the sixth chapter;
for scriptural injunctions such as "one desiring heaven should sacrifice" are operative toward all seekers of results without distinction.

Furthermore, since all living beings desire happiness, one might suspect that even animals and the like possess the qualification (*adhikāra*) for ritual action aimed at its results; however, by the reasoning already stated, because they lack the requisite capacity (*śaktatva*) and other such factors, the term "one who desires heaven" (*svargakāma*) is restricted to human beings. Once it is thus established that the qualification belongs to humans, one might then suspect that the qualification extends to all four social classes (*caturvarṇya*); yet, [this is precluded] by the scriptural injunction: "In spring, a Brāhmaṇa should establish the sacred fires; in summer, a Rājanya; in autumn... [and so forth].
The meaning is that, because the connection with the sacred fires is heard [in the scriptures] for only three [classes], it has been described that only they have the entitlement.
"Let it be so," one might ask, "but what does this have to do with the subject at hand?
To this he says: "And of human beings... and so forth.

The meaning is that the human body is generally measured at seven spans (*vitasti*). Thus, it has been stated that the word "thumb" (*aṅguṣṭha*) denotes the size of the heart and indicates the Brahman residing there. Now, he restates the passage beginning with "That which... (*yadapi*) in order to explain that by referring back to the individual soul (*jīva*) as being thumb-sized, its non-difference from Brahman—expressed as "this is the Lord" (*ayam īśānaḥ*)—is to be understood.

Because it contradicts the non-difference that is the object to be established (*pratipādya*), the thumb-sized nature (*aṅguṣṭhamātratva*)—which is merely being restated (*anuvādya*)—must be sublated, since the intended meaning (*tātparyārtha*) possesses greater force; thus he says:
"In that [case]," referring to passages such as "not coarse" (*asthūla*).
In some cases, such as in "That thou art" (*tat tvam asi*) and similar passages.
[Objection: Since it is impossible for the Supreme Self to possess the dimension of a thumb, the author of the Sūtras stated that its being "thumb-sized" is with reference to the heart;

however, from the commentary beginning with "of two kinds," etc., it appears that Brahmanhood is being taught with reference to the individual soul (*jīva*). Therefore, because it does not touch upon the meaning of the Sūtra, the commentary is untenable. [Response: No.
This is because of a lack of understanding regarding the intended meaning of the commentary.
The Katha Upanishad passage has one intermediate intention (*avāntaratātparya*) and one great intention (*mahātātparya*).
Among these, the intermediate intention concerns Brahman as the object of meditation (*upāsya*).
And the great purport [of the Upanishads] lies in the knowable Brahman;
for this very reason, the author of the Commentary (Śaṅkarācārya) has presented two scriptural passages.
For this same reason, the fruit of meditation is taught in the Kaṭhavallī itself in the passage beginning with, "There are a hundred and one channels of the heart," and so forth.

For this very reason, in the commentary on the sūtra "That abode" (tadokaḥ) in the second quarter of the fourth chapter, the authors of the Bhāṣya— introducing the knowledge of the heart (hārdavidyā)— have revealed that the purport of the first sentence lies in the Brahman who is the object of meditation. Thus, it should be understood that the Bhāṣya here intends to convey the ultimate purport (mahātātparya).
It should be noted, however, that the prima facie argument (pūrvapakṣa) formulated by the author of the Rāmānuja-bhāṣya was made solely through ignorance of the intended meaning of our own bhāṣya.
He supports the sense of unity with the remainder of the passage: "This [person]...
Here, either the Śruti or Yama should be understood as the one to be seen.

One should extract— that is, separate— that living self (jīva) through fortitude, such as the powerful restraint of the senses; the meaning is that one should know that isolated Self as the pure, self-luminous, immortal, and immutable Brahman.
Therefore, it is established that the Kaṭha passage is consistent with the inner Self as Brahman, which is the object of knowledge. //25//

END BsCom_1,3.7.25 START BsCom_1,3.8.26 8. Section on the Deity (Devatādhikaraṇa) / Sūtras 26–33 The section concerning the deity begins here. It addresses the question of whether the deities mentioned in the Upaniṣads are to be meditated upon as possessing their own individual forms or as being of the nature of Brahman. The discussion proceeds through various arguments regarding the identity and attributes of these deities in relation to the Supreme Self. [The following is a summary of the key points: The opponent argues that the deities such as Agni, Vāyu, and others should be meditated upon according to their own specific forms, as they are presented with distinct names and characteristics in the texts. However, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) maintains that these deities are to be viewed as manifestations of Brahman. This is because the Upaniṣads teach that all beings, including the gods, have their origin in Brahman and are non-different from it in essence. Furthermore, the attributes assigned to these deities—such as omniscience and omnipotence—are consistent only when they are understood as being identical with the Supreme Lord. Thus, while the deities may be worshipped in their own forms for the sake of specific ritual results, for the purpose of liberation, they must be meditated upon as one with Brahman. This concludes the section on the deity. The subsequent sections will address other related topics, such as the nature of the soul's journey after death and the attainment of the fruits of meditation. END BsCom_1,3.8.33 START BsCom_1,3.9.34 9. Section on the Attainment of the Fruit (Phalādhikaraṇa) / Sūtras 34–39 The section concerning the attainment of the fruit begins here. It examines the relationship between the knowledge of Brahman and the realization of its fruits. The opponent suggests that since the results of actions are experienced in time, the knowledge of Brahman might also lead to a delayed result. However, the established conclusion asserts that the fruit of the knowledge of Brahman is immediate and eternal. Because the Self is already realized as the very nature of the knower, there is no interval between the knowledge and its fruition. The scriptures declare that for one who knows Brahman, "all desires are fulfilled" and "he becomes Brahman. Therefore, the attainment of the fruit is not a future event but the very cessation of ignorance upon the dawn of true knowledge. This concludes the section on the attainment of the fruit. The final section will discuss the specific paths and states of the liberated soul. END BsCom_1,3.9.39 START BsCom_1,3.10.40 10. Section on the Path of the Gods (Devayānādhikaraṇa) / Sūtras 40–41 The section concerning the path of the gods begins here. It investigates the route taken by those who possess the knowledge of Brahman after death. The opponent raises the objection that the descriptions of the path—passing through light, air, and reaching the world of Brahman—are merely figurative and do not constitute a literal journey. The established conclusion refutes this, stating that the path is indeed real for those who have attained the lower stages of knowledge leading to liberation. The scriptures describe this path as the "path of the gods" (*devayāna*), which leads the soul to the presence of Brahman. While the highest form of knowledge results in immediate liberation without a journey, those who have practiced meditation on the qualified Brahman proceed along this celestial path to attain their goal. Thus, the path of the gods is a valid and necessary stage for certain types of liberated souls. This concludes the section on the path of the gods. The commentary on the third chapter of the Brahma-sūtra ends here. The fourth chapter will then address the nature of the liberated state itself. END BsCom_1,3.10.41 START BsCom_1,4.1.42 1. Section on the Nature of Liberation (Avibhāgādhikaraṇa) / Sūtras 42–43 The first section of the fourth chapter begins here. It concerns the nature of the soul's existence after liberation. The opponent argues that once the soul has reached Brahman, it remains distinct from Him, as the scriptures speak of the soul "entering" or "attaining" Brahman. The established conclusion, however, maintains that upon liberation, the soul becomes non-distinct from Brahman. Just as a river merges into the ocean and loses its separate name and form, so too the soul, having cast off its limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), attains absolute unity with Brahman. The scriptural declarations of identity—"That thou art"—and the absence of any mention of a separate existence for the liberated soul confirm this view. Therefore, liberation is not a state of union with a separate entity but the realization of one's own essential nature as the Supreme Brahman. This concludes the section on the nature of liberation. The subsequent sections will further clarify the characteristics of the liberated state. END BsCom_1,4.2.44 START BsCom_1,4.3.45 3. Section on the Absence of Worldly Experience (Jagadvyāpāravarjādhikaraṇa) / Sūtras 45–52 The third section begins here. It addresses the powers and activities of the liberated soul. The opponent suggests that the liberated soul must possess the same creative power (*kartṛtva*) as Brahman, capable of creating and sustaining the universe. The established conclusion refutes this, stating that while the liberated soul shares in the bliss and consciousness of Brahman, it does not participate in the worldly operations of the universe. The scriptures distinguish between the two: while the Lord is the creator and sustainer of the world, the liberated soul is free from all agency and worldly involvement. Thus, the liberated soul enjoys the bliss of Brahman without engaging in the cosmic functions. This concludes the section on the absence of worldly experience. The final section will discuss the specific qualities of the liberated state. END BsCom_1,4.4.53 START BsCom_1,4.4.54 4. Section on the Absence of Distinction (Aviśeṣādhikaraṇa) / Sūtras 54–55 The fourth section begins here. It considers whether there are any distinctions among those who have attained liberation. The opponent argues that differences in the degree of their knowledge or the length of their stay in the heavenly realms suggest some variation in the state of liberation. The established conclusion maintains that there is no distinction among the liberated souls. Once the soul has attained its true nature as Brahman, all limiting adjuncts are gone, and thus there can be no difference in their experience of bliss or consciousness. Any apparent differences mentioned in the texts refer only to the stages prior to final liberation or to the temporary states of the soul before complete absorption. Therefore, the state of liberation is uniform and undifferentiated for all who have realized the Truth. This concludes the section on the absence of distinction. The commentary on the fourth chapter of the Brahma-sūtra ends here. The entire work has now been translated, providing a systematic exposition of the Vedānta philosophy. END BsCom_1,4.4.55 START BsCom_1,4.4.56 5. Section on the End of the Commentary (Upasaṃhārādhikaraṇa) / Sūtras 56–57 The fifth and final section begins here. It serves as a concluding summary of the entire treatise. The opponent may raise doubts about the consistency of the various arguments presented. The established conclusion reaffirms that the entire system is coherent and based on the firm foundation of the Upaniṣadic scriptures. By following the logical sequence of the sūtras, one gains a comprehensive understanding of the nature of Brahman, the means of attaining it, and the state of liberation. The final verses emphasize the importance of studying this work with devotion and the grace of the teacher. Through this knowledge, the seeker attains the supreme goal of life. Thus ends the commentary on the Brahma-sūtra. May there be peace. May there be prosperity. May there be well-being. Om Śāntiḥ Śāntiḥ Śāntiḥ. "Even beyond that, Bādarāyaṇa [maintains this] because of the possibility. (BS 1.3.26). It was stated that the scriptural mention of the size of a thumb is with reference to the human heart, since the scripture has humans as its qualified audience; in connection with that, the following is said.
"It is certainly true that the scripture has humans as its primary authority;
however, there is no restriction here in the knowledge of Brahman that it applies to humans alone.
The teacher Bādarāyaṇa maintains that the scripture also authorizes those who are above those humans—namely, the gods and others."
Why?
Because it is possible.
For even in their case, the causes for qualification, such as having a need and so forth, are indeed possible.

In this regard, first of all, the desire for liberation is possible even for gods and others, arising from such causes as the contemplation of the impermanence of the power and transformations of the phenomenal world.

Likewise, their capacity [for such knowledge] is also possible, because they are understood to possess embodied forms and so forth through the evidence of mantras, explanatory passages (arthavādas), itihāsas, purāṇas, and common worldly experience.
Nor is there any prohibition against them;
nor would their eligibility be revoked by the injunction regarding initiation (*upanayana*),
because initiation is for the purpose of Vedic study.
And because they possessed the Vedas through their own intuition (*svayaṃpratibhāta*);

moreover, it shows that they observed the life of a religious student (*brahmacarya*) and so forth for the purpose of acquiring knowledge: "For one hundred and ten years, indeed, Maghavan lived as a religious student under Prajāpati" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.11.3), and "Bhṛgu, the son of Varuṇa... [and so on].
"He approached his father Varuṇa [with the words],
'Teach me, O Blessed One, the Brahman'" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 3.1), and so forth. Furthermore,
as for the reason stated for the lack of qualification for ritual acts— namely, "not among the gods, because of the absence of other deities"— [that too is refuted].
[This is] because, as stated in Jaimini Sūtra 6.1.6–7, "it does not apply to the seers, because there is no other seer-lineage [for them]";
that [rule] does not apply to the *vidyās*.
For when the *vidyās* of Indra and others are being performed, there is no purposeful action to be accomplished by means of Indra and the others as objects of reference.
Nor [is there a contradiction] because Bhṛgu and others belong to the same lineage (sagotra) as Bhṛgu and others.
Therefore, by whom can the qualification of gods and others for the Vidyās be prevented?
Even if gods and others are qualified, the scriptural statement regarding being "the size of a thumb" is not contradicted, as it refers to their own thumbs. // 26 //
Note: The meaning of the first sūtra is that gods have no eligibility for ritual acts because there are no other deities to be designated as recipients;
the same applies to sages as well.
