The meaning of the second sūtra is that because there is no other seer (ṛṣi) [to act as an intermediary], one is incapable of performing a rite associated with a seer;
thus, incapacity is the reason [for their exclusion].

Having raised the objection that if the scripture has humans as its qualified audience, then gods and others would lack qualification for the knowledge of Brahman, he says: "Bādarāyaṇa [holds] that even above that [the human realm], [there is qualification], because it is possible."

Now, one might object: "Is it not the case that an inquiry into qualification (*adhikāra*) is not relevant in the chapter on Concordance (*samanvaya-adhyāya*)? To this he says: "The thumb" (*aṅguṣṭha*). "Relevance" (*prasaṅga*) means that what has been brought to mind ought not to be neglected. Here, by stating that humans are qualified, there arises a doubt as to whether deities and others—though mentioned [in other contexts]—possess qualification for hearing the Vedānta and so forth, or not. The prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that they do not, because those who are attached to worldly enjoyment cannot possibly possess dispassion (*vairāgya*) and the other required qualities.
Thus, there is a contextual connection (*prasaṅgikī saṃgati*) between these two sections (*adhikaraṇa*), both of which consist of an inquiry into eligibility (*adhikāra*).

Here, the result of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*)—that because gods and others lack eligibility for knowledge, humans who desire gradual liberation (*kramamukti*) would not engage in meditations such as that on the "small" (*dahara*) which have the fruit of gradual liberation by way of attaining divinity—is that there is no engagement; whereas in the final conclusion (*siddhānta*), there is engagement.

This inquiry is fruitful because liberation is possible through knowledge gained by means such as hearing (śravaṇa) for those who have attained divinity through meditations (upāsanā). Now, one might object that those [gods] who are attached to enjoyment lack the desire for liberation and thus have no qualification; to this, he says: "First of all, there is the desire...

The meaning is that for the gods, whose nature is predominantly *sattva*, the desire for liberation—which is unsurpassed happiness—is possible, since they perceive the pleasure of sense objects as unreal due to its being a modification (*vikāra*) and because it is seen to be tainted by defects such as decay and envy.
One might object: "In cases such as 'svāhā to Indra' (indrāya svāhā), there is no embodied deity distinct from the word ending in the dative case;

and since a word lacks the capacity [to perform an action], there can be no qualification [for the fruit]. To this he says: "In the same way" (tathā). This means "just like the state of being a seeker" (arthitva).
He states that they are not excluded by saying, "And not of these...
The meaning is that there is no prohibition against gods and others qualifying for knowledge (vidyā), unlike the case [of the rule] "A Śūdra is not ordained for the sacrifice.

Now, one might object: even if they possess visible capacity due to having physical bodies, they lack scriptural capacity because of the absence of the initiation ceremony (upanayana); to this he says, "And not..."

The meaning is as follows: those for whom the Vedas have appeared spontaneously through the power of study in a previous birth are "those who remember the Vedas" (*smṛtaveda*); the state of being such is what is intended.

Since we observe the proclamation of the Vedas by Piśācas and others who have entered into children and so forth, it follows that beings of divine origin possess the recollection of previous births; thus, it is logical that those who remember the Vedas should engage in the investigation of their meaning.

Having stated that desire and other factors constitute the grounds for the eligibility of gods and sages for knowledge, he states the scriptural evidence—such as residence in the teacher's house—to support this with the words "Moreover" (*apica*).

Now, it might be argued that the knowledge of Brahman does not qualify the gods and others for practice, because it is the subject matter of the Veda, just like the Agnihotra sacrifice; to this, he says: "As for that which... (yadapi).
The meaning of the first sūtra is that gods have no eligibility for ritual acts, because there are no other deities to be designated as recipients.
Likewise, sages have no eligibility.
The meaning of the second sūtra is that because there is no other seer (ṛṣi), one lacks the capacity for ritual action associated with a seer.
He refutes this by stating "not that," meaning that incapacity is not the limiting condition (upādhi).
The sense is that incapacity is not the cause.
The ellipsis is "for there is nothing by which [the inference] would be incapable.
Furthermore, the sublation of the inference by the scriptural statement, "Whosoever among the gods awakened to that, he indeed became that; so it was with the seers," should also be understood.
Now, one might ask: how can there be a scriptural teaching regarding the thumb-sized [self] with respect to the gods and others?

Because they possess massive bodies, their hearts cannot be the size of our thumb; therefore, they have no qualification [for this meditation] according to the Śrutis. To this, he says: "Even though there is qualification for the gods and others... (26).
If it be argued that there is a contradiction regarding action, we say no, because we observe multiple ways of attaining [the goal]. (BS 1.3.27)

It might be argued as follows: if the qualification of gods and others for the sciences (*vidyā*) were described by accepting their possession of bodies and so forth, then, because they possess bodies, one would also have to accept that Indra and the other deities participate as constituent parts of the ritual through the presence of their own physical forms;
and in that case, there would be a contradiction regarding the ritual.
If it is argued that the status of Indra and others as auxiliary elements (*aṅga*) in a sacrifice is not observed through the presence of their actual forms (*svarūpa-saṃnidhāna*),
and that such presence is impossible because it is illogical for a single Indra to be present in his own form simultaneously in many sacrifices; [then we reply:]...
There is no such contradiction.
Why?
Because there are multiple ways of understanding.
The simultaneous assumption of multiple forms is possible even for a single divine being.
How is this known? From observation.

For instance, having begun with "How many gods are there? and having explained, "Three hundred and three, and three thousand and three," [the text] addresses the question "Which are they? by stating: "These are merely their powers; there are only thirty-three gods" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.9.1, 2).
Thus, by declaring this, the Śruti demonstrates that each individual divine self possesses multiple forms simultaneously.

Likewise, by showing through the process of subsuming the thirty-three gods into six, and so on, that "Which one is the single god? Breath," it demonstrates that the gods have the single form of breath, and thereby shows that this one breath possesses multiple forms simultaneously.
Likewise, Smṛti also says: "O bull among the Bharatas, the Self indeed has many bodies."
Having attained power, the yogi should act; and with all those [powers], he should traverse the earth.
One might obtain sense-objects through some means, or one might perform severe austerity.
And he should withdraw them again, just as the sun withdraws its multitude of rays.

Thus, this kind of reasoning demonstrates that even for yogins who have attained powers such as *aṇimā* (minuteness) and the rest, there is the simultaneous assumption of multiple bodies; how much more so, then, for the gods who are perfected by birth (*ājānasiddha*)?
Furthermore, because the assumption of multiple forms is possible, a single deity, having divided itself into many forms, simultaneously becomes a constituent part (*aṅga*) in many sacrifices.
And it is logical that he is not seen by others due to his employment of such actions as invisibility.

There is another explanation for the statement "because multiple modes of participation are observed": even among those possessing physical bodies, multiple modes of participation as constituent parts (*aṅga*) are observed in injunctions regarding ritual acts.
In some cases, even a single embodied being cannot simultaneously occupy the status of a constituent part in multiple places;
just as when many people are feeding [guests], a single Brāhmaṇa is not fed by all of them at once.
And in some cases, even a single embodied being can simultaneously occupy the status of a constituent part in multiple locations,

just as a single Brahmin is saluted at once by many people who are paying homage. Similarly, since sacrifice consists of both the dedication [of an object] and its relinquishment, many [persons] may dedicate [an offering] to a single embodied deity.
Since each deity will simultaneously relinquish its own respective substance, there is no contradiction whatsoever regarding the ritual action, even though the deities possess corporeal forms.

[This is known] from observation and from the authority of the Śruti; for in the *Nivid* of the *Vaiśvadeva-śāstra*, after the question "How many gods are there? was posed, Yājñavalkya gave the answer to Śākalya: "Three hundred and three, and three thousand and three."
*Nivid* refers to mantra-words that express the number of deities being praised.
*Bala* means the perfection of yoga.
[The powers are: *aṇimā*, *mahimā*, *garimā*, *prāpti*, and *īśitā*.

"Prākamya, vaśitva, and kāmāvasāyitā therein"—these refer to the powers beginning with *aṇimā*. [The term] "those perfected by birth" (*ājānasiddha*) refers to those who have attained excellence from the very moment of their birth.

Now, it was argued that the eligibility of gods and others [for Vedic rites] was stated on the assumption that there is an intended meaning (*tātparya*) regarding the possession of manifest forms for mantras and so forth.
And that [position] is incorrect;

for it is impossible to assume an intention regarding their own literal meaning when those [texts] are devoted to something else, as they would contradict perception and other means of valid cognition. Having raised this objection, he refutes it with four sūtras beginning with "virodhaḥ karmaṇi" (contradiction in action), etc.
The word "would be described" (*varṇyeta*) is to be supplied, with "then" (*tarhi*) understood.
"Svarūpa" means the physical form.
If it were accepted [that the deity exists], the deity would be perceived by direct perception;
yet it is not perceived.

Therefore, since there is an absence of a deity possessing a physical form due to its non-apprehension despite its being suitable for perception, there would be no accomplishment of the ritual action because of the absence of the recipient (*saṃpradāna-kāraka*). Thus he says: "And then...
Furthermore, he says: "Nor... because the status of the physical form as a constituent part (*aṅga*) is contradicted by perception and cannot be established through reasoning.
Consequently, the deity is simply the word itself as qualified by its meaning.
The meaning of the objection is that because she (Prakṛti) is insentient, she has no qualification for knowledge. He refutes this with the words "Not so.
For it is possible for even a single deity to assume multiple bodies through the power of yoga, as is seen in the Śruti and Smṛti.
Therefore, he explains that there is no contradiction regarding ritual action with the words beginning "Why? (kasmāt).
When Śākalya asked Yājñavalkya how many deities are being praised in the Vaiśvadeva hymn, Yājñavalkya gave his answer by means of a *nivid* in the form "Three and... and so forth.
A *nivid* is a word that expresses the number of deities being praised.

Regarding the statement of the number as "three thousand three hundred and six," when asked about the nature of those to be numbered: the "magnitudes" (*mahimānaḥ*) are the manifestations (*vibhūtayaḥ*), namely all the gods. Among these thirty-three gods, there are the eight Vasus, the eleven Rudras, the twelve Ādityas, Indra, and Prajāpati; thus, there are thirty-three gods. These, moreover, [are contained] within the six: fire, earth, wind, the intermediate space, the sun, and the sky.
The meaning is that those glories (mahimānaḥ) are also included within the six deities;
it has been shown that the six deities are contained within the three worlds, the three within the two—namely food and breath—and the two within the one, the breath Hiraṇyagarbha.
This is to be connected with the phrase "even of the thirty-three deities."
Having explained the scriptural vision (*darśana*), he explains the traditional one (*smārta*) with the words "likewise the Smṛti.
"Power" (*bala*) refers to the perfection of yoga (*yogasiddhi*):
"Atomicity (*aṇimā*), magnificence (*mahimā*), lightness (*laghimā*), reach (*prāpti*), and mastery (*īśitā*)."
Irresistible will, mastery, and the power to resolve according to one's desire.
Thus are the eight sovereign powers (*aiśvarya*).
In an instant, the yogi becomes minute, large, light, and heavy;
touching the moon with a finger is the power of attainment (*prāpti*).
Sovereignty (īśitā) is the power of creation;
irresistible will (prākāmya) is the non-obstruction of one's desire;
and mastery (vaśitva) is the power of control.

The distinction is that in [the former case] there is the attainment of desired objects through mere volition, whereas in [the latter] there is the power of determining objects at will (*yatra-kāmāvasāyitā*). "Those established by birth" means those who are perfected from birth.
He states the conclusion: "aneka... (many...).

The status of being an auxiliary (*aṅgabhāva*) consists in the performance of one [act] among many acts; this is stated because it is observed in the world. To express this, he states the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) with the words "in some cases, one.
He then states the positive concomitance (*anvaya*) example relevant to the subject at hand with the words "and in some cases. //27//
If it be argued that [the world] is sound, we say no, because of its origination from this [Brahman], as established by perception and inference. (BS 1.3.28)
Granted that no contradiction regarding karma might arise if one accepts that gods and others possess physical bodies;
however, a contradiction would indeed arise in the case of sound.
How so?

For the authority of the Veda was established on the basis of the innate connection between word and meaning, by the principle of "independence" (*anapekṣatvāt*). Now, however, if a deity possessing a physical body (*vigrahavatī*) is admitted—even if she, through her sovereign power (*aiśvarya*), could consume sacrificial offerings related to multiple rituals simultaneously—nevertheless, because of her possession of a body, she would be subject to birth and death like ourselves; thus, for an eternal word...
If it is argued that, when an eternal relationship with an eternal object is perceived, there would be a contradiction with the established authority of Vedic words—
this contradiction does not exist either.
Why?
Because it originates from that;
for it is precisely from this Vedic word that the world, beginning with the gods, originates.
But surely, in the sūtra "From which the birth, etc., of this [world proceed" (Brahma-sūtra 1.1.2), it was determined that the world originates from Brahman;
how then can it be said here that it originates from the Word?
Furthermore, even if its origin from Vedic words is indeed accepted,

how is the contradiction regarding the word itself thereby avoided? For since the referents— the Vasus, Rudras, Ādityas, Viśvedevas, and Maruts— are themselves non-eternal due to their having an origin, and given their non-eternality, by what means can the non-eternality of the Vedic words "Vasu" and so forth that denote them be prevented?
If it is argued that there is indeed a contradiction regarding words, because it is well known in the world that when Devadatta’s son is born, the name Yajñadatta is given to him, we say: no,
for we observe the eternity of the relationship between words and their meanings in the case of words such as "cow" (go) and so forth.
For it is not the case that because individual instances such as cows and the like possess the quality of being produced, their generic forms (ākṛti) must also possess the quality of being produced.
Indeed, it is only the individual instances of substances, qualities, and actions that are produced, not their generic forms.
Furthermore, the relationship of words is with generic forms, not with individual instances.
Because individuals are infinite, it is impossible to grasp their relationship [with words];
furthermore, since universals (*ākṛti*) are eternal even as individuals arise, no contradiction is observed in the case of words such as "cow" (*go*).

Likewise, it should be understood that even if the origination of individual deities and others is accepted, there is no contradiction in the case of words such as "Vasu," because the universals are eternal.

The specific forms of the gods and others, however, are to be understood from the mantras, explanatory passages (arthavādas), and so forth, through the comprehension that they possess bodies and the like.
Terms such as "Indra" and so on are based on their connection with particular positions, just like terms such as "general" and the like.
Consequently, whoever ascends to a particular position is designated by the terms "Indra" and so forth; thus, no fault arises.
This "origination from speech" is not stated with the intention of referring to a material cause (*upādāna-kāraṇa*), as is the case with [the world's] origination from Brahman.

How then? While the eternal word exists in its nature as the signifier (*vācaka*) and possesses an eternal connection with its object, there occurs the manifestation of the individual objects (*arthavyakti*) capable of being engaged with through verbal usage; therefore, it is said that [the world] has its "origination" (*prabhava*) from this. But how is it understood that the world originates from the word?
By means of perception and inference.
Perception is sacred revelation (śruti), because it possesses authority independently of anything else.
Inference is memory,
because it is dependent [on other means] with respect to its validity;
for those two [scriptures] show creation as preceded by the Word.

"The Śruti states: 'With "ete" Prajāpati created the gods; with "asṛgram," human beings; with "indavaḥ," the ancestors; with "tiraḥ pavitram," the cups (grahas); with "āśavaḥ," the hymn (stotra); with "viśvāni," the recitation (śastra); and with "abhisaubhaga," other creatures. Likewise, elsewhere it is said: 'He, through his mind, entered into union with speech' (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.2.4)."

In various such passages, creation preceded by sound is proclaimed. Smṛti also states: "The beginningless and endless, eternal, divine Speech, consisting of the Vedas, was emitted by the Self-existent in the beginning, from which all activities proceed."
Thus,
this "emission" (utsarga) of speech should also be understood as consisting in the transmission of the tradition,
since no other kind of emission is possible for that which is without beginning or end.
"Likewise, in the beginning, that Great Lord fashioned both names and forms, as well as the performance of the duties of living beings, from the words of the Veda alone."
"But he, at the beginning, fashioned the names and the distinct actions of all beings, as well as their various conditions, from the words of the Veda alone."

And so it is; moreover, it is directly perceived by all of us that when one intends to perform a certain action, one first recollects the word expressive of that action and subsequently performs that action.
In the same way, even for Prajāpati the creator, the Vedic words manifested in his mind prior to creation.
It is understood that subsequently he creates the objects that follow from those [names];
and thus the Śruti says: "He uttered 'Bhūḥ'; he created the earth" (Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa 2.2.4.2).
In this way, such passages show the creation of the worlds beginning with Bhūḥ from the very words "Bhūḥ" and so forth, which have appeared in his mind.
Furthermore, with reference to what kind of sound (*śabda*) is this "origination from sound" being stated? He says: "The *sphoṭa*.

For if the position were that of the phonemes (*varṇa*), since they perish as soon as they arise, it would be untenable for the manifestation of gods and other beings to originate from eternal sounds.
Furthermore, phonemes are subject to arising and destruction, because they are perceived differently with each utterance.

For instance, even when a particular person is not visible, he is specifically identified from the mere hearing of the sound of his recitation as "this is Devadatta who is studying" or "this is Yajñadatta who is studying."
Furthermore, this cognition of change regarding the phonemes is not a false cognition,
because there is no subverting cognition [to contradict it];
nor is it logical that the comprehension of meaning arises from the phonemes.
For each individual phoneme cannot convey the meaning,
because of deviation;
nor is there a cognition of a collection of phonemes.
If it were argued that because phonemes occur in a sequence,
the final phoneme— accompanied by the mental impressions (*saṃskāra*) produced by the experience of each preceding phoneme— will cause the meaning to be understood,
that is not so.
For a word, depending upon the apprehension of its relationship [to its meaning], would cause the object to be understood when it itself is perceived, just like smoke and so forth;

yet there is no perception of the final phoneme accompanied by the mental impressions (*saṃskāra*) produced by the experience of each preceding phoneme, because those impressions are not themselves perceptible.
If it is argued that the final phoneme, accompanied by mental impressions (*saṃskāra*) produced by the preceding phonemes, will cause the meaning to be understood, we say no;
for even the recollection, which is the effect of those impressions, occurs in a temporal sequence.
Therefore, the *sphoṭa* alone is the word.

And that [cognition] manifests instantaneously as the object of a single cognition within the cognizer, whose seed of latent impressions has been deposited by the cognitions of each preceding letter and whose maturation has been produced by the cognition of the final letter.
Nor is this single cognition a memory whose objects are the letters; for since the letters are many, it is impossible for them to be the object of a single cognition.
And because it is recognized as the same with every utterance, that [word] is eternal;
for the cognition of difference pertains only to the phonemes (*varṇa*).
Therefore, from the eternal word in the form of *sphoṭa*, which is the signifier, the world—which consists of actions, factors of action, and results—arises as the signified.
"But it is the phonemes themselves that constitute the word, not something else," says the venerable Upavarṣa.
Now, as for the claim that phonemes are subject to arising and perishing—that is not so;
for there is recognition [of them] through the thought "these are those very same [phonemes]."
If it is argued that recognition occurs due to similarity, as in the case of [re-growing] hair and so forth, we say no;
for it is impossible for recognition to be sublated by another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
If it is argued that recognition is based on the universal form (*ākṛti*), we say no.
Because there is recognition of the individual [letter].

For if, at each utterance, distinct individual manifestations of phonemes were perceived—just as distinct individual cows and so forth are perceived—then that recognition would be based on a universal form (*ākṛti*).
But this is not the case.

For it is indeed the individual phonemes (*varṇavyakti*) themselves that are recognized in each utterance; for the cognition is "the word 'cow' has been uttered twice," and not "two words 'cow' [have been uttered].

But was it not said that even phonemes are perceived as distinct due to differences in utterance, since a distinction is perceived merely from hearing the sounds of the study of Devadatta and Yajñadatta?

To this it is replied: when there is a certain recognition regarding the phonemes (*varṇa*), because phonemes are manifested by conjunctions and disjunctions, this varied cognition regarding the phonemes is caused by the diversity of their manifestors, not by the nature of the phonemes themselves. Furthermore, even by one who maintains that there is a difference between individual phoneme-instances, phoneme-forms (*varṇākṛti*) must be postulated for the sake of establishing recognition.
And in those cases, one must admit that the cognition of difference is caused by external adjuncts (*paropādhika*).

Therefore, it is better to assume that the cognition of difference regarding the individual phonemes themselves is caused by external adjuncts, while the recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*) is based on their own essential nature (*svarūpa*); thus, there is parsimony of hypothesis (*kalpanālāghava*).
And this very recognition is the subverting cognition (*bādhaka-pratyaya*) that invalidates the cognition of difference concerning the phonemes.

For how could a single *saṅ* sound, when uttered by many people at the same time, simultaneously possess multiple forms—namely, as acute (*udātta*), grave (*anudātta*), circumflex (*svarita*), nasalized (*sānunāsika*), and non-nasalized (*niranunāsika*)?
Alternatively, this difference in perception is caused by the sound (*dhvani*) and not by the phoneme (*varṇa*); thus there is no fault.

What, then, is this so-called *dhvani*? It is that which enters the path of the ear of one hearing from a distance who does not perceive the distinction between phonemes (*varṇa*), and which, as one draws near, imposes distinctions such as clarity or indistinctness upon the phonemes.
The specific qualities such as the acute accent (*udātta*) and so forth are based on that [temporal sequence], not on the intrinsic nature of the phonemes (*varṇa*),
because phonemes are recognized as being the same in every utterance.
This being the case, the cognitions of the acute accent and so forth will have a real objective basis (*sālambana*).

Otherwise, since the phonemes (*varṇa*) are recognized as being without distinction, one would have to postulate that the specific qualities such as the acute accent (*udātta*) and so forth are produced by conjunctions and disjunctions [of air].

Furthermore, because conjunctions and disjunctions are imperceptible, it would be impossible to determine that their dependent specific qualities reside in the phonemes; consequently, these cognitions of the acute accent and so forth would be entirely without a basis (*nirālambana*).
Moreover, one should not be so insistent that the recognition of phonemes as identical should be contradicted by the distinctions of the acute accent and so forth.
For it is not possible for one thing that is undivided to possess a division based on the division of another;
indeed, people do not consider a universal (*jāti*) to be divided by the division of individuals (*vyakti*).
Furthermore, since the comprehension of meaning is possible from the phonemes (*varṇa*) themselves, the postulation of *sphoṭa* is purposeless.

If it is argued: "I do not postulate a *sphoṭa*; rather, I perceive it directly through immediate intuition (*pratyakṣa*), because it appears instantaneously in a cognition that has been conditioned by the apprehension of each individual phoneme," we say: no, for even this cognition has the phonemes as its object.
This single cognition, "cow," which occurs subsequent to the apprehension of each individual phoneme, has as its object the entire collection of phonemes and not some other distinct entity.
How is this known?
Because even in this cognition, the phonemes beginning with *ga* persist, whereas those beginning with *da* do not.

For if the object of this cognition were the *sphoṭa*, which is a distinct entity from the letter *ga* and so forth, then the letters *ga* and so forth would be excluded from this cognition just as the letters *da* and so forth are;
but such is not the case.
Therefore, this single cognition is merely a memory whose object is the phonemes themselves.
Now, it was argued that because phonemes are manifold, it is not possible for them to be the object of a single cognition;
to this we reply: it is indeed possible for even a plurality to be the object of a single cognition, as is seen in cases such as "a row," "a forest," "an army," "ten," "a hundred," and "a thousand."

As for the cognition that "this word *gauḥ* is one," that is merely figurative (*aupacārikī*), based on the delimitation of a single meaning among many phonemes (*varṇa*s), just like the cognitions of a forest, an army, and so forth.

Here [the opponent] says: if the phonemes themselves, by occurring in their entirety as the objects of a single cognition, were the word (*pada*), then there would be no comprehension of the specific difference between words in cases such as *jārā*, *rājā*, *kapiḥ*, and *pikaḥ*.
"For those very same phonemes appear here and there [in different words].

To this we reply: even though there is a simultaneous recollection of all the phonemes, just as ants enter into the cognition of a "line" only by following a specific order, so too will the phonemes enter into the cognition of a "word" only by following a specific order.
In that regard, even though there is no difference in the phonemes themselves, the comprehension of distinct words produced by a specific sequence is not contradictory.

In the linguistic usage of elders, these phonemes—being assisted by a specific order and having their connection to particular meanings grasped—appear in one's own usage exactly as they did, within a cognition that reflects upon them as a whole following the apprehension of each individual phoneme. Thus, they [convey] that...
For those who maintain that the letters [themselves] convey that meaning without deviation, the assumption is simpler.
For the proponents of *sphoṭa*, however, there is both the abandonment of what is perceived and the assumption of what is unperceived;
for they would have to assume the heavier theory that "these letters, being apprehended in sequence, manifest the *sphoṭa*, and that *sphoṭa* manifests the meaning."
Furthermore, even if it were the case that different phonemes (varṇa) arise with each utterance,

nevertheless, because one must necessarily admit the existence of phoneme-universals (varṇasāmānya) as the objective basis for recognition (pratyabhijñā), the process by which meaning is conveyed through phonemes— which has been established— must be transferred to those universals. Consequently, there is no contradiction in the view that the manifestation of individual entities such as gods proceeds from eternal words.
FN: "Innate" (*autpattika*) means natural (*svābhāvika*).

From a word denoting a genus such as "substantiality" (*vastutva*), one forms a mental image of the individual instance of that genus intended to be produced; the arising (*prabhava*) of that [instance] from it is what constitutes this "arising from that" (*tatprabhavatva*).
Of the forms and the classes [of words]:
"These swift drops have been poured across the filter,
toward all auspicious fortunes."
Recalling [the creation] by means of the words contained in this mantra, Brahmā created the gods and others.

Therein, the word *etad* (this), which denotes that which is proximate, serves as a reminder of the gods who are proximate by virtue of being the presiding deities (*anugrāhaka*) over the sense organs. The word *agra* (foremost) is a reminder of humans, because blood (*asṛk*) is their primary delight in the body.
The word *indu* is a reminder of the Pitṛs who abide in the moon;
the word *tiraḥpavitra* is a reminder of the Grahas who purify the Soma and spread it within themselves;
the word *āśu* is a reminder of the Stotras that pervade the Ṛks; and the word *viśva* is a reminder of the Śastras that enter into performance immediately after the Stotras.

The meaning of the word "what" (*kiṃ*) is as follows: is it the tradition (*saṃpradāya*), which is the study passed down through the succession of teacher and disciple; or is it the structural states (*saṃsthā*), that is, the various stages; or is it the form of phonemes (*varṇa*), or the form of the *sphoṭa* distinct from them?

It is called *sphoṭa* because it "bursts forth" (*sphuṭate*) when manifested by phonemes (*varṇa*). The meaning manifested by the phonemes is the *sphoṭa*; the eternal word such as "cow" (*gav-ādiśabda*) is its manifestor. With this in mind, the aforementioned [statement] was made; such is the connection with the preceding [text]. The meaning is that because of deviation—since the cognition of meaning is not observed from a single phoneme alone—and since the futility of other phonemes is not observed [if they were redundant], [the word is eternal]. Just as the true nature of a gem (*ratnatattva*) shines forth clearly through many visual cognitions (*cākṣuṣapratyaya*), so too does the *sphoṭa* of words such as "cow."

The meaning is as follows: in that mind wherein the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*)—which have been deposited by the cognitions produced by each individual phoneme beginning with *ga* and which have the *sphoṭa* as their object—constitute the seed; and in that cognitive mind wherein the final impression, produced by the cognition generated by the final phoneme, has reached its culmination; there arises the cognition "this is one word, *gauh*," which, having that [sphoṭa] as its object, appears clearly as a direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
It is logical that the cognition "these very same hairs" following a haircut is an error,
because it contradicts the cognition of difference [between the previous and subsequent states].

The meaning is that the cognition of variety regarding the phonemes arises because they are manifested by the diverse conjunctions and disjunctions of the abdominal air with the locations such as the palate.
That which enters [the ear] is *dhvani*; this is the remainder [of the sentence].
The meaning is that *dhvani* is sound distinct from the phonemes (*varṇa*).
The distinction is that while the phonemes persist in every utterance, the *dhvani* varies.
The meaning is as follows: "imperceptibility" refers to the lack of audibility.

Just as the universal "cowness" (*gotva*) is undifferentiated across various individual instances that are mutually distinct—such as a spotted cow, a hornless one, and so forth—in the same way, the phonemes (*varṇa*) are indeed undifferentiated across the various sounds (*dhvani*).
The construction is: by means of the cause which is the distinction of the sounds, such as the acute accent (*udātta*) and others, [the distinction] belongs to the phonemes as well.
The determination of an object is the ascertainment of its meaning;
reflective awareness is memory;
and the state of linguistic proficiency is the usage of elders.
By the word "successively" (*krama*) and so forth, number (*saṃkhyā*) is understood.
One's own respective linguistic usage (*svasvavyavahāra*) is the state of activity of the middle-aged elder.
Its being "of such a nature" (*tādṛśatva*) consists in its being assisted by the sequence and other factors observed at the time of learning (*vyutpatti*).
The capacity of phonemes (varṇas) to convey meaning is observed,
whereas the sphoṭa is unobserved.

Having accepted that there is no contradiction regarding the action [of cognition], he raises the objection concerning a contradiction regarding the authority of the word (śabda-prāmāṇya) and then refutes it.
"If it be argued that [it is] sound" means: let there be no such consequence; let it not be so named.

In the *Autpattika-sūtra*, the authority of the Veda regarding its own meaning was stated on the grounds that the relationship between word and object—which are beginningless—is itself beginningless, and thus the Veda does not depend on other means of knowledge.

Now, if one accepts that the individual (vyakti) is impermanent, then because its relationship [to the word] would also be impermanent, a person would have to establish the convention (*saṃketa*) of the word after first cognizing the individual through another means of knowledge. Thus, he states "How so? and so forth, arguing that there would be a contradiction regarding its validity due to its dependence on another means of knowledge.
Does the fact that words are impermanent result in the relation being a product, or does it follow from the impermanence of the objects?
It is not the first case; thus he says: "Nor this either."
The meaning of "also" (*api*) is that [words] are like actions in being non-contradictory.
The intention is that since words already exist prior [to their use], by virtue of being the cause for the manifestation of entities such as gods, they are not impermanent.
Here, one raises the objection regarding a contradiction between what precedes and what follows with the word "nanu."
Anticipating the objection that there is no contradiction because sound acts as a cause by being an auxiliary to Brahman, he raises the second alternative with the words "Moreover" (*apica*).
"Impermanence" (*anityatva*) means having a beginning (*sāditva*).
Since objects in their manifested form are impermanent, the impermanence of the relationship between words and those objects is unavoidable.
Therefore, the meaning is that because [the relationship] depends upon a human-made connection, there is a contradiction with its being authoritative (*prāmāṇya*).

Nor should it be argued that even though individual instances (*vyakti*) are non-eternal, the relationship between word and object must be eternal—just as the inherence (*samavāya*) of a genus such as "pot-ness" [is eternal]—because the point of the analogy fails; the sense is that a relationship dependent on both [relata] cannot persist in the absence of either one.

Just as "cowness" and other universals are the denotata of words such as "cow," so too are the forms (ākṛtis) such as "wealth-ness" (vasutva) the referents of words such as "Vasu," and not the individuals; thus he refutes [the objection] with the passage beginning with "no" (na).

He demonstrates that because words, their referents, and the universals are eternal, their relationship is also eternal, with the passage beginning with "for not" (nahi). [He states the reason for this:
"because individuals are infinite."

Nor should it be argued that the denotative power (śakti) resides in individuals as delimited by "cowness" (gotva), because a universal cannot serve as a cognitive proximity (pratyāsatti) and thus all individuals cannot be presented [to consciousness]; for, compared to the apprehension that "cowness is the delimitor of denotability" (śakyatāvacchedaka), the apprehension that "cowness is the denotable" (śakya) is simpler (lāghava).
The sense is that because the individual is obtained through established *ajahallakṣaṇā* (non-abandoning indication), it cannot be said to be unobtainable by other means.
Alternatively, what is refuted here is the view that the word's denotative power (*śakti*) resides solely in individuals, as well as the resulting cognition of logical inconsistency (*anupapatti*).

Even without the individual (vyakti), because the cognition of the genus (jāti) depends on the power of the word, both powers are necessary. And thus, since the individual is beginningless by virtue of its identity with the eternal genus, its relation [to the genus] is also beginningless,
according to the doctrine of the pre-existence of the effect (satkāryavāda).

For this very reason, it is appropriate that "partial indication" (bhāgalakṣaṇā) is stated regarding sentences such as "That thou art" in the *Vākyavṛtti*; for if only the universal were the denoted meaning, there would be no part of the denoted meaning that constitutes the undivided reality (*akhaṇḍārtha*).
Furthermore, from the natural sense of the Sūtra, "Because [the world] originates from That," it is understood that the view of a power residing solely in the individual is refuted.

Indeed, words such as *ḍittha* denote only the individual and are conventional (*sāṃketika*) because they arise immediately after the object; however, words such as *go* (cow) are not merely denotative of the individual nor are they conventional, because they exist even prior [to the individual] as the cause of its production. Rather, they denote a universal (*sāmānya*) that is inextricably linked to the individual and permeates it in both gross and subtle forms.

Nor is it correct to argue that words like *indra* and *candra* are merely denotative of the individual—just like the word *ākāśa*—on the grounds that there is no genus (*jāti*) due to the singularity of the individual *indra* and so forth.
Since the universal (*jāti*) arises through the distinction between past and future individuals (*vyakti*), enough with this elaboration.

Having concluded the example, he states the application to the subject of the illustration (*dārṣṭāntika*) with the words beginning "In individuals" (*vyaktiṣu*); here, "form" (*ākṛti*) means the universal (*jāti*).
Now, what indeed is that individual?
Lest it be argued that the meaning of a word would be a genus such as "Indra-hood" (indratva) and so forth, he says: "But a specific configuration" (ākṛtiviśeṣa).
This means [the meaning is derived] from such expressions as "the thunderbolt-handed one" (vajrahasta) and "the destroyer of cities" (purandara).

Having stated that for words like "Indra," the genus is the ground for their application (*pravṛttinimitta*), he states that the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) is the ground by saying: "by position" (*sthāna*).
Since the locus remains even during the dissolution of individuals, the relationship between word and meaning is eternal; therefore, he says "And thus" (*tataśca*).
He resolves the previously mentioned contradiction by saying "Nor is it so" (*na ca*).
Considering that there is no contradiction in the view that the word is the cause, he introduces the remainder of the Sūtra with the question "But how? (*kathaṃ punar*).
Smṛti is inference because, for the sake of establishing its own authority, it infers a foundational Śruti; [as in the case of]:
"These swift drops have flowed across the filter, possessing all auspicious fortunes."
"Having recollected by means of these words contained in the mantra, Brahmā created the gods and the others.
Therein, the word *ete* (these), being a pronoun, serves to recall the gods.
As for *asṛgraḥ*, they are humans because they delight (*ramante*) in a body where blood (*asṛj*) is predominant."
The word *indu* is a reminder of the ancestors who reside in the moon;
the word *tiraḥ-pavitra* refers to the planets that obscure the pure *soma* within themselves;
and the word *āśu* refers to the hymns (*ṛc*) in the form of chants which flow like tears.
Based on the Vedic scripture, "The Sāman is supported upon the Ṛc," the word *viśva* refers to the Śāstras that enter into the performance following the Stotra.
The word *abhisaubhaga* is a reminder for those endowed with auspiciousness in all respects; such is the meaning of the passage from the Chāndogya Brāhmaṇa.

That Prajāpati brought about a union of mind and speech—that is, he brought about a union consisting of mind and speech as its two forms. The meaning is that he contemplated with his mind the creation manifested by the three Vedas.
The phrase "He created the sun as a ray," and so forth, is the meaning of the word "etcetera" (ādi).

Tradition (*saṃpradāya*) is the study transmitted through the succession of teacher and disciple; its established forms (*saṃsthā*) are its states. That creation of Prajāpati was preceded by sound (*śabda*).
Because it is a creation, like a pot perceived by direct perception; thus, with the words "apica" (furthermore), he states another meaning of the phrase "by means of direct perception and inference.
Then, fearing the undesirable consequence that [the Veda] originates from that [Creator], he raises an objection regarding the nature of the sound-form itself by asking: "Of what essence is it?"
The meaning of the word "what" (*kiṃ*) is: is it the form of the phonemes (*varṇa*), or is it the form of the *sphoṭa* which is distinct from them?

In response to the objection that, because the phonemes are impermanent and the *sphoṭa* does not exist, neither can be the cause of the world, the Grammarian adopts the second position by saying "the *sphoṭa*. That which is manifested—that is, revealed—by the phonemes is the *sphoṭa*; the word "cow" (*gavādiśabda*) and so forth is eternal and is the manifester of that object which is the *sphoṭa*. This [statement] is made with reference to that, and this is how it connects with what precedes.

He refutes that very first position with the word "varṇa" (phoneme). [The opponent argues: "There is no logical inconsistency, because the permanence of phonemes is established by the recognition 'this is that same letter *ga*. To this he replies: 'utpanna' (arisen).

The meaning is that recognition has as its object the universal (*jāti*) of *ga*-ness, because the difference of the perceived *ga*-phoneme is inferred from its possession of contradictory properties such as high pitch (*tāratva*) and low pitch (*mandratva*), as in the cognitions 'the *ga* is high-pitched' and 'the *ga* is low-pitched.'"
[Objection: Is it not the case that the cognition of contradictory properties is an error conditioned by the limiting adjunct (upādhi) of the sound (dhvani)?

To this he says: "And not... The implication is that since phonemes (varṇas) are impermanent, they cannot be the cause of the world. Furthermore, because it is impossible for them to convey meaning, he states with the words "And not from the phonemes," etc., that the sphoṭa must be accepted;
for there is deviation, as one does not observe the comprehension of meaning from a single phoneme.
The meaning is: "and because it would follow that other phonemes would be useless.

Then, having raised the objection that the collection (*samudāya*) of phonemes is the signifier, he says "nor" (*na ca*), meaning that such a collection does not exist for things that are momentary (*kṣaṇika*).

He then raises a further objection: even though there is no inherent concomitance (*sāhitya*) among the phonemes, there is a concomitance by means of an unseen potency (*apūrva*) characterized as a mental impression (*saṃskāra*), just as there is among the *Āgneya* and other sacrifices; thus he says "by means of the prior" (*pūrva*).
Is this *saṃskāra* some distinct entity called *apūrva* produced by the phonemes, or is it the mental impression (*bhāvanā*) produced by the experience of the phonemes?
It cannot be the first, because there is a lack of evidence.
Furthermore, is this [word] a cause for the cognition of an object when it is unknown or when it is known?
It is not the first case; thus he says: "Not that.
A word, accompanied by a mental impression (*saṃskāra*), is a cause for the cognition of an object only when it is known.
The meaning is that it is an indicator because it brings about cognition in dependence upon the apprehension of a relationship, like smoke and so forth.
Regarding the second [alternative], is it known through perception or by means of an effect as a logical mark?
He says "not so" with the words "na ca" (nor).
He raises the second objection with "kārya" (the effect):

[the objection being that] the cognition of the object is the effect, and when that has arisen, the impression (*saṃskāra*) is the cause; and when that has arisen, the [cognition of the object] occurs. He refutes this through mutual dependence (*parasparāśraya*) with the word "no."

The literal meaning is that since the recollection of word-meanings also occurs subsequent to the cognition of the words, it is not tenable for there to be a cognition of the word consisting of the final phoneme together with the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*).
The word "also" (*api*) is intended to highlight the mutual dependence [of these two].
By this, the position that the latent impressions belong to the cognitions themselves is also refuted.
For it is impossible for that [residual impression] to be the cause of the cognition of the object, since its only function is to serve as the cause for the recollection of the phonemes.

Nor should it be argued that the cognition of the object arises from the final phoneme in conjunction with it, while the residual impression alone serves as the cause for the recollection of the phonemes.
The meaning is as follows: at the time prior to the cognition of the object, cultivation (*bhāvanā*) cannot be the cause of the cognition of the object because it does not exist [at that time].
Nor should it be argued that this cultivation—inferred through the recollection of the phonemes (*varṇa*)—becomes the cause of the cognition of the object when conjoined with the final phoneme;

for the recollection of the phonemes, which is its effect and occurs sequentially, also arises immediately after the experience of the final phoneme, and thus the cultivations inferred by it lack conjunction with that final phoneme.
He states the result regarding the possibility of phonemes (*varṇa*) conveying meaning with the words "Therefore" (*tasmāt*).

Anticipating the objection as to what proof there is for the *sphoṭa*, he states that the perception "this is one word" (*ekaṃ padam*) is the means of valid cognition (*pratyakṣapramāṇa*), saying "And that" (*sa ca*).
Just as the true nature of a gem (*ratnatattva*) becomes clearly manifest through many visual cognitions (*cākṣuṣapratyaya*), so too does the *sphoṭa* of words such as "cow" (*gavādi*).

The meaning is this: in that consciousness (*citta*) wherein the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*)—produced by the individual cognitions of each letter beginning with *ga* and having the *sphoṭa* as their object—have been deposited, there arises a final impression (*saṃskāra*) produced by the cognition of the final letter; in that consciousness which possesses such an impression, the cognition "this is one word, *gaur*" occurs, and it appears clearly through its being the object of that [final] perception.

By this, it is shown that the positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) of the phonemes (*varṇa*) with respect to the cognition of the *sphoṭa* is established otherwise (*anyathāsiddhi*). Furthermore, the complete manifestation of the *sphoṭa* does not arise from a single phoneme—

by which other phonemes would be rendered useless— but rather, as has been stated, the complete manifestation of the *sphoṭa* occurs when the mind is refined by numerous impressions (*pratyaya*), like a gem.

One might object: "The cognition that 'one word is one sentence' is not a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) for the existence of the word-sphoṭa and the sentence-sphoṭa, because it is merely a memory (*smṛti*) based on a collection of phonemes. Anticipating this objection, [the author] refutes it with the words "And not...
He states the eternity of the sphoṭa for the purpose of establishing its status as the cause of the universe, with the words "And of that..."

[Objection: Is it not the case that the recognition "this is that very same word" is an error, because there is a cognition of differences such as the acute accent (*udātta*)? To this he replies with the words "difference," etc.
He establishes his final position (*siddhānta*), preceded by the statement of the teacher’s tradition, with the words "the phonemes alone," etc.
The meaning is that a word consisting of a *sphoṭa* distinct from the phonemes does not ascend to [the level of] experience.
He raises the objection that this is an error due to similarity, with the words "due to similarity.
It is reasonable that the cognition "these are those very same hairs" following the shaving of hair is an error.

Because it contradicts the cognition of difference; however, the cognition that "this very same phoneme is this" is indeed valid knowledge (*pramā*), as there is no subverting evidence (*bādhaka*). Thus he says: "No."

He raises the objection that the recognition of phonemes has as its object the [individual] cows and so forth, just like the recognition of "cowness" and the like—this is expressed by the words "pratyabhijñānam" (recognition).
Only when a difference between individuals is established would recognition have a universal (jāti) as its object, as in cases such as: "The water that you drank is the very same water that I drank."
He offers a rebuttal, stating that a distinction between individual instances is not established here in this manner: "No; [it is] the individual instance," and "But this is not so."
The meaning is that it is the cognition of the individual's difference [from others].

He restates that the difference between individuals is established by inference because of their possession of contradictory properties such as being acute (udātta) and so forth—starting with "Now, [one might object]...

Since the cognition of difference has its basis in a difference due to limiting adjuncts (upādhi), like the cognition of difference between the space within a jar and the space in a well, it is otherwise accounted for; therefore, it is set aside by the recognition of the identity of the individual, which is not otherwise accounted for and which rests upon the independent essential nature [of the thing itself].
He provides the answer, "Objection," as follows:

"In this case," the meaning is that the cognition of diversity among the phonemes arises because they are manifested by diverse conjunctions and disjunctions of the air residing within the chest with the locations such as the palate.
Furthermore, he states, "Moreover," that there is no inherent difference among the phonemes due to the conceptual complexity (kalpanā-gaurava) [of postulating such differences].

The meaning is that it is improper to postulate both an infinity of individual phonemes (*varṇavyakti*) and universals (*jāti*); rather than postulating universals such as "g-ness" (*gatva*) for the sake of recognition among the infinite individual instances of the letter *ga*, and then further postulating that distinctions such as acute accent (*udāttatva*) within those universals are merely adventitious (*aupādhika*), it is better to simply postulate that the distinction between individual phonemes is adventitious.
Thus, the postulation of an infinity of individuals and of universals is incorrect.
Now, one might object that since there is no sublation of difference, it cannot be merely adventitious; to this he says: "This [is not so].
Then, let it be that both difference and non-difference are real for the sake of the validity of the two cognitions;
to this he replies: "For how [could it be]?"
The meaning is that because the identity of the two is contradictory, their difference must be merely adventitious (*aupādhika*).

Now, expressing dissatisfaction with the view that—since the conjunction of air and so forth is beyond the senses, it is impossible for the superimposition (*āropa*) of its various qualities, such as the acute accent (*udātta*), to be perceived in the phonemes—he states his own position: "Or rather" (*athavā*).
The meaning is that properties of the sound (*dhvani*), such as acuteness and so forth, appear in the phonemes due to the superimposition of non-difference between the sound and the phoneme.
He states the nature of *dhvani* by means of a question: "What?"—the ellipsis being "that which descends is *dhvani*.
The meaning is that *dhvani* is sound distinct from the phonemes (*varṇa*).

He states that "for a person who has approached [the sound]," that very person superimposes qualities residing in himself, such as highness or lowness, upon the phonemes; this is expressed by the words "pratyāsīdataśca" (and for one drawing near).
He explains the word "ādi" (and so forth) with the word "tad" (that).
Now, one might object that *dhvani* is merely the unmanifested phoneme and not something distinct from it; to this he replies with the words "varṇānām" (of the phonemes).
The meaning is that there is a distinction because the phonemes (varṇas) persist with every utterance while the sound (dhvani) varies.
Otherwise, in the case of whispered recitation (vācika-japa), when the phonemes are indistinct, there would be a cognition of "sound" (dhvani) rather than phonemes;
and when the sound of a drum or similar instrument is perceived merely as "sound-ness," there would be the notion, "this is an indistinct phoneme. This is how it should be understood.

Thus, while stating the merit in his own view regarding the limiting adjunct of sound (*dhvani*), he demonstrates the aforementioned lack of conviction concerning the limiting adjunct of air (*vāyu*) with the words "And thus," etc.
[Objection: Let it be so; what is the fault? To this, he replies: "By conjunction," etc.
The meaning is that [qualities] such as conjunction with air (*vāyusaṃyoga*) are not audible.
Therefore, the intention is that only the audible sound (*śrāvaṇadhvani*) is the limiting condition (*upādhi*) for the superimposition of properties such as high pitch (*udāttatva*).
Thus, it has been stated that even though the sounds possessing contradictory properties are distinct, the phonemes (*varṇa*) that inhere in them do not differ.
He confirms that very point by means of an illustration with the words "apica" (furthermore).

Just as the universal "cowness" (*gotva*) is non-different despite existing in many distinct individuals such as those that are spotted or hornless, so too the phonemes (*varṇa*) are indeed non-different among the various sounds (*dhvani*).
The construction is as follows: "by means of the cause which is the distinction of the sound—such as the acute accent (*udātta*) and so forth—the [distinction] of the phonemes also [occurs]."
The literal meaning [of the phrase] is "because of the contradiction with recognition" (*pratyabhijñāvirodhāt*).

Alternatively, he dispels the doubt that there is a difference between phonemes (*varṇa*) because they are recognized as being qualified by distinctions such as the acute accent (*udātta*) and so forth—by means of an example, [saying] "moreover" (*apica*).
Having established the permanence of phonemes, he refutes the *sphoṭa* in order to state that these very phonemes are the expressive agents: "and from the phonemes" (*varṇebhyaśca*).
Unable to tolerate this conceptualization, he raises an objection with "no.

He says "instantly" (*jhaṭiti*): just as the face [is perceived] by the eye in a cognition associated with a mirror, so too the *sphoṭa* is directly perceived by the ear in a cognition associated with the phonemes, even without any other cause. Whatever object appears in a consciousness is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) therein.

He says that the cognition of "a single word" involves only the phonemes (*varṇa*) appearing [in consciousness], and not some additional *sphoṭa*; therefore, that cognition is not a means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) for the *sphoṭa*.
He states this with the words beginning "of this too" (*asyā api*).

Now, one might object: the *sphoṭa* is the object of the cognition of the word "cow" (*gopada*), whereas the letters *ga*, etc., merely persist because they are its manifestors (*vyañjaka*). To this he replies: "If indeed... (*yadi hi*).

The meaning is that in the cognition of the fire being manifested, one does not observe the persistence of the manifesting smoke. He says "therefore" to indicate that the sphoṭa need not be postulated because it is possible for [the word] to have a collection of phonemes as its objective support, since the postulation of a separate category of entity (padārthāntara) would involve unnecessary complexity (gaurava).

He states that "even for many, unity based on limiting adjuncts (upādhi) is logical" with the words "it is possible. Now, one might ask: while such adjuncts as spatial parts exist there [in the case of a forest], what is the adjunct in the present case? To this he replies: "But that which... [yā tv iti].

The meaning is that a single word is capable of expressing a single object, and a single sentence possesses intentionality toward a single principal object; thus, the designation of "oneness" is applied metaphorically due to the connection with a single object.
Furthermore, the cognition of a single object does not occur once the status of being a single word has been known.
It should not be argued that this involves a circular dependency (anyonyāśraya) because [the status of being a word or sentence] is known only when that [meaning] is known;

for, once the middle-aged person has ascertained— through the inferential mark of the child’s activity— that the phonemes uttered by the superior elder, having been sequentially grasped in a single recollection immediately after hearing the final phoneme, are the cause of a single cognition of an object,
he then ascertains their status as a single word or sentence.

He raises an objection, saying "here he says," [arguing] that since a difference in words is observed even when there is identity of phonemes (*varṇa*), one must accept a word distinct from the phonemes, called *sphoṭa*.
He refutes this, saying "here [it is replied]," [stating] that the perception of a difference in words occurs among the phonemes themselves due to a difference in their sequence of action.

[The opponent objects: "But how can there be a sequence for phonemes that are eternal and all-pervading, or how can they be the cause of the cognition of meaning through the cognition of them as words?"
To this he replies: "By growth" (*vṛddhi*).
At the stage of linguistic acquisition, having perceived the sequence of apprehension corresponding to the sequence of utterance, one superimposes that sequence onto the phonemes being apprehended;
thus, those phonemes are grasped as possessing this sequence, this number, and this capacity for meaning. Then, at the time of the listener's activity, they function in exactly that same way.
The meaning is that [the letters], having ascended to memory, cause their respective objects to be understood.
He concludes the doctrine of permanent letters with the word "varṇa":
the capacity of letters to convey meaning is observed.
The *sphoṭa* has not been observed.
Now, having provisionally accepted the instability of phonemes (*varṇas*), he refutes the *sphoṭa* by means of a bold argument (*prauḍhivāda*) with the words "Even so" (*athāpi*).

Since it is established that stable universals (*sāmānyas*) such as "going" and so forth, when possessed of specific sequences and grasped through their conventional relations, convey meaning, the entire process should be applied to these established universals rather than to an unestablished *sphoṭa*.
The meaning is that [the word] must be postulated.
Having established that phonemes are stable and expressive, he states the resulting conclusion: "And therefore," etc. //28//
And for this very reason, it is eternal. BBs_1,3.29.

Since the eternity of the Veda has been established through arguments such as the non-recollection of an independent author, one might raise the objection that this is contradicted by the admission that individual beings such as gods originate [from it]. Having resolved this with the sūtra "Because [the world] originates from that," he now further solidifies that very established eternity of the Veda with the words: "And for this very reason, there is eternity."
For this very reason, since the world—including gods and other beings of fixed form—originates from the words of the Veda, the eternity of the Vedic word must also be understood.
And thus says a mantra: "By means of sacrifice, they found the path of speech; they discovered her who had entered among the seers" (Ṛgveda 10.71.3).
This shows that speech was already established when it was discovered.

And Vedavyāsa likewise records this: "At the end of the age, the great seers, authorized by the Self-born One, recovered through austerity the Vedas along with the Itihāsas that had disappeared. (29) [Note:
By means of sacrifice, or by their previously performed deeds, they attained the path of speech—that is, the fitness for receiving and the fitness for grasping the Veda.

Then, the ritualists (yājñika)— meaning those who had not previously found it— discovered and obtained that speech which had entered into the sages and was existing there; they discovered it, having found it,
at the beginning of the previous intermediate kalpa (avāntara-kalpa).

He explains the Sūtra—beginning with the words "of the agent" (*kartuḥ*) and so forth—by first restating the contents of the preceding treatise. Having raised the objection that the eternity of the Veda, though established in the previous treatise, is not established in the case of the creation of individual beings such as gods because the words denoting them are also created, [the author] refutes its conventional nature by stating that the birth of individuals arises from words denoting eternal forms; thus, the Veda persists even through the state of the intermediate dissolution (*avāntara-pralaya*).
The meaning is that he confirms this through the inference: "Because He is the cause of the world, He is God.

The meaning of the mantra is as follows: having attained the fitness for obtaining *vāk*—the Veda—through sacrifice (*yajña*) or prior merit (*pūrvasukṛta*), the performers of sacrifice obtained it as it resided within the sages; thus, it is "obtained" (*anuvinnā*).
Previously, at the beginning of an intermediate kalpa. //29//
And because names and forms are the same, there is no contradiction even in the case of recurrence, as is seen from scripture and from tradition. (BS 1.3.30)
Furthermore, it might be argued:

if the individual instances of gods and so forth were to arise and cease only in a continuous stream, just like the individual instances of cattle and so forth, then— due to the non-interruption of the linguistic usage consisting of the signifier, the signified, and the speaker— the contradiction regarding the word would be resolved by means of the permanence of the relationship.
But when the scriptural and traditional texts declare that the entire triple world, having abandoned name and form, dissolves without stain and emerges anew, how can there be no contradiction?
To this it is replied: "Because names and forms are the same. Even then, one must admit the beginninglessness of saṃsāra.
And the Teacher will establish the beginninglessness of saṃsāra in the passage: "It is both logically possible and observed" (Brahma Sūtra 2.1.36).

In a beginningless saṃsāra, just as there is no contradiction in the worldly activity following a waking state—even though the hearing of its origination and dissolution occurs just as in the case of sleep and waking—so too it should be understood regarding the origination and dissolution of different kalpas.

Furthermore, the dissolution and origination [of the senses] are heard in connection with sleep and waking: "When a man is asleep and sees no dream whatsoever, then he becomes one with this vital breath (*prāṇa*) alone; then speech merges into him along with all names, the eye merges into him along with all forms, the ear merges into him along with all sounds, and the mind merges into him along with all thoughts. When he awakes..."

"Just as from a blazing fire sparks fly out in all directions, even so from this Self all the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) go forth according to their respective natures; from the vital breaths the gods, and from the gods the worlds" (Kauṣītaki Upaniṣad 3.3).
This might be so.

During ordinary sleep, there is no contradiction because the worldly transactions of other persons continue uninterrupted, and because one who has awakened from sleep is capable of reconnecting with the transactions of his previous waking state.

However, in the case of the great dissolution (*mahāpralaya*), there is a disparity because all worldly transactions are destroyed, and it is impossible to reconnect with the transactions of another eon, just as it is impossible to reconnect with the transactions of a different lifetime.
This is not a valid objection.

Even though the great dissolution (*mahāpralaya*), which brings all worldly transactions to an end, does occur, it is possible for lords such as Hiraṇyagarbha and others to reconnect with the transactions of a previous *kalpa* through the grace of the Supreme Lord.
Although ordinary living beings are not seen to reconnect with the transactions of another birth,
nevertheless, the lords must not be regarded as being like ordinary beings.

For instance, although there is no difference in their status as living beings, it is observed that among those ranging from humans down to plants, the obstruction of knowledge, power, and so forth, becomes increasingly greater at each successive stage;

likewise, among those ranging from humans up to Hiranyagarbha, the manifestation of knowledge, power, and so forth, also becomes increasingly greater at each successive stage— a fact repeatedly heard in the declarations of Śruti and Smṛti, which cannot be denied.

Consequently, for the lords such as Hiraṇyagarbha and others—who have performed preeminent knowledge and action throughout past kalpas, who appear at the beginning of the current kalpa, and who are graced by the Supreme Lord—the continuity of worldly activity across different kalpas is established, being like one waking from sleep.
Thus says the Śruti: "He who ordains Brahmā in the beginning, and who indeed imparts the Vedas to him..."
"One who desires liberation should indeed seek refuge in that God, who is the light of self-knowledge" (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 6.18).
And Śaunaka and others record: "They were seen by the seers beginning with Madhucchandas.
In each Veda, the seers of the sections (*kāṇḍarṣi*) and so forth are likewise recorded in this manner.

The Śruti also demonstrates that performance by means of a mantra must be preceded by knowledge of the seer (*ṛṣi*): "He who, indeed, sacrifices or teaches with a mantra whose *ṛṣi*, metre (*chandas*), deity (*daivata*), and explanatory passage (*brāhmaṇa*) are unknown, either strikes against a stump or falls into a pit" (Sarvānukramaṇī-pariśiṣṭa).
Having begun thus, it concludes: "Therefore, one should know these [four] for every mantra."
Dharma is prescribed for the attainment of happiness by living beings,
and adharma is prohibited for the avoidance of suffering.

Since attachment and aversion arise toward objects of visible and traditionally heard happiness and suffering, and not toward objects of a different nature, the subsequent creation— which is the fruit of dharma and adharma— when being produced, is necessarily similar to the previous creation.
It is accomplished; and there arises this recollection: "Whatever actions those beings performed in a previous creation, those very same actions they undertake again and again as they are created."

Violent and non-violent, gentle and cruel, righteous and unrighteous, truthful and false—impregnated by these very qualities, beings enter [into new births]; therefore, each finds pleasure in that which accords with its own nature.
Thus,
even as this world dissolves, it dissolves entirely along with its powers;
and it arises only with its powers as its root.
Otherwise, there would be the consequence of their being causeless;
nor is it possible to postulate multiple forms of causal potencies.
Consequently, regarding the streams of worlds such as the earth, which arise intermittently, [there must be a single, uniform cause].
Furthermore, the necessity of the streams of living beings characterized as gods, animals, and humans,

as well as the fixed arrangement of the fruits of the duties of the castes and stages of life within beginningless saṃsāra, should be understood to be as necessary as the necessity of the connection between the sense organs and their objects.

Indeed, it is impossible to imagine that this worldly convention— beginning with the connection between the sense organs and their objects— could be otherwise at each dissolution, as if there were a sixth sense organ and its corresponding object.

And for this reason, because all world-ages (*kalpa*) possess identical linguistic conventions and because the Lords (*īśvara*) are capable of reconnecting with the conventions of previous ages, the particularities (*viśeṣa*) manifest at each new creation with exactly the same names and forms.

And since they possess identical names and forms, even when the recurrence of the world characterized by great creation and great dissolution is admitted, there is no contradiction whatsoever with the authority of the Word (*śabda-prāmāṇya*) and other means of knowledge.
Scripture and tradition both demonstrate this identity of names and forms: "The Creator fashioned the sun and the moon just as before."
"Both heaven and earth, the intermediate space, and then the sky" (Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 10.190.3).
The meaning is that just as the world, beginning with the sun and the moon, was fashioned in the previous kalpa, so too did the Supreme Lord fashion it in this kalpa.
Likewise: "Agni indeed desired, 'May I be the eater of food among the gods.'"
"He offered this cake on eight potsherds to Agni and the Kṛttikās" (Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa 3.1.4.1).

In this injunction for a sacrifice to the lunar mansions (*nakṣatreṣṭi*), such scriptural passages should be cited here, which demonstrate the identity of name and form between the Agni who performed the offering and the Agni to whom the offering was made.
There is also a Smṛti text: "The names of the sages and the visions found in the Vedas..."
At the end of the night, the Unborn One bestows those very same things upon those who have been born.
Just as the various signs of the seasons appear in their recurring cycle according to the season,
so too do these same phenomena reappear at the beginnings of the Yugas.
Just as those who possessed conceit in the past were equal to those here at present,
so too are the gods equal to the gods of the past, both in their forms and indeed in their names.
Expressions of this kind are to be understood in this way.
[Note: By the word "speaker" (abhidhātṛ), both the teacher and the student are meant;
even so—that is, even when the great dissolution and the great creation are accepted.]
Even though the word "atha" (then) occurs at the beginning of the passage, its meaning is "tadā" (at that time).
Prāṇa is the Supreme Self; therein the individual soul (jīva) becomes one with it. The ellipsis is to be supplied as: "then that jīva goes to this prāṇa. From that [state of] the prāṇa-self...
The term "āyatana" means a ball (golaka).
The word "iti" is connected with the phrase "yadyapi" (even though).
There are scriptural declarations such as, "Hiraṇyagarbha came into being," and so forth.
"Whose knowledge is incomparable," and so forth, are the declarations of the Smṛti.
It discards, causes one to understand, and manifests sensation within his intellect.
The Ṛgveda consists of ten maṇḍalas; because there are exactly ten maṇḍalas, the Ṛks contained therein are called "Dāśatayya."
The *ārṣeya* is the connection with the seers (*ṛṣi*);
the *chandas* is the *gāyatrī* and so forth;
the *daivata* is Agni and so forth.
The application [of these] is for a Brahmin; in whichever mantra these [details] are unknown,
[the result is] a stump— that is, an immobile thing— or a pit, that is, hell.
Among those living beings, they are of that very same kind; the sixth faculty is the mind (manas), according to the traditional teaching: "The faculties have the mind as the sixth."
The plural number is used because of the multiplicity of constellations. [He] offered the oblation to be cooked on eight potsherds to Agni, the deity of Kṛttikā.
In the word "deveṣu" (among the gods), the locative case is used in the sense of a sphere or domain.
"At the end of the night" means at the end of the dissolution;
"the signs of the season" refers to new sprouts and so forth;
"in the cycle" means in the recurrence, like a waterwheel.

"Bhāvas" refers to entities (padārthas). One might object: "But since even the universal (jāti) does not exist at the time of the great dissolution (mahāpralaya), the relationship between word and meaning would be non-eternal. Anticipating this doubt, he says "samāna... [referring to the sūtra]. He states the doubt that is to be refuted by the sūtra with the words "athāpi... [referring to the objection].
In the case of a minor dissolution (*avāntarapralaya*), because individual lineages (*vyaktisantati*) of castes continue to exist, the relationship [between word and meaning] persists;

and since worldly usage (*vyavahāra*) remains uninterrupted, it is known [through tradition]. Thus, there would be no contradiction regarding the authority of the Veda based on its independence (*anapekṣatva*).

However, in the case of a total dissolution (*nirlepalaya*), because the relationship [between word and meaning] is destroyed, some person would have to establish the convention (*saṃketa*) anew upon re-creation; consequently, the Veda would lack authority due to its dependence on human intellect (*puruṣabuddhisāpekṣatva*).
The meaning is that because of the destruction of the substratum, namely the teacher, the impermanence of that which is supported [by him] also follows.
Furthermore, even at the time of the great dissolution (*mahāpralaya*), a dissolution without residue is not established,
because of the doctrine of the pre-existence of the effect (*satkāryavāda*).
And thus, since words, their meanings, and their relationship exist in the form of latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) and are merely manifested during a new creation, they are not non-eternal.
Because those manifested names and forms are identical to those of the previous cycle (*kalpa*), no convention (*saṃketa*) need be established by anyone.

He refutes [the objection] with the passage beginning "In that regard, this... [stating] that there is a dependence on convention only in the case of a dissimilar creation, not in the case of a similar creation.

[Objection: Surely, at the first creation, the convention must be established by someone; to this he says, "Even then" (*tadāpi*). The meaning is: even when the great cycle of creation and dissolution has commenced.

[Objection: Granted that the relationship is beginningless in this beginningless *saṃsāra*, nevertheless, since there is a lapse caused by the great dissolution (*mahāpralaya*), how can there be the practical usage of the Vedic meaning in the absence of memory?
Regarding this, he says: "And even though [the world] is beginningless.
There is no contradiction whatsoever;
the ellipsis to be supplied is "of the recollection of the relationship between words and their meanings," and so forth.
Anticipating the objection that dissolution and creation are not established during sleep and waking, he cites the scripture beginning with "svāpa" (sleep).
