Now, at that time in deep sleep, the individual soul (*jīva*) becomes one with the vital breath (*prāṇa*), which is the Supreme Self (*paramātman*); the ellipsis is "he goes to this breath. [He comes] from this Self.
The sense-base (*āyatana*) is the sphere (*golaka*).
The ablative case should be understood in the sense of immediate succession (*ānantarya*), as in "from the fifth" and so forth.

Since there is no existence of sentient beings for that which is imagined like a dream unless it is known, the view that seeing is creation and non-seeing is dissolution—this is the doctrine of "creation upon seeing" (*dṛṣṭisṛṣṭivāda*), which is the intended meaning of the Śruti. This is the sense.
Anticipating the objection that the illustrative example is dissimilar, he refutes it with the words beginning "it might be" (*syāt*).
The phrase "the non-contradictory [connection] such as recollection" (*aviruddham anusandhānādikam*) is the ellipsis to be supplied.
[The point is that] Hiraṇyagarbha and others were devoid of any recollection of a previous kalpa.
Anticipating the objection that [the Lord] is subject to transmigratory existence because He is like ourselves and others, he says: "Even though... (yadyapi).
The construction is: "even though this is so, nevertheless [He is] not like an ordinary being" (na prākṛtavat).

One must also admit that there is excellence (*utkarṣa*) in knowledge and so forth, just as there is inferiority (*nikarṣa*), because there is no sublation (*bādhā*); thus, he says "just as indeed" (*yathā hi*) and so on, [showing] that the inference based on general observation (*sāmānyato dṛṣṭānumāna*) is sublated by scripture and other means supported by logic.
Now, even so, since the Lords of previous kalpas have attained liberation, who would be the one to maintain the continuity (*anusaṃdhātṛ*) in this kalpa? To this, he says "and therefore" (*tataśca*).
The meaning is "due to the excellence of knowledge and so forth.
The intention is that those other than the liberated ones are the synthesizers (anusaṃdhātṛ).
Regarding the superior knowledge of those favored by the Supreme Lord, he cites the previously mentioned scriptural and traditional statements, beginning with "And thus" (tathā ca).

The meaning is: "I take refuge"—that is, I resort to—that God who, at the beginning of the previous kalpa, creates [the world] and sends forth [the Vedas] to that Brahmā, causing them to manifest in his intellect; that God who is my own self-form, shining forth in the intellect arising from the Great Sayings (mahāvākya), the supreme refuge, the state of fearlessness, whose nature is the highest good (niḥśreyasa).

To inspire confidence that this excellence of knowledge belongs not to a single person alone, but to many seers of the Vedic branches (*śākhā-draṣṭṛ*), he says: "They remember. The *dāśatamyas* are the verses (*ṛc*) belonging to the ten maṇḍalas of the Ṛgveda. He further says: "It is remembered," indicating that the seers of the sections (*kāṇḍa*), hymns (*sūkta*), and mantras in the other Vedas as well are recorded by Baudhāyana and others.

Furthermore, he states "the scripture also" to show that the Vedic revelation, which makes known the necessity of knowing the seers (*ṛṣi*) and other details regarding mantras, demonstrates the extraordinary excellence of knowledge possessed by the seers who perceived those mantras.
*Ārṣeya* means connection with a seer;
*chandas* refers to the meters such as *gāyatrī*.
The meaning is: that mantra in which the deity— such as Agni and so forth— the Brāhmaṇa, and the application (viniyoga) are unknown.
"Sthāṇu" means stationary;
"garta" means hell.

Thus, the sense is that since those superior in knowledge have maintained the practice by recollecting the Veda even when it was interrupted for the duration of a kalpa, the Veda's beginninglessness and its independence (anapekṣatva) are not contradictory.
Now he elaborates upon the identity of name and form [of the new being] with those of its predecessors, stating: "And of living beings.
To the question, "What follows from that?", he replies: "Is seen.

It is logical that the fruit of karma performed out of attachment to the pleasures of sense-objects pertaining to this world and the next—such as cattle and so forth—is a resemblance to those very cattle and other things seen [in this life].
In the case of something dissimilar, there is an absence of desire because of the absence of a cause.
Likewise, the fruit of unwholesome action (*adharma*) produced by hatred toward perceived suffering is only a suffering similar to that which was perceived, not happiness;
for otherwise, faults such as the "loss of what was done" (*kṛtahāni*) would ensue—this is the meaning.
Regarding the object established by reasoning, he states the authority [of scripture]: "And tradition (smṛti).
The subsequent creation is of the same nature as the prior creation, because it is the fruit of karma.
The meaning of the word "and" (ca) is the inference that [the creation] was like the previous creation.
Among those living beings, "those very same" means those belonging to the same species. Showing these, he states the cause for attaining them as "violence" (hiṃsra).
In the case of an action, by way of its being prescribed or prohibited, it produces both an *apūrva* (unseen potency) and a mental impression (*saṃskāra*) as an act;
therein, one experiences the fruit from the *apūrva*.
The meaning is that, because it is cultivated by latent dispositions (*saṃskāra*), one subsequently performs actions of that same kind.
He states the inferential mark regarding the latent disposition with the words "therefore":
by the power of the latent disposition alone, either merit or demerit becomes pleasing.
Therefore, from the sign of inclination (*abhiruci*), the formative impressions (*saṃskāra*) of merit and demerit are to be inferred.
That very thing is designated as "intrinsic nature" (*svabhāva*), "primordial matter" (*prakṛti*), or "latent impression" (*vāsanā*).

Having thus explained the similarity of creation through karma, he also states the similarity by virtue of the power of the capacity in the form of the latent impressions of effects dissolved within their own material cause (*upādāna*), beginning with the words "being dissolved" (*pralīyamānam*).
Otherwise, the meaning is that at the dissolution when all residual impressions (*saṃskāra*) have perished, the diversity of the world would be accidental.
Now, one might object: "Let other powers (*śakti*) be postulated as the causes of the world's diversity"; to this, he replies: "And not... (*na ca*).

No potencies other than the *saṃskāra* (latent impression) consisting of the effect merged within ignorance (*avidyā*) should be postulated, because of the absence of evidence and because it would entail excessive complexity (*gaurava*).
However, a potency in the form of an effect merged within its own material cause (*upādāna*) is established by such scriptural texts as "A great banyan tree stands" and "Have faith, my dear.

Therefore, the meaning of the conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that there are no potencies other than ignorance and its effects; rather, ignorance itself, in relation to the Self (*ātman*), is that very potency.

Even regarding the causal signs (*nimitta*), there is no insistence that the effect itself resides within the material cause (*upādāna*) through the operation of ignorance (*avidyā*), or that it is some other power; for the result is the establishment of the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) of the effect within the material cause. He states this result with the words "therefore" (*tataśca*).

Just as for one who has awakened from sleep, an eye of the same class as the previous eye arises, and that [new eye] perceives a form of the same class as the previous form, and not taste or other such objects.

The meaning is that there is a fixed rule: thus, the worlds to be enjoyed, the classes of living beings who are the substrata of enjoyment, and the karmas which are the causes of enjoyment, are exactly like those of the previous worlds due to the power of formative forces (*saṃskāra*).
"Classes" (*nikāya*) means aggregates.
Anticipating the objection that the illustrative example is unestablished, he says: "For not... (*na hi*).
Just as there is no unique object for the sixth sense, the mind— since pleasure and so forth are directly perceivable by the witness-consciousness (sākṣin)—
so too, the meaning is that any alteration in worldly transactional usage is unreal.
The meaning is that the sixth sense-faculty and its object are proximate. He summarizes the stated point with the words "and therefore" (*ataśca*).
The meaning is that, due to the similarity of conventional usage and because of their possible existence, the individual instances (*vyakti*) being conventionally designated are indeed identical.
He connects this with the Sūtra by means of the words "samāna" and so forth.

Looking toward the future, the sacrificer—having desired, "May I become Agni, the eater of food"—offered the oblation to be cooked on eight potsherds to Agni, the deity presiding over the Kṛttikā constellation; this is the meaning.
The plural number is used because of the multiplicity of individual stars within that constellation.

[Objection: "Just as the sacrificer becomes Agni—the future [Agni]—possessing the same name and form as the Agni who is the object of reference, so too in the cases of 'Rudra indeed desired' and 'Viṣṇu indeed desired,' it should be stated in the same way. [Response: That is incorrect.
For Viṣṇu and Rudra do not possess the status of presiding deities (adhikāripuruṣa) in the same way as Agni, because they are heard in scripture to be the causes of the world;
as it is said: "Rudra is indeed one, not two."
Because it would contradict such Vedic and Smṛti texts as "Viṣṇu is one," the locative case in the phrase "in the Vedas" (*vedeṣu*) within that Smṛti is a locative of domain (*viṣaya-saptamī*).
"At the end of the night" means at the end of the dissolution (*pralaya*).
"Signs of the seasons," such as spring and so forth, refer to new sprouts and the like.
"In succession" means in a rotation like that of a water-wheel (*ghaṭīyantra*).
"Entities" (*bhāvāḥ*) refers to things (*padārthāḥ*); the ellipsis is "are equal.

Therefore, since there is no contradiction regarding action or sound even if one accepts the assumption of a physical body (*vigraha*) involving birth and destruction, it is established that the gods possess the qualification for knowledge (*vidyā*). //30//
Jaimini [maintains] that there is no eligibility [for the knowledge of Brahman] for those such as the Madhvas, because of the impossibility [of certain practices]. (BS 1.3.31)
Here, that which was previously asserted—that even gods and others possess the qualification for the knowledge of Brahman—is now being overturned.
The teacher Jaimini considers that gods and others lack such qualification.
Why?
Because of the impossibility [of it] in the Madhu-vidyā and others.

For if one were to admit the qualification for the knowledge of Brahman, then, since there is no difference in their being forms of knowledge (*vidyā*), one would have to admit the qualification for the Madhu-vidyā and others as well;
but this is not possible.
How so? In the passage, "That sun, indeed, is the honey of the gods" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 3.1.1), human beings should approach the sun by meditating upon it as honey.
For if gods and others were admitted to be among the worshippers, what other Āditya could the [central] Āditya worship?

Furthermore, having introduced the five nectars (amṛtas), beginning with the red [color], which depend upon the Āditya, and having taught that the five groups of gods—the Vasus, Rudras, Ādityas, Maruts, and Sādhyas—subsist respectively upon each of those nectars, [the text continues]: "He who thus [knows] this nectar..."

By the passage beginning, "Becoming one of the Vasus alone, with Agni as his mouth, having seen this very nectar, he is satisfied," [the text] shows that those who know the nectars upon which the Vasus and others depend attain the greatness of the Vasus and so forth. But whom else could the Vasus and others know as Vasus and so forth who depend on their nectar?
Or what other greatness, such as that of the Vasus and so forth, would they desire to attain?
Likewise: "Agni is one foot, Vāyu is one foot, Āditya is one foot, the quarters are one foot" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 3.18.2), and "Vāyu indeed is the absorber" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 4.3.1).

In meditations on the self of a deity, such as "The sun is Brahman—this is the instruction" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 3.11.1), it is not possible for those very deities themselves to have the qualification [for such meditation].
Likewise: "These two are indeed Gotama and Bharadvāja; I am Gotama, and this one is Bharadvāja" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.2.4).
In meditations connected with sages such as these, it is not possible for those very sages themselves to have the qualification [to perform them]. // 31 // [FN:

"Five" refers to the five flowers mentioned in the four Vedas—namely, the *praṇava* and the four ritual acts; from these, substances such as soma and clarified butter are offered, resulting in the red, white, and other colors. Red, white, etc.
Black,
supremely black,
as if agitated in its center.

The meaning is as follows: these five nectars, beginning with *rohit*, have been described; they are brought from the solar orb by the solar-ray channels situated in the five directions from east to upward, which correspond to the respective portions of the mantras and consist of apertures present within the honey-bees.
Having been transformed into the nature of fame, splendor, sensory power, vigor, and food, they are meditated upon as being enjoyed by the Vasus and other deities stationed in the five directions;
thus, the attainment of the status of the Vasus and others is stated.
It objects: [the passage] "in the case of the Madhu-vidyā and others" means that the knowledge of Brahman does not qualify the gods and others,
because it is a form of knowledge.
The meaning is: "as in the case of the Madhu-vidyā and other such teachings."
He explains the illustration with the words beginning "How so? and so forth:

one should perform meditation by superimposing the name "honey" upon the sun—because it delights the gods, it is like honey—situated within the honeycomb that is the intermediate space, upon the bamboo staff known as the heavenly world (*dyuloka*).
In that regard, the presiding authority over the sun is not appropriate [for the sacrificer].
He says "among the gods, etc. because of the absence of distinction between the meditator and the object of meditation.

Anticipating the objection that the Vasus and others might have authority there, he says "furthermore," because even they are objects of meditation and goals to be attained, they cannot be the meditators.
The five flowers are the rituals prescribed in the four Vedas and the *praṇava*.
To them, sacrificial materials such as Soma and clarified butter—known as the five nectars (pañcāmṛta), consisting of the red, white, black, dark-beyond-black, and secret [substances]—are offered.

These are brought from the solar orb by means of the solar-ray channels (nāḍīs) situated in the five directions starting from the east and ending above; these channels, which have the form of apertures containing honey and cakes, are brought by the respective portions of mantras and are transformed into the nature of fame, splendor, sensory power, vigor, and food. Thus, they become the sustenance for the Vasus and other deities residing in the five directions.
The meaning is that it has been stated that for one who meditates, there is the attainment of wealth (*vasu*) and so forth.
He explains the meaning of the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) found in the Sūtra with the words "likewise fire" (*tathāgni*).
There are four feet (*pāda*) of the Brahman that is space (*ākāśa*).
Two ears,
two eyes,
and two nostrils.

Regarding the statement "Speech is one," he says that one should perform meditation on the seven seers (*saptarṣi*) within the seven sense organs located at the head and the *camasa* vessels— namely, "these two indeed": the right ear is Gautama,
and the left is Bhāradvāja.
Thus, Viśvāmitra and Vasiṣṭha are in the right eye and nostril; Jamadagni and Kaśyapa are in the left; and Atri is in the voice—this is the meaning.
In this case, because they are themselves objects of meditation for the sages, the sages do not possess the qualification [to perform the rites]. //31//

And for what further reason do gods and others possess the qualification? — START BsCom_1,3.8.32 END 1.3.8.32. And for what further reason do gods and others possess the qualification?
And because of the existence [of the deities] in the luminaries:

that is to say, regarding this circle of light situated in the sky which revolves by day and night and illuminates the world, words denoting deities such as "Āditya" (the Sun) and others are applied to it,
both through worldly convention and through the established usage of scriptural passages (*vākyaśeṣa*).

Furthermore, it is not possible to understand that the sphere of light possesses a body consisting of a heart and other organs, nor that it possesses consciousness, desire, and so forth; for it is understood to be insentient, like a corpse or similar objects.
By this, fire and the others are also explained.
This might be argued:

[The opponent argues: "This fault does not apply, because we understand that gods and others possess embodied forms (vigrahavattva) from the perspective of mantras, arthavādas, itihāsas, purāṇas, and common worldly usage.
[The author replies: No;
for there is no such thing as "worldly usage" (loka) that exists as an independent means of valid cognition (pramāṇa).

For it is said that an object established from means of valid cognition such as perception—without their specific qualifications being analyzed—is established through worldly convention (*lokaprasiddhi*).
However, in this case, none of the means of valid cognition, such as perception, is present.
Even the *Itihāsa* and *Purāṇa*, because they are of human origin, require another source of valid cognition as their basis.

Even the *arthavādas*, being part of a single syntactical unit with an injunction (*vidhi*) and serving the purpose of praise, do not function as independent grounds for establishing the existence of bodies and other attributes of the gods.

Furthermore, the *mantras*—which are employed according to direct Vedic statement (*śruti*) and so forth, and which are integrated into the ritual performance for the purpose of denotation—are said not to be a means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) for any factual matter.
Therefore, there is an absence of qualification (*adhikāra*) for the gods and others [to perform sacrifices]. 32.

Mantras such as "Vajrahastaḥ purandaraḥ" (Indra has the thunderbolt in his hand); explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) such as "He wept" (*sa roroda*); historical narratives and Purāṇas such as "O gods, [I shall give you] the desired enjoyments";
and even in the world, [the representation of] Yama with a staff in his hand.

The meaning is that because the five factors—beginning with *vigraha* (embodiment)—exist in the phrase "they depict Indra, the wielder of the thunderbolt," there is no fault of lack of qualification (*anadhikāradoṣa*).
These five are: embodiment, enjoyment of oblations, sovereignty, and graciousness.
"The fivefold [category] beginning with the body consists of the granting of fruits.
Furthermore, he states "because of their existence as luminaries" (jyotiṣi bhāvāt) to show that gods and others have no eligibility for ritual action anywhere due to the absence of a body.
The meaning is that since words such as Āditya, Sūrya, Candra, Śukra, and Aṅgāraka are used to denote masses of light, there is no god whatsoever who possesses a physical body.
In the supplementary passage of the Madhu-vidyā, "The sun rises in the east and sets in the west," the word *āditya* is well-known to refer specifically to light.
If that were so, let there be eligibility for the spheres of light alone;
to this, he replies: "And not... (na ca).
Anticipating the objection regarding the eligibility (*adhikāra*) of fire and the other [elements], he says: "By this" (*etena*).
The meaning is: because words such as "fire," "wind," and "earth" denote insentient things.
The proponent of the established view (*siddhāntin*) raises an objection with the words: "This might be so," and so forth.

Mantras such as "Vajrahastaḥ purandaraḥ" (The wielder of the thunderbolt is Purandara) and so forth; explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) such as "He wept" (*sa arodīt*) and so forth; and [the statement]: "For the gods, nourished by sacrifice, will grant you the desired enjoyments."
"Being satisfied themselves, they satisfy him with the auspicious fruits of all his desires"—
such are the Itihāsas and Purāṇas.
Furthermore, even in the world, people depict Yama with a staff in his hand.

The meaning is that because the fivefold set beginning with *vigraha* (embodiment) exists in the mantra "Indra, whose hand holds the thunderbolt," there is no defect regarding lack of qualification (*anadhikāra*).
This fivefold set beginning with *vigraha* consists of: embodiment, the enjoyment of oblations, sovereignty, graciousness, and the bestowing of fruits.
He refutes this by stating "no," etc., on the grounds that there is a lack of evidence:
"And not here" means "not in the case of the analysis [of the compound] and so forth."
Anticipating the objection that explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) or mantras might be the basis [for the existence of deities], he says "explanatory passages," and so forth.

The meaning is that the Mīmāṃsakas declare that mantras, being grasped by the injunctions of performance (*prayoga-vidhi*) like rice and other such materials, serve the purpose of denoting things connected with the performance; they do not aim at [establishing] the body (*vigraha*) and so forth which are unknown [from other sources].
Therefore, the meaning is "because of the absence of a body" (verse 32).
But Bādarāyaṇa maintains that there is [the presence of the fires], for it is so stated.
The word "but" (tu) sets aside the prima facie view.
The teacher Bādarāyaṇa, however, maintains that there is eligibility for gods and others as well.

Although there may be an impossibility of eligibility in the Madhu-vidyā and other such meditations which involve a mixture of deities and so forth, nevertheless, there is indeed the possibility of it in the pure knowledge of Brahman.
Since eligibility depends upon factors such as the desire for the result, the capacity, and the absence of prohibitions,
the mere fact that [eligibility] is impossible in some cases does not mean that eligibility should be set aside even where it is possible.
Even among humans, it is not the case that all Brahmins and others are eligible for all rites such as the Rājasūya.

The same principle that applies there will apply here as well. With reference to the knowledge of Brahman (*brahmavidyā*), there is a scriptural vision (*darśana*) indicating the qualification of gods and others [for such knowledge]: "Among the gods, whoever realized That, he alone became That; likewise among the seers (*ṛṣis*), and likewise among human beings" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.4.10).
"They said: 'Come, let us search for that Self, by searching for which one obtains all worlds and all desires.
And so on, beginning with: "Indra, indeed, went forth from among the gods, and Virocana from among the Asuras" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.7.2).
There is also the Smṛti, such as the dialogue between the Gandharva and Yājñavalkya.

As for what was also stated, "because [the word] exists in reference to light," we reply: even those words denoting deities such as Āditya, which have light and so forth as their objective referents, designate that respective divine self who is endowed with consciousness and sovereign power, because they are treated as such in the mantras, arthavādas, and other texts.
For indeed, by virtue of their sovereign power (*aiśvarya*), the deities possess the capacity to abide as they wish in forms consisting of light and so forth, and to assume various bodies at will.
Thus it is heard in the *Subrahmaṇyā* explanatory passage:
"Medhātithi’s ram"—namely, "Indra, having become a ram, carried off Medhātithi, the descendant of Kaṇva" (*Ṣaḍviṃśa-brāhmaṇa* 1.1).
And it is recorded in scripture: "The Sun, having become a person, approached Kuntī.
Furthermore, even in the case of clay and other such materials, conscious presiding agents are admitted, as seen in such passages as "the clay spoke" and "the waters spoke.
However, regarding the elemental constituents such as light, their lack of consciousness is admitted in the case of the sun and so forth.

It has been stated that volitions (*cetanā*) are presiding agents because of the conventional usage of mantras, explanatory passages (*arthavāda*), and so forth, which refer to deities as having a self.
Furthermore, regarding the claim that mantras and explanatory passages lack the capacity to reveal the form and other attributes of a deity because their purpose is not literal—here we reply:
for the presence or absence of conviction is indeed the cause for the existence or non-existence [of a thing].
There is neither the state of being for another purpose nor the state of not being for another purpose.
For instance, even one who has set out for another purpose perceives that grass, leaves, and so forth, which have fallen on the path, simply exist. To this, he replies: "The analogy is unequal."
For in that case (the injunction), there exists a perception directed toward objects such as grass and leaves by which their existence is apprehended;

however, here, because it forms a single syntactical unit with the statement of the injunction for the purpose of praise, it is impossible to determine through an *arthavāda*—whether as a separate entity or otherwise—a cognitive operation directed toward a historical fact (*vṛttānta*). Indeed, in a sentence containing a negative particle such as "One shall not drink liquor," only the prohibition of drinking liquor is understood as the sole meaning due to the connection of the three words.
"Furthermore, because of the connection between the two words 'na' (not) and 'punaḥ surāṃ pibet' (one should not drink liquor), there is also an injunction regarding the drinking of liquor.
To this it is replied: "The comparison is unequal.
It is logical that in the prohibition of drinking liquor, because the syntactical connection of the words is a single unit, no intermediate sentence-meaning is grasped."

However, in the case of the injunction (*vidhi*) and the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*), the words situated within the *arthavāda* first undergo a separate syntactic connection regarding their own specific content; subsequently, by virtue of the requirement for purpose (*kaimarthyavaśena*), they serve to eulogize the injunction as desired.

For instance, in the injunction "One desiring prosperity should sacrifice a white animal to Vāyu" (*vāyavyaṃ śvetamālabheta bhūtikāmaḥ*), the words such as "to Vāyu" (*vāyavya*) occurring in the injunctive statement are connected with the injunction itself;
but this is not the case for these words occurring in the *arthavāda*: "Vāyu is indeed the swiftest deity; he approaches Vāyu with his own share; he [Vāyu] leads him to prosperity."
For it is not the case that [the texts] state, "One should sacrifice to Vāyu," or "One should sacrifice to the swiftest deity," and so forth;
rather, by proclaiming the nature of Vāyu, they establish an intermediate connection and thereby praise the injunction, [showing] that "this ritual has such a specific deity.

Thus, where that intermediate sentence-meaning falls within the scope of another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), there the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) proceeds as a restatement (*anuvāda*) of it.
Where there is a contradiction with another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), there [the statement] is a figurative description (*guṇavāda*).

But where neither of those two [contradiction or lack of contradiction] exists, should it be a figurative description due to the absence of another means of valid cognition, or rather a description of what actually exists due to the non-contradiction with another means of valid cognition? Those who rely on direct perception (*pratīti*) as their refuge must adopt the description of what actually exists, not the figurative description.
By this, the mantra has been explained.
Furthermore, the specific forms of Indra and the other deities are required by the injunctions themselves which enjoin the oblations dedicated to Indra and the rest;
for Indra and the others cannot be brought to mind if they are devoid of a specific form.
Furthermore, it is not possible to offer an oblation to a particular deity unless that deity has ascended into the mind;
for the scripture declares: "One should meditate upon whichever deity the oblation is taken for, as one is about to utter the vaṣaṭ-call" (Ai. Brā. 3.8.1).
Moreover, it is not possible for the mere word to be the actual nature of the object.
Because of the difference between word and object,
that nature of Indra and others which is understood from mantras and arthavādas cannot properly be rejected by one who relies on verbal testimony as a means of knowledge (*śabdapramāṇaka*).

Furthermore, since the Itihāsas and Purāṇas— being possible according to the path already explained— are rooted in mantras and arthavādas, they are capable of establishing the embodied form (*vigraha*) and other attributes of the deities.
It is also possible for [the Veda] to have perception and other means of knowledge as its basis.
For indeed, what was not perceived by us may have been perceived by those of old;
likewise, it is recorded in tradition that Vyāsa and others engaged in direct perception with gods and other beings.
But he who should say that, just as for people of the present day, there was no capacity among those of the past to interact with gods and other beings, would be denying the diversity of the world;
and he might as well say that, just as now, there has never been at any other time a universal sovereign (sārvabhauma) kṣatriya.
Consequently, he would obstruct the injunctions for the Rājasūya and other such sacrifices.
Moreover, he asserts that even at other times, just as now, the duties of the castes and stages of life (*varṇāśramadharma*) were for the most part unsettled;
consequently, the scripture (*śāstra*) which establishes those regulations would be rendered useless.
Therefore, it follows that by virtue of their excellence in merit (*dharmotkarṣa*), the ancients interacted with gods and others through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
Moreover, they remember: "From the study [of sacred texts], there is communion with the chosen deity" (Yogasūtra 2.44), and so forth.
Yoga, which is recorded as having the attainment of powers such as *aṇimā* as its fruit, cannot be rejected on the basis of mere audacity.
Furthermore, scripture proclaims the greatness of yoga: "When the fivefold quality of yoga has arisen—consisting of earth, water, fire, air, and space—and has come into operation..."
"For him there is no disease, no old age, and no death, having attained a body composed of the fire of yoga" (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 2.12).
It is not appropriate to compare the power of even the sages—who were seers of the Mantras and Brāhmaṇas—with our own power.
Therefore, the Itihāsas and Purāṇas are rooted in reality.
Even worldly renown cannot be determined to be without a basis when such a basis is possible.
Therefore, it is logically established that from mantras and other sources there arises the understanding that gods and others possess embodied forms and so forth.
Consequently, since the presence of desire for liberation and other necessary qualifications is possible, the eligibility of gods and others for the knowledge of Brahman is also established.
The views regarding gradual liberation (*kramamukti*) are likewise established in this very way. (33) [Note:
Since it is not possible for everyone to have the qualification for everything everywhere, it follows that [the teaching] is not to be set aside.
That Brahman which one realizes as the inner self (*pratyak*) among the gods...

By the inclusion of the word "etcetera" (ādi), the Itihāsas, Purāṇas, and Dharmaśāstras are understood. A "statement of injunction" (vidhyuddeśa) is an injunctive sentence; by virtue of being syntactically connected with it, the "narrative" (vṛttānta) is the account of past events.
"It is embraced" means it is joined.
The meaning of the sūtra is that through the recitation of mantras, there is the presence of the deity and conversation with them.
With the words beginning "the word 'tu' (but)," he refutes the prima facie position established by the two preceding sūtras.

The argument that "the knowledge of Brahman (brahmavidyā) does not qualify the gods and others because it is a form of knowledge, like the Madhu-vidyā and other such knowledges," is rendered ineffective by the reason stated; thus he says, "Even though... (yadyapi).
The New Moon sacrifice and other such rites do not qualify a Brāhmaṇa as their subject,
because they are ritual acts.
The phrase "like the Rājasūya and other [sacrifices]" expresses a similarity in appearance regarding the reason for its being a *vidyā*; this is indicated by the words "and not" (*na ca*).
The meaning is that the logical principle—that whoever has the eligibility (*adhikāra*) for something is the one entitled to it there—is the same [in both cases].
Since it is not possible for everyone to have eligibility for everything, therefore it cannot be set aside; such is the syntactical connection (*anvaya*).
The meaning is that whichever among the gods and others realized that Brahman as their own inner self (pratyak), he became that Brahman.

Furthermore, there is an indicative mark (liṅga) in the fact that those gods spoke to one another, and subsequently Indra and Virocana—the kings of the gods and the asuras—approached Prajāpati, the bestower of the knowledge of Brahman. This is the sense.

Regarding the question of the Gandharva, "What is this immortal Brahman here?", Yājñavalkya replied, "Him. He states that this is a sign of the eligibility of the gods and others for the *mokṣa-dharma*s, saying "Smārta" (found in the Smṛtis).
Just as, although the term "eye" and so forth is applied to the physical globes in children, those learned in the scriptures accept sense organs distinct from the globes;
and just as, although words like "Sūrya" are applied to light and the like, one must accept deities possessing embodied forms—he says "Jyotirādi" (light and so forth).
The meaning is that it is because it is treated as being conscious in that way.
To the question, "How can a single entity possess both the nature of the insentient and the sentient?", he says: "For there exists... and so forth.
For instance, the conventional usage of "deity" (deva) is heard in connection with having a physical form;
for example, the *arthavāda* related to the *subrahmaṇya*, who is a priest belonging to the group of *udgātṛs*: "O Indra, come! and so forth.
In that context, the address "O Medhātithi’s ram" (*medhātithermeṣa*) is heard as a vocative for Indra; he explains it as "meva."
The meaning is that "Meṣa" is an address to Indra for the purpose of making known that he carried off the Sage after having become a ram;
as for what was said— that the Ādityas and others are indeed insentient like clay and so forth— [that is not the case].
That is not so;
because in every case there exists a dual aspect consisting of the insentient and the sentient, he says "clay" (mṛd).
One might ask: in the sun and other such things, what is the insentient portion and what is the conscious portion?
Regarding this, he says: "But as for 'jyotirādi' (the passages beginning with 'light'), etc.

Mantras and the like are not authoritative with respect to their own literal meaning—the physical form and so forth that appear through the power of the words—because they are intended for another purpose.

He says "even as the statement 'Eat poison'" (yadapi) to indicate that it is like such a sentence. He says "here we reply" (atra brūmaḥ) to show that even from a sentence whose primary intent lies elsewhere, its own literal meaning is to be accepted provided there is no contradiction. He provides an illustration of existence based on mere cognition even regarding an object devoid of intended significance, saying "for instance" (tathā hi).

He raises the objection regarding the disparity—that there is a suffix in the case of "grass" (*tṛṇa*) and so forth, but it is absent in the case of "refutation" (*vigraha*) and so forth—by saying "here he says":
the "enunciation of an injunction" (*vidhyuddeśa*) is the injunctive sentence;
by virtue of being syntactically one with that, the meaning in the explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) is simply that "the injunction is praiseworthy. Thus, the suffix exists [in the sense of praise].

"Vṛttānta" means the actual fact; the meaning is that there is no cognition of its object, such as the analytical compound (vigraha) and so forth. [The opponent objects: "But surely, let there be a cognition of the analytical compound and so forth by means of an intermediate sentence. To this, he says: "Not so" (na hi).
The sense is that there might even be a basis for drinking liquor.

He says, "To this it is replied," because this is not so due to the difference between syntactic unity at the level of a word (*padaikavākyatva*) and syntactic unity at the level of a sentence (*vākyaikavākyatva*).

When the single word *nañ* (the negative particle) connects with the two words "one should drink liquor" (*surāṃ pibet*), then that single unit of syntactic unity at the level of a word produces a single experience of meaning; it does not, however, cause the two words to separately signify the drinking of liquor.

Since a negation is untenable within the context of an injunction (*vidhi*), it cannot serve as a mediating factor for the experience of the sentence-meaning. However, an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) attains syntactic unity with the injunction by making known a connection between existing facts as a means to praise; thus, there is indeed an experience of the analysis (*vigraha*) and so forth—this is the meaning. Now, one might object: "Let the words occurring in the *arthavāda* be directly connected to the injunction, rather than first producing an intermediate understanding of their mutual relation. To this, he says: "For just as... and so on.
He demonstrates the impossibility of direct logical connection with the words "for not" (*na hi*).
Fearing that one might everywhere assume the primary meaning [of a statement] from an *arthavāda*, he analyzes the *arthavādas* with the words "in that case" (*tadyatra*).
This means: "in those *arthavādas* where," such as "Fire is the remedy for cold," and so forth.

The meaning is as follows: since the non-difference [of the post] from the sun in the statement "The sacrificial post is the sun" is contradicted by perception, this is a figurative eulogy (guṇavāda) based on qualities such as brilliance;
whereas in cases such as "Vajrahasta Purandara," where there is neither corroboration nor contradiction by other means of knowledge, it is a statement of an existing fact (bhūtārthavāda).
The word "iti vimṛśya" (having thus reflected) is to be supplied [as the context].

The statement that "a sentence expressing a description of a conflict (vigrahārtavāda) possesses a purport even toward its own literal meaning" is established by the logic: "because, while being subordinate to another [meaning], it is a word whose meaning is unknown and unsublated," like the sentences concerning the *prayāja* offerings. By the phrase "by this [same reasoning]," he extends this principle to the mantras.
The words in the reason (*hetu*) are intended to exclude those [mantras] which are restatements (*anuvāda*) of the Vedānta or which are figurative descriptions (*guṇavāda*).

Furthermore, there is no syntactical split (*vākyabheda*) even when [the text] has both as its purport, because the intermediate meaning is subsumed within the meaning of the great sentence (*mahāvākyārtha*); this is the intended sense.
He states "Moreover" (*api ca*) to show that the corporeal form of the deity must be accepted, just like heaven, on the grounds that [otherwise] the injunction would be untenable.

Now, one might object: since an injunction regarding an action consisting of affliction (kleśa) is untenable without a fruit, let it be that heaven—established by the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) "that which is not mixed with suffering"—is the object of the injunction as its authoritative means of knowledge.
But what is the inconsistency of the injunction without a [deity's] body?
To this, he says: "For not... (na hi).

He states the scriptural authority (*śruti*) as well for the position that mental representation (*cetasyāroha*) must be accepted because the act of relinquishment (*tyāga*) is impossible [without it], using the words "of whom" (*yasyā*).
Therefore, for the sake of mental representation, a physical form (*vigraha*) must be postulated.

Furthermore, because it is recited within the context of ritual action (*karmaprakaraṇa*), the cognition of a physical form must be accepted as a subsidiary element (*aṅga*) of the rite, just like the *prayāja* offerings.
Without that [divine form], the unseen potency (*apūrva*) of ritual action cannot be established.
Furthermore, he states "nor [is it] sound" (*na ca śabda...*) to show that devotion to sound alone as the deity—abandoning the deity who possesses a perfectly serene form—is improper.
Nor should it be argued: "Let the mere generic form (*ākṛti*) be the denotation of the word; what is the need for a physical form?"

Because [the word] is not connected with either an individual (vyakti) or a form (ākṛti), he says "therein" (*tatra*), meaning that since the word requires an object, one must accept a physical form whose nature is known through mantras and other means of valid cognition.

Likewise, he says "itihāsa," etc., meaning that even sources such as history (*itihāsa*) and so forth, which are rooted in mantras and explanatory passages (*arthavāda*), serve as authority for the physical form.
The meaning is that it exists as a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).
He states "perception" (*pratyakṣa*) to show that even the direct perception of deities and so forth by yogins such as Vyāsa is the source for the *itihāsas* and other texts;
[however,] Vyāsa and others were devoid of direct perception of deities and the like.
He refutes the inference—"because of being a living being, like us"—by means of an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*), beginning with the words "But he who... [and so forth].
[According to that logic], everything would be non-different from a jar.
Because it is a real entity, like a jar; thus he might even say that the diversity of the world does not exist.

Likewise, he would assert the non-existence of the kṣatriya caste, the non-existence of the system of castes and stages of life (varṇāśrama), and the lack of order regarding the castes and stages of life.
Because of the unrestrained nature of the intellect,

the meaning is that there is a sublation of the scriptural injunctions regarding the Rājasūya sacrifice and other rites, as well as the scriptural injunctions concerning the established order of duties for the Kṛta and other ages.
Furthermore, he states "apica" (moreover) to show that the direct perception by gods and others is established even from the meaning of the Yoga Sūtras.
The meaning of the aphorism is that through the recitation of mantras, there is the presence of the deity and conversation with them.

Since the greatness of yoga is established by the Śruti and Smṛti, he states "yoga" [in the next sūtra] to show that for yogis, there is direct perception of gods and other beings. [He describes the stages:

from the soles of the feet up to the knees, from the knees up to the navel, from the navel up to the neck, from the neck up to the growth of the hair, and from there to the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra).

The meaning is that when the pentad beginning with earth has arisen and been conquered through *dhāraṇā*, and when the yogic powers such as *aṇimā* have begun to function, the yogin who has attained a body composed of light manifested by yoga is not touched by disease and the like.
He states "in the world" (*loke*) to show that even common renown among painters and others serves as proof for the existence of such a form.
He concludes the subject matter with the words "Therefore" (*tasmāt*).
He states the fruit of this inquiry with the words "Successive" (*krama*):

only when gods and others possess the qualification for the knowledge of Brahman (*brahmavidyā*) are meditations that have the fruit of successive liberation (*kramamukti*) through the attainment of divinity logically possible.

The meaning is that if the gods lacked the qualification [for knowledge], they would have no inclination toward meditations for the sake of gradual liberation due to the absence of knowledge; therefore, the accomplishment of their engagement [in such practices] follows from the determination of their qualification. //33//

Section on the Exclusion of Śūdras (Apaśūdrādhikaraṇa) / Sūtras 34–38 Sūtra 34: "On account of the absence of qualification. Sūtra 35: "And because of the prohibition. Sūtra 36: "And because of the mention of the Smṛti. Sūtra 37: "If it be argued that there is no contradiction because of the existence of the power [to understand], we say no, on account of the absence of the capacity for comprehension. Sūtra 38: "And because of the reference to the three castes. [The commentary explains: It has been stated that the study of the Veda and the performance of rituals are intended for those who possess the qualification for them. Now, a doubt arises as to whether this applies equally to all four castes, including the Śūdra, or if it excludes the Śūdra. The prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa) is that since the desire for knowledge is common to all, and since the Śūdra possesses the capacity for understanding, the Śūdra is also qualified for the study of the Veda and the performance of rituals. The established conclusion (siddhānta) is as follows: The Śūdra is not qualified. Why? Because of the absence of qualification. The qualification for Vedic study consists in the possession of the sacred thread (*upanayana*), which is a rite prescribed by the Veda. Since the Śūdra is not entitled to this rite, he lacks the necessary qualification. Furthermore, the Veda itself prohibits the Śūdra from studying: "The Śūdra is the fourth caste, born of the feet; therefore, he is not entitled to the sacrifice" (*Taittirīya Saṃhitā* 7.1.1.6). Moreover, the Smṛtis declare that the Śūdra is excluded from hearing the Veda, reciting it, and performing Vedic rites. If it be argued that the Śūdra might still have the power to comprehend the meaning of the texts, we say no; such comprehension is impossible without prior study, and study is forbidden to him. Finally, the Veda refers to the three higher castes when prescribing rites, thereby excluding the Śūdra. Therefore, the Śūdra is not qualified for the study of the Veda or the performance of its rituals.
For it is indicated by the mention of Śuka’s lack of respect and his subsequent rushing toward [the teacher].

Just as the restriction that the qualification for knowledge belongs only to humans was set aside and the qualification of gods and others for knowledge was stated, so too might there be a qualification for a Śūdra by setting aside the restriction that the qualification belongs only to the twice-born; it is to dispel this doubt that this section (adhikaraṇa) is commenced.

In that regard, it might first appear that even a Śūdra possesses the qualification [for Vedic study], because both the desire for knowledge and the capacity for it are possible in his case. [However, this is not so,] as it is said: "Therefore, the Śūdra is not entitled to sacrifice" (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 8.1.1.6).
This is because, as in that [previous] case, there is no hearing of a prohibition such as "a Śūdra is not qualified for knowledge.

Furthermore, the fact that a Śūdra lacks the sacred fires (anagnitva)—which is the reason for his lack of qualification for ritual acts—is not an indicative mark (liṅga) that precludes his qualification for knowledge;
for knowledge cannot be realized by one who is devoid of the Āhavanīya and other sacrificial fires.
Furthermore, there exists an indicative mark that supports the eligibility of Śūdras.

For in the Saṃvarga-vidyā, the text refers to Jānaśruti Pautrāyaṇa, who was desirous of hearing, by the word "Śūdra": "O Śūdra, let this chariot with its horses and cows remain yours alone" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 4.2.3).
Moreover, Vidura and others, though born from a Śūdra womb, are recorded in tradition as being endowed with distinguished knowledge.
"Therefore, a Śūdra is entitled to the [acquisition of] knowledge.
This being the position reached, we reply: there is no entitlement for a Śūdra, because of the absence of Vedic study.
For it is one who has studied the Veda and understood the meaning of the Veda who is authorized in matters concerning the Veda;
yet there is no study of the Veda for a Śūdra,
since the study of the Veda is preceded by the initiation ceremony (upanayana).
Furthermore, since the initiation ceremony (*upanayana*) pertains only to the three [upper] castes,
mere desire for it does not constitute a cause for entitlement when there is a lack of capability.
Nor is worldly capability alone the cause for entitlement.
Because in a scriptural matter, scriptural capacity is required;
and because scriptural capacity has been refuted by the refutation of [the Śūdra’s] Vedic study.
Furthermore, this statement, "A Śūdra is not entitled to sacrifice," indicates that he is likewise not entitled to knowledge, since it is based on that same principle.
Because the principle [of qualification] is common [to all].
As for the fact that you consider the hearing of the word "Śūdra" in the Saṃvarga-vidyā to be an indicative mark (liṅga), that is not an indicative mark, because it lacks logical necessity.
For in the case of what is stated by logical reasoning (*nyāya*), the observation of an indicative mark (*liṅga*) serves as a manifestor;
however, no such reasoning exists here.
Furthermore, even if this word "Śūdra" were to authorize a Śūdra for that one specific Saṃvarga-vidyā alone, [it would not apply elsewhere].
Because it has that [specific] as its object,
it does not apply to all forms of knowledge;
furthermore, being situated within an explanatory passage (arthavāda), it is not capable of authorizing a Śūdra in any instance whatsoever.
Moreover, this word "śūdra" can be applied to one who is eligible [for instruction].

How so? It is said: from this speech of the swan, "How can you speak of him as if he were Raikva with the cart? (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 4.1.3), grief arose in Jānaśruti Pautrāyaṇa upon hearing of his own lack of respect.
It is understood that the seer Raikva indicated her by this word "śūdra" in order to demonstrate his own possession of indirect knowledge (parokṣajñatā),
since a śūdra by birth has no entitlement [to such knowledge].
But how, again, is the grief that has arisen indicated by the word "śūdra"?
It is said: because of rushing toward that;
he rushed toward grief, or he was rushed toward by grief.

"Or perhaps it was out of grief that he ran up to Raikva; thus [Raikva] said, 'Śūdra'—because the etymological meaning of the parts of the word is possible here, whereas its conventional meaning is not;
and this very meaning is seen in this narrative. (34)

FN: *Anavakḷptaḥ* means incapable; therefore, because of his lack of fire (*anagnitvāt*). *Aha* is a particle expressing dejection. *Hāretvā* refers to a chariot that comes by means of a necklace (*hāra*) or a gold coin (*niṣka*); *saha gobhiḥ* means together with cows; O Śūdra!
The sense is: "Let this [sacrifice] be yours alone; what is the use of this small thing which is of no utility for my state of householdership?
The word "yajña" (sacrifice) is an elliptical expression for "unqualified for knowledge. As in the injunction, "One should cause the Niṣāda-sthapati to sacrifice," the Niṣāda-sthapati is enjoined.
The Śūdra [is mentioned] in the Saṃvarga-vidyā. The word division is *kaṃ u are*.
The particle *u* has the sense of "also" (*api*).
"You have spoken these words like Raikva standing together with his yoked cart (*yugvā*), his vehicle (*gantrī*), and his wagon (*śakaṭī*).
For his distress (*śuc*) is indeed indicated [by this].
With the word "just as" (*yathā*), he states the connection of this example with the preceding one.

In the preceding section, by demonstrating the application (*samanvaya*) of mantras and other texts to the actual nature (*bhūtārtha*)—such as the embodied form (*vigraha*)—of the gods and others for the sake of establishing their eligibility (*adhikāra*), the application of the Vedāntas to Brahman as the actual reality was likewise reinforced.

Here too, by demonstrating the application of the Vedic term *śūdra* to a Kṣatriya, that [application] is further strengthened; thus, it should be understood that these two incidental sections are included within this chapter on *samanvaya*.

The result is that in the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa), even a Śūdra would be entitled to engage in hearing the Vedānta just like the twice-born, whereas in the final conclusion (siddhānta), such entitlement does not exist.
In this context, the subject matter is the inquiry into Vedānta;

regarding the doubt as to whether it qualifies a Śūdra or not—arising from the possibilities of its feasibility or infeasibility—the prima facie (pūrvapakṣa) position is stated with the words "In that regard, even for a Śūdra," and so forth: "Therefore, due to the absence of sacred fires and the lack of Vedic study, he is incapable."
He states that the Śūdra has the right [to study] even on the basis of the indicative mark (*liṅga*) consisting in the use of the word "Śūdra" for one seeking knowledge, saying: "And it occurs...
It is said that Jānaśruti, having offered six hundred cows and a chariot to his teacher Raikva, said, "Teach me.
Thereupon, Raikva, being destitute and desiring a bride, spoke as follows.
The particle *aha* expresses weariness.
A chariot that goes—meaning one that travels—yoked with a *hāra* (necklace) and a *niṣka* (gold ornament) is called a *hāretvā*. O Śūdra, let that [chariot] be yours along with the cows;
the sense is: "What is the use of this small amount which is of no utility for my household life? This is the intended meaning.

He states "therefore" (*tasmāt*) based on a logical mark (*liṅga*) supported by reasoning: that when the desire for an object and other conditions are present, engagement in the means to achieve the highest good is appropriate because it is natural.
He establishes his own conclusion (*siddhānta*) outside the sūtra itself with the words "there is no qualification for a Śūdra," and so forth.
The meaning is: "of one by whom the meaning of the Veda has been understood at first sight."

The meaning is that the Śūdra lacks the qualification for the inquiry into Vedānta because he lacks the capacity prescribed by the scriptures for investigating the meaning of the Veda—both the Veda itself as consecrated by the rules of formal study (*adhyayana-vidhi*) and the initial knowledge arising therefrom. Due to the absence of these, the logical grounds for the possibility of his possessing the desire [to know] and so forth are not established. Alternatively, the meaning is that only one by whom the meaning of the Veda has been ascertained through the Veda consecrated by formal study has the qualification for the injunctions regarding the meaning of the Veda, and no other.
For even one who has not studied the Veda would possess the qualification for performing the rites according to the meaning of the Veda, which would result in the futility of the injunction to study;

therefore, the meaning is that the Śūdra lacks qualification for the injunctions of hearing (śravaṇa) and so forth, which are the means for attaining the knowledge of Brahman culminating in its fruit.

This is because the same logic applies: namely, the absence of the capacity obtained through the injunction to study, which consists in possessing the knowledge of the meaning of the Veda already studied.
He states that the word "sacrifice" (yajña) is intended as an indicator for the meaning of the Veda, saying, "because the principle is common.
Therefore, the phrase "therefore a Śūdra" means that the principle referred to by that pronoun is equal in both the knowledge of sacrifice and the knowledge of Brahman.
He refutes the previously mentioned indicative mark with the words, "as for that which..."
The meaning is that the principle regarding the possibility of [the Śūdra] possessing the desire for knowledge and so forth has been refuted by the principle of incapacity (*asāmarthya*).

Now, one might object: "In the case of the injunction, 'One should cause the Niṣāda-sthapati to sacrifice,' even though there is an absence of Vedic study, the Śūdra—by virtue of the word 'Śūdra'—should have the right to knowledge in the same way as the Niṣāda has the right to perform the sacrifice.
Anticipating this doubt, he admits the Śūdra's eligibility for the Saṃvarga-vidyā with the words, "If you wish" (*kāmam*).
The meaning is: "because it has that as its object" and "because it is heard there.
In reality, however, because it occurs within an injunctive sentence, even the word *niṣāda* serves to designate the qualified person (*adhikārin*);
whereas the word *śūdra*, being situated in an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) subordinate to the injunction for knowledge, does not indicate a qualified person.

Thinking that a word intended for another purpose cannot convey its own primary meaning due to the logical principle of incapacity (*asāmarthya*) and contradiction, he abandons his initial position and says "Arthavāda... [to express his acceptance].
Then, raising the doubt as to what the meaning of the word "Śūdra" heard here might be, he states the meaning through the Sūtra with the words beginning "And it is possible," etc.
King Jānaśruti by name slept on the roof of his palace at night during the summer heat.
Then, the sages, gratified by the multitude of his virtues such as the giving of food and other gifts, transformed themselves into swans and approached him in the form of a flight for his benefit;
among them, the last swan said to the lead swan:
"O Bhadrākṣa!"
"Do you not see the splendor of this Jānaśruti, which stands pervading the heavens? It will burn you; do not go!
To him, the leader said:

"O, you speak these words to some wretched man who is devoid of knowledge, as if he were Raikva accompanied by his cart (sayugvān)—that is, one standing with a cart (*yugva*) which is a vehicle (*gantrī*). For the splendor of Raikva, the most eminent knower of Brahman (*brahmiṣṭha*), is insurmountable; it is not so for one like you who does not know the Self. This is the meaning.
The intention of the swans was that the king, distressed by our words, would recognize Raikva by his sign—the cart—and thus become possessed of knowledge.
The word division is "kaṃ u are";
the particle *u* has the sense of "also" (*api*).

The logical connection of the aphorism (*sūtra*) is as follows: upon hearing those words of disregard from the swans, grief arose in this king; that [grief] is indicated by Raikva through the word "śūdra," for which the particle *hi* is used.

The particle *hi* serves to illuminate the maxim that when a literal etymological meaning (*yaugika-artha*) is obtainable from the Vedic text, a conventional meaning (*rūḍhi-artha*) that lacks syntactic connection must be abandoned.
Because he ran toward that grief— because he was pursued by that sorrow—
he became a Śūdra, having attained grief; or rather, the king was pursued and overtaken by Grief as its agent.
The meaning is that he went to Raikva either out of grief or by means of some instrument. //34//
And because the status of a Kṣatriya is understood from what follows, on account of the indicative mark [provided] by Caitraratha. (BS 1.3.35)
For this reason as well, Jānaśruti was not a Śūdra by birth;
because, upon examining the context, his status as a Kṣatriya is understood from his subsequent mention alongside Caitraratha Abhipratārin, who was a Kṣatriya.
For later on, in the supplementary portion of the Saṃvarga-vidyā, the Kṣatriya Caitrarathi Abhipratārin is mentioned.
"Now, while Śaunaka Kāpeya and Abhipratārin Kākṣaseni were being served food, a religious student begged from them" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 4.3.5).
And Abhipratārin’s status as a descendant of Citraratha is to be understood from his connection with the Kāpeyas.
For the connection with the Kāpeyas is known from Citraratha’s case, as it is said: "The Kāpeyas indeed performed the sacrifice for Citraratha" (Tāṇḍya Brāhmaṇa 20.12.5).
And generally, those of the same lineage serve as priests for those of the same lineage.
Furthermore, because his status as a lord of the Kṣatra is understood from the statement, "From him was born a lord of the Kṣatra named Caitrarathi," his status as a Kṣatriya must be understood.
The mention of Jānaśruti together with that Kṣatriya Abhipratārin in reference to an identical branch of learning indicates Jānaśruti’s status as a Kṣatriya;
for generally, such co-mention occurs between those who are equals.
Furthermore, Jānaśruti’s status as a Kṣatriya is understood from his exercise of sovereignty, such as by dispatching a charioteer.
Therefore, there is no entitlement for a Śūdra.

[35] *Note:* The word "atha" (now) is intended to introduce the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) immediately following the injunction regarding the Saṃvarga-vidyā. The particle "ha" indicates the commencement of a narrative.

To the domestic priest named Abhipratārin, who was the son of Śunaka and belonged to the Kapiga lineage, the attendant (kṣattṛ) and the charioteer (sūta) were sent by him in search of Raikva. Regarding the word "Śūdra" being used in its etymological sense, he states the indicative mark: "In his being a Kṣatriya... and so forth.
Immediately following the injunction for the Saṃvarga-vidyā, an explanatory passage (arthavāda) begins.

The meaning is that while King Abhipratārin—the descendant of Śunaka belonging to the Kapi lineage—and [the king] who was the descendant of Kakṣasena were seated down to eat, being served by a cook, a young student (baṭu) begged from them.
Now, one might object: "His status as a Caitrarathi is not heard [in the text]," to which [the author] replies: "And his status as a Caitrarathi... [and so forth].
By the Chāndogya scriptural passage, "by this Dvirātra sacrifice," the connection of Citraratha with the Kāpeyas was previously stated;
since Abhipratārin also has that same connection, his descent from the lineage of Citraratha is determined.
For, as a general rule, the family priests of those belonging to royal lineages are themselves descended from the lineage of the [original] family priest—this is the meaning.
Granted that Abhipratārin was the son of Citraratha; but how does that establish his status as a Kṣatriya?
To this, he says: "Therefore... (tasmāt).
The meaning of *citraratha* is Āditya.

That the attendant (*kṣattṛ*) and the charioteer (*sūta*) were sent by him to search for Raikva, as well as [Jānaśruti’s] giving of food, cows, and so forth, are indicative marks (*liṅga*) of Jānaśruti’s status as a Kṣatriya. //35//
Because of the reference to formative forces (*saṃskāra*) and because of the statement regarding their absence. (BBs 1.3.36)

For this reason as well, the Śūdra has no entitlement [to Vedic knowledge]: because in the sections concerning knowledge, purificatory rites such as initiation (*upanayana*) are referred to, as in "He initiated him" (Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa 11.5.3.13) and "‘Teach me,
O Blessed One,’ he approached [him]" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 7.1.1).

"Devoted to Brahman, grounded in Brahman, seeking the Supreme Brahman, [they thought], 'He indeed will tell us all that'; so, with fuel in their hands, they approached the venerable Pippalāda. (Praśna Upaniṣad 1.1) And:
"Without having initiated them... (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 5.11.7).
Thus, the attainment of initiation (*upanayana*) is indeed demonstrated [to be absent];
for the absence of sacramental rites (*saṃskāra*) is declared for the Śūdra:
"The Śūdra is the fourth caste, having but one birth" (Manu 10.4).

This is because of the recollection that they belong to a single caste, and also because of such [scriptural] passages as: "A Śūdra incurs no sin whatsoever, nor does he deserve any sacramental rite" (Manu 10.126). // 36 //
FN: "Adhīhi" means "teach," so to speak.
"Brahmaparāḥ" refers to those who have reached the further shore of the Vedas. "Paraṃ brahma" is the supreme, attributeless Brahman.

"Approached" means having come near. "Without having initiated" means that those of higher caste should be instructed by those of lower caste even without initiation; this is for the purpose of making known the traditional rule (*ācāra*). One who is of a single birth is one who has not been initiated.
In this matter, it is established that the word *śūdra* is purely etymological (yaugika), and thus there is no entitlement for a *śūdra*.
Regarding this, he states another indicative mark (*liṅga*)—namely, "sacramental rite" (*saṃskāra*).
It has been stated previously that initiation (*upanayana*), which is a constituent part of the acquisition of the Veda, does not exist for a *śūdra*.

It is argued here that because the sacrament of initiation (*upanayana*), which is an auxiliary to the acquisition of knowledge, is referred to in all [Vedic texts], and because the Śūdra lacks that, he has no entitlement to knowledge.
In the *Bhāṣya*, the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) includes study, service to the teacher, and other such requirements.
The meaning is that the teacher initiated that disciple.

Nārada also, seeking knowledge while reciting a mantra, approached Sanatkumāra; thus he says: "He studied," meaning "he requested instruction. Bharadvāja and the others—those devoted to Brahman, who had mastered the Vedas, were established in the Brahman with attributes (saguṇa-brahman), and were searching for the supreme, attribute-less (nirguṇa) Brahman—having decided that this Pippalāda would explain everything they desired to know, [approached him].
The meaning is that the six sages approached him.

Now, one might object: since the scripture regarding the Vaiśvānara-vidyā states that the king imparted the knowledge to the sages only after having initiated them, does this not imply that even an uninitiated person has the right to the knowledge? To this, he says: "To them...

By showing in the preceding passage—"They, with fuel in their hands, approached him in the forenoon"—that these Brāhmaṇas had come for the purpose of initiation, the possibility of initiation is established and then [in the present context] precluded.
The meaning is that this is for the purpose of making known the proper conduct, namely that one of lower caste must bring those of higher caste near and instruct them.
"Of a single birth" means one who has not been initiated.
A "sin" is that which is committed by eating what is forbidden to eat. //36//
And because activity occurs when there is a determination of the non-existence of that [object]. (BBs 1.3.37)
For this reason as well, the Śūdra has no entitlement [to Vedic study]:

because Gautama proceeded to initiate and instruct Jābāla once his lack of Śūdra-status had been determined by the speaking of the truth—[as recorded in] Chāndogya Upaniṣad 4.4.5: "A Brāhmaṇa ought not to speak thus; bring fuel, my dear; I will initiate you; you have not departed from the truth."

This is because of the indicative mark (*liṅga*) in the Śruti. [The story is as follows: Satyakāma, whose father had died, asked his mother Jabālā, "I do not know my lineage (*gotra*), nor does my mother know it; however, when I go to the teacher for the sake of initiation (*upanayana*), tell him, 'I am Satyakāma Jābāla'. By this truthful statement, he was known as Satyakāma.
"What is my lineage?
His mother said to him, "Because I was preoccupied with serving your father, I too do not know your father's lineage;
however, I am named Jabālā, and you are named Satyakāma—this much I do know."
Then Jābāla, having approached Gautama, was asked by him, "What is your lineage? and he replied:
"I do not know my lineage, nor does my mother know it; however, my mother told me, 'When you go to a teacher for the sake of initiation, say, "I am Satyakāma Jābāla. "
By this declaration of truth, his lack of Śūdra status is determined.
Having determined that "it is not right for one who is not a Brāhmaṇa to speak this truth after having analyzed it," [he spoke].
"O dear one,
since you have not departed from the truth and have not abandoned the truth,
I shall therefore initiate you."

He states that there is no entitlement for a Śūdra because of the indicative mark (liṅga) found in Gautama’s activity, namely his instruction: "Bring fuel for that purpose" (tadarthaṃ samidhamāhara). This is expressed in the sūtra: "In the absence of that... (tadabhāva...). //37//
Because of the prohibition of hearing, studying, and understanding [the Veda], and because of the Smṛti. (BS 1.3.38)
For this reason as well, there is no entitlement for a Śūdra:
because there exists a prohibition against his hearing, studying, and understanding the meaning of the Smṛti.

It is recorded in the Smṛti that for a Śūdra there is a prohibition against hearing the Veda, a prohibition against studying the Veda, and a prohibition against knowing its meaning and performing its injunctions.
First, there is the prohibition against hearing [the Veda]: "Now, if he should overhear the Veda, his ears are to be filled with molten lead and lac.
And: "A Śūdra is indeed a funeral pyre; therefore, one should not study in the vicinity of a Śūdra.
For this very reason, there is a prohibition against studying [the Veda].
For how could one study what has not been heard when one is not even permitted to study in the presence [of such a person]?
Indeed, it is said that upon the utterance of the Veda there shall be the cutting of the tongue, and upon its retention, the destruction of the body.
For this very reason, by implication, there follows a prohibition regarding the knowledge of the meaning and its practical application: "One should not impart wisdom to a Śūdra."
And [it is said]: "For the twice-born, study, sacrifice, and giving [are the duties].

However, in the case of those such as Vidura and the hunter Dharmavyādha, for whom the arising of knowledge occurred by virtue of impressions (saṃskāra) formed in previous lives, their attainment of the fruit cannot be prevented, because knowledge has an unerring result.
Because of the traditional rule that "one should cause the four castes to hear [it]," which records the eligibility of all four castes for the acquisition of the Itihāsas and Purāṇas;
however, it remains established that there is no eligibility for Śūdras regarding that which is preceded by the Vedas. (38) [Note:
*Trapu* and *jatubhyām* refer to lead and tin, respectively, when heated and melted along with lead and lac.]
"Padyu" means possessed of feet;
that is to say, capable of moving about.
"Mati" is the knowledge of the meaning of the Vedas.
He states that there is no entitlement [to Vedic study] because of the prohibition of hearing and so forth by means of *smṛti*: "Hearing," etc.
The meaning is that for this *śūdra* who hears the Veda being recited by the twice-born through negligence, the penance to be performed is the filling of both ears with heated lead and lac;
"padyu" means possessing feet, that is to say, having a mobile form.
And it exists; "recollection" is the understood remainder [of the sentence].
"Understanding" (mati) is the knowledge of the meaning of the Vedas.
Giving is permanently prohibited for a Śūdra;
however, occasional giving (naimittika-dāna) certainly exists for him.
As for what was said regarding the observed state of being a knower (jñānitva) in Vidura and others—

Regarding this, he says "of those who... Although the attainment of the perfected ones (siddhas) is undeniable, he says "he should cause [them] to hear" in response to the question: how is knowledge to be obtained by practitioners who are Śūdras? //38//
