The Section on Trembling (Kampanādhikaraṇa) / Sūtra 39.
Because of its trembling (kampanāt).
The incidental investigation into the subject matter is concluded;
we shall now proceed with the investigation into the meaning of the sentence that is our primary topic.
"That is to say: whatever there is in this entire world, it quivers, having issued forth from the vital breath (*prāṇa*).
A great terror, like a raised thunderbolt—those who know this become immortal" (Kauṣītaki Upaniṣad 2.6.2).
This statement is characterized by its conformity with the meaning of the verbal root *ejṛ*, "to quiver."

In this passage, it is heard that this entire world vibrates with its support being the vital breath (prāṇa), that some great cause of fear designated by the word "thunderbolt" (vajra) is raised up, and that through the knowledge of that [breath], the attainment of immortality occurs.

In this regard, since there is a lack of understanding as to what that *prāṇa* is and what that terrifying *vajra* is, when an inquiry is undertaken, it is first concluded—on the basis of common usage—that the *prāṇa* is the wind with its fivefold functions (*pañcavṛtti-vāyu*).
And on the basis of common usage alone, the *vajra* would be the thunderbolt (*aśani*).
For it is the greatness of the wind that is being proclaimed here.
How so?
This entire world moves for the sake of being established upon the fivefold wind designated as *prāṇa*;
and it is solely on account of the wind that the great, terrifying thunderbolt is raised up.
For they declare that when the wind transforms itself into the state of Parjanya (the rain-cloud), lightning, thunder, rain, and thunderbolts transform accordingly.
And this immortality results precisely from the knowledge of the wind;
for thus says another scriptural text: "The wind indeed is the individual manifestation (*vyaṣṭi*), the wind is the collective manifestation (*samaṣṭi*); he who knows this conquers recurrent death."
"Therefore, this [element] here must be understood as air.
This being the position reached, we reply: "Brahman alone is what must be understood here.
Why?
Because of the consideration of what precedes and follows;
for we perceive that it is Brahman alone being indicated in the preceding and following portions of the text.
How then could we understand Vāyu to be indicated here in the middle, quite unexpectedly?

In the preceding passage, Brahman was indeed indicated: "That alone is the Bright, that is Brahman, that alone is called the Immortal; in it all worlds are supported, and no one transcends it" (Kauṣītaki Upaniṣad 2.6.1).

Therefore, it is understood that here too, by virtue of proximity and because of the recognition of its having the worlds as its support in the phrase "the whole world moves, impelled by Prāṇa," this very [Brahman] is indicated.
Furthermore, this word "Prāṇa" is employed [in the sense of Brahman], as in "the breath of breath" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.18).
Because of this observation, the quality of being the impeller also belongs only to the Supreme Self and not to air alone.
And so it has been said: "No mortal lives by means of the out-breath (prāṇa) or the in-breath (apāna)."
"But by the other they live, upon which these two depend" (Kāṭhaka Upaniṣad 2.5.5).
And further on: "Out of fear of him the fire burns, out of fear the sun shines;
out of fear Indra and Vāyu, and Death as the fifth, run forth" (Kāṭhaka Upaniṣad 2.6.3).
Thus, it is Brahman alone that will be indicated here, and not Vāyu;
for it has been stated that [Brahman] is the cause of fear for the entire world, including Vāyu.
Therefore, by virtue of proximity, it is that very same [Brahman] which is the "great fear" here as well.
And it is understood that the phrase "the raised thunderbolt" is indicated because it is recognized as a cause of fear;
this word "thunderbolt" (vajra) is also employed here due to its commonality as a cause of fear,
just as one thinks, "The raised thunderbolt might fall upon my very head if I do not carry out his command."

Just as people engage in their duties out of fear and kings and others out of obedience to commands, so too this world—consisting of fire, wind, the sun, and so forth—proceeds in its respective functions out of fear of this very Brahman. Thus, Brahman is terrifying and is compared to a thunderbolt.
Accordingly, another Vedic scripture concerning Brahman states: "Out of fear of Him the wind blows."
"Out of fear of Him the sun rises; out of fear of Him, Agni and Indra, and Death as the fifth, run away. (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.8.1)
Furthermore, because the fruit of immortality is heard [in scripture], it is understood that this is indeed Brahman;
for the attainment of immortality results from the knowledge of Brahman, as stated:
"Only by knowing Him does one pass beyond death; there is no other path for the journey" (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 6.15).
This is because of the wording of the mantra.
As for the fact that immortality is mentioned in some places as resulting from the knowledge of Vāyu, that is relative;
for in that very context, by introducing a different topic, the Supreme Self is described [with the words]: "The end is other than the perishable" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.4).
Thus, because the affliction of air and the other elements is mentioned,
the determination that this refers to the Supreme Self follows from the context as well:
"Other than dharma, other than adharma, other than what is done and not done by us..."
Because the Supreme Self is what is being asked about in the passage: "Tell me that which you see as other than the past and the future" (Kaṭha Upaniṣad 1.2.14).
[FN: *bhīṣā* means through fear.]
The phrase "from this Brahman" means "on account of this cause.
The mention of the "five" is for the purpose of indicating all things, moving and non-moving, from Brahmā down to a blade of grass.
For, by the scriptural statement "he conquers death no more," the conquest of premature death is declared, but not the conquest of the supreme death; thus, [the former] is relative.
Regarding the word "kampanāt" (from trembling),
he states "avasitaḥ" (concluded) to address the concern that this [point] might also be merely incidental;
the meaning is "finished."
The *Kāṭhaka* recites:
"This which..."—the entire world has issued forth from, or been produced from, the vital breath (*prāṇa*); while that conscious Self (*cidātman*), the impeller, exists, it moves and exerts itself.
And that cause called the vital breath is the Great Brahman; it is "fear" because one fears from it.
Regarding that state of being a cause of fear, he provides an illustration: "like a thunderbolt.
The meaning is that it is just like the fear caused by a raised thunderbolt.
He says, "those who," referring to those who know this Brahman called *prāṇa* as being without distinction; they become liberated.
To the question, "How is this sentence cited in this Sūtra?", he says: "This [word].
The meaning is that because the sense of *ejati*—namely, trembling—is what is being defined in the Sūtra, a sentence containing the word *ejati* has been cited.

It is stated by the phrase "known from the word alone" (*śabdādeva pramitaḥ*) that no connection is required for this [citation] due to its consideration within the context of incidental topics (*prāsaṅgika-adhikāra*).

In that regard, it was stated that in the passage concerning the thumb, the restatement of the individual soul (*jīva*) is for the purpose of knowing its identity with Brahman; however, such is not possible here regarding the restatement of the vital breath (*prāṇa*),
because identity is impossible for the vital breath, which is imagined as having a distinct nature of its own.

Therefore, he presents the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa) by way of a counter-example, asserting that this passage is devoted to the meditation on the vital breath (prāṇa), on the grounds of its conventional usage: "The fivefold function [is the vital breath], because of its well-known meaning.

Now, one might object: "In passages such as 'For this very reason, the vital breath [is Brahman],' the scriptural term *prāṇa* was interpreted as referring to Brahman on account of its indicative marks (*liṅga*).
Here too, the state of being the cause of all activity and fearlessness is a mark of Brahman; thus, there is no occasion for a prima facie view, as the matter has already been settled."
Therefore, he says: "And of the wind.
It is well known that the world moves, having obtained its support—that is, its stability—by means of the vital air (prāṇa) as its cause.
Thus, the sense is that there is no clear mark of Brahman here.
And from the Vajra-linga comes the wind; thus he says, "the wind.
Individual manifestation (*vyaṣṭi*) is the particular, while collective totality (*samaṣṭi*) is the universal.
Immediately after [the prima facie view], he states the established conclusion (*siddhānta*): "Brahman alone.

He does so with the words beginning "In the preceding [passage]," etc.
"Bright" (*śukram*) means self-luminous.
The meaning of the syllable *u* is that there is no world whatsoever that does not depend upon Brahman, nor does it ever transcend it.
He explains the grammatical gender used in the Sūtra as "the state of being a mover.
The meaning is that because it is heard in scripture that everything, including the wind, trembles [at its command], Prāṇa must indeed be the Supreme Self.

Anticipating the question of how the word "vajra" can apply to Brahman, he states that it is used in a figurative sense with the words "the word vajra. In the *Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad*, in the passage "Vāyu alone is the individual manifestation," the term "immortality" refers to a relative immortality consisting in the conquest of untimely death (*apamṛtyu*), and not to absolute immortality; for in that very context, after concluding the section on the meditation upon Vāyu with the words "Then Uṣasta questioned him," the Self that is to be known is described, and it is stated that Vāyu and the others are subject to destruction. This is what he expresses with the words beginning "as for [the statement] about Vāyu," and so forth.
Therefore, it is established that the Kāṭhaka passage is connected with that which is to be known. //39//

Because of the perception of light. It is heard in scripture: "This serene being, having arisen from this body and having attained the highest light, appears in its own true form" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.12.3).
In this regard, a doubt arises:
does the word "light" refer to that brilliance which is the object of the eye and dispels darkness, or rather to the supreme Brahman?
What, then, is the initial position?
It is well known that the word "jyotis" (light) denotes "tejas" (fire). Why? Because the word "jyotis" is conventionally established (*rūḍha*) in that sense.

For in the case of [Brahma Sūtra 1.1.24], "Because of the mention of feet, [the light is Brahman]," the word *jyotis* (light), by virtue of the context, abandons its own primary meaning and refers to Brahman; however,
here we do not perceive any such reason for abandoning its own primary meaning.
And so it is stated in the section on the channels: "Now, when he departs from this body, he ascends upwards by means of these very rays" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.6.5).
Thus, the attainment of the sun is declared for the seeker of liberation.
Therefore, it is well-established that light is indeed what is denoted by the word *jyotis*.
This being the case, we reply: the word "light" (jyotis) refers to the Supreme Brahman alone.
Why?
Because of the scriptural vision [of it as such].

For its continuity is seen here in this context as something that must be discussed, because at the beginning of the section, the Self characterized by qualities such as being free from evil— expressed in the words "That Self which is free from evil" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.7.1)— is declared to be the object to be sought and the object to be understood.
And because of the following connection: "I shall explain this very matter to you further" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.9.3),
and "Pleasure and pain do not touch one who exists indeed bodiless" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.12.1).
Furthermore, because this attainment of light is stated for the sake of bodilessness (*aśarīratā*),
and because bodilessness is impossible apart from the state of Brahman; and because of the qualifying descriptions, "the highest light" and "that supreme person" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.12.3).
As for what was said— that the attainment of the sun is taught for one desiring liberation—
that is not ultimate liberation, because it involves movement and departure.
For we shall explain that in ultimate liberation, there is neither movement nor departure.
FN: The section concerning the channels begins with "Now, as for these channels of the heart," and so forth.
Therein, the connection is that the attainment of that [light] by the seeker of liberation is stated in accordance with the solar orb.
This is because of the perception of light.

He cites the passage concerning Prajāpati’s knowledge from the Chāndogya Upaniṣad with the words "This [is the Self]... He states the doubt arising from the two scriptural mentions of the "highest light" with the word "Therein...

The meaning is that the solar light destroys the darkness that obscures objects such as jars; this serves as a supporting factor for the preceding context of Brahman, since there is no possibility of restricting the scope of the word "all" or the like. Thus, the scriptural mention of "Prāṇa" was interpreted as referring to Brahman.

"We do not see anything here that supports the context [of the Self] as being 'that Self which is free from evil,'" he says, stating the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa) by way of a counter-example, beginning with "It is well known" and so forth.
The result of the prima facie view is the worship of the sun; the result of the final conclusion (siddhānta) is liberation through the knowledge of Brahman.

[Objection: But surely, since it has been stated in the *Jyotir-adhikaraṇa* that the word "light" (*jyotis*) refers to Brahman, how can there be a prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*)? To this he says: "Light" (*jyotiḥ*).

The meaning is this: in that case, in the passage concerning the *Gāyatrī*, the word "light" was made to abandon its own primary sense because of its grammatical coordination (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the pronoun "which" (*yat*), which refers back to the previously mentioned Brahman; however, here, since no reason for abandoning its own primary sense is seen, the prima facie position arises.
He states that being on the path beginning with light (*arcir-ādi*) is an indicative mark (*liṅga*), serving as a support for the scriptural mention of "light" (*jyotis*): "And thus" (*tathā ca*).
Having stated the mutual connection between the channels (*nāḍyaḥ*) and the rays (*raśmayaḥ*) in the section beginning, "Now these are the channels of the heart," [the text continues]:
"Then, after the loss of consciousness, at the time when this death occurs, he departs in such a manner; then, at that time..."

It has been stated that by means of these rays connected to the channels, being directed upwards, one goes upward; having gone, one reaches the sun, which serves as the gateway to the world of Brahman (brahmaloka).

In the same way, it must be stated here as well: having risen from the body after death, and having attained the supreme light known as the sun, one goes through that gateway to the world of Brahman and manifests in one's own true nature.
The meaning is that by the two verbal suffixes *ktvā* (in *samutthāya* and *upasaṃpadya*), it appears that the light (*jyotis*) is situated on the path beginning with light (*arcir-ādi*).

Thus, the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) being reached—that this passage concerns gradual liberation through the meditation on the sun situated on the path—the author establishes the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) with the word "Thus" (*evam*).

Since the Self, which was introduced as the subject to be explained, is the very thing to be explained here by the word "light," the scriptural mention of "light" (*jyotiḥ-śruti*)—which would cause a division of the sentence—is sublated by the scriptural mention of the "Highest Person" (*uttama-puruṣa-śruti*), which is supported by the context (*prakaraṇa*) that serves as the unifying factor for the single-sentence nature of the "Light" passage.
This is the state of being.
Furthermore, because the mark (liṅga) of the fruit—which is bodilessness—is present, he states "bodiless" to show that the light is Brahman alone and not the sun.
Nor should it be argued that bodilessness could be attained gradually through reaching the sun.
He says "param" (the supreme) because, by referring back to that very light which was specified as being "other," its bodilessness is determined.
He refutes the previously mentioned inferential mark with the words "yattu" (as for what...).

In the section on the channels (*nāḍīkhaṇḍa*), the attainment of the sun mentioned for the worshiper of the "small space" (*dahara*) is not liberation; therefore, the mention of the sun is appropriate [in that context].

In this context, however, regarding the statement of Prajāpati concerning the knowledge of the attributeless (nirguṇa-vidyā), since the sun situated on the path beginning with light (arcir-ādi-gati) cannot be logically connected [to the self], it would be purposeless; therefore, the intention is that it should be explained by rearranging the scriptural order as follows: "Having directly realized its own true nature, one attains that very supreme light. //40//

The Section Concerning the Designation of Being a Different Entity (Arthāntaratvavyapadeśādhikaraṇa) / Sūtra 41.
Space [is Brahman] because it is designated as being distinct from objects and so forth.

It is heard in scripture: "That which is called space is indeed the bringer-forth of name and form; that which is within these two is Brahman, that is the immortal, that is the Self" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.14.1).
In the inquiry as to whether the word "ether" (ākāśa) refers to the Supreme Brahman or to the well-known elemental ether (bhūtākāśa), it is appropriate to accept the latter;
for the word "ether" is conventionally established in that sense,
and because the "guiding of names and forms" can be attributed to it by way of providing space.
And because no clear characteristic of Brahman, such as being the creator, is heard here;
this being the position reached, it is said in reply: the Supreme Brahman alone must be what is denoted by the word "ether" (ākāśa) here.
Why?
Because of the designation as being "something other than the objects" and so forth;
for by the statement, "That which is between them is Brahman," space is designated as something other than name and form.
And nothing other than Brahman can possibly exist as something other than name and form, because the entire aggregate of modifications is manifested solely through name and form.
Furthermore, the complete accomplishment of name-and-form is not possible anywhere other than in Brahman;
for we hear of Brahman as the agent in such passages as, "Entering with this living self, let me evolve name-and-form" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.3.2).
But surely the individual soul (jīva) also possesses the capacity to carry out perceptual activity regarding names and forms?
Certainly it does;
however, what is intended here is non-difference.
And by the very mention of "carrying forth name-and-form" (nāmarūpanirvahaṇa), the marks of Brahman such as being the creator and so forth are thereby expressed;
furthermore, "That is Brahman, that is the Immortal, that is the Self" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.14) are the marks of the doctrine of Brahman.
This is an elaboration of the very point made in [Brahma-sūtra] 1.1.22: "It is space, because of its characteristic mark. [FN:
The meaning is that it is illogical for name-and-form—the word and its object—to be distinct from that [Brahman] while being included within it, or for them to have it as their creator.]
"Because of the designation [as] 'space'.
He cites the *Chāndogya*: "Space," etc.

Just as the mention of "light" is set aside by the force of the opening statement, so too the words "Brahman" and so forth are set aside by the opening statement regarding "space"; thus he presents the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) by means of this analogy, beginning with "the element," etc.
The fruit in both cases consists of the meditation on Ākāśa through its heard qualities and the knowledge of the qualityless Brahman.

Anticipating the objection that this [sūtra] is a mere repetition of the sūtra "Ākāśas talliṅgāt" (Brahma Sūtra 1.1.22), he refutes it by stating "and because of [its] being the creator, etc.," noting that here, unlike there, no clear indicative mark (liṅga) is heard.

It is logical that the well-known indicative mark *vai* and the scriptural mention of *ākāśa* should be set aside by the two mentions of *brahman* and *ātman* found in the supplementary portion of the passage, which are endowed with multiple indicative marks;

for it is determined that the purport of a sentence lies where there is a convergence of many means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Thus he establishes the final conclusion with the words "the Supreme alone," and so forth.
The meaning is that name and form—namely, word and object—are included within that [Brahman]; therefore, it is illogical for anything other than that to be their creator.

The objection is raised that "being the creator of names and so forth" is not a characteristic mark of Brahman, because it resides in the individual soul (jīva)—this is expressed by the word "nanu. The response is given with "bāḍham" (certainly): in the passage "by this living soul," the agency of that [creation] is stated as belonging to the soul through its non-difference from Brahman, since a direct [agency] is impossible.
Regarding what was stated—that there is no clear indicative mark—he says: "The name. In that case, however, there would be a redundancy.
Regarding this, he says: "As for 'space' (ākāśa).
This investigation is intended to establish that very point.

The sense is that there is no tautology, because it was stated there that the application of the word "space" to Brahman is taken as established, and that doubt and so forth proceed with respect to it. //41//

END BsCom_1,3.12.41 START BsCom_1,3.13.42 13. Section on Deep Sleep and Departure (Suṣuptyutkrāntyadhikaraṇa) / Sūtras 42–43. [The Self is distinct from the body, etc.,] because of deep sleep and departure. (Sūtra 42) [The Self is distinct from the body, etc.,] because [the scripture teaches that the soul] departs [from the body]. (Sūtra 43) In this section, it is established that the individual self (*jīva*) is distinct from the body, the senses, and the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*). Regarding this, some maintain that the individual self is nothing other than the body, the senses, and the internal organ. They argue that since these perish at death, the self must likewise perish; for they claim that consciousness arises from the specific configuration of these elements, just as intoxicating power arises from the mixture of certain ingredients. Furthermore, they point out that while the body is seen to be the locus of experience—as when one says "I am fat" or "I am thin"—it follows that the self is identical with the body. To refute this, the author states: "[The Self is distinct from the body, etc.,] because of deep sleep and departure. The individual self is distinct from the body, the senses, and the internal organ. Why? Because of the scriptural teaching regarding deep sleep (*suṣupti*) and departure (*utkrānti*). For it is taught that during deep sleep, the self becomes one with Brahman, and upon waking, it returns again; and that at the time of death, it departs from the body. If the self were identical with the body, these states would be impossible, as the body does not become one with Brahman nor depart from itself. Therefore, the self is distinct from the body, the senses, and the internal organ. Furthermore, the author states: "[The Self is distinct from the body, etc.,] because [the scripture teaches that the soul] departs [from the body]. It is taught that the individual self departs from the body at the time of death. If the self were identical with the body, such a departure would be impossible. Therefore, the self is distinct from the body, the senses, and the internal organ. Thus, it is established that the individual self is distinct from the body, the senses, and the internal organ. END BsCom_1,3.13.42 START BsCom_1,3.14.44 14. Section on the Nature of the Soul (Jaiminyadhikaraṇa) / Sūtras 44–53. In this section, it is established that the individual self is eternal. Some maintain that the individual self is non-eternal, arguing that it is produced from the elements at birth and perishes at death, just like the body. To refute this, the author states: "[The individual self is eternal,] because of the designation of its existence before [birth]. (Sūtra 44) It is taught that the individual self existed prior to its birth in this world. If the self were non-eternal, it could not have existed prior to birth. Therefore, the self is eternal. Furthermore, the author states: "[The self is eternal,] because of the designation of its existence after [death]. (Sūtra 45) It is taught that the individual self exists even after death. If the self were non-eternal, it could not exist after death. Therefore, the self is eternal. Moreover, the author states: "[The self is eternal,] because of the designation of its going [to another world]. (Sūtra 46) It is taught that the individual self goes to another world after death. If the self were non-eternal, it could not go to another world. Therefore, the self is eternal. Furthermore, the author states: "[The self is eternal,] because of the designation of its returning. (Sūtra 47) It is taught that the individual self returns from another world to this one. If the self were non-eternal, it could not return. Therefore, the self is eternal. Moreover, the author states: "[The self is eternal,] because of the designation of its being the agent. (Sūtra 48) It is taught that the individual self is the agent of actions. If the self were non-eternal, it could not be the agent of actions performed in previous lives. Therefore, the self is eternal. Furthermore, the author states: "[The self is eternal,] because of the designation of its memory. (Sūtra 49) It is taught that the individual self possesses memory. If the self were non-eternal, it could not possess memory of past experiences. Therefore, the self is eternal. Moreover, the author states: "[The self is eternal,] because of the designation of its desire. (Sūtra 50) It is taught that the individual self possesses desire. If the self were non-eternal, it could not possess desire for things experienced in previous lives. Therefore, the self is eternal. Furthermore, the author states: "[The self is eternal,] because of the designation of its intelligence. (Sūtra 51) It is taught that the individual self possesses intelligence. If the self were non-eternal, it could not possess intelligence regarding matters known in previous lives. Therefore, the self is eternal. Moreover, the author states: "[The self is eternal,] because of the designation of its name. (Sūtra 52) It is taught that the individual self has a name. If the self were non-eternal, it could not have a name based on its deeds in previous lives. Therefore, the self is eternal. Furthermore, the author states: "[The self is eternal,] because of the designation of its work. (Sūtra 53) It is taught that the individual self performs works. If the self were non-eternal, it could not perform works that yield results in future lives. Therefore, the self is eternal. Thus, it is established that the individual self is eternal. END BsCom_1,3.14.53 START BsCom_1,3.15.54 15. Section on the Size of the Soul (Aṇvadhikaraṇa) / Sūtras 54–66. In this section, it is established that the individual self is atomic (*aṇu*) in size. Some maintain that the individual self is all-pervading (*vibhu*), arguing that it is taught to be omnipresent in scripture. To refute this, the author states: "[The individual self is atomic,] because of the designation of its going and so forth. (Sūtra 54) It is taught that the individual self goes to another world, returns from there, and moves about within the body. If the self were all-pervading, such movement would be impossible. Therefore, the self is atomic. Furthermore, the author states: "[The self is atomic,] because of the designation of its being measured. (Sūtra 55) It is taught that the individual self is measured by the size of a thumb. If the self were all-pervading, it could not be measured. Therefore, the self is atomic. Moreover, the author states: "[The self is atomic,] because of the designation of its departing [from the heart]. (Sūtra 56) It is taught that the individual self departs from the heart through the veins. If the self were all-pervading, it could not depart from a specific location. Therefore, the self is atomic. (Sūtra 57) It is taught that the individual self is supported by the mind (*manas*). If the self were all-pervading, it would not require support. Therefore, the self is atomic. Moreover, the author states: "[The self is atomic,] because of the designation of its having qualities. (Sūtra 58) It is taught that the individual self possesses qualities such as knowledge and desire. If the self were all-pervading, it would be difficult to account for its limited qualities. Therefore, the self is atomic. Furthermore, the author states: "[The self is atomic,] because of the designation of its being an enjoyer. (Sūtra 61) It is taught that the individual self is minute. If the self were all-pervading, it could not be
"By the distinction between deep sleep and departure.
The phrase "because of designation" is understood to carry over from the previous sūtra.
In the sixth chapter of the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad, it is said: "Which is the Self? It is this person consisting of consciousness among the vital breaths, the light within the heart" (Bṛ. 4.3.7).
Having begun thus, an extensive elaboration concerning the Self has been made.
Therefore, the doubt arises: does this passage aim merely to describe the nature of the transmigrating soul (*saṃsārin*), or does it aim to establish the nature of the non-transmigrating [Self]?
What, then, is the prima facie position?
It has as its object only the true nature of the transmigrating soul.
Why?
Because of the introductory statement and the concluding summary.
Because at the beginning there is the mark of the embodied self in the passage,

"This which consists of consciousness among the vital breaths," and because at the conclusion that same [mark] is not abandoned in the passage, "Verily, this great unborn Self is this which consists of consciousness among the vital breaths" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.22).
Because even in the middle [of the text], by the introduction of states such as the end of a world-cycle (*buddhānta*) and so forth, that very same [Supreme Self] is further elaborated.
This being the case, we reply: this passage has the Supreme Lord alone as its primary subject of instruction, and it does not have the mere embodied soul (*śārīra*) as its subject of explanation.
Why?
Because the Supreme Lord is designated as distinct from the embodied soul both during deep sleep and at the time of departure.

First, regarding deep sleep, the text designates the Supreme Lord as distinct from the embodied soul: "This person, embraced by the conscious Self (prājña-ātman), knows nothing external nor internal" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.3.21).
In that context, the "person" (puruṣa) would be the embodied self (śārīra), because it is the knower;
for when there is the possibility of experiencing both external and internal objects, its negation is possible.
The "wise one" (prājña) is the Supreme Lord (parameśvara).
Because he is never separated from the wisdom characterized by omniscience;

likewise, even at the time of departure, the Supreme Lord is designated as distinct from the individual soul in the passage: "This embodied self, mounted by the conscious self, goes forth uttering [the last breath]" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.3.35).
Even there, the embodied one would be the individual soul (jīva) because of its lordship over the body;
however, the "wise one" (prājña) is that very same Supreme Lord.
Therefore, it is understood from the designation of difference between deep sleep and departure that it is the Supreme Lord alone who is intended here.

As for what was stated—that because of the bodily characteristics at the beginning, middle, and end, this passage has that [the individual soul] as its subject—we reply: in the opening, "This which consists of consciousness among the vital breaths," it is not the nature of the transmigrating soul that is intended to be described; rather, having referred to the nature of the transmigrating soul, it intends to teach its identity with the supreme Brahman.
For the commencement of the subsequent text, beginning with "It meditates, as it were; it moves, as it were," is observed to be intent upon the refutation of the attributes of a transmigrating being.
Likewise, in the conclusion as well, he concludes exactly according to the opening: "He indeed is this great, unborn Self, who consists of consciousness among the vital breaths.

The meaning is that he who is perceived as a transmigrating being consisting of consciousness among the vital breaths—he indeed is this great, unborn Self, the Supreme Lord himself, as has been established by us.

As for those who believe that because of the mention of states such as waking and dreaming in the middle [of the passage], the intention is to describe the nature of the transmigrating soul (saṃsārin)—
they have not even set out in the eastern direction when they are heading toward the western one.
For the author does not intend to describe the state of being a transmigrator or the possession of states by means of the mention of states such as waking and dreaming.
What then? It is the state of being devoid of [fixed] conditions and the state of being a transmigrator.
How is this understood?
Because at every step he asks, "Speak further for the sake of liberation alone."
And at every step he replies: "He is not followed by that, for this person is unattached" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.3.14–15), and also:
"He is not followed by merit, nor followed by evil; for then he has crossed beyond all sorrows of the heart" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.3.22).

Therefore, it should be understood that this sentence is intended solely to establish the nature of one who is not subject to saṃsāra. [FN: "Vijñānamaya" means consisting of or predominantly composed of the intellect (buddhi). The locative case in "prāṇeṣu" is used in the sense of distinction.]
The meaning is that he is distinct from both the vital breath and the intellect.
"Buddhānta" refers to the waking state;
"anvārūḍhaḥ" means presided over or mounted upon.
Uttering terrible sounds,
when the intellect meditates, the self seems to meditate;
when it moves, it seems to move.
The construction is as follows: because one replies "it exists," it is therefore understood.
Consequently, by that property of the state, [the self] remains unaccompanied and untouched, because of its non-substantiality (*asattva*).
"Thereafter" means immediately following the seclusion from desire and so forth.
By means of the distinction between deep sleep and departure [from the body],
when Janaka asked, "Among those things accessible to the notion of 'I', which one is the Self?", Yājñavalkya replied, "This one which...
He is composed of consciousness— that is, he consists primarily of the intellect (*buddhi*).
The seventh case has the sense of distinction (*vyatireka*);
the meaning is that [the Self] is distinct from the vital breath and the intellect.
He states its difference from the mental modification (*vṛtti*) and from ignorance by saying, "inner light" (*antarjyoti*).
The word *puruṣa* means "the Full One. Having observed that both genders [masculine and neuter] are used [for this term], he expresses a doubt with the words "Then what?
In the preceding section, it was stated that the ether is Brahman because of the mention of its distinction from name and form.
That is incorrect;

for just as there is a statement of difference regarding the individual self (*jīvātman*) even though it is non-different [from Brahman] in the passage "embraced by the intelligent Self" (*prājñenātmanā saṃpariṣvaktaḥ*), so too a figurative statement of difference is possible—this is the connection of the objection.
In the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), there is praise of the individual self as the agent and object of action.

In the established conclusion (*siddhānta*), the result is the realization of the identity of the essential nature of the Supreme Self (*paramātman*)—the conscious one (*prājña*) who is distinguished from the individual soul (*jīva*) only by an imagined difference—by means of a restatement (*anuvāda*) of that soul.
The "waking state" (*buddhānta*) refers to the state of being awake.

Since the individual soul is mentioned at the beginning, middle, and end [of the passage], it follows that this statement is intended as a praise of the soul; such being the prima facie view (*pūrva-pakṣa*), the author establishes the conclusion with the words beginning "the Supreme Lord," and so forth.

If the sentence were merely a praise of the individual soul (jīva), then the subsequent statement regarding the Supreme Knower (prājña) as distinct from the individual soul—which would otherwise remain unknown—would be incoherent.
Therefore, when there is a conjunction of the known and the unknown, the unknown must be established by way of restating the known;
for this is the purport of the established doctrine (*siddhānta*), based on the maxim: "The purpose of a sentence lies in what is previously unknown. This is the intended meaning of the conclusion.
He dispels the misconception that the *puruṣa* is the body, the *prājña* is the *jīva*, by means of the passage beginning with "therein, the *puruṣa*...
Since the body cannot be denied because it is subject to sensation, the *puruṣa* must indeed be the *jīva*;
however, the *prājña*—by conventional usage—is the Supreme Self alone. This is the meaning.
Mounted and presiding over it,
emitting terrible sounds,
he meditates when the intellect meditates, and moves when the intellect moves, as if he himself were meditating and moving.

He states "yataḥ" (since) to show that because it is said [in the scripture] to be "in reality devoid of all modification," the intent is not directed toward one who is subject to transmigratory existence.
He states "tathā" (likewise) to show that unity is intended to be expressed in the concluding statement just as it was in the opening statement.
He explains [the meaning] with "yo 'yam" (this which...).

He states that the presentation of the various stages does not possess the characteristics of the individual soul (jīva), because its purpose is to establish oneness by means of purifying the referent "thou" (tvam); thus he says, "Since [he is] not [perceived] in the waking state.
He states that non-transmigration is understood through the question and answer; thus he says, "From this point onward," which means immediately after the discrimination of desire and so forth.
"And it becomes" means: because he speaks thus, it is understood; such is the construction.
By that, he remains unaccompanied by and untouched by the properties of the various states.
Because of its non-attachment, even in deep sleep the reality of the Self remains untouched by merit and demerit.
For since the Self in deep sleep transcends all sorrow, the meaning of the Śruti is that "all sorrows belong only to the heart. //42//
[The self exists] because of the words "husband" and so forth. (BS 1.3.43)
For this reason as well, it should be understood that this passage is intended solely to establish the nature of the non-transmigrating Self;

for in this passage, words such as "Lord" (pati) and others are intended to establish the nature of the non-transmigrating Self and to negate the nature of the transmigrating Self. Expressions such as "the controller of all, the ruler of all, the sovereign of all" are of the nature of establishing the character of the non-transmigrating Self.
"By good action he does not become greater, nor indeed by bad action smaller"—such passages negate the nature of one who is subject to transmigratory existence.
Therefore, it is understood that the Supreme Lord, who is not subject to transmigratory existence, is the one spoken of here. // 43 //
Thus ends the third quarter of the first chapter in the *Śārīrakamīmāṃsābhāṣya* composed by the venerable Śaṅkara Bhagavatpāda.
[FN: *Vaśī* means independent;

"Not dependent" means [not subject to anything else].
"Īśāna" (the Lord) is one who possesses the power of restraint;

Therefore, it is established that the thematic consistency of the sixth chapter pertains to the unity of the meaning of the purified "thou" (tvaṃ). //43//

Section 1: The Topic Concerning the Inferential [Self] (Ānumānikādhikaraṇa). Sūtras 1–7.

If it be argued that for some [schools], the [self] is inferential, we say no; because [the scripture] shows that it is grasped as presented in the allegory of the body, and [the Lord] declares it so.
Having proposed the inquiry into Brahman (*brahmajijñāsā*), the definition of Brahman was stated: "That from which the origin, etc., of this [world proceed]" (Brahma-sūtra 1.1.2).

Anticipating the objection that the aforementioned characteristics belong equally to the Pradhāna as well, that [objection] was refuted on the grounds that it lacks scriptural authority: "Because of [the word] 'seeing,' that which lacks scriptural authority [is not Brahman]" (Brahma-sūtra 1.1.5).

Furthermore, it has been elaborated upon in the preceding section that the Vedānta texts possess a uniform direction toward the doctrine of Brahman as the cause, and not toward the doctrine of the Pradhāna as the cause.
Now, however, this remaining doubt is raised: that which was stated regarding the Pradhāna’s lack of scriptural authority is unproven.
Because in certain scriptures there are heard words that appear to designate *pradhāna* as the primary cause,
it follows that the causality of *pradhāna* is established by the Veda itself and has been accepted by great supreme sages such as Kapila and others.

Therefore, until it is demonstrated that those words have another meaning, the teaching that the omniscient Brahman is the cause of the world, even though it has been established, would become confused.
Therefore, the subsequent portion of the text proceeds to demonstrate that those [passages] have another purpose.
Even that which is inferential—that is, the *pradhāna* determined through inference—is found, according to some reciters of the Veda, to be expressed by words.
For it is read in the *Kaṭhaka*: "Greater than the Great is the Unmanifest; greater than the Unmanifest is the Person" (1.3.11).

In this context, those very entities known as Mahat, the Unmanifest (avyakta), and Puruṣa, which are established by tradition (smṛti) in their specific names and sequence, are here recognized. Among them, it is called "the Unmanifest" because it is so established by tradition, and because the etymological derivation is possible— namely, that it is "unmanifest" (avyakta) due to its being devoid of sound and other qualities.
If it is argued that the *pradhāna* well-known from the *Smṛti* is what is being denoted,
and that its status as "not being based on the Word" (*aśabdatva*) is untenable because it possesses the quality of sound (*śabdavat*),
and that this very *pradhāna* is the cause of the world due to its establishment through *Śruti*, *Smṛti*, and reasoning; [then we reply:]
This is not so;
for this passage from the Kāṭhaka does not have as its primary purport the existence of the "Great" (mahat) and the "Unmanifest" (avyakta) as established by Smṛti and logical reasoning.
Indeed, that which is well-known from Smṛti—an independent cause consisting of the three qualities (triguṇa), namely Pradhāna—is not recognized here in such a form.
For here, it is recognized through identification as "the unmanifest" being merely sound;
and that sound, because the term is etymological (yaugika), is applied to anything else that is subtle and very difficult to perceive, whether manifest or unmanifest,
yet this term is not conventionally established (rūḍha) for any specific thing.
As for the conventional usage of those who propound the Pradhāna, that being merely technical to them, does not serve as a basis for determining the meaning of the Veda.
Nor does the comprehension of an identical meaning arise from a mere similarity in sequence when there is no recognition of that specific form;
for one who sees a cow in the place of a horse does not, unless he is deluded, conclude, "This is a horse."
Furthermore, in the investigation of this context, the *pradhāna* postulated by others is not perceived,
because it is understood through the metaphorical representation of the body.
For here, the body, represented as a chariot, is what is grasped by the term "the unmanifest" (*avyakta*).
Why?
Because of the context and by process of elimination.

For the immediately preceding passage shows the metaphorical construction of the chariot and its driver for those who maintain the existence of the self and the body: "Know the Self as the rider, and the body indeed as the chariot."
Know, however, that the intellect is the charioteer and the mind is the reins.
The wise say that the senses are the horses and their objects are the paths;
they say that the self, when joined with the senses and the mind, is the enjoyer.
By means of those [faculties] such as the senses when they are unrestrained, one enters into saṃsāra;
but by means of them when they are restrained, one reaches the further shore of the path—that supreme abode of Viṣṇu—having been shown [the way].

In response to the inquiry, "What is that end of the path, the supreme abode of Viṣṇu?", the text shows the Supreme Self—the end of the path and the supreme abode of Viṣṇu—as being superior to those very things previously mentioned, namely the senses and so forth: "Higher than the senses are the objects; higher than the objects is the mind."
"But higher than the mind is the intellect; higher than the intellect is the Great Self;

higher than the Great is the Unmanifest; higher than the Unmanifest is the Puruṣa. There is nothing higher than the Puruṣa; that is the culmination, that is the supreme goal" (Kāṭhaka Upaniṣad 1.3.10–11).

In this context, those very same things—the senses and so forth—which were previously introduced as the horses and other parts in the metaphorical description of the chariot, are here also adopted in order to avoid abandoning what was introduced and introducing what was not.
Among these, the senses, the mind (*manas*), and the intellect (*buddhi*) have identical names both previously and here.
As for the objects—namely, sound and the other sense-objects which were described as the range of the horses that are the senses—their superiority over the senses is established.
This is because of the well-known scriptural statement: "The senses are the seizers, and the objects are the over-seizers" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.2);
and because the mind is superior to the objects.
Since the functioning of objects and the senses is rooted in the mind,
the intellect (buddhi) is higher than the mind;
for it is by ascending to the intellect that the world of objects approaches the enjoyer.
The Great Self, which is higher than the intellect, is that which was introduced as the charioteer in the passage, "Know the Self as the rider in the chariot.
Why? Because...
Because of the word "self" (ātman),
and because it is logical for the enjoyer to be distinct from the instruments of enjoyment;
furthermore, its greatness is established by virtue of its lordship.
Alternatively, it is recited thus: "Mind, the Great One, Intellect, Brahmā, Forethought, Consciousness, the Lord, Wisdom, Perception, Cognition, and Memory."

According to the Smṛti, and according to the Śruti, "He who in the beginning created Brahmā and who indeed delivered the Vedas to him" (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 6.18), that intellect of Hiraṇyagarbha, the first-born, is the supreme foundation of all intellects;
it is this which is here called the "Great Self" (mahān ātmā).

And that [intellect], having already been grasped previously by the very mention of "intellect" (buddhi), is here taught separately; for it is possible for it to be superior even to our own cognitions. However, on this view, the mention of the "Person" (puruṣa) as the supreme one, whose object is the Supreme Self, should be understood as referring to the Self who is the rider of the chariot.

Since, from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārthataḥ*), there is no difference between the Supreme Self (*paramātman*) and the conscious self (*vijñānātman*), only the body remains as such. Thus, while sequentially enumerating the other [categories] beginning with the senses— which were introduced here precisely for the purpose of showing the supreme state— the author indicates that the body, which remains as the subject under discussion, is what is referred to here by the final term "the unmanifest" (*avyakta*).
It is understood as follows:

for the sake of the enjoyer who possesses ignorance and is conjoined with the body, senses, mind, intellect, objects, and sensations, the intended meaning here is the realization of the inner self as Brahman, achieved by defining the course of transmigration and liberation through the metaphorical conception of the body and other factors as a chariot and so forth.
And thus: "This Self, hidden in all beings, does not shine forth;
but it is seen by subtle seers through their sharp and subtle intellect."

(Verse 1.3.12) Having thus stated the difficulty of comprehending the supreme state of Viṣṇu, he shows the yoga for the purpose of its comprehension: "The wise man should restrain speech in the mind; he should restrain that [mind] in the self consisting of knowledge; he should restrain knowledge in the great self; and he should restrain that [great self] in the peaceful self."
(Kārikā 1.3.13).
This is what is meant: one should restrain speech within the mind; having abandoned the activity of the external senses such as speech and so forth, one should abide in the mind alone.

Furthermore, the mind—which is directed toward the conceptualization of objects—one should fix within the intellect (*buddhi*), which is designated by the word "knowledge" and has the nature of ascertainment, by perceiving the defects of conceptual construction.
One should restrain even that intellect by bringing it to a state of subtlety within the Great Self (mahat), which is the experiencer, or within the supreme intellect;

and one should establish the Great Self within the peaceful Self, which possesses the context of the Supreme Person, at the ultimate pinnacle. Thus, when considering the preceding and following passages, there is no room here for the Pradhāna imagined by others. // 1 //

In this section, in order to state the connection between the three topics and the topic of "seeing" (*īkṣati*), he restates what has preceded: "Brahman," etc.; because it is not expressed by that word.
The meaning is: "because the Pradhāna is devoid of Vedic words.

In the *Īkṣaty-adhikaraṇa*, the uniformity of purport (*gati-sāmānya*) and the absence of scriptural authority (*aśabdatva*) were asserted; therein, the uniformity of purport of the Vedāntas with respect to Brahman was elaborated.

Now, having raised the objection that the "absence of scriptural authority" (*aśabdatva*) regarding *pradhāna* is unestablished, the matter is investigated; this constitutes the connection by way of an objection (*ākṣepasaṃgati*).

Consequently, by this investigation into the absence of scriptural authority, the concordance (*samanvaya*) of the Vedāntas with regard to Brahman is further strengthened; thus, the connection with the entire chapter (*adhyāyasaṃgati*) for these three topical sections (*adhikaraṇa*) should also be understood.
Here, the term "the Unmanifest" (*avyakta*) is the subject matter (*viṣaya*).

Regarding the doubt as to whether this [term] refers to the *pradhāna* mentioned previously or to the body mentioned earlier—due to both the *smṛti* and the context—the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) maintains that the word "unmanifest" (*avyakta*) refers to the *pradhāna*, which is not well-known [in the Veda], just as it was shown in the sixth chapter that the [text] refers to Brahman, which was previously unknown. Thus, he states: "The inferential" (*ānumānikam*).
By the use of the word "also" (*api*), he indicates that this objection regarding the lack of scriptural authority (*aśabdatva*) is raised while nevertheless accepting Brahman.
Furthermore, since Brahman and Pradhāna are both causes by way of option, the result is the failure of the restrictive rule that the Vedāntas have their harmony (*samanvaya*) in Brahman alone;

whereas in the Siddhānta, this restrictive rule is established—this is the distinction. Since these sections (*adhikaraṇas*) consist of investigations into words, it should be understood that this constitutes the connection (*saṅgati*) for this section (*pāda*).
He says "sound, etc. because the word *avyakta* refers to *pradhāna* due to its established usage in the Smṛtis and because yoga is possible through its being devoid of sound, touch, and so forth.

The Smṛti states: "The cause is called Prakṛti," and so forth;
the Nyāya principle holds: "Whatever is limited is of an insentient nature.

Stating the meaning of the negative particle (*nañ*) in the Sūtra, he establishes his conclusion with the words "not this" (*naitad*).

He provides the reason for the absence of intent regarding the claim that the Pradhāna is Vedic with the words "for not" (*na hi*). [Objection: But surely the Pradhāna is Vedic because it is recognized here; to this he replies: "for not here" (*na hy atra*).
