and saying "Not the first," he explains why it cannot be the former.
He states the second [objection] with the words "But that which...
The meaning is that human convention is not the cause for determining the meaning of the various Vedas, because human cognition is diverse.
As for the claim that because of the recognition of the sequence found in the Smṛti, the sequential meaning must also be based on the Smṛti alone—to this he replies: "And not by sequence...

The meaning is as follows: since there is no apprehension of its [the Vedic] form through the recognition of that form based on position, the negative particle *na* is transposed [to yield the sense]: when there is a recognition of what is not of that form—that is, of what is contrary to that form.

Regarding the point that when a cognition of a contrary object arises in place of an object whose form was previously known, the [prior] cognition no longer exists, he provides an illustration with the words "for not" (*na hi*).
Anticipating the objection that in the present case there is no contrary cognition, he states "by the context" (*prakaraṇāt*), meaning that by virtue of the context, there is a cognition of the body.

"Arranged as a metaphorical representation of the body" (*śarīrarūpakavinyasta*) means that the body itself has been arranged through the metaphorical comparison (*rūpaka*) of its similarity to a chariot.

The meaning of the Sūtra is this: since that which was read in the middle position between *ātman* and *buddhi* in the preceding passage is also grasped here by the word *avyakta*, which likewise stands in the middle, the *pradhāna* is not Vedic.

Anticipating the objection, "Why should the sequence of the Smṛti be abandoned?", he states, beginning with "For what reason," that the Vedic sequence is stronger because it is supported by context and other factors;
he explains both of these points with the words "For thus."
The fashioning of forms is the conceptualization of resemblance;
the rein is the tether for the horse.
When the charioteer of the intellect is discerning, it then draws back the horses of the senses from the path of treacherous objects by means of the mind.

If one is undiscriminating, then one sets those [senses] in motion, bound by the reins of the mind; thus, it is appropriate that the mind functions as the bridle for those horses. For them—the horses—*gocarān* means paths.

Now, one might object: since experience is possible for the conscious Self (cidātman) by its own nature, what is the need for chariots and so forth? To this he says: "The Self" (ātmā). The meaning is that the state of being an experiencer arises through the false imagination of the body and other such things; it does not exist inherently, because [the Self] is by nature unattached (asaṅga). Now, stating that there is a destination to be reached by means of those chariots and so forth, he utters the subsequent passage beginning with "By them," etc., in order to fulfill the expectation [of the reader].
Even though the body is the subject under discussion, one might think that the term "unmanifest" (*avyakta*) refers to *pradhāna*; therefore, he says: "In that [context], it is that which...
Having thus cleared up the context, he establishes that the body remains as the referent by means of the passage beginning with "In that case, the senses...
Anticipating the objection that objects (*artha*) were not previously mentioned, he justifies their status as being "beyond" [the senses] by saying: "The objects..."
The sense faculties (indriya) are called "graspers" (graha) because they seize and bind the human beast. Their status as graspers is dependent upon their objects;
for in the absence of an object, they are incapable of acting.
For it is heard in the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad that "the objects of the senses (viṣaya) are the 'over-graspers' (atigraha), superior to the [physical] graspers (graha).
The sense is that their superiority refers to excellence, not to being more internal.
The mind (*manas*) is determinate cognition (*savikalpaka-jñāna*); the intellect (*buddhi*) is indeterminate cognition characterized by ascertainment (*niścayātmikā*);
and from the word "Self" (*ātman*), it follows that He alone is beyond the intellect.
The word "is recognized" (*pratyabhijñāyate*) is to be supplied as the ellipsis.

Alternatively, he says "or" (*athavā*), stating that the Great One (*mahān*) is the collective intellect (*samaṣṭibuddhi*) which is to be known through terms such as Brahmā, by virtue of its non-difference from Hiraṇyagarbha;
it is the power of reflection (*mananaśakti*).
The pervasive one,
the certainty of existence,
Brahmā, the Self.
The basis for the category of objects of enjoyment,
immediate certainty,
and the power of fame.
The power of regulation,

the determination of the three periods of time, that which manifests consciousness, and the collective intellect (samaṣṭibuddhi) which grasps all past objects superimposed upon it— this is the meaning.

Regarding the statement that this intellect belongs to Hiraṇyagarbha, he cites scripture with the words "He who... One might ask: "But how can that [intellect] be mentioned when it is not the subject under discussion?
And if it is so mentioned, what wrong has the Pradhāna done? To this, he says: "And that..."
"Hiruk" means separately.
The meaning is that what was previously stated without distinction through the intellect of individuality (vyaṣṭi-buddhi) is here stated as being "beyond" (para) by way of distinction.
In that case, the chariot and the charioteer would remain as two [remaining entities].
He says "no" with the words "But in this [case]...
Therefore, he states that the chariot alone remains with the words "Thus, in this way...";
the meaning is: among those six categories previously mentioned.
He states the result of the remainder [of the argument] with the words "the others. The ellipsis is "whether it be the Veda or Yama.
Thus, the portion of the sūtra beginning with "and he shows" has been explained.
Furthermore, he states with the words beginning "In the body" (*śarīra*) that there is no room for proponents of duality in a treatise whose primary purport is the oneness of Brahman and the Self.
"Experience" (*bhoga*) means sensation.

He states with the words beginning "And likewise this" (*tathā caiṣa*) that there are indicative marks (*liṅga*) for the injunctions regarding yoga, which serve as the cause for knowledge—the hidden meaning and the object to be known—within the *Kāṭhaka* text, which has oneness as its ultimate intent.
The foremost [speech] is born from the maturation of meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
In this context, the elision of the second case ending in the word *vāc* is Vedic (*chāndasa*), as is the lengthening of the vowel in *manasi*. //1//
But it is subtle, because of its worthiness [to be so]. (BBs 1.4.2)
It has been stated, both by way of direct argument and by the exhaustion of other possibilities, that the body is the referent of the term "unmanifest" (avyakta) and not the Pradhāna.

Now, this objection is raised: how is the body worthy of being called "unmanifest," given that because it is gross, this body is more clearly perceived and thus more appropriately termed "manifest," whereas the word "unmanifest" implies something indistinct?
To this, the following is said: here, however, the body is intended in its subtle form as a cause, because the subtle is worthy of being designated by the term "unmanifest" (avyakta).
Although this gross body does not itself deserve the term "unmanifest," nevertheless, the subtle elements that constitute its origin do deserve the term "unmanifest."
Furthermore, the word *prakṛti* is seen used for a modification (*vikāra*), as in the Vedic text: "Mix the intoxicating [Soma] with cows" (Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 9.46.4), and as the Śruti says:
"In the beginning, this was indeed undifferentiated (*avyākṛta*)" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.4.7).

Thus, this very world—which is distinguished by manifested name and form (*vyākṛta-nāmarūpa*)—is shown to have been in a prior state where name and form were unmanifested (*parityakta-vyākṛta-nāmarūpa*), existing in the condition of seed-potency and joined with the term "unmanifest" (*avyakta*). [Note:

Because the modifications (*vikāra*) are non-different from primordial matter (*prakṛti*), the unmanifest nature of *prakṛti* is figuratively attributed to its modification. One should mix, that is, blend, the *matsara* (Soma) with "cows," meaning with the products of cows, namely milk.

Indeed, at that time, in the prior state, this world was unmanifest (avyākṛta), that is, unevolved (avyakta). He explains the Sūtra as a response to an objection, beginning with the words "This has been stated," and so forth.

The meaning is that because there is no difference between cause and effect, the term "unmanifest" (avyakta), which denotes the primal nature (mūlaprakṛti), indicates the transformation (vikāra) by way of secondary indication (lakṣaṇā).
"Mix the exhilarating Soma with cows—that is, with products of the cow and with milk;
that is to say, make it blended.
This is the second person plural form in the imperative mood derived from the root *śrīñ* (meaning "to cook" or "to mix").
He states the proof for the fact that the effect is fit for the designation "unmanifest" by virtue of its unmanifest nature: "And scripture [says so].
The meaning is: "In the prior state, this world was indeed unevolved (avyākṛta).
It is in the state of being a latent impression (saṃskāra), a power in the form of a seed. //2//
Because it is dependent on that, it is purposeful. (BS 1.4.3)

Here it is objected: If this world, whose name and form are unmanifest, were admitted to exist in a prior state as a seed-nature, fit for the designation "unmanifest," and if the body were likewise asserted to be fit for the designation "unmanifest" by virtue of that [seed-nature],
then, this being the case, the very doctrine of the Primal Matter (pradhāna) as the cause would result.
"Because this very world is accepted as being in the state of *pradhāna* during its prior condition.
To this it is replied: "If we were to accept some independent prior condition of the world as its cause, then we would be falling into the doctrine of *pradhāna* as the cause."
We, however, accept that this prior state of the world is dependent upon the Supreme Lord (parameśvara) and not independent;
and that [dependence] must necessarily be accepted,
for it is meaningful.
For without her, the Lord’s status as creator cannot be established,
since activity is impossible for one devoid of power;
and furthermore, there would be no rebirth for those who have attained liberation.
Why?
Because that seed-potency is burnt away by knowledge.
For the seed-potency, which consists of ignorance, is designated by the term "the unmanifest" (avyakta); it rests upon the Supreme Lord, is composed of māyā, and is the great sleep.

In that [state] in which the transmigrating individual souls lie, devoid of the awakening to their own true nature, this is the unmanifest (avyakta). It is designated by the word "ether" (ākāśa) in some places, according to the Vedic scripture: "In this very Imperishable, O Gārgī, the ether is woven like warp and woof" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.8.11).
In other places, it is expressed by the word "Imperishable" (akṣara), according to the scripture: "Higher than the high Imperishable" (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 2.1.2).

In some places it is indicated that she is *māyā*, from the wording of the mantra: "One should know *māyā* as *prakṛti*, but the Great Lord (*maheśvara*) as the wielder of *māyā*" (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 4.10).
For that *māyā* is indeed unmanifest (*avyakta*).
This is because it is impossible to determine whether [the unmanifest] is identical to or different from that [mahat].
This very thing is called "the unmanifest is beyond the mahat," because the mahat originates from the unmanifest; here, "mahat" refers to the intellect (buddhi) of Hiraṇyagarbha.
But when the *jīva* is "great," even then, because the state of being a *jīva* is dependent upon the Unmanifest (*avyakta*), it is said that "the Unmanifest is beyond the Great.
For the Unmanifest is indeed ignorance (*avidyā*).
It is precisely through its possession of ignorance that the entire continuous worldly activity of the *jīva* proceeds.
The state of being "higher than the Great" (mahat) is attributed metaphorically by way of non-difference to its modification, namely the body.

Even though the senses and so forth, like the body, are equally its modifications, it is the body alone that is grasped by the term "the Unmanifest" (avyakta) through this metaphorical attribution of non-difference;
for the senses and so forth have already been grasped by their own respective names, and the body remains as the only thing left over.
Others, however, explain it thus: the body is indeed twofold, gross and subtle.
The gross is that which is perceived here;

the subtle is that which will be described later: "In proceeding to the next state, it goes enveloped [by the elements], as is determined by the questions and the explanations" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.1.1).
Both of these bodies were previously designated as the "chariot" without distinction; however, here it is the subtle body that is grasped by the word "unmanifest" (avyakta),
because the subtle is worthy of being called "unmanifest."
Furthermore, because the conventional usage of bondage and liberation depends upon it, that [Self] is superior to the individual soul (jīva).
Just as objects are superior to the senses because the functioning of the senses depends upon objects, so too is that [Self] superior.
However, they [the opponents] must state this:

Since both bodies have been mentioned without distinction as being like chariots in the preceding passage, and since both are equally the subject matter remaining under discussion, how can we claim to understand the meaning of the scripture such that only the subtle body is grasped here and not the gross one? One cannot challenge what is not stated in the text. If it is argued that the word *avyakta* (unmanifest) used in the scripture is capable of denoting only the subtle body and not the other, because the latter is manifest (*vyakta*), we say: no.
Because the comprehension of meaning depends upon syntactic unity;
for these two [passages], the preceding and the succeeding, do not convey any meaning without attaining syntactic unity,
since that would entail the abandonment of what was introduced by another [text] and the introduction of what was not intended.
Furthermore, there can be no comprehension of syntactic unity (ekavākyatā) without an expectancy (ākāṅkṣā).

In that case, while there remains an expectancy for both bodies to be grasped, if a connection is not admitted according to that expectancy, the very status of being a single sentence is subverted; how then could there be a comprehension of the meaning of what has been revealed in scripture?
Nor should it be thought that only the subtle body is grasped here because it is difficult to purify.
However, the gross [element] is not included because it is easily purified due to its visible loathsomeness;
for no purification of anything is intended here,
as there is no verb in this context that prescribes a process of purification.
However, because it was mentioned immediately prior, this is what is intended here: "What is that supreme abode of Viṣṇu?
For, after stating, "This is superior to that; this is superior to that," he says, "There is nothing whatsoever superior to the Puruṣa.
Nevertheless, since the refutation of the inferential [soul] is established in every respect, let it be so named.
Nothing of ours is cut off. // 3 // [FN:
"Then" (tarhi) means at that time.
"Consisting of illusion" (māyāmayī) means comparable to well-known illusions.]

Due to the distinctions of limiting adjuncts such as the intellect (*buddhi*), there is the plural expression "individual souls" (*jīvas*). Because it is unconditioned, it is the nature of space (*ākāśa*); because it does not cease without the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*), it is the imperishable (*akṣara*).
The distinction is that it is called *māyā* because its effects are manifold;
that [unmanifest] is the *avyakta*.
This should be understood as being like the expression "cattle and bulls" (*gobalīvarda*).
The state of being established within a single cognition through mutual expectancy among words that convey a single meaning is "unity of sentence" (*ekavākyatā*).
Expectancy for being apprehended is unity of sentence.
The meaning is: by that state of being characterized by *bībhatsā*, which is loathing or disgust, in which it is observed.
"In every way" means even when either the gross or the subtle [object] is apprehended.
He explains the Sūtra as a response to the suspicion of a deviation from established tenets (*apasiddhānta*), beginning with the words "Here it is said," and so forth.
"Then" (*tarhi*) means at that time.

This being the case—meaning, provided that the prior state denoted as "subtle" is accepted—it is argued that there is no deviation from established doctrine (apasiddhānta), because one accepts that [the subtle state] is imagined within the Lord and is subject to His control; this is stated in the passage beginning with "To this it is said.
It was previously stated that ignorance (avidyā) must be admitted for the sake of establishing the creative agency of the immutable Brahman.
He states that it must also be accepted for the sake of establishing the distinction between bondage and liberation: "Of the liberated ones," etc.

The meaning is that that [nescience] through whose destruction liberation occurs must be accepted; for if creation were to take place without it, there would be the undesirable consequence of the liberated ones being bound again.
He states its distinction from the "Primal Nature" (pradhāna) which is conceived as a self-sufficient reality by others, beginning with the words "ignorance" (avidyā) and so forth:
it is "consisting of illusion" (māyāmayī), meaning it is compared to well-known illusion; in the world, it is dependent on another, like the illusion of a magician.
He states that this [avidyā] must also be accepted as the limiting adjunct (upādhi) for the differentiation of individual souls (jīva), saying "the great deep sleep" (mahāsuṣupti).
The plural expression "individual souls" is used because of the distinctions among the limiting adjuncts such as the intellect (buddhi) and so forth.
He also cites scripture regarding avidyā, saying "that very thing" (tadetad).
It is called "space" (ākāśa) because it is the cause of space;
it is the "imperishable" (akṣara) because there is no end to it apart from gnosis;
and it is "illusion" (māyā) because of its manifold activity—such is the distinction.

Now, he states that ignorance (avidyā) is fit to be designated by the word "unmanifest" (avyakta) because it cannot be defined as either different from or non-different from Brahman—this is expressed by the words "the unmanifest.

To the question, "How is it that this [ignorance] is superior to the Great One (mahat)? he replies with "that which is called this. The syntactical connection is as follows: when the intellect (buddhi) is the Great One, then [ignorance] is said to be superior because it is the cause of that [intellect].
Because a reflection is dependent upon its limiting adjunct (*upādhi*), he states that the adjunct is superior to the reflection with the words "But when...
He clarifies the reason with the word "ignorance" (*avidyā*).
Even though the unmanifest (*avyakta*) is superior, what happens to the body?
He says this with the words "And that" (tacceti).
Now, one might ask: since the senses and so forth are also non-different from the Unmanifest, why is their state of being unmanifest and their status as the "higher" not mentioned?
To this he replies: "Even though... (satyapi).
He introduces the commentary of another author on these two sūtras with the words "But others [say]":
"The subtle parts of the fivefold-composed elements (pañcīkṛtabhūta) are the originators of the gross body.
It will be stated that for every individual soul, there exists a subtle body (sūkṣmaśarīra) which is fixed as the substratum of the subtle body (liṅga)."

The meaning is that, upon attaining another body, he goes to the next world joined with that [subtle body]. Anticipating the objection as to how that [subtle body] can be superior to the great self (mahat), he explains the second sūtra: "And because it is dependent on that," [and] "it has a purpose."
He states the example found in the Sūtra with the word "yathā" (just as).
He refutes that explanation with the words "tair" (by them).

He raises an objection, fearing that by the force of the term "avyakta" (the unmanifest), even the "sthūla" (gross) which is the subject at hand might be abandoned, using the phrase "āmnātasya" (of what is traditionally taught).

"Syntactic unity (*ekavākyatā*) consists in words that convey a single meaning being mounted upon a single cognition through mutual expectancy. Since, in your view, this [unity] is absent, how can there be comprehension of meaning?"—thus he answers with "No. To the question, "Why should there not be comprehension of meaning even without that?", he says: "For not..."

The meaning is that, since the word "body" (śarīra) conventionally refers to the gross [body] which is the subject under discussion, it would be improper to use the term "unmanifest" (avyakta) to refer to the subtle elements (bhūtasūkṣma), which are not the subject at hand; thus, there would be a loss of the primary topic.
To the objection that "let there be a single coherent sentence," he replies with "And not... (na ca).
To the question "What follows from that?", he says "In that case... (tatra).
When there is syntactic unity through mutual expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*), the two bodies under discussion are to be understood by the term "the unmanifest" (*avyakta*);
the sense is that their expectancy is equal.
Purity is the certainty regarding the non-self.
For that purpose, only the subtle [self] should be sought as the object of apprehension;
for when it is grasped as non-different from the Self due to its subtlety, it is difficult to purify.

He raises an objection—beginning with "na ca"—on the grounds that for the gross [body], the realization of its non-selfhood and the resulting dispassion are easily attained through the perception of its manifest foul odor and so forth, just like garlic and similar things.
The meaning is: "by that state of being," namely that in which loathsomeness and disgust are perceived.
He refutes [the objection] with the words "since" (*yataḥ*); for here, it is not impurity that is intended for the sake of detachment (*vairāgya*).

Because there is no such injunction, however, the supreme state of Viṣṇu is intended to be expressed; therefore, the sense is that the aforementioned gross [body] alone should be understood by the term "unmanifest" (avyakta) for the purpose of showing that [supreme state].

Furthermore, since the subtle [body], which is included within the causal body (liṅga), is already grasped by the mention of the senses and so forth, it is not grasped separately by the two terms "unmanifest" (avyakta) and "body" (śarīra).
Having conceded this, he says: "In every way.
This means even when there is the apprehension of either a gross or a subtle object.
[He replies: "Let it be so named."
The meaning is that the unmanifest (avyakta) must indeed be subtle. //3//
Furthermore, the Sāṃkhyas maintain that *pradhāna* is an object of knowledge, as they say: "Liberation results from the knowledge of the distinction between the *guṇas* and the *puruṣa*.
For it is not possible to know the distinction of the *puruṣa* from the *guṇas* without first knowing the nature of the *guṇas*.
Moreover, in some instances, they maintain that *pradhāna* is to be known for the sake of attaining specific supernatural powers (*vibhūti*).
If this unmanifest were not stated here as an object of knowledge,
then the word "unmanifest" would be merely a fragment;
for there is no sentence here stating that "the unmanifest is to be known and to be meditated upon."
Furthermore, it cannot be maintained that knowledge of an entity not taught [in scripture] constitutes a human goal;
for this reason as well, the *pradhāna* is not denoted by the word "Unmanifest" (*avyakta*).

For us, however, this presentation is faultless, as it is intended to reveal the supreme abode of Viṣṇu alone by following the sequence of the body and other elements fashioned through the metaphor of the chariot. // 4 //
Regarding the point that the unmanifest (avyakta) is not the Pradhāna, there is a further sūtra for the sake of providing another reason: "Because it is an object of knowledge" (jñeyatva).

The meaning is that the distinction (antara)—that is, the difference—of the Puruṣa from the Pradhāna, which consists of the qualities (guṇas) such as Sattva and so forth, arises from the knowledge of that [distinction].
The connection is that by those who say "it is not possible," the Pradhāna is remembered as being an object of knowledge.

The author states "In some places... to show that the Pradhāna is not only intended by them to be an object of knowledge (*jñeya*) as the counter-correlate of difference, but also for the sake of attaining powers such as *aṇimā* through its meditation.

He says "Nor [is it] untaught" because, even in the absence of an injunction to know it, the Pradhāna possesses an implied knowability (*jñeyatva*) insofar as it is accessible to the cognition generated by the word "unmanifest" (*avyakta*).

The meaning is this: since knowledge is only capable of being known as fruitful when it has been taught—and since teaching is inappropriate for that which is fruitless—and since no instruction regarding the knowledge of the Unmanifest is given, its accessibility through fruitful knowledge remains unestablished.
He states the conclusion: "Therefore" (tasmāt).
The meaning is: because it is not stated that [the self] is to be known through the fruitful knowledge desired by the Sāṃkhyas.
Now, one might object: since the body is also not mentioned as being an object of knowledge, how can it be included here?
Regarding this, he says: "But for us...

The meaning is that, in our view, since the single entity called Viṣṇu alone is the object of knowledge, it is appropriate to introduce the body by means of the term "the unmanifest" (avyakta) for the purpose of perceiving Him.

The intended sense is that the Pradhāna is not recognized merely from a common word, because there is no restrictive factor due to the non-statement of any characteristic mark found in the Smṛti. //4//
If it is argued that [the self] speaks, we say no; for the wise one does not speak, as is clear from the context.
Here the Sāṃkhya says: "Because of the non-statement of its being an object of knowledge" is unproven.
How so?

For indeed, later on, there is a statement regarding the Pradhāna—denoted by the word *avyakta*—that it is an object of knowledge: "That which is without sound, without touch, without form, imperishable, and likewise without taste, eternal, and without smell."
Having perceived that which is without beginning or end, greater than the great, and eternal, one is liberated from the jaws of death.
(Kārikā 2.3.15).
For here, that very same Pradhāna which is described in Smṛti as being beyond the Mahat and devoid of sound and other qualities is indicated as the object to be perceived;
therefore, this is indeed the Pradhāna.
And that very [Self] is what is designated by the word "unmanifest.
To this we reply: here the *pradhāna* (primordial matter) is not indicated as the object to be perceived;
rather, it is understood that the wise Supreme Self (*paramātman*) is indicated here as the object to be perceived.
Why?
Because of the context;
for the context of a wise person extends far.

This is because of such scriptural indications as, "There is nothing higher than the Puruṣa; that is the limit, that is the supreme goal," and because of the statement regarding its difficulty of knowing—namely, "This Self, hidden in all beings, does not shine forth"—which expresses a desire for that very [Puruṣa] to be known.
Furthermore, it is because the restraint of speech and other faculties is prescribed for the sake of knowing that [Self] alone, in the passage, "The wise man should restrain speech in the mind."
And because it has the result of liberation from the mouth of death;
for the Sāṃkhyas do not maintain that one is liberated from the mouth of death merely by perceiving the Pradhāna alone.
For their accepted doctrine is that one is liberated from the mouth of death through the knowledge of the conscious Self.
In all the Vedānta texts, it is the conscious Self alone that is described as having the attributes of being beyond sound and so forth.
Therefore, neither the Pradhāna nor anything else is intended here as the object of knowledge, nor is it designated by the word "unmanifest" (avyakta). [Note:
In the phrases beginning with "beyond sound" (aśabda), the word "eternal" (nitya) is to be connected with each term.]
Anticipating the objection based on the indicative mark (*liṅga*), he refutes it with the words "if it is argued that [the text] says so" (*vadatīti cet*).
For here, the connection is that exactly such [a thing] has been indicated.
The rest is clear. //5//
And for these three alone there is such an introduction and inquiry. (BBs 1.4.6)
For this reason as well, the Pradhāna cannot be denoted by the word "Unmanifest" (avyakta), nor can it be the object of knowledge (jñeya).

Because in this text, the Kaṭhavallīs, we observe that the introduction of the three categories—the fire, the individual soul (jīva), and the Supreme Self (paramātman)—is presented as the subject matter to be explained by virtue of the granting of boons;
and the questions likewise concern only those subjects.
There is no question or presentation of another [topic] beyond this.
In that regard, first, there is the question concerning fire: "O Death, you know that fire which leads to heaven; tell it to me, who am full of faith" (Kauṣītaki Upaniṣad 1.1.13).
"Regarding this doubt concerning the deceased man—some say he exists, and others say he does not exist—may I be instructed by you in this; this is the third of my boons."
"Thus [ends] the question concerning the individual soul (jīva):

'Tell me that which you see as other than dharma and other than adharma, other than what has been done and what has not been done by us, and other than what has been and what is yet to be. (Kārikā 1.1.20)

The statement, "Thus [he spoke] regarding the Supreme Self" (Kāṭhaka Upaniṣad 1.2.14), concerns the Paramātman; the reply as well, "He told him about that Agni, the source of the worlds— how many bricks he has, or how they are arranged" (Kāṭhaka Upaniṣad 1.1.15), concerns Agni.
"Come, I shall declare to you this secret, eternal Brahman,
and how the self becomes [otherwise] upon reaching death, O Gautama. Some embodied beings enter a womb for the sake of assuming a body."
"Others follow the Post, according to their karma and according to their learning" (Kauṣītaki Upaniṣad 2.5.6–7).
This refers, by way of interruption, to the individual soul (jīva):
"The wise one is neither born nor does he die" (Kauṣītaki Upaniṣad 1.2.18).
Thus, there is an extensive elaboration concerning the Supreme Self;
however, there is no such question regarding the Pradhāna. And because it was not asked, it is not to be introduced [into the discussion].

Here he asks: Is this very question concerning the self— namely, "There is this doubt regarding a person after death"— being drawn back again as "Apart from dharma, apart from adharma," or is a different, entirely new question being raised?
What follows from this? If it were argued that this very same question is being reintroduced,

then because two questions concerning the Self would result in becoming one— the question concerning fire and the question concerning the Self— it should not have been stated that there is a presentation of three questions.

If it should be argued that "this is another unprecedented question being raised," then just as there is no fault in assuming a question apart from the granting of the boons, so too there would be no fault in assuming the introduction of *pradhāna* (primordial matter) apart from a question.
To this, it is replied: We do not at all assume any question here apart from the granting of the boons, because of the force of the opening of the passage.
Indeed, from the beginning of the granting of boons until its conclusion, the discourse in the Kaṭha Upaniṣads is observed to take the form of a dialogue between Mṛtyu and Naciketas.
It is said that Mṛtyu granted three boons to Naciketas, who had been sent by his father. Naciketas, it is said, chose benevolence as the first of those boons.
By the second [question] he asks about the knowledge of fire (agnividya), and by the third, the knowledge of the Self (ātmavidya),
as indicated by the words "That which [exists] when one has died" and "This is the third of the boons" (Kauṣītaki Upaniṣad 1.1.20).

In that regard, if this new question—"Is he other than dharma?"—were raised as something distinct, then the statement would be contradicted by the assumption of a question even apart from the granting of the boon.
[Objection: But surely this must be a new question because of the difference in what is to be asked;
for the previous question had the individual soul (jīva) as its subject matter.

This doubt regarding the deceased—namely, the doubt as to whether a human being exists or does not exist—is expressed by the term "vicikitsā. Furthermore, the *jīva* (the living soul) deserves the question "Is it other than dharma and so forth? because it is the object of the domain of dharma and the like; however, the wise one, having transcended dharma and the like, deserves the question "Is it other than dharma and so forth? because he is beyond them.
Furthermore, the shadow of the two questions is not seen to be the same;
for the former has existence and non-existence as its object, whereas the latter has past entities such as the *dharmas* as its object.
Therefore, due to the absence of recognition [between them], there is a difference between the questions.
If it is argued that there is no carrying forward of the preceding [subject] into the subsequent [question], we say no;

for the oneness of the individual soul (jīva) and the supreme conscious one (prājña) is admitted. There would be a distinction between the questions due to a distinction in what is to be asked only if the individual soul were different from the supreme conscious one.
However, there is no difference [between them],
based on other scriptural passages such as "That thou art" (tattvamasi).

Furthermore, in this context, the answer to the question "Is it other than dharma?"— namely, "The wise one is neither born nor dies"— establishes the non-difference between the embodied soul and the Supreme Lord by means of the negation of birth and death.
It demonstrates this:
for a negation is meaningful only when there is a possibility [of the claim being made].
And the possibility of birth and death through contact with a body belongs to the embodied soul (*śārīra*), not to the Supreme Lord (*parameśvara*).
Likewise: "The wise person does not grieve, having realized the great, all-pervading Self by which one perceives both the state of dreaming and the state of waking."

(Kārikā 2.4.4) Thus, by showing that the cessation of sorrow occurs through the contemplation of the individual soul (*jīva*)—which is characterized by greatness and omnipresence and is the seer in both the dreaming and waking states—it demonstrates that the *jīva* is not other than the *prājña*.
For the established doctrine of the Vedānta is that the cessation of sorrow results from the realization of the *prājña*.
Likewise, further on: "What is here, that is there; what is there, that is likewise here."

"He goes from death to death who perceives here as if there were multiplicity" (Kaṭha Upaniṣad 2.4.10); thus [the text] refutes the view of a distinction between the individual soul (*jīva*) and the supreme conscious being (*prājña*).

Likewise, immediately following the question regarding the existence or non-existence of the individual soul, Death, though attempting to entice Naciketas with various desires beginning with the words "Choose another boon, O Naciketas," [is rebuffed].

When he did not waver, Death approached him, [addressing him] by demonstrating the distinction between the higher and lower goals and by demonstrating the distinction between knowledge and ignorance: "I consider Naciketas to be one who desires knowledge; many desires did not distract you" (Katha Upaniṣad 1.2.4).

Having thus praised [the questioner] and commending his very question, he said: "The wise man, having realized through the attainment of the yoga of the supreme self that ancient God—who is difficult to see, entered into the secret, placed in the cave, dwelling in the abyss—casts off both joy and sorrow."

Thus, it is understood from this as well that the non-difference (*abheda*) of the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Supreme Lord (*prājña*) is precisely what is intended here. Furthermore, if Naciketas, having received great praise from Death for the reason of his question, were to set that aside and propose another question immediately after the praise,
then all that praise would have been extended out of place.
Therefore, the phrase "other than dharma" is a restatement of that very question, "That which one knows after death.
As for the objection raised regarding the difference in the form of the questions, that is no fault;
for it is precisely that same specific point which is being asked again.
For in the former [passage], the existence of the Self as distinct from the body and so forth was questioned, whereas in the latter, its state of being beyond saṃsāra is questioned.
As long as ignorance does not cease, the individual soul's (jīva) status as a transmigrating being and its being the object of dharma and the like do not cease.
But upon the cessation of that [ignorance], it is realized through the scriptural text "That thou art" (tat tvam asi) that it is indeed the Prājña (the Supreme Consciousness).
Furthermore, there is no difference whatsoever in the nature of the object itself between its state when it is possessed by ignorance and its state when that ignorance has been removed.
For example, suppose someone, seeing a rope fallen in thick darkness, mistakes it for a snake; terrified and trembling, he flees.
Then another person says to him, "Do not be afraid! This is not a snake; it is merely a rope."
And upon hearing that, he would abandon the fear produced by the snake, as well as his trembling and flight;
yet there would be no difference whatsoever in the object itself between the time when it was perceived as a snake and the time when that perception had vanished.
This case should be understood in exactly the same way.
Consequently, even such passages as "It is neither born nor does it die" serve as answers to the question regarding existence.
However, the Sūtra must be interpreted with reference to the distinction between the individual soul (jīva) and the conscious principle (prājña), which is imagined through ignorance.

For, although the subject of the question concerns the oneness of the Self, in the previous section there was merely a doubt concerning the existence of something distinct from the body at the time of death, and there was no removal of the nature of transmigratory existence, such as agency and so forth.
It is surmised that the former refers to the individual soul (jīva),
whereas the latter, because it mentions the transcendence of dharma and so forth, refers to the conscious one (prājña).
Consequently, the conceptualization of fire, the individual soul, and the supreme self is appropriate.
But in the case of the postulation of Pradhāna, there would be an inconsistency: there would be neither the granting of boons, nor the question, nor the answer. [Note:
Since Death said to Naciketas, "Choose three boons," Naciketas asked questions regarding exactly those three, and Death provided the corresponding explanations.]

"O Death, you who have granted me a boon, do you remember the fire that was for the sake of heaven? When one has departed—meaning when dead—is there another [self] distinct from the body? There is this doubt. Therefore, the meaning is: may I know this reality of the self without uncertainty."
"Śrutamupanyāsam" means that whose commencement has the granting of a boon as its primary subject. "Prahitāya" means sent toward the realm of Yama.
Because it is the object of experience and because it is the basis,
it is logically connected [to the term];
"end" refers to a state.
The connection is that by means of which witness the knower perceives, that is the Self.
Whatever consciousness exists here in this body, that very same exists there in the sun and so forth.
The meaning is: setting aside that which is the subject of the question, that is, the question itself.
The word "iti" marks the conclusion of the specific statement (viśeṣokti).
Furthermore, he states that the Pradhāna is not included here because there is no question or answer regarding it in this Kaṭhavallī; thus he says, "of the three.
When Mṛtyu said to Naciketas, "Choose three boons," Naciketas made his inquiry concerning those three alone.
And the presentation was made by Death;
the meaning is that it was not by anyone else.
He recites the three questions in sequence, beginning with "In that regard, first... and so on.
O Death, you who have granted me boons, do you remember the fire that is the cause of heaven? When one has departed, when one has died,
there is a doubt as to whether there exists something other than the body.
The meaning is: "Therefore, may I know this reality of the Self without doubt.
He states the next three [questions] in sequence, beginning with the reply: "The answer also...
Because the Virāj-self is to be meditated upon as the cause of the worlds, the fire-altar consisting of the worlds and so forth was described by Death to Naciketas.

The meaning is that he stated everything regarding how, in what manner, by what nature, to what extent, and in what sequence the fire-altar is constructed. The point is that, by the statement "Come now, I shall speak of Brahman," the passage beginning with "And as one attains death" is the answer concerning the individual soul (jīva), even though it was separated from the question about the soul by the discourse on Brahman, because it is appropriate [to that context].

As for the meaning of the sentence: "I shall explain how the self becomes after reaching death. He states what was promised with the words "yonim" (the womb). He states the cause for attaining the bodies of moving and non-moving beings with the word "yathā" (as).
"Śruta" means "reverential meditation.
In the Sūtra, the first *ca* (and) has the sense of "because.
Thus, since only these three are presented and questioned, the construction is: "Therefore, the Unmanifest is not the Pradhāna."
He introduces a sutra regarding the point already stated with the words "here he says.
He asks what follows from two alternative positions—whether there is one question or two questions—with the words "And what [follows] from this" (*kiñcātaḥ*).
Here, the suffix *tasi* is used in the sense of the locative case (*saptamī-arthe*).

And here, in both of these two positions, the meaning is "why? The proponent of the prima facie view (pūrvavādī) states, beginning with "That very [one]... that if the question is identical, there is a lack of consistency with the Sūtra; whereas if there is a difference, the status of Pradhāna as being based on scripture (śrautatva) is established.
Taking the position that the question is identical, the proponent of the final view (siddhāntin) says: "To this, it is replied."
The ellipsis is "by which the primary accomplishment would occur.
He explains that if one were to assume a fourth question, there would be a contradiction with the introduction concerning the three boons, using the words "vara" and so forth;
that is, she is the one whose introduction consists of the granting of boons.

"To him who has been sent forth"—that is, dispatched toward the world of Yama—"and who has returned here again from that world to the mortal realm, may my father be as well-disposed as before"; thus he first chose this boon.

To the objection, "Why should there not be a distinction between the questions, such that the second boon is the science of life (*jīvavidyā*) and the third is the science of Brahman (*brahmavidyā*)?", he replies with the words, "This which... [and so on].

The meaning is that, because the statement "the third" occurs after beginning with the word *prete* (when the body has perished), the third boon is indeed the knowledge of the individual self (*jīvātman*).
Since this is the case at the commencement of the passage, he says "therein" (*tatra*) to show that another question is not appropriate.

He raises an objection with the words "But surely" (*nanu*), etc., suggesting that since there is a distinction between the individual self and the Lord (*īśvara*)—as indicated by the marks of being untouched by the nature of death and so forth—the distinction between the two questions is established, and thus the [alleged] contradiction of the passage is justified.

Because they are the objects of experience and because they are the bases [of cognition], the difference in questions is not due solely to a difference in what is to be asked, but also because of the lack of similarity between the two question-phrases; thus he says, "by way of the shadow of the question. He refutes the claim that the difference in what is to be asked is unestablished with the words beginning with "no," and so forth.

Furthermore, by negating birth and other attributes in response to Brahmā’s question while describing the true nature of the individual soul (jīva), Yama indicates the identity of the two; thus he says, "here and elsewhere.
To the objection that the statement of Śiva regarding that negation is unproven, he replies, "being" (satī);
[the word] *bhāgin* means "endowed with" or "connected with."
Therefore, the meaning is that the true nature of the individual soul (jīva) has been stated by negating birth and so forth as attained through ignorance.
Furthermore, the individual soul is non-different from Brahman,
because it is the object of the knowledge that is the cause of liberation.
He says "like Brahman" and "so in dream";
*anta* means state.
The connection is: that Witness by whom the knower perceives, [one should know] Him as the Self.
Having raised the objection that the reason is inconclusive, he states the contradiction with the Śruti, "Only by knowing Him," using the word *prājña*.
Furthermore, since difference is censured after non-difference has been declared, he says *tathā* (so it is), meaning that non-difference alone is real;
for the consciousness that exists here in this body is the very same as that which exists there in the sun and so forth.

Thus, the meaning is that he who perceives a false multiplicity as if it were real within this Brahman, which is indivisible and of a single essence, is a "seer of difference" (bhedadarśī); he goes from death to death and is not liberated from the fear of saṃsāra.

Furthermore, the connection is that non-difference is understood through the answer He gave immediately after the question concerning the individual soul (jīva), namely, "Him, who is difficult to see.

He states that the status of [the Self] as Brahman is established by the sign of praising both the questioner and the question itself, which indicates the extreme rarity of what was asked, beginning with the words "another boon," and so forth.

Even when told, "Choose sons and the like," Naciketas did not waver from the knowledge of the Self, having rendered sense-objects contemptible; for it is heard in scripture: "Naciketas chose nothing other than that.

Then Yama, being satisfied, declared the distinction between the paths of worldly enjoyment and liberation by saying, "One is better, and the other indeed is dearer," and then demonstrated this by stating, "Far apart and leading in opposite directions are these two: ignorance and what is knowledge. This is the meaning.
*Preyas* is that which is most dear, such as heaven and the like; *viṣūcī* refers to those with contrary fruits,
namely ignorance (*avidyā*) and ritual action (*karman*).
Knowledge is the realization of reality.

I consider you to be one who desires knowledge— that is, one who seeks knowledge— because even though many objects of desire, such as sons and the like, were offered by me to you, and though they were difficult to obtain, they did not cause you to become greedy.

The literal meaning [of the verse] is that, having praised the questioner by saying "you have not made him greedy," he further praises the question itself by saying, "O Naciketas, may you be such a questioner as this.
He states, "yatpraśna... (regarding which question), because this praise would not be appropriate under the view that the questions are distinct.
The meaning is that if, after receiving praise for a question, one were to set aside that very question and raise another instead, then the praises would be rendered out of context.
"Therefore" means because there is no difference in the subject matter to be questioned.

He refutes the claim that there is a difference between the two questions because of the lack of similarity between the question and its explicit statement by saying "As for what [was said]," and so forth. To the question, "How can the individual soul (jīva), which is the substratum of attributes such as dharma, be Brahman? he replies with the words "as long as...

He further says, "nor is there the state of possessing ignorance," in order to show that if the state of being Brahman were to occur only after the destruction of ignorance, it would be adventitious and impermanent.

He shows the advantage that, since the identity of the individual soul (*jīva*) with Brahman is innate, the answer given to the question regarding Brahman also serves as the answer to the question regarding the individual soul—this is expressed by the words "And therefore, it is not born. To the objection, "If there is oneness of the individual soul and Brahman, how then is the Sūtra [B.S. 1.4.6] which speaks of 'the three' to be understood?", he replies: "But the Sūtra...
He states that the distinction between the questions is merely a conceptual construction based on the imagined distinction [between the two], saying: "And therefore..."

The sense is that because the *pradhāna* is distinct from the Supreme Self (*paramātman*) by virtue of being non-self (*anātmatva*), it is impossible for it to be included within the third boon. //6//
And there is the mention of the "Great One" (mahat). BBs_1,4.7.

Just as the word "Great" (*mahat*), though employed by the Sāṃkhyas for the first-born [evolute] which is mere existence (*sattāmātra*), does not denote that same thing even when used in Vedic application—
as in "The Self of the intellect is the Great One beyond" (*Kāṭhaka Upaniṣad* 1.3.10) and "The great, all-pervading Self" (*Kāṭhaka Upaniṣad* 1.2.22).
Because of reasons such as the use of the word "Self" (ātman) in passages beginning with, "I know this great Person" (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 3.8),
the term "unmanifest" (avyakta) likewise cannot denote the Pradhāna in Vedic usage.
And for this reason, this inferential [cognition] does not possess the nature of verbal testimony. // 7 //

He says "and like the word 'mahat'" (mahadvacca), meaning that the Vedic term *avyakta* does not have as its object the specific principles (tattva) unique to the Sāṃkhya system, because it is a Vedic word, just like the word *mahat*.
He explains the Sūtra with the words "Just as," and so forth.

Furthermore, it should be understood that there is no deviation (vyabhicāra) regarding terms such as "space" (ākāśa), because space and the like are common to other philosophical systems; thus, they cannot be established as being unique to the Sāṃkhya, and since the probandum (sādhya) also exists [in those cases], [the reason is not inconclusive].
"In mere existence" means in the primordial transformation of primordial nature (prakṛti), which has existence as its primary quality;
that is to say, in non-conceptual cognition (nirvikalpaka-buddhi).

The connection [of the passage] is as follows: because of the use of the word "Self" (*ātman*) in the phrase "the Self is great," and because of the transcendence of grief and the state of being beyond darkness in such passages as "having known Him, one does not grieve" and "beyond darkness," the word "great" (*mahat*) does not denote the Sāṃkhya principle.
He concludes the subject of the discussion with the words: "And therefore" (ataśca) //7//

Just as the *unnetṛ* is not a separate person but is included among the four principal priests, so too the *chamasādhvaryus* are included among them. Furthermore, the term "cup-priest" (*chamasādhvaryu*) is a descriptive compound (*karmadhāraya*) meaning "the cup-priest who is an *adhvaryu*," and thus it does not denote a distinct office. "Like the *camasa* [cup], because there is no distinction.
(BBs 1.4.8) Furthermore, the proponent of *pradhāna* states that the scriptural non-mention of *pradhāna* remains unestablished.
Why?
From the wording of the mantra: "The one unborn female, red, white, and black, producing many offspring of similar form;
the one unborn male lies beside her, enjoying her, while another unborn male leaves her after she has been enjoyed" (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 4.5).
For in this mantra, the words red, white, and black denote the qualities of rajas, sattva, and tamas respectively.
The red quality is *rajas* because its nature is to color;
the white quality is *sattva* because its nature is luminosity; the black quality is *tamas* because its nature is to obscure.
That [Prakṛti] is designated by the qualities (dharmas) of its constituent parts in their state of equilibrium as "red, white, and black.
Furthermore, it may be called "Unborn" (ajā),
because it is accepted that "the root-primal nature (mūlaprakṛti) is not a modification."

and although there exists the state of being gross primordial matter (sthūlaprakṛti) in the five subtle elements (tanmātras),
nevertheless, since the eternal Self and Ākāśa are mentioned separately [from them], the five— sattva, rajas, tamas, mahat, and ahaṅkāra— must be established as distinct categories.
The intention is that within this pair of pentads—the mind and the five elements—there exists no property that either conforms to or excludes the other pentad.
To the objection that such a property might not exist, he says: "by which."
The meaning is "by means of the dharma.
He clarifies this with the words "for not," [showing that] intermediate numbers enter into a great number.

Just as in the expression "the two Aśvins, the seven Ṛṣis, and the eight Vasus—thus seventeen," the numbers two and so forth enter [into the total] by taking the specific qualities such as being an Aśvin;
it cannot be otherwise. This is the meaning.

He raises an objection with an example, beginning with "Now" (*atha*), suggesting that by means of the two words "five," which denote a number smaller than their own referent, the larger number pervaded by them is actually indicated through secondary signification (*lakṣaṇā*).
He refutes [the objection] that "since the primary meaning will be stated later, figurative indication (lakṣaṇā) is not appropriate" with the words "that too is not so.
Previously, by accepting the non-compounding of the two words *pañca* and *jana*, the perception of the number twenty-five was rejected;
now he says "and moreover," stating that because the compound is certain, there is no such perception.
He states the reason for this compound by saying "by means of technical terminology.
This is the meaning: in this mantra, the first word *pañca* has its initial vowel accented (udātta), while the second is entirely unaccented (anudātta).
Furthermore, the word *jana* has its final syllable accented (*antodātta*).

Thus, without a compound of the words *dvitīya*, *pañca*, and *jana*, it would not be possible for the final vowel *a* to be accented while the preceding vowels remain unaccented; for by the rule *asamāsasya*, the final syllable of a non-compound is prescribed as accented, and by the rule *anudāttaṃ padamekavarjam*, in a word where there is an acute (*udātta*) or circumflex (*svarita*) accent on a particular phoneme, [all other phonemes in that word are unaccented].

By the very injunction that "with the exception of that one [syllable] which is prescribed as such, the remainder of that word becomes unaccented (anudātta)," the fact of its being a single word is determined by the mantra's own final udātta accent. However,

in the *Bhāṣika*— the treatise prescribing the accentuation for the *Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa*— an exception is adopted in the rule "svarito 'nudātto vā," according to which whatever was unaccented or circumflex (svarita) in the state of a mantra becomes udātta in the state of a Brāhmaṇa.
Thus, by the rule "the final [vowel] is acute, [and] the preceding [vowels] are grave," it follows that in the state of Brahman, the vowels preceding the final vowel would attain acuteness; however,
according to the sūtra "the final [vowel] is grave [if it is acute]," acuteness is prescribed for the final vowel in the state of a mantra when it is pronounced as joined with what follows,
and consequently, the vowel *ā* following the final *na*, being recited in conjunction with the word *ākāśaḥ*, becomes grave.
This term "final-udātta accent" is technical; by means of it, the status of being a single word is determined through the Brāhmaṇa accent.
However, the author of the *Prakaṭārtha* has explained that the final-udātta accent well-known among reciters (*pāṭhaka*) is the technical term.
That explanation was refuted by the author of the *Kalpataru*.
Since the reciters study the word *pañcajana* with the final syllable unaccented (*antānudātta*), the claim that this is merely a matter of established usage among readers is unfounded.

Thus, there is a distinction: the accentuation in the mantra "pañca pañcajanāḥ" has the acute (*udātta*) on the final syllable, whereas in the Brāhmaṇa passage "yasmin pañca pañcajanāḥ," the accentuation has the grave (*anudātta*) on the final syllable.
In both cases, the formation of a compound is established because it constitutes a single word.
He states that it is a single word also because of its usage in the *Taittirīyaka*: "And in another usage," etc.

The remainder of the mantra for taking the clarified butter (*ājya*) is: "O clarified butter, I take you for the support—that is, for the sustenance—of the five *pañcajanas*, who are specific classes of deities."

The body of the deities, which is established in the mechanism of their activity (*karma-yantre*), is itself the *dhartram* (the support) here, serving as the substratum for the enjoyment of [their] enemies;

"for that" means for the sake of its non-deficiency—this is the statement of the sacrificer (*yajamāna*). To the question, "Let there be this compound; what follows from it?", he says: "And because of being fully satisfied."

The meaning is that repetition (*vīpsā*) is the intended exclusion; for in its absence, because there is no apprehension of two groups of five, the cognition of the number twenty-five remains unestablished.
The literal meaning of the words is as follows: one group of five is the first "five," and another group of five is the second "five"; thus, there is no apprehension of them as "five times five.
Furthermore, even under the view that this is not a compound (*asamāsa*), is there a mutual connection between the two fivenesses expressed by the two occurrences of the word "five"?
Or rather, is there a connection between those two and pure persons, or is there a connection of another "fiveness" with persons characterized by the state of being five?
It is not the first case; thus he says: "Nor [is there a connection] of the number five... and so forth.

The qualifier is the *anvaya* (syntactic connection). He states the reason for this non-connection (*ananvaya*) with the words "of the subordinate" (*upasarjanasya*). It must be stated that all subordinate elements are connected only with the principal element, which is the qualificand (*viśeṣya*).
The meaning is that there would be a mutual connection of the qualities [only] if it resulted in a split of the sentence (*vākyabheda*).
In the second case, there would be the cognition of the number ten, not the cognition of the number twenty-five. He raises the third alternative with "But surely... (*nanu*).

The meaning is that when "five-ness" (pañcatva) is connected to those things already qualified by five-ness, because "five-ness" is also connected to the "five-ness" that serves as the qualifier, there arises the cognition of "twenty-five.
He refutes this by pointing out the disparity with the example, saying, "We say no.
In the case of the compound *pañcānāṃ pūlānāṃ samāhāraḥ* ("the collection of five bundles"), the formation of the compound is prescribed by the rule *saṃkhyāpūrvo dviguḥ*.

The meaning is this: because the suffix *ṅīp* is prescribed by the rule "tato 'dvigoḥ" (*Pāṇini 4.1.22*), when there is a comprehension of a collective (*samāhāra*), and when the expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) arises as to how many those collectives are, it is appropriate for the word "five" (*pañca*) to be construed with another word [as a qualifier].

However, in the case of "pañcajanāḥ," since the feminine suffix *ṅīp* is absent, a collective is not perceived; furthermore, because the number five is already attributed to the "people" (*jana*) from the outset, there is no expectancy for a number. Thus, the word "five" is not construed [with "people"], because syntactic connection (*anvaya*) is dependent upon such expectancy.

"Differentiation" (*bheda*) means a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*). Now, one might object: "Even if people have no further expectation, there may still be an expectation as to how many there are of those five which serve as qualifiers; therefore, let another 'fiveness' (*pañcatva*) serve as a qualifier. Anticipating this, he says, "Even though it exists... He answers by stating that there is no contradiction with the rule regarding non-qualifiers (*nopasarjana-nyāya*), for he maintains that a non-qualifier does not connect with another non-qualifier, but only with the principal element (*pradhāna*); thus he says, "In that case... and so forth.
Having thus explained [the argument] by way of "diversity" (*nānābhāvāt*), he explains it by way of "excess" (*atirekāt*) with the words beginning "and because of excess.
Excess means surplus.
Is the self included among the twenty-five principles denoted by the word "people" (*jana*), or is it not?
Having stated "not today," he points out the fault in the second [alternative] with the words "in another object" (*arthāntara*).
Likewise, having conceptualized space, he refutes it with the word "similarly" (*tathā*).
The fault already mentioned is the excess of number (*saṃkhyādhikya*).
The meaning is that there would be a total number of twenty-seven, consisting of the twenty-five principles (tattvas), the self (ātman), and space (ākāśa).
Nor should it be argued that this [number] is intended by counting sattva, rajas, and tamas separately,
because it would be redundant for space to be mentioned separately [if it were already included].
In that eternal Self, the establishment of the principles (tattvas) would contradict the scriptural statement, because in your view, the independent Pradhāna itself has no substratum;
furthermore, it would contradict the supplementary passage, "There is no diversity here," since you are an advocate of true non-duality (satyadvaitavādin).
Moreover, even if the number twenty-five were perceived, the Sāṅkhya principles would not be grasped; thus he asks, "And how? (kathaṃ ca).
Does the apprehension of reality arise from the word "person" (*jana*), or by means of its number? Such is the meaning of the word "how" (*katham*).
He states that it is not the first case with the words "not [from] 'person'"; he states that it is not the second case with the words "to another object" (*arthāntara*).
"What is that other referent for which this sentence has meaning?"—thus he asks, "How so?

First, he states that among the various types of compounds such as *karmadhāraya*, the *saṃjñā* (proper name) compound is stronger based on the statement of an authoritative source (*āptokti*), saying: "It is said.
Words denoting direction and words denoting number are compounded with a following word ending in a case-suffix when a proper name is intended.
As in the examples "the southern fire" (dakṣiṇāgniḥ) and "the seven sages" (saptarṣayaḥ), and so forth; and this compound is a variety of the tatpuruṣa. //11//
Who, then, are those who are called the "five peoples"? To this it is said:
"Prāṇa and the others [are the five], because of the supplementary passage.

(BBs 1.4.12) In the mantra following "In whom the five groups of five people [dwell]," five things beginning with prāṇa are specified for the purpose of defining the nature of Brahman: "The breath of breath, the eye of the eye, the ear of the ear, the food of food... (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.18).

"Those who know the mind of the mind"— it is these [beings] mentioned in the remainder of the sentence that are intended here as the "five people" (pañcajana) due to their proximity. But how can the word *jana* (person/being) be applied to the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) and so forth?

Or how could the word "people" (*jana*) be applied to the [subtle] principles (*tattva*)? Since the deviation from conventional usage is equal in both cases, it is by virtue of the remainder of the sentence that the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) and so forth alone must be understood. Furthermore, because of their connection with people, the vital breaths and so forth come to share the designation "people."
Furthermore, the word *puruṣa* is used for the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) in the passage, "These indeed are the five Brahman-puruṣas" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 3.13.6),
and there is the Brāhmaṇa text, "The vital breath is indeed the father; the vital breath is indeed the mother," and so forth.

And by virtue of the power of the compound, it is not contradictory for the word to have conventional meaning (*rūḍhatva*) as a whole. But how can conventional meaning be resorted to when there has been no prior usage?
He says: "It is possible, as in the case of words such as *udbhid*."
For when a word of unknown meaning is employed in proximity to a word of well-known meaning, its referent is restricted by that co-utterance (*samabhivyāhāra*),
as in the cases "one should sacrifice with the *udbhid*," "he cuts the sacrificial post (*yūpa*)," and "he prepares the altar (*vedī*).

Likewise, this term *pañcajana*, whose status as a technical name (*saṃjñā*) is understood from its grammatical derivation as a compound and which stands in need of a named object (*saṃjñin*), will apply to the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) and so forth mentioned in the remainder of the sentence with which it is co-uttered.

By some, however, the five *pañcajanāḥ* are explained as gods, ancestors, *gandharvas*, *asuras*, and *rakṣases*; by others, they are taken to be the four social classes (*varṇas*) with the *niṣādas* as the fifth; and in another instance, it says: "by the people (*viś*) consisting of the fivefold. (Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 8.53.7)

Thus, the application of the word *pañcajana* is seen as referring to the [five] classes of beings (*prajā*). Even if that interpretation were accepted here, there would be no contradiction whatsoever. However, the Teacher (Bādarāyaṇa) stated, "The breath and so forth [are the five], because of the supplementary passage," with the intention that there is no comprehension of the twenty-five principles here. || 12 || @----------------------
Note: The word *uta* has the sense of "also.
The meaning is that those who know the Self, which is the witness of that [Self] and the impeller of the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) and so forth, are the knowers of Brahman.
The word *jana* means a word denoting people; that is to say, the term *pañcajana*.
One born from a Brāhmaṇa father and a Śūdra mother is a Niṣāda.
Having stated that the word *pañcajana* is a technical designation (*saṃjñā*), he cites the Sūtra for the purpose of identifying those who bear that designation: "Who, then, are they?
In the Vedic text, the word *uta* has the sense of "also" (*api*).
The meaning is that those who know the Self as the witness of that [prāṇa] and so forth, which impels them, are the knowers of Brahman.
He raises an objection regarding the mode of application by which the word *pañcajana* is used for the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) and so forth: "But how?

He replies: "Just as for you the word *jana* is used figuratively for the *tattvas*, so for me the word *pañcajana* is used figuratively for the vital breaths and so forth," thus saying, "In the *tattvas*..."

If it is argued that, since the equality of deviating from conventional usage (rūḍhi) is the same in both cases, the [sixteen] principles themselves should be accepted, he says: "But when there is equality" (samāne tu).

The meaning is that only those established in the Śruti, which are immediate and independent of anything else of the same class, are to be accepted; not those established in Smṛti, which are remote and dependent on heterogeneous factors.
He states the connection [between the term] *pañcajana* and the seeds of the [five] characteristics (*lakṣaṇabīja*) with the word "jan" (*jana*). "Jana" is a synonym for "pañcajana.

Just as in the case of words such as *puruṣa* and *mitra*, it is logical that the word *pañcajana* indicates the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) and so forth; thus he says, "and it is a word denoting people (*janavacana*)."
One might object: "Are not the *mahat* and other principles called 'people' (*janāḥ*) because they are born?

And since the *pradhāna* is a 'producer' (*jana*), why resort to conventional meaning (*rūḍhi*)—thereby necessitating the effort of figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*)—when a literal etymological derivation (*yoga*) is possible? To this, he says: "In a compound...

The meaning is that, just as the word *aśvakarṇa*—which is a collection of phonemes—is conventionally established (*rūḍhi*) to mean a tree, so too the word *pañcajana* is purely conventional and does not consist of an etymological derivation based on the power of its constituent parts.
He raises an objection, saying "How so?", on the grounds that there is no conventional usage (*rūḍhi*) because of the absence of prior usage.
[The author replies: There is indeed usage in works such as the *Amarakośa*, which states, "The five classes of men (*pañcajanāḥ*) are males.
Even while conceding the absence of such usage, he says, "It is possible... (*śakyeti*).

In the previous commentary, it was stated that the word *pañcajana* has a conventional meaning (*rūḍhi*) among humans, and based on that, a figurative sense (*lakṣaṇā*) was applied to the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) and so forth.
However, here it should be understood that the conventional meaning itself is being asserted for the vital breaths and so forth as a bold argument (*prauḍhivāda*).
He explains this summary with the words beginning "well-known" (*prasiddha*).

Regarding the statement, "One desiring cattle should sacrifice with the *udbhid*," there arises a doubt as to whether the word *udbhid* signifies a quality (*guṇa*) to be enjoined or is the name of a ritual action (*karmanāmadheya*). Since the word *udbhid* is well-known in common usage for things such as a spade, it would contradict established usage if it were the name of a sacrifice; therefore, it is initially argued that it is an injunction of a quality within the *Jyotiṣṭoma*. However, the final conclusion (*rāddhānta*) is as follows: the meaning is "one should effect the desired result by means of a sacrifice" (*yajeta* = *yāgena iṣṭaṃ bhāvayet*). Thus, the sentence enjoins a sacrifice, and the word *udbhid* is its name. This is because, if it were a quality, it would necessitate the assumption of a new result (cattle) and a new instrument (the *udbhid*), whereas as a name, it merely serves to refer back to the sacrifice already known from the context. Furthermore, the name *udbhid* is justified by the fact that this sacrifice "pierces" (*udbhinatti*) or brings about the attainment of cattle. Therefore, the word *udbhid* is the name of the sacrifice.

Therefore, because the unfamiliar word *udbhidā* ending in the instrumental case is placed in grammatical apposition with the familiarly understood term *yāgena* (by means of sacrifice), it is determined to be the name of that [sacrifice]; for there is no contradiction with the established meaning that "it pierces" (i.e., accomplishes) cattle, and since it is impossible to enjoin a quality (*guṇavidhi*) in a sacrifice like the Jyotiṣṭoma which has already been performed,

and because enjoining it as a quality would entail the fault of metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*)— namely, connecting the sacrifice with the quality called *udbhid* through the sense of possession (*matvartha*)— the word *udbhid* is indeed the name of the ritual action.

Similarly, from its co-occurrence with words whose well-known meanings are suitable for cutting—such as "it cuts"—it is understood that the word *yūpa* (sacrificial post) refers to a specific type of wood; and from its co-occurrence with "he makes," it is understood that the word *vedi* (altar) refers to a specific prepared plot of ground suitable for consecration.

Likewise, the meaning is that the word *pañcajana* is determined to denote the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) and so forth, due to its co-occurrence with words whose meanings are well-established, such as "vital breath."
He states the two views of those who hold a partial position (ekadeśins) with the words "by some," and so forth.
A Niṣāda is one born from a Brāhmaṇa father and a Śūdra mother.
With the words "in some cases," he states another meaning for the term *pañcajana* according to the Veda (*śruti*).

The meaning is as follows: since one enters with the "pañcajanya" progeny, that progeny is called *viś* (the people); it is logical that sounds were created for the purpose of summoning Indra by means of that *viś* in the form of human beings, because it is impossible to summon Indra apart from sound. Thus, even if one takes "progeny" (*prajā*) in its general sense according to the Śruti, there is no contradiction. Anticipating the objection regarding a contradiction with the Sūtra, the Teacher says: "But the Teacher... (*ācāryastu*).
Therefore, the intention is that there is no contradiction in explaining the term *pañcajana* as referring to something other than the principles (*tattva*) of Sāṃkhya. //12//
The five "people" (pañcajana) might indeed be the vital breaths and so forth among the Mādhyandinas, who record food among the vital breaths and the rest.

But how could the five people (*pañcajana*) of the Kāṇvas be "breath and so forth" (*prāṇādayaḥ*), given that they do not mention food among breath and the rest? To this, he reads the following reply: "For some, [they are so] by means of light, since food is absent. (BBs 1.4.13)
Even if food were not present for the Kāṇvas, their number five would still be completed by means of light (*jyotis*).

For they too, in the mantra preceding "In whom the five sets of five people [dwell]," study light precisely for the purpose of defining the nature of Brahman: "That is the light of lights, which the gods worship.
But how is it that this light, being recited equally by both groups, is included in the number five by some, while by others it is not?
He says it is "due to a difference in requirement.

For the Mādhyandinas, because they obtain the five classes of beings (pañcajana) such as prāṇa and others recited in the same mantra, they have no requirement for the light (jyotis) recited in this other mantra.
However, because the Kāṇvas do not obtain that [light], they have a requirement for it.
Furthermore, due to a difference in perspective, there is both the inclusion and exclusion of *jyotis* even within the same mantra;
just as, despite the *Atirātra* sacrifice being identical, the *ṣoḍaśin* cup is either included or excluded based on a difference in scriptural statement (*vacana*), so it is here.
Thus, in this way, there is no established scriptural authority whatsoever regarding the existence of a primary principle (*pradhāna*).
As for the objections based on Smṛti and logical reasoning, they will be refuted later [in Sūtra 13].

Here, just as in the case of the optional inclusion or exclusion of the *ṣoḍaśin* cup, there is an option regarding the Jyotiṣṭoma due to the syntactical split (*vākya-bheda*). He takes up the Sūtra as a response to this doubt: "They might be... [Sūtra 12].
The meaning is that the gods worship that Brahman which is the light of lights, such as the sun and other luminaries.
Now, one might object: "But this light mentioned by the word *jyotis* ending in the genitive case exists in both recensions (śākhā) as the sun and so forth;

therefore, it is not logical to propose an alternative (vikalpa) that it is accepted by the Kāṇvas to complete the number five, but not by others. Thus he raises the doubt with the words, "How then? (*kathaṃ punar iti*).
The proponent of the established doctrine (siddhāntin) states "dependence" (*apekṣā*) to show that an option (*vikalpa*) is logical due to a specific requirement.

Just as in the case of the *atirātra* sacrifice, where there is an option—either "one takes the *ṣoḍaśin* cup" or "one does not take it"—due to the division of sentences, so too, by virtue of the presence or absence of the recitation in different Vedic branches (*śākhā*), there is an option regarding the *jyotis*.
[Objection: But surely an option is appropriate for an action (*kriyā*), not for a thing (*vastu*).
True.

Here too, according to the difference of Vedic recensions (śākhā), there is the possibility of an alternative interpretation in the act of meditation—that one should contemplate with the mind that place where the five [elements], beginning with breath, are established, either together with Sāman or together with Light; thus, what was stated regarding the unscriptural nature of Pradhāna is faultless. He concludes this with the words "Thus, therefore."
Nevertheless, because it is argued that the Pradhāna alone is the cause of the world on the basis of both Smṛti and reasoning, he says: "Smṛti... (Sūtra 1.1.13).
