The Section Concerning Being the Cause (Kāraṇatvādhikaraṇa). Sūtras 14–15.
And because of the statement regarding space and so forth as being causes in accordance with what has been taught [in the scriptures],
the definition of Brahman has been established,
and the uniformity of the purport of the Vedānta passages concerning Brahman has been established.
And it has been established that the Pradhāna is not denoted by the words [of the Vedas].

To this, another objection is raised: it is not possible to understand either that Brahman is the cause of birth and so forth, or that there is a uniformity of purport (*gatisāmānya*) among the Vedānta passages concerning Brahman.
Why?
Because of the observation of contradictions;
for in each Vedānta text, a different account of creation is found due to the diversity of sequences and other details.
For instance, in one place it says: "From the Self, space was produced" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.1).
Thus, the creation beginning with space is recorded in some places; in others, it begins with fire, as in "It created fire" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.2.3);
and in others, it begins with breath, as in "It created breath, and from breath, faith" (Praśna Upaniṣad 6.4).
Thus, in some places the origin of the worlds is recorded as occurring without any sequence: "He created these worlds:
water, light-rays, death, and waters" (Aitareya Upaniṣad 4.2.1).
Likewise, in other places creation preceded by non-existence is taught: "In the beginning, this was indeed non-existent; from that, truly, the existent was born" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.7).
And [it is said]: "In the beginning, this was indeed non-existent; that became existent; that developed" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 3.19.1).

In some places, by refuting the doctrine of non-existence (asat-vāda), the process of creation is affirmed as being preceded by existence: beginning with "On this point, some say that in the beginning this was indeed non-existent," [the text continues] "But how indeed, my dear, could it be so? He said: How could the existent be born from the non-existent? (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.2.2).
"In the beginning, my dear, this was indeed Being alone" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.2.1, 2);

in another place, the evolution of the world is described as having itself as its own agent: "In the beginning, this was indeed undifferentiated; it was differentiated by name and form" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.4.7).

Since there are thus various contradictions and since a conceptual alternative regarding a real entity is untenable, it is not logical that the Vedānta texts have as their primary purpose the determination of the cause of the world.
Since it is established by both scripture and reasoning that there must be the acceptance of another cause [for the world], this being the position reached, we reply:
although there is a discrepancy regarding the order and other details concerning the ether and so forth created in each Vedānta text, there is no discrepancy whatsoever regarding the Creator.
Why?
Because it is designated as being exactly as described.

For just as in one Vedānta text the omniscient, omnipotent, universal self, unique and without a second, is designated as the cause, so too is He designated in other Vedānta texts in that very same way;
for example: "Brahman is truth, knowledge, and infinite" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.1).

In this context, first, by means of the word "knowledge" (jñāna) and by the subsequent statement regarding its object—namely, its being the desirer [of desires]—he characterized Brahman as conscious; and by stating that it is not dependent on another, he declared the Lord to be the cause.

Furthermore, by means of the subsequent word "Self" (ātman) referring to that very same subject, and by describing the process of entering into the interior through the succession of sheaths beginning with the body, he established it as the innermost Self (pratyagātman) within all. [This is seen in the passage:
"May I become many, may I be born forth. (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.6)
Thus, by praising the benefit of becoming manifold with reference to the Self, [the text] declared the non-difference of the created modifications from their creator.

Likewise, by the instruction regarding the creation of the entire world in the passage, "He created all this, whatever exists here" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.6), it declares the creator to have been without a second prior to creation.

Therefore, that very same characteristic by which Brahman is known as the cause here is known elsewhere as well: "In the beginning, this was indeed Being, one only, without a second; it thought, 'May I be many, may I grow forth';
it created fire" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.2.1, 3).

Likewise, there is the passage: "In the beginning, this universe was indeed the Self alone; there was nothing else whatsoever, not even a blinking thing. He thought: 'Let me now create the worlds'" (Aitareya Upaniṣad 1.1.1, 2).
Since such a collection of passages, which define the nature of the cause, is consistent in its meaning across every Vedānta text, [the conclusion follows].

However, a discrepancy regarding the effect is observed in some places, such as the creation beginning with ether (*ākāśa*) in one instance and beginning with fire (*tejas*) in another; that is, discrepancies of this kind are seen.
Yet, it cannot be argued that because of such discrepancies concerning the effect, the cause—Brahman—is not intended to be understood as non-discrepant across all Vedānta texts.
For that would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
And the Teacher [Śaṅkara] will resolve even the disagreement regarding the subject of the effect, beginning with the sūtra "Not so, because of the non-hearing [of ether]" (Brahma-sūtra 2.3.1).
Even if there were disagreement concerning the effect, it would not matter, because it is not what is intended to be taught;
for this manifold expansion of creation and so forth is not what is sought to be established.
For no human goal (puruṣārtha) is seen or heard anywhere as being dependent upon that [meditation on the individual self]; nor can such a dependence be postulated,
because it is understood from the beginning and the conclusion that those various passages concerning the individual self form a single syntactical unity with the sentences whose subject is Brahman.

And it demonstrates that the manifold expansion of creation and so forth serves the purpose of realizing Brahman: "Seek, my dear, the root of water by means of food as the sprout; seek, my dear, the root of fire by means of water as the sprout; seek, my dear, the root of Being by means of fire as the sprout" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.8.4).
Furthermore, it is understood that the manifold expansion of creation and so forth is taught through analogies such as clay in order to declare the non-difference of the effect from its cause.

And thus those who know the tradition say: "The creation described in various ways through examples such as clay, iron, and sparks is a means for [understanding] the descent [of the Absolute]; there is no difference whatsoever."
(Māṇḍūkya 3.15).
However, the fruit connected with the realization of Brahman is heard in scripture: "The knower of Brahman attains the Supreme" (Taittirīya 2.1);
"The knower of the Self crosses over sorrow" (Chāndogya 7.1.3).
"Only by knowing Him does one go beyond death" (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 3.8).

And this result is directly perceived when the realization of the Self as non-transmigrating occurs through the instruction "That thou art," because the transmigrating nature of the Self is thereby sublated. // 14 //
Note: By the inclusion of the word "etc. (*ādi*), non-sequential order is also understood.
The meaning of the word "water" (*ambhas*) is the heavenly world, which abounds in bodies consisting of water.
The intermediate space (*antarikṣa*) world, pervaded by the rays of the sun, is "rays" (*marīci*).
*Mara* means one subject to death; *martya* means mortal.
"Abundant waters" refers to the waters in the netherworld (*pātālaloka*), according to the meaning of the Vedic revelation (*śruti*).
*Prakriyā* means creation (*sṛṣṭi*).
In that regard, concerning that cause,
some outsiders [hold this view] with respect to that object, namely, the object of Brahman.
"Acting while looking on" means possessing activity;
this is because it does not contradict the meaning [of the term].
"By the sprout" refers to the effect.
The repetition "in one way and another" (*anyathānyathā*) is to be understood as an intensive distributive sense.
This is for the purpose of entry [into the teaching] and for the generation of the cognition of Brahman;
therefore, even though there is a difference in those [appearances], there is no division in Brahman.
There is no contradiction regarding the object of knowledge.

Furthermore, because space and so forth are designated as such by being stated to function as causes, [the author] restates what has preceded in order to explain the connection with the present passage, saying: "It has been established."

By means of the three preceding sections, it has been established through the demonstration that the Pradhāna is not based on the Śruti—that Brahman alone, characterized as the cause of the world, is present in the mind; and that the Vedāntas have their systematic unity (*samanvaya*) in that very same non-differentiated Brahman which is present in the mind.
In this regard, the objection is raised that the definition (*lakṣaṇa*) and the systematic unity (*samanvaya*) are indeed unestablished.
He states the connection of this [section] with the words "In that context" (*tatra*), in response to the objection that it arises from observing contradictions among the *śrutis*.
Nor should it be said that the investigation of non-contradiction has no connection with this chapter because it belongs to the second chapter;
for once the concordant harmony (*samanvaya*) is established, the removal of contradictions with other means of knowledge such as *smṛti* constitutes the subject matter of the second chapter.

Since there is a mutual contradiction among the Śrutis that propound the cause of the world as the literal meaning (*vācyārtha*) of the term "That" (*tat*), and since the lack of determination regarding the literal meaning results in the failure to establish the concordance (*samanvaya*) with the indicated sense (*lakṣya*), the investigation into non-contradiction—which establishes that [concordance]—is appropriately situated right here.
Nor should it be argued that the non-contradiction of the Śrutis concerning creation should likewise be investigated right here;
for in the case of a creation imagined like a dream, there is simply no contradiction at all.
Why, then, is that reflection undertaken in the second chapter?
We reply: it is for the purpose of settling the understanding of those with coarse intellects.

Here, however, for the sake of those with subtle vision, the contradiction with the scriptural texts regarding the meaning of the word *tat* (That) is resolved so that they may attain knowledge of the concordance (*samanvaya*) in the meaning of the sentence.

Although the contradiction with the scriptural texts concerning the meaning of the term "thou" (tvaṃpadārtha) must here be resolved, nevertheless, since the falsity of bondage was indicated by the first aphorism, non-contradiction is established.
The author of the Sūtras considers that the detailed exposition of the phenomenal world (prapañca), however, will follow as an occasion for instructing those of dull intellect.
In this context, the scriptural passages regarding the cause of the world constitute the subject matter.

Regarding the doubt as to whether those [meditations] are authoritative with respect to Brahman or not, the opponent offers a counter-example (*pratyudāharaṇa*) to establish the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), explaining the aforementioned objection with the words "In every Vedānta," and so forth. He argues that while there may be an option (*vikalpa*) regarding the action of meditating on food and light as being either one or two, such options are impossible regarding the causal reality itself— such as whether the cause is non-existent or existent— and therefore [the texts concerning Brahman] lack authority.
The connection with the chapter on *Śruti* (Scripture) is established by proving the concordance (*samanvaya*) of the Vedānta texts;
the connection with the section (*pāda*) is established by stating the concordance of words such as "non-existent" (*asat*) with the existent cause (*sat-kāraṇa*).
In the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), the result is the failure to establish that concordance.
The distinction is that its establishment occurs within the final conclusion (*siddhānta*).
First, he demonstrates the contradiction with creation through both succession and non-succession, beginning with the words "For instance, in some cases...
That Supreme Self created the worlds.
The world of heaven, abounding in bodies composed of water, is the meaning of the word *ambhaḥ*.
The intermediate space (*antarikṣa*), pervaded by the rays of the sun, is *marīcīḥ*.
*Maraḥ* is the world of mortals (*martyaloka*).
The meaning of the Vedic text is that the netherworlds consist predominantly of water.

Having stated the contradiction with respect to creation, he states the contradiction with respect to the cause: "In the same way," [meaning] the cause consists of name and form that are unmanifest and non-existent.
For that reason, it is manifested as existent.
To express this same meaning, he cites the Chāndogya passage: "Non-existent indeed [was this in the beginning].
Does this mean it was merely a void?
"No," he says, "it was *tatsat*.
The meaning is that it was indeed Brahman, uncontradicted.
That world, which existed as the self of Brahman, became fully manifested at the time of creation.
"Process" means creation;
"therein" means in that cause;
"some" refers to the outsiders.
The Śruti itself refutes their view— why?—
and explains the meaning of the words "kutaḥ" (whence) and "evam" (thus) with the word "katham" (how).
It states its own position with the word "sat" (Being).
This very world, it is said, was indeed in a state of non-manifestation (*avyākṛta*), consisting of its cause, at that prior time.
He summarizes the contradiction among the Śrutis with the word "thus" (*evam*).
Anticipating the doubt as to what is logical here, he states "Smṛti... [etc.], asserting that it is logical for the Vedāntas to indicate the *pradhāna* established by other means of knowledge.
In this regard, having acknowledged the contradiction in the act of creation, he removes the contradiction regarding the Creator with the words "even though" (*satyapi*).
Having made the formal proposition that there is no contradiction whatsoever in Brahman’s being the cause of ether and the other elements, he states the reason for it with the word "why? (*kutaḥ*).
He explains its being exactly as it is by saying "omniscient" (*sarvajña*).
He states, beginning with "tadyathā" (just as), that the causality [of Brahman] possesses attributes such as omniscience, as seen in every Vedānta text;
"tadviṣayeṇa" means by that which has Brahman as its object;
"cetanam" means the omniscient one.

From the Śruti text, "He made Himself alone," His independence from being impelled by another is established; from the text, "From this very Self," His nature as the innermost Self (pratyagātman) is established;
and from His desire for manifoldness, His non-duality even during the period of manifestation is established.
He states that just as omniscience and other attributes belong to the Cause in the *Taittirīyaka*, they are likewise seen in the *Chāndogya* and other texts: "That which is the definition here...
[means] that which is active (*miṣat*), i.e., possessed of function.
Because its meaning is not contradicted—that is, because its meaning is non-contradictory—the implication is that there is no disagreement regarding the Cause.

Nevertheless, fearing that because there is contradiction regarding the effects, there might also be contradiction regarding the cause, [the author] refutes this with the words beginning "But as for the object which is the effect.

He says "due to over-extension" (atiprasaṅgāt) to show that if the creations in dreams were different every day, then even the seer—who is recognized through the recognition "I am he"—would be subject to the consequence of being multiple.
Having thus conceded the contradiction regarding the creation, it was stated that there is no contradiction regarding the creator.
Now, [the author] explains that he will both accept [this view] and resolve [the objection]: "He will accept it" and "He will resolve it.

Then, anticipating the objection—"For what purpose, then, do the Śrutis describe creation in various different ways?"—he states, beginning with "It may be," in order to make known that there is no intended meaning (atātparya) regarding creation.
He establishes this lack of intended meaning by showing that contradiction in matters where there is no intended meaning is not a fault, saying: "For indeed... (na hi).

Since the creation passages can achieve their purposeful meaning by being subordinate to the fruit-bearing statements concerning Brahman, a separate result for their own sake need not be postulated, as that would entail a split in the sentence (*vākyabheda*); thus he says, "nor can it be postulated.
Since syntactic unity is established by reasoning, scripture also demonstrates it; thus he says, "and it shows."

Having stated that the purpose of the creation texts is for the sake of knowing the causal Brahman by means of the "sprout" (śuṅga)—which is to say, by means of the effect as a sign (liṅga)—he states the knowledge of the non-duality of the cause, which culminates in the fruit, beginning with the words "mṛdādi.

Thus, since there is no intentionality regarding creation—which is fruitless and intended for another purpose—contradiction is not a defect; in this regard, he cites the consensus of the elders with the words "tathā ca.
The repetition "anyathā-anyathā" is to be understood as an intensive (vīpsā).
For the sake of descent and for the birth of Brahmā;
therefore, even though there is a difference in that [manifestation], there is no division within Brahman.
The meaning is that there is no contradiction regarding the object of knowledge.
The fact that the knowledge of Brahman is the culmination of creation has been stated;
to establish that, he declares its fruit with the word "Brahman. The grammatical construction is: "He transcends death. //14//
Furthermore, as for the contradiction regarding the cause that was shown— beginning with "In the beginning, this was indeed non-existent" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 3.19.1)— that must be resolved.
To this it is replied: Because of the drawing together [of the passages].
"In the beginning, this was indeed non-existent" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.7).
Thus, it is not the non-existent that is taught here as the cause;
for [it says], "He becomes non-existent indeed,
if he knows Brahman as non-existent."

Having determined that Brahman— characterized by existence— is the inner self (pratyagātman) through the series of sheaths beginning with the one made of food (*annamaya*), by means of the refutation of the doctrine of non-existence in the passage, "If one knows that 'Brahman exists,' then they know him as existing," and having then drawn back upon that very same subject under discussion in the words, "He desired," [the text proceeds] with the manifestation of the world (*saprapañca*).

Having caused the creation to be heard from that [text] and having concluded with "That they call the Truth," the text introduces this verse— "In the beginning, this was indeed non-existent"— with the words "On this very point, there is also this verse," referring back to that same subject matter already under discussion. If, however, "non-existent" (asat) were intended here to mean a soulless void, then by citing one thing while drawing a conclusion about another, the statement would become incoherent.

Therefore, since the word "existent" (sat) is generally well-known as referring to an object that has been manifested with name and form, Brahman—though indeed existent before its origination—is figuratively described as if it were non-existent (asat), with reference to the absence of such manifestation.
This same interpretation applies to the passage: "In the beginning, this was indeed non-existent" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 3.19.1).
This is because of the retrospective reference [in the Upanishad] stating, "That was Being" (*tatsadāsīt*).

For if one were to admit an absolute non-existence, what would be the point of retrospectively referring to it as "That was Being"? As it says: "On this point, some say: 'In the beginning, this was indeed Non-being' (*taddhaika āhurasadevedamagra āsīt*). (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.2.1)
In this case as well, this presentation of the opinion of "some" (ekīya-mata) is not intended to refer to another scriptural passage;
for a choice between alternatives is impossible regarding an established entity (vastu), unlike the case of ritual action (kriyā).

Therefore, it should be understood that this is merely a presentation and subsequent refutation of a false position imagined by those of dull intellect, intended solely to strengthen the true position accepted by the scriptures.
Even in the passage, "In the beginning, this was indeed undifferentiated" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.4.7), the differentiation of the world is not described as occurring without a presiding agent,

because of the subsequent reference to the presiding agent through the statement, "He entered here even to the tips of the fingernails," which shows that the agent has entered into the differentiated effects.

For if one were to accept a grammatical interpretation that lacks a presiding subject, then by the pronoun *saḥ* (he), which refers back to the immediately preceding subject, what could be drawn in as entering into the activity?
Moreover, the entry of this conscious Self into the body is heard in scripture;
for once entered, its consciousness is heard of in the passage: "Seeing with the eye, hearing with the ear, thinking with the mind."
Furthermore, it is understood that just as this world is currently being differentiated by name and form under the supervision of a presiding agent, so too was it at the beginning of creation;
for it is impossible to conceive of a hypothesis contrary to what is observed.
Another scriptural passage also confirms this: "Entering with this living self, let me differentiate names and forms" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.3.2).
Thus, [the text] shows that the manifestation of the world occurs precisely with a supervisor.

Furthermore, the verbal suffix in the form "vyākriyata" (it was manifested) should be understood as a reflexive-passive construction (*karmakartari*) even while the Supreme Lord exists as the agent of manifestation, in consideration of ease;
just as one says, "The field is being reaped by itself," even though the reaper is actually present.

Alternatively, this [action] denoted by the verbal suffix (*lakāra*) should be understood as depending upon an agent implied by the meaning of the action itself, just as in the expression "the village is being gone to" (*gamyate grāmaḥ*). // 15 // @---------------------- FN:
That, in that [Brahman].
The verse is the mantra;
the supervisor is the agent;
the eye is the seer.
The ear is called the hearer, and the mind is called the thinker;
this refers to the present time, to now.

Having thus resolved the contradiction regarding the process of creation—which was not directly stated in the Sūtra—he takes up the next Sūtra (*yat punar*) in order to dispel the direct contradiction with Śruti concerning the existence or non-existence of the Cause.

The construction is as follows: since he determines that Brahman is characterized by existence and then cites a verse in reference to that very [Brahman], it follows that in this verse, that which is "without self" (nirātman) or non-existent is not what is being taught.
In this regard, there is a verse in the form of a mantra concerning the True Self (*sadātman*):

"By the word 'non-existent' (*asat*), Brahman is indicated through the term 'the non-existent' [referring to] supersensuous objects, because of the attraction toward the True Self. He says "therefore" (*tasmāt*) to explain this.
Nor should it be argued that *pradhāna* alone is what is being indicated.

The sense is that there would be the fault of excessive resort to figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā-gaurava*) for numerous words such as "Brahman" and others which have the meaning of volition (*cetanā*).
Having applied the aphorism (*sūtra*) to the *Taittirīyaka* scripture, he applies it to the *Chāndogya* and other texts with the words "This very same...

The meaning is that because the previously mentioned "non-existent" (*asat*) is drawn back (*samākarṣāt*) by the word "That" (*tat*), which has the same referent as "Being" (*sat*), there is no [doctrine of] emptiness (*śūnyatva*).

Now, one might object: "Is it not improper to characterize [the injunction] as having non-existent words, since the scriptures themselves have shown an option—just as in the case of the *uditahoma* and *anuditahoma*—according to the differences between their own respective schools? To this, he says: "taddhaika" (Regarding that, some...). This does not mean "some followers of a particular Vedic branch."
However, the meaning is that those situated outside the Veda are those who stand within the beginningless wheel of saṃsāra.

The intention is that since the existence of reality (sadvāda) alone is desired by the Śrutis through the refutation of emptiness (śūnya), figurative interpretation (lakṣaṇā) is appropriate for dispelling the appearance of contradiction with them.
As for what was said—that in some places creation is described as being without an agent—[that refers to a different context].
He says "no" to that, stating: "For this [world] is indeed that.

The presiding overseer (*adhyakṣa*) is the agent (*kartṛ*). Now, one might object that it is precisely the absence of an agent that is being referred to; therefore, he says: "And this belongs to the conscious one."
The meaning is that the eye is called the seer, the ear the hearer, and the mind the thinker.
He says "moreover" (apica) to present the argument: "The first effect has a creator, because it is an effect, like a jar."
"At present" means now. [Objection:

But surely, if there exists an agent other than the *karmakāraka* (the object as a grammatical factor), it is contradictory for the verbal suffix (*lakāra*) to denote the agent when the object itself is [intended to be expressed]. To this, he says: "It is being manifested. This is with respect to the accomplishment of the object without effort.
The meaning is that agency is merely figuratively attributed [to Brahman].
Having explained that the world manifests itself as already accomplished, he explains how it is manifested by someone else with the words "or else" (yadvā).
Therefore, since there is no contradiction among the scriptural texts, it is established that the concordance [of the Vedas] is achieved through the medium of the cause. //15//

Section concerning Bālāki (Bālakyādhikaraṇa) / Sūtras 16–18.
Because of the mention of the world.
In the Kauṣītaki Brāhmaṇa, in the dialogue between Bālāki and Ajātaśatru, it is heard: "O Bālāki, he who is the maker of these, whose work this is—he indeed is to be known" (KauṣB 4.19).
In this regard, there arises a doubt: is the individual soul (jīva) taught as the one to be known, or the principal vital breath (mukhya prāṇa), or the supreme self (paramātman)?
What, then, is the initial conclusion?
That it is the vital breath (prāṇa).
Why?
Because of the scriptural statement, "He whose work this is," and because action characterized by motion has the vital breath (*prāṇa*) as its substratum,
and because the word "prāṇa" is seen in the complementary passage, "Then he becomes one in this very prāṇa."

Furthermore, because the word *prāṇa* is well-known in its primary sense as the vital breath, Prāṇa is also the agent of those persons previously mentioned by Bālāki—such as "the person in the sun," "the person in the moon," and so forth—for those deities are particular states of Prāṇa. As it is said:
"Which one is the single deity? Prāṇa. He is Brahman; they call him *Tyat*. (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.9.9).
This is because it is well-known from another Vedic text.
Furthermore, it is the individual soul (jīva) that is taught here as the object to be known;
for him too, action characterized by merit and demerit can be made known through the statement, "Of whom this is the action."
He too, by virtue of being the enjoyer, is logically established as the agent of these persons who constitute the instruments of enjoyment; moreover,
a characteristic mark of the individual soul (jīva) is perceived in the remainder of the passage,
because Ajātaśatru, desiring to awaken Bālāki— who had approached him seeking knowledge— intends to make known that agent of the persons who was introduced as the object to be known.

By addressing a sleeping man and observing that he does not hear the sounds of address, it is demonstrated that the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) and so forth are not the experiencer; then, by his awakening upon being struck with a staff, it is demonstrated that the living self (*jīva*), distinct from the vital breaths and so forth, is the experiencer.
Likewise, further on, the characteristic mark of the living self is understood: "Just as a chief enjoys [the wealth] along with his own people, or as his own people [enjoy]..."
"Just as [people] eat from the merchant, even so this conscious self (prajñātman) eats through these selves; even so these selves eat this self" (Kauṣītaki Brāhmaṇa Upaniṣad 4.20).
Furthermore, because it is the sustainer of the vital breaths (prāṇabhṛt), it is appropriate for the individual soul (jīva) to be designated by the word "prāṇa."
Therefore, either the individual soul (jīva) or the chief vital breath (mukhya-prāṇa) must be understood here, and not the Supreme Lord, because no characteristic mark of Him is perceived.
This being the position reached, we reply: this creator of these persons must indeed be the Supreme Lord.
Why?
Because of the force of the context.
For here, Bālāki began a conversation with Ajātaśatru, saying, "I shall tell you about Brahman."
Having described several persons, such as Āditya and others, who possessed the view of the non-primary Brahman, he became silent.

Ajātaśatru, refuting him on the grounds that he was speaking of a non-primary Brahman, said, "Indeed, you have been speaking falsely to me; let me tell you of Brahman," and introduced another as the one to be known, the creator of that [non-primary Brahman].
If even he were a possessor of the view of the non-primary Brahman, the initial premise would be contradicted.
Therefore, this must be the Supreme Lord alone.
Furthermore, the agency of these persons cannot be conceived as independent of the Supreme Lord.
Moreover, the phrase "he whose work this is" does not refer to action characterized by physical movement or action characterized by merit and demerit.
Because neither of those two is the subject under discussion,
and because they have not been mentioned;
nor is this a designation of the persons.
This is because they are specified as "the maker of these persons"; furthermore,
due to the discrepancy in gender and number, this is not a designation for the action of making whose object is the person, nor for the fruit of the action,
since both of those are already included by the word "maker" itself.
By process of elimination, the entire world, which is present before the eyes, is indicated by the word "this" (*etac-chabda*).
And because it is being created, at that very moment the world is the object (*karman*).
But is it not the case that the world has neither been introduced as the subject matter (*aprakṛta*) nor has it been previously mentioned (*asaṃśabdita*)?
This is true;

nevertheless, since no specific qualification is mentioned, it is understood that this designation refers to any object present by virtue of its proximity in a general sense, and not to any particular thing,
because there is an absence of the presence of any specific [qualification].

And since in the preceding [passage] the world itself was understood to be referred to without qualification—despite the specific mention of persons who constitute only a portion of that world—it is understood here as well that the world alone is being referred to.
This is what is meant: "He who is the creator of these persons who constitute a portion of the world"—what is the purpose of this qualification?

The phrase "for whom the entire world without exception is [his] karma" uses the word "or" (*vā*) to exclude the notion that his agency is limited to only a single part. The inclusion of this qualification is intended to demonstrate that those persons whom Bālāki proclaimed and regarded as Brahman are not actually Brahman.

Thus, according to the method of the Brahmins and wandering mendicants (*brāhmaṇaparivrājaka*), the creator of the world is taught as that which is to be known through both the general and the particular.
And the Supreme Lord is determined in all the Vedāntas to be the creator of the entire world. (16) [FN:
This world is whose work.]
By the etymological derivation "that which is being done," the meaning is "the effect" (kārya);
that is the vital breath (prāṇa).
"Tyat" means the remote (parokṣa).
The construction is as follows: because it awakens the individual soul (jīva), therefore there exists the awakening of one who was asleep, which is a characteristic mark of the jīva.
This is like the case when it is said, "Brāhmaṇas should be fed, and the wandering mendicant [should also be fed]"; by means of both the general and the particular, it includes all nearby Brāhmaṇas.
This is because [the word 'jīva'] denotes the world.
He states the subject matter with the words "Kauṣītaki.
Bālāki is the son of Balākā; the king spoke to that brāhmaṇa, beginning with "He who...
It is not merely the creator of the sun and so forth, but rather the creator of the entire world, as he says: "Of whom..."
This world is the *karma* (action) of that [Lord]; by the etymological derivation (*vyutpatti*) "that which is acted upon" (*kriyate*), the meaning is "the effect" (*kārya*).
Regarding the word *karma*, he states a doubt based on both its etymological and conventional meanings (*yogarūḍhibhyām*) with the words "therein" (*tatra*).

In the previous case, the word "non-existent" (asat) was interpreted by the force of words such as "Being" (sat) occurring within a single sentence. Here, however, because there is a difference in sentences, it is impossible to interpret the word "Prāṇa" and so forth—found in Bālāki’s statement "I shall tell you Brahman"—as referring to Brahman, due to the presence of the word "Brahman" [in the king's response]. Thus, he states the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa) by way of a counter-example: "What, then... and so on.

In the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), because the sentence is intent upon the meditation on the vital breath (*prāṇa*) and so forth, the concordance (*samanvaya*) with Brahman is not established; in the final view (*siddhānta*), the concordance with Brahman as the object of knowledge is established—this is the result [of the discussion].
Now, regarding deep sleep:
the word "the seer" (*draṣṭṛ*) is to be supplied as the remainder [of the sentence].

Since it has been heard that the vital breath (prāṇa) is the agent of all things, [the author] asks, "How so? and replies with the words, "And these... He provides the authority for the statement that the sun and other deities are modifications of the vital breath whose essence is the Sūtra, by citing the passage beginning, "Whose glories are all the gods," as shown in the preceding sentence.
Therefore, because it consists of all the gods, that Prāṇa is Brahman;
"Tyat" means the remote or transcendent.
The meaning is: "because it is to be known solely through the scripture.

He states another prima facie view: "or the individual soul (jīva). The construction is as follows: because it awakens the individual soul, therefore there exists the awakening of one who was asleep, which is a characteristic mark of the individual soul.
The two of them approached a sleeping man.

The King addressed him, calling out, "O Bṛhatpāṇḍaravāsa! O Soma-rāja!"—having thus awakened him and demonstrated that the vital breath (*prāṇa*) and other such functions are not the Self because they do not recognize the call—he raised him up with a blow from his staff; the meaning is that he awakened the individual soul (*jīva*).
[The soul] is the chief, who eats what is brought by his own servants and kinsmen, and his own kinsmen depend upon him for their livelihood.

In this way, the individual soul (jīva) also experiences through the sun and other [deities] by means of light and other instruments of enjoyment; and they, in turn, subsist upon the soul by receiving the oblation and so forth. Thus, the state of being an enjoyer is stated to be a characteristic mark of the soul. Now, one might ask: "How can the word 'prāṇa'—which is heard in the scripture as 'the breath becomes unified'—refer to the soul? To this he says: "And because it is the sustainer of the vital breaths" (prāṇabhṛttvāt). He establishes the final conclusion (siddhānta) outside the scope of the sūtra itself with the word "evam" (thus).
And that Bālāki, having been refuted by the king after describing persons in the form of individual limiting adjuncts (liṅga) under the delusion that they were Brahman, remained silent.

[The author] says, "If even he," meaning that he too ought to have known [the true Brahman], because one must state that the Brahman being described by the king is indeed Brahman; otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) of the king himself being a speaker of falsehood.
This is the sense.

The primary agency of action is a characteristic mark (liṅga) of Brahman alone, because both the vital breath (prāṇa) and the individual soul (jīva) lack independence, being subject to its control; thus he says: "And agency...
As for what was stated—that the word *karman* denotes motion and unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*), and thereby brings to mind the vital breath and the individual soul—[the following refutes that].
He says "no" to that with the words "of which" (*yasya*).
It is logical to grasp one of several possible meanings from a word that has multiple meanings based on either the context (*prakaraṇa*) or a governing word (*upapada*).

Since neither context nor a governing word is present here, there arises a doubt as to which meaning should be grasped; the point is that, due to the proximity of the word "person" (*puruṣa*) as the agent and the connection [implied] by the verbal root *kṛ* (to do) in the sense of "it is being done," the term refers to the world (*jagat*).

[The opponent argues: "Since there is a reference to the subject at hand by the word 'this' (*etad*), let the 'persons' (*puruṣāḥ*) mentioned previously be indicated by the word 'action' (*karman*). To this, he says: "Nor [is it that].
The meaning is that because of tautology, and because it is improper to refer to persons (which are plural) by means of a neuter singular pronoun.

[The opponent objects: "But surely the meaning of the root *kṛ* (to do/make) is the activity of the agent who produces the person; its fruit is the birth of the person. Therefore, let the word 'action' (*karman*) denote one or the other of these. To this, he says: "Nor [is it that]."
Regarding the phrase "by the word 'agent'":
since agency is impossible without both action and its fruit, the meaning is that those two are indeed included by the word "agent" itself.
He acknowledges the statement that "for the world as well, these two do not exist [as primary] in this context," saying: "True."

For context and the like serve to restrict the scope of a pronoun; in their absence, everything present in the mind is grasped in a general sense. And here, since there is no such restricting factor, the pronoun, which denotes "all," refers to the word *karman* as the designator of whatever is to be done that is present in the mind. Thus he says: "Nevertheless... (*tathāpi*).
Furthermore, he states that by the mention of "one part of the world," the "world" is what is under discussion—referring to the phrase "as before.
Since the inclusion of the "world" already entails the inclusion of the "persons," he says "this has been stated" to show that the separate mention [of persons] would otherwise be redundant;
the connection is with the words "he is to be known."
The word "or" (*vā*) is intended to dispel the misconception that agency is attributed solely to a person.

Just as in the statement "the Brahmins are to be fed, as well as the wandering mendicants," the word "Brahmin" excludes those who are not wandering mendicants, so too here the word "action" (*karman*) refers to the world other than the person. He says "thus":
let it be that the creator of the world is to be known.
To the question, "What does this have to do with the Supreme Lord? he says: "In the Supreme Lord... (verse 16).

If it be argued that [the passage does not refer to Brahman] because of the characteristic marks of the individual soul (jīva) and the chief vital breath (mukhya-prāṇa), that has already been explained. (BS 1.4.17)

Therefore, that which was stated—that because of the marks of the individual soul (*jīva*) and the marks of the chief vital breath (*mukhyaprāṇa*) found in the supplementary passage, it is logical to grasp one of those two here and not the Supreme Lord—must be refuted.

This has already been refuted in the Sūtra: "Not so, because of the threefoldness of meditation; because [meditation] is resorted to elsewhere, it is connected with that here as well" (Brahma-sūtra 1.1.31).
For if this were the case, three kinds of meditation would result here: meditation on the individual soul (jīva), meditation on the principal vital breath (mukhyaprāṇa), and meditation on Brahman.
And this is not reasonable;
for it is understood from both the opening and the conclusion that this passage has Brahman as its subject matter.
In that regard, it has already been shown that the opening statement has Brahman as its object;

furthermore, the concluding passage is also seen to have Brahman as its object because of the mention of a result that is unsurpassed: "Having cast off all evils, he who knows this attains the preeminence, sovereignty, and lordship over all beings."
If this is so, then surely this passage would also be determined by the very determination of the *Pratardana* passage.
It is not so determined;
for the statement "and whose work this is" was not established there as having Brahman as its object.
Therefore, the doubt regarding the individual soul (*jīva*) and the principal vital breath (*mukhya-prāṇa*) that arises here is set aside.
Furthermore, the word "prāṇa" is seen to refer to Brahman in such passages as, "For the mind, my dear, is fastened to prāṇa" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.8.2).
Even the marks of the individual soul must be interpreted with the intention of non-difference, since the introductory and concluding sections pertain to Brahman. // 17 //

Note: The distinction is that *śraiṣṭhya* is the excellence of superior qualities, *ādhipatya* is the state of being a ruler or controller, and *svārājya* is the state of being independent or not subject to control.

Having stated the established conclusion (*siddhānta*), he refutes the seed of the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) by restating it: "On account of the indicative marks (*liṅga*) of the individual soul (*jīva*) and the chief vital breath (*mukhyaprāṇa*). He recalls what has already been said: "It is threefold.
"Preeminence" (*śraiṣṭhya*) means the excellence of qualities (*guṇādhikya*).
"Sovereignty" (ādhipatya) means the state of being a ruler;
"self-rule" (svārājya) means the state of not being ruled—this is the distinction.

He raises the objection that this would be a tautology by saying, "But if it is so," on the grounds that it has already been stated: "When a single unified meaning is possible, a split in the sentence (vākya-bheda) is indeed not desired."

He states "No," etc., to show that since the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa) arises through the conventional meaning of the word *karman*, the commencement of this [sūtra] is appropriate for the purpose of refuting it.
He explains the application of the word *prāṇa* and the characteristic mark (*liṅga*) of the individual soul (*jīva*) with the words "The word *prāṇa* also... [Sūtra 1.1.18]:
"The mind is the individual soul. (1.1.17)
Jaimini, however, [holds that the passage] has another purpose, on account of both the question and the explanation; and likewise some [teachers] maintain this.
Furthermore, one should not dispute here whether this sentence primarily concerns the individual soul (jīva) or primarily concerns Brahman;
for the teacher Jaimini considers that the reference to the individual soul in this sentence is for another purpose, namely for the sake of realizing Brahman.
Why?
[The nature of the Self is determined] by means of both questions and explanations.

First, regarding the question: when the individual soul (jīva), as distinct from the vital breaths (prāṇas) and so forth, has been awakened by the awakening of the person in deep sleep, there is seen a further question concerning that which is distinct from the individual soul: "O Bālāki, where did this person lie here? Where did he become this? From whence did he come? (Kauṣītaki Brāhmaṇa Upaniṣad 4.19).

The reply is also given in such passages as: "When, being asleep, he sees no dream whatsoever, then he becomes one with this very prāṇa," and so forth, up to: "From this Self the prāṇas proceed each to its own abode; from the prāṇas the gods, and from the gods the worlds" (Kauṣītaki Upaniṣad 4.20).

Furthermore, at the time of deep sleep, the individual soul (jīva) attains oneness with the supreme Brahman, and from that supreme Brahman the world, beginning with the vital breaths, is born; such is the established doctrine of the Vedānta. Therefore, that state of sleep in which this soul possesses a nature characterized by lack of consciousness and transparency—a state devoid of specific cognitions produced by limiting adjuncts (upādhi)—is its true essential form.
Since that arrival consists in the destruction of that [ignorance],
it is understood that the Supreme Self is what is taught here as the object to be known.
Moreover, some followers of the Vājasaneya branch, in this very dialogue between Bālāki and Ajātaśatru, clearly use the term "consisting of consciousness" (vijñānamaya).

The sacred texts, having taught the individual soul (*jīva*), teach the Supreme Self (*paramātman*) as distinct from it, in response to the question: "Where was this person consisting of consciousness (*vijñānamaya-puruṣa*) then? Whence did he come? (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.1.16).
In the reply as well, it is said: "He lies in that space (*ākāśa*) which is within the heart."
Furthermore, the word "ether" (*ākāśa*) is applied to the Supreme Self in the passage, "In this, there is a small ether" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.1.1).

And since the text declares that "all these selves emerge from this one," thereby teaching the emergence of the conditioned selves from another source, it is understood that they are teaching the Supreme Self alone as the cause.

Moreover, the refutation of the vital breaths (*prāṇa*)—by means of the awakening of the person in deep sleep—is an additional argument establishing the teaching of that which is distinct from the vital breaths and the rest. 18.
Note: "Niḥsaṃbodhatā" means being devoid of specific cognition;
"svacchatā" means being devoid of the impurity of distraction.
It has been stated that Brahman itself is indicated by the characteristic mark of the living soul (jīva).
Now, it is said that Brahman is to be grasped through the mention of the individual soul (*jīva*) by means of its characteristic marks; thus [the text] says, "For another purpose" (*anyārtham*).
Regarding the fact that the reference to the individual soul is for the sake of knowing Brahman as residing within the soul, he poses the question: "Who is this?
(*kaiṣaḥ*). O Bālāki, where did this person lie in such a way that this lying down—consisting of the absence of specific cognition—took place?
The meaning is: "In what substratum did he take his rest?
He asks "Where [did he go]? for the purpose of knowing the locus of the state of unification.
In such a way that this becoming would consist of unification, where was this person when he slept?
The meaning is: "By what means does he attain unity? He asks for the source of his arising with the word "from where" (*kutaḥ*).
The sense is: from where has the person come, such that this arrival takes the form of a loss of unity?
Having stated the question, he provides the explanation with the words "the reply.
The meaning is that Brahman alone, denoted by the term *prāṇa*, is the substratum of both the bed and the house, as well as the cause of one's rising from them.
Since *prāṇa* is mentioned in the answer, he says "and at the time of deep sleep" to show that the question also concerns *prāṇa*.
The meaning here is that Prāṇa is Brahman because it is the cause of the world and because of its identity with the individual soul (jīva).
He concludes that the mention of the jīva has another purpose with the words "Therefore" (tasmāt).
"Lack of consciousness" (niḥsaṃbodhatā) means being devoid of specific cognition.
Transparency is the state of being devoid of the impurity of distraction;
it is the unity of essential nature, free from the delusion of difference. [The author] states this with the words "upādhi" (limiting adjunct).

Furthermore, since both the question and the explanation have Brahman as their subject matter, [the author] cites the corroboration from another Vedic branch: "Moreover, some followers of other branches [teach] thus."
Now, it might be argued that space (*ākāśa*) was stated there to be the locus of deep sleep, not Brahman; therefore, he says "ākāśa" [in the commentary].

Furthermore, because it is, by way of its limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), the cause of the birth of the self as the knower (*pramātṛ*), he says "sarva" [in the commentary] to show that space is indeed Brahman.
Having thus explained the Sūtra as having the purpose of refuting the individual soul (*jīva*), he explains it again as being intended to refute the vital breath (*prāṇa*), saying "prāṇa."

In this passage, Jaimini considers the instruction regarding Prāṇa to be for the purpose of attaining knowledge of Brahman, because it is understood from the stated question and its explanation that the purport of the sentence is Brahman.

Furthermore, certain followers of other Vedic schools (śākhins), who likewise teach a living self (jīvātman) distinct from Prāṇa, preclude Prāṇa from being the meaning of the sentence; such is the construction of the Sūtra.
The meaning of the commentary is that the teaching of a soul distinct [from the vital breath] is also a further supporting reason for the refutation of the vital breath (*prāṇa*).
Therefore, it is established that this passage is consistent with Brahman. //18//

END BsCom_1,4.5.18 START BsCom_1,4.6.19 6. The Section on the Connection of the Sentences (Vākyānvayādhikaraṇa) / Sūtras 19–22 The section concerning the connection of the sentences [of the Upaniṣads] begins here. This section addresses whether the Upaniṣadic texts are intended for the purpose of ritual action (*karma*) or for the purpose of knowledge (*jñāna*). Sūtra 19: *śeṣatvāt puruṣārthavādo yathānyeṣv iti jaiminiḥ* // Because they are subordinate [to rituals], they are merely commendatory statements regarding the person’s welfare, as in other cases; so says Jaimini. Sūtra 20: *ācāradarśanāt* // Because we observe [the performance of] traditional practices [by those who know the Upaniṣads]. Sūtra 21: *tadvacanād āmnāyasya prāmāṇyam* // The authority of the sacred tradition (*āmnāya*) [is established] because of the teaching of that [Brahman] [in the Upaniṣads]. Sūtra 22: *mantrāyurvedaprāmāṇyavac ca tatprāmāṇyam āptaprāmāṇyāt* // And its authority is like the authority of mantras and the Ayurveda, because of the authority of the trustworthy person (*āpta*). [In this section, the author refutes the view of Jaimini and others who maintain that the Upaniṣads are merely subordinate to ritual acts or are for the sake of praising the performer, and establishes instead that their primary purpose is the realization of Brahman. END BsCom_1,4.6.22 START BsCom_1,4.7.23 7. The Section on the Non-difference of the Meditations (Avibhāgādhikaraṇa) / Sūtras 23–25 The section concerning the non-differentiation [of meditations] begins here. This section addresses whether meditations (*upāsana*) on the same object are identical or distinct. Sūtra 23: *avibhāgo vacanāt* // There is no division [between the meditations], because of the scriptural statement. Sūtra 24: *vyatihāro viśiṃṣanti hītaravat* // There is an exchange [of attributes between the two forms of meditation], for they distinguish [them] like the other [meditations]. Sūtra 25: *saiva hi satyādayaḥ* // For it is that very [same meditation] which possesses the qualities of truth and so forth. [In this section, the author establishes that meditations on the same object are essentially one, despite differences in the description of their attributes, and that certain qualities may be exchanged between different forms of the same meditation. END BsCom_1,4.7.25 START BsCom_1,4.8.26 8. The Section on the Optionality of the Meditations (Kāmyādhikaraṇa) / Sūtras 26–28 The section concerning optional meditations begins here. This section addresses whether meditations performed for specific desires are optional or mandatory. Sūtra 26: *kāmyāstu yathākāmaṃ samuccīyeran na vā pūrvahetvabhāvāt* // But the optional meditations may be combined according to one's desire, or not, because of the absence of the previous reason [for non-division]. Sūtra 27: *aikakarmyād iti cen na codanāpravibhāgāt* // If it be argued that they must be combined because they constitute a single act, we say no, because of the distinction between the injunctions (*codanā*). Sūtra 28: *darśanāc ca* // And because we observe [this distinction in practice]. [In this section, the author concludes that meditations for specific desires are optional and need not be combined, as they are distinct acts with separate purposes. END BsCom_1,4.8.28 START BsCom_1,4.9.29 9. The Section on the Non-restriction of Meditations (Aikāśramyādhikaraṇa) / Sūtras 29–32 The section concerning the non-restriction [to a single stage of life] begins here. This section addresses whether a person must remain in one stage of life (*āśrama*) or may choose among them. Sūtra 29: *aikaśramyaṃ tv ācāryāḥ pratyakṣavidhānād gārhasthasya* // But the teachers [maintain] a single stage of life, because the householder's state is directly enjoined by scripture. Sūtra 30: *vīrahā vā eṣa devānāṃ yo 'gnim udvāsayate* // "Verily, he is a slayer of heroes among the gods who lets the sacred fire go out. Sūtra 31: *parāmarśaṃ jaiminir acodanāc ca* // Jaimini [considers the mention of other stages] to be a mere reference, because there is no injunction [for them]. Sūtra 32: *anuṣṭheyaṃ bādarāyaṇaḥ sāmyaśruteḥ* // It is to be performed [as an option], Bādarāyaṇa [says], because of the scriptural statement of equality. [In this section, the author refutes the view that only the householder's life is mandatory and establishes that all four stages of life are equally valid options for the seeker of liberation. END BsCom_1,4.9.32 START BsCom_1,4.10.33 10. The Section on the Liberation of the Released Soul (Anārabdhādhikara�aṇa) / Sūtras 33–34 The section concerning the non-commencement [of the fruits of actions] begins here. This section addresses whether the soul released from the body is liberated immediately or remains for some time. Sūtra 33: *anārabdhakārye eva tu pūrve tadavadheḥ* // But only those [actions] whose effects have not yet begun [are destroyed]; for that is the limit [set by scripture]. Sūtra 34: *agnihotrādi tu tatkāryāyaiva taddarśanāt* // But the Agnihotra and other such rites are for the sake of that very [attainment of Brahman], because of the scriptural vision [of that effect]. [In this section, the author establishes that while the fruits of actions already commenced are exhausted through experience, the fruits of uncommenced actions are destroyed by knowledge, and that even obligatory rites like the Agnihotra serve the ultimate goal of liberation. END BsCom_1,4.10.34 START BsCom_1,4.11.35 11. The Section on the Departure of the Soul (Arthāntarādhikaraṇa) / Sūtras 35–37 The section concerning the departure [of the soul] begins here. This section addresses whether the soul departs from the body at death or not. Sūtra 35: *tadoko 'grajvalanaṃ tatprakāśitadvāro vidyāsāmarthyāt taccheṣagatyanusmṛtiyogāc ca hārdānugṛhīto raśmibhir udkramiṣyat* // The flame arises first at his dwelling-place; the door is illuminated by that [flame]; by the power of knowledge, and by the application of the recollection of the path which is the remainder of that [knowledge], being favored by the one in the heart, he shall depart by means of the rays [of the sun]. Sūtra 36: *niśi neti cen na sambandhasya yāvaddehabhāvitvād darśayati ca* // If it be argued that [the soul does not depart] at night, we say no, because the connection [of the soul with the body] lasts as long as the body exists, and scripture shows this. Sūtra 37: *ataścāyane 'pi dakṣiṇe* // And therefore
Because of the connection of the sentences.

In the Maitreyī-brāhmaṇa of the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad, it is studied: beginning with "Verily, not for the sake of the husband is a husband dear," and continuing until "Verily, not for the sake of all is all dear; rather, for the sake of the Self (ātman) all becomes dear; the Self, indeed..."

"Verily, this Self, Maitreyī, is to be seen, heard, reflected upon, and meditated upon; for by the seeing, hearing, thinking, and knowing of this Self, all this is known" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upani�sad 4.5.6).

Regarding this, a doubt arises: is it the individual self (*vijñānātman*) that is taught here in the form of being "to be seen," "to be heard," and so forth, or rather the supreme Self (*paramātman*)?
But whence arises this doubt?
It is because the instruction regarding the conscious self (*vijñānātman*) begins with the agent of enjoyment as indicated by the beloved one;
what, then, is the prima facie position?
Regarding the teaching that consciousness is the self:
why?
Because of the force of the introductory statement.
For everything in the world— such as husband, wife, children, and wealth— which is of the nature of an object of enjoyment, becomes dear because it exists for the sake of the Self; thus,
having first introduced the Self as the enjoyer indicated by these "dear" things, what other Self could this [Self] be that is subsequently taught as the one to be seen and so forth?

Even in the middle [of the passage], by stating that "this great being, infinite and boundless, consisting of nothing but a mass of consciousness, arising from these elements, perishes after them; there is no consciousness after death," the text shows that this very great being which is to be seen is the object of vision precisely as the conscious self (vijñānātman), since it describes the emergence of that same subject from the elements in the form of the conscious self.
Likewise, by concluding with the word "knower" in the phrase, "By what, my dear, should one know the knower?", the text shows that it is indeed the knowing self (vijñānātman) that is taught here.

Therefore, the claim that the knowledge of all arises from the knowledge of the Self must be regarded as merely figurative, since the entire range of objects of enjoyment exists for the sake of the enjoyer.
This being the position reached, we reply: this is indeed an instruction concerning the Supreme Self.
Why?
Because of the syntactical connection (*vākyānvaya*).
For when this sentence is examined in its proper sequence from beginning to end, it is observed that its constituent parts are connected toward the Supreme Self (*paramātman*).

How so? That is established as follows: Having heard from Yājñavalkya that "there is no hope for immortality through wealth," Maitreyī—desiring immortality, saying, "What should I do with that by which I might not become immortal? Tell me only that which the Blessed One knows"—to her, Yājñavalkya teaches this knowledge of the Self.
The declarations of the Śruti and Smṛti state that there is no immortality apart from the knowledge of the Supreme Self.
Likewise, the statement that through the knowledge of the Self all is known cannot be understood in its primary sense unless it refers to the knowledge of the Supreme Cause.
Nor can this be taken as being merely figurative.

For this reason, having asserted that "by the knowledge of the Self, all is known," the text immediately thereafter establishes that very point with the passage beginning, "Brahman would desert him who sees Brahman as other than the Self," and so forth.

For he who perceives the world—consisting of the Brahmins, the Kṣatriyas, and the rest—as existing independently apart from the Self, that very world of Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, and so on, which was falsely perceived, rejects that person of false vision; thus, the view of duality is sublated.
The statement, "All this is what this Self is," introduces the non-difference of the entire aggregate of things from the Self;
and by means of the analogies of the drum and so forth (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.5.8),
it confirms that very non-difference.

Furthermore, by stating, "This Rigveda is the breath of this great Being" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.5.11), and so forth, the text explains that the Self under discussion is the cause of the manifold expansion of names, forms, and actions, thereby leading one to understand Him as the Supreme Self.
The same is the case in the section concerning the Single Goal (ekāyana-prakriyā) [Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.5.12].

By explaining that this entire phenomenal world—including its objects, sense organs, and internal instruments—is a single resort (*ekāyana*), without interior or exterior, and a mass of pure consciousness (*prajñānaghana*), [the text] leads one to understand this as the Supreme Self (*paramātman*).
Therefore, it is understood that this instruction regarding seeing and so forth refers to the Supreme Self alone. (19) [Note:
This is the immediate reality.]
Great and undivided;
real and true;
infinite and eternal.
If it is shoreless, all-pervading, and of a single flavor;
if it is the knower and the agent of cognition—then it cannot be attained by wealth or by the ritual action (karman) accomplished through it. This is the meaning.
"There is no other path," "not by action," and so forth are the declarations of the Śruti;
"liberation comes from knowledge alone," and so forth are the declarations of the Smṛti.
It obstructs and causes one to fall away from the path to the higher good.
"Name" refers to the Ṛgveda and so forth; "sacrifice" and "oblation" refer to ritual action.
"And this world" refers to form (*rūpa*);
it is the process (*prakriyā*) because of its connection with the context (*prakaraṇa*) of the sentence.
He states the subject sentence: "The Bṛhad...
Since the body and so forth are dear because they are subordinate to the Self, the Self alone is the most beloved of all;
therefore, having abandoned everything else, the Self alone is to be seen.
The meaning is that hearing and other such acts should be performed for the sake of vision [of the truth]. "By those indicative of what is dear" refers to husbands, wives, and so forth.
The meaning is: "by means of beloved objects of enjoyment, which are inferred to be [characteristic of] the living being.

Just as the subject matter of the sentence "I shall declare Brahman to you" is determined to be Brahman by the force of its opening statement, so too, because this sentence begins with the living being (jīva), its subject matter is the living being; thus he sets forth the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa) by means of this analogy, beginning with "What, then... and so on.

The result is that, in the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), the sentence has as its purport the meditation on the individual soul (*jīva*), whereas in the established conclusion (*siddhānta*), it is the concordance with the inner Brahman as the object of knowledge.
This [Brahman] is the immediate (*pratyak*).
Great and undivided;
real and true;
infinite and eternal.
It is shoreless, all-pervading, and of the single essence of consciousness.

Having arisen in a state of equilibrium from these elements—which are produced in the form of cause and effect—and having experienced birth conditioned by those elements, it perishes following those very elements as they are led away.
The meaning of the scripture is that after death conditioned by limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), there is no longer any specific cognition.
"The knower" means the agent of cognition.
When the enjoyer is known, it is a figurative expression (upacāra) that "the object of enjoyment is known.

He establishes the final position—that the sentence has the status of a means of valid knowledge regarding Brahman—because the purport (tātparya) is understood to reside in Brahman alone through the syntactic connection (anvaya) of the sentence with such indicative marks (liṅga) as being accessible through the knowledge that is the means to liberation: "Thus... [he says].
"Not by wealth" means not by the ritual action accomplished through it.

Since the knowledge of all through the knowledge of one is established by means of proving non-difference after first censuring difference, its figurative nature is untenable; thus he says, "And this is not figurative," and so forth.
He rejects [the distinction] and causes one to fall away from the path to excellence;

for just as the specific differences among the sounds of a drum, a conch, and a lute, when grasped merely by their commonality as "sound," are imagined within that generality and do not differ from it— just like silver grasped through the perception of mother-of-pearl.
Thus, having ascertained that everything appearing as a self-nature is merely the Self, he says, "from the drum" (*dundubhyāt*).
In this way, because the proposition that all knowledge is attained through a single knowledge is primary, there is the ascertainment of Brahman;
and he also states, "of this Great One," because of the indicative mark (*liṅga*) of being the creator of all.
The name consists of the *Ṛgveda* and so forth; the action consists of the sacrifice (*iṣṭa*) and the oblation (*huta*);
and the form consists of this world and the world beyond.

Furthermore, he states that the passage, "Just as the ocean is the one goal of all waters," serves as an indicative mark (*liṅga*) for the Self’s nature as Brahman, because it establishes the Self as the primary locus of dissolution for the entire phenomenal world (*prapañca*): "In the same way, the one goal... etc.
(Chāndogya Upaniṣad 7.10.1).

As for what was further stated—that because the opening passage indicates what is dear, this instruction regarding seeing and so forth refers only to the individual self (vijñānātman)—to this we reply:
"The sign [of the Self] is for the sake of establishing the initial proposition; thus [says] Āśmarathya. (BBs 1.4.20)

There is a proposition here: "When the Self is known, all this becomes known," and "All this is that which is this Self. This indicative mark—the mention of the Self, who is indicated by what is dear, as being the object of vision and so forth—points to the fulfillment of that proposition. For if the individual self (vijñānātman) were other than the Supreme Self, then even upon the knowledge of the Supreme Self, the individual self would not be known; thus, the proposition that through the knowledge of one everything is known would be lost.

Therefore, the teacher Āśmarathya maintains that the opening statement is made by way of the aspect of non-difference between the individual self (vijñānātman) and the supreme self (paramātman) for the purpose of establishing the thesis.

The view of Āśmarathya is that because there exists both difference and non-difference between the individual soul (jīva) and Brahman, this introduction of the individual soul [in the Chāndogya Upaniṣad] serves to establish the initial proposition regarding their non-difference. //20//
"Audulomi maintains that [the soul] is thus [pure] because it is about to depart. (BS 1.4.21)

The teacher Auḍulomi maintains that this introduction [to the subject] by way of non-difference is possible because the individual self (*vijñānātman*)—which has become turbid through contact with the limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) of the aggregate of body, senses, mind, and intellect; which has not yet attained clarity through the practice of means such as knowledge and meditation; and which is about to emerge from the aggregate of the body and so forth—is capable of attaining identity with the Supreme Self (*paramātman*).

And there is a scriptural passage to this effect: "This serene being (*saṃprasāda*), having risen up from this body and having reached the highest light, appears in its own true form" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.12.3).

And in another place, [the scripture] indicates by means of the illustration of a river that name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) has the individual soul (*jīva*) as its substrate: "As rivers flowing along reach their end in the ocean, casting off name and form;
so the knower, liberated from name and form, attains the divine Person, higher than the high" (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 3.2.8).

Just as in the world rivers reach the ocean, casting off name and form which have themselves as their substrate, so too does the individual soul [cast off name and form which have itself as their substrate].

For in that context, the meaning understood for the sake of the correspondence between the illustration and the illustrated is that "having abandoned name-and-form (nāmarūpa), one approaches the Supreme Person.
[FN: *Samutthāna* means departure (*utkrānti*).
There is indeed a distinction during the state of transmigratory existence.]
The view of Auḍulomi is that non-difference exists only in liberation. He states the proof for this: "And scripture.
Here, *samutthāna* means departure (from the body).

Now, having raised the objection that because transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*) is adventitious (*aupādhika*), there is always non-difference [between the self and Brahman], he states—by means of the force of an illustration—that transmigratory existence is inherent (*svābhāvika*), beginning with the words "kvacicca" (and in some cases).
He explains the illustration of the rivers from the text, "Just as rivers flowing reach the ocean, casting off name and form," with the words "yathā loke" (as in the world). //21//
"Because of abiding," says Kāśakṛtsna. (BS 1.4.22)
The teacher Kāśakṛtsna maintains that this introductory statement regarding non-difference is appropriate because this very Supreme Self exists even in the form of the individual soul (vijñānātman).

To this effect, the Brāhmaṇa passage— “Having entered with this living self (jīva), let me evolve names and forms” (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.3.2)— and others of a similar kind, demonstrate that the Supreme Self itself exists in the state of the individual soul.
And there are scriptural passages such as: "The Wise One, having fashioned all forms and made their names, sits calling them by those names" (Taittirīya Āraṇyaka 3.12.7).
Furthermore, in the creation of fire and the other elements, there is no separate creation of the individual soul.
This has been heard [in scripture],
by which it would follow that the individual soul (*jīva*) is a modification distinct from the Supreme Self.
However, the view of the teacher Kāśakṛtsna is that the individual soul is the unmodified Supreme Lord and not something other than Him.

As for Āśmarathya, although he intends the non-difference of the individual soul from the Supreme, nevertheless, because he mentions its dependence on the latter in the phrase "for the sake of establishing the initial proposition," it is understood that some degree of the relation of cause and effect is also intended.

In the view of Auḍulomi, however, difference and non-difference are clearly understood as being dependent upon different states. In this regard, it is understood that the opinion of Kāśakṛtsna conforms to the Śruti.
This is because it follows the meaning intended to be established by such scriptural passages as "That thou art" (*tattvam asi*).
This being the case, immortality is logically possible through the knowledge of that [Self].

For if the individual soul (*jīva*) were admitted to be of the nature of a modification (*vikāra*), then upon the dissolution of the modification back into its primordial material cause (*prakṛti*), the consequence would be its destruction; thus, immortality through the knowledge of that [Self] would not be logically possible.

And therefore, since name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) cannot exist with respect to its own substrate, name-and-form is metaphorically attributed to the individual soul (*jīva*) by depending upon limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*).
For this very reason, even the birth of the soul, which is heard of in some places through the illustration of sparks from a fire, must be understood as depending solely upon limiting adjuncts.

As for what was also stated—that by showing the emergence of the very subject under discussion, the Great Being who is to be seen, from the elements in the form of the conscious self (*vijñānātman*), [the text] shows that it is this conscious self alone who is to be seen—[this too is explained as follows].
In this case as well, the same threefold sūtra should be applied:
"Āśmarathya [holds that] the sign [of the soul's existence] is the establishment of the proposition.
Here, the following has been proposed: "When the Self is known, everything becomes known," and "All this is what this Self is" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.4.6).

And this has been established: because the entire manifold of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) arises from one source and merges into one, and because the non-difference of cause and effect is demonstrated through the analogies of the drum and so forth;

furthermore, Āśmarathya maintains that this sign indicates the fulfillment of that very proposition—that the Great Being who is to be seen emerges from the elements in the form of the conscious self (*vijñānātman*).
The Teacher (Ācārya) considers that since there is indeed non-difference, the proposition that "by the knowledge of one, there is the knowledge of all" is logically consistent.
"Because it will depart [from the body] in this state," says Auḍulomi.

The teacher Auḍulomi maintains that this declaration of non-difference arises because it is possible for the conscious self (vijñānātman), which is about to depart, to become unified with the Supreme Self when it is serene through the power of knowledge, meditation, and so forth.
"Because of its abiding, [it is so]—thus says Kāśakṛtsna":
the teacher Kāśakṛtsna maintains that this declaration of non-difference is appropriate because this very Supreme Self abides even in this form of the conscious self.

But is this not a statement of annihilation, namely: "Having arisen from these elements, one perishes after them; there is no consciousness after death" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.4.12)? How then can this be a statement of non-difference? This is not a fault.

This statement regarding "destruction" is intended to mean the destruction of specific cognitions (*viśeṣavijñāna*), not the annihilation of the Self; for, after the question was raised—"In this very matter, O Blessed One, do not confuse me; there is no consciousness after death"—the Śruti itself demonstrated another meaning: "Truly, I do not speak of delusion; this Self, O friend, is indestructible and its nature is non-perishing."
"But there is for him a dissociation from the *mātrās*.
This is what is meant: this Self, which is a mass of consciousness, is indeed immutable and eternal; there is no possibility of its destruction.
However, through knowledge (*vidyā*), there occurs for it a dissociation from the *mātrās*—characterized by the elements and the senses—which are produced by ignorance (*avidyā*).

Furthermore, because there is an absence of the specific cognition under discussion in the state of non-relational negation (*saṃsargābhāva*), it has been stated that "there is no consciousness after death. As for the argument that— because the passage concludes with a word denoting an agent in the statement, "But by what, my dear, should one know the knower?"— this must be understood as referring to the self consisting of cognition (*vijñānātman*) alone—
that too must be refuted by the very view of Kāśakṛtsna.

Furthermore, beginning with "For where there is duality as it were, there one sees another" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.4.13), the scripture elaborates upon that very same person's specific cognition characterized by seeing and so forth within the sphere of ignorance; then, with "But where for him everything has become the Self alone, then by what and whom should he see? and so on, it describes that very same cognition characterized by seeing and so forth within the sphere of knowledge.
It declares the absence of specific cognition (*viśeṣavijñāna*).
Furthermore, suspecting that one might cognize the self even in the absence of objects, it says: "O, by what could one cognize the cognizer?

Therefore, since the sentence is intent upon establishing the absence of specific cognition, it is understood that the element of consciousness alone is indicated by the agentive suffix *tṛc* (the suffix *-tṛ*), based on its prior state as an agent.
It has already been demonstrated above that the position of Kāśakṛtsna is supported by scripture;

therefore, this meaning must be accepted by all proponents of Vedānta: the distinction between the individual consciousness and the supreme Self is not ultimate, but is caused by the limiting adjuncts (upādhi) such as the body, which are fashioned from name-and-form presented by ignorance, as stated in "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone, one only without a second" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.2.1).
"Self alone is all this" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 7.25.2); "Brahman alone is all this" (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 2.2.11); "All this which is here is the Self" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.4.6).
This is because of such scriptural passages as, "There is no other seer than this" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.7.23), and "There is nothing else besides this that sees" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.8.11).
And from the Smṛtis: "Vāsudeva is all" (Gītā 7.19);
"Know Me also as the Knower of the Field in all fields, O Bhārata" (Gītā 13.2);
and "The Supreme Lord abiding equally in all beings" (Gītā 13.27).
