From such [views] as these, and from the censure of the perception of difference, [it is said]: "He who thinks, 'That one is one and I am another,' does not know, like a beast" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.4.10); and "He goes from death to death, who perceives here as if there were multiplicity" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.19).
From such passages as these,
and because all modifications are denied of the Self in the text, "This indeed is that great unborn Self, undecaying, undying, immortal, fearless Brahman" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.25).
Otherwise, it would be impossible for those seeking liberation to possess a cognition free from contradiction, and it would be impossible for that cognition to have a perfectly certain object;
for it is held that a cognition regarding the Self which is free from contradiction is what brings all inquiry to an end.
And from the Śruti: "Those whose purpose is well-ascertained through the realization of the knowledge of Vedānta" (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 3.2.6), and also:
"What delusion, what sorrow can there be for him who perceives oneness? (Īśā Upaniṣad 7).
And because of the recollection of the characteristics of one whose wisdom is established (Gītā 2.54):

once the right vision (*samyagdarśana*)— which has as its object the identity of the Knower of the Field (*kṣetrajña*) and the Supreme Self (*paramātman*)— is established, then, since there is only a difference in name between the Knower of the Field and the Supreme Self,

any insistence on a distinction between the selves of the type "this Knower of the Field is different from the Supreme Self" or "this Supreme Self is different from the Knower of the Field" is meaningless.
For this Self is indeed one, though it is designated in many ways through the mere difference of names; as it is said:
"Brahman is truth, knowledge, and infinite;
he who knows it as hidden in the cave [of the heart]" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.1).
This was said with reference to a certain single cave; and there is nothing other than Brahman that is hidden within the cave, for [the scripture] says:
"Having created that, it entered into that very thing" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.6).
Thus, because the scripture itself declares the entry of the Creator,
those who insist otherwise, by subverting the meaning of the Vedānta, obstruct right vision— the very door to the highest good—
and they imagine that liberation is something produced and therefore impermanent.
And they do not accord with reason. // 22 // [FN:
*Dhīraḥ* means the Omniscient One.
*Rūpāṇi* refers to the bodies of moving and unmoving things.]
Having discerned and fashioned them, having assigned names to them, and having entered into them, one performs acts such as addressing others while speaking and so forth.
"Delusion" (moha) refers to speech that causes delusion.
"Of indestructible nature" (anucchittidharmā) means that which does not possess destruction (ucchitti), that is, annihilation.

[He refers to] some [view] as being different from the locus of the individual soul (jīva). But as for those beginning with Āśmarathya, he states the established conclusion (siddhānta): "Because of its abiding" (avasthiteḥ).

The meaning is that, for the purpose of making known the absolute non-difference [of the two], the attributes of Brahman, such as being the object of vision and so forth, are stated after first introducing the individual soul (*jīva*). By this, it is not the case that this section (*adhikaraṇa*) exists merely to show that the marks of the individual soul have Brahman as their ultimate referent,
because that has already been explained in the *Pratardana-adhikaraṇa*.

Nor can it be for the purpose of establishing Brahman by way of restating the individual soul (jīva), because that has already been addressed in the section on "deep sleep and departure" (Suṣuptyutkrāntyadhikaraṇa).
Therefore, the objection that this present section is redundant is refuted.

Since it is necessary to establish the identity of Brahman by means of the individual soul (jīva) as the subject of reference, a doubt may arise regarding both difference and non-difference. To address this, this [section] is commenced to demonstrate that while the status of being the subject of reference and so forth occurs through an imagined difference, there is absolute non-difference in its own nature.

Furthermore, the indicative mark (*liṅga*) for this demonstration is to be understood as follows: the statement of the attributes of Brahman occurs without even mentioning another substratum (the *dharmin*)—namely, Brahman—as distinct from the individual soul which was introduced by the word "Self" (*ātman*). For if there were both difference and non-difference, one would have to mention two distinct substrata.
The wise one is the omniscient Lord.

Having fashioned and created all forms and effects, and having assigned their names, He who exists entering into those [entities] such as the intellect and so forth, performing speech and other functions—he who knows Him becomes immortal even here in this world. Thus he says, "The mantra," indicating that the mantra also demonstrates the identity of the individual soul (jīva) and the Supreme (para).
To the objection that there can be no identity because the individual soul (jīva) is a modification (vikāra) of Brahman, he says: "And not fire...
He demonstrates the three views by distinguishing them, beginning with the words "Kāśa... and so forth. [He asks:
"How much [of it]? etc.
The meaning is that even where there is non-difference, difference also exists.
Regarding that, he states the acceptability of the final view [of Śaṅkara] with the words "In that regard, Kāśī...

The intended meaning is that, just as in the statement "This is that Devadatta," the absolute non-difference between the higher and the lower is what is sought to be established through sentences such as "That thou art" (*tattvamasi*).
The meaning is "because of following that.
He states, "And thus," [meaning] that this very position must be accepted even because the scriptural teaching that liberation comes from knowledge would otherwise be inexplicable;
the meaning is "if there were absolute non-difference."
It should also be understood that the cessation of an imagined distinction is possible through knowledge, whereas that of a real one is not.
Regarding what was stated— that transmigratory existence (saṃsāra) is inherent based on the analogy of the river—
he says "Therefore" (ataśca) to refute that.
The meaning is that the individual soul (jīva) is Brahman because it is devoid of name and form.
To the objection that there is both difference and non-difference between the soul and Brahman based on the scriptural texts concerning its origin, he says: "For this very reason.
This means precisely because liberation would be impossible if the origin were inherent to the soul's nature.

In this prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*), three seeds [of doubt] have been stated: the commencement with the individual soul (*jīva*), the declaration of non-difference from the Supreme Self through the scriptural statement regarding "rising up" (*samutthāna*), and the word "knower" (*vijñātṛ*).
Among these, the first seed has been refuted by the three sūtras.
Now, having restated the second, he refutes it in the same manner, beginning with the words "As for what was also said," and so forth.

Regarding the proposition that "from the knowledge of the Self comes the knowledge of all," the reason for this is stated as "all this is what this Self is"—that is, non-difference (*avyatireka*). By the demonstration of that [non-difference], the very proposition is established; such is the construction [of the argument].
That from which there is an emanation of one [thing]...
The meaning is: because of the state of that in which there is dissolution into one [source].
"Arising" (*samutthāna*) means the expression of non-difference; this is what is intended.
Having raised the objection that "birth and destruction have been mentioned, but not non-difference," he refutes it with the words beginning "But surely... (*nanu*).

"You have deluded me with this very statement that there is no consciousness for one who is dead, because it would follow that the Self, whose nature is knowledge, would perish in the absence of knowledge. Thus addressed by Maitreyī, the Sage said: "No, indeed" (na vā are). [This refers to] delusion—that is, a statement causing delusion—[for the Self is] indestructible, being devoid of any cause for destruction.
Therefore, the meaning of "having the nature of non-annihilation" (*anucchittidharma*) is that it does not possess the quality of destruction.
He states, with the words "even that which... and so forth, that the third seed must be refuted by means of the very same third position.
Furthermore, since both of the first two positions accept a distinction between existence and difference, the objection as to "by what [means]" is not tenable.

In the view of Kāśakṛtsna, however, because there is absolute non-difference [of the self] from consciousness, there is an absence of causal agents; thus, that [view] is logical. Since it follows the Śruti, the meaning is that in his view, the status of being a knower—which is imagined by the mind—is stated with respect to the liberated Brahman-self by way of a former state (*bhūtapūrvagatyā*), and this must be so resolved. Furthermore, since a consideration of the preceding and following parts of the passage reveals that the sentence has the liberated self as its subject, the status of being a knower is merely a restatement of what is imagined; therefore, one cannot conclude that the passage refers to the individual soul (*jīva*) on the basis of that indicative mark. Thus he says: "Moreover" (*api ca*).
Regarding the question of what the reason is for the view of Kāśakṛtsna alone being acceptable among the views of the Ṛṣis,
he says: "It has been shown," and "And because it is supported by scripture."
Furthermore, he states that [the Self] possesses the nature of being known through Śruti and Smṛti by means of the passage beginning with "sadeva" and so forth.
This is connected to the proposition that the difference among causes is not ultimately real.

He says, "sa vā eṣa," because if one holds the position of both difference and non-difference, the Self would possess modifications such as birth and so on, and thus its negation [of such modifications] would be impossible.

He says "and otherwise" (*anyathā ca*) because if difference were real, it would be sublated by the valid cognition of that [difference], and thus the unimpeded knowledge "I am Brahman" could not arise.

Anticipating the objection that there might be valid cognition because non-difference also exists, he says "well-ascertained" (*suniścita*), meaning that due to the contradiction between difference and non-difference, there would instead be doubt.
He says "without exception" (*nirapavāda*) to show that such unimpeded knowledge must indeed exist.

He cites a Smṛti passage as well to show that it is only for one who possesses the uncontradicted certainty "I am Brahman" that grief and other afflictions are removed—this is expressed by the words "sthitā" (established).
The sense is that wisdom becomes firmly established only in absolute oneness, not in the state of both difference and non-difference.
Now, an objection may be raised: the individual soul and the Supreme Self are inherently distinct.
Because they possess non-synonymous names, like a pillar and a jar; to this he says, "And when [the substrate] persists.

Anticipating the objection, "How then can there be a distinction between non-synonymous names? he says, "For one [is the same]," because of the difference in limiting conditions (nimitta) such as being the individual soul (jīva) or being the Lord (īśvara).
Furthermore, since the individual soul (jīva) resides in the cave that consists of ignorance and its products— the forms of cognition—
and because of the Vedic scripture stating that "Brahman is hidden in that very [cave]," he says "Not so," asserting that Brahman is indeed the soul due to their identity of location.
"Only one certain [person]" means other than the individual soul (jīva).
To the objection, "Why could there not be two in a single cave?", he says: "And not... [the rest].
There is no difference [between the two], because the individual soul (jīva) is the Creator himself through his entry [into the body].

If it is argued: "But if there were absolute non-difference, then since the soul is clearly manifest, Brahman too would be clearly manifest; therefore, there must be a difference between the two based on their being clear and unclear respectively," we say: No.

For just as the original object (bimba) is not clearly manifest even when its reflection in a mirror is clear, the establishment of contradictory attributes is possible through an imagined difference (kalpitabheda).

He states the fault of those who are insistent on a distinction between truths with the words "But those who... The meaning is as follows: because of the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) of two substances that are neither cause nor effect—as in "That art thou" (*tat tvam asi*)—the meaning of the Vedānta is absolute non-difference; the realization of that alone is the means to the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*), and its sublation is not tenable. Furthermore, those who maintain both difference and non-difference postulate a produced liberation through knowledge and ritual action.
In that regard, impermanence is the defect.
As for the claim that even what is produced is permanent, that is contradicted by the logical principle that "whatever is to be accomplished through action is impermanent."

The sense is that, for us, since the destruction of what is harmful is to be accomplished through knowledge and consists merely in the eternally liberated Self, the defect of impermanence does not apply.
Therefore, it is established that the Maitreyī Brāhmaṇa is consistent with the inner Brahman. //22//

Section on Primordial Matter (Prakṛtyadhikaraṇa) / Sūtras 23–27 [The opponent argues: Since the world is seen to be composed of pleasure, pain, and delusion, it must have for its cause something that consists of pleasure, pain, and delusion; and that [cause] is Primordial Matter (prakṛti). For it is established by inference that the cause must possess the same qualities as the effect. Furthermore, since the world is finite, it must have a cause; and that which is the cause of this manifold world is Primordial Matter. Moreover, since the world is organized, it must have an intelligent creator; yet, because that creator is not perceived, we conclude that it is Primordial Matter itself, which is the cause of the world, acting through the agency of an intelligent being. Therefore, the doctrine of Brahman is refuted by the Sāṃkhya system. To this we reply: This is not so. Because the world is seen to be composed of pleasure, pain, and delusion, it does not follow that its cause is something consisting of pleasure, pain, and delusion. For even if the cause consisted of pleasure, pain, and delusion, it would still be impossible for it to produce an effect characterized by pleasure, pain, and delusion, just as a painting cannot be produced from a single color. Furthermore, since the world is finite, it does not necessarily follow that it has a cause; for it is observed that things such as mountains and trees, though finite, are without cause. Moreover, the fact that the world is organized does not prove that it has an intelligent creator; for organization is seen even in things like clouds and crystals, which lack an intelligent creator. And as for the claim that Primordial Matter acts through the agency of an intelligent being, that is untenable; for if Primordial Matter were dependent on an intelligent being, it would lose its status as the independent cause of the world. Therefore, the doctrine of Brahman remains unrefuted. Thus ends the Section on Primordial Matter. Sūtras 23–27.
And [Brahman is] the material cause, because that would not contradict the initial proposition and the illustrative examples.
Just as Dharma is to be inquired into because it is the cause of worldly prosperity (*abhyudaya*), so too Brahman is to be inquired into because it is the cause of the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*);
and Brahman is defined as "that from which the origin, etc., of this [world proceed]" (Brahmasūtra 1.1.2).
Thus it has been defined.

And since that definition applies equally to clay, gold, and so forth being the material cause (*prakṛti*) of jars, necklaces, and the like, as it does to the potter, the goldsmith, and so forth being the instrumental cause (*nimitta*), a doubt arises as to what the nature of Brahman’s causality might be.
In this regard, it appears that there might be only a mere efficient cause (nimittakāraṇa).
Why?
Because of the scriptural hearing of agency preceded by deliberation (īkṣāpūrvakakartṛtva).

For the agency of Brahman is understood to be preceded by reflection, based on such scriptural passages as, "He reflected" (Praśna Upaniṣad 6.3) and "He created the vital breath" (Praśna Upaniṣad 6.4).
Furthermore, agency preceded by deliberation is observed only in instrumental causes such as potters and the like;
moreover, in the world, the accomplishment of the fruit of an action is seen to be preceded by multiple causal factors. This same principle is appropriate to apply to the primal creator as well.
And because of the well-known status of being a lord (*īśvara*).

For in the case of lords such as kings, Vaivasvata, and others, it is perceived that they are merely efficient causes (*nimittakāraṇa*); likewise, it is appropriate to understand that the Supreme Lord (*parameśvara*) also possesses only the nature of an efficient cause.
Furthermore, this world, which is an effect, is observed to have parts, to be insentient, and to be impure.
The cause must also be of that very same nature, because a similarity between cause and effect is observed;
yet Brahman is not understood to have such characteristics, for it is said: "It is without parts, without activity, tranquil, irreproachable, and stainless" (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 6.19).
From such scriptural passages as these,

and by the method of elimination (*pāriśe�syāt*), one must accept that there exists another material cause for the world, distinct from Brahman, which possesses qualities such as impurity and is well-known from the Smṛtis;
for the scriptural teaching regarding Brahman as the cause culminates in its being merely the efficient cause (*nimittatvamātra*).
This being the case, we reply: Brahman must be accepted as both the material cause (*prakṛti*) and the efficient cause (*nimittakāraṇa*), and not merely as the efficient cause alone. Why?
Because there is no contradiction between the proposition (*pratijñā*) and the illustrative example (*dṛṣṭānta*).
In this way, both the proposition and the example are consistent with the sacred scripture (*śruti*).

First, the proposition is as follows: "Have you ever asked for that instruction by which the unheard becomes heard, the unthought becomes thought, and the unknown becomes known? (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.1.2).
And in that case, it is understood that when one thing is known, everything else that is dependent upon it is also known;
for the knowledge of everything is possible through the knowledge of the material cause (*upādānakāraṇa*), since the effect is not distinct from its material cause.
However, the effect is not non-distinct from its efficient cause (*nimittakāraṇa*).
In the world, we observe that a carpenter is distinct from the palace [he builds].

Furthermore, the scriptural illustration—"Just as, my dear, by means of a single lump of clay, all that is made of clay becomes known; the modification is a mere verbal handle, a name, while the reality is simply 'clay'"—is recorded as referring exclusively to the material cause (*upādāna-kāraṇa*).

Likewise, [there are the examples]: "By means of a single piece of copper, all that is made of copper would be known" and "By means of a single nail-cutter, all that is made of black iron would be known" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.1.4–6).
Similarly, in another place there is the proposition: "O Venerable One, when what is known does all this become known? (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 1.1.2).
The illustration is: "Just as plants grow upon the earth" (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 1.1.7).
Likewise, the proposition is: "When the Self—unique and non-dual—is seen, heard, thought, and known, all this is known."

"The example is as follows: 'Just as when a drum is being beaten, one would not be able to grasp the external sounds, but by grasping the drum, or the striking of the drum, the sound is grasped' (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.5.6–7).
In this way, according to the circumstances, the proposition and the example in each Vedānta text are to be understood as establishing [the Self] as the material cause."

Since this is a fifth case-ending (*pañcamī*), as in the passage "from which indeed these beings are born" (*yato vā imāni bhūtāni jāyante*), it should be understood as referring specifically to the *apādāna* characterized as the material cause (*prakṛti*), according to the specific grammatical rule: "The source of the agent of birth is the material cause" (*janikartuḥ prakṛtiḥ*, Pāṇini 1.4.30).
Its status as the efficient cause (*nimittatva*), however, is to be understood from the absence of any other presiding agent.

For just as in the world clay, gold, and so forth—which serve as material causes—proceed by depending upon presiding agents such as potters and goldsmiths, it is not so with Brahman, which exists as the material cause; for prior to creation, there is no other presiding agent to be depended upon, as is established by the definitive statement that "it was one only, without a second. Furthermore, the absence of any other presiding agent should be understood as being declared precisely through the non-contradiction of the initial proposition and the illustrative examples.

For if a controller (*adhiṣṭhātṛ*) were admitted as distinct from the material cause (*upādāna*), then, since it would again be impossible for all cognitions to arise from a single cognition, there would be a contradiction of both the proposition and the illustrative example.

Therefore, because there is no other controller, the Self possesses the status of an agent (*kartṛtva*); and because there is no other material cause, it possesses the status of primordial nature (*prakṛtitva*). (23) [Note:
*vimarśaḥ* means doubt.]
Partless and without components,
inactive and immovable,
tranquil and unchanging.
"Niravadya" means free from all defects. "Loha" means gold.
"Nakhanikṛntana" refers either to a nail-cutter made of black iron or to a lump of iron.
The meaning is that "particular sound" (*viśeṣaśabda*) refers to a sound that is related to the striking of a drum by way of being its product (*janya*).
Regarding the phrase "and the *prakṛti*," he recalls the preceding context with the words "just as" (*yathā*) in order to state the connection of this [term] with the defining sūtra (*lakṣaṇasūtra*).
For in that context, the general characteristic of being the cause of the world was stated in order to bring Brahman to mind;

having thereby established the concordance of all the Vedāntas with respect to Brahman thus brought to mind, this [present inquiry] is commenced because of a desire for specific knowledge as to whether that causality consists merely of agency, or whether it takes the form of both material causality and agency.
And thus, since the knowledge of the general [nature] is the cause for the inquiry into the particular, there is a connection between them.

Although it would have been more logical to place this immediately after that [first chapter], nevertheless, because it is easier to refute the view that the Lord is merely the agent by means of the Vedānta texts whose purport is already ascertained, this is written at the end of the section on *samanvaya*.
Since the definition-sūtra (*lakṣaṇa-sūtra*) is connected to the beginning of the chapter, this [present topic] is also connected to the beginning of the chapter.
In the preceding section, the view that the sentence refers to the individual soul (jīva) was refuted on the grounds that the proposition concerning the identity of all consciousness is primary;

however, that [refutation] is incorrect, because the proposition is merely figurative due to the difference between the agent and the material cause—this is the objection raised by the words beginning with "tatra nimitta... (In that regard, the efficient cause...).

The result of the prima facie (pūrvapakṣa) and final (siddhānta) positions is the establishment of duality and non-duality respectively. By the scriptural statement "having deliberated" (īkṣāpūrvaka), the agency [of Brahman] is determined;
and thus, Brahman is not the material cause (prakṛti).
Because of being an agent;
for whoever is the agent of something is not its material cause,
just as a potter is the agent of a jar— this is the meaning.
He says "aneka... [in the verse], meaning: "The world has a distinct agent and material cause, because it is an effect, like a jar.
Brahman is not the material cause.
Because of its being a Lord (īśvara), like a king and so forth; thus he says: "because of its being a Lord.
The world does not have Brahman as its material cause (prakṛti).
Because it is of a different character from that;
for whatever is thus is so, like a jar produced by a potter who is of a different character [from the jar]—thus he says, "And the effect. It is partless, meaning devoid of constituent parts.
It is inactive and immovable, peaceful and unchanging, faultless, and with all defects cast away.
The reason for this is stated as "stainless" (*nirañjana*).
This means it is empty of darkness, which is like eye-ointment (*añjana*).
If one asks, "In that case, what is the similar material cause (*upādāna*) of the world? he replies: "By the method of elimination" (*pāriśeṣyāt*).
Thinking that when Brahman is negated, Primordial Matter (prakṛti) remains as the primary [cause], he establishes his own position with the words "and Primordial Matter" (prakṛtiśca).
By the word "and" (ca), the inclusion of its being the instrumental cause (nimitta) is understood.
He says "thus" (evam) to show that in this way, since the causality consists of both forms, there is no contradiction between those two [scriptural passages].

To the objection, "Why should knowledge of all effects not arise from knowledge of the agent as well? he says: "But there is no non-distinction from the efficient cause. Since clay and other materials serve as the examples (*dṛṣṭānta*), it must be stated that Brahman, the subject of the example (*dārṣṭāntika*), is the material cause; thus he says: "The example also...
The meaning is that since modification is merely a name beginning with speech and does not exist in reality, it is logical that knowledge of the modification arises from knowledge of the real cause.
For the sake of establishing the commonality of the destination (*gati-sāmānya*), the *Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad* also states the proposition and the illustration—thus [it is said] "in another place as well.
Furthermore, the *Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad* also says "so with respect to the Self.

Just as the statement "the jar shines" implies an underlying, pervasive luminosity which is the primordial nature (*prakṛti*), and that apart from this there are no modifications (*vikāra*), so too this meaning is made clear by means of an illustration (*dṛṣṭānta*), which is now stated.
Due to the commonality of sound produced by the drum being struck, the hearer would not be able to apprehend the specific external sounds separately from the apprehension of the general sound.

However, through the apprehension of the general sound, the specific sound produced by the striking of the drum is apprehended; or, through the apprehension of that [specific sound], its further particular sub-varieties are apprehended.

Therefore, the meaning is that just as particularities, which are to be grasped through the apprehension of the commonality of sound, are imagined within the universal, so too are jars and other objects, which are illuminated by the light of the Self, imagined within the Self.

Having stated that Brahman is the material cause (prakṛti) based on the evidence of the non-contradiction between the proposition and the example, he further states it by means of the ablative case-ending (*pañcamī*) in the word "yataḥ" (from which). The syntactical connection is that in the scriptural passage "yato vā," the ablative case "yataḥ" is to be understood as denoting the material cause.

The meaning of the sūtra is that the source (prakṛti) of an effect that is being born—that is, the agent of birth—is designated as the *apādāna*. The result of this designation is the application of the fifth case-ending (*pañcamī*) to the source, according to the rule "the fifth case is used for the *apādāna*.
Having thus established Brahman’s status as the source, he establishes its status as the agent by stating "it is the efficient cause" (*nimittatvam*).

He states that the following inferences—such as "Brahman must be presided over by a creator distinct from itself, because it is a material cause, like clay and so forth"—are sublated by scripture: "prior to creation... (prāgutpatteḥ).
He applies the Sūtra even to the point that Brahman alone is the creator of the world: "adhiṣṭhātrāntareti" (by another presiding agent). //23//
And for what reason [is it said that] the Self does not possess the nature of being an agent?— START BsCom_1,4.7.24— END BsCom_1,4.7.23.
And because of the teaching of desire (*abhidhyā*).

The teaching of desire—namely, "He desired: 'May I be many, may I procreate,'" and "He thought: 'May I be many, may I procreate'"—indicates that the Self possesses both agency (*kartṛtva*) and the nature of being the material cause (*prakṛtitva*).
In this context, it is understood that He is the agent because His activity is independent and preceded by such desire.
Because the desire for multiplicity expressed in the words "May I be many" has the inner self (pratyagātman) as its object, it is also understood that the individual soul is the source (prakṛti).
[The commentary notes: *Abhidhyā* means the volition of creation.
By the four sūtras beginning with "For what reason? (*kutaśca*), he establishes that it is not contradictory for a single entity to possess both types of causality.
Covetousness is the volition for creation. //24//
And because both are directly stated [in scripture]. (BS 1.4.25)
This is a further argument for [Brahman] being the material cause (*prakṛti*).
For this reason as well, Brahman is the material cause:
because both the origin and the dissolution are recorded in scripture as having Brahman itself as their direct cause—“Verily, all these beings arise from Ākāśa alone.”
"They merge back into space" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 1.9.1).
For it is well known that whatever originates from something and into which it dissolves, that is its material cause (upādāna),
just as the earth is the material cause of rice, barley, and so forth.
By stating "from space itself" (*ākāśādeva*), [the text] shows the non-appropriation of any other material cause (*upādāna*) for that which has been directly perceived as being direct.
Furthermore, the dissolution (*pratyastamaya*) of an effect is never observed to occur anywhere other than its material cause. (25) [FN:
*Abhyuccaya* means an additional reason.]
The phrase "another cause for abundance" (abhyuccayahetvantaram) refers to the following construction:

the author of the Sūtras demonstrates through the word "directly" (sākṣāt) that there is no grasping of any other material cause, as indicated by the restrictive particle "only" (eva) in the expression "from space alone" (ākāśādeva). //25//
Because of self-activity and transformation. (BS 1.4.26)
For this reason as well, Brahman is the primal source (prakṛti):
because in the context of the exposition of Brahman, the passage "It made itself by itself" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.7) shows that the Self is both the object and the agent.
The word "the self" (*ātmānam*) indicates the object (*karman*),
while "he made himself" (*svayamakuruta*) indicates the agent (*kartṛ*).
But how can it be possible for that which already exists as an established entity and is situated as an agent to be further brought about as something being made?
We say it is because of transformation (*pariṇāma*).
For although the Self is already established as existing, it transformed itself specifically into the nature of a modification (*vikāra*).
And such transformation into the nature of a modification is observed in primal materials (*prakṛti*) such as clay.
Furthermore, from the qualification "itself" (*svayam*), it is understood that [Brahman] does not depend on any other cause.
Alternatively, "from transformation" (*pariṇāmāt*) may be a separate sūtra; its meaning is this: for this reason as well, Prakṛti is Brahman.

For this reason, the transformation of Brahman itself into the form of its modifications is recorded in grammatical coordination [with Brahman] in such passages as: "It became the manifest and the unmanifest, the defined and the undefined" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.6). // 26 //
FN: "Sat" refers to the three perceptible elements; "tyat" refers to the two imperceptible elements;
and "nirukta" refers to that which can be defined, such as a jar and the like.
"Indefinable" (anirukta) means that which cannot be described, such as the form of a dove and so forth. "Self-action" (ātmakṛti) is action related to the self.
The relationship of the self to the action consists in its being both the object and the locus [of that action].

An objection is raised: "But surely the substratum of an action is already established, whereas its object is that which is to be accomplished; thus, for a single entity to possess both [states] is contradictory. To this, he asks: "How then? He replies: "Because of transformation," meaning that just as clay possesses the status of being the object of an action through its non-difference from the transformation to be accomplished, so too does the Self.
He says: "The Self... [referring to the passage beginning with *ātmānam*].
The word "non-contradiction" (*avirodha*) is to be supplied as the remainder [of the sentence].
He provides an example for the fact that even what is already established may be something to be accomplished, using the phrase "as having the nature of a modification" (*vikārātmanā*).

Now, one might object: since the accusative case in the phrase "the Self of Brahman" (*brahmaṇa ātmānam*) indicates that it is to be accomplished in the form of an effect, let Brahman be the material cause, while the agent be someone else; to this he replies with the words "and by itself" (*svayam iti ca*).

In order to establish that Brahman is the object of the act of creation (*kṛtikarma*), he explains the term "because of transformation" (*pariṇāmāt*) and then offers another interpretation, stating that it is a separate sūtra. The meaning is that Brahman is the material cause (*prakṛti*), based on the scriptural statement of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) regarding transformation, such as "Brahman is *sat* (being) and *tyat* (becoming)," which is like the expression "the clay is the jar. Here, *sat* refers to the three perceptible elements (*bhūta*).
The meaning is that both the perceptible— the two elements— and the definable, such as jars and the like, as well as the indefinable, such as the form of a pigeon and so forth, became Brahman alone.

In this sūtra, the word "transformation" (pariṇāma) refers merely to an effect, and not to a transformation consisting of a real effect, because the doctrine of illusory manifestation (vivarta-vāda) will be stated later in the sūtra "tadananyatvam... (II.1.14). //26//
For it is also sung as the womb (yoni). BBs_1,4.27.

For this reason as well, Brahman is recited in the Vedāntas as the *prakṛti* and the *yoni*: "The agent, the Lord, the Person, the Brahman-source" (Muṇḍaka 3.1.3), and "That source of beings which the wise perceive" (Muṇḍaka 1.1.6).
Furthermore, the word *yoni* is understood in common usage to denote *prakṛti*, as in: "The earth is the source (*yoni*) of herbs and trees."
Even in the case of the female womb, there exists the status of being the material cause (*upādāna-kāraṇa*) with respect to the embryo by way of the vaginal opening.
Furthermore, the word *yoni* is seen in some instances to denote "place," as in: "O Indra, a place has been prepared for you to sit" (*Ṛgveda Saṃhitā* 1.104.1).
However, in this context, based on the remainder of the passage, its denotation as "material cause" is accepted, as in: "Just as a spider emits and withdraws [its thread]" (*Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad* 1.1.7).
From such passages as these,
Brahman’s status as the material cause is established.

As for what was further stated— that in the world, agency preceded by deliberation is observed only in efficient causes such as potters and the like, and not in material causes, and so forth— [this is now addressed].
To that it is replied: one must not proceed here as one does in the world. For this matter is not accessible through inference;
since this matter is accessible through scripture, it must be understood here exactly according to the scripture.
We have already stated that the word [Īśvara] indicates that the Lord is the material cause (prakṛti);
furthermore, we shall explain all of this in detail later. // 27 // [FN:
The agent who possesses the power of action.]
The Lord, the controller;
the Person, the inward-facing one;
Brahman, the full.
"Yoni" means "prakṛti" (primordial nature).

O Indra, for your sitting—that is, for your dwelling—a yoni, a place, has been made by me; it was fashioned. And he states that the word "yoni" implies the state of being primordial nature with the words: "and the yoni."
The agent, possessed of the power of action; the Lord, the controller;
the Person, the inward-facing one.
The meaning is that the wise perceive through meditation Brahman, which is full, as the source, that is, primordial nature (prakṛti).

Now, since the word "yoni" is seen to be used even for a female womb that is not a source of appropriation (*anupādāna*), he says: "of the female womb. Here, "blood" is the meaning of the word as a constituent part (*avayava*).
The word "yoni" can also mean "place," but that [meaning] is not to be understood here by such terms as "source of beings" (*bhūtayoni*) and the like.
He says "in some places" because it would contradict the remainder of the illustrative statements concerning the spider (*ūrṇanābhi*) and so forth.
[The verse says: "O Indra, for your sitting—that is, for your dwelling—a womb, a place, has been made by me"; this is the meaning.
Having restated the inferences (anumāna) stated by the proponent (*pūrvapakṣin*), he states the sublation by scripture (*āgamabādha*) with the words "But as for that which... and so forth.

Now, one might object: since inference is independent of scripture, there can be no sublation by it; to this he replies, "For not... The subject (*pakṣa*)—the creator of the world—is established by scripture alone.

The meaning is as follows: since an inference for one who possesses eternal agency is impossible due to the contradiction of the pervasion (vyāpti) that "whatever is an action is produced by a body," there is indeed a sublation (bādha) by the scripture teaching [the Lord's] nature as material cause (prakṛtitva), which must be relied upon when one takes the Lord taught in the Śruti as the subject (pakṣa) and attempts to prove His lack of being a material cause.
As for what was stated—that Brahman cannot be the material cause of the world because of its dissimilarity—[that too is refuted].
Regarding this, he says: "And again" (*punaśca*).
This means starting from the point beginning with "Not so, because of the difference in characteristics" (*na vilakṣaṇatvāt*).
Therefore, it is established that the nature of Brahman as the cause consists of both forms [of being the material and the efficient cause]. //27//
END BsCom_1,4.7.27 START BsCom_1,4.7.28 8. Section on the Interpretation of All [Scriptures] (Sarvavyākhyānādhikaraṇa) / Sūtra 28.
By this, all [theories] have been explained, have been explained.

Beginning with the sūtra "Because of seeing, [the cause] is not that which is not based on scripture" (Brahma-sūtra 1.1.5), the doctrine of the Pradhāna as the cause has been repeatedly raised as an objection and refuted by the sūtras themselves.
For there are certain fallacious marks (*liṅgābhāsa*) that support this position which appear at first glance to those of dull intellect within the Vedāntas; moreover,
because it accepts the non-difference of cause and effect,
it is closely related to the Vedāntic doctrine and has been adopted by some authors of *Dharma-sūtras*, such as Devala and others, in their own works.
Therefore, he has exerted great effort toward refuting that [theory], rather than refuting the theories of atoms and other such causes;
nevertheless, those too must be refuted because they stand as counter-positions to the doctrine of Brahman as the cause.
Furthermore, some Vedic indicative mark might appear to those of dull intellect at first glance as a support for them as well.

Therefore, according to the maxim of "overthrowing the chief wrestler," he extends [the argument] by stating: "By this collection of logical arguments for the refutation of the doctrine of Pradhāna as the cause, all doctrines asserting atoms and other such causes are also to be understood as explained by way of being refuted;
for like Pradhāna, they too lack scriptural authority and are contradicted by scripture."
The repetition of the words "it has been explained, it has been explained" indicates the completion of the chapter. // 28 //
By this, all [other views] have been explained.
To state the purport of this section on extended application (*atideśādhikaraṇa*), he restates what has preceded with the words "on account of seeing" (*īkṣateḥ*).
He states the reasons for the primary refutation of the doctrine of Pradhāna with the words "for that," and so forth.
If it is argued that the theories of atoms and so forth should be disregarded because they are weak, he says: "But even those... [referring to the phrase *te 'pi tu*].
To the question, "How can they be opponents if they are rootless? he says: "Of those... [referring to the phrase *teṣām*].
For instance, in the Chāndogya Upaniṣad, in order to make known that [Brahman] is the cause of the world, a father said to his son,
"Break one of these banyan seeds.
The son replied, "It has been broken, O Venerable Sir."

Again, when the father asked, "What do you see here?", he replied, "Nothing, O Blessed One. Thereupon the father said, "In that case, you do not see even the atom (aṇimāna). Thus, from the word "nothing," the doctrines of emptiness and intrinsic naturelessness are understood.
The doctrine of atoms (paramāṇuvāda) follows from the word "aṇu.

In this way, indicative marks such as "In the beginning, this was indeed non-existent" and "Subtler than the subtle" are to be understood. Here, when a doubt arises as to whether the doctrines of atoms and so forth are based on the Vedas (śrauta) or not, the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa) is that they are Vedic because of the force of words like "non-existent" and "atom. To this, [the author] extends the argument by saying "by this [same reasoning]."
Because this [section] is an extended application (*atideśa*), it does not require a separate introduction (*saṃgati*) and so forth.

Since the words "nothing" (*na kiṃcana*) and "non-existent" (*asat*) refer to an entity that is incapable of being perceived by the senses, and since the word "atom" (*aṇu*) intends something subtle, these doctrines lack scriptural authority; like the doctrine of *pradhāna*, they are not based on the Vedas.
Furthermore, [the doctrine of Pradhāna] is sublated by the scriptural texts concerning Brahman as the cause;
therefore, it is established that Brahman alone is the supreme cause, and that the concordance of all Vedānta texts applies to Him alone. //28//
Thus ends the fourth quarter of the first chapter in the Śārīrakamīmāṃsābhāṣya composed by the venerable Paramahaṃsa Parivrājaka Ācārya, the worshipful Śrī Śaṅkara Bhagavatpāda.
Thus ends the first chapter, titled "Samanvaya" (Harmonization), in the venerable Śāṅkarabhāṣya on the Brahma-sūtras. 1.4.28. End.

Thus ends the fourth quarter of the first chapter, titled "The Consistency of Even Those Words That Are Doubtful, Such as the Unmanifest and Others."
Thus ends the first chapter, named "Harmonization," in the venerable Śaṅkara-bhāṣya on the Brahma-sūtras.
